Course map

Diskrete Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie — Niki Kilbertus, script version of 24 June 2026

One page per subchapter of the script, in the script's own order and with the script's own numbering. Every chapter page walks the same route: the plain-language picture first, then the exact definitions and theorems, then the proofs, then easy examples before hard ones, then the exercise-sheet tasks and old-exam tasks that belong to that subchapter, and finally a summary sheet and a self-test. (The background page B1 is the one exception: it is a map into your Analysis guide, so it has no summary sheet and no self-test of its own.)

How to read a page

Every claim on every page carries a coloured label that says where it comes from. A label is never used for a source the material does not come from. Where one passage really has two sources — an exam task that I then extended, say — it carries both labels next to each other rather than one blended label:

Script 1.6 stated in the lecture script, at that number Sheet 1 · Ex 4 an exercise-sheet task WiSe25 · P1a an old-exam task My addition written by me, not in any official document Analysis guide a link into your own MA0902 guide, opening in a new tab

The My addition label covers three things: background the script assumes you already have (from Discrete Structures, Analysis or Linear Algebra), proofs the script leaves as "Exercises" or omits entirely, and the interactive widgets. Where an official solution is wrong, the page says so and gives the corrected answer: either in a red box of its own, or — when only one step is affected — in a note labelled Note on the official solution beside that step.

Proofs sit inside collapsed grey strips so you can read a page for the statements first and open the arguments on a second pass. Nothing is hidden that you need.

The pages

Background pages B1–B5 come first. They teach what this course assumes but never explains. Anything your Analysis guide already covers is linked there rather than repeated — B1 is the full map. Gaps it does not cover get pages of their own: set algebra and countability (B2), counting (B3), measure theory and the Lebesgue integral (B4), and linear algebra with the change-of-variables formula (B5).

All pages are written: background pages B1–B5, chapter pages 0, 1.1–1.4, 2.1–2.4 and 3.1–3.5, and the script's appendix A.1.

Three structural habits of these three exams

1. Every exam opens with a True/False block (P1), worth 5–12 credits. In WiSe 25/26 and SoSe 2025 you have to justify each answer, and one counterexample is enough to earn the points. In SoSe 2026 P1 you only mark true or false, with no justification at all (5 credits), and a second, justified True/False block follows as P2 (12 credits).

2. All three exams ask you to state a named result with all its assumptions. In WiSe 25/26 and SoSe 2025 this is the whole of P2 (6 credits): the strong law of large numbers plus the definition of almost-sure convergence, and the central limit theorem plus the definition of convergence in distribution. In SoSe 2026 it is P3a, Jensen's inequality (3 of the 5 credits of P3). This is pure recall of the exact wording, assumptions included.

3. The last problem is always a long applied one built from a story (duck hunt, tennis schedule, randomized response). These are worth 10–13 credits and chain several subchapters together: two for the tennis problem (§1.4 and §1.1), three for the duck hunt (§1.2, §2.1, §2.2), five for the randomized-response problem (§1.4, §2.1, §3.1, §3.2, §3.3).
