Every row of that table was verified numerically before it was written: for example \(\int_0^\infty x^{3}e^{-2x}\mathrm dx\) evaluates to \(0.375\) and \(3!/2^{4}=6/16=0.375\); \(\int_\R e^{-z^{2}/2}\mathrm dz = 2.5066283 = \sqrt{2\pi}\); \(\Gamma(3.5)=3.3233510\) and \(2.5\,\Gamma(2.5)=3.3233510\); and for \(Y\sim\Gamma(4,2)\), \(\int_0^\infty y^{-1}p_Y(y)\mathrm dy =0.6666667=\beta/(\alpha-1)=2/3\). The odd-function row is the one that saves the most time in an exam: spotting it turns a three-line calculation into the word "odd".

Worked example — a whole density problem, start to finish SoSe25 · P3a–c

\(p_X(x)=\dfrac{x}{c}\) for \(x\in[0,2]\) and \(0\) otherwise, for some constant \(c\in\R\).

(a) Find \(c\). Impose "total area \(=1\)", integrating over the support \([0,2]\) only, and pull the constant \(1/c\) out by linearity:

\[ 1=\int_0^2\frac{x}{c}\,\mathrm dx=\frac1c\int_0^2 x\,\mathrm dx =\frac1c\left[\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_0^{2}=\frac1c\left(\frac{4}{2}-0\right)=\frac{2}{c} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=2 . \]

Then add the non-negativity line, which the official solution writes out as well: with \(c=2>0\) and \(x\ge0\) on \([0,2]\), \(p_X(x)=x/2\ge0\), so it is a valid density. Check: \(\int_0^2 x/2\,\mathrm dx=1.0000000\). ✓

(b) The cdf, all three branches. \(F_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}p_X(t)\,\mathrm dt\). Below the support there is nothing to collect; above it everything has been collected; in between, integrate from the left end of the support:

\[ \int_0^{x}\frac t2\,\mathrm dt=\left[\frac{t^{2}}{4}\right]_0^{x}=\frac{x^{2}}{4}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<0,\\[2pt] \dfrac{x^{2}}{4},&0\le x\le 2,\\[4pt] 1,&x>2.\end{cases} \]

All three branches are required for full credit. Two checks that cost five seconds each: \(F_X(2)=4/4=1\) ✓, and differentiating the middle branch gives \(2x/4=x/2=p_X(x)\) ✓.

(c) Mean and median. The mean weights each \(x\) by its density:

\[ \E[X]=\int_0^2 x\cdot\frac{x}{2}\,\mathrm dx=\int_0^2\frac{x^{2}}{2}\,\mathrm dx =\left[\frac{x^{3}}{6}\right]_0^{2}=\frac{8}{6}=\frac43\approx1.3333 . \]

The median \(m\) solves \(F_X(m)=\tfrac12\), so \(m^{2}/4=\tfrac12\), \(m^{2}=2\), \(m=\sqrt2\approx1.4142\) — and the root \(-\sqrt2\) is discarded because it is outside the support \([0,2]\). Checks: numerical integration gives \(\E[X]=1.3333333\) ✓, and \(F_X(\sqrt2)=2/4=0.5\) ✓. Note \(\E[X]=1.333<1.414=m\): this density leans to the right, so its balance point sits to the left of its middle.

Fuller treatment: Analysis 8.1 — Definition of the integral, Analysis 8.2 — Important properties (linearity, additivity, symmetry), Analysis 8.3 — Antiderivatives (the fundamental theorem, both directions). The measure-theoretic version of "integral", which is the one the DPT script actually defines, is on B4 — Measure and integration, and B4 also explains why for every density in this course the two notions give the same number. In DPT: §1.3 primer, §2.1 expectation, TT3 on the exam page.

Improper integrals (to \(\infty\)) and when they diverge

Most DPT integrals run out to \(\infty\), or start at a point where the integrand blows up. Such an integral is called improper [uneigentliches Integral], and it is defined as a limit of ordinary integrals with finite limits. Sometimes that limit is a finite number ("the integral converges"), and sometimes it is \(+\infty\) ("it diverges"). Divergence is not an error — twice in this course it is the answer.

How to compute one My addition

Infinite upper limit. \(\displaystyle\int_a^{\infty}f(x)\,\mathrm dx:=\lim_{b\to\infty}\int_a^{b}f(x)\,\mathrm dx\). In practice: find an antiderivative \(F\), write \([F(x)]_a^{b}=F(b)-F(a)\), and then let \(b\to\infty\). If \(F(b)\) has a finite limit, that limit goes in; otherwise the integral is \(+\infty\).

Blow-up at the lower limit. If \(f\) is unbounded near \(a\), \(\displaystyle\int_a^{b}f:=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int_{a+\varepsilon}^{b}f\), where \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) means \(\varepsilon\) shrinks to \(0\) from above.

Both ends infinite: split at any convenient point, for instance \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}=\int_{-\infty}^{0}+\int_0^{\infty}\), and both halves must converge separately.

Notation in an exam. Writing \(\bigl[-e^{-\lambda x}\bigr]_0^{\infty}\) directly is accepted everywhere in this course, with the understanding that the symbol \(\infty\) at the top means "take the limit". Doing it in one line costs nothing and is what every official solution does.

The two convergence rules that decide every case here My addition

Rule 1 — powers, the \(1/x^{p}\) test. For \(p>0\):

\[ \int_1^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm dx}{x^{p}} =\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{p-1}&\text{if }p>1\quad\text{(converges)},\\[6pt] +\infty&\text{if }p\le1\quad\text{(diverges)};\end{cases} \qquad \int_0^{1}\frac{\mathrm dx}{x^{p}} =\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{1-p}&\text{if }p<1,\\[6pt] +\infty&\text{if }p\ge1.\end{cases} \]
In words: out at infinity you need the integrand to decay faster than \(1/x\); down at zero you need it to blow up slower than \(1/x\). The borderline case \(p=1\) diverges at both ends — that is the function \(1/x\), whose antiderivative \(\ln x\) creeps to \(\infty\) without ever settling.

Rule 2 — the exponential beats every power. For every \(a>0\) and every \(n\ge0\), \(x^{n}e^{-ax}\to0\) as \(x\to\infty\), and \(\int_0^{\infty}x^{n}e^{-ax}\,\mathrm dx=\dfrac{n!}{a^{n+1}}\) is always finite. So any integral whose integrand carries a genuine factor \(e^{-ax}\) with \(a>0\) converges at the \(+\infty\) end, no matter what polynomial sits in front of it. This is why boundary terms like \(\bigl[-x e^{-\lambda x}\bigr]_0^{\infty}\) evaluate to \(0\) at the top.

Checks. \(\int_1^{\infty}x^{-1.5}=2.000000=1/(1.5-1)\) ✓; \(\int_1^{\infty}x^{-3}=0.500000=1/(3-1)\) ✓; and for \(p=1\) the truncated integrals \(\int_1^{B}\mathrm dx/x\) equal \(4.605\), \(9.210\), \(13.816\) at \(B=10^{2},10^{4},10^{6}\) — exactly \(\ln B\), growing without bound. ✓

Convergent case — a heavy-ish tail that still normalises Sheet 10 · Ex 3(i)

\(p_X(x)=\dfrac{2c^{2}}{x^{3}}\) for \(x\ge c\), with \(c>0\). The tail is a power, so use Rule 1 with \(p=3>1\):

\[ \int_c^{\infty}\frac{2c^{2}}{x^{3}}\,\mathrm dx =2c^{2}\lim_{b\to\infty}\int_c^{b}x^{-3}\,\mathrm dx =2c^{2}\lim_{b\to\infty}\left[-\frac{1}{2}x^{-2}\right]_c^{b} =2c^{2}\left(0-\left(-\frac{1}{2c^{2}}\right)\right)=1 . \]

The step \(\int x^{-3}=\tfrac{x^{-2}}{-2}\) is the power rule with \(a=-3\), and \(b^{-2}\to0\) is Rule 1 doing its work. Check at \(c=2.5\): the numerical value is \(1.0000000\) ✓, and the mean \(\int_c^{\infty}x\,p_X(x)\,\mathrm dx=5.0000000=2c\) ✓ (here the integrand behaves like \(1/x^{2}\), still \(p>1\), so the mean exists).

Divergent case 1 — a mean that does not exist My addition

Change the exponent in the example above from \(3\) to \(2\): \(q(x)=\dfrac{c}{x^{2}}\) for \(x\ge c\) is still a perfectly valid density (\(\int_c^\infty c\,x^{-2}\mathrm dx=1\)), but its mean is

\[ \int_c^{\infty}x\cdot\frac{c}{x^{2}}\,\mathrm dx=c\int_c^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm dx}{x} =c\bigl[\ln x\bigr]_c^{\infty}=+\infty . \]

Rule 1 with \(p=1\): divergent. Check at \(c=2.5\): cutting the integral at \(10^{3},10^{5},10^{7}\) gives \(14.98\), \(26.49\), \(38.00\) — it keeps climbing, by the same \(c\ln 100=11.51\) for every factor of \(100\), which is what \(\ln\) does. ✓

This is what "a heavy tail" means: the tail is not thin enough for the balance point to exist. The famous example in this course is the Cauchy distribution, whose density \(\tfrac{1}{\pi(1+x^{2})}\) also decays like \(1/x^{2}\) and therefore has no mean — which is why it is the standard counterexample to the law of large numbers (§2.1, §2.4). When a task says "does \(\E[X]\) exist?", it is asking you to run Rule 1 on the tail.

Divergent case 2 — the \(n=1\) case on Sheet 10 Sheet 10 · Ex 2, note

The maximum likelihood estimator of \(\lambda\) for exponential data is \(\hat\lambda_{\mathrm{mle}}=n/\sum_i X_i\). To check whether it is unbiased you need \(\E[\hat\lambda]\), and for \(n=1\) that is \(\E[1/X_1]\) with \(X_1\sim\Exp(\lambda)\):

\[ \E\!\left[\frac1{X_1}\right]=\int_0^{\infty}\frac1x\,\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\,\mathrm dx . \]

The trouble is at the lower end, not at infinity. Near \(x=0\) the factor \(e^{-\lambda x}\) is close to \(e^{0}=1\), so the integrand behaves like \(\lambda/x\), and \(\int_0\frac{\mathrm dx}{x}\) diverges by Rule 1 with \(p=1\). So \(\E[\hat\lambda_{\mathrm{mle}}]\) is undefined for \(n=1\). Check (\(\lambda=2\)): cutting the integral at \(\varepsilon=10^{-2},10^{-4},10^{-6}\) gives \(6.71\), \(15.88\), \(25.09\) — again climbing like \(\ln(1/\varepsilon)\), without limit. ✓

How to write it in an exam. Three sentences are enough, and all three earn their keep: "Near \(0\), \(\tfrac1x\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\ge \tfrac{\lambda}{e}\cdot\tfrac1x\) for \(x\in(0,1/\lambda]\). Since \(\int_0^{1/\lambda}\tfrac{\mathrm dx}{x}=+\infty\), the integral diverges by comparison. Hence \(\E[1/X_1]\) does not exist and the estimator is not unbiased for \(n=1\)." Name the comparison, name the divergent benchmark, state the conclusion.

Fuller treatment: Analysis 9.1 — Improper integrals (the definition as a limit, and the comparison test), Analysis 5.2 — Growth rates (why the exponential beats every power), Analysis 9.4 — Estimating sums and series. In DPT: §2.1, the existence of \(\E[X]\), §3.2, Sheet 10 Ex 3. The measure-theoretic statement of the same thing — \(\E[X]\) exists precisely when \(\E|X|<\infty\) — is on B4.

Substitution and integration by parts

Two rules cover every integral this course sets that is not already in the table. Substitution [Substitutionsregel] is the chain rule read backwards; integration by parts [partielle Integration] is the product rule read backwards. Learning which to reach for is most of the battle, so each rule below comes with a one-line "what to pick".

Substitution My addition

\[ \int_a^b f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)\,g'(x)\,\mathrm dx \;=\; \int_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u)\,\mathrm du . \]

How you actually use it. Set \(u=g(x)\). Differentiate to get \(\dfrac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm dx}=g'(x)\), and treat that as \(\mathrm du=g'(x)\,\mathrm dx\) — a formal bookkeeping move, and the rule above is what makes it legitimate. Then replace three things at once: the inner expression by \(u\), the piece \(g'(x)\,\mathrm dx\) by \(\mathrm du\), and — this is the step that gets forgotten — both limits, \(a\mapsto g(a)\) and \(b\mapsto g(b)\).

What to pick. \(u\) is the inside of the composition: the exponent of an \(e\), the thing under a square root, the bracket raised to a power. Then look for its derivative sitting as a factor elsewhere in the integrand — if it is there (up to a constant), the substitution will work.

The one that is always safe: a linear substitution \(u=\alpha x+\beta\) with \(\alpha\neq0\), where \(\mathrm du=\alpha\,\mathrm dx\), so \(\mathrm dx=\mathrm du/\alpha\). Nothing can go wrong except forgetting the \(1/\alpha\).

Substitution examples My addition

S1 — the exponential normalisation, \(u=\lambda x\). With \(\mathrm du=\lambda\,\mathrm dx\), the limits \(0\mapsto0\) and \(\infty\mapsto\infty\):

\[ \int_0^{\infty}\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\,\mathrm dx=\int_0^{\infty}e^{-u}\,\mathrm du =\bigl[-e^{-u}\bigr]_0^{\infty}=0-(-1)=1 . \]

The factor \(\lambda\) in front of the density is precisely the \(\mathrm du/\mathrm dx\) the substitution needs — which is a good way to remember why \(\Exp(\lambda)\) has that constant. Check (\(\lambda=1.7\)): \(1.0000000\). ✓

S2 — standardising a normal, \(z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\). This is the substitution of the second half of the course: it turns any \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^{2})\) into \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), so that a single table of \(\Phi\)-values serves every normal distribution. Here \(\mathrm dz=\tfrac{1}{\sigma}\mathrm dx\), so \(\mathrm dx=\sigma\,\mathrm dz\), and the limits \(-\infty,\infty\) are unchanged:

\[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}}\,\mathrm dx =\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^{2}/2}\,\sigma\,\mathrm dz =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-z^{2}/2}\,\mathrm dz =\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=1 . \]

The \(\sigma\) from \(\mathrm dx\) cancels the \(\sigma\) in the constant — that cancellation is the whole reason the density is written with \(1/\sigma\) in front. Check (\(\mu=3.2\), \(\sigma=1.8\)): the integral is \(1.0000000\) ✓ and \(\int x\,p(x)\,\mathrm dx=3.2000000=\mu\) ✓. The probability version of the same move is \(\P(X\le x)=\Phi\!\bigl(\tfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\bigr)\), used in every clt task (TT8).

S3 — \(\displaystyle\int x e^{-x^{2}/2}\,\mathrm dx\), \(u=x^{2}/2\). The inside of the exponential is \(x^{2}/2\); its derivative is \(x\); and an \(x\) is sitting right there as a factor. So \(\mathrm du=x\,\mathrm dx\) and

\[ \int x e^{-x^{2}/2}\,\mathrm dx=\int e^{-u}\,\mathrm du=-e^{-u}+C=-e^{-x^{2}/2}+C . \]

Over a symmetric interval this integral is \(0\), because \(x e^{-x^{2}/2}\) is an odd function: \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}z e^{-z^{2}/2}\mathrm dz=0.0000000\) ✓, which says \(\E[\mathcal N(0,1)]=0\). Keep the antiderivative anyway — example P2 below needs it.

S4 — turning an exponential into a uniform. Let \(X\sim\Exp(\lambda)\) and set \(U:=e^{-\lambda X}\). For \(u\in(0,1)\), using that \(t\mapsto e^{-\lambda t}\) is decreasing so the inequality flips,

\[ \P(U\le u)=\P\bigl(e^{-\lambda X}\le u\bigr)=\P\Bigl(X\ge-\tfrac1\lambda\ln u\Bigr) =e^{-\lambda\cdot(-\frac1\lambda\ln u)}=e^{\ln u}=u , \]

which is the cdf of \(\Unif(0,1)\). So \(U\sim\Unif(0,1)\). This is the inverse of the transformation in micro-example 5 of part 1, and the same substitution written at the level of integrals reads \(\int_0^{\infty}h(e^{-\lambda x})\,\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\,\mathrm dx =\int_0^{1}h(u)\,\mathrm du\), with \(u=e^{-\lambda x}\) and \(\mathrm du=-\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\mathrm dx\) absorbing the sign into the swapped limits. Check: simulating \(400\,000\) draws with \(\lambda=1.3\) gives \(U\) a sample mean \(0.5005\) and sample variance \(0.0833\), against \(\tfrac12=0.5\) and \(\tfrac1{12}=0.0833\) for \(\Unif(0,1)\). ✓

The one trigonometric substitution DPT needs: \(x=\sin u\) Sheet 8 · Ex 3(ii)

A \(\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) in the integrand is the signal. Substituting \(x=\sin u\) makes it disappear, because \(\sin^{2}u+\cos^{2}u=1\) gives \(\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}u}=\cos u\) (and \(\cos u\ge0\) on \([-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2]\), so no absolute value is needed there). With \(x=\sin u\) you also get \(\mathrm dx=\cos u\,\mathrm du\), and the limits move as \(x=0\mapsto u=0\), \(x=1\mapsto u=\tfrac\pi2\).

Two identities do the rest. Learn them as facts — both come straight out of the addition formulas in Analysis 5.3: putting \(y=x\) in \(\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y\) gives the first, and putting \(y=x\) in \(\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y\) gives \(\cos 2v=\cos^{2}v-\sin^{2}v=1-2\sin^{2}v\) (using \(\cos^{2}+\sin^{2}=1\)), which rearranges to the second.

IdentityWhat it is for
\(2\sin u\cos u=\sin(2u)\) turns a product \(\sin u\cos u\) into a single sine, so it can be squared cleanly
\(\sin^{2}v=\tfrac12-\tfrac12\cos(2v)\) turns a square of a sine into something with an obvious antiderivative (\(\int\cos(av)\,\mathrm dv=\tfrac1a\sin(av)\))

Worked — \(\E[X^{2}]\) for the uniform disc. Its marginal density is \(p_X(x)=\tfrac2\pi\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) on \([-1,1]\) (worked below). The integrand is even, so double the half from \(0\) to \(1\), then substitute — one \(\cos u\) comes from \(\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\), the other from \(\mathrm dx\):

\[ \E[X^{2}]=\frac2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}x^{2}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\,\mathrm dx =\frac4\pi\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2}u\,\cos^{2}u\,\mathrm du =\frac1\pi\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2}(2u)\,\mathrm du , \]

the last step being \(\sin^{2}u\cos^{2}u=\tfrac14(2\sin u\cos u)^{2}=\tfrac14\sin^{2}(2u)\), identity one. Identity two with \(v=2u\) finishes it:

\[ \frac1\pi\int_0^{\pi/2}\Bigl(\frac12-\frac{\cos(4u)}{2}\Bigr)\mathrm du =\frac1\pi\Bigl[\frac u2-\frac{\sin(4u)}{8}\Bigr]_0^{\pi/2}=\frac1\pi\cdot\frac\pi4=\frac14 , \]

the \(\sin(4u)\) term vanishing because \(\sin(2\pi)=\sin0=0\). With \(\E[X]=0\) by the odd-function rule, \(\Var[X]=\tfrac14\). Checks: \(\int_0^1x^{2}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\mathrm dx=0.1963495=\pi/16\) ✓; \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2}(2u)\mathrm du=0.7853982=\pi/4\) ✓; \(\int_{-1}^{1}x^{2}p_X(x)\mathrm dx =0.2500000\) ✓; and at \(u=0.734\), \(2\sin u\cos u=0.9947211=\sin(2u)\) ✓, \(\sin^{2}u=0.4486923=\tfrac12-\tfrac12\cos(2u)\) ✓.

Note on the official solution. Sheet 8 Ex 3(ii) prints this chain as \(\tfrac2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}x^{2}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\,\mathrm dx=\tfrac4\pi\int_{-1}^{1}x^{2}\sqrt{1-x^{2}} \,\mathrm dx=\tfrac1\pi\int_0^{\pi/2}(2\sin u\cos u)^{2}\mathrm du\). The middle expression is wrong: doubling is only allowed together with halving the range, so it must read \(\tfrac4\pi\int_{0}^{1}\). As printed the middle term equals \(\tfrac12\), twice the correct \(\tfrac14\); the first and last terms are both right, so the final answer is unaffected.

One free fact on top, used in Sheet 8 Ex 3(iii): a whole number of periods of a sine integrates to \(0\), so \(\int_0^{2\pi}\sin(k\theta)\mathrm d\theta=0\) for every integer \(k\neq0\) (check at \(k=2\): \(-0.0000000\) ✓) — which is why the covariance of the uniform disc vanishes with no work. Fuller treatment: Analysis 5.3 — Trigonometric functions, Analysis 8.4 — The substitution rule.

Integration by parts My addition

\[ \int_a^b u(x)\,v'(x)\,\mathrm dx \;=\; \bigl[u(x)\,v(x)\bigr]_a^b \;-\; \int_a^b u'(x)\,v(x)\,\mathrm dx . \]

What the rule does. It trades the integral you have for a different one, plus a boundary term. It is worth doing only if the new integral is easier than the old one.

What to pick. Choose \(u\) to be the factor that gets simpler when differentiated, and \(v'\) to be the factor you can integrate. In this course that decision is almost automatic:

  • integrand \(=\) polynomial \(\times\) exponential \(\Rightarrow\) \(u=\) the polynomial (each round of by-parts lowers its degree by one), \(v'=\) the exponential;
  • integrand contains \(\ln x\) with nothing else convenient \(\Rightarrow\) \(u=\ln x\) (it turns into \(1/x\)), \(v'=\) the rest.

Boundary terms at \(\infty\). Evaluate \([uv]_a^{\infty}\) as a limit. When \(v\) carries a factor \(e^{-ax}\) with \(a>0\), Rule 2 of the previous section makes the term \(0\) at the top, and saying "\(x^{n}e^{-ax}\to0\) as \(x\to\infty\)" is the line that justifies it.

Integration-by-parts examples My addition

P1 — the mean of \(\Exp(\lambda)\). Take \(u=x\) (so \(u'=1\)) and \(v'=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) (so \(v=-e^{-\lambda x}\)):

\[ \E[X]=\int_0^{\infty}x\,\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\,\mathrm dx =\underbrace{\bigl[-x e^{-\lambda x}\bigr]_0^{\infty}}_{=\,0-0\,=\,0} +\int_0^{\infty}e^{-\lambda x}\,\mathrm dx =\left[-\frac{1}{\lambda}e^{-\lambda x}\right]_0^{\infty}=\frac1\lambda . \]

The boundary term vanishes at the top because the exponential beats the factor \(x\), and at the bottom because of the factor \(x=0\). The sign of the second term became \(+\) because the rule's minus met the minus inside \(v\). Check (\(\lambda=2.2\)): \(0.4545455=1/2.2\). ✓

P2 — the variance of \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) Sheet 8 · Ex 5. The task is \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x^{2}e^{-x^{2}/2}\,\mathrm dx\). Split the \(x^{2}\): take \(u=x\) and \(v'=x e^{-x^{2}/2}\), whose antiderivative is \(v=-e^{-x^{2}/2}\) by example S3 above. Then

\[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x^{2}e^{-x^{2}/2}\,\mathrm dx =\underbrace{\bigl[-x e^{-x^{2}/2}\bigr]_{-\infty}^{\infty}}_{=\,0} +\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^{2}/2}\,\mathrm dx =\sqrt{2\pi} . \]

Dividing by \(\sqrt{2\pi}\) gives \(\E[Z^{2}]=1\), and since \(\E[Z]=0\) that is \(\Var[Z]=1\). Check: \(\int_\R x^{2}e^{-x^{2}/2}\mathrm dx=2.5066283=\sqrt{2\pi}\) ✓ and \(\int_\R z^{2}\varphi(z)\,\mathrm dz=1.0000000\) ✓. Choosing \(u=x^{2}\), \(v'=e^{-x^{2}/2}\) instead leads nowhere, because \(e^{-x^{2}/2}\) has no antiderivative in elementary functions — that choice is the trap.

P3 — a conditional expectation Sheet 7 · Ex 1. With \(u=y\), \(v'=e^{-y}\), \(v=-e^{-y}\):

\[ \int_x^{\infty}y e^{-y}\,\mathrm dy =\bigl[-y e^{-y}\bigr]_x^{\infty}+\int_x^{\infty}e^{-y}\,\mathrm dy =\bigl(0+x e^{-x}\bigr)+e^{-x}=(x+1)e^{-x} . \]

The boundary term at the lower limit contributes \(+x e^{-x}\) because \(-(-x e^{-x})=x e^{-x}\). Checks: at \(x=0\) the value is \(1.0000000\) versus \((0+1)e^{0}=1\) ✓; at \(x=1\), \(0.7357589\) versus \(2e^{-1}=0.7357589\) ✓; at \(x=2.5\), \(0.2872975\) versus \(3.5\,e^{-2.5}\) ✓.

P4 — the tail formula \(\E[X]=\int_0^{\infty}\P(X>x)\,\mathrm dx\), for \(X\ge0\) with density \(p\) and cdf \(F\). Take \(u=x\) and \(v'=p(x)\). The clever choice is \(v(x)=-\bigl(1-F(x)\bigr)=-\P(X>x)\): this is a legitimate antiderivative of \(p\), because \(\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\bigl[-(1-F(x))\bigr]=F'(x)=p(x)\), and any antiderivative may be used. Then

\[ \E[X]=\int_0^{\infty}x\,p(x)\,\mathrm dx =\underbrace{\bigl[-x\,\P(X>x)\bigr]_0^{\infty}}_{=\,0\ \text{when }\E[X]<\infty} +\int_0^{\infty}\P(X>x)\,\mathrm dx . \]
In words: instead of weighting each value by its density, sweep a horizontal line up the picture and add the widths of the survival function. For \(\Exp(\lambda)\) it reads \(\int_0^{\infty}e^{-\lambda x}\mathrm dx=\tfrac1\lambda\), which is the mean, with no by-parts work at all. Check (\(\lambda=0.8\)): \(1.2500000=1/0.8\). ✓

The discrete twin, \(\E[X]=\sum_{k\ge1}\P(X\ge k)\) for \(X\) with values in \(\N_0\), is the same identity with a sum in place of the integral, and it is the fast route to \(\E[X]\) for the geometric distribution (§2.1).

P5 — \(\int\ln x\,\mathrm dx\), the "multiply by 1" trick. There is only one factor, so invent a second: \(u=\ln x\) (\(u'=1/x\)) and \(v'=1\) (\(v=x\)). Then

\[ \int_1^{e}\ln x\,\mathrm dx=\bigl[x\ln x\bigr]_1^{e}-\int_1^{e}x\cdot\frac1x\,\mathrm dx =(e\cdot1-1\cdot0)-\bigl[x\bigr]_1^{e}=e-(e-1)=1 , \]

so the antiderivative of \(\ln x\) is \(x\ln x-x+C\). Checks: \(\int_1^{e}\ln x\,\mathrm dx =1.0000000\) ✓, and \(\int_0^{1}\ln u\,\mathrm du=-1.0000000\) ✓ — the second of these is the integral that WiSe25 · P3c obtains by a probabilistic argument instead (§2.1).

Which rule, in five seconds My addition

  • Do you see a function and its derivative multiplied together? → substitution (\(x e^{-x^{2}/2}\): the \(x\) is the derivative of \(x^{2}/2\)).
  • Do you see polynomial \(\times\) exponential with no matching derivative? → by parts, \(u=\) the polynomial (\(x e^{-\lambda x}\), \(x^{2}e^{-ax}\)).
  • Is the integrand already a table row, possibly after pulling out a constant? → look it up, do not integrate (the table).
  • Is the integrand odd and the interval symmetric? → the answer is \(0\), with no work.
  • Do you see a function's derivative over the function itself? → \(\ln\) of the bottom, \(\int f'/f=\ln|f|\).
  • Do you see \(\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\)? → the substitution \(x=\sin u\).
  • Is the integrand a density in disguise? → its integral over the support is \(1\), so \(\int_0^{\infty}x^{n}e^{-ax}\mathrm dx\) can be read off from the Gamma density instead of computed.

Fuller treatment: Analysis 8.4 — Integration rules, and inside it integration by parts and the substitution rule; Analysis 8 — mixed exercises for drill. In DPT: §1.3, the Gamma integrals, §2.3, the Gaussian, §2.1, Sheet 7 Ex 1, TT3 and TT4 on the exam page. The multivariate version — substitution with a Jacobian determinant — is on B4 and in §2.3, transformations.

Standardise, then fold with \(\Phi\)

Every central-limit task ends the same way: you are asked for a probability about a normal variable, and the answer is not a number but an expression in \(\Phi\), the cdf of the standard normal (\(\Phi(z)=\P(Z\le z)\) for \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\)). Two moves, in this order. Both were worth credit on two of the three past papers.

Move 1 — standardise; move 2 — fold My addition

1. Standardise. Subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation. For any \(X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^{2})\),

\[ \P(X\le x)=\P\Bigl(\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\le\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\Bigr) =\Phi\Bigl(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\Bigr) , \]

which is substitution S2 above done at the level of probabilities. Dividing by \(\sigma>0\) does not flip the inequality.

2. Fold. The bell curve \(\varphi(z)=\tfrac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^{2}/2}\) is even: \(\varphi(-z)=\varphi(z)\), since only \(z^{2}\) appears. So the area left of \(-z\) equals the area right of \(+z\), which is

\[ \Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z),\qquad\text{and therefore}\qquad \P\bigl(|Z|\ge a\bigr)=2\bigl(1-\Phi(a)\bigr)=2\,\Phi(-a)\quad (a\ge0). \]
In words: a two-sided event \(\{|Z|\ge a\}\) is two identical tails, so compute one tail and double it. Writing \(2\Phi(-a)\) rather than \(2(1-\Phi(a))\) is the same number and is what the official solutions print.

Checks: \(\Phi(1.5)+\Phi(-1.5)=0.9331928+0.0668072=1.0000000\) ✓. At \(a=2\): \(2(1-\Phi(2))=0.0455003\), \(2\Phi(-2)=0.0455003\), and integrating the bell curve directly, \(2\int_2^{\infty}\varphi(z)\,\mathrm dz=0.0455003\) ✓. At \(a=1.96\) all three give \(0.0499958\) — the familiar \(5\%\).

Worked — the exam's own line WiSe25 · P4c

There \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{mle}}\) has \(\E[\hat\theta]=\theta\) and \(\Var[\hat\theta]=\theta^{2}/(2n)\), so its standard deviation is \(\theta/\sqrt{2n}\). The central limit theorem says the standardised estimator is approximately \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). Asked for \(\P(|\hat\theta-\theta|\ge\varepsilon)\), standardise inside the absolute value — dividing both \(|\hat\theta-\theta|\) and \(\varepsilon\) by the same positive number \(\theta/\sqrt{2n}\) — and then fold:

\[ \P\bigl(|\hat\theta-\theta|\ge\varepsilon\bigr) =\P\Bigl(\Bigl|\tfrac{\hat\theta-\theta}{\theta/\sqrt{2n}}\Bigr|\ge\tfrac{\varepsilon\sqrt{2n}}{\theta}\Bigr) \;\approx\; 2\,\Phi\!\Bigl(-\frac{\sqrt{2n}\,\varepsilon}{\theta}\Bigr) . \]

Check (\(n=200\), \(\varepsilon=0.2\), \(\theta=1\)): the argument is \(-4\), so the approximation is \(2\Phi(-4)=6.334\cdot10^{-5}\), against the Chebyshev bound \(\theta^{2}/(2n\varepsilon^{2})=0.0625000\) from part (b) — the same quantity, three orders of magnitude apart, which is exactly what part (d) asks you to comment on. The identical move with \(\hat\theta-\theta\) replaced by \(Z_n\) is SoSe26 · P4d: \(\P(|Z_n|\ge a)\approx2(1-\Phi(a))=2\Phi(-a)\).

Used in DPT for: every confidence interval and every two-sided test, where the quantile \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\) is defined by exactly this folding (§3.3, and the \(\Phi\)-table at §3.3); Sheet 9, Sheet 11; and TT8 on the exam page. There is nothing to integrate — \(e^{-z^{2}/2}\) has no elementary antiderivative, which is why the answer is left in terms of \(\Phi\).

Two variables: double integrals, regions, polar coordinates

Up to here every integral had one variable. From §2.3 onwards DPT hands you two random variables at once — a pair \((X,Y)\) with a joint density \(p(x,y)\), a function of two inputs whose total volume is \(1\). Every question about the pair ("what is \(\P(X\le Y)\)?", "what is the density of \(X+Y\)?", "what is the density of \(X\) alone?") turns into an integral over a region of the plane. That is all a double integral is used for in this course. This section gives you the four shapes of region that actually occur and nothing else.

A double integral is two ordinary integrals, done one after the other My addition

The symbol \(\iint_B f(x,y)\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy\) — "integrate \(f\) over the region \(B\) in the plane" — is computed by iterated integration [iterierte Integration]: freeze one variable, integrate over the other, then integrate the result. Written out:

\[ \iint_B f(x,y)\,\mathrm d(x,y)\;=\;\int_{\;x\text{ ranges over its whole span}} \Biggl(\underbrace{\int_{\;y\text{ ranges over the slice of }B\text{ at that }x} f(x,y)\,\mathrm dy}_{\text{inner: }x\text{ is a frozen constant here}}\Biggr)\mathrm dx . \]
In words: cut the region into vertical strips. For each fixed \(x\), the strip is a one-dimensional interval in \(y\); integrate along it. That gives a number depending on \(x\). Then integrate that number over all \(x\).

The only thing that can go wrong is the inner limits. The outer limits are always plain numbers. The inner limits are allowed to contain the outer variable, and that is exactly how a non-rectangular region gets described.

Rule 1 — when the region is a rectangle, the two integrals separate My addition

If \(B=[a,b]\times[c,d]\) (a rectangle: \(x\) between \(a\) and \(b\), \(y\) between \(c\) and \(d\), with no interaction) and the integrand splits as \(f(x,y)=g(x)h(y)\), then

\[ \iint_B g(x)h(y)\,\mathrm d(x,y)=\Bigl(\int_a^b g(x)\,\mathrm dx\Bigr)\cdot\Bigl(\int_c^d h(y)\,\mathrm dy\Bigr). \]

Why this is worth knowing: for independent \(X\) and \(Y\) the joint density is a product, \(p(x,y)=p_X(x)\,p_Y(y)\). So every probability over a rectangle collapses into two one-variable integrals you already know how to do, and you never write a double integral at all.

D1 — a rectangle, done both ways My addition

Compute \(\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^2 xy\,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx\). Inner first, with \(x\) frozen so that it comes out of the \(y\)-integral as a constant:

\[ \int_0^2 xy\,\mathrm dy = x\int_0^2 y\,\mathrm dy = x\left[\frac{y^{2}}{2}\right]_0^{2}=x\cdot 2=2x, \qquad\text{then}\qquad \int_0^1 2x\,\mathrm dx=\bigl[x^{2}\bigr]_0^{1}=1 . \]

By Rule 1 the same thing in one line: \(\bigl(\int_0^1x\,\mathrm dx\bigr)\bigl(\int_0^2y\,\mathrm dy\bigr) =\tfrac12\cdot2=1\). Check: numerical double integration gives \(1.0000000\). ✓

Rule 2 — swapping the order is free when the integrand is \(\ge0\) My addition

If \(f(x,y)\ge0\) everywhere on \(B\), then

\[ \int\!\!\Bigl(\int f\,\mathrm dy\Bigr)\mathrm dx\;=\;\int\!\!\Bigl(\int f\,\mathrm dx\Bigr)\mathrm dy \]

— both orders give the same answer, including the answer \(+\infty\). This is Tonelli's theorem [Satz von Tonelli], the non-negative half of the Fubini–Tonelli pair. Densities and probabilities are never negative, so in DPT you may always swap, and you should swap the moment one order looks harder than the other. (For an integrand that changes sign the theorem needs \(\iint|f|<\infty\) first; that case does not occur in this course's exercises.) The slow version, with the counterexample that shows why the condition is not decoration, is on B4 — Fubini and Tonelli.

Reading the inner limits off a region — the four shapes DPT uses My addition

Draw the region. Then, for the order "\(\mathrm dy\) inside, \(\mathrm dx\) outside", ask: for this fixed \(x\), where does \(y\) start and where does it stop?

RegionPicture in one lineWritten as an iterated integralWhere it comes from
rectangle \(a\le x\le b\), \(c\le y\le d\) a box \(\int_a^b\int_c^d\cdots\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx\) independent pair on bounded supports
triangle \(\{x\le y\}\) inside \([0,\infty)^2\) everything above the diagonal \(\int_0^{\infty}\!\int_{x}^{\infty}\cdots\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx\)
or \(\int_0^{\infty}\!\int_{0}^{y}\cdots\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy\)		 \(\P(X\le Y)\); "who arrives first"; Sheet 7 Ex 1
half-plane \(\{x+y\le z\}\), \(z\) fixed below the line \(y=z-x\) \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\,z-x}\cdots\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx\) the cdf of a sum \(X+Y\); convolution
wedge \(\{x\le t\,y\}\), \(t>0\), \(y>0\) below a ray through the origin \(\int_0^{\infty}\!\int_0^{\,t y}\cdots\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy\) the cdf of a ratio \(X/Y\) (SoSe25 · P1d)
disc \(\{x^{2}+y^{2}\le R^{2}\}\) a filled circle \(\int_{-R}^{R}\!\int_{-\sqrt{R^{2}-x^{2}}}^{\,+\sqrt{R^{2}-x^{2}}}\cdots\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx\), or polar coordinates below Both are needed. Polar for areas and for integrands that depend only on \(x^{2}+y^{2}\) or are symmetric in the angle (the Gaussian integral; Sheet 8 Ex 3(iii)). The \(x,y\) slice \(\pm\sqrt{R^{2}-x^{2}}\) for a marginal density (D5, Sheet 8 Ex 3(i)) — polar coordinates cannot express "integrate out \(y\)", because \(y\) is not one of their coordinates.

The one habit that prevents the standard mistake: after you write the limits, check that the outer ones are numbers and that the inner ones mention only the outer variable. If the outer limits still contain a variable, you have swapped the two lines by accident.

D2 — the triangle \(\{x\le y\}\): "which of the two happens first?" My addition

\(X\sim\Exp(\lambda)\) and \(Y\sim\Exp(\mu)\) independent, with \(\lambda=2\), \(\mu=3\). Independence makes the joint density the product \(p(x,y)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\cdot\mu e^{-\mu y}\) on \(x,y\ge0\). Then

\[ \P(X\le Y)=\iint_{\{x\le y\}}p(x,y)\,\mathrm d(x,y) =\int_0^{\infty}\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\underbrace{\Bigl(\int_x^{\infty}\mu e^{-\mu y}\,\mathrm dy\Bigr)}_{=\,e^{-\mu x}}\mathrm dx =\int_0^{\infty}\lambda e^{-(\lambda+\mu)x}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu} . \]

Each step: the inner integral is the exponential table row \(\int_x^{\infty}\mu e^{-\mu y}\mathrm dy =\bigl[-e^{-\mu y}\bigr]_x^{\infty}=0-(-e^{-\mu x})=e^{-\mu x}\); then \(e^{-\lambda x}e^{-\mu x}=e^{-(\lambda+\mu)x}\) by the exponential rule \(e^{a}e^{b}=e^{a+b}\); then the same table row again with rate \(\lambda+\mu\), which gives \(\lambda\cdot\frac1{\lambda+\mu}\). Checks: \(\lambda=2,\mu=3\) gives \(0.4000000=2/5\) ✓, and doing the integral in the other order (\(\int_0^{\infty}\!\int_0^{y}\)) gives \(0.4000000\) as well ✓ — that is Rule 2 in action.

D3 — the half-plane \(\{x+y\le z\}\): the density of a sum My addition

\(U,V\) independent and \(\Unif(0,1)\) — that is, each has density \(1\) on \([0,1]\) and \(0\) elsewhere. What is \(\P(U+V\le z)\) for \(z=0.6\)? The region is the part of the unit square below the line \(u+v=0.6\), a right triangle with legs \(0.6\):

\[ \P(U+V\le 0.6)=\int_0^{0.6}\!\!\int_0^{\,0.6-u}1\,\mathrm dv\,\mathrm du =\int_0^{0.6}(0.6-u)\,\mathrm du=\left[0.6u-\frac{u^{2}}{2}\right]_0^{0.6}=0.36-0.18=0.18 . \]

In general \(\P(U+V\le z)=z^{2}/2\) for \(0\le z\le1\); differentiating in \(z\) gives the density \(p_{U+V}(z)=z\) there. Checks: \(z=0.6\) gives \(0.1800000=0.6^{2}/2\) ✓; \(z=1.4\) gives \(0.8200000=1-(2-1.4)^{2}/2\) ✓ (above \(z=1\) the triangle is cut off by the square, so the formula changes — a reminder to draw the picture rather than trust one formula everywhere).

The general statement this produces is the convolution formula [Faltung]: differentiating \(\P(X+Y\le z)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{z-x}p_X(x)p_Y(y)\,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx\) under the integral sign gives

\[ p_{X+Y}(z)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p_X(x)\,p_Y(z-x)\,\mathrm dx . \]

Check on \(X,Y\) independent \(\Exp(1)\): the formula gives \(\int_0^{z}e^{-x}e^{-(z-x)}\mathrm dx=z e^{-z}\), and at \(z=2\) numerical integration returns \(0.2706706=2e^{-2}\) ✓ — the \(\Gamma(2,1)\) density, which is where the Gamma family comes from (§1.3).

D4 — the wedge \(\{x\le t\,y\}\): the density of a ratio SoSe25 · P1d

\(X,Y\) independent \(\Exp(1)\). For \(t>0\), the event \(\{X/Y\le t\}\) is \(\{X\le tY\}\) (multiplying by \(Y>0\) does not flip the inequality). So

\[ \P\bigl(X/Y\le t\bigr)=\int_0^{\infty}e^{-y}\Bigl(\int_0^{\,t y}e^{-x}\,\mathrm dx\Bigr)\mathrm dy =\int_0^{\infty}e^{-y}\bigl(1-e^{-ty}\bigr)\mathrm dy=1-\frac{1}{1+t}=\frac{t}{1+t} . \]

The last step used the table row twice: \(\int_0^{\infty}e^{-y}\mathrm dy=1\) and \(\int_0^{\infty}e^{-(1+t)y}\mathrm dy=\frac1{1+t}\). Check at \(t=2\): numerical double integration gives \(0.6666667=2/3\) ✓. Differentiating in \(t\) gives the density of the ratio, \(p(t)=1/(1+t)^{2}\) on \(t>0\).

The whole recipe for a ratio, a sum or a maximum is the same three lines: (i) write the event as a region of the plane; (ii) integrate the joint density over it, inner limits first; (iii) differentiate the resulting cdf in the parameter to get a density. Nothing about it is specific to which function of \((X,Y)\) you took.

D5 — marginal densities: integrating the other variable out

Given the joint density \(p_{X,Y}\) of a pair, the marginal density [Randdichte] of \(X\) alone is what you get by forgetting \(Y\). "Forgetting" means adding up all the ways \(Y\) could have come out, and adding up over a continuous variable is integrating.

The rule, and the only hard part Script §1.4, Thm 1.68

\[ p_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm dy ,\qquad p_Y(y)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm dx . \]
In words: to get the density of \(X\), integrate the joint density over \(y\), leaving \(x\) alone. The variable you integrate is the one you are throwing away.

The only hard part is the limits. They are not \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\) in practice: the joint density is \(0\) outside its region, so the integral runs over the slice of the region at that \(x\) — the same vertical strip as in the iterated-integration box above, and the same indicator-to-limits move as in "integrate only over the support". The answer is a function of \(x\), and you must also say for which \(x\) it is non-zero.

Worked — the uniform disc Sheet 8 · Ex 3(i)

\((X,Y)\) is uniform on the unit disc \(D=\{(x,y) : x^{2}+y^{2}\le1\}\). "Uniform" means constant density on \(D\); since the disc has area \(\pi\) and the total must be \(1\), that constant is \(1/\pi\): \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)=\tfrac1\pi\chi_D(x,y)\).

The slice. Fix an \(x\). The condition \(x^{2}+y^{2}\le1\) is \(y^{2}\le1-x^{2}\), i.e. \(|y|\le\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\). So \(y\) runs from \(-\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) to \(+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) — and that requires \(1-x^{2}\ge0\), so there is a slice only for \(x\in[-1,1]\); outside that, \(p_X(x)=0\). Then

\[ p_X(x)=\int_{-\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}^{\,+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\frac1\pi\,\mathrm dy =\frac1\pi\cdot\Bigl(\sqrt{1-x^{2}}-\bigl(-\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\bigr)\Bigr) =\frac{2}{\pi}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\qquad\text{for }|x|\le1 . \]

The integrand did not depend on \(y\), so the integral is just "constant × length of the interval", and the length is twice the half-width. By the symmetry between the two coordinates, \(p_Y(y)=\tfrac2\pi\sqrt{1-y^{2}}\) on \([-1,1]\). Checks: \(\int_{-1}^{1}p_X=1.0000000\) ✓ (a marginal is a density, so this is the free error-check); at \(x=0.6\) the slice integral gives \(0.5092958\) and the formula \(\tfrac2\pi\sqrt{1-0.36}=0.5092958\) ✓. The mean is \(0\) by the odd-function rule, and \(\E[X^{2}]=0.2500000=\tfrac14\), which is the trig-substitution box.

Why polar coordinates are the wrong tool here, even though the region is a disc: "integrate out \(y\)" is a statement about the coordinate \(y\), and after the change to \((r,\theta)\) there is no \(y\) left to integrate out. Polar coordinates are for Sheet 8 Ex 3(iii) — the covariance, where the integrand \(xy=r^{2}\cos\theta\sin\theta\) becomes \(\tfrac12 r^{2}\sin(2\theta)\) and the \(\theta\)-integral over a full turn is \(0\) (§2.1). Check: integrating \(xy/\pi\) over the disc numerically gives \(0.0000000\) ✓.

A second instance, with an unbounded slice Sheet 7 · Ex 1

\(p_{X,Y}(x,y)=e^{-y}\chi_A(x,y)\) with \(A=\{0\le x\le y\}\). For \(x\ge0\) the slice at that \(x\) is \(y\in[x,\infty)\), so \(p_X(x)=\int_x^{\infty}e^{-y}\mathrm dy=e^{-x}\). Slicing the other way, at a fixed \(y\ge0\) the variable \(x\) runs over \([0,y]\) and the integrand does not depend on \(x\), so \(p_Y(y)=\int_0^{y}e^{-y}\mathrm dx=y\,e^{-y}\). Checks: \(p_X(0.8)=0.4493290=e^{-0.8}\) ✓; \(p_Y(1.3)=0.3542913=1.3\,e^{-1.3}\) ✓. Both marginals are needed for what that exercise actually asks: the conditional densities \(p_{X\mid Y=y}=p_{X,Y}/p_Y\) and \(p_{Y\mid X=x}=p_{X,Y}/p_X\), from which it computes \(\E[X\mid Y=y]=y/2\) and \(\E[Y\mid X=x]=x+1\) (§2.1). A marginal is also the standard way to disprove independence, since \(p_{X,Y}=p_Xp_Y\) fails here — \(e^{-x}\cdot y e^{-y}\ne e^{-y}\chi_A(x,y)\) — and that is the move Sheet 8 · Ex 3(iii) makes for the disc.

Polar coordinates, and the Gaussian integral

For an integrand that depends on the distance from the origin, the \(x,y\) slice \(\pm\sqrt{R^{2}-x^{2}}\) leads to an integral nothing simplifies. Polar coordinates [Polarkoordinaten] describe the same point by a distance and an angle instead:

\[ x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta,\qquad r\ge0,\ \ \theta\in[0,2\pi) , \]

where \(r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\) is the distance from the origin and \(\theta\) is the angle measured anticlockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis. In these coordinates a disc of radius \(R\) is simply \(0\le r\le R\), \(0\le\theta<2\pi\) — a rectangle again.

The factor \(r\) is not optional My addition

\[ \iint f(x,y)\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy=\iint f(r\cos\theta,\,r\sin\theta)\;\boxed{r}\;\mathrm dr\,\mathrm d\theta . \]
In words: a small patch at distance \(r\) with side lengths \(\mathrm dr\) and angle \(\mathrm d\theta\) is not a square of area \(\mathrm dr\,\mathrm d\theta\); it is a curved rectangle whose arc side has length \(r\,\mathrm d\theta\), so its area is \(r\,\mathrm dr\,\mathrm d\theta\). Patches far out are bigger, and the factor \(r\) is the bookkeeping for that.

Sanity check: the area of a disc of radius \(2\) is \(\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{2}r\,\mathrm dr\,\mathrm d\theta=2\pi\cdot\bigl[\tfrac{r^{2}}2\bigr]_0^{2}=2\pi\cdot2=4\pi\). Numerically \(12.5663706=4\pi\) ✓. Leaving out the \(r\) would have produced \(2\pi\cdot2=4\pi\) as well only by accident of this example — for radius \(3\) the correct \(9\pi=28.27\) versus the wrong \(6\pi=18.85\) shows the difference.

Why \(\int_{\R}e^{-z^{2}/2}\,\mathrm dz=\sqrt{2\pi}\) — the one place polar coordinates earn their keep My addition

\(e^{-z^{2}/2}\) has no antiderivative built from powers, exponentials, logarithms and trigonometric functions, so one-variable methods cannot touch it. Call the unknown number \(I\), square it (Rule 1 read backwards turns the product of two one-variable integrals into a double one), and switch to polar, where \(x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}\) and the plane is \(r\in[0,\infty)\), \(\theta\in[0,2\pi)\):

\[ I^{2}=\iint_{\R^{2}}e^{-(x^{2}+y^{2})/2}\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy =\int_0^{2\pi}\Bigl(\underbrace{\int_0^{\infty}r e^{-r^{2}/2}\mathrm dr}_{=\,1}\Bigr)\mathrm d\theta =2\pi\quad\Longrightarrow\quad I=\sqrt{2\pi}. \]

The inner integral is the substitution \(u=r^{2}/2\), \(\mathrm du=r\,\mathrm dr\), giving \(\int_0^{\infty}e^{-u}\mathrm du=1\) — the factor \(r\) that polar coordinates supplied is exactly the factor that substitution needed, which is the whole reason the trick works. Checks: \(\int_0^{\infty}re^{-r^{2}/2}\mathrm dr=1.0000000\) ✓ and \(\int_{\R}e^{-z^{2}/2}\mathrm dz=2.5066283=\sqrt{2\pi}\) ✓.

In words: the \(\sqrt{2\pi}\) in the normal density is not a magic constant. It is the number that makes the bell curve enclose area \(1\).

The Jacobian, in one line, for the two cases that occur My addition

Substitution in two variables is the same idea as in one: change coordinates, and multiply by "how much the change stretches area". That stretch factor is the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant [Jacobi-Determinante] \(|\det J|\), where \(J\) is the matrix of all partial derivatives of the new coordinates' map. Two cases are enough here.

  • Linear map. \(x=au+bv\), \(y=cu+dv\). Then \(J=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\), \(\det J=ad-bc\), and \(\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy=|ad-bc|\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv\). The one-dimensional special case \(x=\sigma u+\mu\) has stretch factor \(|\sigma|\) — that is the \(1/\sigma\) in the \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^{2})\) density.
  • Polar map. \(x=r\cos\theta\), \(y=r\sin\theta\). Then \(J=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&r\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\det J=r\cos^{2}\theta+r\sin^{2}\theta=r(\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta)=r\), using \(\cos^{2}+\sin^{2}=1\). That is the factor \(r\) from the box above.

The general statement — \(\int_{T(B)}f=\int_B (f\circ T)\,|\det J_T|\) in \(\R^{n}\), with determinants, matrix inverses and worked examples — is on B5 — change of variables, and the regions-and-slices side of it is on B4 — integrating over regions. In DPT it appears as Proposition 2.51 (§2.3, transformations); the one-dimensional version \(p_Y(y)=p_X(g^{-1}(y))\,\bigl|\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dy}g^{-1}(y)\bigr|\) is the case \(n=1\), where "\(|\det J|\)" is just the absolute value of a derivative — worked in full at the transformation formula.

Fuller treatment: your Analysis guide builds differential calculus in several variables (Analysis 11.2 — partial derivatives, the Jacobian matrix) but it never integrates in two variables, so the double integral itself is a genuine gap — it is written up on B4. In DPT: §2.3 transformations, §2.3 the Gaussian, Sheet 7 Ex 1, exam task type TT4.

Convex functions and Jensen

A function is convex [konvex] when its graph curves upward like a bowl: every straight line segment joining two points of the graph lies above the graph. Concave [konkav] is the mirror image — an upside-down bowl, chords below the graph. DPT needs this for exactly one reason: Jensen's inequality, which says that averaging and applying a convex function do not commute, and which direction the error goes.

The test you can actually run in an exam My addition

Let \(g\) be twice differentiable on an interval \(I\). Then

\[ g''(x)\ge0\ \text{ for all }x\in I\ \Longleftrightarrow\ g\text{ is convex on }I,\qquad g''(x)\le0\ \text{ for all }x\in I\ \Longleftrightarrow\ g\text{ is concave on }I . \]

The three-second procedure: differentiate twice, look at the sign, write one sentence naming the interval. That is it. \(g''\) is the derivative of \(g'\); \(g'\ge0\) rising means the slope keeps increasing, which is exactly "curving upward".

The exam sentence, in the form that scores: "\(g(x)=x^{2}\) satisfies \(g''(x)=2>0\) for all \(x\in\R\), hence \(g\) is convex on \(\R\)." Name the function, give \(g''\), give the sign, give the interval, say the word.

When \(g\) is not differentiable — the only such case here is \(g(x)=|x|\), which has a corner at \(0\) — use the definition directly: \(g\) is convex if \(g(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\le\alpha g(x)+(1-\alpha)g(y)\) for all \(x,y\) and all \(\alpha\in[0,1]\). For \(|\cdot|\) this is the triangle inequality (above), so \(|x|\) is convex without any second derivative.

The list to memorise — six functions, with their second derivatives My addition

\(g(x)\)\(g'(x)\)\(g''(x)\)VerdictWhat Jensen then says
\(x^{2}\) on \(\R\)\(2x\)\(2>0\)convex \(\E[X]^{2}\le\E[X^{2}]\) — i.e. \(\Var[X]\ge0\)
\(e^{x}\) on \(\R\)\(e^{x}\)\(e^{x}>0\)convex \(e^{\E[X]}\le\E[e^{X}]\) — the moment-generating direction
\(-\ln x\) on \((0,\infty)\)\(-1/x\)\(1/x^{2}>0\)convex \(-\ln\E[X]\le\E[-\ln X]\), i.e. \(\E[\ln X]\le\ln\E[X]\)
\(1/x\) on \((0,\infty)\)\(-1/x^{2}\)\(2/x^{3}>0\)convex \(1/\E[X]\le\E[1/X]\)
\(|x|\) on \(\R\)undefined at \(0\)—convex (by definition) \(|\E[X]|\le\E[|X|]\)
\(\sqrt x\) on \((0,\infty)\)\(\tfrac12x^{-1/2}\)\(-\tfrac14x^{-3/2}<0\)concave \(\E[\sqrt X]\le\sqrt{\E[X]}\) — inequality the other way
\(\ln x\) on \((0,\infty)\)\(1/x\)\(-1/x^{2}<0\)concave \(\E[\ln X]\le\ln\E[X]\)
\(x^{3}\) on \(\R\)\(3x^{2}\)\(6x\), sign changes at \(0\)neither on \(\R\) Jensen does not apply — convex only on \([0,\infty)\)

Numerical spot-checks of the second derivatives (difference quotient \(\frac{g(x+h)-2g(x)+g(x-h)}{h^{2}}\) with \(h=10^{-4}\)): \(x^{2}\) at \(x=1\): \(+2.000000\) versus \(2\) ✓; \(e^{x}\) at \(x=0.7\): \(+2.013753\) versus \(e^{0.7}=2.013753\) ✓; \(-\ln x\) at \(x=2\): \(+0.250000\) versus \(1/4\) ✓; \(\sqrt x\) at \(x=4\): \(-0.031250\) versus \(-\tfrac14\cdot4^{-3/2}=-1/32\) ✓; \(\ln x\) at \(x=3\): \(-0.111111\) versus \(-1/9\) ✓; \(1/x\) at \(x=2\): \(+0.250000\) versus \(2/8\) ✓.

The last row is the trap the exams like: a function can be convex on part of its domain and concave on another part. Jensen needs convexity on an interval that contains all the values \(X\) can take. Saying "on \(\R\)" when the function is only convex on \([0,\infty)\) loses the credit.

Jensen's inequality, as the exam wants it written Script 2.42 SoSe26 · P3a

Assumptions: \(X\) a real random variable with \(\E[|X|]<\infty\) (its expectation exists and is finite), and \(g:\R\to\R\) convex. Conclusion:

\[ g\bigl(\E[X]\bigr)\;\le\;\E\bigl[g(X)\bigr] . \]

SoSe26 · P3a gave 3 credits for this statement alone, one credit each for: "\(\E[X]\) is finite", "\(g:\R\to\R\) is convex", and the inequality with the correct direction. Part (b) then asked you to check convexity of a concrete \(g\) and apply it — which is the \(g''\ge0\) line from the box above, and nothing more. So the whole Analysis content of that 5-credit problem is: differentiate twice, read the sign, name the interval.

In words: for a bowl-shaped \(g\), the average of the outputs is at least the output of the average. Spreading \(X\) out can only push \(\E[g(X)]\) up. For a concave \(g\) the inequality flips, because \(g\) concave means \(-g\) convex.

Numeric check with \(X\) uniform on \(\{1,2,6\}\), so \(\E[X]=3\): with \(g(x)=x^{2}\), \(g(\E[X])=9.000000\) and \(\E[g(X)]=\tfrac{1+4+36}{3}=13.666667\), and \(9\le13.67\) ✓ — the gap \(13.666667-9=4.666667\) is precisely \(\Var[X]\). With the concave \(g=\ln\): \(\E[\ln X]=0.828302\le\ln\E[X]=1.098612\) ✓.

Fuller treatment: Analysis 7.6 — Convexity [Krümmungsverhalten] for the equivalence between \(g''\ge0\), the chord condition and the tangent-below condition. In DPT the probability side lives on §2.2 — Jensen's inequality (with a widget that moves the two points of the chord), and the exam-statement drill is on the exam page.

Complex numbers, only as much as §2.3 needs

Characteristic functions [charakteristische Funktionen] are defined as \(\varphi_X(t)=\E[e^{itX}]\), and the letter \(i\) in that formula is the only reason complex numbers appear in this course. You do not need complex analysis. You need five facts.

The five facts My addition

  1. What \(i\) is. \(i\) is a symbol with \(i^{2}=-1\). A complex number [komplexe Zahl] is \(z=a+bi\) with \(a,b\in\R\); \(a\) is the real part, \(b\) the imaginary part. You add and multiply exactly as with real numbers, replacing \(i^{2}\) by \(-1\) whenever it appears: \((2+3i)(1-i)=2-2i+3i-3i^{2}=2+i+3=5+i\).
  2. Modulus. \(|z|=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\) — the distance of \(z\) from \(0\) in the plane whose axes are the real and imaginary parts. It behaves like the absolute value: \(|zw|=|z|\,|w|\) and \(|z+w|\le|z|+|w|\). This is the \(|\cdot|\) that lets you write \(|\varphi_X(t)|\le1\).
  3. Euler's formula [Eulersche Formel]. For real \(t\), \[ e^{it}=\cos t+i\sin t . \] This is a definition-level fact you use as a rewriting rule: whenever a sum of \(e^{itx}\)-terms needs simplifying, expand it into cosine and sine.
  4. \(|e^{it}|=1\) for every real \(t\). Because \(|e^{it}|=\sqrt{\cos^{2}t+\sin^{2}t}=\sqrt{1}=1\), using the Pythagorean identity \(\cos^{2}+\sin^{2}=1\). Check at \(t=1.3\): \(|\cos 1.3+i\sin1.3|=1.0000000\) ✓. Consequence used constantly: \(|\varphi_X(t)|=|\E[e^{itX}]|\le\E[|e^{itX}|]=\E[1]=1\), so a characteristic function always exists and never exceeds \(1\) in modulus — no integrability condition is ever needed, unlike for moment-generating functions.
  5. Differentiating \(e^{ict}\) in \(t\). The real chain rule carries over unchanged, with the constant \(ic\) treated like any other constant: \[ \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}e^{ict}=ic\,e^{ict}. \] Check with \(c=2\) at \(t=0.4\): the numerical derivative is \(-1.434712+1.393413\,i\) and \(2i\,e^{0.8i}=-1.434712+1.393413\,i\) ✓. Repeating it gives \(\tfrac{\mathrm d^{n}}{\mathrm dt^{n}}e^{itx}=(ix)^{n}e^{itx}\), which at \(t=0\) is \((ix)^{n}\) — that is the whole content of "\(\E[X^{n}]=i^{-n}\varphi_X^{(n)}(0)\)" (Remark 2.47(iii)), the alternative route to means and variances that SoSe26 · P4 accepted for full marks.

The one limit the central limit theorem's proof uses Script 2.64, proof

\[ \text{if }z_n\to z\text{ in }\mathbb{C},\qquad\text{then}\qquad\Bigl(1+\frac{z_n}{n}\Bigr)^{n}\longrightarrow e^{z} \quad(n\to\infty). \]

Here \(\mathbb{C}\) is the set of complex numbers. This is the complex version of the real limit \((1+x/n)^{n}\to e^{x}\) from the three limits; the statement is the same and only the number system changed. Checks with \(z=i\): \((1+i/n)^{n}\) equals \(0.570790+0.882508\,i\) at \(n=10\), \(0.540573+0.841892\,i\) at \(n=1000\), \(0.540305+0.841475\,i\) at \(n=10^{5}\), converging to \(e^{i}=\cos1+i\sin1=0.540302+0.841471\,i\) ✓.

Where it is used. In the CLT proof the characteristic function of the standardised sum is \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t)=\bigl(\varphi_{X}(t/\sqrt n)\bigr)^{n}\), and a Taylor expansion (next section) turns the bracket into \(1-\frac{t^{2}}{2n}+o(1/n)\). Then the limit above with \(z_n=-\tfrac{t^{2}}2+n\cdot o(1/n)\to-\tfrac{t^{2}}{2}\) gives \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t)\to e^{-t^{2}/2}\), the characteristic function of \(\mathcal N(0,1)\).

A concrete instance you can check by hand — the one SoSe26 · P4b builds: if \(X_i=\pm1\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) each, then \(\varphi_{X}(t)=\tfrac12 e^{it}+\tfrac12e^{-it}=\cos t\) (Euler's formula, since the sine terms cancel), so \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t)=\cos^{n}(t/\sqrt n)\). At \(t=1\): \(0.601359\) for \(n=10\), \(0.606024\) for \(n=100\), \(0.606526\) for \(n=10^{4}\), \(0.606531\) for \(n=10^{6}\) — converging to \(e^{-1/2}=0.606531\) ✓.

Fuller treatment: Analysis 1.1 — Complex numbers [komplexe Zahlen] for the arithmetic, and B1 — calculus with complex-valued functions for the derivative rules and this limit written out with its proof, which your Analysis script states for real arguments only. In DPT: §2.3 — characteristic functions and §2.4 — the central limit theorem.

Taylor to second order and little-o

Near a point, a smooth function looks like a parabola. Taylor's formula to second order [Taylorformel] writes down that parabola and names the leftover. DPT uses exactly one instance of it, in the proof of the central limit theorem, so this section covers that one instance and stops.

The expansion, and what \(o(s^{2})\) means My addition

If \(f\) is twice differentiable at \(0\), then for \(s\) near \(0\)

\[ f(s)=f(0)+f'(0)\,s+\tfrac12 f''(0)\,s^{2}+o(s^{2}) . \]

Each piece: \(f(0)\) is the height at \(0\); \(f'(0)s\) tilts the line to the right slope; \(\tfrac12f''(0)s^{2}\) bends it to the right curvature; and \(o(s^{2})\) — read "little-o of \(s^{2}\)" [Landau-Symbol] — is a placeholder for whatever is left over.

In words, what \(o(s^{2})\) says: the leftover is so small that even after dividing it by \(s^{2}\) it still goes to \(0\) as \(s\to0\). Formally, \(r(s)=o(s^{2})\) means \(r(s)/s^{2}\to0\). It is not a specific function; it is a promise about size. You never compute an \(o(s^{2})\), you only carry it along and discard it at the end.

The three expansions that occur:

\[ e^{s}=1+s+\tfrac{s^{2}}2+o(s^{2}),\qquad \cos s=1-\tfrac{s^{2}}2+o(s^{2}),\qquad e^{is}=1+is-\tfrac{s^{2}}2+o(s^{2}) . \]

The third is the first with \(s\) replaced by \(is\), using \(i^{2}=-1\) in the square term: \(\tfrac{(is)^{2}}{2}=\tfrac{i^{2}s^{2}}{2}=-\tfrac{s^{2}}{2}\).

Watching the leftover shrink — a numeric example My addition

Take \(f(s)=\cos s\), whose expansion is \(1-s^{2}/2+o(s^{2})\). The table shows the true value, the parabola, the error, and — the column that matters — the error divided by \(s^{2}\).

\(s\)\(\cos s\)\(1-s^{2}/2\)errorerror\(/s^{2}\)
\(0.5\)\(0.8775826\)\(0.8750000\)\(2.58\cdot10^{-3}\)\(1.03\cdot10^{-2}\)
\(0.1\)\(0.9950042\)\(0.9950000\)\(4.17\cdot10^{-6}\)\(4.17\cdot10^{-4}\)
\(0.01\)\(0.9999500\)\(0.9999500\)\(4.17\cdot10^{-10}\)\(4.17\cdot10^{-6}\)

The last column is the point. It is not enough that the error shrinks — the error divided by \(s^{2}\) shrinks too, by a factor of about \(100\) each time \(s\) shrinks by \(10\). That is what "\(o(s^{2})\)" asserts.

Where DPT uses it: the one step of the CLT proof Script 2.64

Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be independent and identically distributed with \(\E[X_1]=0\) and \(\Var[X_1]=1\), and let \(Z_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\). Apply the expansion to \(f(t)=\varphi_{X_1}(t)\), whose first two derivatives at \(0\) are \(\varphi'(0)=i\,\E[X_1]=0\) and \(\varphi''(0)=i^{2}\E[X_1^{2}]=-1\):

\[ \varphi_{X_1}(s)=\underbrace{\varphi(0)}_{=\,1}+\underbrace{\varphi'(0)}_{=\,0}s +\tfrac12\underbrace{\varphi''(0)}_{=\,-1}s^{2}+o(s^{2}) =1-\frac{s^{2}}{2}+o(s^{2}) . \]

Put \(s=t/\sqrt n\), so \(s^{2}=t^{2}/n\), and raise to the \(n\)-th power (independence turns the sum into a product of characteristic functions):

\[ \varphi_{Z_n}(t)=\Bigl(\varphi_{X_1}\bigl(t/\sqrt n\bigr)\Bigr)^{n} =\Bigl(1-\frac{t^{2}}{2n}+o\bigl(\tfrac1n\bigr)\Bigr)^{n}\;\longrightarrow\;e^{-t^{2}/2} \]

by the limit \((1+z_n/n)^{n}\to e^{z}\) from the previous section. And \(e^{-t^{2}/2}\) is the characteristic function of \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), which by the continuity theorem gives \(Z_n\to\mathcal N(0,1)\) in distribution.

In words: the whole CLT proof is "expand to second order, discard the leftover, recognise the \(e\)-limit". The first moment drops out because the variables are centred, the second moment supplies the \(-t^{2}/2\), and every higher moment is swallowed by the \(o\). That is also why the theorem needs finite, non-zero variance and nothing more.

Fuller treatment: Analysis 6.1 — Landau symbols [Landau-Symbole] for \(o\) and \(O\), and Analysis 10.1 — Taylor's formula for the general expansion with its remainder term. In DPT: §2.3 and §2.4 — the central limit theorem; \(o(\cdot)\) as a symbol to read is in the notation table at the top of this page.

The cheat card

This is the part to reread the evening before the exam. Left column: the words that appear on the paper. Middle: the Analysis move those words demand. Then: where on this page it is written out, and where in DPT it is used. Every row is drawn from a task that actually appeared on one of the three past papers or on the eleven exercise sheets — the task-type codes TT1–TT15 are the ones used on the exam page.

Honesty note. Three past papers is a small sample, and the rows are weighted by what those three happened to ask. Read the table as "what has been asked", never as "what will be asked". The rows are ordered roughly by how often the move was needed, not by difficulty.

If the DPT task says … … the Analysis move is … … on this page … … and DPT uses it in
"Determine the constant \(c\) such that \(p\) is a density" Set \(\int p=1\) over the stated support only, pull \(c\) out by linearity, solve. Then add the line \(p\ge0\). Integration TT3; SoSe25 · P3a
"Compute the cdf \(F_X\)" Integrate the density from the left end of the support up to \(x\); write all three branches (\(0\) below, formula on, \(1\) above). Integration TT3; SoSe25 · P3b
"Compute \(\E[X]\)" for a density \(\int x\,p(x)\,\mathrm dx\) over the support; for \(x^{n}e^{-ax}\) read off \(n!/a^{n+1}\) instead of integrating. The integral table §2.1; SoSe25 · P3
"Compute \(\E[X]\)" for a pmf Sum a series: geometric \(\sum q^{k}=\frac1{1-q}\), exponential \(\sum\frac{\lambda^{k}}{k!}=e^{\lambda}\), index shift, telescoping. Series §1.2; every discrete mean
"Compute \(\E[X]\) or \(\Var[X]\) for \(\Geo(p)\) / \(\NegBin(r,p)\)" The differentiated geometric series \(\sum_{k\ge1}kq^{k-1}=\frac1{(1-q)^{2}}\) and \(\sum_{k\ge2}k(k-1)q^{k-2}=\frac2{(1-q)^{3}}\), with \(q=1-p\). Series §1.2; Lemma 2.26(v),(vi)
"Compute the characteristic function of \(\Poi(\lambda)\)" \((e^{it})^{k}=e^{ikt}\), then the exponential series with the complex argument \(\lambda e^{it}\): \(\varphi(t)=\exp(\lambda(e^{it}-1))\). Series §2.3; Sheet 8 Ex 1
"Compute \(\Var[X]\)" \(\E[X^{2}]-\E[X]^{2}\); the \(\E[X^{2}]\) integral is one row further down the same table (\(2/a^{3}\) for \(\Exp\)). The integral table TT6; §2.1
"Determine the median / the \(\alpha\)-quantile" Solve \(F(m)=\tfrac12\) — usually \(1-e^{-\lambda m}=\tfrac12\), so apply \(\ln\) and divide. Discard roots outside the support. Solving with \(\ln\) TT3; SoSe25 · P3c
… and the cdf is a quadratic, e.g. \((r+3)^{2}/15=0.05\) Complete the square with \(x^{2}+bx=(x+\tfrac b2)^{2}-\tfrac{b^{2}}4\), take \(x=-a\pm\sqrt c\), then keep the root inside the support and say why. Quadratic equations Sheet 5 Ex 1(iv),(v); Sheet 7 Ex 4(i)
"Compute the cdf" and the density has several pieces Each branch starts from the value already accumulated: \(F(r)=F(0)+\int_0^{r}p\). Check the branches agree where they meet, and that the last one ends at \(1\). Quadratic equations Sheet 5 Ex 1(ii)
"Derive the density of \(Y=g(X)\)" cdf route: \(\P(g(X)\le y)\), invert the inequality (flip if \(g\) decreases), then differentiate with the chain rule. The safe route when \(g\) is not monotone. Differentiation TT4; WiSe25 · P3a
"… with the hint \(p_Y(y)=p_X(g^{-1}(y))\bigl|\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dy}g^{-1}(y)\bigr|\)" Invert \(g\) algebraically, differentiate the inverse, take the absolute value, and map the old support through \(g\) — that last step is separately marked. Transformation formula TT4; SoSe25 · P3d, WiSe25 · P3a
"Determine the maximum likelihood estimator" \(\ln\) turns the product \(\prod p_\theta(x_i)\) into a sum; differentiate in \(\theta\); set \(=0\); solve. \(\ln\) rules, Differentiation TT5; §3.2
"Determine the mle" and the model has two parameters (\(\nabla_\theta\ell=0\)) Differentiate in each parameter with the other frozen (that is all \(\partial\) means), solve the first, substitute it into the second. Partial derivatives §3.2; script Ex 3.28 (Gaussian)
"Show that \(\hat\theta\) is indeed a maximum" \(\ell''(\hat\theta)<0\) for a local maximum; for a global one, show \(\ell'>0\) left of \(\hat\theta\) and \(\ell'<0\) right of it. Finding a maximum TT5; WiSe25 · P4a
"Bound \(\P(|Y-\E[Y]|\ge\varepsilon)\)" Chebyshev: compute \(\E[Y]\) and \(\Var[Y]\) as a labelled step, then divide by \(\varepsilon^{2}\) and simplify the algebra. Rearranging inequalities TT7; SoSe25 · P5c
"Bound \(\P(|Z|\ge a)\)" with Markov Square both sides first: \(|Z|\ge a\iff Z^{2}\ge a^{2}\) (both sides non-negative, so squaring preserves the inequality), then Markov on \(Z^{2}\). Rearranging inequalities TT7; SoSe26 · P4d
"How large must \(n\) be so that … \(\le0.05\)?" Set the bound equal to the budget, solve for \(n\), then round in the safe direction and say which direction that is and why. Rearranging inequalities TT7; §2.2
"Is the estimator asymptotically unbiased / consistent?" Take \(n\to\infty\) of the bias or the variance, using the limit rules and \(\tfrac1n\to0\). Limit rules TT6; §3.2
"Show \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\binom nk p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}=\dots\)" (Poisson limit) The \(e\)-limit \(\bigl(1-\tfrac\lambda n\bigr)^{n}\to e^{-\lambda}\), plus \(\tfrac{n!}{(n-k)!\,n^{k}}\to1\) for fixed \(k\). The three limits §1.2, Thm 1.42; Sheet 3 Ex 3
"Show that \(\sum_k p(k)=1\)" Recognise the geometric or exponential series; shift the index so it starts where the standard formula starts. Series §1.2; Sheets 2–4
"Show the memorylessness \(\P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=\P(X>t)\)" Split the exponential: \(e^{-\lambda(s+t)}=e^{-\lambda s}e^{-\lambda t}\), then cancel. \(\exp\) rules §1.4; Sheet 5
"Compute \(\int x\,e^{-\lambda x}\,\mathrm dx\)" (or any polynomial \(\times\) exponential) Integration by parts with \(u=\) the polynomial; the boundary term at \(\infty\) vanishes because \(\exp\) beats every power. By parts §2.1; TT3
"Compute \(\int x\,e^{-x^{2}/2}\,\mathrm dx\)" (function times its own derivative) Substitution \(u=x^{2}/2\), \(\mathrm du=x\,\mathrm dx\). Substitution §2.3; Sheet 8
Any integral of an odd function over a symmetric interval Write \(0\) and the word "odd". No computation. The integral table Sheet 6 Ex 3(ii); \(\E[\mathcal N(0,1)]=0\)
"Show \(\E[X]=\infty\)" / "does the integral converge?" The \(1/x^{p}\) test at \(\infty\): converges for \(p>1\), diverges for \(p\le1\). Improper integrals §2.1; the Cauchy distribution
"Compute \(\P(X\le Y)\)" for an independent pair Double integral over the triangle \(\{x\le y\}\): inner limits \(\int_x^{\infty}\), outer \(\int_0^{\infty}\). Double integrals Sheet 7 Ex 1; §2.3
"Determine the density of \(X+Y\)" / "of \(X/Y\)" Write the event as a region (half-plane \(\{x+y\le z\}\), wedge \(\{x\le ty\}\)), integrate the joint density over it, differentiate the result. Double integrals TT4; SoSe25 · P1d
"Determine the marginal density \(p_X\)" \(p_X(x)=\int p_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm dy\) over the slice of the region at that \(x\) — for a disc that is \(y\in[-\sqrt{R^{2}-x^{2}},+\sqrt{R^{2}-x^{2}}]\), not polar coordinates. State for which \(x\) the answer is non-zero. Marginal densities Sheet 5 Ex 3, Sheet 7 Ex 1, Sheet 8 Ex 3(i); Thm 1.68
A joint density written with a product of indicators \(\chi_A(x,y)\chi_{\R_{\ge0}}(y)\) All conditions must hold at once: intersect them and read the limits off. A product \(\prod_i\chi_{[0,\theta]}(x_i)\) collapses to \(\theta\ge\max_i x_i\). Integrate over the support Sheet 7 Ex 1 & 2(ii), Sheet 10 Ex 1(i)
"Compute \(\int x^{2}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\,\mathrm dx\)" (a \(\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) anywhere) Substitute \(x=\sin u\), \(\mathrm dx=\cos u\,\mathrm du\), \(\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}u}=\cos u\); then \(2\sin u\cos u=\sin 2u\) and \(\sin^{2}v=\tfrac12-\tfrac12\cos 2v\). Trig substitution Sheet 8 Ex 3(ii); §2.1
An integrand that is a function's derivative over the function \(\int\frac{f'}{f}\mathrm dx=\ln|f|+C\); fix the constant with a known value such as \(f(0)=1\). \(\int f'/f\) Sheet 5 Ex 2, the "\(\Leftarrow\)" half; §1.4
A \(\Gamma(\alpha,\beta)\) or \(\chi^{2}\) mean, or \(\E[1/Y]\) The recursion \(\Gamma(\alpha+1)=\alpha\Gamma(\alpha)\) reduces every such integral to \(\Gamma(\alpha)\): \(\E[Y]=\alpha/\beta\), \(\E[1/Y]=\beta/(\alpha-1)\). The integral table Sheet 10 Ex 2(iii); Lemma 2.27(iii),(v)
"State Jensen's inequality" / "show \(g\) is convex" \(g''\ge0\) on the interval, then one sentence naming function, sign and interval. Convexity TT2 (model answer); SoSe26 · P3a,b
"Show \(\E[X]^{2}\le\E[X^{2}]\)" Jensen with \(g(x)=x^{2}\), convex because \(g''=2>0\) on all of \(\R\). Convexity §2.2; Sheet 10 Ex 4(ii)
"Compute the characteristic function \(\varphi_X(t)\)" Sum \(\sum e^{itx}p(x)\), then Euler: \(e^{iu}=\cos u+i\sin u\); use \(|e^{it}|=1\) for bounds. Complex numbers TT12; SoSe26 · P4a
"Show \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t)\to e^{-t^{2}/2}\)" Taylor to second order, then the limit \(\bigl(1+\tfrac{z_n}{n}\bigr)^{n}\to e^{z}\). Taylor §2.4; SoSe26 · P4b
"Read off a moment from \(\varphi_X\)" \(\E[X^{n}]=i^{-n}\varphi^{(n)}(0)\); differentiate with \((\sin)'=\cos\), \((\cos)'=-\sin\), \((e^{ict})'=ic\,e^{ict}\). Differentiation SoSe26 · P4c; §2.3, Rem 2.47(iii)
"Give the answer in terms of \(\Phi\)", "\(\P(|Z|\ge a)\approx\dots\)" Stop integrating. Standardise inside the bars, then fold with \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\): \(\P(|Z|\ge a)=2(1-\Phi(a))=2\Phi(-a)\). Standardise and fold TT8; WiSe25 · P4c, SoSe26 · P4d
"\(\sup\)", "\(\inf\)", "\(A_n\uparrow A\)", "\(\lceil x\rceil\)" Read the symbol, do not compute anything: least upper bound, greatest lower bound, an increasing set sequence, rounding up. Notation, sup and inf §1.1; §3.3, the size of a test

What Analysis gives you and what it does not

Almost everything on this page is in your Analysis script somewhere, and the "fuller treatment" line at the end of each section points at it. Five things are not, and no amount of rereading Analysis will produce them. Page B1 works through the evidence item by item (B1 — what Analysis does not give you); this is the short list.

TopicIn your Analysis guide?Where to read it instead
Limits, series, \(\exp\), \(\ln\), derivatives, one-variable integrals, improper integrals, substitution, by parts, convexity, Taylor, Landau \(o\), complex arithmetic and Euler Yes, all of it Chapters 1–3, 5–10 — every section above links the exact anchor
Measure theory: \(\sigma\)-algebras, measures, the Lebesgue integral, null sets, monotone and dominated convergence, Fubini No — it builds the Riemann integral only B4, the largest background page; needed from Definition 1.17 onwards
Counting: permutations, \(\binom nk\) as a count, urn models, inclusion–exclusion No — \(\binom nk\) appears once, inside the binomial theorem, and nothing is ever counted B3; this is Discrete Structures material
Set algebra for arbitrary index families: \(\bigcup_{\alpha\in I}\), de Morgan, power sets, pre-images No B2
Double integrals and the multi-dimensional change of variables with \(|\det J|\); determinants and matrix inverses Partly — the Jacobian matrix is defined (Ch. 11.3), the integral formula is not B4 for regions and slices, B5 for \(|\det J|\); the fast version is above on this page
Calculus with complex-valued functions; \((1+z_n/n)^{n}\to e^{z}\) for complex \(z_n\); differentiating under an improper integral Partly — complex numbers and Euler are there, the calculus is stated for real functions B1 — complex-valued calculus and B1 — the Leibniz rule

Practical consequence for a week of revision: the Analysis on this page is recall work — you have seen it and need it back. B2–B5 are new work. If time is short, the ordering that pays is this page first (it unlocks the credits in Problems 3–5), then B3 counting (it unlocks Problem 1 and the discrete distributions), then the vocabulary half of B4 — enough to read \(\sigma\)-algebra, measurable and density without stopping.

How to read this page

You do not need to read this page top to bottom. It is a lookup page. Start with the prerequisite map just below: for every section of the course it lists what you must already know and where to learn it. When a probability page says "by monotone convergence" or "because the series converges absolutely" and you want the underlying statement, come here, find the row, and follow the link.

The last column says why this course needs it — which definition, theorem or exercise would stop working without it. That is the part worth skimming once, because it tells you which bits of Analysis are load-bearing for this course and which are not needed at all.

Three topics that the course uses but your Analysis guide does not treat fully are written out at the end of this page: interior and open sets, differentiating an integral and complex numbers for characteristic functions.

What from Analysis this course does not use

Worth knowing, so you do not revise the wrong things:

  • Differential equations (Analysis Ch. 12) — the largest chapter of your Analysis guide, and not used anywhere in Discrete Probability Theory.
  • Curve sketching (Ch. 7.7) and the mean value theorem as such.
  • Radius of convergence (Ch. 10.2) — power series appear here only as the two named series \(e^x\) and \(\ln(1+x)\), never as objects to analyse.
  • n-th roots via the intermediate value theorem (Ch. 4.2).
  • l'Hospital's rule (Ch. 7.4) — I searched the script, all twelve exercise sheets and the three old exams: it is never used, and no limit in this course needs it.

Two things that look skippable but are not. Each is used exactly once, so do not revise them in depth — but do know they exist: the Cauchy product (Ch. 3.3) justifies multiplying \(r\) geometric series when checking that the negative binomial pmf sums to 1 (Example 1.39(v)), and differentiating an integral with respect to a parameter (Ch. 9.2, extended below) is the "Leibniz integral rule" of Remark 2.22(v).
