Five facts from Analysis you will use every week

These come up so often that it is worth having them stated here, so you do not have to leave the page. Each links back to the full treatment.

1. Monotone bounded sequences converge Analysis 2.2

If \(x_1\le x_2\le\cdots\) and there is a \(C\) with \(x_n\le C\) for all \(n\), then \(\lim_n x_n\) exists and equals \(\sup_n x_n\) (the supremum, fact 5 below). Same downwards, with the infimum.

Example: \(x_n=1-\tfrac1n\) gives \(0,\tfrac12,\tfrac23,\tfrac34,\dots\). It increases and stays below \(C=1\), so it converges; its limit is \(1=\sup_nx_n\). Notation: \(x_n\uparrow x\) means "\(x_n\) increases and converges to \(x\)"; \(x_n\downarrow x\) means "decreases and converges to \(x\)".

Here: this is what makes \(\mu(A_k)\uparrow\mu(\bigcup_i A_i)\) in Proposition 1.19(iv) a statement about a real limit rather than a formal symbol. Full treatment →

2. Geometric series Analysis 3.1

For \(|q|<1\): \(\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}q^{j}=\frac{1}{1-q}\), and the partial sums are \(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^j=\frac{1-q^n}{1-q}\). For \(|q|\ge1\) the series diverges. Example: \(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\tfrac18+\dots=\frac1{1-1/2}=2\).

Here: \(\sum_{\omega\ge1}(1-p)^{\omega-1}p=1\), which is why the geometric pmf is a pmf. Full treatment →

3. The exponential series and \(e\) as a limit Analysis 2.2, 3.4

\(\displaystyle e^{x}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{k}}{k!}\) for every real \(x\), and \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\Bigl(1+\frac{x}{n}\Bigr)^{n}=e^{x}\). Here \(k!=1\cdot2\cdots k\) (with \(0!=1\)). Example with \(x=1\): \(1+1+\tfrac12+\tfrac16+\tfrac1{24}\approx2.708\), already close to \(e\approx2.718\); and \((1+\tfrac1{10})^{10}\approx2.594\), approaching \(e\) more slowly.

Here: the first gives \(\sum_\omega e^{-\lambda}\lambda^\omega/\omega!=1\) for the Poisson pmf and \(e^{-1}\) for derangements; the second is the engine of the Poisson limit theorem. the limit for general \(x\) (Lemma 6.24) → · \(x=1\), the definition of \(e\) → · the series →. For a varying \(x_n\to x\), also complex, see below.

4. Absolute convergence licenses rearrangement Analysis 3.3

If \(\sum_k|a_k|<\infty\), then every reordering of \(\sum_k a_k\) converges to the same value — and you may also group the terms into blocks freely. If the series converges but not absolutely, Riemann showed you can rearrange it to converge to any number you like. Example: \(1-\tfrac12+\tfrac13-\tfrac14+\dots\) converges (to \(\ln2\)) but not absolutely, because \(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac13+\dots=\infty\); so its value depends on the order of the terms.

Here: a pmf has non-negative terms summing to 1, so it converges absolutely, and that is the licence for splitting \(\sum_{\omega\in\bigcup_i A_i}p(\omega)=\sum_i\sum_{\omega\in A_i}p(\omega)\) in Lemma 1.35. Without non-negativity the proof collapses. Full treatment →

5. Supremum: the recipe Analysis 1.2

The supremum [Supremum] \(\sup M\) of a set \(M\) of real numbers is its least upper bound: the smallest number that is \(\ge\) every element of \(M\). The infimum [Infimum] \(\inf M\) is the greatest lower bound. Unlike a maximum or minimum, they need not belong to \(M\).

To show \(s=\sup M\): (1) \(a\le s\) for all \(a\in M\) (\(s\) is an upper bound); (2) for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an \(a\in M\) with \(a>s-\varepsilon\) (nothing smaller is an upper bound). Then check whether \(s\in M\) to decide if it is also the maximum.

Example: \(M=\{1-\tfrac1n\mid n\ge1\}=\{0,\tfrac12,\tfrac23,\dots\}\). (1) Every element is \(\le1\). (2) Given \(\varepsilon>0\), pick \(n>\tfrac1\varepsilon\); then \(1-\tfrac1n>1-\varepsilon\). So \(\sup M=1\). But \(1\notin M\), so \(M\) has no maximum. On the other side, \(\inf M=\min M=0\).

Here: Sheet 2 Exercise 1(iii). And the fact that \(\sup\) of an increasing sequence is its limit is what makes the counterexample there work. Full treatment →

One notation clash to keep straight My addition

Your Analysis script says \(0\notin\N\): it writes \(\N=\{1,2,3,\dots\}\) and \(\N_0=\N\cup\{0\}\). The Discrete Probability script says the opposite in Convention 1.1: \(\N=\{0,1,2,\dots\}\), and writes \(\N_{>0}\) when it wants to exclude zero.

So the same symbol means different sets in your two courses. When a probability statement says "for a sequence \((A_i)_{i\in\N}\)", the sequence starts at \(A_0\). When Analysis says "\(\forall n\in\N\)", it starts at 1. This bites most often in index shifts inside sums — renaming the summation index, e.g. \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_{n-1}=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}a_m\) with \(m=n-1\); a worked explanation is on B3.

Interior points, open and closed sets My addition

What it is for. Many statements in this course only work "away from the edge" of a set. The clearest case is maximum likelihood: Definition 3.27 says the likelihood equation \(\nabla_\theta\ell=0\) finds the maximiser if the maximum is in the interior of \(\Theta\). The words interior, boundary, open and closed make "away from the edge" precise. Your Analysis guide defines closed and compact sets (Analysis 4.4) and the norms that measure distance in \(\R^k\) (Analysis 1.3), and it uses the phrase "interior point" for a point of an open interval (Analysis 7.1) — but it never defines the interior, nor an open subset of \(\R^k\). Here it is.

A picture first. Take the interval \([0,1]\) on the number line. The point \(0.5\) is surrounded by points of \([0,1]\) on both sides: you can wiggle it a little (say by \(0.1\)) in either direction and stay inside. The point \(0\) is different: every step to the left, however small, leaves the interval. \(0.5\) is an interior point; \(0\) is a boundary point.

Definitions

Let \(A\subseteq\R^k\) (for \(k=1\), a subset of the number line). Write \(B_r(x):=\{y\in\R^k\mid\|y-x\|<r\}\) for the open ball of radius \(r>0\) around \(x\): all points at (Euclidean) distance less than \(r\) from \(x\). For \(k=1\) this is just the interval \((x-r,x+r)\).

  • \(x\) is an interior point [innerer Punkt] of \(A\) if some ball around \(x\) lies completely inside \(A\): there is an \(r>0\) with \(B_r(x)\subseteq A\). The set of all interior points is the interior [Inneres] of \(A\), written \(A^\circ\) or \(\operatorname{int}A\).
  • \(x\) is a boundary point [Randpunkt] of \(A\) if every ball around \(x\) contains points of \(A\) and points outside \(A\). The set of boundary points is the boundary \(\partial A\).
  • \(A\) is open [offen] if every point of \(A\) is an interior point, i.e. \(A=A^\circ\).
  • \(A\) is closed [abgeschlossen] if its complement \(\R^k\setminus A\) is open. Equivalently (this is the definition in Analysis 4.4): limits of convergent sequences in \(A\) stay in \(A\). A closed set contains its whole boundary.

Examples with numbers

  • \(A=[0,1]\). For \(x=0.3\) take \(r=0.3\): then \(B_{0.3}(0.3)=(0,0.6)\subseteq[0,1]\), so \(0.3\) is interior. In general for \(0<x<1\) take \(r=\min(x,1-x)\), the distance to the nearer end. For \(x=0\), every ball \((-r,r)\) contains \(-r/2\notin A\) and \(0\in A\), so \(0\) is a boundary point; the same for \(1\). Hence \([0,1]^\circ=(0,1)\) and \(\partial[0,1]=\{0,1\}\). \([0,1]\) is closed, not open.
  • \(A=(0,1)\) is open: its interior is itself. It is not closed: \(\tfrac1n\in(0,1)\) but \(\tfrac1n\to0\notin(0,1)\).
  • \(A=(0,\infty)\) (e.g. the possible values of a variance \(\sigma^2\)): open, since for \(x>0\) the ball \((x/2,\,3x/2)\) stays positive.
  • In \(\R^2\): the parameter set \(\Theta=\R\times(0,\infty)\) of the Gaussian \((\mu,\sigma^2)\) is open — around any \((\mu,\sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma^2>0\), the disc of radius \(\sigma^2/2\) keeps the second coordinate positive. So every point is interior.
  • A set can be neither open nor closed: \([0,1)\).

Why "interior" matters for maximum likelihood

At an interior maximum \(x_0\) of a differentiable \(f\) you can move a little both left and right. Moving right cannot increase \(f\), so \(f'(x_0)\le0\); moving left cannot either, so \(f'(x_0)\ge0\); together \(f'(x_0)=0\) (Analysis 7.1). At a boundary point you can only move one way, and the argument breaks. Example: three coin tosses, all heads, Bernoulli model with \(\Theta=[0,1]\). The likelihood is \(L(p)=p^3\), largest at \(p=1\) — a boundary point — where \(L'(1)=3\neq0\). Solving \(L'(p)=0\) would give \(p=0\), the minimum. So: always check whether the maximiser can sit on the boundary of \(\Theta\) before solving the likelihood equation. Used in §3.2, Definition 3.27.

The same words appear in Remark 1.14 (the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra is generated by the open sets) and in Sheet 2 Exercise 5.

In words: an interior point has some room around it inside the set; a boundary point touches the outside no matter how closely you look. Open sets consist only of interior points; closed sets contain their whole boundary.

Differentiating an integral with respect to a parameter My addition

What it is for. Sometimes the thing you want to differentiate is itself an integral that depends on a number \(c\) — through its limits, through the integrand, or both. This happens in Remark 2.22(v) (the median minimises \(\E|X-c|\); the script says "using Leibniz integral rule"), in Lemma 1.49 (a pdf is the derivative of the cdf), and in Remark 2.47(iii) (moments from derivatives of the characteristic function). Your Analysis guide covers the two basic cases separately (Analysis 8.3 — FTC and Analysis 9.2 — parameter integrals); this section puts them together.

Case 1 — the parameter is the upper limit: the fundamental theorem

If \(f\) is continuous and \(F(c):=\int_a^c f(x)\,\mathrm dx\), then \(F'(c)=f(c)\). Picture: moving the right edge from \(c\) to \(c+h\) adds a thin strip of width \(h\) and height about \(f(c)\), so the area grows at rate \(f(c)\). Numbers: \(F(c)=\int_0^cx^2\,\mathrm dx=\tfrac{c^3}{3}\), and indeed \(F'(c)=c^2=f(c)\).

Lower limit: \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dc}\int_c^bf(x)\,\mathrm dx=-f(c)\), because \(\int_c^b=\int_a^b-\int_a^c\) and the first part does not depend on \(c\). A function as the limit: by the chain rule, \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dc}\int_a^{h(c)}f(x)\,\mathrm dx=f(h(c))\,h'(c)\). The same holds with \(a=-\infty\) when the improper integral converges: \(\int_{-\infty}^c=\int_{-\infty}^{a}+\int_a^c\), and the first part is a constant.

In probability: the cdf \(F(c)=\int_{-\infty}^cp(x)\,\mathrm dx\) has \(F'(c)=p(c)\) wherever \(p\) is continuous at \(c\).

Case 2 — the parameter sits inside the integrand, limits fixed

If \(f(x,c)\) and its partial derivative \(\partial_cf(x,c)\) (differentiate in \(c\), treating \(x\) as a constant) are continuous on \([a,b]\times[c_1,c_2]\), then

\[ \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dc}\int_a^bf(x,c)\,\mathrm dx=\int_a^b\partial_cf(x,c)\,\mathrm dx \]

(Analysis 9.2, Satz 9.8). Numbers: \(\int_0^1 e^{cx}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{e^c-1}{c}\) for \(c\neq0\); differentiating under the integral gives \(\int_0^1xe^{cx}\,\mathrm dx\), which at \(c=1\) is \(\bigl[(x-1)e^x\bigr]_0^1=1\); differentiating the formula gives \(\frac{ce^c-(e^c-1)}{c^2}\), which at \(c=1\) is \(e-e+1=1\) ✓.

Case 3 — both at once: the Leibniz rule

\[ \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dc}\int_a^{c}f(x,c)\,\mathrm dx=f(c,c)+\int_a^{c}\partial_cf(x,c)\,\mathrm dx . \]

The first term is Case 1 (the edge moves), the second is Case 2 (the height changes). Check: \(G(c)=\int_0^c(c-x)\,\mathrm dx=\tfrac{c^2}{2}\), so \(G'(c)=c\). The rule gives \(f(c,c)=c-c=0\) plus \(\int_0^c1\,\mathrm dx=c\) ✓.

The median minimises \(\E|X-c|\) (Remark 2.22(v)), without the Leibniz rule

Let \(X\) have a continuous pdf \(p\), cdf \(F\), and \(\E|X|<\infty\). Split at \(c\) and pull \(c\) out of each integral (it is a constant for the integration variable \(x\)):

\[ g(c):=\E|X-c|=\int_{-\infty}^{c}(c-x)p(x)\,\mathrm dx+\int_{c}^{\infty}(x-c)p(x)\,\mathrm dx =cF(c)-\int_{-\infty}^{c}xp(x)\,\mathrm dx+\int_{c}^{\infty}xp(x)\,\mathrm dx-c\bigl(1-F(c)\bigr), \]

using \(\int_{-\infty}^cp=F(c)\) and \(\int_c^\infty p=1-F(c)\). Now only Case 1 and the product rule are needed: \(\bigl(cF(c)\bigr)'=F(c)+cp(c)\); \(\bigl(\int_{-\infty}^cxp\bigr)'=cp(c)\); \(\bigl(\int_c^\infty xp\bigr)'=-cp(c)\); \(\bigl(c(1-F(c))\bigr)'=(1-F(c))-cp(c)\). Adding with the signs above, the four \(cp(c)\) terms cancel:

\[ g'(c)=F(c)-\bigl(1-F(c)\bigr)=2F(c)-1 . \]

So \(g'(c)=0\iff F(c)=\tfrac12\): \(c\) is a median. And \(g'<0\) to the left, \(g'>0\) to the right, so it is a minimum. Numbers: for \(X\sim\Unif(0,1)\) and \(0\le c\le1\), \(g(c)=\tfrac{c^2}2+\tfrac{(1-c)^2}{2}\), \(g'(c)=2c-1=2F(c)-1\) ✓, minimum at \(c=\tfrac12\).

When may you differentiate under an improper integral or an expectation?

Analysis 9.2 needs a bounded rectangle. For \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\) or \(\E[\cdot]\) the standard sufficient condition is a dominating function: if \(|\partial_tf(x,t)|\le g(x)\) for all \(t\) near the point of interest, with \(\int g<\infty\), then you may swap \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\) and \(\int\). This comes from the dominated convergence theorem (B4). Example: \(\varphi_X(t)=\E[e^{itX}]\). Here \(\partial_te^{itx}=ixe^{itx}\) and \(|ixe^{itx}|=|x|\), so if \(\E|X|<\infty\) then \(\varphi_X'(t)=\E[iXe^{itX}]\) and \(\varphi_X'(0)=i\,\E[X]\) — Remark 2.47(iii) with \(n=1\). (Complex derivatives: next section.) The script itself, in Remark 2.22(v), writes "assuming we can interchange differentiation and expectation" and does not ask you to check it; Remark 2.47(iii) adds no condition either.

In words: moving the edge of an integral changes it by the height at the edge; changing the integrand changes it by the integral of the change; if both happen, add the two effects.

Complex numbers: what this course needs My addition

What it is for. Characteristic functions (§2.3) are \(\varphi_X(t)=\E[e^{itX}]\): complex-valued functions of a real \(t\). The central limit theorem (§2.4) is proved with them. You need five facts; the first three are in your Analysis guide (Analysis 1.1 — complex numbers, 3.4 — exp on \(\mathbb C\), 5.3 — Euler's formula), the last two are not.

1. Complex numbers, modulus, conjugate

A complex number is \(z=a+ib\) with real \(a\) (real part, \(\operatorname{Re}z\)) and real \(b\) (imaginary part, \(\operatorname{Im}z\)), where \(i^2=-1\). Picture it as the point \((a,b)\) in the plane. Its modulus [Betrag] \(|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) is the distance from \(0\); its conjugate \(\bar z=a-ib\) is the mirror image in the horizontal axis, and \(z\bar z=a^2+b^2=|z|^2\). Numbers: \(z=3+4i\) has \(|z|=\sqrt{9+16}=5\), \(\bar z=3-4i\), \(z\bar z=9+16=25\). Rules: \(|zw|=|z||w|\) and the triangle inequality \(|z+w|\le|z|+|w|\).

2. Euler's formula and the unit circle

For real \(t\): \(e^{it}=\cos t+i\sin t\). So \(e^{it}\) is the point \((\cos t,\sin t)\), reached by walking an arc of length \(t\) counter-clockwise around the circle of radius 1. Hence \(|e^{it}|=\sqrt{\cos^2t+\sin^2t}=1\). Numbers: \(e^{i\pi/2}=0+i\cdot1=i\), \(e^{i\pi}=-1\), \(e^{2\pi i}=1\).

3. The exponential function on \(\mathbb C\)

\(e^z=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{z^k}{k!}\) converges for every complex \(z\), and \(e^{w+z}=e^we^z\) still holds. So \(e^{it}e^{is}=e^{i(t+s)}\), and a series like \(\sum_k\frac{(\lambda e^{it})^k}{k!}\) equals \(\exp(\lambda e^{it})\) — the key step in computing the characteristic function of \(\Poi(\lambda)\), which comes out as \(e^{-\lambda}\exp(\lambda e^{it})=\exp\bigl(\lambda(e^{it}-1)\bigr)\). Also \(|e^{a+ib}|=e^{a}\,|e^{ib}|=e^a\), and \(\exp\) is continuous on \(\mathbb C\).

4. Differentiating a complex-valued function of a real variable

Write \(f(t)=u(t)+iv(t)\) with real \(u=\operatorname{Re}f\), \(v=\operatorname{Im}f\). Then \(f'(t):=u'(t)+iv'(t)\): differentiate the real and imaginary parts separately. The usual rules (sum, product, chain rule with a real inner function) remain true — multiply out into real and imaginary parts and apply the real rules to each. Key example: for real \(c\),

\[ \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}e^{ict}=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\bigl(\cos(ct)+i\sin(ct)\bigr) =-c\sin(ct)+ic\cos(ct)=ic\bigl(\cos(ct)+i\sin(ct)\bigr)=ic\,e^{ict}, \]

using \(i\cdot i=-1\) in the third step. So the familiar rule \((e^{ct})'=ce^{ct}\) survives with \(ic\) in place of \(c\). Repeating: \(\frac{\mathrm d^n}{\mathrm dt^n}e^{itx}=(ix)^ne^{itx}\), which at \(t=0\) is \(i^nx^n\) — the source of \(\E[X^n]=i^{-n}\varphi^{(n)}_X(0)\) in Remark 2.47(iii). Taylor works the same way (apply it to \(u\) and \(v\)): \(e^{it}=1+it-\tfrac{t^2}{2}+o(t^2)\) as \(t\to0\), where \(o(t^2)\) means "divided by \(t^2\), it tends to 0" (Analysis 6.1, 10.1). Numbers: \(t=0.1\): \(e^{0.1i}=\cos0.1+i\sin0.1\approx 0.99500+0.09983i\), and \(1+0.1i-0.005=0.995+0.1i\) — already very close.

5. \((1+z_n/n)^n\to e^z\) for complex \(z_n\to z\)

The CLT proof (step (vi), §2.4) ends with \(\bigl(1-\tfrac{t^2}{2n}+o(\tfrac1n)\bigr)^n\to e^{-t^2/2}\), and the \(o\)-term may be complex. The real version \((1+\tfrac xn)^n\to e^x\) for fixed real \(x\) is Analysis 6.3, Lemma 6.24, proved with logarithms — which does not carry over to complex numbers. Here is a proof that does. Claim: if \(z_n\in\mathbb C\) and \(z_n\to z\), then \((1+\tfrac{z_n}{n})^n\to e^z\).

Proof supplied by me — the script only cites the real limit

Tool (telescoping). For complex \(a,b\): \(a^n-b^n=(a-b)(a^{n-1}+a^{n-2}b+\dots+b^{n-1})\) (multiply out: everything cancels except \(a^n\) and \(-b^n\)). The bracket has \(n\) terms, each of modulus at most \(m^{n-1}\) with \(m:=\max(|a|,|b|)\), so \(|a^n-b^n|\le n\,|a-b|\,m^{n-1}\).

Choose \(w:=\tfrac{z_n}{n}\), \(a:=1+w\), \(b:=e^{w}\). Then \(b^n=e^{nw}=e^{z_n}\) by the functional equation. A convergent sequence is bounded, so there is \(M\) with \(|z_n|\le M\) for all \(n\), hence \(|w|\le M/n\).

Bound \(m\). \(|a|\le1+|w|\le e^{|w|}\) (since \(e^s=1+s+\tfrac{s^2}2+\dots\ge1+s\) for \(s\ge0\)), and \(|b|=e^{\operatorname{Re}w}\le e^{|w|}\). So \(m^{n-1}\le e^{(n-1)|w|}\le e^{M}\).

Bound \(|a-b|\). \(b-a=e^w-1-w=\sum_{k\ge2}\frac{w^k}{k!}\), so \(|a-b|\le\sum_{k\ge2}\frac{|w|^k}{k!}=|w|^2\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{|w|^j}{(j+2)!}\le|w|^2e^{|w|}\le\frac{M^2}{n^2}e^{M}\).

Combine. \(\bigl|(1+\tfrac{z_n}n)^n-e^{z_n}\bigr|\le n\cdot\frac{M^2e^M}{n^2}\cdot e^M =\frac{M^2e^{2M}}{n}\to0\). And \(e^{z_n}\to e^z\) because \(\exp\) is continuous. By the triangle inequality, \(\bigl|(1+\tfrac{z_n}n)^n-e^z\bigr|\le\bigl|(1+\tfrac{z_n}n)^n-e^{z_n}\bigr|+|e^{z_n}-e^z|\to0\). ∎

Applied to the CLT: \(1-\tfrac{t^2}{2n}+o(\tfrac1n)=1+\tfrac{z_n}{n}\) with \(z_n=-\tfrac{t^2}{2}+n\cdot o(\tfrac1n)\to-\tfrac{t^2}{2}\), so the limit is \(e^{-t^2/2}\). Numbers (real case): \((1-\tfrac{1}{2\cdot100})^{100}\approx0.6058\), and \(e^{-1/2}\approx0.6065\).

In words: complex numbers are points in the plane; \(e^{it}\) walks around the unit circle; you differentiate a complex function by differentiating its two real coordinates; and "\((1+\text{something}/n)^n\to e^{\text{limit of something}}\)" stays true for complex somethings.

Background · B2 · assumed by §1.1

Sets, families and countability

Mengen, Familien, Abzählbarkeit

Why this page exists My addition

Definition 1.2 of the script says: "we generally assume familiarity with common concepts and notation from set theory — this is a short reminder". It then points to its Appendix A.1. That appendix is a list of bare definitions with no examples. You can read it on its own page: the script's own appendix A.1. This page explains every concept of that appendix again, slowly and with numbers, and adds what the appendix leaves out.

Your Analysis guide Chapter 1 covers quantifiers, countability and the number systems. It does not cover set algebra: unions over an arbitrary index set, de Morgan's laws, power sets and pre-images. This page fills that gap. It also covers the distributive laws for families of sets, the pre-image of a composition \(g\circ X\), and why \(\pow(\N)\) is uncountable (countability).

Everything here is used on the §1.1 page. If you can answer the self-test at the bottom, you have what §1.1 assumes.

The big picture

A probability space has three parts. There is a set \(\Omega\) (Greek capital omega) of all possible outcomes. There is a collection \(\Aa\) (a curly A) of subsets of \(\Omega\), the events. And there is a function \(\P\) that gives each event in \(\Aa\) a probability.

So the objects of this course live on three different levels. Take one roll of a die:

  • Elements: an outcome, such as \(3\). It lies in \(\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\).
  • Sets of elements: an event, such as "even" \(=\{2,4,6\}\). It is a subset of \(\Omega\).
  • Sets of sets: a collection of events, such as \(\Aa=\bigl\{\emptyset,\{2,4,6\},\{1,3,5\},\Omega\bigr\}\). Its members are themselves sets.

Nearly every confusion in Chapter 1 is a mix-up between these levels. This page makes the levels automatic.

In words: Chapter 1 is not hard because the ideas are deep. It is hard because the objects are stacked three deep and the notation does not warn you when you slip a level.

Sets, elements, subsets

The vocabulary Script A.1

A set [Menge] is a collection of distinct objects. The objects are its elements [Elemente]. We write \(x\in A\) for "\(x\) is an element of \(A\)" and \(x\notin A\) for "\(x\) is not an element of \(A\)".

There are two ways to write a set down.

  • By listing: \(\{1,2,3\}\), or \(\{a,b,\dots,*,\odot\}\) — the elements between curly brackets. The order and repetitions do not matter: \(\{1,2\}=\{2,1\}=\{1,1,2\}\). A set with exactly one element, \(\{x\}\), is a singleton.
  • By a property: \(\{x\in\R \mid x^2<2\}\), read "the set of all \(x\) in \(\R\) such that \(x^2<2\)". Here \(\R\) is the set of real numbers and the bar \(\mid\) means "such that".

Subset [Teilmenge]. \(A\subseteq B\) means: every element of \(A\) is also in \(B\). In symbols, \(\forall x\in A: x\in B\), where \(\forall\) means "for all". We then also call \(B\) a superset of \(A\) and write \(B\supseteq A\). Example: \(\{1,2\}\subseteq\{1,2,3\}\). Also \(\{1,2\}\subseteq\{1,2\}\): a set is allowed to equal the other one.

Proper subset [echte Teilmenge]. \(A\subsetneq B\) means \(A\subseteq B\) and \(A\ne B\): \(B\) has at least one extra element. Example: \(\{1,2\}\subsetneq\{1,2,3\}\), but \(\{1,2\}\) is not a proper subset of \(\{1,2\}\).

A warning about \(\subset\). Definition 1.2 says the script uses \(\subseteq\) for "subset, equality allowed" and \(\subsetneq\) for "proper subset", tries to avoid the bare symbol \(\subset\) altogether, and adds that where \(\subset\) does slip in it "probably" means \(\subseteq\) — and asks you to point it out. The exercise sheets do slip: Sheet 0 Exercise 5 writes \(K\subset\{1,\dots,52\}\) and Sheet 3 Exercise 3 writes \((p_n)_{n\in\N}\subset[0,1]\), both meaning \(\subseteq\). Read \(\subset\) as \(\subseteq\) unless the text insists on \(A\ne B\).

Equality. \(A=B\) means \(A\subseteq B\) and \(B\subseteq A\): the two sets have exactly the same elements.

Two rules for \(\subseteq\). It is reflexive: \(A\subseteq A\) for every set \(A\). It is transitive: if \(A\subseteq B\) and \(B\subseteq C\), then \(A\subseteq C\). Example: \(\{1\}\subseteq\{1,2\}\) and \(\{1,2\}\subseteq\{1,2,3\}\) give \(\{1\}\subseteq\{1,2,3\}\).

Empty set. \(\emptyset\) is the set with no elements. It is a subset of every set \(B\). The reason: the statement "\(\forall x\in\emptyset: x\in B\)" has nothing to check, so it is true.

The single most important technique: proving \(A = B\) My addition

Two sets are equal exactly when each contains the other (\(\Longleftrightarrow\) means "exactly when", or "if and only if"):

\[ A = B \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A\subseteq B \ \text{ and } \ B\subseteq A. \]

So every proof that two sets are equal has two halves. Both halves have the same shape: take an arbitrary element of the left side and show that it lies in the right side. "Arbitrary" means you assume nothing about the element except that it lies in the left side. That is why the argument covers every element at once.

This is the shape of Sheet 1 Exercises 1, 2, 3 and 6, Sheet 3 Exercises 1 and 2, and every proof in §1.1. Sometimes each step works in both directions (written \(\iff\)). Then you can write both halves as one chain of \(\iff\)-steps. The de Morgan and pre-image proofs below do this.

Set operations

The five operations Script A.6, Definition 1.2; \(\Delta\) from Corollary 1.10

Let \(A,B\subseteq \Omega\). Here \(\Omega\) is the surrounding set, sometimes called the "universe". The symbol \(:=\) means "is defined as".

  • Union [Vereinigung]: \(A\cup B := \{x \mid x\in A \ \text{or}\ x\in B\}\). "Or" in mathematics is always inclusive: \(x\) may be in both.
  • Intersection [Schnitt]: \(A\cap B := \{x \mid x\in A \ \text{and}\ x\in B\}\).
  • Difference [Differenz], which the script calls the relative complement of \(B\) in \(A\): \(A\setminus B := \{x \mid x\in A \ \text{and}\ x\notin B\}\). Read "\(A\) without \(B\)".
  • Complement [Komplement]: \(A^c := \Omega\setminus A\), everything in the universe that is not in \(A\). This one depends on \(\Omega\). The complement of \(\{1\}\) inside \(\{1,2\}\) is \(\{2\}\); inside \(\{1,2,3\}\) it is \(\{2,3\}\). Always know what the universe is.
  • Symmetric difference [symmetrische Differenz]: \(A\,\Delta\,B := (A\setminus B)\cup(B\setminus A)\), the elements that lie in exactly one of the two sets. (\(\Delta\) is the Greek capital delta.) This is the one operation the appendix does not list: the script introduces it later, in the middle of Corollary 1.10, with exactly this formula.

\(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint [disjunkt] if \(A\cap B=\emptyset\): they have no element in common. Example: \(\{1,2\}\) and \(\{3\}\) are disjoint; \(\{1,2\}\) and \(\{2,3\}\) are not.

The script writes \(A\mathbin{\dot\cup}B\) (a union sign with a dot) for a union of sets that happen to be disjoint. The dot adds no new meaning. It only tells the reader "these sets are disjoint", so that additivity of probabilities may be used.

Venn diagrams [Venn-Diagramme] draw each set as a circle inside a rectangle (the universe \(\Omega\)); overlaps show intersections. The script's appendix remarks that they help your intuition but are not proofs: a picture with two circles shows one situation, while a proof must cover every possible pair of sets. The widget below is a Venn diagram you can click.

Widget — the Venn playground My addition

Click the four regions to switch them on and off. The panel lists every standard expression and tells you which ones describe exactly the region set you have selected. Switch on "only A" and "neither" to see \(B^c\); switch on "neither" alone to watch \((A\cup B)^c\) and \(A^c\cap B^c\) light up together — that is de Morgan.

Worked example with real sets My addition

Take \(\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\) (a die), \(A=\{2,4,6\}\) ("even"), \(B=\{4,5,6\}\) ("at least 4").

ExpressionValueIn words
\(A\cup B\)\(\{2,4,5,6\}\)even or at least 4
\(A\cap B\)\(\{4,6\}\)even and at least 4
\(A\setminus B\)\(\{2\}\)even but below 4
\(A^c\)\(\{1,3,5\}\)odd
\(A\,\Delta\,B\)\(\{2,5\}\)exactly one of the two holds
\((A\cup B)^c\)\(\{1,3\}\)neither
\(A^c\cap B^c\)\(\{1,3\}\)not even and not ≥ 4 — same set ✓

The last two rows give the same set. That is one instance of de Morgan's law (below). The general law says this is no coincidence of this die: it happens for all sets.

Indexed families and big unions

Start with an example. Take the labels \(I=\{1,2,3\}\) and the three sets \(A_1=\{a\}\), \(A_2=\{a,b\}\), \(A_3=\{b,c\}\). Each label \(i\in I\) carries one set \(A_i\). This labelled collection is a family. The formal version:

Definition — family, index set Script A.7

Let \(I\) be a non-empty set (\(I\ne\emptyset\)). For each \(\alpha\in I\) (\(\alpha\) is the Greek letter alpha, used as a label) let \(A_\alpha\) be a set. Then \(\{A_\alpha \mid \alpha\in I\}\), also written \((A_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}\), is a family of sets [Familie von Mengen] (or collection of sets). \(I\) is its index set [Indexmenge].

The definition allows two things that often surprise people:

  • Repetition: \(A_\alpha = A_\beta\) is allowed for \(\alpha\ne\beta\). Example: \(A_1=A_2=\{0\}\). Think of a family as a labelling: two labels may carry the same set.
  • Empty members: \(A_\alpha=\emptyset\) is allowed. This makes the padding trick below legal.

The index set may be finite (\(I=[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}\)), countably infinite (\(I=\N\)) or uncountable (\(I=\R\)); these words are explained in the countability section. Which case you are in decides whether the axioms of a σ-algebra (the event collections of §1.1) can be applied.

Union and intersection over a family Script 1.2

\[ \bigcup_{\alpha\in I}A_\alpha := \{x \mid \exists \alpha\in I: x\in A_\alpha\}, \qquad \bigcap_{\alpha\in I}A_\alpha := \{x \mid \forall \alpha\in I: x\in A_\alpha\}. \]

Here \(\exists\) means "there exists" and \(\forall\) means "for all". So:

  • \(x\) is in the union if at least one of the sets contains \(x\);
  • \(x\) is in the intersection if every one of the sets contains \(x\).

In the example above, \(\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i=\{a,b,c\}\) and \(\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i=\emptyset\), since no letter lies in all three sets.

De Morgan's laws (below) are what you get when you negate these two statements. Negating quantifiers is Analysis 1.1.

Infinite families My addition

Interval notation: \([a,b]\) contains both endpoints, \((a,b)\) neither, and \([a,b)\) only \(a\). \(\N_{>0}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}\).

  • \(A_n=\bigl[0,1-\tfrac1n\bigr]\) for \(n\in\N_{>0}\). These grow: \(A_1=\{0\}\), \(A_2=[0,\tfrac12]\), \(A_3=[0,\tfrac23]\), … and \(\bigcup_n A_n=[0,1)\). Note the union is not \([0,1]\): no single \(A_n\) contains 1, and the union only collects what is in some member.
  • \(B_n=\bigl(-\tfrac1n,\tfrac1n\bigr)\). These shrink, and \(\bigcap_n B_n=\{0\}\): a number \(x\ne0\) fails to be in \(B_n\) as soon as \(\tfrac1n<|x|\), which happens for some \(n\) by the Archimedean property.
  • \(C_q=\{q\}\) for \(q\in\Q\). Here \(I=\Q\) is countably infinite and \(\bigcup_{q\in\Q}C_q=\Q\), where \(\Q\) is the set of fractions (rational numbers). This family is why \(\Q\) is a Borel set (§1.1): a countable union of single points.

The first two are exactly the shapes that appear in Proposition 1.19(iv) and (v) — increasing and decreasing families — and in Lemma 1.24, where \((-\infty,x_n]\) grows or shrinks.

The padding trick My addition — used all over §1.1

The union axiom of a σ-algebra talks about a sequence \((A_i)_{i\in\N}\), that is, countably many sets \(A_0,A_1,A_2,\dots\) (in this course \(\N=\{0,1,2,\dots\}\)). Suppose you only have finitely many, \(A_0,\dots,A_m\). Then extend the family with empty sets:

\[ B_i:=\begin{cases}A_i,& i\le m,\\ \emptyset,& i>m,\end{cases} \qquad\text{then}\qquad \bigcup_{i\in\N}B_i=\bigcup_{i=0}^{m}A_i, \]

This works because adding \(\emptyset\) to a union changes nothing: no \(x\) lies in \(\emptyset\), so a padded member never supplies the "at least one". Example: \(\{1\}\cup\{2\}\cup\emptyset\cup\emptyset \cup\dots=\{1,2\}\).

For intersections, pad with \(\Omega\) instead. Every \(x\) lies in \(\Omega\), so a padded member never blocks the "every one": \(\bigcap_{i\in\N}B_i=\bigcap_{i=0}^{m}A_i\) when \(B_i=\Omega\) for \(i>m\).

Used in: Sheet 1 Ex 3 and Corollary 1.10 (finite unions and intersections stay in \(\Aa\), even though axiom (iii) of Definition 1.6 only speaks about infinite sequences); Definition 1.17, where finite additivity is squeezed out of σ-additivity by padding with \(\emptyset\); and, through that, the proofs of Proposition 1.19.

de Morgan's laws

Lemma 1.3 de Morgan Script 1.3

Small case first. For two sets: \((A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c\) ("not in either" is the same as "not in \(A\) and not in \(B\)") and \((A\cap B)^c=A^c\cup B^c\) ("not in both" is the same as "missing from at least one"). The die table above checked the first one. The general version:

For a family \(\{A_i\}_{i\in I}\) of subsets of \(\Omega\), with any index set \(I\):

\[ \Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i\Bigr)^{c}=\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i^{c}, \qquad \Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i\Bigr)^{c}=\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i^{c}. \]
Proof of the first law, in full Sheet 1 · Ex 1

The whole proof is the negation rule for quantifiers, written with sets. The rule: "it is not true that some \(i\) works" is the same as "every \(i\) fails". Below, \(\neg\) means "not". The chain of \(\iff\)-steps proves both inclusions at once:

\[ \begin{aligned} x\in\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i\Bigr)^{c} &\iff x\notin\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i && \text{definition of complement}\\ &\iff \neg\bigl(\exists i\in I: x\in A_i\bigr) && \text{definition of union}\\ &\iff \forall i\in I:\ x\notin A_i && \text{negating }\exists\text{ gives }\forall\\ &\iff \forall i\in I:\ x\in A_i^{c} && \text{definition of complement}\\ &\iff x\in\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i^{c} && \text{definition of intersection} \end{aligned} \]

Since every step is an "if and only if", the two sets have exactly the same elements, so they are equal. The second law is the same chain with \(\exists\) and \(\forall\) swapped — or, more cheaply, apply the first law to the family \((A_i^c)_{i\in I}\) and take complements of both sides, using \((A^c)^c=A\). ∎

Why this matters so much here: the definition of a σ-algebra (Definition 1.6) has an axiom for unions and an axiom for complements, and no axiom for intersections. So every time you need an intersection to stay inside \(\Aa\), you go through de Morgan:

\[ \bigcap_{i}A_i=\Bigl(\bigcup_{i}A_i^{c}\Bigr)^{c}. \]

Distributive laws, also for families

The picture. For numbers you know \(a\cdot(b+c)=a\cdot b+a\cdot c\): multiplying "distributes" over adding. Sets have the same rule with \(\cap\) in the role of \(\cdot\) and \(\cup\) in the role of \(+\). Unlike for numbers, it also works the other way round (\(\cup\) distributes over \(\cap\)). Intersecting a union with \(B\) is the same as intersecting each piece with \(B\) and then uniting the results.

The distributive laws [Distributivgesetze] My addition — the script uses them without stating them

Two sets first. For sets \(A,B,C\):

\[ A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C),\qquad A\cup(B\cap C)=(A\cup B)\cap(A\cup C). \]

Check with a die. \(\Omega=\{1,\dots,6\}\), \(A=\{2,4,6\}\), \(B=\{4,5,6\}\), \(C=\{1,2\}\).

  • First law. Left: \(B\cup C=\{1,2,4,5,6\}\), so \(A\cap(B\cup C)=\{2,4,6\}\). Right: \(A\cap B=\{4,6\}\), \(A\cap C=\{2\}\), union \(\{2,4,6\}\) ✓.
  • Second law. Left: \(B\cap C=\emptyset\), so \(A\cup\emptyset=\{2,4,6\}\). Right: \(A\cup B=\{2,4,5,6\}\), \(A\cup C=\{1,2,4,6\}\), intersection \(\{2,4,6\}\) ✓.

The family version — this is the one the course needs. For any set \(B\) and any family \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) (finite, countable or larger index set \(I\)):

\[ B\cap\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i\Bigr)=\bigcup_{i\in I}\bigl(B\cap A_i\bigr),\qquad B\cup\Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i\Bigr)=\bigcap_{i\in I}\bigl(B\cup A_i\bigr). \]
Proof — one chain of equivalences
\[ \begin{aligned} x\in B\cap\bigcup_{i}A_i &\iff x\in B\ \text{ and }\ \exists i\in I: x\in A_i && \text{definitions of }\cap\text{ and }\bigcup\\ &\iff \exists i\in I:\ \bigl(x\in B \text{ and } x\in A_i\bigr) && \text{see below}\\ &\iff \exists i\in I:\ x\in B\cap A_i && \text{definition of }\cap\\ &\iff x\in\bigcup_{i}(B\cap A_i) && \text{definition of }\bigcup \end{aligned} \]

The second step: the statement "\(x\in B\)" does not mention \(i\) at all, so it makes no difference whether we say it before "there is an \(i\)" or inside it. Since every step is an "if and only if", both sets have the same elements (double inclusion, above). The second law is the same chain with "or" instead of "and" and \(\forall\) instead of \(\exists\). ∎

An infinite example. \(B=[0,\tfrac12]\) and \(A_n=[0,1-\tfrac1n]\) for \(n\ge1\) (from the families section). Left: \(\bigcup_nA_n=[0,1)\), so \(B\cap[0,1)=[0,\tfrac12]\). Right: \(B\cap A_1=\{0\}\) and \(B\cap A_n=[0,\tfrac12]\) for every \(n\ge2\) (because then \(1-\tfrac1n\ge\tfrac12\)); their union is \([0,\tfrac12]\) ✓.

Disjointness survives. If the \(A_i\) are pairwise disjoint, so are the \(B\cap A_i\): they are smaller (\(B\cap A_i\subseteq A_i\)), and smaller sets cannot start to overlap.

In words: "in \(B\) and in at least one \(A_i\)" means the same as "in at least one of the pieces \(B\cap A_i\)". Cutting a union with \(B\) cuts each piece with \(B\), and disjoint pieces stay disjoint.

Where the course uses it My addition

σ-additivity proofs. To show that \(A\mapsto\P(A\cap B)\) (and hence the conditional probability \(\P(A\mid B)=\P(A\cap B)/\P(B)\)) is σ-additive, take pairwise disjoint \(A_1,A_2,\dots\). Then \((\bigcup_nA_n)\cap B=\bigcup_n(A_n\cap B)\) with disjoint pieces, so \(\P\bigl((\bigcup_nA_n)\cap B\bigr)=\sum_n\P(A_n\cap B)\). That is Theorem 1.70(i) = Sheet 4 Ex 2, worked on the §1.4 page.

Splitting an event by cases. If \(B_1,B_2,\dots\) cut \(\Omega\) into disjoint pieces, then \(A=A\cap\Omega=A\cap\bigcup_iB_i=\bigcup_i(A\cap B_i)\), a disjoint union. This is the first line of the law of total probability (Theorem 1.70(ii)) and of splitting the win event in exam task WiSe25 P6a (§1.4 exams).

The power set, and \(2^\Omega\)

Definition — power set Script A.3, 1.2

The power set [Potenzmenge] of \(\Omega\) is \(\pow(\Omega) := \{A \mid A\subseteq\Omega\}\): the set whose elements are all the subsets of \(\Omega\).

Example. For \(\Omega=\{1,2,3\}\): \(\pow(\Omega)=\bigl\{\emptyset,\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\},\{1,2,3\}\bigr\}\), eight elements.

The level jump is the point. \(\Omega\) holds outcomes; \(\pow(\Omega)\) holds sets of outcomes. So \(A\in\pow(\Omega)\) and \(A\subseteq\Omega\) say exactly the same thing. You will see both.

Examples, including the ones that look strange Script A.4

  • \(\pow(\{*,\odot\})=\bigl\{\emptyset,\{*\},\{\odot\},\{*,\odot\}\bigr\}\) — four elements.
  • \(\pow(\emptyset)=\{\emptyset\}\). Read that carefully: the empty set has exactly one subset, namely itself, so its power set has one element and is not empty.
  • \(\pow(\{\emptyset\})=\bigl\{\emptyset,\{\emptyset\}\bigr\}\) — two elements.
  • \(|\pow(\Omega)|=2^{|\Omega|}\) for finite \(\Omega\), where \(|\Omega|\) is the number of elements of \(\Omega\). Reason: building a subset means one yes/no decision per element, so there are \(2\cdot2\cdots2\) possibilities by the product rule (page B3). For \(\Omega=\{1,2,3\}\) that is \(2^3=8\), matching the list above.

Indicator functions, and why \(\pow(\Omega)\) is written \(2^\Omega\) Script 1.2, A.5

For \(A\subseteq\Omega\), the indicator function [Indikatorfunktion] \(\one_A:\Omega\to\{0,1\}\) is

\[ \one_A(\omega)=\begin{cases}1,&\omega\in A,\\ 0,&\omega\notin A.\end{cases} \]

Read the symbol. The letter in \(\one_A\) is the Greek lower-case chi, \(\chi\). That is the script's own notation (Definition 1.2 writes \(\chi_A\) with \(\chi_A(a)=1\) if \(a\in A\) and \(\chi_A(a)=0\) otherwise), and this guide keeps it on every page. Other books write \(\mathbf 1_A\) or \(\mathbb 1_A\) for the same function, which is why it is called an indicator and not a "chi-function".

The notation \(2^\Omega\) usually means "the set of all maps \(\Omega\to\{0,1\}\)". Such a map says, for each element, 1 ("in") or 0 ("out"). Example with \(\Omega=\{1,2,3\}\): the subset \(\{1,3\}\) belongs to the map \(1\mapsto1,\ 2\mapsto0,\ 3\mapsto1\), which is its indicator \(\one_{\{1,3\}}\). The rule

\[ \pow(\Omega)\to 2^{\Omega},\qquad A\mapsto \one_A \]

is a one-to-one correspondence (a bijection, see below): each subset gives one in/out pattern, and each in/out pattern describes exactly one subset. That is why the script (Remark A.5) also writes \(2^\Omega\) for the power set.

Worth knowing for later: indicators turn set operations into arithmetic — \(\one_{A\cap B}=\one_A\one_B\) and \(\one_{A^c}=1-\one_A\). In §2.1 this becomes \(\P(A)=\E[\one_A]\) ("probability equals the expected value of the indicator"), which is how counting problems turn into expectation problems. SoSe25 P5a (duck hunt) is built entirely on that move.

Cartesian products and tuples

Definition Script 1.2, Convention 1.64

The Cartesian product [kartesisches Produkt] is \(X\times Y := \{(x,y) \mid x\in X,\ y\in Y\}\), the set of ordered pairs. "Ordered" means \((x,y)=(x',y')\) exactly when \(x=x'\) and \(y=y'\), so \((1,2)\ne(2,1)\) — unlike the set \(\{1,2\}=\{2,1\}\).

Example: \(\{1,2\}\times\{a,b,c\}=\{(1,a),(1,b),(1,c),(2,a),(2,b),(2,c)\}\), with \(2\cdot3=6\) elements.

\(X^n := X\times\cdots\times X\) (\(n\) factors) is the set of \(n\)-tuples \((x_1,\dots,x_n)\). For finite \(X\), \(|X^n|=|X|^n\).

Notation the script uses constantly: \([n]:=\{1,\dots,n\}\) for \(n\in\N_{>0}\). So \([6]^2\) is the sample space of two dice, with \(|[6]^2|=36\).

Maps, images and pre-images

Definition My addition — the script uses these without defining them

A map [Abbildung] (or function) \(f:X\to Y\) assigns to each \(x\in X\) exactly one \(f(x)\in Y\). \(X\) is the domain [Definitionsbereich], \(Y\) the codomain [Zielmenge].

Running example. \(X=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\), \(Y=\{0,1,2,3,4\}\), \(f(x)=x^2\). So \(f(-2)=f(2)=4\), \(f(-1)=f(1)=1\), \(f(0)=0\).

For subsets \(A\subseteq X\) and \(B\subseteq Y\):

\[ f(A) := \{f(x) \mid x\in A\}\subseteq Y \quad\text{(\textbf{image} [Bild] of } A\text{)}, \] \[ f^{-1}(B) := \{x\in X \mid f(x)\in B\}\subseteq X \quad\text{(\textbf{pre-image} [Urbild] of } B\text{)}. \]

In words: the image collects the outputs of the points in \(A\). The pre-image collects all inputs whose output lands in \(B\). In the example: \(f(\{1,2\})=\{1,4\}\); \(f^{-1}(\{4\})=\{-2,2\}\); \(f^{-1}(\{0,1\})=\{-1,0,1\}\); \(f^{-1}(\{3\})=\emptyset\), since no square equals 3.

Three standard words:

  • \(f\) is injective [injektiv] if different inputs always give different outputs. The example is not: \(f(-1)=f(1)\).
  • \(f\) is surjective [surjektiv] if every \(y\in Y\) is the output of some input. The example is not: nothing maps to 2 or 3.
  • \(f\) is bijective [bijektiv] (a bijection, a one-to-one correspondence) if it is both. Then every \(y\in Y\) comes from exactly one \(x\), and \(f\) has an inverse function. Example: \(g:\{1,2,3\}\to\{a,b,c\}\) with \(g(1)=a\), \(g(2)=b\), \(g(3)=c\).

The mistake to avoid: \(f^{-1}\) is not an inverse function

\(f^{-1}(B)\) is defined for every map \(f\), invertible or not. It is not a function \(Y\to X\); it is a map \(\pow(Y)\to\pow(X)\), taking sets to sets. When \(f\) is not injective, \(f^{-1}(\{y\})\) may contain several elements (above, \(f^{-1}(\{4\})=\{-2,2\}\)). When \(f\) is not surjective, it may be empty (above, \(f^{-1}(\{3\})=\emptyset\)). Neither is a problem.

This matters because the whole theory of random variables is built on pre-images: a map \(X\) is measurable when \(X^{-1}(B)\) is an event for every \(B\), and nobody ever requires \(X\) to be invertible.

The pre-image toolbox Sheet 1 · Ex 2 (i)–(iii)

For \(f:X\to Y\), subsets \(A,B\subseteq Y\) and a collection \(\mathcal C\subseteq\pow(Y)\) (a set whose members are subsets of \(Y\)). Items 1–3 are exactly parts (i), (ii), (iii) of the sheet; item 4 is mine, and nothing extra has to be proved for it:

  1. \(A\subseteq B \implies f^{-1}(A)\subseteq f^{-1}(B)\);
  2. \(f^{-1}\bigl(\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal C}A\bigr)=\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal C}f^{-1}(A)\);
  3. \(f^{-1}(A^c)=\bigl(f^{-1}(A)\bigr)^c\);
  4. My addition and, as a consequence of (2) and (3), \(f^{-1}\bigl(\bigcap_{A\in\mathcal C}A\bigr)=\bigcap_{A\in\mathcal C}f^{-1}(A)\).
Proofs — each is a one-line chain of equivalences

(1) Let \(x\in f^{-1}(A)\). By definition \(f(x)\in A\). Since \(A\subseteq B\), also \(f(x)\in B\), i.e. \(x\in f^{-1}(B)\). ✓

(2)

\[ x\in f^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal C}A\Bigr) \iff f(x)\in\bigcup_{A}A \iff \exists A\in\mathcal C:\ f(x)\in A \iff \exists A:\ x\in f^{-1}(A) \iff x\in\bigcup_{A}f^{-1}(A). \;✓ \]

(3)

\[ x\in f^{-1}(A^{c}) \iff f(x)\in A^{c} \iff f(x)\notin A \iff x\notin f^{-1}(A) \iff x\in\bigl(f^{-1}(A)\bigr)^{c}. \;✓ \]

(4) By de Morgan twice and (2),(3): \(f^{-1}(\bigcap_A A)=f^{-1}\bigl((\bigcup_A A^c)^c\bigr) =\bigl(f^{-1}(\bigcup_A A^c)\bigr)^c=\bigl(\bigcup_A f^{-1}(A^c)\bigr)^c =\bigl(\bigcup_A f^{-1}(A)^c\bigr)^c=\bigcap_A f^{-1}(A)\). ✓ ∎

In words: pre-images commute with everything — unions, intersections, complements. That is the entire reason \(f^{-1}(\mathcal B)\) is a σ-algebra whenever \(\mathcal B\) is (Sheet 1 Ex 6).

Forward images do not commute with complements SoSe26 · P2b

Images satisfy \(f(A\cup B)=f(A)\cup f(B)\), but in general

\[ f(A\cap B)\subseteq f(A)\cap f(B) \quad\text{(can be strict)}, \qquad f(A^{c})\ne f(A)^{c}. \]

Why: if \(f\) glues two points together, a value can be reached both from inside \(A\) and from outside it, so it lands in \(f(A)\) and in \(f(A^c)\).

Concretely, with \(X=\{1,2,3\}\), \(Y=\{a,b\}\), \(f(1)=f(2)=a\), \(f(3)=b\) and \(A=\{2\}\): \(f(A)=\{a\}\) and \(f(A^c)=f(\{1,3\})=\{a,b\}\), which is not \(\{a\}^c=\{b\}\).

This asymmetry is the entire content of exam task SoSe26 P2b, worked on the §1.1 page.

Widget — pre-image explorer My addition

A small map \(f:\{1,\dots,6\}\to\{a,b,c\}\). Click elements of the codomain to build a set \(B\); the panel shows \(f^{-1}(B)\), then checks the complement identity for pre-images and the matching one for forward images, with \(A:=f^{-1}(B)\).

What to try. The first map hits all three values \(a,b,c\); the second never outputs \(c\). Pick the second map and put \(c\) into \(B\): the pre-image line stays green, while the forward-image line turns red. Reason: \(f(A)^c\) contains \(c\) (nothing in \(A\) maps to \(c\)), but \(f(A^c)\) cannot contain \(c\), because no input maps to \(c\) at all. With \(A=f^{-1}(B)\) that is the only way the forward identity can fail — which is why the warning box above uses a set \(A\) that is not a pre-image.

Choose \(B\subseteq\{a,b,c\}\):

Composition of maps, and the pre-image of a composition

The picture. Often you first compute one quantity and then feed it into a formula: roll a die, subtract 3, then square the result. Doing one map after another is called composition. The question this section answers: which outcomes lead to a final result in a set \(B\)? Answer: go backwards through the maps one at a time.

Definition and the key identity My addition — the identity the script needs for Lemma 2.2

For maps \(X:\Omega\to Y\) and \(g:Y\to Z\), the composition [Verkettung, Komposition] \(g\circ X:\Omega\to Z\) (read "\(g\) after \(X\)") is \((g\circ X)(\omega):=g\bigl(X(\omega)\bigr)\): first apply \(X\), then \(g\). In probability one simply writes \(g(X)\). (Analysis 4.1 uses composition for continuity.)

For every \(B\subseteq Z\):

\[ (g\circ X)^{-1}(B)=X^{-1}\bigl(g^{-1}(B)\bigr). \]

Note the order: the map applied last (\(g\)) is undone first.

Proof
\[ \omega\in(g\circ X)^{-1}(B)\iff g\bigl(X(\omega)\bigr)\in B\iff X(\omega)\in g^{-1}(B)\iff\omega\in X^{-1}\bigl(g^{-1}(B)\bigr). \]

Step 1 is the definition of pre-image for \(g\circ X\); step 2 is the definition of pre-image for \(g\), applied to the point \(X(\omega)\); step 3 is the definition of pre-image for \(X\). ∎

Worked example with numbers My addition

\(\Omega=\{1,\dots,6\}\) (a die), \(X(\omega)=\omega-3\), \(g(x)=x^2\). Then \(g\circ X\) sends \(1\mapsto4,\ 2\mapsto1,\ 3\mapsto0,\ 4\mapsto1,\ 5\mapsto4,\ 6\mapsto9\). Take \(B=\{1,4\}\).

  • Backwards in two steps. \(g^{-1}(\{1,4\})=\{-2,-1,1,2\}\) (the numbers whose square is 1 or 4). Then \(X^{-1}(\{-2,-1,1,2\})=\{1,2,4,5\}\) (the \(\omega\) with \(\omega-3\) in that set).
  • Directly. From the list, \(g(X(\omega))\in\{1,4\}\) exactly for \(\omega=1,2,4,5\) ✓.

A cdf-style example. With \(g(x)=x^2\) and \(B=(-\infty,y]\) for some \(y\ge0\): \(g^{-1}\bigl((-\infty,y]\bigr)=[-\sqrt y,\sqrt y]\), so \(\{X^2\le y\}=\{-\sqrt y\le X\le\sqrt y\}\). This is exactly the first step of the cdf method for the distribution of \(g(X)\).

Why it matters: \(g(X)\) is again a random variable My addition

A random variable \(X\) is a map whose pre-images \(X^{-1}(B)\) of Borel sets \(B\) are events (Definition 1.50). If \(g:\R\to\R\) is measurable (pre-images of Borel sets are Borel sets — true for every continuous or monotone \(g\), see B4), then \(g^{-1}(B)\) is a Borel set, so \((g\circ X)^{-1}(B)=X^{-1}(g^{-1}(B))\) is an event. That is the whole proof that \(X^2\), \(e^X\), \(-\ln U\), … are random variables (§1.3), used in Sheet 4 Ex 4 and in the exam tasks SoSe25 P3d and WiSe25 P3a (\(X=g(U)\), §1.3 exams).

Where the script relies on it. Lemma 2.2 opens with "let \(g:\R\to\R\) be a measurable function. Then \(Y=g(X)\) is also an RVRV" and gives no proof; the missing line is exactly the identity above. Example 1.52 supplies the other half — "continuous functions are measurable with respect to their Borel-σ-algebras" — which is what makes \(g^{-1}(B)\) a Borel set for the \(g\) this course uses.

In words: to find the outcomes that end up in \(B\) after two maps, first find the middle values that \(g\) sends into \(B\), then find the outcomes that \(X\) sends to those middle values.

Countability, and the arithmetic of it

The definition and Cantor's argument are in your Analysis guide Analysis 1.1

A set \(A\) is countable [abzählbar] if it is empty or there is a surjective map \(f:\N\to A\). Think of \(f\) as a numbered list \(f(0),f(1),f(2),\dots\) that eventually reaches every element of \(A\); repetitions are allowed. A set that is not countable is uncountable [überabzählbar].

Examples. \(\{a,b\}\) is countable: the list \(a,b,b,b,\dots\) works. The even numbers \(\{0,2,4,\dots\}\) are countable: \(f(n)=2n\). Here \(f\) is even a bijection with \(\N\); such a set is called countably infinite [abzählbar unendlich]. \(\Z=\{\dots,-1,0,1,\dots\}\) is countable via the list \(0,1,-1,2,-2,\dots\). \(\Q\) is countable; \(\R\) is not, by Cantor's diagonal argument. Your guide has both, with the diagonal widget: Analysis 1.1 — Countability →

Careful with the words — but not in the way you might expect. In this course "countable" already includes the finite case. Definition 1.2 spells it out: "a countable (i.e., finite or countably infinite) collection of sets". Definition 1.34 writes "at most countable" [höchstens abzählbar] for the very same thing, only more explicitly, so that nobody reads "countable \(\Omega\)" as "infinite \(\Omega\)" and excludes a six-sided die. Your Analysis guide uses "countable" in exactly this wide sense too. The one phrase that really does exclude finite sets is "countably infinite". So: whenever you meet "countable" or "at most countable" in this course, finite sets are allowed; only "countably infinite" rules them out.

The four facts this course actually uses My addition

Sheet 1 lets you use the first two without proof. Learn all four by heart.

  1. A subset of a countable set is countable.
  2. A countable union of countable sets is countable. If \(A_0,A_1,\dots\) are each countable, so is \(\bigcup_i A_i\).
  3. A finite product of countable sets is countable — in particular \(\Q\times\Q\) is countable.
  4. The set of finite subsets of \(\N\) is countable, and so is the set of finite sequences over a finite alphabet.
Why (2) is true, and where it is used My sketch

Empty sets add nothing to a union, so leave them out. (If nothing is left, the union is empty and therefore countable, and there is nothing to prove. If only finitely many are left, repeat the last one over and over — repeating a set changes no union, and now there are infinitely many rows to work with.) List each remaining \(A_i\) as \(a_{i,0},a_{i,1},a_{i,2},\dots\) (possible since \(A_i\) is countable: that is what a surjection \(\N\to A_i\) gives you). Arrange these lists as the rows of an infinite grid, and walk the grid along anti-diagonals: first \(a_{0,0}\); then \(a_{1,0},a_{0,1}\); then \(a_{2,0},a_{1,1},a_{0,2}\); and so on. Each anti-diagonal is finite, so every entry is reached after finitely many steps. That walk is a surjection \(\N\to\bigcup_i A_i\). ∎

This is the same anti-diagonal walk your Analysis guide uses to list \(\Q\).

Used here in three places:

  • Sheet 1 Exercise 4(iii): the co-countable sets form a σ-algebra — the union case needs exactly (2).
  • Sheet 2 Exercise 5: there are only countably many intervals \([a,b)\) with \(a,b\in\Q\), because \(\Q\times\Q\) is countable — that is (3). Without it, "every open set is a countable union of rational intervals" would fail and the Borel σ-algebra argument would collapse.
  • Theorem 1.27: the group of finite coin-flip changes is countable, by (4).

Two more facts, with their reasons My addition

(5) Every infinite set contains a countably infinite subset. Let \(\Omega\) be infinite. Pick any element \(\omega_0\in\Omega\). The rest, \(\Omega\setminus\{\omega_0\}\), is not empty (otherwise \(\Omega\) would have only one element), so pick \(\omega_1\) in it. After \(n\) picks, the rest \(\Omega\setminus\{\omega_0,\dots,\omega_{n-1}\}\) is still not empty, because a set with only \(n\) elements is finite and \(\Omega\) is not. So the picking never gets stuck, and it produces distinct elements \(\omega_0,\omega_1,\omega_2,\dots\); the set \(\{\omega_0,\omega_1,\dots\}\) is countably infinite. (Making infinitely many picks one after the other, with no rule saying which element to take, is a mild use of the axiom of choice, the "countable choice" version; the course uses it silently.) Used in the guide's proof of Sheet 1 Ex 4(iv), where distinct \(\omega_0,\omega_1,\dots\) are picked.

(6) The power set of \(\N\) is uncountable — it has the same size as \(\R\). The script states this in its motivation (p. 8) without an argument; the Motivation page gives the diagonal step in short form. Here is the whole thing, in three steps:

  1. Subsets are 0/1-sequences. A subset \(S\subseteq\N\) is described by its indicator (above): the sequence \(\one_S(0),\one_S(1),\one_S(2),\dots\) of 0s and 1s. Example: the even numbers give \(1,0,1,0,\dots\).
  2. No list contains every subset (a diagonal argument, as in Cantor's proof for \(\R\), Analysis 1.1). Suppose \(S_0,S_1,S_2,\dots\) were a list of all subsets of \(\N\). Build \(D:=\{n\in\N\mid n\notin S_n\}\). For every \(n\), the sets \(D\) and \(S_n\) disagree about the number \(n\): if \(n\in S_n\) then \(n\notin D\), and if \(n\notin S_n\) then \(n\in D\). So \(D\) is none of the \(S_n\) — but it is a subset of \(\N\), and the list was supposed to contain all of them. That is impossible, so no such list exists. Example: if the list begins \(S_0=\{0,1\}\), \(S_1=\emptyset\), \(S_2=\{0,2,4,\dots\}\), \(S_3=\N\), then \(0\in S_0\Rightarrow0\notin D\); \(1\notin S_1\Rightarrow1\in D\); \(2\in S_2\Rightarrow2\notin D\); \(3\in S_3\Rightarrow3\notin D\). \(D\) already differs from each of the first four sets.
  3. Same size as \(\R\) (sketch). A 0/1-sequence \(d_0,d_1,d_2,\dots\) is the binary expansion \(0.d_0d_1d_2\ldots\) of a number in \([0,1]\). Only countably many numbers have two expansions (such as \(0.1000\ldots=0.0111\ldots\) in binary), which does not change the size, and \([0,1]\) has the same size as \(\R\).

The proof pattern. Step 2 is a proof by contradiction [Widerspruchsbeweis]: assume the opposite of what you want (here: "a complete list exists"), deduce something impossible, and conclude that the assumption was false. The model example is Analysis 1.1 — \(\sqrt2\) is not rational. The script's proofs of Theorems 1.27 and 1.28 (the Vitali section) and Sheet 2 Ex 5 have the same shape.

In words: an infinite set always has room for an endless list of different elements; but the collection of all subsets of \(\N\) is too big for any list, because from any list you can build a subset it misses.

Equivalence relations, partitions, and the axiom of choice

These three ideas appear in exactly one place in this course — the Vitali construction, Theorem 1.28 — but that proof is unreadable without them.

Definition — equivalence relation My addition

A relation \(\sim\) on a set \(X\) (a rule that, for each pair, either holds or does not) is an equivalence relation [Äquivalenzrelation] if it is

  • reflexive: \(x\sim x\) for all \(x\);
  • symmetric: \(x\sim y \implies y\sim x\);
  • transitive: \(x\sim y\) and \(y\sim z\) \(\implies\) \(x\sim z\).

The equivalence class [Äquivalenzklasse] of \(x\) is \([x]:=\{y\in X \mid y\sim x\}\), the set of everything equivalent to \(x\). (These square brackets have nothing to do with \([n]=\{1,\dots,n\}\) or with intervals.)

Small example. On \(X=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\) let \(x\sim y\) mean "\(x\) and \(y\) have the same parity" (both even or both odd). All three rules hold. There are two classes: \([1]=[3]=[5]=\{1,3,5\}\) and \([2]=[4]=[6]=\{2,4,6\}\).

Classes partition the set My addition

The equivalence classes of \(\sim\) are non-empty, pairwise disjoint (any two different classes are disjoint), and their union is \(X\). In other words, they cut \(X\) into blocks with no overlaps and no leftovers. Such a cutting is called a partition [Partition, Zerlegung]. In the parity example the blocks are \(\{1,3,5\}\) and \(\{2,4,6\}\).

Proof

Non-empty: \(x\in[x]\) by reflexivity.

Cover: every \(x\) lies in its own class, so the union of all classes is \(X\).

Disjoint: suppose \([x]\cap[y]\ne\emptyset\), say \(z\sim x\) and \(z\sim y\). By symmetry \(x\sim z\), and with transitivity \(x\sim y\). Then for any \(w\in[x]\) we get \(w\sim x\sim y\), so \(w\in[y]\), giving \([x]\subseteq[y]\); by the same argument with the roles swapped, \([y]\subseteq[x]\). Hence \([x]=[y]\). So two classes are either identical or disjoint — never partially overlapping. ∎

The example you need: the Vitali relation

On \(X=[0,1)\) define \(x\sim y :\iff x-y\in\Q\).

  • Reflexive: \(x-x=0\in\Q\) ✓
  • Symmetric: if \(x-y\in\Q\) then \(y-x=-(x-y)\in\Q\) ✓
  • Transitive: if \(x-y\in\Q\) and \(y-z\in\Q\) then \(x-z=(x-y)+(y-z)\in\Q\), since a sum of rationals is rational ✓

Each class is a set like \(\{\,x+q \bmod 1 \mid q\in\Q\,\}\). Here "\(\bmod 1\)" means: keep only the part after the decimal point, so the result stays in \([0,1)\). Example: the class of \(0\) is \(\Q\cap[0,1)\), and the class of \(\sqrt2-1\approx0.414\) contains \(0.414\ldots+\tfrac12=0.914\ldots\). Each class is countably infinite — it holds exactly one point for each rational \(q\in\Q\cap[0,1)\), because if \((x+q)\bmod 1=(x+q')\bmod 1\) with \(q,q'\in[0,1)\) then \(q-q'\) is a whole number smaller than 1 in size, hence \(0\), so \(q=q'\) — and dense in \([0,1)\): every interval, however short, contains a point of it. There are uncountably many classes. If there were only countably many, \([0,1)\) would be a countable union of countable sets, hence countable (fact 2 above) — but it is not.

The axiom of choice My addition

The axiom of choice [Auswahlaxiom] says: given any family of non-empty sets, there is a function picking one element out of each. For finitely many sets this is unremarkable — you just pick. For an uncountable family with no rule saying which element to take, it is a genuine extra assumption about what mathematics permits.

Why it appears here: the Vitali set \(V\) is built by choosing one representative from each of uncountably many equivalence classes, with no rule for choosing. That non-constructive step is exactly why \(V\) can be so badly behaved that no translation-invariant probability can measure it. You cannot write down a non-measurable set; you can only prove one exists.
