  • If the correct value is none of the printed values, then no label is correct: \(T = \emptyset\), so \(\P(T) = 0\%\). But 0 % is printed (label C), so the correct value would be printed after all. Contradiction.

Every candidate contradicts itself, so the question has no consistent answer. It is a liar paradox wearing a multiple-choice costume, not a probability problem.

In words: the model \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\) is perfectly fine. What fails is the question, which asks about a quantity that is defined in terms of its own answer. Probability theory does not repair badly posed questions — it only makes the breakage visible.

Gap in the official solution: it checks the three printed values but never says why no other value can be correct. The missing case: suppose the true probability were some value not printed at all (say 75 %). Then no label is correct, so \(T = \emptyset\) and \(\P(T) = 0\). But then the true probability is 0 %, which is printed (as C), so this case contradicts itself too. Only with this fourth case is "no consistent answer" fully proved. (Two smaller things: the official solution uses the symbol \(T\) without ever saying what it stands for — it is the set of labels carrying the correct value — and it announces "this gives a contradiction" before the three cases instead of drawing the conclusion after them.)

Old-exam tasks

What the old exams take from this page

I checked all three available exams (WiSe25, SoSe25, SoSe26) task by task. No task asks about the puzzles, the history or the philosophy of Chapter 0. The script brackets that material as "— Philosophical Interlude —".

What does get examined is the vocabulary the motivation section introduces informally: \(\Omega\), events, \(\P\), pmf, probability space, \(\sigma\)-algebra. These are defined properly on the next page, where SoSe26 P2b, WiSe25 P1a and WiSe25 P1c are worked. The simplest of them can already be solved with the three \(\sigma\)-algebra rules above:

True or false: a \(\sigma\)-algebra on three points WiSe25 · P1a

"On \(\Omega = \{\circ, \triangle, \star\}\), the set \(\{\emptyset, \{\circ\}, \{\star\}, \{\circ,\star\}, \Omega\}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra."

False. Rule 2 (closed under complements) fails: \(\{\circ\}\) is in the collection, but its complement \(\Omega \setminus \{\circ\} = \{\triangle, \star\}\) is not. One missing set is enough for a counterexample. This matches the official solution.

Formulas from this page

pmf conditions
\(p(\omega) \ge 0\) and \(\sum_{\omega\in\Omega} p(\omega) = 1\)
events from pmf

Things to be able to say out loud

  • \(\Omega\) is chosen, not discovered — it holds the outcomes we care about.
  • \(p\) takes outcomes, \(\P\) takes sets of outcomes.
  • On an uncountable \(\Omega\), every single outcome has probability zero, and yet whole sets of outcomes — an interval such as \([0.15,0.46]\) — still have positive probability.
  • \(\pow(\Omega)\) is too big to be the event space for the uniform law on \([0,1]\), which is why \(\sigma\)-algebras exist.
  • Randomness in this course models our ignorance, not a mechanism in nature.

Exam focus

The puzzles and the philosophy have never been examined. The \(\sigma\)-algebra rules have (WiSe25 P1a, SoSe26 P2b). The habit worth carrying into the exam is the one Sheet 0 drills: before computing anything, write down \(\Omega\), \(\Aa\) and \(\P\) explicitly, and say whether the outcomes in \(\Omega\) are equally likely. The official old-exam solutions that use the Laplace distribution (for example SoSe25 P1a) state the model first in exactly this way.

Self-test

Section 1.1 · Lectures 1–2 (15 & 22 April 2026)

Probability spaces

Wahrscheinlichkeitsräume

What this page covers Script §1.1, pp. 11–19

Everything from Convention 1.1 to Remark 1.33. The script's own section goal: "Introduce a concise mathematical framework to talk about probability and distributions."

Worked in place: Sheet 1 (all six tasks), Sheet 2 (Ex. 1, 3, 5), Sheet 3 (Ex. 1, 2), and the old-exam tasks WiSe25 P1a, WiSe25 P1c, WiSe25 P6c, SoSe26 P2b.

This is the most abstract page of the course and the one that pays back most. Four separate exam tasks come from it, spread over two of the three past exams we have (WiSe 25/26 and SoSe 2026; SoSe 2025 happens to contain none).

The big picture

The previous page ended with a problem. On a continuous sample space (for example all numbers in \([0,1]\)) we cannot give every subset a probability. This page repairs that. It builds three objects, in this order:

  1. a \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\Aa\) — the list of subsets that will get a probability. It is small enough to leave out a few badly behaved sets. It is large enough to contain every set we will ever ask about.
  2. a measure \(\mu\) — a rule that gives each set on that list a "size". The size behaves like length, area and volume behave.
  3. a probability measure \(\P\) — a measure whose total size is exactly 1.

That is the whole plan. Everything else on this page is one of three things: a consequence of these three definitions, a worked example, or a proof that the caution was necessary.

In words: in this course, "probability" means "a way of measuring the size of sets, scaled so that the whole space has size 1". Your intuitions about lengths and areas carry over. Bigger sets are not smaller. Pieces that do not overlap add up. The whole is the sum of its parts.

Primer: the notation this section uses My addition

Cross-references Analysis guide

Quantifier negation: Analysis 1.1. Supremum: Analysis 1.2. Sequences, \(\uparrow\), \(\downarrow\): Analysis 2.1 and 2.2. Full set algebra (families, de Morgan, pre-images): B2. What a measure-theoretic integral is: B4.

Page 0 covered sets, subsets, power sets, unions, intersections, complements, \(\N\), \(\Q\), \(\R\), and countability. This section adds five more things, all of which the script uses without introduction.

1. Indexed families and unions over an index set

An index set \(I\) is a set whose elements are used as labels. Writing \((A_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}\) or \(\{A_\alpha \mid \alpha \in I\}\) means: for each label \(\alpha\) we have a set \(A_\alpha\). The index set may be finite (\(I = \{1,2,3\}\)), countably infinite (\(I = \N\)), or uncountable (\(I = \R\)). Sets may repeat: \(A_\alpha = A_\beta\) for \(\alpha \ne \beta\) is allowed. Some sets may be empty. This is the script's Definition A.7. Example: with \(I=\{1,2,3\}\) and \(A_1=\{a\}\), \(A_2=\{a,b\}\), \(A_3=\{b,c\}\) we get \(\bigcup_i A_i=\{a,b,c\}\) and \(\bigcap_i A_i=\emptyset\) (no letter is in all three).

The union and intersection over such a family are defined by what it means to belong to them:

\[ \bigcup_{\alpha\in I} A_\alpha = \{\omega \mid \exists \alpha \in I : \omega \in A_\alpha\}, \qquad \bigcap_{\alpha\in I} A_\alpha = \{\omega \mid \forall \alpha \in I : \omega \in A_\alpha\}. \]

Here \(\exists\) reads "there exists" and \(\forall\) reads "for all". So \(\omega\) is in the union if it is in at least one of the sets, and in the intersection if it is in every one of them.

The script asks, in the middle of Definition 1.2: "How do the above two points include the finite collection case?" The answer mine: take \(I = \N\) and set \(A_i = \emptyset\) for all \(i\) beyond the ones you care about. Since adding \(\emptyset\) to a union changes nothing, \(\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i = A_0 \cup \dots \cup A_m\). For intersections you pad with \(\Omega\) instead, because intersecting with \(\Omega\) changes nothing. Learn this padding trick now: it is what turns finite statements into the countable ones the axioms actually speak about, and it reappears in Sheet 1 Exercise 3 and in the derivation of finite additivity from \(\sigma\)-additivity (Definition 1.17).

2. Disjoint unions and the symbol \(\mathbin{\dot\cup}\)

Two sets are disjoint if \(A \cap B = \emptyset\) — they share no element. A family is pairwise disjoint if no two of its members share an element. The script writes \(A \mathbin{\dot\cup} B\) to signal "this is a union of sets that happen to be disjoint". The symbol is an ordinary union; the dot is a reminder to the reader that additivity may be applied.

3. \([n]\), and \(\subseteq\) versus \(\subsetneq\)

\([n] := \{1,\dots,n\}\) for \(n \in \N_{>0}\). The script uses \(\subseteq\) for "subset, equality allowed" and \(\subsetneq\) for "proper subset, equality not allowed". It tries to avoid \(\subset\) entirely, and says that where \(\subset\) does appear it "probably" means \(\subseteq\) — and invites you to point it out.

4. The indicator function \(\one_A\)

For \(A \subseteq \Omega\), the indicator function [Indikatorfunktion] \(\one_A : \Omega \to \{0,1\}\) is defined by \(\one_A(\omega) = 1\) if \(\omega \in A\) and \(\one_A(\omega) = 0\) otherwise — "is \(\omega\) in \(A\)? yes = 1, no = 0". The script uses the Greek letter \(\chi\) (chi) for it; other books write \(\mathbf 1_A\).

This is what makes the notation \(2^\Omega\) for the power set sensible: a subset \(A \subseteq \Omega\) is the same information as a map \(\Omega \to \{0,1\}\), namely \(\one_A\), which decides for each element whether it is in (1) or out (0). The correspondence \(\pow(\Omega) \to 2^\Omega\), \(A \mapsto \one_A\), is one-to-one.

5. Monotone limits: \(\uparrow\), \(\downarrow\), and \(\sup\)

For real numbers, \(x_n \uparrow x\) means the sequence \(x_1 \le x_2 \le \dots\) increases and converges to \(x\); \(x_n \downarrow x\) means it decreases to \(x\). For sets, the same arrows mean the sets grow or shrink: \(A_0 \subseteq A_1 \subseteq \cdots\) growing, or \(A_0 \supseteq A_1 \supseteq \cdots\) shrinking.

(Full treatment with an explorer widget: Analysis 1.2 — sup, inf.) The supremum \(\sup S\) of a set \(S \subseteq \R\) is its least upper bound: a number \(u\) is an upper bound if \(x \le u\) for every \(x \in S\), and \(\sup S\) is the smallest upper bound. Example: \(\sup\{\tfrac12,\tfrac23,\tfrac34,\dots\} = 1\), although 1 is not in the set. Sheet 2 Exercise 1(iii) states this definition explicitly, so the course does not assume you know it. For an increasing sequence, \(\sup_n x_n = \lim_n x_n\); for a general sequence the two can differ. The infimum \(\inf S\) is the mirror image: the largest lower bound. For a decreasing sequence, \(\inf_n x_n = \lim_n x_n\).

A function \(F\) is right-continuous at \(x\) if \(F(x_n) \to F(x)\) for every sequence \(x_n \downarrow x\) — approaching \(x\) from above reproduces the value at \(x\). It may still jump when approached from below. Picture a staircase whose steps include their left endpoint.

Conventions and set operations

Convention 1.1 — 0 is a natural number Script 1.1

Throughout the course, \(\N = \{0,1,2,\dots\}\).

Why it matters: many German textbooks start \(\N\) at 1. When the script writes "for a sequence \((A_i)_{i\in\N}\)" the sequence starts at \(A_0\), and when Proposition 1.19 writes \(A_0 \subseteq A_1 \subseteq \cdots\) the index really does begin at zero. Where a statement needs the positive integers, the script writes \(\N_{>0}\).

Definition 1.2 — set operations Script 1.2

For any set \(\Omega\): the power set \(\pow(\Omega) := \{A \mid A \subseteq \Omega\}\); for \(A \subseteq \Omega\), the complement \(A^c := \Omega \setminus A \subseteq \Omega\). For a countable collection \((\Omega_i)_{i\in\N}\),

\[ \bigcup_{i\in\N}\Omega_i = \{\omega \mid \exists i \in \N: \omega \in \Omega_i\}, \qquad \bigcap_{i\in\N}\Omega_i = \{\omega \mid \forall i \in \N: \omega \in \Omega_i\}, \]

and the same for an arbitrary (possibly uncountable) index set \(I\). Disjoint unions are written \(\mathbin{\dot\cup}\); \([n] := \{1,\dots,n\}\).

The script notes it "generally assumes familiarity" with this and points to Appendix A.1 for a longer refresher.

Lemma 1.3 de Morgan's laws Script 1.3

Let \(\{A_i\}_{i\in I}\) be a family of sets indexed by a set \(I\). Then

\[ \Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i\Bigr)^{c} = \bigcap_{i\in I}A_i^{c}, \qquad \Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i\Bigr)^{c} = \bigcup_{i\in I}A_i^{c}. \]

The script's proof line reads, in full: "Proof. Exercises." — it is Sheet 1, Exercise 1, worked below.

In words: "not (in at least one of them)" is the same as "in none of them"; "not (in all of them)" is the same as "missing from at least one". These two identities are the engine of nearly every \(\sigma\)-algebra proof in the course, because a \(\sigma\)-algebra is closed under unions and complements but says nothing directly about intersections.

Convention 1.4 — non-empty \(\Omega\) Script 1.4

Throughout the lecture, unless stated otherwise, \(\Omega\) is a non-empty set.

Why: if \(\Omega = \emptyset\) then \(\pow(\Omega) = \{\emptyset\}\) and the only candidate measure would need \(\P(\emptyset) = 1\) and \(\P(\emptyset) = 0\) at once. The convention removes a degenerate case rather than a real one.

Remark 1.5 — samples, events, event systems Script 1.5

The script includes an illustration (adapted from Georgii, 2015) showing three levels stacked on top of each other. Redrawn here:

Reading it from the bottom: a single outcome \(\omega\) is a point of \(\Omega\). An event \(A\) is a set of outcomes, so it is a point one level up, inside \(\pow(\Omega)\). An event system such as a \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\Aa\) is a set of events, so it is a point one level higher still, inside \(\pow(\pow(\Omega))\).

In words: keeping these three levels straight is most of the difficulty of this section. When a statement confuses you, ask which level each symbol lives on. Writing \(\omega \in \Aa\) or \(A \in \Omega\) is a level error and is always wrong.

\(\sigma\)-algebras

Definition 1.6 \(\sigma\)-algebra Script 1.6

We call \(\Aa \subseteq \pow(\Omega)\) a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) if

  1. \(\Omega \in \Aa\),
  2. for each \(A \in \Aa\) we have \(A^c \in \Aa\), and
  3. for each sequence \((A_i)_{i\in\N}\) in \(\Aa\) we have \(\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i \in \Aa\).

Reading each part. \(\Aa\) is a set whose elements are subsets of \(\Omega\) — that is what \(\Aa \subseteq \pow(\Omega)\) says. (i) The certain event is on the list. (ii) If you can measure "\(A\) happens", you can measure "\(A\) does not happen". (iii) If you can measure each of countably many events, you can measure "at least one of them happens".

Where the \(\sigma\) comes from: it marks the word countably in (iii). Without it — only finite unions — the structure is called an algebra, and it is too weak: limits of events would fall outside it.

Note of mine: \(\emptyset \in \Aa\) is not listed as an axiom because it follows: \(\Omega \in \Aa\) by (i), so \(\Omega^c = \emptyset \in \Aa\) by (ii). Several official solutions verify "\(\emptyset \in \Aa\)" where the definition asks for "\(\Omega \in \Aa\)". Both are fine, but in an exam quote the axiom as stated.

Widget — the \(\sigma\)-algebra lab My addition

Take \(\Omega = \{1,2,3,4\}\), which has \(2^4 = 16\) subsets. Click subsets to put them into your collection \(\Aa\). The checker tests the three axioms of Definition 1.6 one at a time and names the first witness that fails. "Generate \(\sigma(\Aa)\)" closes your collection up into the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra containing it — that is Lemma 1.8 made concrete. The widget opens on the WiSe25 P1a preset, which needs only three points, so it switches to \(\Omega=\{1,2,3\}\) and 8 subsets; the other presets switch back to \(\{1,2,3,4\}\). In that preset read \(1=\circ\), \(2=\triangle\), \(3=\star\), so the exam's collection \(\{\emptyset,\{\circ\},\{\star\},\{\circ,\star\},\Omega\}\) appears as \(\{\emptyset,\{1\},\{3\},\{1,3\},\Omega\}\).

Presets:

Proposition 1.7 intersection of \(\sigma\)-algebras Script 1.7

Let \(I\) be a non-empty index set (finite, countable or even uncountable) and let \(\Aa_\alpha\) be a \(\sigma\)-algebra over \(\Omega\) for every \(\alpha \in I\). Then \(\Aa := \bigcap_{\alpha\in I}\Aa_\alpha\) is also a \(\sigma\)-algebra over \(\Omega\).

Script proof: "Exercises." — it is Sheet 1, Exercise 5, worked below.

Why \(I \ne \emptyset\) is assumed My addition: with no \(\alpha\) at all, the condition "\(X\in\Aa_\alpha\) for every \(\alpha\in I\)" holds for every \(X\) (there is nothing to check). So the "intersection" would have to be read as "all subsets of \(\Omega\)", that is \(\pow(\Omega)\). That happens to be a \(\sigma\)-algebra too, but it needs a separate convention. Assuming \(I\ne\emptyset\) avoids the special case.

The union is a different story. The union of two \(\sigma\)-algebras is usually not one; that is Sheet 1 Exercise 4(ii). Intersecting keeps only sets that everybody agrees about, and the axioms survive; uniting throws together sets from two different systems whose combinations belong to neither.

Lemma 1.8 generator of a \(\sigma\)-algebra Script 1.8

For a system of subsets \(\mathcal E \subseteq \pow(\Omega)\),

\[ \sigma(\mathcal E) := \bigcap\{\Aa \mid \Aa \text{ is a } \sigma\text{-algebra on } \Omega \text{ and } \mathcal E \subseteq \Aa\} \]

is the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) containing \(\mathcal E\). We call \(\mathcal E\) the generator and \(\sigma(\mathcal E)\) the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by \(\mathcal E\).

Proof supplied by me — the script states this without proof

Step 1: the family being intersected is non-empty. We need at least one \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) that contains \(\mathcal E\). The power set \(\pow(\Omega)\) is one: it satisfies the three axioms of Definition 1.6 (this is Example 1.9(ii) below), and it contains every subset of \(\Omega\), in particular every member of \(\mathcal E\). So the intersection is over a non-empty family and Proposition 1.7 applies.

Step 2: \(\sigma(\mathcal E)\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra. Immediately from Proposition 1.7, since it is an intersection of a non-empty family of \(\sigma\)-algebras on \(\Omega\).

Step 3: it contains \(\mathcal E\). Let \(E \in \mathcal E\). Every \(\Aa\) appearing in the intersection satisfies \(\mathcal E \subseteq \Aa\), so \(E \in \Aa\) for every such \(\Aa\). Being in all of them is precisely being in their intersection, so \(E \in \sigma(\mathcal E)\).

Step 4: it is the smallest such. Let \(\mathcal B\) be any \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\) with \(\mathcal E \subseteq \mathcal B\). Then \(\mathcal B\) is one of the sets being intersected, and an intersection is contained in each of its members, so \(\sigma(\mathcal E) \subseteq \mathcal B\). ∎

Why "smallest" is worth having. It converts an existence question into a containment check. To prove \(\sigma(\mathcal E) \subseteq \mathcal B\) you never have to describe \(\sigma(\mathcal E)\) — you only have to show \(\mathcal E \subseteq \mathcal B\) and that \(\mathcal B\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra. Sheet 2 Exercise 5, Sheet 3 Exercise 1 and Sheet 3 Exercise 2 are all won by exactly this move.

Example 1.9 \(\sigma\)-algebras Script 1.9

  1. \(\{\emptyset,\Omega\}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\), called the trivial \(\sigma\)-algebra. Check: \(\Omega\) is in it; the complements are \(\emptyset^c = \Omega\) and \(\Omega^c = \emptyset\), both in it; any union of copies of \(\emptyset\) and \(\Omega\) is again \(\emptyset\) or \(\Omega\).
  2. The power set \(\pow(\Omega)\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\). Check: every subset of \(\Omega\) is in it, so any requirement of the form "this subset must be in it" holds automatically.
  3. For every \(A \subseteq \Omega\), \(\sigma(\{A\}) = \{\emptyset, \Omega, A, A^c\}\). Check: this collection is closed under complements (the four complements are \(\Omega, \emptyset, A^c, A\)) and under unions (any union of these four is one of the four again — e.g. \(A \cup A^c = \Omega\)), and it contains \(A\). By Lemma 1.8 the generated \(\sigma\)-algebra is the smallest one containing \(A\); no member can be dropped, since each is forced by the axioms. Note the degenerate cases: if \(A = \emptyset\) or \(A = \Omega\) the list collapses to the trivial \(\sigma\)-algebra.

Corollary 1.10 \(\sigma\)-algebras are closed under set operations Script 1.10

Let \(\Aa\) be a \(\sigma\)-algebra over \(\Omega\) and \(A, B \in \Aa\). Then

\[ \Omega,\quad A\cup B,\quad A\cap B,\quad A\setminus B,\quad A\,\Delta\,B := (A\setminus B)\cup(B\setminus A) \]

are all in \(\Aa\), and for a countable index set \(I\) with \(\{A_i \mid i \in I\}\subseteq\Aa\) we have \(\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i \in \Aa\). (\(A\,\Delta\,B\) is the symmetric difference: the elements in exactly one of the two sets.)

The script gives no proof; it is Sheet 1, Exercise 3, worked below.

In words: the three axioms look stingy — only complements and countable unions — but they buy you every finite and countable set operation. In practice you may treat a \(\sigma\)-algebra as closed under anything you can build from countably many unions, intersections and complements.

Measurable spaces and Borel sets

Definition 1.11 measurable space, measurable sets Script 1.11

A measurable space [Messraum] is a tuple (an ordered pair) \((\Omega,\Aa)\) where \(\Omega\) is a set and \(\Aa\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\). The elements of \(\Aa\) are called measurable sets.

Note what is absent: no measure yet. A measurable space only says which sets we are allowed to measure, not how big they are. Adding the "how big" gives a measure space (Definition 1.17); requiring total size 1 gives a probability space (Definition 1.20).

Overview 1.12 why the word "measure" Script 1.12

The idea behind measurability is literally to measure the size of mathematical objects. We have good intuition for the size of

  1. subsets of \(\R\): the length of intervals,
  2. subsets of \(\R^2\): the area of surfaces,
  3. subsets of \(\R^3\): the volume of solids.

A rigorous formalism is needed for the corner cases: what volume should a line in 3D space have? What about the volume of an uncountable collection of points?

The script then makes the point that pays off later: we can also measure mass. To get the total mass of the earth's outer crust, take the density of the material and integrate it over the volume of the crust. "Integrate the density over a measure of volume to get a measure of mass" is the key idea behind densities. Another instance: integrate population density over an area to get a number of people.

Example 1.13 the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\R^n\) Script 1.13

Let \(\Omega = \R^n\) for \(n \in \N_{>0}\). The \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by the open boxes

\[ \bigl\{(a_1,b_1)\times(a_2,b_2)\times\cdots\times(a_n,b_n) \;\bigm|\; a_i < b_i \text{ for all } i\in[n]\bigr\} \;\subseteq\; \pow(\R^n) \]

is called the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\R^n\), written \(\mathcal B^n\). For \(n=1\) we simply write \(\mathcal B\).

Unpacking the notation. \((a,b)\) is the open interval \(\{x \in \R \mid a < x < b\}\); \(X \times Y := \{(x,y) \mid x \in X, y \in Y\}\) is the Cartesian product, so an open box in \(\R^2\) is an open rectangle and in \(\R^3\) an open brick. The generator is the set of all such boxes, for all choices of endpoints.

What \(\mathcal B\) contains. Far more than intervals. Since \(\sigma\)-algebras are closed under countable operations (Corollary 1.10): \([a,b] = \bigcap_{k\ge1}\bigl(a-\tfrac1k,\,b+\tfrac1k\bigr)\) is Borel; \(\{x\} = [x,x]\) is Borel; \(\Q = \bigcup_{q\in\Q}\{q\}\) is Borel, being a countable union of singletons. Every set you will ever write down explicitly is Borel. The sets that are not have to be conjured with the axiom of choice — see Theorem 1.28.

Remark 1.14 topological view on \(\mathcal B\) Script 1.14

If you know what a topology \(\mathcal O\) on a set \(\Omega\) is, you can try to prove that the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal B^n\) on \(\R^n\) is \(\sigma(\mathcal O^n)\), where \(\mathcal O^n\) is the standard topology on \(\R^n\).

Translation, for those who do not: a topology is a chosen collection of subsets declared "open"; the standard one on \(\R^n\) declares \(A\) open when every point of \(A\) has a small ball around it still inside \(A\). The remark says: generating from all open sets gives the same \(\sigma\)-algebra as generating from open boxes alone. The reason is that every open set is a countable union of boxes with rational corners. Sheet 2, Exercise 5 proves exactly this (with half-open rational intervals), and it is worked below, so you do not need any topology.

Lemma 1.15 induced \(\sigma\)-algebra Script 1.15

Let \((\Omega,\Aa)\) be a measurable space and \(B \subseteq \Omega\) a non-empty subset. Then

\[ \Aa|_B := \Aa \cap B := \{A \cap B \mid A \in \Aa\} \]

is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(B\), called the induced \(\sigma\)-algebra or the restriction of \(\Aa\) to \(B\). For \(\mathcal E \subseteq \pow(\Omega)\) we have \(\sigma(\mathcal E)|_B = \sigma(\mathcal E|_B)\).

Proof of the first claim supplied by me; the second claim is Sheet 3 Exercise 2

Note first that the ambient set is now \(B\), so "complement" inside \(\Aa|_B\) means \(B \setminus \cdot\), not \(\Omega\setminus\cdot\). Check the three axioms of Definition 1.6.

(i) \(B \in \Aa|_B\). Take \(A = \Omega\), which lies in \(\Aa\) by axiom (i). Then \(\Omega \cap B = B\). ✓

(ii) closed under complements in \(B\). Let \(C \in \Aa|_B\), so \(C = A \cap B\) for some \(A \in \Aa\). Then

\[ B \setminus C = B \setminus (A\cap B) = B \cap (A \cap B)^c = B \cap (A^c \cup B^c) = (B\cap A^c)\cup(B\cap B^c) = A^c \cap B, \]

where the second step is "\(X\setminus Y = X\cap Y^c\)", the third is de Morgan (Lemma 1.3), the fourth is distributivity of \(\cap\) over \(\cup\), i.e. \(X\cap(Y\cup Z)=(X\cap Y)\cup(X\cap Z)\) (B2 — distributive laws), and the last uses \(B \cap B^c = \emptyset\) together with \(S\cup\emptyset=S\). Since \(A^c \in \Aa\) by axiom (ii), the set \(A^c \cap B\) is of the required form. ✓

(iii) closed under countable unions. Let \(C_i = A_i \cap B\) with \(A_i \in \Aa\) for \(i \in \N\). Intersection distributes over union, so

\[ \bigcup_{i\in\N} C_i = \bigcup_{i\in\N}(A_i \cap B) = \Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i\Bigr)\cap B, \]

and \(\bigcup_i A_i \in \Aa\) by axiom (iii). ✓ ∎

Convention 1.16 — which \(\sigma\)-algebra is meant Script 1.16

In this course we always assume non-empty "continuous spaces" \(A \subseteq \R^n\) to be equipped with the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra restricted to \(A\), that is \(\mathcal B^n|_A\), and countable spaces to be equipped with their power set.

In words: from here on, whenever the script writes \([0,1]\) or \(\R\) or \(\{1,\dots,6\}\) without naming a \(\sigma\)-algebra, this convention has silently supplied one. In an exam, if you are asked to "set up the probability space", writing \(\Aa = \pow(\Omega)\) for a discrete \(\Omega\) and \(\Aa = \mathcal B|_\Omega\) for a continuous one is exactly what is expected.

Measures

Definition 1.17 measure, measure space Script 1.17

Let \((\Omega,\Aa)\) be a measurable space. We call \(\mu : \Aa \to [0,\infty]\) a measure [Maß] if

  1. \(\mu(\emptyset) = 0\),
  2. it is non-negative: \(\mu(A) \ge 0\) for all \(A \in \Aa\), and
  3. it is \(\sigma\)-additive: for all countable collections \((A_i)_{i\in\N}\) of pairwise disjoint sets in \(\Aa\),
\[ \mu\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i\Bigr) = \sum_{i\in\N}\mu(A_i). \]

The triple \((\Omega,\Aa,\mu)\) is then called a measure space.

Reading the pieces. The domain is \(\Aa\), not \(\pow(\Omega)\) — that restriction is the whole point of the previous subsection. The codomain \([0,\infty]\) includes \(+\infty\), so a measure may give a set infinite size (the length of \(\R\) is \(\infty\)). Condition (ii) is in fact implied by the codomain being \([0,\infty]\); the script lists it for emphasis. Condition (iii) is the only real condition: the size of a pile of non-overlapping pieces is the sum of their sizes.

Worth knowing: \(\sigma\)-additivity implies finite additivity. Given disjoint \(A, B\), set \(A_0 = A\), \(A_1 = B\) and \(A_i = \emptyset\) for \(i \ge 2\). These are still pairwise disjoint, their union is \(A \cup B\), and the infinite sum is \(\mu(A)+\mu(B)+0+0+\cdots\) using \(\mu(\emptyset) = 0\). So \(\mu(A\mathbin{\dot\cup}B) = \mu(A)+\mu(B)\). The same padding works for any finite number of pairwise disjoint sets \(A_0,\dots,A_m\) — set \(A_i=\emptyset\) for \(i>m\) — so \(\mu(A_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}A_m)=\mu(A_0)+\cdots+\mu(A_m)\). This padding step is used in almost every proof below (the proof of Proposition 1.19(i) uses it with three pieces).

Calculating with \(\infty\) in \([0,\infty]\) My addition

Because a measure may take the value \(+\infty\), the course calculates in the extended half-line \([0,\infty]=[0,\infty)\cup\{+\infty\}\). Here \(\infty\) is not a real number but a symbol for "bigger than every real number", and only these rules are allowed:

  • \(a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty\) for every \(a\in[0,\infty]\). Example: the length of \([0,1]\cup[2,\infty)\) is \(1+\infty=\infty\).
  • \(c\cdot\infty=\infty\) for \(c>0\), and by convention \(0\cdot\infty=0\) (a set of length 0 repeated "infinitely thick" still has no size — this convention is standard in measure theory).
  • \(\infty-\infty\) is not defined. That is why the subtraction rule in Proposition 1.19(ii) below needs \(\mu(A)<\infty\).
  • A series \(\sum_i a_i\) of terms \(a_i\ge0\) always has a value in \([0,\infty]\): its partial sums only grow, so they either converge to a real number or grow beyond every bound (value \(\infty\)). No convergence check is needed, which is why the right-hand side of \(\sigma\)-additivity always makes sense. Example: \(\sum_{i}c\) for a constant \(c\ge0\) is \(0\) if \(c=0\) and \(\infty\) if \(c>0\) — the fact the Vitali proofs turn on.

More detail: B4 — arithmetic in \([0,\infty]\); series with value \(+\infty\): Analysis 3.1.

Remark 1.18 \(\sigma\)-additivity is only countable Script 1.18

\(\sigma\)-additivity is defined only for countable collections. For uncountable collections the sum becomes problematic. The script's example: every single point \(\{x\}\) in \([0,1]\) has length 0, yet their uncountable union is \([0,1]\), which has length 1. If additivity were allowed over uncountable families we would conclude \(1 = 0\).

This is the same wall you hit on page 0 when trying to build a uniform distribution on \([0,1]\) from single-point probabilities. The axiom is written "countable" on purpose.

Proposition 1.19 basic properties of measures Script 1.19

Let \((\Omega,\Aa,\mu)\) be a measure space, \(A, B \in \Aa\), and \((A_i)_{i\in\N}\subseteq\Aa\). Then

  1. \(\mu(A\cup B) + \mu(A\cap B) = \mu(A) + \mu(B)\),
  2. \(\mu(B\setminus A) = \mu(B) - \mu(A)\), if \(A \subseteq B\) and \(\mu(A) < \infty\),
  3. \(\mu\) is monotone: \(A \subseteq B \implies \mu(A) \le \mu(B)\),
  4. \(\mu\) is continuous from below: \(\mu(A_k) \uparrow \mu\bigl(\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i\bigr)\) for \(A_0 \subseteq A_1 \subseteq A_2 \subseteq \cdots\),
  5. \(\mu\) is continuous from above: \(\mu(A_k) \downarrow \mu\bigl(\bigcap_{i\in\N}A_i\bigr)\) for \(A_0 \supseteq A_1 \supseteq \cdots\) with \(\mu(A_0) < \infty\),
  6. \(\mu\) is \(\sigma\)-subadditive: \(\mu\bigl(\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i\bigr) \le \sum_{i\in\N}\mu(A_i)\).

The script states all six without proof. All six are used constantly, so here they are.

Proofs of (i)–(vi) supplied by me — the script gives none

Throughout, "additivity" means the finite additivity derived in Definition 1.17 by padding with \(\emptyset\).

(i) \(\mu(A\cup B)+\mu(A\cap B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\). Split \(A\cup B\) into three pairwise disjoint pieces:

\[ A\cup B = (A\setminus B)\;\dot\cup\;(A\cap B)\;\dot\cup\;(B\setminus A). \]

All three are in \(\Aa\) by Corollary 1.10, and they are disjoint because each element of \(A \cup B\) is in exactly one of "only \(A\)", "both", "only \(B\)". Additivity gives

\[ \mu(A\cup B)=\mu(A\setminus B)+\mu(A\cap B)+\mu(B\setminus A). \]

Splitting \(A\) and \(B\) the same way, \(A = (A\setminus B)\,\dot\cup\,(A\cap B)\) and \(B = (B\setminus A)\,\dot\cup\,(A\cap B)\), so

\[ \mu(A)+\mu(B)=\mu(A\setminus B)+\mu(A\cap B)+\mu(B\setminus A)+\mu(A\cap B). \]

The first three terms on the right are exactly \(\mu(A\cup B)\), so the right-hand side equals \(\mu(A\cup B)+\mu(A\cap B)\). ✓

(ii) \(\mu(B\setminus A)=\mu(B)-\mu(A)\) when \(A\subseteq B\), \(\mu(A)<\infty\). Because \(A\subseteq B\), we may split \(B = A \,\dot\cup\, (B\setminus A)\) — every element of \(B\) is either in \(A\) or not, and the two pieces do not overlap. Additivity:

\[ \mu(B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B\setminus A). \]

Now subtract \(\mu(A)\) from both sides. This last step is where \(\mu(A) < \infty\) is needed: if \(\mu(A)=\infty\) then \(\mu(B)=\infty\) too and "\(\infty-\infty\)" is not a number. ✓

(iii) monotonicity. From the same split, \(\mu(B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B\setminus A)\ge\mu(A)\), since \(\mu(B\setminus A)\ge 0\) by non-negativity. No finiteness is needed here, because nothing is subtracted. ✓

(iv) continuity from below. Turn the growing sequence into disjoint rings:

\[ B_0 := A_0, \qquad B_k := A_k\setminus A_{k-1}\ (k\ge1). \]

Each \(B_k \in \Aa\) by Corollary 1.10. They are pairwise disjoint: for \(j < k\) we have \(B_j \subseteq A_j \subseteq A_{k-1}\) while \(B_k\) avoids \(A_{k-1}\) by construction. And they rebuild the sets:

\[ \bigcup_{i=0}^{k}B_i = A_k, \qquad \bigcup_{i\in\N}B_i=\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i, \]

the first by induction (adding the ring \(B_k\) to \(A_{k-1}\) gives \(A_k\)), the second because every \(\omega\) in some \(A_i\) lies in \(B_k\) for the smallest such index \(k\). Now apply \(\sigma\)-additivity and then the definition of an infinite sum as the limit of partial sums:

\[ \mu\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i\Bigr)=\sum_{i\in\N}\mu(B_i) =\lim_{k\to\infty}\sum_{i=0}^{k}\mu(B_i) =\lim_{k\to\infty}\mu(A_k). \]

The last equality is finite additivity applied to the \(k+1\) disjoint pieces \(B_0,\dots,B_k\): \(\sum_{i=0}^{k}\mu(B_i)=\mu\bigl(\bigcup_{i=0}^{k}B_i\bigr)=\mu(A_k)\).

The sequence \(\mu(A_k)\) increases by (iii), so the limit is an increasing limit: the arrow \(\uparrow\) is justified. ✓

(v) continuity from above. Flip the shrinking sequence into a growing one inside \(A_0\). Put \(C_k := A_0\setminus A_k\). Since \(A_k \supseteq A_{k+1}\), removing a smaller set leaves more: \(C_0 \subseteq C_1 \subseteq \cdots\). Their union is

\[ \bigcup_{k\in\N}C_k=\bigcup_{k\in\N}(A_0\setminus A_k)=A_0\setminus\bigcap_{k\in\N}A_k, \]

by de Morgan (Lemma 1.3) inside \(A_0\): being outside some \(A_k\) is being outside the intersection. Apply (iv) to \((C_k)\):

\[ \mu(C_k)\uparrow\mu\Bigl(A_0\setminus\bigcap_i A_i\Bigr). \]

Because \(A_k \subseteq A_0\) and \(\mu(A_0)<\infty\), monotonicity gives \(\mu(A_k)\le\mu(A_0)<\infty\), so (ii) applies to both sides:

\[ \mu(A_0)-\mu(A_k)\;\uparrow\;\mu(A_0)-\mu\Bigl(\bigcap_i A_i\Bigr). \]

Subtracting the whole line from the finite number \(\mu(A_0)\) reverses the arrow and gives \(\mu(A_k)\downarrow\mu(\bigcap_i A_i)\). ✓

Why \(\mu(A_0)<\infty\) cannot be dropped my addition: take \(\Omega=\R\) with the length measure (called Lebesgue measure; it gives \([a,b]\) the size \(b-a\)) and \(A_k=[k,\infty)\). Then \(\mu(A_k)=\infty\) for every \(k\), so the sequence \(\mu(A_k)\) stays at \(\infty\). But \(\bigcap_k A_k=\emptyset\) (no real number is \(\ge k\) for every \(k\)), and \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\). So \(\mu(A_k)\) does not converge to \(\mu(\bigcap_k A_k)\). This is the standard counterexample, and it is the reason (iv) carries no finiteness assumption while (v) does.

(vi) \(\sigma\)-subadditivity. Disjointify again, this time by removing everything seen before:

\[ B_0:=A_0,\qquad B_k:=A_k\setminus(A_0\cup\cdots\cup A_{k-1})\ (k\ge1). \]

These are in \(\Aa\), pairwise disjoint (an element enters at the first index where it appears and is excluded ever after), and \(\bigcup_i B_i=\bigcup_i A_i\). Crucially \(B_k\subseteq A_k\), so \(\mu(B_k)\le\mu(A_k)\) by monotonicity (iii). Hence

\[ \mu\Bigl(\bigcup_i A_i\Bigr)=\mu\Bigl(\bigcup_i B_i\Bigr)=\sum_i\mu(B_i)\le\sum_i\mu(A_i). \]

Equality holds, for example, when the \(A_i\) are pairwise disjoint (then \(B_k=A_k\)). ∎

In words: (i) inclusion–exclusion for two sets; (ii) subtracting a piece subtracts its size; (iii) bigger sets are not smaller; (iv) and (v) a measure respects limits of growing and shrinking sequences; (vi) overlapping pieces can only over-count.

Widget — continuity of measures, and when it fails My addition

Proposition 1.19(iv)–(v) with the length measure \(\lambda\). Move \(k\): the shaded set is \(A_k\); the dots are \(\lambda(A_1),\lambda(A_2),\dots\). From below, the lengths climb to the length of the union; from above, they fall to the length of the intersection — unless the lengths are infinite.

Probability measures

Definition 1.20 probability measure, probability space Script 1.20

Let \((\Omega,\Aa)\) be a measurable space. A measure \(\P:\Aa\to[0,\infty]\) is called a probability measure [Wahrscheinlichkeitsmaß] if \(\P(\Omega)=1\). The triple \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\) is then called a probability space [Wahrscheinlichkeitsraum]. In this case \(\Aa\) is called the event space or the set of events of interest.

That single extra line is Kolmogorov's axiomatisation. Unpacked, a probability measure satisfies: \(\P(A)\ge0\); \(\P(\Omega)=1\); and \(\P\) is \(\sigma\)-additive. Everything in this course follows from those three.

Immediate consequences worth memorising:

  • \(\P(A) \le 1\) for every \(A\), by monotonicity (Prop. 1.19(iii)) with \(A\subseteq\Omega\).
  • \(\P(A^c) = 1-\P(A)\), by Prop. 1.19(ii) with \(A \subseteq \Omega\) and \(\P(A)\le1<\infty\). This is Sheet 2 Exercise 1(i).
  • \(\P(\emptyset)=0\), from the measure axiom (i) — or from \(\P(\Omega^c)=1-1\).

Overview 1.21 probability as measure Script 1.21

Intuitively, the fact that probability is essentially a measure is the idea that we "measure the likelihood" of something happening. The machinery developed for measuring subsets of arbitrary spaces is exactly what we need to assign probabilities consistently — to measure the "size of subsets" according to their probability.

The script's diagram (which is also on the title page of the script), redrawn:

Left: the experiment produces an outcome somewhere in \(\Omega\); three events \(A, B, C\) are marked. Middle: those events, and everything you can build from them with complements and countable unions, make up the \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\Aa\). Right: \(\P\) sends each event to a number in \([0,1]\).

Theorem 1.22 inclusion–exclusion principle Script 1.22

Let \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\) be a probability space and \(A_1,\dots,A_n \in \Aa\) any finite collection of events (\(n\in\N_{>0}\)). Then

\[ \P\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}A_i\Bigr) =\sum_{k=1}^{n}(-1)^{k-1}\!\!\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n}\!\!\P\bigl(A_{i_1}\cap\cdots\cap A_{i_k}\bigr). \]

Script proof: "Exercises." — it is Sheet 2, Exercise 3.

Reading the double sum. The outer sum runs over the number \(k\) of sets being intersected. The inner sum runs over every way of choosing \(k\) indices out of \(n\) in increasing order — there are \(\binom{n}{k}\) such choices, where \(\binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}\) is the binomial coefficient [Binomialkoeffizient], the number of \(k\)-element subsets of an \(n\)-element set (B3 — binomial coefficients). The sign \((-1)^{k-1}\) is \(+\) for odd \(k\) and \(-\) for even \(k\). For \(n=3\) it reads

\[ \P(A\cup B\cup C)=\P(A)+\P(B)+\P(C)-\P(A\cap B)-\P(A\cap C)-\P(B\cap C)+\P(A\cap B\cap C), \]

which is exactly Sheet 2 Exercise 1(iv).

In words: add the pieces; you have double-counted every pairwise overlap, so subtract them; you have now removed the triple overlaps once too often, so add them back; and so on, alternating.

The counting version of this principle, with a proof by counting and the derangement example, is on B3 — inclusion–exclusion.

Proof by induction on \(n\) Sheet 2 · Ex 3 — restructured by me for readability

The method my addition: a proof by induction [vollständige Induktion] shows a statement for every \(n=1,2,3,\dots\) in two steps. Base case: prove it for \(n=1\). Induction step: assume it for some \(n\) (the induction hypothesis, IH) and deduce it for \(n+1\). Then it holds for 1, hence for 2, hence for 3, and so on — like dominoes. Taught from scratch in Analysis 2.2 — three tools.

Write \([n]=\{1,\dots,n\}\) and, for a non-empty \(S\subseteq[n]\), write \(A_S:=\bigcap_{i\in S}A_i\). Write \(|S|\) for the number of elements of \(S\) (its cardinality). Choosing an increasing tuple \(i_1<\cdots<i_k\) is the same as choosing a subset \(S\) of size \(k\), so the claim can be restated more compactly as

\[ \P\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}A_i\Bigr)=\sum_{\emptyset\ne S\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{|S|-1}\P(A_S). \tag{$\star$}\]

Base case \(n=1\). Only \(S=\{1\}\) occurs, with \((-1)^{0}=1\), so both sides are \(\P(A_1)\). ✓

The two-set case, which we will reuse. \(A\cup B=(A\setminus B)\,\dot\cup\,B\) — every element of the union is either in \(B\), or in \(A\) but not \(B\). Additivity gives \(\P(A\cup B)=\P(A\setminus B)+\P(B)\). Also \(A=(A\setminus B)\,\dot\cup\,(A\cap B)\), so \(\P(A\setminus B)=\P(A)-\P(A\cap B)\) by Prop. 1.19(ii) (all quantities are \(\le1\), hence finite). Substituting,

\[ \P(A\cup B)=\P(A)+\P(B)-\P(A\cap B). \tag{$\dagger$}\]

Induction step \(n\to n+1\). Assume \((\star)\) holds for \(n\). Put \(U:=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}A_i\). By \((\dagger)\) applied to \(U\) and \(A_{n+1}\),

\[ \P\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n+1}A_i\Bigr)=\P(U)+\P(A_{n+1})-\P(U\cap A_{n+1}). \]

Now handle the last term. Intersection distributes over union:

\[ U\cap A_{n+1}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(A_i\cap A_{n+1}\bigr)=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}B_i, \qquad B_i:=A_i\cap A_{n+1}. \]

That is a union of \(n\) events, so the induction hypothesis applies to it. For \(\emptyset \ne S\subseteq[n]\) we have \(\bigcap_{i\in S}B_i=\bigl(\bigcap_{i\in S}A_i\bigr)\cap A_{n+1}=A_{S\cup\{n+1\}}\), hence

\[ \P(U\cap A_{n+1})=\sum_{\emptyset\ne S\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{|S|-1}\P\bigl(A_{S\cup\{n+1\}}\bigr). \]

Putting the three pieces together and flipping the sign of the last sum:

\[ \P\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n+1}A_i\Bigr) =\underbrace{\sum_{\emptyset\ne S\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{|S|-1}\P(A_S)}_{\text{(1)}} +\underbrace{\P(A_{\{n+1\}})}_{\text{(2)}} +\underbrace{\sum_{\emptyset\ne S\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{|S|}\P\bigl(A_{S\cup\{n+1\}}\bigr)}_{\text{(3)}}. \]

Every non-empty \(T\subseteq[n+1]\) appears exactly once, with the right sign. There are three mutually exclusive cases for such a \(T\):

  • \(n+1\notin T\). Then \(T\subseteq[n]\) and \(T\) contributes once, in (1), with sign \((-1)^{|T|-1}\). ✓
  • \(T=\{n+1\}\). It contributes once, in (2), with sign \(+1=(-1)^{1-1}\). ✓
  • \(n+1\in T\) and \(T\ne\{n+1\}\). Then \(T=S\cup\{n+1\}\) for the unique non-empty \(S=T\setminus\{n+1\}\subseteq[n]\), and it contributes once, in (3), with sign \((-1)^{|S|}=(-1)^{|T|-1}\). ✓

So the right-hand side equals \(\sum_{\emptyset\ne T\subseteq[n+1]}(-1)^{|T|-1}\P(A_T)\), which is \((\star)\) for \(n+1\). ∎

A remark of mine. The official solution proves the same thing but keeps the "\(i_1<\cdots<i_k\)" tuple notation, which forces an index shift \(k \to k-1\) near the end and is hard to follow. Switching to subsets \(S\) removes the shift entirely. There is also a slicker proof using indicator functions and the identity \(\one_{(\bigcup A_i)^c}=\prod_i(1-\one_{A_i})\) (\(\prod_i\) = the product over all \(i\); see B3 — product notation), but it needs expectations, which arrive only in §2.1.

The bonus part of Sheet 2 Exercise 3 asks you to show the dual formula \(\P(A_1\cap\cdots\cap A_n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(-1)^{k-1}\sum_{\{i_1,\dots,i_k\}\subseteq[n]} \P(A_{i_1}\cup\cdots\cup A_{i_k})\). In subset notation, with \(U_S:=\bigcup_{i\in S}A_i\): \(\P(A_{[n]})=\sum_{\emptyset\ne S\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{|S|-1}\P(U_S)\). The official solution does not work the bonus; here is a full solution mine.

Step 1 (complement). By de Morgan (Lemma 1.3), \(\bigcap_{i=1}^n A_i=\bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i^c\bigr)^c\), so \(\P(A_{[n]})=1-\P\bigl(\bigcup_i A_i^c\bigr)\).

Step 2 (apply \((\star)\) to the events \(A_i^c\)).

\[ \P\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i^c\Bigr)=\sum_{\emptyset\ne S\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{|S|-1} \P\Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in S}A_i^c\Bigr). \]

Step 3 (complement again). By de Morgan, \(\bigcap_{i\in S}A_i^c=(U_S)^c\), so \(\P\bigl(\bigcap_{i\in S}A_i^c\bigr)=1-\P(U_S)\). Substituting and splitting the sum:

\[ \P(A_{[n]})=1-\sum_{\emptyset\ne S\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{|S|-1} +\sum_{\emptyset\ne S\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{|S|-1}\P(U_S). \]

Step 4 (the constant sum equals 1). There are \(\binom nk\) subsets of size \(k\), so \(\sum_{S\ne\emptyset}(-1)^{|S|-1}=\sum_{k=1}^n\binom nk(-1)^{k-1}=1-\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk(-1)^k =1-(1-1)^n=1\), by the binomial theorem \((a+b)^n=\sum_k\binom nk a^kb^{n-k}\) with \(a=-1,b=1\). So the first two terms give \(1-1=0\), and what remains is exactly the claimed formula. ∎

Check with \(n=2\): \(\P(A_1\cap A_2)=\P(A_1)+\P(A_2)-\P(A_1\cup A_2)\), which is \((\dagger)\) rearranged. ✓

Small slips in the official induction: the base case is labelled "(IH)" instead of "base case" and starts at \(n=2\) (the case \(n=1\) is trivially true, so no harm).

Widget — inclusion–exclusion, term by term My addition

420 points are scattered once in the box and never move. Three circular events \(A, B, C\) sit on top of them; the sliders move and resize the circles. The panel computes both sides of Theorem 1.22 for \(n = 3\): the direct count of \(A \cup B \cup C\), and the seven-term alternating sum. They agree in every configuration, which is what "identity" means.

Cumulative distribution functions

Definition 1.23 cumulative distribution function (cdf) Script 1.23

Let \(\P\) be a probability measure on \((\R,\mathcal B)\). The cumulative distribution function [Verteilungsfunktion] of \(\P\) is

\[ F_\P:\R\to[0,1],\qquad x\mapsto\P\bigl((-\infty,x]\bigr), \]

often written just \(F\) when \(\P\) is clear.

Reading it. \((-\infty,x]\) is everything up to and including \(x\). So \(F(x)\) answers "what is the probability of landing at or below \(x\)?" Note the definition applies only to measures on the real line — it uses the order structure of \(\R\), which an abstract \(\Omega\) does not have.

Why bother, when we already have \(\P\)? Because \(F\) is a single function \(\R\to[0,1]\), while \(\P\) is a function on the enormous collection \(\mathcal B\). Theorem 1.25 below says no information is lost: the small object determines the big one.

Widget — build a cdf and read the jumps My addition

Put probability mass on the three points \(0, 1, 2\) and watch the staircase. The open circle at the left of each step and the filled circle at the right are the picture of right-continuity (Lemma 1.24(ii)); the height of each jump is \(\P(\{x\})\) (Lemma 1.24(iv)). The preset reproduces Sheet 2, Exercise 1(vi): the sum of two fair coin flips.

Lemma 1.24 properties of cdfs Script 1.24

Let \((\R,\mathcal B,\P)\) be a probability space and \(F\) the cdf of \(\P\). Then

  1. \(F\) is monotonically increasing: \(x \le y \implies F(x)\le F(y)\).
  2. \(F\) is right-continuous: for all \(x_n\downarrow x\) in \(\R\), \(F(x_n)\downarrow F(x)\).
  3. \(F\) has a left-hand limit: for all \(x_n\uparrow x\), \(F(x_n)\uparrow F(x^-):=\P\bigl((-\infty,x)\bigr)\).
  4. the discontinuities correspond to singleton probabilities: \(F(x)-F(x^-)=\P(\{x\})\) for all \(x\in\R\).
  5. \(\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0\) and \(\lim_{x\to\infty}F(x)=1\).

(Background: \(x_n\downarrow x\) means the sequence decreases and converges to \(x\), i.e. approaches \(x\) from the right; \(x_n\uparrow x\) approaches from the left. One-sided limits of a function, defined through exactly such sequences, are stated in Analysis 9.1; continuity via sequences in Analysis 4.1.)

Proof of (i)–(v) supplied by me — the script gives none

Everything is an application of Proposition 1.19 to cleverly chosen sequences of sets.

(i) monotone. If \(x\le y\) then \((-\infty,x]\subseteq(-\infty,y]\), because any \(t\le x\) also satisfies \(t\le y\). Monotonicity of measures, Prop. 1.19(iii), gives \(\P((-\infty,x])\le\P((-\infty,y])\), i.e. \(F(x)\le F(y)\). ✓

(ii) right-continuity. Let \(x_n\downarrow x\), so \(x_1\ge x_2\ge\cdots\) and \(x_n\to x\). The sets \(A_n:=(-\infty,x_n]\) then shrink: \(A_1\supseteq A_2\supseteq\cdots\). Their intersection is

\[ \bigcap_{n}(-\infty,x_n]=(-\infty,x], \]

because \(t\le x_n\) for every \(n\) holds exactly when \(t\le\inf_n x_n=x\). Since \(\P(A_1)\le1<\infty\), continuity from above (Prop. 1.19(v)) applies and gives \(\P(A_n)\downarrow\P((-\infty,x])\), i.e. \(F(x_n)\downarrow F(x)\). ✓

(iii) left-hand limit. Let \(x_n\uparrow x\) with \(x_n < x\). The sets \(A_n:=(-\infty,x_n]\) now grow. Their union is

\[ \bigcup_n(-\infty,x_n]=(-\infty,x), \]

the open half-line: if \(t<x\) then, since \(x_n\to x\), some \(x_n\) exceeds \(t\), so \(t\in A_n\); conversely every \(t\in A_n\) satisfies \(t\le x_n<x\). Continuity from below (Prop. 1.19(iv)) gives \(F(x_n)\uparrow\P((-\infty,x))=F(x^-)\). ✓

(iv) jumps are point masses. \((-\infty,x)\subseteq(-\infty,x]\) and the difference of the two sets is exactly \(\{x\}\). Both have finite measure, so Prop. 1.19(ii) gives

\[ \P(\{x\})=\P\bigl((-\infty,x]\bigr)-\P\bigl((-\infty,x)\bigr)=F(x)-F(x^-). \;✓ \]

In particular \(F\) is continuous at \(x\) exactly when \(\P(\{x\})=0\).

(v) the two limits. \(F\) is monotone by (i). For a monotone function it is enough to check one sequence in each direction: if \(x\le -n\) then \(0\le F(x)\le F(-n)\), and if \(x\ge n\) then \(F(n)\le F(x)\le 1\), so \(F(x)\) is squeezed as soon as \(F(-n)\to0\) and \(F(n)\to1\). Take \(A_n:=(-\infty,-n]\); these shrink with \(\bigcap_n A_n=\emptyset\) (no real number is below every \(-n\)) and \(\P(A_0)\le1<\infty\), so Prop. 1.19(v) gives \(F(-n)\downarrow\P(\emptyset)=0\). Take \(B_n:=(-\infty,n]\); these grow with \(\bigcup_n B_n=\R\), so Prop. 1.19(iv) gives \(F(n)\uparrow\P(\R)=1\). ∎

A note on (iii). The statement is only interesting for sequences with \(x_n<x\); if some \(x_n\) equalled \(x\) the union would be \((-\infty,x]\) and the limit would be \(F(x)\), not \(F(x^-)\). So the arrow \(\uparrow\) in the script has to be read here as "increasing to \(x\) from strictly below", i.e. \(x_0\le x_1\le\cdots\), \(x_n\to x\) and \(x_n<x\) for every \(n\).

In words: a cdf is a staircase that never goes down, starts at height 0 on the far left, ends at height 1 on the far right, and includes the right-hand endpoint of every step. The height of a step at \(x\) is the probability of the single point \(x\).

Theorem 1.25 correspondence of cdfs Script 1.25

For any \(F:\R\to[0,1]\) that satisfies (i), (ii) and (v) of Lemma 1.24, there exists a unique probability measure \(\lambda_F\) on \((\R,\mathcal B)\) such that \(F_{\lambda_F}=F\). For any probability measure \(\P\) on \((\R,\mathcal B)\) we have \(\P=\lambda_{F_\P}\).

In words: cdfs and probability measures on the real line are the same information in two formats. Monotone + right-continuous + limits 0 and 1 is not just necessary for being a cdf — it is sufficient. Give me such an \(F\) and I can hand you back the measure, and there is only one.

Why this is the most useful theorem on the page. It means you may always specify a distribution by writing down a single function of one real variable. Every named continuous distribution in §1.3 is introduced this way, and the "determine the cdf" exam task SoSe25 P3b is implicitly invoking it. (WiSe25 P3b and WiSe25 P5 also work with a cdf, but they are given one rather than asked to construct it.)

The script gives no proof, and none is expected of you. For orientation: existence comes from Carathéodory's extension theorem — one defines the measure on intervals by \(\lambda_F((a,b]):=F(b)-F(a)\) and extends it to all of \(\mathcal B\); uniqueness comes from the fact that the intervals \((a,b]\) are closed under intersection and generate \(\mathcal B\). Note the contrast with WiSe25 P1c below, where the generator is not closed under intersection and uniqueness fails.

Caveat 1.26 the measure problem Script 1.26

Generally, we cannot construct useful (probability) measures on the power set of infinite spaces. Therefore we need \(\sigma\)-algebras to talk meaningfully about probability theory.

Why \(\sigma\)-algebras are unavoidable: the Vitali theorems

Both proofs below are proofs by contradiction [Widerspruchsbeweis]: to show that something does not exist, assume it does, compute, and arrive at an impossible statement (here: \(1=0\) or \(1=\infty\)). Since correct steps cannot lead from a true assumption to a false conclusion, the assumption must be false. The model example is the proof that \(\sqrt2\) is irrational: Analysis 1.1 — √2 is not rational. The step "a countable sum of one constant is \(0\) or \(\infty\)" uses the rules for \([0,\infty]\) from the box after Definition 1.17.

Theorem 1.27 Vitali, 1905 Script 1.27

Let \(\Omega=\{0,1\}^{\N}\) be the sample space of infinitely many repeated coin tosses. For \(n\in\N\) define \(T_n:\Omega\to\Omega\) by

\[ \omega=(\omega_n)_{n\in\N}\;\mapsto\;T_n(\omega):=(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_{n-1},\,1-\omega_n,\,\omega_{n+1},\dots), \]

the map that flips the result of the \(n\)-th coin toss. For \(A\in\pow(\Omega)\) let \(T_n(A):=\{T_n(\omega)\mid\omega\in A\}\). Then there does not exist a probability measure \(\P\) on the power set \(\pow(\Omega)\) satisfying the invariance property \(\P(T_n(A))=\P(A)\) for all \(A\in\pow(\Omega)\) and \(n\in\N\).

Unpacking \(\{0,1\}^{\N}\): an element is an infinite sequence of 0s and 1s, one per toss — \(\omega = (0,1,1,0,1,\dots)\). This set is uncountable, with the same size as \([0,1]\) (read the sequence as binary digits). The map \(T_n\) leaves every toss alone except the \(n\)-th, which it flips (\(1-0=1\), \(1-1=0\)). Example: \(T_2(0,1,1,0,\dots)=(0,0,1,0,\dots)\) if we count the tosses as first, second, third, …

A small indexing slip in the script: since \(0\in\N\) (Convention 1.1), the sequence \((\omega_n)_{n\in\N}\) starts with \(\omega_0\), but the formula for \(T_n\) lists it from \(\omega_1\). Nothing depends on this; read the formula as "change entry \(n\), keep all others".

Proof sketch supplied by me — the script states this without proof

The argument has the same shape as Theorem 1.28 below, which the script does prove in full.

1. A countable collection of moves. Let \(G\) be the set of all maps obtained by composing finitely many of the \(T_n\) — that is, all "flip the tosses in a finite set \(S\subseteq\N\)" operations. Each such map is determined by the finite set \(S\), and the collection of finite subsets of \(\N\) is countable (there are countably many of size 1, of size 2, and so on, and a countable union of countable sets is countable). So \(G\) is countable.

2. An equivalence relation. Declare \(\omega\sim\omega'\) when they differ in only finitely many positions — equivalently, when \(\omega'=g(\omega)\) for some \(g\in G\). This is an equivalence relation: every \(\omega\) differs from itself in zero places; the relation is symmetric because flipping back undoes a flip; and it is transitive because a finite set union a finite set is finite.

3. Choose representatives. Using the axiom of choice, pick exactly one element from each equivalence class and collect them into \(V\subseteq\Omega\).

4. The translates tile \(\Omega\). The sets \(g(V)\) for \(g\in G\) are pairwise disjoint (two representatives in the same class would have to be equal) and their union is all of \(\Omega\) (every \(\omega\) is \(g\)-related to its own representative). So \(\Omega=\dot\bigcup_{g\in G}g(V)\), a countable disjoint union.

5. The contradiction. Each \(g\) is a composition of finitely many \(T_n\), so repeated use of the invariance property gives \(\P(g(V))=\P(V)\) for every \(g\in G\). By \(\sigma\)-additivity,

\[ 1=\P(\Omega)=\sum_{g\in G}\P\bigl(g(V)\bigr)=\sum_{g\in G}\P(V). \]

The right-hand side is a countably infinite sum of one and the same number. If \(\P(V)=0\) it is 0; if \(\P(V)>0\) it is \(+\infty\). It can never be 1. Contradiction. ∎

Theorem 1.28 Vitali set on \([0,1)\) Script 1.28

Let \(\Omega=[0,1)\) and for \(A\subseteq[0,1)\) and \(q\in\Q\) define the rational translate modulo 1 by

\[ A\oplus q:=\{(x+q)\bmod 1 \mid x\in A\}. \]

Then there does not exist a probability measure \(\P\) on \(\pow([0,1))\) such that

  1. \(\P([a,b))=b-a\) for all \(0\le a\le b\le1\),
  2. \(\P(A\oplus q)=\P(A)\) for all \(A\in\pow([0,1))\) and \(q\in\Q\).

In particular, there exists a subset \(V\subseteq[0,1)\) that is not in \(\mathcal B\), i.e. not Borel measurable.

Notation help: \(x \bmod 1\) is the fractional part of \(x\) — what is left after discarding the whole-number part, so \(1.7 \bmod 1 = 0.7\). Adding \(q\) modulo 1 is "slide everything to the right by \(q\), and whatever falls off the right end reappears at the left": bend \([0,1)\) into a circle and rotate it.

Proof the script's own proof, with my annotations in italics

Define an equivalence relation on \([0,1)\) by

\[ x\sim y \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; x-y\in\Q. \]

An equivalence relation is a way of declaring elements "the same for present purposes"; it must be reflexive (\(x\sim x\), true since \(x-x=0\in\Q\)), symmetric (true since \(-(x-y)\) is rational whenever \(x-y\) is) and transitive (true since a sum of rationals is rational). It carves \([0,1)\) into disjoint equivalence classes, each consisting of numbers differing from one another by a rational.

Using the axiom of choice, pick one representative from each equivalence class and collect them in a set \(V\subseteq[0,1)\). This is the classical Vitali set.

(Equivalence relations and the axiom of choice are set up from scratch on B2.)

The axiom of choice says that from any family of non-empty sets one can simultaneously pick an element of each. Here the family is uncountable and there is no rule that names the picks — this non-constructive step is exactly why \(V\) can be so badly behaved.

For each \(q\in\Q\cap[0,1)\) define \(V_q:=V\oplus q\).

These sets are pairwise disjoint. Suppose \(x\in V_q\cap V_r\). Then

\[ x=(v+q)\bmod1=(w+r)\bmod1 \]

for some \(v,w\in V\). Thus \((v+q)-(w+r)\) is an integer, so \(v-w\) differs from \(r-q\) by an integer and is therefore rational. Hence \(v\) and \(w\) lie in the same equivalence class. Since \(V\) contains exactly one representative from each class, \(v=w\), and then \(q=r\).

They cover all of \([0,1)\). For any \(x\in[0,1)\), let \(v\in V\) be the chosen representative of the class of \(x\). Then \(x-v\in\Q\), so after reducing modulo 1 we obtain some \(q\in\Q\cap[0,1)\) with \(x=(v+q)\bmod1\in V_q\). Therefore

\[ [0,1)=\bigcup_{q\in\Q\cap[0,1)}V_q. \]

And \(\Q\cap[0,1)\) is countable, so this is a countable disjoint union — exactly the situation \(\sigma\)-additivity speaks about.

The contradiction. By \(\sigma\)-additivity and translation invariance,

\[ 1=\P([0,1))=\sum_{q\in\Q\cap[0,1)}\P(V_q)=\sum_{q\in\Q\cap[0,1)}\P(V). \]

The first equality uses assumption (i) with \(a=0,b=1\); the third uses assumption (ii), which forces every translate to have the same measure as \(V\) itself.

But \(\Q\cap[0,1)\) is countably infinite. Hence the right-hand side is either 0 if \(\P(V)=0\), or \(+\infty\) if \(\P(V)>0\). It can never equal 1 — a contradiction.

So no such probability measure on \(\pow([0,1))\) exists. Moreover, \(V\) cannot be Borel measurable: otherwise all \(V_q\) would also be Borel measurable. We will see that we can define a cdf for the uniform distribution on \([0,1)\), and Theorem 1.25 then guarantees a uniform measure on \(\mathcal B|_{[0,1)}\), under which all \(V_q\) have the same probability. Again \(\sigma\)-additivity on the partition of \([0,1)\) into the \(V_q\) leads to the same contradiction. ∎

That last paragraph is the sharpest part. The first half of the proof says "no measure on the whole power set". The second half says something stronger and more concrete: the measure we do have, the uniform one on the Borel sets, cannot possibly have \(V\) in its domain. So \(\mathcal B|_{[0,1)} \subsetneq \pow([0,1))\) — the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra on \([0,1)\) (that is, \(\mathcal B\) restricted to \([0,1)\) in the sense of Lemma 1.15) really is strictly smaller than the power set, and we have a named example of what is missing.

Remark 1.29 how to interpret the two Vitali theorems Script 1.29

The invariance property in Theorem 1.27 states that every sequence of coin tosses should be exactly as probable as the one where the \(n\)-th flip came out differently. The invariance in Theorem 1.28 states that the probability of a set of locations in \([0,1)\) should not change if the set is shifted by a rational amount around the circle. Both are very natural symmetry principles.

The point of the theorems is not that these symmetries are unreasonable. The point is that demanding them on the full power set is too much. If we insist on using \(\pow(\Omega)\) for infinite spaces, then even very natural symmetry requirements become inconsistent with countable additivity. So while \(\pow(\Omega)\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra, it is generally too large for a useful probability theory on infinite spaces, and we must work with a smaller \(\sigma\)-algebra of measurable sets.

The second construction makes this concrete: \(V\subseteq[0,1)\) cannot be assigned a translation-invariant probability compatible with interval length, and is a concrete example of a non-Borel subset of \([0,1)\). "This is one of the central reasons \(\sigma\)-algebras are not just technical decoration but genuinely necessary."

Interpretations of probability

The script marks this stretch "— Start Philosophical Interlude —". No exam task has ever come from it. Read it once; it is what gives the axioms their meaning.

Remark 1.30 interpretations of probability Script 1.30

Connecting back to Remark 0.9: the probability space \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\) does not necessarily represent a physically real source of randomness, but rather our ignorance or the limits of our knowledge. \(\P\) is our best description, and \(\Omega\) a convenient representation of the outcomes. Randomness is thus typically not "in nature" but "in our model". Probability theory is a quantitative framework for reasoning consistently about uncertainty, not an explanation of some intrinsic source of randomness. The script's working premise from here on: probability is useful.

In practice we call \(A\in\Aa\) an event and \(\P(A)\) the probability that \(A\) happens. An event may consist of several outcomes: "rolling a 1 or a 3" is a valid event, with probability \(\tfrac13\) for a fair die, even though only one of the two can occur in any given roll. The three common interpretations:

  1. naive: "nature is not sure" what it does, and \(\P(A)\) is the degree of uncertainty with which it decides for \(A\);
  2. frequentist: \(\P(A)\) is the relative frequency with which \(A\) tends to occur under the same external conditions;
  3. subjective: \(\P(A)\) is the degree of certainty with which, based on my personal assessment of the situation, I am willing to bet on \(A\).

Viewpoint 1.31 probability from gambling: the Dutch book argument Script 1.31

We started directly with Kolmogorov's axioms. Besides "falling from the heavens", they can also be derived from other principles. The Dutch book arguments show that if a person's subjective probabilities violate the axioms of probability, a bettor can construct a list of bets that guarantees that person loses money. Consequently, rational belief assignments must obey the axioms of probability to avoid inconsistency.

A concrete instance, mine: suppose you claim \(\P(A)=0.6\) and \(\P(A^c)=0.6\), violating \(\P(A)+\P(A^c)=1\). I sell you a ticket paying 1 € if \(A\) happens, for 0.60 €, and another paying 1 € if \(A^c\) happens, for 0.60 €. You have paid 1.20 € and exactly one of the two tickets pays out 1 €. You lose 0.20 € no matter what happens. This is what "guaranteed to lose" means, and it is the reason the relative in Example 0.3 finally asks the doctor for betting odds: a bet is a way of forcing a vague degree of belief to become a number that obeys the axioms.

Viewpoint 1.32 probability from logic and partial beliefs Script 1.32

Jaynes (2003) builds the axioms of probability by extending classical logic to settings with uncertainty due to incomplete information. Leaning on basic principles of rational reasoning — consistency, and the ability to rank plausibility — he shows that any system for manipulating degrees of belief must obey the rules of probability. This motivates the axioms as the unique rational calculus for reasoning under uncertainty.

The script adds, disarmingly: "I would have loved to take this approach in the lecture as well, but due to a lack of time we just dumped the final framework onto you."

The script also recommends a podcast on the "Logic and Use of Probability" with the philosopher Branden Fitelson. It explains how probabilities can (and cannot) be used to judge how strongly evidence supports or undermines a scientific claim.

Remark 1.33 Bayes vs. frequentist Script 1.33

It is often said there are two approaches to probability.

  • The frequentist approach interprets probabilities as long-run relative frequencies of events in repeated trials. The parameters of the underlying experiment are considered fixed but unknown.
  • The Bayesian approach interprets probability as a degree of belief, or credence, allowing uncertainty about the parameters to be modelled directly with probability distributions. Bayesians have less trouble talking about events that by their nature can only happen once.

Bayesians rely on prior beliefs — one must start with some credences. Frequentists rely on repeatedly sampling from identical distributions, at least conceptually, and avoid prior beliefs. The script promises more detail later; it arrives in §3.5.

Here the script marks "— End Philosophical Interlude —". The mathematics resumes in §1.2.

Exercise-sheet tasks

Sheet 1, Exercise 1 — de Morgan's laws Sheet 1 · Ex 1

Prove, for \(\Omega\ne\emptyset\) and an arbitrary family \(\{A_\alpha\in\pow(\Omega)\mid\alpha\in I\}\):

\[ \Bigl(\bigcap_\alpha A_\alpha\Bigr)^c=\bigcup_\alpha A_\alpha^c,\qquad \Bigl(\bigcup_\alpha A_\alpha\Bigr)^c=\bigcap_\alpha A_\alpha^c. \]

The method: prove set equality by proving two inclusions

\(X=Y\) means \(X\subseteq Y\) and \(Y\subseteq X\) (the script's Definition A.1 in Appendix A.1). To show \(X\subseteq Y\), take an arbitrary \(x\in X\) and derive \(x\in Y\). "Arbitrary" is what makes the conclusion hold for all elements. This is the standard shape of every set-identity proof in this course; it is set up with worked examples on B2 — subsets and set equality.

Proof of the second identity in full the sheet's argument, written out step by step

"\(\subseteq\)": Let \(x\in\bigl(\bigcup_\alpha A_\alpha\bigr)^c\). By definition of complement, \(x\notin\bigcup_\alpha A_\alpha\). By definition of union, "\(x\) is in the union" means "there exists \(\alpha\) with \(x\in A_\alpha\)"; so its negation means for every \(\alpha\), \(x\notin A_\alpha\), that is \(x\in A_\alpha^c\) for every \(\alpha\). By definition of intersection, \(x\in\bigcap_\alpha A_\alpha^c\). Since \(x\) was arbitrary, \(\bigl(\bigcup_\alpha A_\alpha\bigr)^c\subseteq\bigcap_\alpha A_\alpha^c\).

"\(\supseteq\)": Let \(x\in\bigcap_\alpha A_\alpha^c\). Then \(x\in A_\alpha^c\) for every \(\alpha\), i.e. \(x\notin A_\alpha\) for every \(\alpha\). So there is no \(\alpha\) with \(x\in A_\alpha\), which means \(x\notin\bigcup_\alpha A_\alpha\), i.e. \(x\in\bigl(\bigcup_\alpha A_\alpha\bigr)^c\).

Both inclusions hold, so the two sets are equal. The first identity follows by the same argument with the roles of \(\exists\) and \(\forall\) swapped — or by applying the proved identity to the family \((A_\alpha^c)\) and taking complements. ∎

On the official solution. It works the first identity \(\bigl(\bigcap_\alpha A_\alpha\bigr)^c=\bigcup_\alpha A_\alpha^c\) and says the second one "follows analogously"; what is written out above is that second one. The official argument is correct, but it compresses its very first step: from \(x\in\bigl(\bigcap_\alpha A_\alpha\bigr)^c\) it concludes at once "there exists an \(\alpha\in I\) such that \(x\notin A_\alpha\)". That step is the negation of a "for all" statement — \(x\) lies in the intersection exactly when \(x\in A_\alpha\) for every \(\alpha\), so \(x\) lies outside it exactly when that fails for at least one \(\alpha\) (Analysis 1.1 — quantifiers and their negation). Everything after that is the same element chase as above.

Sheet 1, Exercise 2 — inverse images Sheet 1 · Ex 2

Let \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\) be non-empty, \(f:\Omega_1\to\Omega_2\) an arbitrary map and \(\mathcal C\subseteq\pow(\Omega_2)\) a collection of subsets. Show: (i) \(A\subseteq B \implies f^{-1}(A)\subseteq f^{-1}(B)\); (ii) \(f^{-1}\bigl(\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal C}A\bigr)=\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal C}f^{-1}(A)\); (iii) \(f^{-1}(A^c)=\bigl(f^{-1}(A)\bigr)^c\).

First, what \(f^{-1}\) means here My addition — the sheet does not define it

For \(A\subseteq\Omega_2\), the inverse image [Urbild] is

\[ f^{-1}(A):=\{\omega\in\Omega_1 \mid f(\omega)\in A\}. \]

This does not require \(f\) to be invertible. \(f^{-1}\) is not a function \(\Omega_2\to \Omega_1\); it is a map \(\pow(\Omega_2)\to\pow(\Omega_1)\) taking sets to sets. It always exists, for every \(f\). Confusing it with an inverse function is the single most common mistake in this exercise.

Proofs Sheet 1 · Ex 2, rewritten by me for precision

(i) Let \(\omega\in f^{-1}(A)\). By definition \(f(\omega)\in A\). Since \(A\subseteq B\), also \(f(\omega)\in B\), so \(\omega\in f^{-1}(B)\). ✓

(ii) Chain of equivalences, each step just unfolding a definition:

\[ \omega\in f^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal C}A\Bigr) \iff f(\omega)\in\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal C}A \iff \exists A\in\mathcal C: f(\omega)\in A \iff \exists A\in\mathcal C: \omega\in f^{-1}(A) \iff \omega\in\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal C}f^{-1}(A). \;✓ \]

(iii) Same style:

\[ \omega\in f^{-1}(A^c)\iff f(\omega)\in A^c\iff f(\omega)\notin A \iff \omega\notin f^{-1}(A)\iff\omega\in\bigl(f^{-1}(A)\bigr)^c. \;✓ \;\;∎ \]

On the official solution. Its proofs say things like "there exists \(a\in A\) such that \(f(\omega)=a\)", which is a roundabout way of writing \(f(\omega)\in A\); and in (iii) the "\(\Longleftarrow\)" direction asserts "there exists \(a\in A^c\) such that \(f(\omega)=a\)" as though it were given, when it is the thing being derived. The conclusions are all correct — the write-ups are just loose. The equivalence-chain form above is shorter and cannot go wrong.

Why this exercise matters: these three properties are exactly the three \(\sigma\)-algebra axioms in disguise. They are what makes Exercise 6 and Sheet 3 Exercise 1 work, and they are why inverse images behave and forward images do not — the content of SoSe26 P2b.

Sheet 1, Exercise 3 — closure properties (= Corollary 1.10) Sheet 1 · Ex 3

\(\Aa\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra over \(\Omega\ne\emptyset\), \(A_0,A_1,A_2,\dots\in\Aa\), \(m\in\N\). Show that \(\Omega\), \(A_0\setminus A_1\), \(\bigcup_{i=0}^{m}A_i\), \(\bigcap_{i=0}^{m}A_i\) and \(\bigcap_{i\in\N}A_i\) are in \(\Aa\).

Proof Sheet 1 · Ex 3

\(\Omega\in\Aa\). This is axiom (i) of Definition 1.6 directly. (The official solution derives it as \(\Omega=\emptyset^c\), which presupposes \(\emptyset\in\Aa\) — also fine, but it is one step longer than necessary given how the script states the axioms.)

Finite unions. Axiom (iii) speaks about infinite sequences, so pad. Define

\[ B_i:=\begin{cases}A_i & i\le m,\\ \emptyset & i>m.\end{cases} \]

Each \(B_i\in\Aa\) (the \(A_i\) by assumption, \(\emptyset=\Omega^c\) by axioms (i) and (ii)). By axiom (iii), \(\bigcup_{i\in\N}B_i\in\Aa\). Since adding \(\emptyset\) changes no union, \(\bigcup_{i\in\N}B_i=\bigcup_{i=0}^{m}A_i\). ✓

Finite intersections. By axiom (ii), \(A_0^c,\dots,A_m^c\in\Aa\). By the finite-union result just proved, \(\bigcup_{i=0}^{m}A_i^c\in\Aa\). By axiom (ii) again its complement is in \(\Aa\), and by de Morgan (Lemma 1.3)

\[ \bigcap_{i=0}^{m}A_i=\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=0}^{m}A_i^c\Bigr)^{c}\in\Aa. \;✓ \]

Countable intersections. Identical, using axiom (iii) instead of the finite-union result: \(\bigcap_{i\in\N}A_i=\bigl(\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i^c\bigr)^c\in\Aa\). ✓

\(A_0\setminus A_1\in\Aa\). An element is in \(A_0\setminus A_1\) when it is in \(A_0\) and not in \(A_1\), so \(A_0\setminus A_1=A_0\cap A_1^c\). Here \(A_1^c\in\Aa\) by axiom (ii), and the intersection of the two sets \(A_0, A_1^c\) is in \(\Aa\) by the finite-intersection result (with \(m=1\)). ✓ (We prove this after intersections on purpose. The official solution states it first and calls it "immediate", although it uses the intersection result proved later.)

Symmetric difference (in Corollary 1.10 but not on the sheet): \(A\,\Delta\,B=(A\setminus B)\cup(B\setminus A)\) is a union of two sets already shown to be in \(\Aa\). ∎

Two further slips in the official solution: in the finite-intersection step it says the complements are in \(\Aa\) "by (i)" — it is axiom (ii); and the finite-union step switches from \(m\) to \(n\) and from \(A_0\) to \(A_1\) mid-formula. The ideas are right.

Method to reuse — the two moves that solve almost every \(\sigma\)-algebra exercise

1. Pad with \(\emptyset\) to turn a finite union into a countable one (and with \(\Omega\) for intersections). 2. Go through complements to turn an intersection into a union, via de Morgan. Between them they cover Sheet 1 Ex 3, Ex 4(iii), Ex 6, and most of Sheet 3.

Sheet 1, Exercise 4 — true or false? Sheet 1 · Ex 4

This is the exercise most directly rehearsing the exam's opening problem. Use the widget above to experiment with (i) and (ii).

(i) Is \(\Aa=\{\emptyset,\{1,2\},\{1,4\},\{2,3\},\{3,4\},\{1,2,3,4\}\}\) a \(\sigma\)-algebra over \(\Omega=\{1,2,3,4\}\)?

False. The union property fails: \(\{1,2\}\in\Aa\) and \(\{2,3\}\in\Aa\), but \(\{1,2\}\cup\{2,3\}=\{1,2,3\}\notin\Aa\).

My addition. Complements do not give a witness here. Every listed set has its complement in the list: \(\emptyset\leftrightarrow\Omega\), \(\{1,2\}\leftrightarrow\{3,4\}\), \(\{1,4\}\leftrightarrow\{2,3\}\). So the union is the axiom that breaks, and one union is enough to show it.

A quick sanity check, mine: a \(\sigma\)-algebra on a finite \(\Omega\) always has \(2^k\) members for some \(k\). (Its smallest non-empty members split \(\Omega\) into \(k\) blocks, and every member is a union of some of the blocks: \(2^k\) choices.) This collection has 6 members, and 6 is not a power of 2. So it cannot be a \(\sigma\)-algebra. Use this to know the answer fast, then write the union witness.

(ii) If \(\Aa_1,\Aa_2\) are \(\sigma\)-algebras over \(\Omega\), is \(\Aa_1\cup\Aa_2\)?

False. Take \(\Omega=\{1,2,3,4\}\) and

\[ \Aa_1=\{\emptyset,\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\Omega\},\qquad \Aa_2=\{\emptyset,\{1,4\},\{2,3\},\Omega\}. \]

Each is a \(\sigma\)-algebra (each is \(\sigma(\{A\})=\{\emptyset,\Omega,A,A^c\}\) from Example 1.9(iii), with \(A=\{1,2\}\) and \(A=\{1,4\}\) respectively). But \(\{1,2\},\{2,3\}\in\Aa_1\cup\Aa_2\) while \(\{1,2\}\cup\{2,3\}=\{1,2,3\}\) lies in neither, so it is not in the union.

Contrast with Proposition 1.7: intersections of \(\sigma\)-algebras are \(\sigma\)-algebras. Intersecting keeps only sets both systems already contain, and any union of such sets is in both systems by their own axioms. Uniting creates pairs that no single system was ever asked about.

(iii) Is \(\Aa:=\{A\subseteq\Omega \mid A \text{ or } A^c \text{ is countable}\}\) a \(\sigma\)-algebra?

True. Call a set co-countable if its complement is countable. (Why these facts hold: B2 — countability arithmetic.) Permitted facts, given on the sheet: a countable union of countable sets is countable; a subset of a countable set is countable.

(a) \(\Omega\in\Aa\). \(\Omega^c=\emptyset\) is finite, hence countable. ✓ (The official solution checks \(\emptyset\in\Aa\) instead; the script's axiom (i) asks for \(\Omega\). Both hold, and each implies the other by axiom (ii), but quote the axiom as written.)

(b) complements. Let \(A\in\Aa\). If \(A\) is countable then \(A^c\) is co-countable, so \(A^c\in\Aa\). If \(A\) is co-countable then \(A^c\) is countable, so \(A^c\in\Aa\). ✓

(c) countable unions. Let \(A_0,A_1,\ldots\in\Aa\). Two cases:

  • All \(A_i\) countable. Then \(\bigcup_i A_i\) is a countable union of countable sets, hence countable, hence in \(\Aa\). ✓
  • Some \(A_j\) is uncountable. Since \(A_j\in\Aa\), its complement \(A_j^c\) must be countable. By de Morgan, \(\bigl(\bigcup_i A_i\bigr)^c=\bigcap_i A_i^c\subseteq A_j^c\), a subset of a countable set, hence countable. So the union is co-countable, hence in \(\Aa\). ✓ ∎

(iv) Is \(\Aa:=\{A\subseteq\Omega\mid A \text{ or } A^c \text{ is finite}\}\) a \(\sigma\)-algebra if and only if \(\Omega\) is finite?

True. An "if and only if" needs both directions.

"\(\Leftarrow\)" (\(\Omega\) finite \(\Rightarrow\) \(\Aa\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra). If \(\Omega\) is finite then every subset of \(\Omega\) is finite, so the condition "\(A\) or \(A^c\) finite" holds for every \(A\), giving \(\Aa=\pow(\Omega)\), which is always a \(\sigma\)-algebra by Example 1.9(ii). ✓

"\(\Rightarrow\)" by contraposition (\(\Omega\) infinite \(\Rightarrow\) \(\Aa\) not a \(\sigma\)-algebra). Rewritten by me — see the note below. Contraposition means: instead of "\(P\Rightarrow Q\)" we prove the equivalent "not \(Q\) \(\Rightarrow\) not \(P\)". Since \(\Omega\) is infinite it contains a countably infinite subset; list it as \(\omega_0,\omega_1,\omega_2,\dots\) with all \(\omega_i\) distinct. (Why such a list exists: pick any \(\omega_0\in\Omega\); then pick \(\omega_1\in\Omega\setminus\{\omega_0\}\), then \(\omega_2\in\Omega\setminus\{\omega_0,\omega_1\}\), and so on. After finitely many picks only finitely many points are used up, and \(\Omega\) is infinite, so there is always something left to pick. Making infinitely many such choices is formally an appeal to the (countable) axiom of choice, see B2; the course uses it without comment.) Put

\[ A:=\{\omega_0,\omega_2,\omega_4,\dots\}=\bigcup_{i\in\N}\{\omega_{2i}\}. \]

Each singleton \(\{\omega_{2i}\}\) is finite, hence lies in \(\Aa\), and the union is countable — so axiom (iii) would force \(A\in\Aa\). But \(A\) is infinite, and \(A^c\) is infinite too, because it contains all of \(\omega_1,\omega_3,\omega_5,\dots\). So \(A\notin\Aa\), and axiom (iii) fails. Therefore \(\Aa\) is not a \(\sigma\)-algebra. ∎

A slip in the official solution

The printed solution opens the "\(\Rightarrow\)" direction with "Assume that \(\Omega\) is not countable", then immediately says "We can further assume that \(\Omega\) is countable infinity and not uncountable". The first sentence should read "Assume that \(\Omega\) is not finite" — the contraposition of "\(\Aa\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\Rightarrow\) \(\Omega\) finite" negates finite, not countable. The argument that follows is the right one; only the word is wrong. The version above avoids the detour ("restrict to a countable subset") by exhibiting \(A\) directly.

Sheet 1, Exercise 5 — intersections of \(\sigma\)-algebras (= Proposition 1.7) Sheet 1 · Ex 5

Proof Sheet 1 · Ex 5

Let \(\Aa:=\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}\Aa_\alpha\) with each \(\Aa_\alpha\) a \(\sigma\)-algebra over \(\Omega\) and \(I\ne\emptyset\). By the definition of an intersection (\(\forall\) in Definition 1.2), \(X\in\Aa\) means: \(X\in\Aa_\alpha\) for every \(\alpha\in I\). We check the three axioms of Definition 1.6 one by one.

(i) \(\Omega\in\Aa_\alpha\) for each \(\alpha\), since each is a \(\sigma\)-algebra. Being in all of them, \(\Omega\in\Aa\). ✓
