(ii) Let \(A\in\Aa\). Then \(A\in\Aa_\alpha\) for every \(\alpha\). Each \(\Aa_\alpha\) is closed under complements, so \(A^c\in\Aa_\alpha\) for every \(\alpha\), hence \(A^c\in\Aa\). ✓

(iii) Let \(A_0,A_1,\ldots\in\Aa\). Then all \(A_i\in\Aa_\alpha\) for every \(\alpha\). Each \(\Aa_\alpha\) is closed under countable unions, so \(\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i\in\Aa_\alpha\) for every \(\alpha\), hence \(\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i\in\Aa\). ✓ ∎

The shape of this proof is worth noticing: each axiom is verified "pointwise in \(\alpha\)". Nothing about \(I\) is used except that it is a set — which is why the statement holds for uncountable \(I\) as well, and why Lemma 1.8 may intersect over the (usually enormous) family of all \(\sigma\)-algebras containing \(\mathcal E\).

The sheet then states, as Remark 1, that this makes \(\sigma(S)\) well-defined for any non-empty \(S\subseteq\pow(\Omega)\) — which is Lemma 1.8 of the script. Note the notational mismatch: the sheet writes \(\Aa_\sigma(S)\) and, in its displayed formula, "\(\Aa\subseteq S\)" where it means \(S\subseteq\Aa\). The script's Lemma 1.8 has it right.

Sheet 1, Exercise 6 — pre-image and push-forward \(\sigma\)-algebras Sheet 1 · Ex 6

With \(f:\Omega_1\to\Omega_2\) and \(\Aa,\mathcal B\) \(\sigma\)-algebras over \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\), show that

\[ f^{-1}(\mathcal B):=\{f^{-1}(B)\mid B\in\mathcal B\} \quad\text{and}\quad f_*(\Aa):=\{B\subseteq\Omega_2 \mid f^{-1}(B)\in\Aa\} \]

are \(\sigma\)-algebras over \(\Omega_1\) and \(\Omega_2\) respectively.

Proof Sheet 1 · Ex 6, with the axiom (i) check corrected

The push-forward \(f_*(\Aa)\), over \(\Omega_2\).

(i) \(\Omega_2\in f_*(\Aa)\): we need \(f^{-1}(\Omega_2)\in\Aa\). Every \(\omega\in\Omega_1\) satisfies \(f(\omega)\in\Omega_2\), so \(f^{-1}(\Omega_2)=\Omega_1\in\Aa\) by axiom (i). ✓ (The official solution checks \(\emptyset\in f_*(\Aa)\) via \(f^{-1}(\emptyset)=\emptyset\). True, but it is the wrong axiom: Definition 1.6(i) asks for the whole space.)

(ii) Let \(B\in f_*(\Aa)\), so \(f^{-1}(B)\in\Aa\). By Exercise 2(iii), \(f^{-1}(B^c)=\bigl(f^{-1}(B)\bigr)^c\), which is in \(\Aa\) by axiom (ii). Hence \(B^c\in f_*(\Aa)\). ✓

(iii) Let \(B_0,B_1,\ldots\in f_*(\Aa)\), so each \(f^{-1}(B_j)\in\Aa\). By Exercise 2(ii),

\[ f^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcup_{j\in\N}B_j\Bigr)=\bigcup_{j\in\N}f^{-1}(B_j)\in\Aa \]

by axiom (iii). Hence \(\bigcup_j B_j\in f_*(\Aa)\). ✓

The pre-image \(f^{-1}(\mathcal B)\), over \(\Omega_1\). Same three steps, run the other way.

(i) \(\Omega_1=f^{-1}(\Omega_2)\) and \(\Omega_2\in\mathcal B\), so \(\Omega_1\in f^{-1}(\mathcal B)\). ✓

(ii) An element of \(f^{-1}(\mathcal B)\) has the form \(f^{-1}(B)\) with \(B\in\mathcal B\). Then \(\bigl(f^{-1}(B)\bigr)^c=f^{-1}(B^c)\) by Exercise 2(iii), and \(B^c\in\mathcal B\), so the complement is again of the required form. ✓

(iii) For \(f^{-1}(B_j)\), \(j\in\N\), Exercise 2(ii) gives \(\bigcup_j f^{-1}(B_j)=f^{-1}\bigl(\bigcup_j B_j\bigr)\), and \(\bigcup_j B_j\in\mathcal B\), so the union is again of the required form. ✓ ∎

In words: \(f^{-1}\) commutes with all three set operations, so it carries \(\sigma\)-algebras to \(\sigma\)-algebras in both directions. The forward image \(f(\cdot)\) does not commute with complements, and that is precisely what SoSe26 P2b exploits.

Sheet 2, Exercise 1 — six true/false statements Sheet 2 · Ex 1

(i) For a probability space, \(\P(\Omega\setminus A)=1-\P(A)\) for all \(A\in\Aa\).

True. \(\P\) is \(\sigma\)-additive, hence finitely additive. \(A\) and \(\Omega\setminus A\) are disjoint and their union is \(\Omega\), so

\[ 1=\P(\Omega)=\P\bigl(A\,\dot\cup\,(\Omega\setminus A)\bigr)=\P(A)+\P(\Omega\setminus A), \]

and rearranging gives the claim. The rearrangement is legitimate because \(\P(A)\le1\) is finite.

(ii) For a measure space and \(A,B\in\Aa\) with \(\mu(A\cap B)<\infty\): \(\mu(B\setminus A)=\mu(B)-\mu(A\cap B)\).

True. Split \(B\) into the part inside \(A\) and the part outside: \(B=(B\setminus A)\,\dot\cup\,(A\cap B)\). These are disjoint and both in \(\Aa\) by Corollary 1.10, so additivity gives \(\mu(B)=\mu(B\setminus A)+\mu(A\cap B)\). Subtract \(\mu(A\cap B)\), which is permitted because it is finite.

Note the improvement over Prop. 1.19(ii): the statement does not assume \(A\subseteq B\), and it subtracts \(\mu(A\cap B)\) rather than \(\mu(A)\). When \(A\subseteq B\) we have \(A\cap B=A\) and the two coincide.

(iii) \(\P\bigl(\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i\bigr)=\sup_{i\in\N}\P(A_i)\) for any sequence \((A_i)\).

False. Take \(\Omega=\{0,1\}\), \(\Aa=\pow(\Omega)\), \(\P(\{0\})=\P(\{1\})=\tfrac12\), and

\[ A_0=\{0\},\qquad A_i=\{1\}\ \text{ for all } i\ge1. \]

Then \(\bigcup_i A_i=\{0,1\}=\Omega\), so the left-hand side is 1, while every \(\P(A_i)=\tfrac12\) and so the supremum is \(\tfrac12\). Since \(1\ne\tfrac12\), the statement fails.

Two notes of mine. First, the official solution writes "\(A_n=\{1\}\) for each \(n>1\)", which leaves \(A_1\) undefined; taking \(i\ge1\) as above closes the gap. Second, and more useful for the exam: the statement becomes true if the sequence is increasing, \(A_0\subseteq A_1\subseteq\cdots\), because then \(\P(A_i)\) is an increasing sequence, its supremum is its limit, and continuity from below (Prop. 1.19(iv)) gives exactly this equality. The counterexample works only because the sequence jumps around. Examiners like this distinction.

(iv) \(\P(A\cup B\cup C)=\P(A)+\P(B)+\P(C)-\P(A\cap B)-\P(A\cap C)-\P(B\cap C)+\P(A\cap B\cap C)\).

True. It is Theorem 1.22 with \(n=3\): the \(k=1\) terms are the three singles with sign \(+\), the \(k=2\) terms the three pairs with sign \(-\), and the \(k=3\) term the triple with sign \(+\).

(v) Is \(\bigl(\N,\pow(\N),\mu\bigr)\) with \(\mu(A)=0\) for finite \(A\) and \(\mu(A)=\infty\) for infinite \(A\) a measure space?

False. \(\sigma\)-additivity fails. Take \(A_n=\{n\}\) for \(n\in\N\) — pairwise disjoint, each finite, so \(\mu(A_n)=0\). Their union is \(\N\), which is infinite, so \(\mu(\N)=\infty\). Then

\[ \infty=\mu(\N)=\mu\Bigl(\bigcup_{n\in\N}A_n\Bigr)\;\ne\;\sum_{n\in\N}\mu(A_n)=\sum_{n\in\N}0=0. \]

Worth noticing: the other two axioms do hold — \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\) since \(\emptyset\) is finite, and \(\mu\ge0\) always. So this is a clean example that \(\sigma\)-additivity is the axiom with teeth. It is also finitely additive on disjoint sets in every case: if \(A,B\) are both finite, \(A\cup B\) is finite and \(0=0+0\); if at least one is infinite, \(A\cup B\) is infinite and \(\infty=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\). So \(\mu\) is finitely additive but not \(\sigma\)-additive — finite additivity is strictly weaker than \(\sigma\)-additivity.

(vi) For the sum of two fair coin flips (sides counting as 0 or 1), is the cdf \(F(x)=0,\ \tfrac14,\ \tfrac34,\ 1\) on \(x<0\), \([0,1)\), \([1,2)\), \(x\ge2\)?

True. Model: \(\Omega=\{0,1,2\}\) for the possible sums, with

\[ \P(\{0\})=\tfrac14,\qquad \P(\{1\})=\tfrac12,\qquad \P(\{2\})=\tfrac14, \]

because of the four equally likely flip pairs \((0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\), one gives sum 0, two give sum 1, one gives sum 2. Then by Definition 1.23,

\[ F(x)=\P\bigl((-\infty,x]\bigr)=\sum_{n\in\{0,1,2\},\,n\le x}\P(\{n\}), \]

so \(F(x)=0\) for \(x<0\); \(F(x)=\tfrac14\) on \([0,1)\); \(F(x)=\tfrac14+\tfrac12=\tfrac34\) on \([1,2)\); and \(F(x)=1\) for \(x\ge2\). ✓

Set the cdf widget above to weights \(1,2,1\) and you get exactly this staircase. Check the three jump heights against Lemma 1.24(iv): \(\tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac14\) — the point masses.

Sheet 2, Exercise 5 (bonus) — other generators of \(\mathcal B^n\) Sheet 2 · Ex 5

Show \(\sigma(\mathcal E_1)=\sigma(\mathcal E_2)\) where \(\mathcal E_1\) is the set of open subsets of \(\R^n\) and \(\mathcal E_2=\{[a,b)\mid a,b\in\Q^n,\ a<b\}\).

Reading the vector notation my addition. Here \(a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\) and \(b=(b_1,\dots,b_n)\) are vectors with rational entries (\(\Q^n\) = all \(n\)-tuples of rationals). For vectors, \(a<b\) is meant componentwise [komponentenweise]: \(a_i<b_i\) for every \(i=1,\dots,n\). And \([a,b)\) is the half-open box \([a,b):=[a_1,b_1)\times\cdots\times[a_n,b_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n[a_i,b_i)\), where \(\times\) is the Cartesian product and \(\prod\) here means "Cartesian product of the \(n\) intervals" (product notation: B3). Example with \(n=2\): \(a=(0,1)\), \(b=(2,3)\) satisfy \(a<b\) because \(0<2\) and \(1<3\), and \([a,b)=[0,2)\times[1,3)\) is a rectangle containing its bottom and left edges but not its top and right edges. By contrast \(a=(0,5)\), \(b=(2,3)\) are not comparable: neither \(a<b\) nor \(b<a\). Vectors in \(\R^n\): Analysis 11 — linear algebra you need.

The universal method for "same generated \(\sigma\)-algebra"

Show \(\mathcal E_1\subseteq\sigma(\mathcal E_2)\) and \(\mathcal E_2\subseteq\sigma(\mathcal E_1)\). Then Lemma 1.8's minimality does the rest: \(\sigma(\mathcal E_2)\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra containing \(\mathcal E_1\), so it contains the smallest such, namely \(\sigma(\mathcal E_1)\); and symmetrically. You never have to describe either \(\sigma\)-algebra.

Proof for \(n=1\), written out my version; the official one does general \(n\) and is hard to read in the PDF

Part 1: \(\mathcal E_1\subseteq\sigma(\mathcal E_2)\). Let \(A\subseteq\R\) be open. By definition of "open", for every \(x\in A\) there is \(\varepsilon_x>0\) with \((x-\varepsilon_x,\,x+\varepsilon_x)\subseteq A\). Because the rationals are dense in \(\R\) (Analysis 1.2, Satz 1.10) — every non-empty open interval contains a rational — we can choose rationals \(a_x,b_x\) with

\[ x-\varepsilon_x < a_x \le x < b_x < x+\varepsilon_x, \]

so that \(x\in[a_x,b_x)\subseteq A\) and \([a_x,b_x)\in\mathcal E_2\). Hence

\[ A=\bigcup_{x\in A}[a_x,b_x). \]

The union is over possibly uncountably many \(x\) — but the distinct sets appearing are all of the form \([a,b)\) with \(a,b\in\Q\), and there are only countably many of those, because \(\Q\times\Q\) is countable. So \(A\) is a countable union of members of \(\mathcal E_2\), hence \(A\in\sigma(\mathcal E_2)\) by axiom (iii). ✓

Part 2: \(\mathcal E_2\subseteq\sigma(\mathcal E_1)\). Let \(a<b\) be rationals. Then

\[ [a,b)=\bigcap_{k\ge1}\Bigl(a-\tfrac1k,\;b\Bigr). \]

Check both inclusions. If \(a\le x<b\) then \(x>a-\tfrac1k\) for every \(k\), so \(x\) is in every set on the right. Conversely if \(x\) is in every \((a-\tfrac1k,b)\) then \(x<b\), and \(x>a-\tfrac1k\) for all \(k\) forces \(x\ge a\) (if \(x<a\) we could pick \(k\) with \(\tfrac1k<a-x\) and get a contradiction). ✓

Each \((a-\tfrac1k,b)\) is an open interval, hence in \(\mathcal E_1\), and a countable intersection of members of \(\sigma(\mathcal E_1)\) stays in \(\sigma(\mathcal E_1)\) by Corollary 1.10. So \([a,b)\in\sigma(\mathcal E_1)\). ✓

By the method above, \(\sigma(\mathcal E_1)=\sigma(\mathcal E_2)\). ∎

For general \(n\), replace intervals by boxes: \(\prod_i(x_i-\varepsilon,x_i+\varepsilon)\) in Part 1 with rational corners, and \([a,b)=\bigcap_{k\ge1}\bigl(a-\tfrac1k\vec1,\,b\bigr)\) in Part 2, where \(\vec1=(1,\dots,1)\), so \(a-\tfrac1k\vec1=(a_1-\tfrac1k,\dots,a_n-\tfrac1k)\) moves every lower corner coordinate down by \(\tfrac1k\). Nothing else changes. (The official proof uses open balls \(B_r(x)\) instead of boxes — all points whose Euclidean distance from \(x\) is less than \(r\); distance and balls: Analysis 1.3 — norms.)

Connection to Example 1.13. The script defines \(\mathcal B^n\) from open boxes, while this exercise starts from all open sets. Part 1 above shows every open set is a countable union of rational boxes, so the two generators give the same \(\sigma\)-algebra — which is also the content of Remark 1.14, without needing the word "topology".

Two typos in the sheet's Remark 1 Spotted by me

The sheet lists ten further generators \(\mathcal E_3,\dots,\mathcal E_{12}\) of \(\mathcal B^n\). Two are almost certainly misprinted: \(\mathcal E_4:=\{B_r(x)\mid x\in\Q^n,\ r\in\Q_{>9}\}\) was meant to read \(r\in\Q_{>0}\) (open balls \(B_r(x)\) = all points at distance less than \(r\) from \(x\), with positive rational radius). Note: even as printed the claim is not false, at least for \(n=1\). Differences of big intervals give small ones, e.g. \((-10,10)\setminus(-9.5,10.5)=(-10,-9.5]\), so the small intervals are still generated. And \(\mathcal E_5:=\{A\subseteq\R^{N}\mid A\text{ closed}\}\) should read \(\R^{n}\). The remaining eight are correct as printed. Useful ones to remember: (Vocabulary used in that list: a set \(A\subseteq\R^n\) is closed [abgeschlossen] if limits of convergent sequences in \(A\) stay in \(A\) — e.g. \([0,1]\) is closed, \((0,1]\) is not, since \(\tfrac1k\to0\notin(0,1]\); equivalently, its complement is open. A set is compact [kompakt] if it is closed and bounded, like \([0,1]\). Both: Analysis 4.4; see also B1 — interior, open and closed.) \(\mathcal B\) is generated by the half-lines \(\{(-\infty,b]\mid b\in\Q\}\) alone — which is why Definition 1.23 can get away with defining a cdf from those sets only.

Sheet 3, Exercise 1 — generators and measurability Sheet 3 · Ex 1

Let \((X,\Aa_X)\) and \((Y,\Aa_Y)\) be measurable spaces, \(f:X\to Y\), and \(\mathcal E_Y\subseteq\Aa_Y\). Show \(\sigma\bigl(f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y)\bigr)=f^{-1}\bigl(\sigma(\mathcal E_Y)\bigr)\), and then that \(f\) is \(\Aa_X\)–\(\sigma(\mathcal E_Y)\)-measurable if and only if \(f^{-1}(E)\in\Aa_X\) for all \(E\in\mathcal E_Y\).

The word "measurable" is used here before the script defines it My addition

The script's Definition 1.50 (on the §1.3 page) says: \(f\) is \(\Aa_X\)–\(\Aa_Y\)-measurable if \(f^{-1}(B)\in\Aa_X\) for every \(B\in\Aa_Y\). In words: the pre-image of every measurable set is measurable. That one line is all you need here. A random variable is exactly such a map, so this exercise is the tool that makes random variables usable in practice.

Proof my version; the official solution is correct but very compressed

Part 1: the identity \(\sigma(f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y))=f^{-1}(\sigma(\mathcal E_Y))\).

"\(\subseteq\)". By Sheet 1 Exercise 6 (applied with \(\mathcal B=\sigma(\mathcal E_Y)\)), the collection \(f^{-1}(\sigma(\mathcal E_Y))\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(X\). It contains \(f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y)\), because \(\mathcal E_Y\subseteq\sigma(\mathcal E_Y)\) and pre-images preserve inclusions (Sheet 1 Ex 2(i)). By Lemma 1.8, \(\sigma(f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y))\) is the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra containing \(f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y)\), so it is contained in this one. ✓

"\(\supseteq\)". This direction needs a trick: build a \(\sigma\)-algebra on the \(Y\) side out of the thing we want to prove something about. Put

\[ \tilde{\Aa}:=\bigl\{B\subseteq Y \;\bigm|\; f^{-1}(B)\in\sigma\bigl(f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y)\bigr)\bigr\}. \]

This is exactly the push-forward \(f_*\bigl(\sigma(f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y))\bigr)\), which is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(Y\) by Sheet 1 Exercise 6. It contains \(\mathcal E_Y\): for \(E\in\mathcal E_Y\) we have \(f^{-1}(E)\in f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y)\subseteq\sigma(f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y))\), so \(E\in\tilde{\Aa}\). By minimality (Lemma 1.8), \(\sigma(\mathcal E_Y)\subseteq\tilde{\Aa}\).

Now unwind what that says: for every \(B\in\sigma(\mathcal E_Y)\) we have \(f^{-1}(B)\in\sigma(f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y))\) — which is precisely \(f^{-1}(\sigma(\mathcal E_Y))\subseteq\sigma(f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y))\). ✓

Part 2: measurability need only be checked on a generator.

"\(\Rightarrow\)": if \(f^{-1}(B)\in\Aa_X\) for all \(B\in\sigma(\mathcal E_Y)\), then in particular for all \(B\in\mathcal E_Y\), since \(\mathcal E_Y\subseteq\sigma(\mathcal E_Y)\). ✓

"\(\Leftarrow\)": suppose \(f^{-1}(E)\in\Aa_X\) for all \(E\in\mathcal E_Y\), i.e. \(f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y)\subseteq\Aa_X\). Since \(\Aa_X\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra containing \(f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y)\), minimality gives \(\sigma(f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y))\subseteq\Aa_X\). By Part 1 the left side equals \(f^{-1}(\sigma(\mathcal E_Y))\), so \(f^{-1}(B)\in\Aa_X\) for every \(B\in\sigma(\mathcal E_Y)\) — which is the definition of \(\Aa_X\)–\(\sigma(\mathcal E_Y)\)-measurability. ✓

Part 3: the case \(\sigma(\mathcal E_Y)=\Aa_Y\) (the sheet's last claim). Then "\(\Aa_X\)–\(\sigma(\mathcal E_Y)\)-measurable" is the same as "\(\Aa_X\)–\(\Aa_Y\)-measurable", and "\(f^{-1}(E)\in\Aa_X\) for all \(E\in\mathcal E_Y\)" is the same as \(f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y)\subseteq\Aa_X\) (the set of all these pre-images lies in \(\Aa_X\)). So Part 2 reads: \(f\) is \(\Aa_X\)–\(\Aa_Y\)-measurable \(\iff f^{-1}(\mathcal E_Y)\subseteq\Aa_X\). ✓ ∎

In words — and this is the payoff: to prove a function into \(\R\) is measurable you do not have to check all Borel sets. It is enough to check the half-lines \((-\infty,b]\), because they generate \(\mathcal B\). That is why "\(\{X\le b\}\) is an event for every \(b\)" is the usual working definition of a real random variable.

A wrong cross-reference in the official solution

Sheet 3's solution cites "Ex.Sh. 0, Ex. 2-(i)" for the preservation of subsets under inverse images, and "Ex.Sh. 0, Ex. 6" for pre-image and push-forward \(\sigma\)-algebras. Sheet 0 contains neither: its six tasks are dice, urns, PINs, a bug detector, aces and the self-referential question. The intended references are Sheet 1, Exercise 2(i) and Sheet 1, Exercise 6.

Sheet 3, Exercise 2 — restriction commutes with generation Sheet 3 · Ex 2

For \(\Omega\ne\emptyset\), \(\emptyset\ne A\subseteq\Omega\) and \(\mathcal E\subseteq\pow(\Omega)\): \(\sigma\bigl(\mathcal E|_A\bigr)=\sigma(\mathcal E)\big|_A\). This is the second half of Lemma 1.15.

Proof Sheet 3 · Ex 2

The whole exercise is one observation: restricting to \(A\) is taking a pre-image. Let \(\iota_A:A\hookrightarrow\Omega\) be the inclusion map, \(\iota_A(a)=a\) for \(a\in A\) — it does nothing except regard an element of \(A\) as an element of \(\Omega\). For any \(B\subseteq\Omega\),

\[ \iota_A^{-1}(B)=\{a\in A\mid\iota_A(a)\in B\}=\{a\in A\mid a\in B\}=A\cap B. \]

So "intersect with \(A\)" and "take \(\iota_A^{-1}\)" are the same operation, and therefore \(\mathcal E|_A=\iota_A^{-1}(\mathcal E)\) and \(\sigma(\mathcal E)|_A=\iota_A^{-1}(\sigma(\mathcal E))\). Now apply Exercise 1 with \(f=\iota_A\):

\[ \sigma\bigl(\mathcal E|_A\bigr)=\sigma\bigl(\iota_A^{-1}(\mathcal E)\bigr) \overset{\text{Ex. 1}}{=}\iota_A^{-1}\bigl(\sigma(\mathcal E)\bigr)=\sigma(\mathcal E)\big|_A. \;\;∎ \]

Why this is useful. Convention 1.16 equips a subset \(A\subseteq\R^n\) with \(\mathcal B^n|_A\). This exercise says you may compute that either by generating on \(\R^n\) and then restricting, or by restricting the generators first and generating inside \(A\) — the answer is the same. Without it, "the Borel sets of \([0,1]\)" would be ambiguous.

Typo in the official solution: it writes \(\iota_A:A\hookrightarrow X\) and "for all \(B\subseteq X\)"; the set is called \(\Omega\) in this exercise.

Old-exam tasks

WiSe 25/26, Problem 1a — is this a \(\sigma\)-algebra? WiSe25 · P1a · 3 credits

Statement. On \(\Omega=\{\circ,\triangle,\star\}\), the set \(\{\emptyset,\{\circ\},\{\star\},\{\circ,\star\},\Omega\}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra. True or false? Justify by a proof or a concrete counterexample.

Official answer: False. The complement \(\Omega\setminus\{\circ\}=\{\triangle,\star\}\) is not in the set.

My verification: correct. Definition 1.6(ii) demands \(A^c\in\Aa\) for every \(A\in\Aa\). Taking \(A=\{\circ\}\) gives \(A^c=\{\triangle,\star\}\), which does not appear in the listed collection — the listed sets containing \(\triangle\) are only \(\Omega\) itself. One witness is enough to refute a "for all" statement.

Exam technique for this recurring question type

Check in this order, it is the fastest:

  1. Count. A \(\sigma\)-algebra on a finite \(\Omega\) has \(2^k\) members. Here there are 5 members — not a power of 2 — so it is already dead. (This shortcut is mine; it will not earn the credits on its own, because the marking scheme asks for a witness. Use it to know the answer instantly, then write the witness.)
  2. Complements. Pair every listed set with its complement and look for an unpaired one. Here \(\emptyset\leftrightarrow\Omega\) is the only pair that closes. The other three listed sets are all unpaired: \(\{\circ\}^c=\{\triangle,\star\}\) ✗ (the official witness), \(\{\star\}^c=\{\circ,\triangle\}\) ✗ and \(\{\circ,\star\}^c=\{\triangle\}\) ✗. Any one of the three is a complete answer — you need exactly one.
  3. Unions. Only if complements pass.

Then write one line: name the set, name its complement, say it is absent. The marking scheme for this problem gives 3 credits and the solution is two lines long.

WiSe 25/26, Problem 1c — does agreeing on a generator force two measures to agree? WiSe25 · P1c · 3 credits

Statement. Let \(\Omega\) be a set, \(\mathcal L\subseteq\pow(\Omega)\), and let \(\mathcal S\) be the \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal S=\bigcap\{\Aa\mid\Aa\text{ is a }\sigma\text{-algebra on }\Omega \text{ and }\mathcal L\subseteq\Aa\}\) — that is, \(\mathcal S=\sigma(\mathcal L)\) in the notation of Lemma 1.8. Then for any two probability measures \(\P_1,\P_2\) on \((\Omega,\mathcal S)\) with \(\P_1(L)=\P_2(L)\) for all \(L\in\mathcal L\), it already holds that \(\P_1=\P_2\). True or false?

Official answer: False, with \(\Omega=\{1,2,3,4\}\), \(\mathcal L=\bigl\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\}\bigr\}\), hence \(\mathcal S=\pow(\Omega)\), and

\[ \P_1=\tfrac13\delta_1+\tfrac13\delta_2+\tfrac13\delta_3,\qquad \P_2=\tfrac16\delta_1+\tfrac12\delta_2+\tfrac16\delta_3+\tfrac16\delta_4, \]

that is, the pmfs (probability mass functions: the list of probabilities of the single points) \(p_1=(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13,0)\) and \(p_2=(\tfrac16,\tfrac12,\tfrac16,\tfrac16)\) on \(\{1,2,3,4\}\). (\(\delta_k\) is the Dirac measure at \(k\): \(\delta_k(A)=1\) if \(k\in A\) and 0 otherwise. A weighted sum of Diracs is just a pmf written compactly.)

My verification: correct, and here is every step.

Step 1 — is \(\mathcal S\) really \(\pow(\Omega)\)? Start from \(\{1,2\}\) and \(\{2,3\}\) and close under the axioms. Complements give \(\{3,4\}\) and \(\{1,4\}\). Intersections (legitimate by Corollary 1.10) give

\[ \{1,2\}\cap\{2,3\}=\{2\},\quad \{1,2\}\cap\{1,4\}=\{1\},\quad \{2,3\}\cap\{3,4\}=\{3\},\quad \{3,4\}\cap\{1,4\}=\{4\}. \]

All four singletons are in \(\mathcal S\); every subset of \(\Omega\) is a union of singletons, so \(\mathcal S=\pow(\Omega)\). ✓

Step 2 — do the two measures agree on \(\mathcal L\)?

\[ \P_1(\{1,2\})=\tfrac13+\tfrac13=\tfrac23,\qquad \P_2(\{1,2\})=\tfrac16+\tfrac12=\tfrac23 \;✓ \] \[ \P_1(\{2,3\})=\tfrac13+\tfrac13=\tfrac23,\qquad \P_2(\{2,3\})=\tfrac12+\tfrac16=\tfrac23 \;✓ \]

Step 3 — are they different? \(\P_1(\{4\})=0\) while \(\P_2(\{4\})=\tfrac16\). ✓ Also both are genuine probability measures: the weights are non-negative and sum to 1 in each case (\(3\times\tfrac13=1\); \(\tfrac16+\tfrac12+\tfrac16+\tfrac16=1\)). The statement is refuted.

(The printed solution renders the shared value as "32", an artefact of the PDF; it is \(\tfrac23\).)

The deeper point, which the exam does not state My addition

Agreeing on a generator does force equality — provided the generator is closed under intersection (such a collection is called a \(\pi\)-system). That is the uniqueness theorem behind Theorem 1.25, and it is why a cdf determines a measure: the half-lines \((-\infty,x]\) are closed under intersection, since \((-\infty,x]\cap(-\infty,y]=(-\infty,\min(x,y)]\).

The counterexample works precisely because \(\mathcal L\) here is not closed under intersection: \(\{1,2\}\cap\{2,3\}=\{2\}\notin\mathcal L\). The two measures were built to agree on the two listed sets while disagreeing on \(\{2\}\) — and nothing in the hypothesis pins \(\{2\}\) down. If you are asked this in an exam, the one-sentence reason is: the generator is not \(\cap\)-stable, so the uniqueness argument does not apply, and here is a counterexample.

SoSe 2026, Problem 2b — is the forward image of a \(\sigma\)-algebra a \(\sigma\)-algebra? SoSe26 · P2b · 3 credits

Statement. Let \(\Omega,\Omega'\) be sets, \(\Aa\) a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega\), and \(f:\Omega\to\Omega'\) an arbitrary function. Then \(f(\Aa):=\{f(A)\mid A\in\Aa\}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega'\). True or false, with justification.

Official answer: False. Take \(\Omega=\{1,2,3\}\), \(\Omega'=\{a,b\}\), \(f(1)=f(2)=a\), \(f(3)=b\), and \(\Aa=\{\emptyset,\{1,3\},\{2\},\Omega\}\). Although \(f\) is surjective (every element of \(\Omega'\) is hit by \(f\)), the forward images are \(f(\Aa)=\{\emptyset,\{a\},\{a,b\}\}\), which is not a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\Omega'\) because it contains \(\{a\}\) but not its complement \(\{b\}\).

My verification: correct. Two things need checking.

Is \(\Aa\) a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\{1,2,3\}\)? \(\Omega\in\Aa\) ✓. Complements: \(\emptyset^c=\Omega\) ✓, \(\{1,3\}^c=\{2\}\) ✓, \(\{2\}^c=\{1,3\}\) ✓, \(\Omega^c=\emptyset\) ✓. Unions: the only non-trivial one is \(\{1,3\}\cup\{2\}=\Omega\) ✓. So yes — it is \(\sigma(\{\{2\}\})\) in the form of Example 1.9(iii).

Are the images right? \(f(\emptyset)=\emptyset\); \(f(\{1,3\})=\{f(1),f(3)\}=\{a,b\}\); \(f(\{2\})=\{a\}\); \(f(\Omega)=\{a,b\}\). Removing the duplicate, \(f(\Aa)=\{\emptyset,\{a\},\{a,b\}\}\), and \(\{a\}^c=\{b\}\) is absent. ✓

In words — why forward images misbehave: \(f^{-1}\) commutes with complements (Sheet 1 Ex 2(iii)), but \(f\) does not. When \(f\) glues 1 and 2 together, the set \(\{2\}\) and its complement \(\{1,3\}\) both send an element to \(a\), so their images overlap instead of partitioning \(\Omega'\). In general \(f(A^c)\) and \(f(A)^c\) can differ when \(f\) is not injective (when two different points have the same image), as here.

Marking scheme: 1 point for "false", 2 points for a valid counterexample together with naming which \(\sigma\)-algebra property fails. Name the failing axiom explicitly — a counterexample without that sentence loses points.

The pairing to remember: pre-images always work (Sheet 1 Ex 6), forward images generally do not (this task). If you are asked about \(f\) and \(\sigma\)-algebras, the first question is which direction the map goes.

WiSe 25/26, Problem 6c — inclusion–exclusion in a tournament WiSe25 · P6c · 4 credits

Statement. You play a four-match tournament with the schedule SWWS — strong opponent, weak, weak, strong. Your win probability is \(p\) against the strong player and \(q\) against the weak player, with \(0<p<q<1\), and matches are independent. You win the tournament if you win at least two non-consecutive matches. Compute your probability of winning.

Note: the full problem also uses independence, which is §1.4 material. It is placed on this page because part (c) is the only exam appearance of Theorem 1.22, and because the inclusion–exclusion bookkeeping is the whole difficulty. "Independent" here means only that probabilities of match results multiply.

Solution. Let \(A_i\) be the event of winning match \(i\). With schedule SWWS,

\[ \P(A_1)=p,\quad \P(A_2)=q,\quad \P(A_3)=q,\quad \P(A_4)=p. \]

The pairs of non-consecutive indices in \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) are \((1,3)\), \((1,4)\) and \((2,4)\) — the pairs \((1,2),(2,3),(3,4)\) are consecutive and do not count. So the winning event is \(E_{13}\cup E_{14}\cup E_{24}\) with \(E_{ij}:=A_i\cap A_j\). By independence,

\[ \P(E_{13})=pq,\qquad \P(E_{14})=p^2,\qquad \P(E_{24})=qp. \]

For the pairwise intersections, note that \(E_{ij}\cap E_{kl}\) is the event of winning all the matches in \(\{i,j\}\cup\{k,l\}\):

\[ \P(E_{13}\cap E_{14})=\P(A_1\cap A_3\cap A_4)=p\,q\,p=p^2q, \] \[ \P(E_{13}\cap E_{24})=\P(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3\cap A_4)=p\,q\,q\,p=p^2q^2, \] \[ \P(E_{14}\cap E_{24})=\P(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_4)=p\,q\,p=p^2q, \]

and the triple intersection is again all four matches: \(\P(E_{13}\cap E_{14}\cap E_{24})=p^2q^2\). Theorem 1.22 with \(n=3\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \P(\text{win}) &= \bigl(pq+p^2+pq\bigr)-\bigl(p^2q+p^2q^2+p^2q\bigr)+p^2q^2\\ &= 2pq+p^2-2p^2q-p^2q^2+p^2q^2\\ &= 2pq+p^2-2p^2q \;=\; p\bigl(2q+p-2pq\bigr). \end{aligned} \]

My verification: the official answer is correct. I also checked it by listing all \(2^4=16\) win/loss patterns by computer (e.g. \(p=0.3,q=0.7\) gives \(0.384\) both ways). The printed solution has two typos. First, it writes \(\P(E_{13}\cup E_{14}\cup E_{14})\), where the last term should be \(E_{24}\). Second, the bracket opened after the minus sign is closed only after the triple-intersection term, so as printed the line reads \(\ldots-\bigl(\P(E_{13}\cap E_{14})+\P(E_{13}\cap E_{24})+\P(E_{14}\cap E_{24})+\P(E_{13}\cap E_{14}\cap E_{24})\bigr)\) — which would subtract the triple term instead of adding it. The very next line of the official solution has the signs right, so it is a typesetting slip only. Two sanity checks of my own:

  • \(q=1\) (you always beat the weak player): the formula gives \(p(2+p-2p)=p(2-p)=2p-p^2\). Check directly: with \(A_2,A_3\) certain, the non-consecutive pairs \((1,3)\) and \((2,4)\) reduce to "win match 1" and "win match 4", so the winning event is \(A_1\cup A_4\), with probability \(p+p-p^2=2p-p^2\) by \((\dagger)\). ✓
  • \(p=0\) (you never beat the strong player): the formula gives 0. Correct, since every non-consecutive pair contains match 1 or match 4. ✓

The trap in this task is thinking the \(E_{ij}\) are independent because the \(A_i\) are. They are not — \(E_{13}\) and \(E_{14}\) both contain \(A_1\). Inclusion–exclusion is needed exactly because they overlap.

The two proof moves that solve most exercises

  1. Pad with \(\emptyset\) (for unions) or with \(\Omega\) (for intersections) to turn finite statements into the countable ones the axioms speak about.
  2. Route through complements: \(\bigcap_i A_i=\bigl(\bigcup_i A_i^c\bigr)^c\). A \(\sigma\)-algebra has no intersection axiom, so every intersection argument goes this way.
  3. For "smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra" claims, never describe \(\sigma(\mathcal E)\). Show \(\mathcal E\subseteq\mathcal B\) for a \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal B\) and invoke minimality (Lemma 1.8).

Exam focus

This page has produced four exam tasks in the three past exams we have — more than any other subchapter of Chapter 1. Three of them (WiSe25 P1a, WiSe25 P1c, SoSe26 P2b) sat in an opening True/False problem, where a single clean witness is worth full credit; the fourth (WiSe25 P6c) was one part buried inside a long applied problem.

  • "Is this a \(\sigma\)-algebra?" (WiSe25 P1a). Check complements first; count members and compare with \(2^k\) as a private shortcut. Write one witness.
  • "Do these constructions preserve \(\sigma\)-algebras?" (SoSe26 P2b). Pre-images: yes. Forward images: no. Intersections: yes. Unions: no. Memorise those four.
  • "Does agreeing on a generator determine the measure?" (WiSe25 P1c). Only if the generator is closed under intersection. Otherwise build a four-point counterexample.
  • Inclusion–exclusion (WiSe25 P6c). Appears inside long applied problems, not on its own. Watch for events that overlap because they share an underlying match, draw or trial.
  • Marking schemes reward naming the failed axiom. "False, because \(\{a\}\in f(\Aa)\) but \(\{b\}=\{a\}^c\notin f(\Aa)\), so Definition 1.6(ii) fails" is a full-credit answer; "False, see counterexample" is not.

Not examined so far: the Vitali theorems, the philosophical interlude (Remarks 1.30, 1.33 and Viewpoints 1.31, 1.32), and Theorem 1.25's proof.
