Discrete probability spaces and distributions

Diskrete Wahrscheinlichkeitsräume und Verteilungen

What this page covers Script §1.2, pp. 20–29

Everything from Definition 1.34 to Example 1.43. The script's section goal: "Introduce common discrete probability distributions and learn how to perform computations in discrete probability spaces." (The script's lecture marker "— Lecture 3" sits just before Example 1.39, so Definition 1.34 to Remark 1.38 were still part of Lecture 2.)

Worked in place: Sheet 0 (Ex. 2, 3, 4, 5 — Ex. 1 and 6 are on the Chapter 0 page), Sheet 2 (Ex. 2, 4), Sheet 3 (Ex. 3, 4), Sheet 4 (Ex. 1).

After the abstract §1.1 (previous page), this page is concrete: almost everything is counting. It also introduces the seven named discrete distributions. You will use them for the rest of the course.

The big picture

A reminder of the setting. In §1.1 a probability space is a triple \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\):

  • \(\Omega\) is the sample space [Ergebnisraum] — the set of all possible outcomes;
  • \(\Aa\) is the \(\sigma\)-algebra [\(\sigma\)-Algebra] — the collection of subsets of \(\Omega\) ("events") that we are allowed to give a probability;
  • \(\P\) is the probability measure — it assigns a number in \([0,1]\) to each event.

§1.1 had to be careful because of uncountable sets like \([0,1]\). This page deals with the easy case: \(\Omega\) is at most countable. That means \(\Omega\) is finite, or its elements can be listed as \(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\dots\) (like \(\N\)). Then there is no difficulty at all. We can let every subset be an event, i.e. \(\Aa=\pow(\Omega)\), the power set [Potenzmenge] (the set of all subsets of \(\Omega\); see B2).

And the whole measure \(\P\) shrinks to a list of numbers: one probability per outcome. That list is called the pmf. Example: a fair die has the list \(\tfrac16,\tfrac16,\tfrac16,\tfrac16,\tfrac16,\tfrac16\).

The page has three parts:

  1. The pmf (Def. 1.34, Lem. 1.35): on a countable \(\Omega\), giving \(\P\) is the same as giving a pmf. Every probability is then a sum.
  2. Counting (Lem. 1.36, Rem. 1.37, Ex. 1.40, Ex. 1.41): if all outcomes are equally likely, then \(\P(A)=|A|/|\Omega|\), where \(|A|\) is the number of elements of \(A\). Probability becomes counting. The hard part is not the arithmetic. It is choosing \(\Omega\) so that "equally likely" is really true.
  3. The catalogue (Ex. 1.39, Thm. 1.42): seven named distributions that appear again and again, and one theorem linking two of them.

The section ends with Bertrand's paradox (Ex. 1.43). It is the continuous version of the warning in Example 1.41: "choose at random" means nothing until you say how you choose.

Primer: everything you need to count My addition

Cross-references

The full counting toolkit with proofs and widgets is background page B3; this primer is the short version. The series come from your Analysis guide: geometric series, exponential series, \((1+x/n)^n\to e^x\) (Lemma 6.24), absolute convergence and rearrangement.

The script assumes counting methods from Discrete Structures [Diskrete Strukturen]. Here they are from scratch. Every fact below is used on this page.

1. The product rule

If a choice is made in \(k\) stages, with \(n_1\) options at the first stage, \(n_2\) at the second (whatever happened first), and so on, the total number of results is \(n_1 \cdot n_2 \cdots n_k\).

Why: for each of the \(n_1\) first choices there are \(n_2\) continuations, giving \(n_1 n_2\) results after two stages; repeat. Example: a 3-letter code from \(\{a,b\}\) has \(2\cdot2\cdot2=8\) possibilities.

2. Factorials

\(n! := n\cdot(n-1)\cdots2\cdot1\) for \(n\in\N_{>0}\), and \(0! := 1\) by convention. So \(4! = 24\), \(1! = 1\).

\(n!\) is the number of ways to arrange \(n\) distinct objects in a row: \(n\) choices for the first position, \(n-1\) for the second, and so on, by the product rule. The convention \(0!=1\) is not arbitrary — there is exactly one way to arrange nothing (the empty arrangement), and it is what makes the formulas below work at the edges.

3. Binomial coefficients

For \(0\le k\le n\),

\[ \binom{n}{k} := \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!} \]

read "\(n\) choose \(k\)". It counts the \(k\)-element subsets of an \(n\)-element set (this is proved below, in the proof of Lemma 1.36(iii)). Example: \(\binom42=\frac{24}{2\cdot2}=6\), and indeed \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) has the six 2-element subsets \(\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{1,4\},\{2,3\},\{2,4\},\{3,4\}\). We set \(\binom{n}{k}=0\) when \(k<0\) or \(k>n\), since there are no such subsets.

Facts used below, with reasons:

  • \(\binom{n}{k}=\binom{n}{n-k}\): choosing which \(k\) to take is the same as choosing which \(n-k\) to leave.
  • \(\binom{n}{0}=\binom{n}{n}=1\): one empty subset, one full subset.
  • Binomial theorem: \((x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}x^k y^{n-k}\). Why: expanding the product \((x+y)(x+y)\cdots(x+y)\) means choosing \(x\) or \(y\) from each of the \(n\) factors; a term \(x^ky^{n-k}\) arises once for each way of picking the \(k\) factors that contribute \(x\), and there are \(\binom{n}{k}\) such ways.

4. Two series you will need

  • Geometric series: \(\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}q^{j}=\dfrac{1}{1-q}\) for \(|q|<1\). (The symbol \(\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\) means "add up the terms for \(j=0,1,2,\dots\) forever", i.e. the limit of the partial sums. Example: \(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\dots=\frac{1}{1-1/2}=2\).)
  • Exponential series: \(e^{x}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{x^{k}}{k!}\) for every real \(x\). This is the definition of \(e^x\) used in Sheet 2 Exercise 4 and in checking that the Poisson pmf sums to 1.

5. Product notation and the power laws

The capital Greek letter \(\prod\) (pi, for "product") is the multiplication version of \(\sum\): \(\prod_{i=1}^{n}a_i:=a_1\cdot a_2\cdots a_n\), "multiply the numbers \(a_i\) for \(i=1,2,\dots,n\)". Example: \(\prod_{i=1}^{3}\frac{i}{i+1}=\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac34=\frac14\) (each numerator cancels the previous denominator). If there are no factors at all (e.g. \(\prod_{i=1}^{0}\)), the product is \(1\), for the same reason that an empty sum is \(0\): multiplying by nothing changes nothing. Rules and more examples: B3 — product notation.

The pmfs below are full of powers such as \((1-p)^{k-1}\) or \(p^r\). Three power laws [Potenzgesetze] do all the work, for any number \(a\neq0\) and whole numbers \(m,k\):

  • \(a^{m+k}=a^m\cdot a^k\) — e.g. \(2^{3+2}=32=8\cdot4\). Read backwards it splits a power: \((1-p)^{n-k}=(1-p)^n\cdot(1-p)^{-k}\), used in the Poisson limit proof below.
  • \(a^{-k}=\dfrac1{a^k}\) and \(a^0=1\) — e.g. \(2^{-3}=\tfrac18\). This is forced by the first law: \(a^{k}\cdot a^{-k}=a^{0}=1\).
  • \((a^m)^k=a^{mk}\) and \((ab)^k=a^kb^k\) — e.g. \((2^2)^3=64=2^6\), \((2\cdot3)^2=36=4\cdot9\).

Your Analysis guide proves the same laws for real exponents: Analysis 5.2 — general powers.

6. Complement counting

When an event says "at least one", count the opposite. Write \(A^c\) for the complement [Komplement] of \(A\) inside \(\Omega\), i.e. \(A^c:=\Omega\setminus A\), the set of all outcomes that are not in \(A\). (Three notations for the same thing appear in this course and on this page: \(A^c\), \(\Omega\setminus A\) and \(\bar A\). They mean the same set; the script mostly writes \(\Omega\setminus A\).) Every outcome is in exactly one of \(A\) and \(A^c\), so \(|A| = |\Omega| - |A^c|\), and dividing by \(|\Omega|\) gives \(\P(A)=1-\P(A^c)\). "At least one six in six dice" has a messy direct count (overlaps everywhere); "no six at all" is a clean product. This trick solves Sheet 0 Ex 1(iii), Sheet 0 Ex 3(ii), Sheet 0 Ex 5(ii), Sheet 2 Ex 2, Sheet 3 Ex 4(ii) and Sheet 4 Ex 1(ii).

7. What "uniformly at random" is allowed to mean

The formula \(\P(A)=|A|/|\Omega|\) only holds when every element of \(\Omega\) has the same probability. It is not the definition of probability. It is what the Laplace distribution \(\Lap_\Omega\) (Example 1.39(i)) gives. Half the work in every counting exercise is choosing \(\Omega\) so that this assumption is true. Example 1.41 shows in detail what goes wrong otherwise.

Discrete probability spaces and the pmf

Definition 1.34 discrete probability space, pmf Script 1.34

Let \(\Omega\) be an at most countable set. A probability measure \(\P\) on \((\Omega,\Aa:=\pow(\Omega))\) is called a discrete probability measure, and \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\) a discrete probability space. The map

\[ p:\Omega\to[0,1],\qquad \omega\mapsto p(\omega):=\P(\{\omega\}) \]

is called the probability mass function (pmf) [Zähldichte] for \(\P\).

Reading the notation. \(p:\Omega\to[0,1]\) says: \(p\) is a function that takes an outcome and returns a number between 0 and 1. \(\omega\mapsto\P(\{\omega\})\) says what that number is: the probability of the event "the outcome is exactly \(\omega\)".

"At most countable" means finite or countably infinite. The \(\sigma\)-algebra is fixed to be the full power set. This is allowed because the Vitali problem of Theorem 1.28 (a set that cannot be given a probability) only happens on uncountable spaces. It matches Convention 1.16, which says countable spaces always carry their power set.

The curly braces matter. \(p(\omega)\) is a number attached to an element. \(\P(\{\omega\})\) is the probability of the one-element set \(\{\omega\}\). The definition says the two numbers are equal, but the inputs are different kinds of objects.

Example of mine: a die loaded towards six, \(\Omega=[6]=\{1,\dots,6\}\), with \(p(1)=\dots=p(5)=0.1\) and \(p(6)=0.5\). Then \(\P(\text{even})=p(2)+p(4)+p(6)=0.1+0.1+0.5=0.7\). Lemma 1.35 says this "add up the pmf" rule always works.

Lemma 1.35 correspondence between pmf and \(\P\) Script 1.35

  1. Let \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\) be a discrete probability space. Then \(\P\) is uniquely determined by its pmf \(p\).
  2. Let \(\Omega\) be countable and \(p:\Omega\to[0,1]\) with \(\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}p(\omega)=1\). Then
\[ \P:\pow(\Omega)\to[0,1],\qquad A\mapsto\sum_{\omega\in A}p(\omega) \]

is a discrete probability measure on \((\Omega,\pow(\Omega))\) with pmf \(p\).

(\(\sum_{\omega\in A}p(\omega)\) means: add \(p(\omega)\) over all outcomes \(\omega\) in \(A\). If \(A\) is infinite this is a series; since all terms are \(\ge0\), the order of adding does not matter.)

In words: on a countable space, "probability measure" and "list of non-negative numbers that add up to 1" are the same thing. This saves a lot of work: you never have to check \(\sigma\)-additivity by hand (\(\sigma\)-additivity is condition (iii) of Definition 1.17: the probability of a union of countably many pairwise disjoint events equals the sum of their probabilities). You only check two things about a list of numbers: each is \(\ge0\), and they add up to 1.

Proof supplied by me — the script states this without proof

(i) \(p\) determines \(\P\). Let \(A\subseteq\Omega\) be any event. Since \(\Omega\) is at most countable, so is \(A\), and we may write it as a disjoint union of its own singletons:

\[ A=\dot\bigcup_{\omega\in A}\{\omega\}. \]

These singletons are pairwise disjoint (different elements) and all lie in \(\Aa=\pow(\Omega)\). Definition 1.17 states \(\sigma\)-additivity for a family \((A_i)_{i\in\N}\) indexed by all of \(\N\); if \(A\) is finite we therefore list its singletons first and then set all remaining \(A_i:=\emptyset\). This changes nothing, because \(\P(\emptyset)=0\) adds zeros to the sum, and it puts the family into the shape Definition 1.17 asks for. \(\sigma\)-additivity then gives

\[ \P(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}\P(\{\omega\})=\sum_{\omega\in A}p(\omega). \]

So the value of \(\P\) at every event is computed from \(p\) alone: two probability measures with the same pmf agree everywhere, which is what "uniquely determined" means. ✓

(ii) every summable list gives a measure. Define \(\P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}p(\omega)\) and check the axioms of Definition 1.17 plus \(\P(\Omega)=1\).

  • \(\P(\emptyset)=0\): the empty sum is 0 by convention.
  • non-negativity: a sum of numbers in \([0,1]\) is \(\ge0\).
  • \(\sigma\)-additivity: let \(A_0,A_1,\dots\) be pairwise disjoint. Every \(\omega\in\bigcup_i A_i\) lies in exactly one \(A_i\), so each term \(p(\omega)\) appears exactly once on each side of
\[ \sum_{\omega\in\bigcup_i A_i}p(\omega)\;=\;\sum_{i\in\N}\;\sum_{\omega\in A_i}p(\omega). \]

The step that needs care is regrouping an infinite sum. It is legitimate here because all terms are non-negative and the total is finite (it is at most 1), so the series converges absolutely (i.e. the sum of the absolute values \(|p(\omega)|\) is finite — here the absolute values are the terms themselves, since every \(p(\omega)\ge0\)); and an absolutely convergent series may be rearranged and grouped arbitrarily without changing its value (Analysis 3.3, rearrangement theorem). This is the same fact the script appeals to on page 8 when it says "analysis then tells us that any subseries also converges". If the \(p(\omega)\) could be negative, the rearrangement would not be allowed.

  • \(\P(\Omega)=1\): this is the assumption \(\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}p(\omega)=1\).
  • its pmf is \(p\): \(\P(\{\omega\})\) is a sum over a one-element set, namely \(p(\omega)\). ✓ ∎

Urn models: the four ways to draw Script 1.36

An urn [Urne] is a box holding \(n\) objects that we can tell apart (numbered \(1,\dots,n\)). We draw \(k\) times. Two yes/no questions fix the model:

  • With or without replacement [mit/ohne Zurücklegen] — is a drawn object put back before the next draw?
  • Ordered or unordered [mit/ohne Reihenfolge] — does the order in which the objects came out belong to the outcome?

Two yes/no choices give four models. Each has its own \(\Omega\) and its own size \(|\Omega|\).

Notation. \([n]:=\{1,\dots,n\}\). \([n]^k\) is the set of all lists (tuples) \((\omega_1,\dots,\omega_k)\) of length \(k\) with entries in \([n]\). In this course \(0\) is a natural number: Convention 1.1 of the script fixes \(\N=\{0,1,2,\dots\}\), so \(\N_0\) and \(\N\) mean the same set, and \(\N_{>0}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}\), \(\N_{\ge r}=\{r,r+1,r+2,\dots\}\). (Many school books use \(\N\) for \(\{1,2,3,\dots\}\); here it contains \(0\). This matters below: the Poisson distribution lives on \(\N\) and its outcome \(0\) is allowed.) The script writes \(\N_0^{\,n}\) in Lemma 1.36(iv) and \(\N^4\) in Example 1.40(iii) for the same kind of set. Script 1.1

A tiny example first: \(n=3\) objects, \(k=2\) draws My addition

  • (i) with replacement, ordered: \((1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(2,2),(2,3),(3,1),(3,2),(3,3)\) — \(9=3^2\) outcomes.
  • (ii) without replacement, ordered: \((1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(2,3),(3,1),(3,2)\) — \(6=\frac{3!}{1!}\) outcomes (no repeats allowed).
  • (iii) without replacement, unordered: \(\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\}\) — \(3=\binom32\) outcomes (\((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\) become the same set).
  • (iv) with replacement, unordered: record how often each object was drawn, \((a_1,a_2,a_3)\): \((2,0,0),(0,2,0),(0,0,2),(1,1,0),(1,0,1),(0,1,1)\) — \(6=\binom{3+2-1}{2}\) outcomes.

Widget — the four urn models side by side My addition

Set \(n\) (objects in the urn) and \(k\) (draws) and read off all four sample-space sizes at once, with the formula each one uses. The bars are drawn on a logarithmic scale, because the counts differ by orders of magnitude.

Lemma 1.36 classical urn models Script 1.36

An urn with \(n\in\N_{>0}\) distinct objects and \(k\in\N_{>0}\) draws.

  1. With replacement, ordered. \(\Omega=[n]^k\), \(\;|\Omega|=n^k\).
  2. Without replacement, ordered. \(\Omega=\bigl\{(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_k)\in[n]^k \bigm| \omega_i\ne\omega_j \text{ for } i\ne j\bigr\}\), \(\;|\Omega|=\dfrac{n!}{(n-k)!}\).
  3. Without replacement, unordered. \(\Omega=\{S\subseteq[n] \mid |S|=k\}\), \(\;|\Omega|=\dbinom{n}{k}\).
  4. With replacement, unordered. \(\Omega=\Bigl\{(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\N_0^{\,n} \Bigm| \sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i=k\Bigr\}\), \(\;|\Omega|=\dbinom{n+k-1}{k}\), where \(a_i\) counts how often object \(i\) is drawn.

Note on (iv): the outcome is not a tuple of draws but an occupancy vector — how many times each object came out. That is what "unordered with replacement" has to mean: once you forget the order, all that is left of the \(k\) draws is a multiset [Multimenge] — a collection in which an object may appear several times but the order is not recorded — and a multiset is the same information as the list of counts. Cases (ii) and (iii) require \(k\le n\): you cannot draw more distinct objects than the urn holds, so for \(k>n\) both sample spaces are empty. Case (iii) reports this correctly, because \(\binom{n}{k}=0\) for \(k>n\) by the convention in the primer. Case (ii) needs a word of care: the quotient \(\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}\) is not defined for \(k>n\), since \((n-k)!\) would be the factorial of a negative number. The form the proof actually produces, \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)\), is defined for every \(k\), and for \(k>n\) one of its factors is \(n-n=0\), so it gives \(0\) — which is the right answer. Read \(\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}\) as a shorthand that is valid only while \(k\le n\). (clarification mine)

Proofs of the four counts supplied by me — the script states them without proof

(i) \(|[n]^k| = n^k\). An outcome is a tuple \((\omega_1,\dots,\omega_k)\). Each of the \(k\) positions is filled independently with any of the \(n\) objects, because the object is replaced after every draw. By the product rule, \(\underbrace{n\cdot n\cdots n}_{k}=n^k\). ✓

(ii) \(n!/(n-k)!\). Now the objects already drawn are gone. The first draw has \(n\) options, the second \(n-1\), …, the \(k\)-th has \(n-k+1\). By the product rule the count is

\[ n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)\cdot(n-k)\cdots1}{(n-k)\cdots1}=\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}. \;✓ \]

(iii) \(\binom{n}{k}\). Count the ordered outcomes of (ii) in a second way. Every \(k\)-element subset \(S\) can be written out in \(k!\) different orders (arrange \(k\) distinct objects — see the factorial fact in the primer), and every ordered outcome of (ii) arises from exactly one subset in exactly one of its orders. So

\[ \bigl(\text{number of }k\text{-subsets}\bigr)\cdot k! \;=\; \frac{n!}{(n-k)!} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{number of }k\text{-subsets}=\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}=\binom{n}{k}. \;✓ \]

(This "count the same set in two ways" argument is called double counting. It is also the proof that \(\binom nk\), defined in the primer by a formula, really counts \(k\)-subsets.)

(iv) \(\binom{n+k-1}{k}\) — "stars and bars". An outcome is a list of counts \((a_1,\dots,a_n)\) of non-negative integers adding to \(k\). Encode such a list as a row of symbols: write \(a_1\) stars, then a bar, then \(a_2\) stars, then a bar, …, then a bar, then \(a_n\) stars. For example with \(n=4\), \(k=6\) the occupancy \((3,0,2,1)\) becomes

\[ \star\star\star \mid \;\mid \star\star \mid \star . \]

Every such row has exactly \(k\) stars and \(n-1\) bars, so \(n+k-1\) symbols in total. And the encoding is reversible: from any arrangement of \(k\) stars and \(n-1\) bars you read off the counts by looking at the gaps between bars. So occupancy vectors correspond one-to-one with arrangements, and an arrangement is determined by choosing which \(k\) of the \(n+k-1\) positions hold stars:

\[ |\Omega|=\binom{n+k-1}{k}. \;✓ \;\;∎ \]

Sanity check against case (i) with \(n=4\), \(k=6\): ordered gives \(4^6=4096\) outcomes, unordered gives \(\binom{9}{6}=84\). Far fewer — and, crucially, the 84 are not equally likely if the underlying mechanism is 6 independent choices. That is precisely the content of Example 1.41.

Remark 1.37 where each urn model applies Script 1.37

ModelThe script's examples
with replacement, orderedrepeated independent trials — wheels of fortune, generating random passwords
without replacement, orderedsequentially picking distinct items — assigning prizes to distinct winners
without replacement, unorderedsimple random sampling without replacement — drawing lottery numbers
with replacement, unordereddistributing indistinguishable balls into distinguishable bins — identical resources among agents

How to choose, in practice My addition

Ask two questions about the story, not about the answer you want.

  1. Can the same object appear twice? Yes → with replacement. No → without.
  2. Would swapping two of the draws give a different outcome as far as the question is concerned? Yes → ordered. No → unordered.

And then a third, which is the one people forget: are the outcomes of the \(\Omega\) I just chose equally likely? Ordered models are safe here, because the underlying mechanism usually acts on positions. Unordered models are safe when the mechanism itself is unordered (drawing a handful of lottery balls at once). If in doubt, use the ordered model — it is always defensible, and order-blind events can still be counted inside it. Sheet 0 Exercise 5 solves the same question both ways and gets the same answer, precisely because of this.

Remark 1.38 discrete probability measures on \(\R\) Script 1.38

Let \(\Omega\subseteq\R\) be countable and \(p\) a pmf on \(\Omega\). The probability measure \(\P\) on \((\R,\mathcal B)\) given by

\[ \P:\mathcal B\to[0,1],\qquad A\mapsto\sum_{\omega\in\Omega\cap A}p(\omega) \]

and the corresponding cdf

\[ F:\R\to[0,1],\qquad x\mapsto\sum_{\omega\in\Omega\cap(-\infty,x]}p(\omega) \]

are called discrete.

Symbols. \(\mathcal B\) is the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\R\) (the events built from intervals; see B4). The cdf [Verteilungsfunktion] of Definition 1.23 is \(F(x)=\P((-\infty,x])\), the probability of landing at or below \(x\). \(\Omega\cap A\) keeps only the mass points that lie in \(A\).

What this achieves. It moves a discrete distribution onto the real line, so the cdf tools of §1.1 apply. All the mass sits on a countable set, and there is none anywhere else. So the cdf is a staircase: flat between the mass points, and jumping up by \(p(\omega)\) at each one — exactly Lemma 1.24(iv) (jump height \(=\P(\{x\})\)). The cdf widget on the §1.1 page draws this for \(\Omega=\{0,1,2\}\).

Example of mine: a fair coin coded as \(\Omega=\{0,1\}\), \(p(0)=p(1)=\tfrac12\). Then \(F(x)=0\) for \(x<0\), \(F(x)=\tfrac12\) for \(0\le x<1\), and \(F(x)=1\) for \(x\ge1\). Also \(\P([0.2,0.9])=0\), because no mass point lies in that interval.

The seven named discrete distributions Script 1.39

This is the catalogue you must know by heart. Every later chapter uses it. Exam problems open with a line like "let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be iid \(\Ber(p)\)" and never define it — see the old-exam section below for which of the seven actually turn up.

Each distribution below is a pmf in the sense of Definition 1.34: a sample space \(\Omega\) plus a number \(p(\omega)\) for each outcome. The letters in brackets, like \(n\) and \(p\) in \(\Bin(n,p)\), are parameters: fixed numbers you choose to fit the situation (number of trials, success probability, …). For each one I also check that the masses add up to 1, so that Lemma 1.35(ii) makes it a genuine probability measure.

Two pieces of vocabulary used from here on My addition

The symbol \(\sim\). "\(X\sim\Bin(n,p)\)" is read "\(X\) is distributed as [ist verteilt wie] \(\Bin(n,p)\)", and it means: the quantity \(X\) takes the value \(\omega\) with probability \(p_{\Bin(n,p)}(\omega)\). A superscript, as in \(X_1,\dots,X_m\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\Bin(n,p)\) (\(m\) quantities, each binomial with the same \(n\) and \(p\)), adds that the \(X_i\) are independent and identically distributed — the same distribution each, and none of them influencing the others (Definition 1.79, §1.4). Here \(X\) is a random variable [Zufallsvariable]: informally, a number read off the outcome, such as "how many of the six dice showed a six". The precise definition only comes in §1.3 (next page); on this page \(\sim\) appears only in pointers to later chapters and in Example 1.41, and nothing on this page depends on it.

The word "support". The support [Träger] of a distribution is the set of outcomes it can actually produce — for us simply the sample space \(\Omega\) listed with each pmf below. Saying "\(\Geo(p)\) has support \(\N_{>0}\)" is saying "a \(\Geo(p)\) outcome is one of \(1,2,3,\dots\), never \(0\)". Getting a support wrong (starting \(\Geo\) at \(0\), or confusing \(\{0,1\}^n\) with \(\{0,\dots,n\}\)) is the classic way to lose marks here.

Widget — the distribution explorer My addition

Pick a distribution and move its parameters. The left panel is the pmf \(p(\omega)\); the right panel is the cdf \(F(x)=\sum_{\omega\le x}p(\omega)\) from Remark 1.38. The readout checks that the displayed masses sum to 1 — a useful habit, since a pmf that does not sum to 1 is not a pmf.

The script's figures Script 1.39, figures. Next to each distribution the script plots its pmf (bars) and its cdf (staircase) for one parameter choice: Uniform with \(N=10\) (\(\Omega=[10]\)), \(\Hyp(50,20,15)\), \(\Ber(0.7)\), \(\Bin(20,0.4)\), \(\NegBin(5,0.5)\), \(\Geo(0.3)\), \(\Poi(5.5)\). The explorer above opens on the script's values for Hyp, Bin, NegBin, Geo and Poi; for the uniform figure move the Lap slider to \(N=10\), and for \(\Ber(0.7)\) choose Bin with \(n=1\), \(p=0.70\) (the pmf of \(\Bin(1,p)\) is the pmf of \(\Ber(p)\)). What to see in them: the uniform pmf is flat at \(0.1\) and its cdf climbs in equal steps of \(0.1\); \(\Hyp(50,20,15)\) and \(\Bin(20,0.4)\) peak near 6 and 8 (at "sample size × fraction of successes"); \(\NegBin(5,0.5)\) starts at 5; \(\Geo(0.3)\) is largest at 1 and then falls; \(\Poi(5.5)\) peaks at 5. Every cdf rises from 0 to 1.

(i) Laplace / uniform distribution \(\Lap_\Omega\) Script 1.39(i)

For a finite sample space \(\Omega\), the pmf is

\[ p_{\Lap_\Omega}:\Omega\to[0,1],\qquad \omega\mapsto\frac{1}{|\Omega|}. \]

When it applies: every outcome in a finite set is equally likely — drawing a card from a well-shuffled deck.

Sums to 1: \(|\Omega|\) outcomes each of mass \(1/|\Omega|\).

Consequence: for any \(A\subseteq\Omega\), \(\P(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}1/|\Omega|=|A|/|\Omega|\). This is the counting formula, and it is only available for this distribution. Exercise sheet 0 writes it \(U_\Omega\), the script writes it \(\Lap_\Omega\) — the same object under two names, an inconsistency between the two documents.

(ii) Hypergeometric distribution \(\Hyp(N,K,n)\) Script 1.39(ii)

Parameters \(N\in\N\), \(K\in\{0,\dots,N\}\), \(n\in\{0,\dots,N\}\). Sample space \(\Omega=\{\max(0,n+K-N),\dots,\min(n,K)\}\) and pmf

\[ p_{\Hyp(N,K,n)}(\omega)=\frac{\dbinom{K}{\omega}\dbinom{N-K}{n-\omega}}{\dbinom{N}{n}}. \]

When it applies: sampling without replacement. Counting defectives in a quality-control sample of size \(n\) from a batch of \(N\) items containing \(K\) defectives.

Reading the formula: the denominator counts all ways to choose the sample of size \(n\) from \(N\) items (urn model (iii)). The numerator counts the favourable ones: choose \(\omega\) of the \(K\) defectives and the remaining \(n-\omega\) from the \(N-K\) good items. So this is just \(|A|/|\Omega|\) with a cleverly split count.

Why the strange sample space: you cannot draw more defectives than exist (\(\omega\le K\)) or more than you drew (\(\omega\le n\)) — hence \(\min(n,K)\). And if the batch has only \(N-K\) good items and you draw \(n\) of them, you are forced to take at least \(n-(N-K)=n+K-N\) defectives — hence the \(\max(0,\cdot)\).

Sums to 1: by Vandermonde's identity \(\sum_{\omega}\binom{K}{\omega}\binom{N-K}{n-\omega}=\binom{N}{n}\), which itself is a counting argument: split the choice of \(n\) items from \(N\) according to how many came from the \(K\) marked ones.

(iii) Bernoulli process \(\Ber(n,p)\) and Bernoulli distribution \(\Ber(p)\) Script 1.39(iii)

For \(p\in[0,1]\) and \(n\in\N_{>0}\), on \(\Omega=\{0,1\}^n\):

\[ p_{\Ber(n,p)}\bigl(\omega=(\omega_i)_{i\in[n]}\bigr)=p^{\sum_{i\in[n]}\omega_i}\, (1-p)^{\,n-\sum_{i\in[n]}\omega_i}. \]

For \(n=1\) we write \(\Ber(p):=\Ber(1,p)\), the Bernoulli distribution, with pmf

\[ p_{\Ber(p)}(\omega)=\begin{cases}p & \omega=1,\\ 1-p & \omega=0.\end{cases} \]

When it applies: \(\Ber(p)\) is a single binary trial — a biased coin flip, or whether a manufactured part passes inspection. \(\Ber(n,p)\) captures repeated coin tosses. The script notes the extension to trials with more than two outcomes (repeatedly rolling a die) is called a Bernoulli scheme.

The distinction students lose marks on: \(\Ber(n,p)\) is not \(\Bin(n,p)\)

\(\Ber(n,p)\) lives on \(\{0,1\}^n\) — its outcomes are the whole sequences of results, so \(|\Omega|=2^n\). \(\Bin(n,p)\) lives on \(\{0,\dots,n\}\) — its outcomes are the number of successes, so \(|\Omega|=n+1\). The binomial is obtained from the Bernoulli process by counting successes, which is why the binomial coefficient \(\binom{n}{\omega}\) appears in the binomial pmf and not in the Bernoulli one: it counts how many sequences give the same total.

The script itself flags a second trap here: "we overload the symbol \(p\)" to mean both the pmf and the probability parameter, and it will keep doing so. In \(p_{\Ber(n,p)}\) the subscript \(p\) is a number and the function \(p\) is a pmf. The meaning is clear from context — but write them apart in your own solutions.

Sums to 1: expand the product \(\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(p+(1-p)\bigr)=1\) (the symbol \(\prod\) means "multiply the \(n\) factors"; see primer item 5). Choosing \(p\) from factor \(i\) corresponds to \(\omega_i=1\), choosing \((1-p)\) to \(\omega_i=0\), so the \(2^n\) terms of the expansion are exactly the \(2^n\) values of the pmf.

(iv) Binomial distribution \(\Bin(n,p)\) Script 1.39(iv)

For \(p\in[0,1]\), \(n\in\N_{>0}\), on \(\Omega=\{0,\dots,n\}\):

\[ p_{\Bin(n,p)}(\omega)=\binom{n}{\omega}p^{\omega}(1-p)^{\,n-\omega}. \]

When it applies: the number of successes in \(n\) independent trials — the number of heads in ten flips of a coin with success probability \(p\).

Sums to 1: the binomial theorem, \(\sum_{\omega=0}^{n}\binom{n}{\omega}p^\omega(1-p)^{n-\omega}=\bigl(p+(1-p)\bigr)^n=1^n=1\).

Exam sighting: WiSe25 P5a asks you to show that \(n\widehat F_n(t)\sim\Bin\bigl(n,F_{X_1}(t)\bigr)\) for the empirical cdf [empirische Verteilungsfunktion] \(\widehat F_n(t):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\one_{(-\infty,t]}(X_i)\), i.e. the fraction of the \(n\) observed values that are \(\le t\) (here \(\one_{(-\infty,t]}(X_i)\) is \(1\) if \(X_i\le t\) and \(0\) otherwise) — the argument is "each indicator is a \(\Ber(F(t))\) trial, they are independent, so the count is binomial".

(v) Negative binomial distribution \(\NegBin(r,p)\) Script 1.39(v)

For \(p\in[0,1]\), \(r\in\N_{>0}\), on \(\Omega=\N_{\ge r}\):

\[ p_{\NegBin(r,p)}(\omega)=\binom{\omega-1}{r-1}p^{r}(1-p)^{\,\omega-r}. \]

When it applies: \(\omega\) is the total number of trials needed to observe \(r\) successes — the number of free-throw attempts until a basketball player makes \(r\) baskets.

A convention difference worth knowing My addition

Many textbooks and software libraries define the negative binomial on the number of failures before the \(r\)-th success, so their support starts at 0 and their pmf is \(\binom{\omega+r-1}{r-1}p^r(1-p)^{\omega}\). This script counts total trials, so the support starts at \(r\). If you look up a formula elsewhere, check which convention it uses before plugging into an exam.

Reading the formula: for the \(r\)-th success to land exactly on trial \(\omega\), that last trial must be a success (factor \(p\)), and among the first \(\omega-1\) trials exactly \(r-1\) must have been successes — there are \(\binom{\omega-1}{r-1}\) ways, each of probability \(p^{r-1}(1-p)^{\omega-r}\).

Sums to 1: substitute \(m=\omega-r\ge0\) and use the negative binomial series \(\sum_{m\ge0}\binom{m+r-1}{r-1}q^m=(1-q)^{-r}\) (valid for \(0\le q<1\)) with \(q=1-p\), giving \(p^r\cdot p^{-r}=1\). Why the series holds: \((1-q)^{-r}\) is the product of \(r\) geometric series \(\sum_{j\ge0}q^j\). Multiplying them out, the coefficient of \(q^m\) is the number of ways to write \(m=j_1+\dots+j_r\) with \(j_i\ge0\) — by stars and bars (Lemma 1.36(iv) with \(n=r\), \(k=m\)) this is \(\binom{m+r-1}{m}=\binom{m+r-1}{r-1}\).

Why "multiplying them out" is allowed: these are infinite sums, so expanding the product term by term needs a theorem, not just algebra. The theorem is the Cauchy product [Cauchy-Produkt]: if \(\sum_j a_j\) and \(\sum_k b_k\) converge absolutely (the sums of the absolute values \(|a_j|\), \(|b_k|\) are finite), then \(\bigl(\sum_j a_j\bigr)\bigl(\sum_k b_k\bigr)=\sum_{m\ge0}\sum_{j+k=m}a_jb_k\): multiply every term by every term and collect the products by total index \(m\). A geometric series with \(0\le q<1\) has non-negative terms and a finite sum, so it converges absolutely, and the theorem applies \(r-1\) times in a row. Check with \(r=2\), \(q=\tfrac12\): \((1-\tfrac12)^{-2}=4\), and \(\sum_{m\ge0}(m+1)(\tfrac12)^m=1+1+\tfrac34+\tfrac12+\tfrac5{16}+\dots\) indeed approaches 4. Full statement and proof: Analysis 3.3 — the Cauchy product.

A small gap in the script: it allows \(p\in[0,1]\), but for \(p=0\) every mass is 0, so the total is 0, not 1. \(\NegBin(r,0)\) is not a distribution (you never reach a success). Read the parameter range as \(p\in(0,1]\). The same applies to \(\Geo(p)\) below.

Note \(\NegBin(1,p)=\Geo(p)\): put \(r=1\) and \(\binom{\omega-1}{0}=1\), leaving \(p(1-p)^{\omega-1}\).

(vi) Geometric distribution \(\Geo(p)\) Script 1.39(vi)

For \(p\in[0,1]\), on \(\Omega=\N_{>0}\):

\[ p_{\Geo(p)}(\omega)=(1-p)^{\,\omega-1}p. \]

When it applies: the number of trials until the first success — the number of customers arriving until the first sale.

Convention warning again: some books count the failures before the first success and so start at 0. This script starts at 1.

Sums to 1: geometric series, as derived on page 0: \(\sum_{\omega\ge1}(1-p)^{\omega-1}p = p\cdot\frac{1}{1-(1-p)}=1\). This needs \(p>0\) (so that \(q=1-p<1\)); for \(p=0\) all masses are 0 — see the note under \(\NegBin\).

Reading the formula: the first success at trial \(\omega\) means \(\omega-1\) failures (each with probability \(1-p\)) and then one success (probability \(p\)). Example with \(p=0.3\): \(p(1)=0.3\), \(p(2)=0.7\cdot0.3=0.21\), \(p(3)=0.7^2\cdot0.3=0.147\).

This is exactly the distribution derived from scratch in the script's motivation section, with \(p=\tfrac1{52}\) for the "how many reshuffles until the ace of hearts" game.

(vii) Poisson distribution \(\Poi(\lambda)\) Script 1.39(vii)

For \(\lambda\in\R_{>0}\), on \(\Omega=\N\):

\[ p_{\Poi(\lambda)}(\omega)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{\omega}}{\omega!}. \]

When it applies: it approximates the count of rare events at a fixed rate in a fixed interval — the number of phone calls an operator receives in an hour when calls arrive at rate \(\lambda\).

Sums to 1: by the exponential series, \(\sum_{\omega\ge0}\frac{\lambda^\omega}{\omega!}=e^{\lambda}\), so the total is \(e^{-\lambda}e^{\lambda}=1\). Note this also explains where the factor \(e^{-\lambda}\) comes from: it is exactly the normalising constant.

The parameter \(\lambda\) is the expected count — the script records this in Lemma 2.26(vii) but deliberately skips the computation; the derivation is on the §2.1 page of this guide. Theorem 1.42 below says where \(\Poi(\lambda)\) comes from.

Urn models in action Script 1.40

Example 1.40 urn model applications Script 1.40

Urn models are typically paired with the uniform distribution — we assume \(\Lap_\Omega\) on \((\Omega,\pow(\Omega))\) for the sample spaces of Lemma 1.36. Then any event \(A\subseteq\Omega\) has \(\P(A)=|A|/|\Omega|\), since all urn sample spaces are finite. "In short, computing probabilities reduces to counting sizes of sets, which in turn often comes down to combinatorics."

(i) Password collision. You and a friend each generate an 8-character alphanumeric password (62 symbols). What is the probability they are identical?

Sampling with replacement, ordered: \(\Omega=[62]^8\), so \(|\Omega|=62^8\). Fix your friend's password; yours matches it in exactly one of the \(|\Omega|\) equally likely ways. Hence

\[ \P(\text{collision})=\frac{1}{62^{8}}\approx4.58\cdot10^{-15}. \]

(ii) Handing out exercises. Five probability exercises are distributed among five students. What is the probability that the student first in the alphabet gets exercise 1 and the student last in the alphabet gets exercise 5?

Sampling without replacement, ordered: \(\Omega=\{(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_5)\in[5]^5\mid\omega_i\text{ pairwise different}\}\), with \(|\Omega|=5!=120\). The event \(A\) consists of all tuples with \(\omega_1=1\) and \(\omega_5=5\); once those two are fixed, the remaining three exercises can be given out in any order, so \(|A|=3!=6\). Hence

\[ \P(A)=\frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}=\frac{6}{120}=\frac{1}{20}. \]

The script notes this can also be obtained by conditioning, which arrives in §1.4: \(\P(A)=\tfrac15\cdot\tfrac14\).

(iii) Coffee mugs in meeting rooms. PhD students randomly leave their 6 identical coffee mugs in any of 4 meeting rooms. What is the probability that exactly one room ends up with no mug?

Modelled as with replacement, unordered (balls into bins):

\[ \Omega=\Bigl\{(a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4)\in\N^4 \Bigm| \sum_{i=1}^{4}a_i=6\Bigr\}, \qquad |\Omega|=\binom{4+6-1}{6}=\binom{9}{6}=84. \]

Count the event \(A\) = "exactly one room empty" in two steps:

  1. Choose which room is empty: \(\binom41=4\) ways.
  2. Distribute all 6 mugs among the other 3 rooms with each of those rooms non-empty. Writing \(b_1+b_2+b_3=6\) with \(b_i\ge1\): first place one mug in each of the three rooms, then distribute the remaining \(6-3=3\) mugs freely among the three. That is the same urn model again with \(n=3\), \(k=3\): \(\binom{3+3-1}{3}=\binom53=10\) ways.

So \(|A|=4\cdot10=40\) and

\[ \P(A)=\frac{40}{84}=\frac{10}{21}\approx0.476. \]

The substitution in step 2 is worth naming: to count solutions of \(b_1+\dots+b_m=k\) with every \(b_i\ge1\), set \(c_i:=b_i-1\ge0\); then \(c_1+\dots+c_m=k-m\), which is the unrestricted problem with \(k-m\) in place of \(k\). It converts "at least one each" into "any number each", and it reappears in many exercises.

Example 1.41 gotcha! model misspecification Script 1.41

The script now takes the mug example apart, and this is the most important paragraph on the page.

Reading A. If the outcome we record is the occupancy tuple \((a_1,\dots,a_4)\) itself, we are in "with replacement, unordered" and the computation above gives \(\tfrac{10}{21}\) — under the additional assumption, usually left implicit, that all occupancy vectors are equally likely.

Reading B. If instead we read the story literally as "each of the 6 students independently chooses one of the 4 rooms", the proper model is "with replacement, ordered": \(\Omega=[4]^6\) with the uniform distribution, so \(|\Omega|=4^6=4096\). Writing \(X_i(\omega):=\omega_i\) for the room chosen by student \(i\), the students are \(X_1,\dots,X_6\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\Lap_{[4]}\), and the occupancy numbers become derived quantities \(N_j:=\sum_{i=1}^{6}\one_{\{j\}}(X_i)\), \(j\in[4]\). (\(\one_{\{j\}}(X_i)\) is 1 when student \(i\) chose room \(j\) and 0 otherwise, so \(N_j\) counts the students in room \(j\); "iid" means independent and identically distributed and is defined in Definition 1.79.)

Now count \(A\) = "exactly one room empty" in this space. Choose the empty room: \(\binom41=4\) ways. Fix it, say room 4. Then all 6 students choose among rooms 1, 2, 3, giving \(3^6\) ordered outcomes — but we must exclude those in which one of rooms 1, 2, 3 is also empty. Apply inclusion–exclusion (Theorem 1.22) to the three events \(L_i\) = "room \(i\) is empty", \(i=1,2,3\), inside this set of \(3^6\) outcomes. Because all \(3^6\) outcomes are equally likely, every probability in Theorem 1.22 is a count divided by \(3^6\), so we may cancel that denominator and work with counts throughout. The counts are: \(|L_i|=2^6\) (all six students pick one of the two remaining rooms), and there are \(\binom31=3\) choices of \(i\); \(|L_i\cap L_j|=1^6=1\) (all six pick the single remaining room) for each of the \(\binom32=3\) pairs; and \(|L_1\cap L_2\cap L_3|=0^6=0\), since the six students cannot all avoid all three rooms. Therefore the number of outcomes lying in none of the \(L_i\) is

\[ 3^6-\binom31 2^6+\binom32 1^6-\binom33 0^6 = 729-192+3-0 = 540 . \]

These 540 ordered outcomes are exactly the ones that use all three of the rooms 1, 2, 3 at least once. (The script writes the same line without the last term, which is \(0\) anyway.) Hence

\[ |A|=\binom41\Bigl(3^6-\binom31 2^6+\binom32 1^6\Bigr)=4\cdot540=2160, \qquad \P(A)=\frac{2160}{4^6}=\frac{2160}{4096}=\frac{135}{256}\approx0.527. \]

Both answers are "correct". \(\tfrac{10}{21}\approx0.476<\tfrac12\) and \(\tfrac{135}{256}\approx0.527>\tfrac12\) simply belong to different modelling choices, which have to be made very explicit. Under the "students place mugs iid" model the occupancy tuples are not equally likely: \((3,1,1,1)\) can arise in many more ordered ways than \((6,0,0,0)\).

In words: the formula \(\P(A)=|A|/|\Omega|\) is not wrong in either case. What differs is the claim "all elements of \(\Omega\) are equally likely", and that claim is a statement about the physical mechanism, not about mathematics. Choosing an unordered \(\Omega\) and then assuming uniformity is the single most common modelling error in this subject.

A check of mine, to make the asymmetry concrete: the tuple \((6,0,0,0)\) arises from exactly \(1\) ordered outcome (all six students pick room 1), while \((3,1,1,1)\) arises from \(\frac{6!}{3!\,1!\,1!\,1!}=120\) ordered outcomes. Under Reading A both get probability \(1/84\); under Reading B they get \(1/4096\) and \(120/4096\). A factor of 120 between two models of the same story.

The Poisson limit theorem

Widget — watching \(\Bin(n,\lambda/n)\) become \(\Poi(\lambda)\) My addition

Fix \(\lambda\) and increase \(n\). The bars are the binomial pmf with \(p_n=\lambda/n\); the outlined bars behind them are the Poisson pmf with the same \(\lambda\). The readout gives the largest gap between the two, which shrinks to 0 — that is Theorem 1.42.

Theorem 1.42 Poisson limit theorem Script 1.42

Let \((p_n)_{n\in\N}\subseteq[0,1]\) with a fixed \(\lambda:=\lim_{n\to\infty}n\,p_n\in\R_{>0}\). Then for all \(\omega\in\N\),

\[ \lim_{n\to\infty}p_{\Bin(n,p_n)}(\omega)=p_{\Poi(\lambda)}(\omega). \]

Symbols. \((p_n)_{n\in\N}\) is a sequence of success probabilities, one for each number of trials \(n\). The assumption \(np_n\to\lambda\) says the expected number of successes, \(n\cdot p_n\), settles down at \(\lambda\). The standard choice is \(p_n=\lambda/n\).

A number example of mine: \(n=100\), \(p=0.03\), so \(\lambda=3\). Probability of no success: binomial \(0.97^{100}\approx0.0476\); Poisson \(e^{-3}\approx0.0498\). Already close.

The script's own gloss: "the pmf of the binomial distributions converges to the Poisson distribution for large \(n\) while \(np\) remains finite, i.e. \(p\) simultaneously has to become small as \(n\) grows in a controlled way. This controlled dependence of \(p\) on \(n\) (not an actual dependence) is such that, in the limit, on average we should expect \(\lambda\) successes among the \(n\) trials."

In words: many trials, each very unlikely, with the average number of successes held fixed — that is a Poisson. This is why Poisson is the distribution for rare events: radioactive decays, typos per page, server requests per second.

Proof Sheet 3 · Ex 3, with one step made rigorous by me

Fix \(\omega=k\in\N\). Start from the binomial pmf:

\[ p_{\Bin(n,p_n)}(k)=\binom{n}{k}p_n^{k}(1-p_n)^{n-k}. \]

Step 0: \(p_n\to0\). Since \(np_n\to\lambda\) with \(\lambda\) finite and \(n\to\infty\), write \(p_n\) as a product of two sequences whose limits we know:

\[ p_n=(np_n)\cdot\frac1n\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\lambda\cdot0=0. \]

This uses the product rule for limits (if \(a_n\to a\) and \(b_n\to b\), both finite, then \(a_nb_n\to ab\); Analysis 2.1 — rules for limits) with \(a_n=np_n\to\lambda\) and \(b_n=\tfrac1n\to0\). (Do not write "\(\lambda/\infty\)": \(\infty\) is not a number, and the limit rules only apply to finite limits.) This is needed three times below.

Step 1: the binomial coefficient. Writing out the factorials,

\[ \binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{(n-k)!\,k!}=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{k!}, \]

a product of exactly \(k\) factors over \(k!\). Therefore

\[ \frac{\binom{n}{k}}{n^k/k!}=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{n^{k}} =\underbrace{\frac{n}{n}\cdot\frac{n-1}{n}\cdots\frac{n-k+1}{n}}_{k\text{ factors}}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1, \tag{1}\]

because \(k\) is fixed while \(n\to\infty\), so each of the \(k\) factors \(\frac{n-j}{n}=1-\frac jn\) tends to 1, and a product of finitely many convergent factors converges to the product of the limits (the product rule for limits, used \(k-1\) times; Analysis 2.1).

Step 2: the power of \(p_n\). By the power law \((ab)^k=a^kb^k\) from primer item 5, read from right to left with \(a=n\), \(b=p_n\),

\[ n^{k}p_n^{k}=(np_n)^{k}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\lambda^{k}, \tag{2}\]

since \(np_n\to\lambda\) and raising to a fixed power \(k\) is continuous (sequence criterion for continuity: if \(f\) is continuous and \(x_n\to x\), then \(f(x_n)\to f(x)\); Analysis 4.1). Equivalently: \((np_n)^k\) is a product of \(k\) copies of \(np_n\), and the product rule for limits applies.

Step 3: the leftover factor. Split \((1-p_n)^{n-k}=(1-p_n)^{n}\,(1-p_n)^{-k}\), using the power law \(a^{m+k}=a^ma^k\) with \(m=n-k\) (primer item 5). By Step 0, \(p_n\to0\), so \(1-p_n\to1\); in particular \(1-p_n>\tfrac12\) for all large \(n\), so we never divide by \(0\). The function \(x\mapsto x^{-k}\) is continuous at \(x=1\), so the sequence criterion for continuity gives

\[ (1-p_n)^{-k}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1^{-k}=1. \tag{3}\]

Step 4: the exponential factor. This is the only delicate step. (Background: Analysis 6.3, Lemma 6.24 proves \((1+\tfrac xn)^n\to e^x\) for a fixed real \(x\), also by taking logarithms, though it finishes with the derivative of \(\ln\) at \(1\) rather than with the series bound used here; the log series is in Analysis 9.3; \(\ln\) as the inverse of \(\exp\), with \(\ln(a^n)=n\ln a\) and \(e^{\ln a}=a\), is Analysis 5.2.) Take logarithms, using \(\ln(a^n)=n\ln a\):

\[ \ln\bigl((1-p_n)^{n}\bigr)=n\ln(1-p_n). \]

For small \(x\) the Taylor expansion is \(\ln(1-x)=-x-\tfrac{x^2}{2}-\tfrac{x^3}{3}-\cdots =-x\bigl(1+\tfrac x2+\tfrac{x^2}{3}+\cdots\bigr)\), so \(\ln(1-x)=-x\,(1+\varepsilon(x))\) with \(\varepsilon(x)=\tfrac x2+\tfrac{x^2}{3}+\tfrac{x^3}4+\cdots\) (the series is valid for \(0\le x<1\)).

Why \(\varepsilon(x)\to0\) as \(x\to0\) my addition: take \(0\le x\le\tfrac12\). Every term of \(\varepsilon(x)\) is \(\ge0\), and each denominator \(2,3,4,\dots\) is at least 2, so

\[ 0\le\varepsilon(x)\le\frac x2+\frac{x^2}2+\frac{x^3}2+\cdots=\frac x2\,(1+x+x^2+\cdots) =\frac x2\cdot\frac1{1-x}\le\frac x2\cdot2=x, \]

using the geometric series \(1+x+x^2+\dots=\frac1{1-x}\) and \(1-x\ge\tfrac12\). So \(0\le\varepsilon(x)\le x\), and squeezing gives \(\varepsilon(x)\to0\). Numbers: \(x=0.1\) gives \(\ln(0.9)\approx-0.10536=-0.1\,(1+0.0536)\), so \(\varepsilon(0.1)\approx0.054\le0.1\) ✓. Since \(p_n\to0\) (Step 0), \(p_n\le\tfrac12\) for all large \(n\), so the bound applies. Substituting \(x=p_n\):

\[ n\ln(1-p_n)=-\,n\,p_n\,\bigl(1+\varepsilon(p_n)\bigr)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}-\lambda\cdot1=-\lambda, \]

using \(np_n\to\lambda\), \(1+\varepsilon(p_n)\to1\) and the product rule for limits. Since \((1-p_n)^n=e^{n\ln(1-p_n)}\) (this is \(e^{\ln a}=a\) applied to \(a=(1-p_n)^n\)) and \(\exp\) — which is just another way of writing \(x\mapsto e^{x}\) — is continuous (Analysis 4.1),

\[ (1-p_n)^{n}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}e^{-\lambda}. \tag{4}\]

Putting it together. Write the pmf so that each converging piece is visible:

\[ \binom{n}{k}p_n^{k}(1-p_n)^{n-k} =\underbrace{\frac{\binom{n}{k}}{n^{k}/k!}}_{\to1\ (1)}\cdot \underbrace{\frac{(np_n)^{k}}{k!}}_{\to\lambda^{k}/k!\ (2)}\cdot \underbrace{(1-p_n)^{n}}_{\to e^{-\lambda}\ (4)}\cdot \underbrace{(1-p_n)^{-k}}_{\to1\ (3)} . \]

A product of finitely many convergent sequences converges to the product of the limits, so

\[ \lim_{n\to\infty}p_{\Bin(n,p_n)}(k)=1\cdot\frac{\lambda^{k}}{k!}\cdot e^{-\lambda}\cdot1 =\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{k}}{k!}=p_{\Poi(\lambda)}(k). \;\;∎ \]

A gap in the official solution Noted by me

The printed solution justifies Step 4 by writing \(\lim_n(1-p_n)^n=\lim_n\bigl(1-\tfrac{np_n}{n}\bigr)^n\) and then citing the standard limit \(e^{-x}=\lim_n\bigl(1-\tfrac xn\bigr)^n\). That standard limit is stated for a fixed \(x\), whereas here the quantity \(x_n=np_n\) changes with \(n\) — it only tends to \(\lambda\). The conclusion is right, but it needs the extra argument that \(\bigl(1-\tfrac{x_n}{n}\bigr)^n\to e^{-\lambda}\) whenever \(x_n\to\lambda\), which is exactly what the logarithm computation in Step 4 supplies. If you reproduce the official version in an exam you will most likely still get the credits; the version above is the one that is airtight.

Rule of thumb for using it my addition: the Poisson approximation to \(\Bin(n,p)\) is good when \(n\) is large and \(p\) small; a common rule is \(n\ge50\) and \(p\le0.1\) (textbooks differ). Set \(\lambda=np\) and compare in the widget above.

Bertrand's paradox Script 1.43

The script brackets this as a Philosophical Interlude. It is the continuous echo of Example 1.41: the same question, three defensible models, three different answers.

Example 1.43 the ambiguity of "random" Script 1.43

Consider a circle of radius \(R\). What is the probability that a randomly chosen chord is longer than the side of an inscribed equilateral triangle? Posed by Joseph Bertrand in 1889.

Vocabulary, since the script assumes it: a chord is a straight segment joining two points on the circle. An inscribed equilateral triangle has all three vertices on the circle and all three sides equal; its side length is \(s=R\sqrt3\), and the perpendicular distance from the centre to any of its sides (the apothem) is \(R/2\). We want \(\P(\text{chord length}>R\sqrt3)\).

Where \(R\sqrt3\), \(R/2\) and \(2\pi/3\) come from (school geometry):

  • Radians [Bogenmaß]: an angle is measured by the length of the arc it cuts out of a circle of radius 1. The full turn \(360^\circ\) is the whole circumference \(2\pi\), so \(120^\circ=\tfrac13\cdot2\pi =\tfrac{2\pi}3\). On a circle of radius \(R\) every length scales by \(R\): arc length \(=\) angle \(\cdot R\), circumference \(2\pi R\), disc area \(\pi R^2\).
  • The three vertices of the equilateral triangle split the circle into three equal arcs, so each side is seen from the centre \(O\) under the angle \(\tfrac{2\pi}3=120^\circ\).
  • Drop the perpendicular from \(O\) to one side. It cuts the \(120^\circ\) angle in half, giving a right triangle with hypotenuse \(R\) (centre to vertex) and angle \(60^\circ\) at \(O\). Its side next to that angle is the apothem \(R\cos60^\circ=R\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac R2\); its opposite side is half the triangle side, \(R\sin60^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2R\). So the side is \(s=2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}2R=R\sqrt3\). (Check by Pythagoras: \((\tfrac R2)^2+(\tfrac{\sqrt3}2R)^2=\tfrac14R^2+\tfrac34R^2=R^2\) ✓.) Sine and cosine: Analysis 5.3.

Widget — three ways to pick a chord My addition

Each method draws chords by its own rule. Long chords (longer than \(R\sqrt3\)) are drawn in the accent colour, short ones faint. Run all three and watch the three running fractions settle on 1/3, 1/2 and 1/4 — three answers to one question.

Method 1 — random endpoints: \(\P_1=\tfrac13\) Script 1.43

Choose two points uniformly and independently on the circumference and join them. Fix one endpoint \(A\). For the chord to be longer than \(s\), the second endpoint \(B\) must lie on the arc between the vertices \(V_1,V_2\) of an equilateral triangle \(AV_1V_2\) — the arc not containing \(A\). That favourable arc subtends an angle of \(2\pi/3\) at the centre \(O\), so it has length \((2\pi/3)R\), out of a total circumference of \(2\pi R\):

\[ \P_1=\frac{(2\pi/3)R}{2\pi R}=\frac13. \]

Method 2 — random radial point: \(\P_2=\tfrac12\) Script 1.43

Choose one radius uniformly at random (uniform angle), then a point \(P\) uniformly along that radius. Each chord is determined by its midpoint, obtained by drawing the chord perpendicular to the radius through \(P\). The chord is longer than \(s\) exactly when its midpoint lies within distance \(R/2\) of the centre, since \(R/2\) is the apothem of the inscribed equilateral triangle. \(P\) is uniform along a segment of length \(R\), and the favourable part has length \(R/2\):

\[ \P_2=\frac{R/2}{R}=\frac12. \]

Method 3 — random midpoint: \(\P_3=\tfrac14\) Script 1.43

Choose a point \(M\) uniformly at random from the area of the circle and use it as the chord's midpoint. The chord is longer than \(s\) exactly when \(M\) lies inside the concentric circle of radius \(R/2\). Comparing areas, not lengths:

\[ \P_3=\frac{\pi(R/2)^2}{\pi R^2}=\frac{(R/2)^2}{R^2}=\frac14. \]

What the paradox shows Script 1.43

We obtained three different probabilities — \(1/3\), \(1/2\), \(1/4\) — for the same event, and all seem justified, in that violating their respective assumptions would appear to violate the problem description. Bertrand's paradox highlights that when talking about infinite spaces, the phrase "randomly choose one of \(X\)" is ambiguous until the precise mechanism of randomness is specified. Each method implicitly defines a different probability measure over the set of chords.

The reason they differ, in one sentence: the three methods put uniform measure on three different parameterisations of the set of chords — arc length, radial distance, and area — and a map that is uniform in one coordinate is not uniform in another. Method 2 and Method 3 both describe a chord by its midpoint, but Method 2 spreads midpoints uniformly along a radius while Method 3 spreads them uniformly over the disc, which concentrates them near the rim (an annulus at radius \(r\) has area proportional to \(r\), not constant).

The script links two videos for animations. Both are external; the mathematics above is complete without them.

Exercise-sheet tasks

Sheet 0, Exercises 2–5 Sheet 0

Sheet 0's preamble prescribes the recipe: build \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\), put the discrete uniform distribution on \(\Omega\), and count. Exercises 1 and 6 are on the Chapter 0 page; the four here are all urn models in disguise.

Sheet 0, Exercise 2 — an urn with 3 red and 2 blue balls Sheet 0 · Ex 2

Two balls are drawn uniformly at random without replacement. Find: (i) both red; (ii) exactly one red; (iii) the second ball is blue; (iv) given the second is blue, the first is red; (v) given at least one is blue, exactly one is blue.

Probability space. Label the balls so that \(R=\{1,2,3\}\) are red and \(B=\{4,5\}\) blue, \(E=\{1,\dots,5\}\). Model two successive draws, ordered, without replacement — urn model 1.36(ii) with \(n=5\), \(k=2\):

\[ \Omega=\{(\omega_1,\omega_2)\in E^2\mid\omega_1\ne\omega_2\},\quad \Aa=\pow(\Omega),\quad \P=U_\Omega, \]

so \(|\Omega|=5\cdot4=20\). Write \(R_i=\{\omega\mid\omega_i\in R\}\) and \(B_i=\{\omega\mid\omega_i\in B\}\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\).

(i) \(|R_1\cap R_2|=3\cdot2=6\) (three reds first, two reds left), so \(\P=\tfrac6{20}=\tfrac3{10}\).

(ii) "exactly one red" \(=(R_1\cap B_2)\,\dot\cup\,(B_1\cap R_2)\) — the dot on the union sign, \(\dot\cup\), is the script's and the sheet's way of recording that the two sets are disjoint (no outcome lies in both), which is why their sizes may simply be added — with \(|R_1\cap B_2|=3\cdot2=6\) and \(|B_1\cap R_2|=2\cdot3=6\), total 12, so \(\P=\tfrac{12}{20}=\tfrac35\).

(iii) \(B_2=(R_1\cap B_2)\,\dot\cup\,(B_1\cap B_2)\) with \(6\) and \(2\cdot1=2\), so \(|B_2|=8\) and \(\P(B_2)=\tfrac8{20}=\tfrac25\).

Worth pausing on: \(\tfrac25=|B|/|E|\) — the probability that the second ball is blue equals the probability that the first is. The reason is symmetry: the map that swaps the two coordinates, \((\omega_1,\omega_2)\mapsto(\omega_2,\omega_1)\), is a bijection of \(\Omega\) onto itself (it is its own inverse) which carries \(B_1\) onto \(B_2\), so the two sets have the same size. Looking at one draw on its own therefore gives the same answer whichever draw you pick; only the joint behaviour of the two draws differs — as parts (iv) and (v) show. This fact saves time in many exercises.

(iv) By the definition of conditional probability (Definition 1.69, which for the uniform distribution is just "restrict the counting to \(B_2\)"):

\[ \P(R_1\mid B_2)=\frac{\P(R_1\cap B_2)}{\P(B_2)}=\frac{|R_1\cap B_2|}{|B_2|}=\frac68=\frac34. \]

(v) Let \(A=B_1\cup B_2\) ("at least one blue") and \(C=(R_1\cap B_2)\,\dot\cup\,(B_1\cap R_2)\) ("exactly one blue"). Complement counting: \(\Omega\setminus A=R_1\cap R_2\) with 6 elements, so \(|A|=20-6=14\); and \(|C|=12\) from part (ii). Since \(C\subseteq A\),

\[ \P(C\mid A)=\frac{|C|}{|A|}=\frac{12}{14}=\frac67. \]

Compare (iv) and (v): \(\tfrac34\) versus \(\tfrac67\). Knowing which ball is blue is different information from knowing some ball is blue. This is the same asymmetry as Exercise 5 below and as the two-card box of Example 0.4.

Sheet 0, Exercise 3 — a 4-digit PIN Sheet 0 · Ex 3

A PIN is chosen uniformly from \(\{0000,\dots,9999\}\). Find: (i) all four digits distinct; (ii) at least one digit repeated; (iii) exactly one pair; (iv) the PIN is a palindrome.

Probability space. A PIN is an ordered tuple of digits, so with replacement, ordered on \(E=\{0,\dots,9\}\):

\[ \Omega=\{0,\dots,9\}^4,\quad \Aa=\pow(\Omega),\quad \P=U_\Omega,\quad |\Omega|=10^4 . \]

(i) Let \(D=\{\omega\in\Omega\mid\omega_i\ne\omega_j\text{ for }i\ne j\}\) be the event "all four digits distinct". Choosing four distinct digits in order is urn model 1.36(ii) with \(n=10\), \(k=4\): \(|D|=10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7=5040\), so

\[ \P(D)=\frac{5040}{10^4}=\frac{63}{125}=0.504. \]

(ii) The complement of (i): \(\P(\Omega\setminus D)=1-\tfrac{63}{125}=\tfrac{62}{125}\).

(iii) Let \(E_{\text{pair}}\) be the event "exactly one pair": one digit appears exactly twice, and the other two digits are distinct from each other and from the repeated one. Build such a PIN in four successive steps:

  • choose the repeated digit \(d\): 10 ways;
  • choose which two of the four positions carry \(d\): \(\binom42=6\) ways;
  • fill the first remaining position from \(\{0,\dots,9\}\setminus\{d\}\): 9 ways;
  • fill the last position from the remaining 8 digits: 8 ways.
\[ |E_{\text{pair}}|=10\cdot6\cdot9\cdot8=4320,\qquad \P=\frac{4320}{10^4}=\frac{54}{125}=0.432. \]

Why this does not double-count: the last two steps fill two specific positions (the ones left over, in left-to-right order), so each PIN is produced exactly once. If instead you chose an unordered pair of digits for those two slots you would have to divide by 2 — and taking 9·8 already accounts for the order of the slots.

(iv) Write \(\Pi\) (capital Greek pi, the sheet's name for this event) for the set of palindromes. A palindrome satisfies \(\omega_1=\omega_4\) and \(\omega_2=\omega_3\), so it is determined by \((\omega_1,\omega_2)\in\{0,\dots,9\}^2\): \(|\Pi|=100\) and \(\P(\Pi)=\tfrac{100}{10^4}=\tfrac1{100}\).

Sheet 0, Exercise 4 — the bug detector and the base rate Sheet 0 · Ex 4

2 % of submissions contain a bug. The detector flags 90 % of buggy submissions and 5 % of bug-free ones. Among 10 000 submissions: (i) how many buggy ones are flagged? (ii) how many bug-free ones? (iii) given a submission was flagged, what is the probability it contains the bug?

Probability space. Model the population itself as the sample space: \(\Omega=\{1,\dots,10\,000\}\), \(\Aa=\pow(\Omega)\), \(\P=U_\Omega\), so \(\P(A)=|A|/10\,000\). "Choosing a submission uniformly at random" is then just picking a point of \(\Omega\). Let \(B\) = buggy and \(F\) = flagged. Reading off the percentages:

\[ |B|=0.02\cdot10\,000=200,\qquad |B\cap F|=0.9\cdot200=180,\qquad |\bar B\cap F|=0.05\cdot9800=490, \]

where \(\bar B=\Omega\setminus B\).

(i) 180.   (ii) 490.

(iii) \(|F|=|B\cap F|+|\bar B\cap F|=180+490=670\), and since \(B\cap F\subseteq F\),

\[ \P(B\mid F)=\frac{\P(B\cap F)}{\P(F)}=\frac{|B\cap F|}{|F|}=\frac{180}{670}=\frac{18}{67}\approx0.269. \]

In words — the base-rate effect: even though the detector is fairly accurate, most flagged submissions are false positives, because the bug is rare. There are 49 times as many clean submissions as buggy ones, so even a 5 % false-positive rate produces more false alarms (490) than true ones (180).

This is Bayes' theorem (Theorem 1.70) done by counting, and it needs no theory at all when the population is finite and uniform. The script's own worked Bayes computation is Example 1.72 (who wrote a passage, given its British spelling); it has the same three-number shape, though not the extreme rarity that produces the base-rate effect here. Whenever a task hands you the three numbers of a testing problem — how common the condition is (here 2 %), how often the test says "yes" when the condition is present (here 90 %), and how often it says "yes" when it is absent (here 5 %) — build a table of counts for a concrete population such as 10 000. It is faster and far less error-prone than manipulating the formula.

Sheet 0, Exercise 5 — two aces, two kinds of information Sheet 0 · Ex 5

(i) You are dealt two cards and look at the first: it is an ace. What is the probability the second is also an ace? (ii) Same deal, but you do not look; someone truthfully tells you at least one of your two cards is an ace. Is the probability that both are aces the same?

Probability space. Number the cards \(\{1,\dots,52\}\) with \(K\subset\{1,\dots,52\}\), \(|K|=4\), the aces. Draw two in order without replacement:

\[ \Omega=\{(\omega_1,\omega_2)\mid\omega_1\ne\omega_2\},\quad |\Omega|=52\cdot51=2652, \qquad K_i=\{\omega\mid\omega_i\in K\}. \]

(i) \(|K_1\cap K_2|=4\cdot3=12\) and \(|K_1|=4\cdot51=204\), so

\[ \P(K_2\mid K_1)=\frac{|K_1\cap K_2|}{|K_1|}=\frac{12}{204}=\frac{3}{51}=\frac1{17}. \]

(ii) Now the conditioning event is \(A=K_1\cup K_2\) ("at least one ace"). Complement counting: \(|\bar K_1\cap\bar K_2|=48\cdot47=2256\), so \(|A|=2652-2256=396\). Since \(K_1\cap K_2\subseteq A\),

\[ \P(K_1\cap K_2\mid A)=\frac{12}{396}=\frac1{33}\;\ne\;\frac1{17}. \]

The same answer in the unordered model. Take \(\tilde\Omega=\{\tilde\omega\subseteq\{1,\dots,52\}\mid|\tilde\omega|=2\}\) with \(U_{\tilde\Omega}\) — urn model 1.36(iii):

\[ \P(K_1\cap K_2\mid A)=\frac{\binom42}{\binom{52}{2}-\binom{48}{2}}=\frac{6}{1326-1128}=\frac{6}{198}=\frac1{33}. \;✓ \]

Both models agree, because the event in question does not depend on order — a useful check that the modelling was consistent.

In words: the two conditioning events carry different information. Knowing that a specific card is an ace is stronger than knowing that some card in the pair is. Naming a position eliminates more possibilities.

A typo in the official solution: it cites "Gregorii, S2.3.1" for the unordered model; the reference is to Georgii (2015), the book listed in the script's literature section.

Sheet 2, Exercise 2 — at least one six in six dice Sheet 2 · Ex 2

\(\Omega_0=\{\text{⚀},\dots,\text{⚅}\}\) is the set of faces of a fair die. Let \(p\) be the probability of obtaining at least one ⚅ when throwing six fair dice at once. Compute \(p\), setting up the probability space properly.

Solution

Probability space. Six dice thrown at once, each showing one of six faces — with replacement, ordered (the dice are distinguishable, even if only conceptually):

\[ \Omega=\{\text{⚀},\dots,\text{⚅}\}^6,\quad \Aa=\pow(\Omega),\quad \P(A)=\frac{|A|}{6^6}. \]

The event. \(A=\{\omega\in\Omega\mid\omega_j=\text{⚅ for at least one }j\in[6]\}\).

Complement counting. "No six at all" means every entry comes from the five non-six faces:

\[ p=\P(A)=1-\P(\Omega\setminus A)=1-\frac{|\{\text{⚀},\dots,\text{⚄}\}^6|}{|\Omega|} =1-\frac{5^6}{6^6}=1-\frac{15625}{46656}=\frac{31031}{46656}\approx0.6651. \]

Why the direct count is a bad idea: the sets "die \(j\) shows a six" overlap heavily, so a direct count needs inclusion–exclusion with \(2^6-1=63\) terms. The complement is one product. The official solution gives the answer as \(\approx0.665\); the exact fraction is \(31031/46656\).

Connection to the distributions: the number of sixes among six dice is \(\Bin(6,\tfrac16)\), and \(\P(A)=1-p_{\Bin(6,1/6)}(0)=1-\binom60(\tfrac16)^0(\tfrac56)^6\) — the same computation seen through Example 1.39(iv). Note \(np=1\), so the Poisson approximation with \(\lambda=1\) would give \(1-e^{-1}\approx0.632\): in the right ballpark, but \(n=6\) is far too small for Theorem 1.42 to be accurate.

The Chevalier de Méré — whom Remark 0.1 of the script names, though for a different question, the problem of points — is also said to have bet on getting at least one six in four rolls of a single die. That is exactly the computation above with four dice instead of six: \(1-(5/6)^4\approx0.518\), just over a half, which is why the bet was profitable. (The historical anecdote is my addition; the script does not mention this bet.)

Sheet 2, Exercise 4 — nobody gets their own sheet back Sheet 2 · Ex 4

A tutor redistributes \(n\) anonymously submitted sheets at random. What is the probability that nobody gets their own sheet back? How does it behave as \(n\to\infty\)?

Solution

Probability space. A redistribution is a bijection of \([n]\) to itself, i.e. drawing \(n\) distinct balls in order — urn model 1.36(ii) with \(k=n\):

\[ \Omega=\{\omega=(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_n)\in[n]^n\mid\omega_i\ne\omega_j\ \forall i\ne j\}, \qquad |\Omega|=n!, \qquad \P=U_\Omega. \]

Here \(\omega_i\) is the sheet handed to student \(i\), and \(\forall\) is the standard shorthand for "for all", so the condition reads "\(\omega_i\ne\omega_j\) for all \(i\ne j\)" — no sheet is handed out twice.

The events. \(A_i=\{\omega\mid\omega_i=i\}\) — "student \(i\) gets their own sheet". Fixing one coordinate leaves \((n-1)!\) arrangements of the rest, so

\[ \P(A_i)=\frac{(n-1)!}{n!}=\frac1n. \]

More generally, fixing \(k\) distinct coordinates leaves \((n-k)!\) arrangements:

\[ \P(A_{i_1}\cap\cdots\cap A_{i_k})=\frac{(n-k)!}{n!}. \]

Inclusion–exclusion (Theorem 1.22). For each \(k\) there are \(\binom nk\) choices of \(k\) indices, and each contributes the same value, so the inner sum collapses to a single product:

\[ \sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n}\P(A_{i_1}\cap\cdots\cap A_{i_k}) =\binom nk\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{n!} =\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{n!}=\frac1{k!}. \]

That cancellation is the whole trick. Therefore

\[ \P\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}A_i\Bigr)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(-1)^{k-1}\frac1{k!}, \]

and the event we want is the complement — nobody gets their own sheet:

\[ \P\Bigl(\text{no fixed point}\Bigr)=1-\sum_{k=1}^{n}(-1)^{k-1}\frac1{k!} =\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{k!}. \]

(The last step: the \(k=0\) term of the right-hand sum is \(1\), and for \(k\ge1\) we have \(-(-1)^{k-1}=(-1)^k\).)

The limit. By the exponential series with \(x=-1\),

\[ \lim_{n\to\infty}\P(\text{no fixed point})=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}=e^{-1}\approx0.3679. \]

In words: whether there are 5 students or 5 000, the chance that nobody gets their own sheet back is about 37 %. The convergence is extremely fast — already at \(n=5\) the value is \(\tfrac{11}{30}=0.36\overline{6}\) (the bar marks the digit 6 repeating for ever), within \(0.002\) of the limit \(0.3679\). Such a fixed-point-free permutation is called a derangement [fixpunktfreie Permutation].

A stale cross-reference: the official solution cites "Lemma 1.33 (without replacement ordered draw)". In the current version of the script the urn models are Lemma 1.36. The script is a living document and its numbering has shifted since the sheet was written — when a sheet and the script disagree on a number, trust the script.

Sheet 3, Exercise 4 — Agathe and the overcrowded subway Sheet 3 · Ex 4

At Marienplatz a train departs every 10 minutes, so crowded that only one person boards each time, with every person on the platform equally likely to be the one. Between trains, two new people arrive. Agathe and Balthasar start alone on the platform. Find the probability that Agathe boards (i) the \(n\)-th train, (ii) at the latest the \(n\)-th train.

Solution

Track the crowd first. Each cycle removes one person and adds two, so the platform grows by exactly one per train. It starts at 2, so when the \(n\)-th train arrives there are \(n+1\) people waiting. (Check: \(n=1\) gives 2 ✓; \(n=2\) gives 3 ✓.)

Everyone present is equally likely to board, so given that Agathe is still there when train \(i\) arrives, she boards it with probability \(\tfrac1{i+1}\) and fails to with probability \(1-\tfrac1{i+1}=\tfrac{i}{i+1}\).

(i) Agathe boards the \(n\)-th train exactly when she misses trains \(1,\dots,n-1\) and then boards train \(n\). Each factor is a probability given that she is still waiting, and such step-by-step probabilities multiply (the multiplication rule for conditional probabilities, §1.4; think "a fraction of a fraction"). The misses give:

\[ \prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\Bigl(1-\frac1{i+1}\Bigr)=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{i}{i+1} =\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac34\cdots\frac{n-2}{n-1}\cdot\frac{n-1}{n}=\frac1n. \]

(The symbol \(\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\) means "multiply the factors for \(i=1,\dots,n-1\)"; see primer item 5 or B3.)

This is a telescoping product (name mine): the numerator of each factor cancels the denominator of the previous one, leaving only the first numerator (1) and the last denominator (\(n\)). Multiplying by the probability of boarding train \(n\):

\[ \P(\text{Agathe boards train }n)=\frac1n\cdot\frac1{n+1}=\frac1{n(n+1)}. \]

(ii) "Boards at the latest with train \(n\)" is the complement of "misses all of the first \(n\) trains". The same telescoping product, now with \(n\) factors, gives \(\prod_{i=1}^{n}\tfrac{i}{i+1}=\tfrac1{n+1}\), so

\[ \P(\text{boards by train }n)=1-\frac1{n+1}=\frac{n}{n+1}. \]

Two checks of mine.

  • Consistency: summing (i) should give (ii). Indeed \(\sum_{m=1}^{n}\frac1{m(m+1)}=\sum_{m=1}^{n}\bigl(\frac1m-\frac1{m+1}\bigr)=1-\frac1{n+1}\) ✓ — another telescoping sum (the same idea as Analysis 3.1 — a telescoping series), using the partial-fraction split \(\frac1{m(m+1)}=\frac1m-\frac1{m+1}\).
  • It is a genuine pmf: letting \(n\to\infty\) gives \(\sum_{m\ge1}\frac1{m(m+1)}=1\), so Agathe boards eventually with probability 1 — despite the platform growing without bound. The distribution of her boarding train is a legitimate pmf on \(\N_{>0}\) (Lemma 1.35(ii)), and it is a nice example of a distribution that is not one of the seven named ones.

Note on the official solution: part (ii) says "from part (a), the latter occurs with probability \(\tfrac1{n+1}\)", but part (a) computed \(\tfrac1n\) for missing the first \(n-1\) trains. The intended reading is "the same telescoping product, run one step further", and the answer \(\tfrac{n}{n+1}\) is correct.

Sheet 3, Exercise 3 — the Poisson limit theorem Sheet 3 · Ex 3

This is exactly Theorem 1.42, and it is worked in full inside the theorem box above, together with a note on the one step the official solution glosses.

Sheet 4, Exercise 1 — rolling a tetrahedron \(k\) times Sheet 4 · Ex 1

A fair tetrahedron (a four-sided die) has faces labelled 1, 2, 3, 4. It is rolled \(k\ge1\) times. \(E\) = "the same number appears in every roll"; \(F\) = "the product of the \(k\) numbers is even". Compute (i) \(\P(E)\), (ii) \(\P(F)\), (iii) \(\P(E\cup F)\).

This sheet belongs to §1.4 by date, but it uses only Laplace counting and inclusion–exclusion, so it lives here, next to the other counting tasks.

Solution

Model. An outcome is the list of results \(\omega=(x_1,\dots,x_k)\) with each \(x_i\in[4]=\{1,2,3,4\}\), so \(\Omega=[4]^k\) (all lists of length \(k\) from \([4]\)) and \(|\Omega|=4^k\) (four choices per roll, multiplied over \(k\) rolls — the product rule from the counting page). "Fair" means every list is equally likely, so we use the Laplace distribution: \(\P(A)=|A|/|\Omega|\) (Script 1.39(i)).

(i) \(E=\{(1,\dots,1),(2,\dots,2),(3,\dots,3),(4,\dots,4)\}\) has 4 elements, so

\[ \P(E)=\frac{4}{4^k}=\Bigl(\frac14\Bigr)^{k-1}. \]

(The last step: \(4/4^k=1/4^{k-1}\) by cancelling one factor 4.)

(ii) Counting "even product" directly is messy, so use the complement \(F^c\) = "product is odd". A product of whole numbers is odd exactly when every factor is odd (one even factor makes the whole product even). So \(F^c=\{1,3\}^k\), with \(2^k\) elements, and

\[ \P(F)=1-\P(F^c)=1-\frac{2^k}{4^k}=1-\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)^{k}. \]

(The complement rule \(\P(F)=1-\P(F^c)\) is Proposition 1.19(ii) with \(B=\Omega\), \(A=F^c\), using \(\P(\Omega)=1\) — see §1.1.)

(iii) Inclusion–exclusion for two sets (Proposition 1.19(i), or Theorem 1.22 with \(n=2\); §1.1): \(\P(E\cup F)=\P(E)+\P(F)-\P(E\cap F)\). The event \(E\cap F\) = "all rolls equal and product even" means all rolls equal some \(i\) with \(i^k\) even, i.e. \(i\in\{2,4\}\). So \(|E\cap F|=2\) and \(\P(E\cap F)=2/4^k=\tfrac12(\tfrac14)^{k-1}\). Therefore

\[ \P(E\cup F)=\Bigl(\frac14\Bigr)^{k-1}+1-\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)^{k}-\frac12\Bigl(\frac14\Bigr)^{k-1} =\frac12\Bigl(\frac14\Bigr)^{k-1}+1-\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)^{k}. \]

Check of mine. For \(k=1\) every single roll is "all equal", so \(E=\Omega\) and \(\P(E\cup F)\) must be 1. The formula gives \(\tfrac12\cdot1+1-\tfrac12=1\) ✓. For \(k=2\): \(\tfrac18+1-\tfrac14=\tfrac78\); directly, the only pairs outside \(E\cup F\) are the unequal all-odd pairs \((1,3),(3,1)\), i.e. \(2/16=\tfrac18\) ✓.

In words: count all-equal lists (4 of them), count odd-product lists (all odd, \(2^k\)), and correct for the overlap (the two all-even constant lists).

Official solution: checked — all three results are correct. One line in (iii) is sloppy: it writes \(E\cap F=E\cap\{(x_1,\dots,x_k)\mid x_i\in\{2,4\}\ \forall i\}\). But the second set is "all rolls even", not \(F\) ("product even"; e.g. \((1,2)\in F\)). The intersection with \(E\) happens to be the same, \(\{(2,\dots,2),(4,\dots,4)\}\), so the count \(|E\cap F|=2\) is right.

Old-exam tasks

No exam task is purely about §1.2 — but its objects are everywhere

I checked all three available exams task by task. None asks you to set up an urn model or to derive a discrete pmf from scratch. What the exams do instead is use the distributions of Example 1.39 as building blocks inside problems belonging to later chapters:

WhereWhat it uses from this pageBelongs to
WiSe25 P5a — empirical cdf each \(\one_{(-\infty,t]}(X_i)\sim\Ber(F(t))\); their sum is \(\Bin(n,F(t))\) §3.2
SoSe25 P5a — duck hunt each hunter's target \(S_j\sim\Lap_{[m]}\), so \(\P(S_j\ne i)=\tfrac{m-1}{m}\) §2.1
SoSe26 P5 — randomised response the sensitive attribute \(A\sim\Ber(p)\), the observed answers \(Y_i\sim\Ber(q(p))\), where \(q(p)=rp+\tfrac{1-r}2\) is a known function of \(p\) §3.1, §3.2, §3.3
SoSe26 P1a, P1b — true/false, mark one answer \(X\sim\Ber(p)\) and \(Y:=1-X\); "for two Bernoulli RVs, \(\Cov[X,Y]=0\) implies independence" (\(\Cov\) is the covariance [Kovarianz], defined in §2.1; it measures whether two quantities tend to be large together) §2.1
SoSe26 P4 — characteristic functions \(\P(X_j=\pm1)=\tfrac12\), a shifted-and-scaled \(\Ber(\tfrac12)\) §2.3
SoSe25 P4a–d — estimating and testing a Poisson rate; P4d light bulb factory \(X_i\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\Poi(\lambda)\); the pmf \(e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x/x!\) is given as a hint and used for the likelihood; defectives per batch modelled as \(\Poi(\lambda)\) §3.2
WiSe25 P1d — true/false on the sample mean \(X_1,X_2,\dots\sim\Poi(2)\), whose mean is the parameter 2 §2.4
SoSe25 P1a — true/false counterexample the Laplace distribution on \(\Omega=\{0,1\}\) as the simplest possible probability space §1.4
SoSe26 P2c — true/false counterexample \(X\) uniform on \(\{-1,0,1\}\), i.e. \(\Lap_{\{-1,0,1\}}\) §2.1

What to take from this. You will not be asked "state the hypergeometric pmf". You will be asked a question whose first line is "let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be iid \(\Ber(p)\)", and you are expected to know without being told what that means, what its support is, and what its mean and variance are (Lemma 2.26). Learn the catalogue as vocabulary, not as a topic.

The inclusion–exclusion technique used in Example 1.41 and in Sheet 2 Exercise 4 is examined — see WiSe25 P6c, worked on the §1.1 page.

Summary sheet

The four urn models

orderedunordered
with replacement\(n^k\)\(\binom{n+k-1}{k}\)
without replacement\(\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}\)\(\binom{n}{k}\)

Memory hook: the two without entries differ by \(k!\) (the orderings of one subset); the two ordered entries are the ones your intuition reaches for first.

The seven distributions

NameSupport \(\Omega\)pmf \(p(\omega)\)Models
\(\Lap_\Omega\)finite \(\Omega\)\(1/|\Omega|\)all outcomes equally likely
\(\Hyp(N,K,n)\)\(\{\max(0,n{+}K{-}N),\dots,\min(n,K)\}\)\(\binom{K}{\omega}\binom{N-K}{n-\omega}/\binom{N}{n}\)defectives in a sample drawn without replacement
\(\Ber(n,p)\)\(\{0,1\}^n\)\(p^{\sum\omega_i}(1-p)^{n-\sum\omega_i}\)the sequence of \(n\) binary trials
\(\Bin(n,p)\)\(\{0,\dots,n\}\)\(\binom{n}{\omega}p^\omega(1-p)^{n-\omega}\)the number of successes in \(n\) trials
\(\NegBin(r,p)\)\(\N_{\ge r}\)\(\binom{\omega-1}{r-1}p^r(1-p)^{\omega-r}\)total trials to reach \(r\) successes
\(\Geo(p)\)\(\N_{>0}\)\((1-p)^{\omega-1}p\)trials until the first success
\(\Poi(\lambda)\)\(\N\)\(e^{-\lambda}\lambda^\omega/\omega!\)rare events at rate \(\lambda\)

Relations between them

  • \(\Ber(p)=\Ber(1,p)\); counting the successes of \(\Ber(n,p)\) gives \(\Bin(n,p)\).
  • \(\NegBin(1,p)=\Geo(p)\).
  • \(\Bin(n,\lambda/n)\to\Poi(\lambda)\) as \(n\to\infty\) — Theorem 1.42.
  • \(\Hyp\) is the without-replacement analogue of \(\Bin\); for \(N\) much larger than \(n\) the two are close, since removing a few items barely changes the composition. (not in the script)
