Traps

  • \(\E[XY]=\E[X]\E[Y]\) and \(\Var[X+Y]=\Var[X]+\Var[Y]\) need independence (or at least uncorrelatedness); \(\E[X+Y]=\E[X]+\E[Y]\) does not.
  • \(\Var[X-Y]=\Var[X]+\Var[Y]\) for independent \(X,Y\) — plus, not minus.
  • \(\Var[2X]=4\Var[X]\ne2\Var[X]\).
  • Uncorrelated \(\not\Rightarrow\) independent (except for two Bernoullis, and jointly Gaussian vectors, §2.3).
  • \(\E[g(X)]\ne g(\E[X])\) in general (Jensen, §2.2).
  • \(\E[Y\mid X=x]\) is a number; \(\E[Y\mid X]\) is a random variable.
  • Medians need not be unique; means need not exist.

Exam focus

Every exam has used this page. Recurring shapes: mean and variance of a count via indicators (SoSe25 P5, duck hunt: 8 credits), true/false on covariance versus independence (SoSe26 P1a, P1b, P2c, P2d), laws of total expectation / variance (WiSe25 P1b), and means and variances of averages as the first step of every estimator and every Chebyshev or clt problem (SoSe26 P4c, P5c; WiSe25 P5a–c; WiSe25 P4b on §2.2), and LOTUS to evaluate an integral (WiSe25 P3c). Know the table by heart.

Self-test

Section 2.2 · Lecture 8 (10 June 2026)

Basic probability inequalities

Grundlegende Ungleichungen der Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie

What this page covers Script §2.2, pp. 70–72

Everything from Theorem 2.38 (Markov) to Remark 2.45: Markov's, Chebyshev's and Jensen's inequalities, with their examples and remarks. The script's section goal: "Introduce fundamental inequalities that provide bounds on probabilities without requiring full knowledge of the distribution but only relying on properties like the mean or variance."

Worked in place: Sheet 8 Ex 2, Sheet 9 Ex 2(i), (iii), Sheet 10 Ex 4, and the old-exam tasks SoSe25 P5c, WiSe25 P4b, SoSe26 P3a, P3b, SoSe26 P4d.

Elsewhere: the parts of Sheet 9 Ex 1–2 that need the central limit theorem or the law of large numbers, and Sheet 9 Ex 3–4 (which use Markov and Chebyshev to prove modes of convergence), are on §2.4. Everything here builds on means and variances from §2.1.

The big picture

Often you do not know the whole distribution of a random quantity. You know only a summary: its mean [Erwartungswert], maybe its variance [Varianz]. Still you want a guarantee about a probability. The inequalities on this page give such guarantees. Each one holds for every distribution with that summary.

A concrete question (my example). Your bus comes after a random waiting time \(X\) (in minutes). A waiting time is never negative, so \(X\ge0\). On average you wait 10 minutes. How likely is a wait of at least an hour?

  • Markov uses only the mean: \(\P(X\ge60)\le\frac{10}{60}=\frac16\). Why: suppose more than a sixth of all days had waits of 60 minutes or more. Those days alone would contribute more than \(\frac16\cdot60=10\) to the average. The average would then be above 10 — a contradiction.
  • Chebyshev also uses the standard deviation [Standardabweichung], say 5 minutes. A wait of 60 is 50 minutes above the mean, which is 10 standard deviations. Chebyshev gives \(\P(X\ge60)\le\frac{5^2}{50^2}=0.01\). More information gives a sharper bound.
  • Jensen answers a different kind of question: how does \(\E[g(X)]\) compare with \(g(\E[X])\)? If the ticket price grows like \(X^2\), the average price is at least the price of the average wait: \(\E[X^2]\ge(\E[X])^2=100\).

In words: Markov — a non-negative quantity is rarely much larger than its mean. Chebyshev — any quantity is rarely many standard deviations away from its mean. Jensen — averaging and then applying a convex function gives at most as much as applying the function and then averaging.

Cross-references

Convex functions and the second-derivative test: Analysis 7.6. Tangent lines: Analysis 6.2. The logarithm is strictly increasing: Analysis 5.2. Mean, variance, indicators, the median's optimality: §2.1.

0. Symbols and words used on this page

  • Probability space [Wahrscheinlichkeitsraum] \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\): \(\Omega\) is the set of all possible outcomes \(\omega\); \(\Aa\) is the collection of events (subsets of \(\Omega\)) that get a probability; \(\P\) assigns each event its probability (sets, measure background).
  • Real random variable [reelle Zufallsvariable] \(X:\Omega\to\R\): a rule that turns each outcome into a number. The script abbreviates it "RVRV" (real-valued random variable).
  • \(\E[X]\) or \(\mu\): the mean (expected value). \(\Var[X]=\E[(X-\mu)^2]\) or \(\sigma^2\): the variance, the mean squared distance from \(\mu\). \(\sigma=\sqrt{\Var[X]}\): the standard deviation (§2.1).
  • Indicator [Indikatorfunktion] \(\one_A\) of an event \(A\), written \(\chi_A\) in the script and on this page: the random variable that is 1 when \(A\) happens and 0 otherwise. Its mean is \(1\cdot\P(A)+0\cdot\P(\text{not }A)=\P(A)\).
  • Almost surely [fast sicher] (a.s.) / "with probability 1": a statement may fail only on an event of probability 0.
  • Independent [unabhängig], written \(X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\); iid = independent and identically distributed (all have the same distribution).
  • Median [Median] \(m\): a number with \(\P(X\le m)\ge\frac12\) and \(\P(X\ge m)\ge\frac12\) — the "middle" of the distribution (§2.1).
  • clt = central limit theorem [zentraler Grenzwertsatz]: sums of many iid variables are approximately normal. \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) is the standard normal distribution and \(\Phi\) its cdf (cumulative distribution function [Verteilungsfunktion]), that is \(\Phi(a)=\P(Z\le a)\) for \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) (§2.4).
  • "iff" = "if and only if". \(\lceil x\rceil\) (ceiling) = the smallest integer \(\ge x\), e.g. \(\lceil1.58\rceil=2\).

1. A function below another gives a smaller mean

Everything on this page rests on one fact, the monotonicity of expectation (Proposition 2.4(iv)): if \(Y(\omega)\le Z(\omega)\) for every outcome \(\omega\), then \(\E[Y]\le\E[Z]\). Combine it with \(\P(A)=\E[\one_A]\) (box 0). This gives a recipe: to bound \(\P(A)\) from above, find a random variable that is at least \(\one_A\) everywhere and whose mean you know.

Example. For \(X\ge0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\): \(\one_{\{X\ge\varepsilon\}}\le\frac X\varepsilon\). Check both cases: where \(X\ge\varepsilon\), the left side is 1 and the right side is \(\ge1\); where \(X<\varepsilon\), the left side is 0 and the right side is \(\ge0\). Taking \(\E\) gives \(\P(X\ge\varepsilon)\le\E[X]/\varepsilon\) — that is Markov's inequality. The picture below shows the step function lying under the line.

2. Convex and concave functions

A function \(g:\R\to\R\) is convex [konvex] if for all \(x_1,x_2\) and all \(t\in[0,1]\)

\[ g\bigl(tx_1+(1-t)x_2\bigr)\le t\,g(x_1)+(1-t)\,g(x_2). \]

Picture: \(tx_1+(1-t)x_2\) runs over the segment between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\); the right side runs over the straight chord joining \((x_1,g(x_1))\) and \((x_2,g(x_2))\). Convex means: the graph never rises above any of its chords — it "holds water". Concave means the reverse inequality (\(-g\) is convex).

  • Test: if \(g\) is twice differentiable, \(g\) is convex iff \(g''\ge0\) everywhere (Analysis 7.6); strictly convex if \(g''>0\).
  • Convex: \(x^2\) (\(g''=2\)), \(e^x\) (\(g''=e^x\)), \(|x|\) (not differentiable at 0, but the chord test holds), \(-\ln x\) on \((0,\infty)\) (\(g''=1/x^2\)), \(1/x\) on \((0,\infty)\).
  • Concave: \(\ln x\), \(\sqrt x\) on \((0,\infty)\); linear functions are both convex and concave.
  • Tangent below the graph. A differentiable convex \(g\) lies above each of its tangent lines: \(g(x)\ge g(x_0)+g'(x_0)(x-x_0)\) for all \(x\). (A convex function without a derivative still has a "supporting line" through every point that stays below the graph.)

3. Absolute values inside events

\(\{|Y|\ge\varepsilon\}=\{Y\ge\varepsilon\}\cup\{Y\le-\varepsilon\}\): "far from 0 on either side". So \(\P(Y\ge\varepsilon)\le\P(|Y|\ge\varepsilon)\) — a two-sided bound also bounds each single side. The exercises use this to turn "the server is overloaded" (one side) into a Chebyshev question (two sides).

Markov's inequality

The idea. A non-negative quantity cannot often be much larger than its mean. If it were, the large values alone would already push the mean up too far. Primer box 1 turned this into a one-line proof. The script states a more general version: first transform \(X\) by an increasing function \(f\), then use the mean of \(f(X)\).

Theorem 2.38 Markov's inequality Script 2.38

Let \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\) be a probability space and \(X:\Omega\to\R\) a real random variable. Write \(S_X=\operatorname{im}(X)=X(\Omega)\) for the set of values that \(X\) can take ("im" = image). Let \(f:S_X\to\R_{\ge0}\) be monotonically increasing [monoton wachsend] (\(x\le y\Rightarrow f(x)\le f(y)\)) with values \(\ge0\). Then for every \(\varepsilon\in\R\) with \(f(\varepsilon)>0\):

\[ \P(X\ge\varepsilon)\le\frac{\E[f(X)]}{f(\varepsilon)}. \]

The usual special case (take \(f(x)=x\)). Let \(X\) be non-negative, i.e. \(\P(X\ge0)=1\). Then for every constant \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[ \P(X\ge\varepsilon)\le\frac{\E[X]}{\varepsilon}. \]

(The script's statement also assumes that \(X\) has a density that is integrable. The general proof below does not use this. Only the second proof, written with integrals, needs it. One more piece of small print (mine): the script writes "for each \(\varepsilon\in\R\)", but \(f\) is only defined on \(S_X\), so \(f(\varepsilon)\) makes sense only for \(\varepsilon\in S_X\). Read the theorem as: for every \(\varepsilon\in S_X\) with \(f(\varepsilon)>0\). In the special case \(f(x)=x\) this is no restriction, because the bound \(\E[X]/\varepsilon\) is then defined for every \(\varepsilon>0\) anyway.)

Proof Script — each step explained

General version. Look at a single outcome \(\omega\). Two cases.

  • If \(X(\omega)\ge\varepsilon\): \(f\) is increasing, so \(f(X(\omega))\ge f(\varepsilon)\). The indicator \(\one_{\{X\ge\varepsilon\}}\) equals 1 here.
  • If \(X(\omega)<\varepsilon\): the indicator equals 0.

In both cases \(f(\varepsilon)\one_{\{X\ge\varepsilon\}}\le f(X)\one_{\{X\ge\varepsilon\}}\le f(X)\). The last step holds because \(f\ge0\), so dropping the indicator (replacing 0 by \(f(X)\ge0\)) can only make things larger. Now take expectations (monotonicity, Proposition 2.4(iv)) and divide by \(f(\varepsilon)>0\):

\[ \P(X\ge\varepsilon)=\E[\one_{\{X\ge\varepsilon\}}]=\E\Bigl[\tfrac{f(\varepsilon)}{f(\varepsilon)}\one_{\{X\ge\varepsilon\}}\Bigr] \le\E\Bigl[\tfrac{f(X)}{f(\varepsilon)}\one_{\{X\ge\varepsilon\}}\Bigr]\le\frac{\E[f(X)]}{f(\varepsilon)}. \]

Special case with a density \(p_X\) (the function whose integral gives probabilities, \(\P(X\ge\varepsilon)=\int_\varepsilon^\infty p_X(x)\,\mathrm dx\)). Since \(X\ge0\), the mean is \(\E[X]=\int_0^\infty x\,p_X(x)\,\mathrm dx\). Split this integral at \(\varepsilon\) and throw away the left part:

\[ \begin{aligned} \E[X]&=\int_0^\varepsilon x\,p_X(x)\,\mathrm dx+\int_\varepsilon^\infty x\,p_X(x)\,\mathrm dx \ \ge\ \int_\varepsilon^\infty x\,p_X(x)\,\mathrm dx &&\text{the first integrand is }\ge0\\ &\ge\int_\varepsilon^\infty\varepsilon\,p_X(x)\,\mathrm dx=\varepsilon\,\P(X\ge\varepsilon) &&x\ge\varepsilon\text{ on the range of integration} \end{aligned} \]

and divide by \(\varepsilon>0\). The discrete case is the same with sums.

Notes on the script's proof. (1) The script first shows that \(f\) is measurable — a technical condition that makes \(f(X)\) a random variable, so that \(\E[f(X)]\) makes sense (B4 — measurable functions). It cites "Exercise 2.1", which is not on the sheets, and its displayed set mixes \(\ge\) and \(>\). A short argument: for increasing \(f\), every set \(\{x:f(x)\ge a\}\) is an interval of the form \([A,\infty)\) or \((A,\infty)\), with \(A=\inf\{x:f(x)\ge a\}\) (the largest lower bound of that set, the infimum [Infimum]; see Analysis 1.2) — or the empty set, or all of \(S_X\). Why an interval: if \(f(x)\ge a\) and \(y\ge x\), then \(f(y)\ge f(x)\ge a\), so the set contains everything to the right of any of its points. Intervals are Borel sets, which is what measurability asks for. (2) It claims \(\{f(x)\ge f(\varepsilon)\}=\{x\ge\varepsilon\}\); that is only true for strictly increasing \(f\), but only the inclusion \(\{x\ge\varepsilon\}\subseteq\{f(x)\ge f(\varepsilon)\}\) is used, and that holds for every increasing \(f\).

How good is it? The script: Markov is "very crude/loose, but requires hardly any assumptions on the distribution of \(X\)"; the bound uses only the mean. It helps only for \(\varepsilon>\E[X]\). For \(\varepsilon\le\E[X]\) the right side is \(\ge1\), and every probability is \(\le1\) anyway. Still, it cannot be improved in general (mine). Take \(0<\mu\le\varepsilon\) and let \(X=\varepsilon\) with probability \(\frac\mu\varepsilon\), \(X=0\) otherwise. Then \(\E[X]=\varepsilon\cdot\frac\mu\varepsilon=\mu\) and \(\P(X\ge\varepsilon)=\frac\mu\varepsilon\) — exactly the bound.

In words: the probability that a non-negative quantity reaches \(\varepsilon\) is at most its mean divided by \(\varepsilon\).

Example 2.39 website hits Script 2.39

A website has on average \(\E[X]=50\) hits per day. How likely are at least 150 hits on a given day? The number of hits is never negative, so Markov applies. With \(\varepsilon=150\) (the script calls it \(a\)):

\[ \P(X\ge150)\le\frac{\E[X]}{150}=\frac{50}{150}=\frac13 . \]

So at least 150 hits happen with probability at most \(\frac13\). The script adds: this bound is "quite general and might not be very tight".

For comparison: if the hits were Poisson distributed, \(\Poi(50)\), then \(\P(X\ge150)\approx3.5\cdot10^{-30}\) (computed numerically). Markov knows nothing about the shape. So it must allow the worst case: a distribution with a third of its mass at 150 and the rest at 0.

Widget — the true tail against the Markov and Chebyshev bounds My addition

For a chosen distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), the curves show, for thresholds \(t>\mu\): the true \(\P(X\ge t)\) (black), Markov's \(\mu/t\) (blue) and Chebyshev's \(\sigma^2/(t-\mu)^2\) (orange), capped at 1. All four distributions are non-negative, so Markov applies; the Chebyshev curve is the two-sided bound for \(\P(|X-\mu|\ge t-\mu)\), used here as a bound for the one-sided \(\P(X\ge t)\) (primer box 3). The vertical axis is logarithmic, so every factor of 10 is one grid step. The "extremal" distribution makes Markov exact at \(t=4\).

Chebyshev's inequality

The idea. Apply Markov not to \(X\) but to the squared distance from the mean, \((X-\mu)^2\), whose mean is the variance. A small variance then forces \(X\) to stay close to \(\mu\) with high probability.

Theorem 2.40 Chebyshev's inequality Script 2.40

Let \(X\) be a real random variable with finite mean \(\E[X]\) and finite variance \(\Var[X]>0\). Then for every \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[ \P\bigl(|X-\E[X]|\ge\varepsilon\bigr)\le\frac{\Var[X]}{\varepsilon^2}. \]

The "\(k\) standard deviations" form (mine; Example 2.41 uses it): with \(\varepsilon=k\sigma_X\),

\[ \P\bigl(|X-\mu|\ge k\sigma_X\bigr)\le\frac1{k^2}. \]

At most \(\frac14\) of the mass lies 2 or more standard deviations from the mean, at most \(\frac19\) at 3 or more — for every distribution.

Proof Script, with one step repaired

Let \(Y:=X-\E[X]\). Then \(|Y|\ge0\), and \(f(x)=x^2\) is increasing on \([0,\infty)\) with \(f(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^2>0\). Markov (Theorem 2.38) applied to the random variable \(|Y|\) with this \(f\):

\[ \P(|X-\E[X]|\ge\varepsilon)=\P(|Y|\ge\varepsilon)\le\frac{\E[|Y|^2]}{\varepsilon^2}=\frac{\E[(X-\E[X])^2]}{\varepsilon^2}=\frac{\Var[X]}{\varepsilon^2}. \]

Note on the script's proof. It applies Theorem 2.38 "with \(f(x)=x^2\)" to \(X\) directly and writes \(\P(|X|\ge\varepsilon)\le\varepsilon^{-2}\E[X^2]\). But \(x^2\) is not increasing on \(\R\), and Theorem 2.38 bounds \(\P(X\ge\varepsilon)\), not \(\P(|X|\ge\varepsilon)\). Applying it to \(|X|\) (or \(|Y|\)), as above, fixes both points; the conclusion is unchanged. Also, the assumption \(\Var[X]>0\) is not needed: if \(\Var[X]=0\), then \(X=\E[X]\) almost surely (Proposition 2.8(i)) and the left side is 0.

Markov versus Chebyshev Script. Chebyshev needs more information (mean and variance), but it can give much better (tighter) bounds.

One-sided use. \(\P(X\ge\mu+\varepsilon)\le\P(|X-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/\varepsilon^2\) (primer box 3). This is how the exercises bound "overload" or "loss" events.

In words: the probability of landing at least \(\varepsilon\) away from the mean is at most the variance divided by \(\varepsilon^2\). At least \(k\) standard deviations away happens with probability at most \(1/k^2\).

Example 2.41 three standard deviations Script 2.41

\(X\) has mean \(\mu_X=10\) and variance \(\sigma_X^2=4\), so \(\sigma_X=2\). How likely is a deviation of 3 standard deviations or more, i.e. of 6 or more? Chebyshev with \(\varepsilon=6\) (the script writes "\(k=3\)", meaning \(\varepsilon=k\sigma_X=3\cdot2\)):

\[ \P(|X-10|\ge6)\le\frac{4}{36}=\frac19 . \]

So \(X\) lies outside \((4,16)\) with probability at most \(\frac19\), whatever its distribution, as long as mean and variance are finite.

Small wording slip in the script: it asks for "more than" 3 standard deviations but computes \(\P(|X-10|\ge6)\), i.e. "at least". The bound \(\frac19\) covers both, since \(\{|X-10|>6\}\subseteq\{|X-10|\ge6\}\). For a normal distribution the true value is about 0.0027 (the "99.7 % rule"). Chebyshev pays for its universality. It is exact for the three-point distribution \(X\in\{\mu-k\sigma,\mu,\mu+k\sigma\}\) with probabilities \(\frac1{2k^2},1-\frac1{k^2},\frac1{2k^2}\) (check: its variance is \(2\cdot\frac1{2k^2}(k\sigma)^2=\sigma^2\), and \(\P(|X-\mu|\ge k\sigma)=\frac1{k^2}\)).

Widget — how conservative is \(1/k^2\)? My addition

For several distributions — each with its own mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\) — the bars show the true \(\P(|X-\mu|\ge k\sigma)\). Measuring the deviation in units of \(\sigma\) makes the five numbers comparable. The dashed line is Chebyshev's bound \(1/k^2\). Only the extremal three-point distribution touches it. ("Double exponential" is the distribution with density \(\frac1{2b}e^{-|x-\mu|/b}\); most textbooks call it the Laplace distribution, but in this course "Laplace" [Laplace-Verteilung] means the uniform distribution on a finite set \(\Lap_\Omega\) of Example 1.39(i), so the name is avoided here.)

Widget — how many samples do I need? Chebyshev versus the clt My addition

You measure \(n\) iid quantities \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) and average them: \(\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\), the sample mean [Stichprobenmittel]. It has \(\E[\bar X_n]=\mu\) and \(\Var[\bar X_n]=\sigma^2/n\) (linearity, and Proposition 2.8(iii),(iv) for the variance). You want \(\bar X_n\) within \(\varepsilon\) of \(\mu\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha\). Chebyshev (guaranteed): \(\frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}\le\alpha\iff n\ge\frac{\sigma^2}{\alpha\varepsilon^2}\). The clt (approximate, §2.4): \(n\ge\bigl(z\,\sigma/\varepsilon\bigr)^2\) with \(\Phi(z)=1-\frac\alpha2\). The same "solve \(\Var/\varepsilon^2\le\alpha\) for the unknown" step appears in SoSe25 P5c (there the unknown is the width \(k\), not \(n\)) and in Sheet 9 Ex 2(iii) (there a given \(n\) is checked).

Jensen's inequality

The idea with two points. Let \(X\) be \(x_1\) or \(x_2\), each with probability \(\frac12\). Then \(\E[X]\) is the midpoint and \(\E[g(X)]=\frac12g(x_1)+\frac12g(x_2)\) is the midpoint of the chord. For a convex \(g\) the chord lies above the graph, so \(\E[g(X)]\ge g(\E[X])\). With other probabilities you move along the chord — that is exactly the definition of convexity with \(t=\P(X=x_1)\). Jensen's inequality says the same holds for any distribution.

Theorem 2.42 Jensen's inequality Script 2.42

Let \(X\) be a real random variable with finite \(\E[X]\), and \(g:\R\to\R\) convex, i.e. \(g(tx_1+(1-t)x_2)\le tg(x_1)+(1-t)g(x_2)\) for all \(x_1,x_2\in\R\), \(t\in[0,1]\). Then

\[ \E[g(X)]\ge g(\E[X]). \]

If \(g\) is strictly convex, equality holds iff \(X=\E[X]\) with probability 1 (\(X\) is almost surely constant). If \(g\) is concave, the inequality reverses: \(\E[g(X)]\le g(\E[X])\).

Script typo: the convexity condition is written with \(f\) instead of \(g\). Also, for functions like \(-\ln\) or \(\sqrt{\ }\) that live only on \((0,\infty)\), the theorem is used for \(X\) with values in that interval (Example 2.43(i) does this). Does \(\E[g(X)]\) have to exist? No extra assumption is needed: by the tangent-line property (primer box 2) \(g(X)\ge a+bX\) for suitable constants \(a,b\), and \(\E[a+bX]=a+b\E[X]\) is a finite number, so \(\E[g(X)]\) is either a real number or \(+\infty\). In the second case the inequality \(\E[g(X)]\ge g(\E[X])\) is true for the trivial reason that \(+\infty\) is larger than any number.

Proof sketch for differentiable \(g\) Script — each step explained

Step 1: the tangent line. A differentiable convex \(g\) lies above each of its tangent lines (primer box 2). Take the tangent at the point \(x_0=\E[X]\). It is the first-order Taylor approximation

\[ L(x)=g(\E[X])+g'(\E[X])\,(x-\E[X]). \]

Step 2: plug in \(X\). Since \(g(x)\ge L(x)\) for every number \(x\), also \(g(X)\ge g(\E[X])+g'(\E[X])(X-\E[X])\) for every outcome.

Step 3: take expectations. One reason per line:

\[ \begin{aligned} \E[g(X)]&\ge\E\bigl[g(\E[X])+g'(\E[X])(X-\E[X])\bigr] &&\text{monotonicity of }\E\\ &=\E[g(\E[X])]+\E\bigl[g'(\E[X])(X-\E[X])\bigr] &&\text{linearity of }\E\\ &=g(\E[X])+g'(\E[X])\,\E[X-\E[X]] &&g(\E[X]),\,g'(\E[X])\text{ are constants}\\ &=g(\E[X])+g'(\E[X])\,(\E[X]-\E[X]) &&\text{linearity; }\E[\text{constant}]=\text{constant}\\ &=g(\E[X])+g'(\E[X])\cdot0=g(\E[X]). \end{aligned} \]

Without a derivative. The script remarks that a rigorous proof for non-differentiable \(g\) uses a supporting line: a straight line through \((\E[X],g(\E[X]))\) that stays below the graph. For convex \(g\) such a line always exists, and it replaces the tangent in the steps above.

Concave: apply the result to the convex \(-g\), which gives \(\E[-g(X)]\ge-g(\E[X])\); multiplying by \(-1\) flips the inequality to \(\E[g(X)]\le g(\E[X])\).

Equality for strictly convex \(g\) (mine). Put \(D:=g(X)-L(X)\). Strict convexity means \(g(x)>L(x)\) for every \(x\ne\E[X]\), so \(D\ge0\) everywhere, and \(D=0\) exactly on the event \(\{X=\E[X]\}\). Equality \(\E[g(X)]=g(\E[X])\) means \(\E[D]=0\) (because \(\E[L(X)]=g(\E[X])\), as computed in step 3). A non-negative random variable with mean 0 is 0 almost surely — here is the one line that shows it, using Markov's inequality (Theorem 2.38) itself: for every \(n\in\N\), \(\P(D\ge\frac1n)\le n\,\E[D]=0\), and \(\{D>0\}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{D\ge\frac1n\}\) is a countable union of events of probability 0, hence has probability 0 (\(\sigma\)-subadditivity, Proposition 1.19(vi)). So \(D=0\) almost surely, i.e. \(X=\E[X]\) almost surely. Conversely, if \(X=\E[X]\) almost surely then both sides equal \(g(\E[X])\), so equality holds.

In words: for a convex \(g\), "first average, then apply \(g\)" gives at most as much as "first apply \(g\), then average". For a concave \(g\) it is the other way round.

Widget — the chord lies above the curve My addition

\(X\) takes the value \(x_1\) with probability \(t\) and \(x_2\) with probability \(1-t\). The orange point \((\E[X],\E[g(X)])\) sits on the chord; the blue point \((\E[X],g(\E[X]))\) on the curve. The gap between them is the "Jensen gap".

Example 2.43 applications of Jensen Script 2.43

(i) \(g(x)=-\ln x\) is convex on \((0,\infty)\) (\(g''=1/x^2>0\)). For a positive \(X\): \(\E[-\ln X]\ge-\ln\E[X]\), i.e. \(\E[\ln X]\le\ln\E[X]\): the logarithm of the mean is at least the mean of the logarithm. This is the AM–GM inequality in disguise (worked out by me): for \(X\) uniform on positive numbers \(a_1,\dots,a_n\), \(\frac1n\sum\ln a_i\le\ln\frac1n\sum a_i\); exponentiating (\(\exp\) is increasing) gives \(\sqrt[n]{a_1\cdots a_n}\le\frac{a_1+\dots+a_n}n\) — geometric mean \(\le\) arithmetic mean.

(ii) Mean \(\mu\), median \(m\), standard deviation \(\sigma\), finite variance. Then \(|\mu-m|\le\sigma\): the mean and the median are never more than one standard deviation apart. The chain, one reason per step:

\[ \begin{aligned} |\mu-m|&=\bigl|\E[X-m]\bigr| &&\text{linearity: }\E[X-m]=\mu-m\\ &\le\E\bigl[|X-m|\bigr] &&\text{Jensen with the convex }g(x)=|x|\\ &\le\E\bigl[|X-\mu|\bigr] &&\text{the median minimises }c\mapsto\E|X-c|\text{ (Remark 2.22(v))}\\ &=\E\Bigl[\sqrt{(X-\mu)^2}\Bigr]\le\sqrt{\E[(X-\mu)^2]}=\sigma &&\text{Jensen with the concave }\sqrt{\ }\text{, applied to }(X-\mu)^2 \end{aligned} \]

Check with Example 2.21: for \(\Exp(\lambda)\), \(\mu-m=\frac{1-\ln2}{\lambda}\approx\frac{0.31}{\lambda}\le\frac1\lambda=\sigma\) ✓. Other everyday consequences: \(\E[X^2]\ge(\E[X])^2\) (i.e. \(\Var\ge0\)), \(\E[e^X]\ge e^{\E[X]}\) (SoSe26 P3b), \(\E[1/X]\ge1/\E[X]\) for \(X>0\).

Remark 2.44 "Jensen oh Jensen" Script 2.44

Jensen's inequality is "infamous among researchers, because it's always 'the wrong way round'". The script quotes Francis Bach: "Jensen's inequality is often not in the direction that you would hope it to be."

A memory aid for the direction: \(g(x)=x^2\) gives \(\E[X^2]\ge(\E X)^2\), which you know is right because the difference is the variance. Convex — "function of the mean is smaller".

Remark 2.45 concentration inequalities Script 2.45

Markov and Chebyshev bound the probability that \(X\) is large or far from its mean — how concentrated the mass is. When a function of many (typically independent) random variables "does not depend too much on any single one of them" (a sum or an average, say), much stronger results hold: its distribution concentrates tightly around its mean. These concentration inequalities (Chernoff, Hoeffding, Azuma, McDiarmid, Bennett, Bernstein) are a cornerstone of statistics and machine learning. Markov and Chebyshev give polynomial bounds in \(\varepsilon\); for sums of independent bounded variables one gets exponential bounds. ("Polynomial in \(\varepsilon\)": the bound falls like a power, e.g. \(1/\varepsilon^2\). "Exponential": it falls like \(e^{-c\varepsilon^2}\), far faster.) The script links to a short online overview and to a standard reference book on concentration inequalities, to give a feeling for what the different variants look like.

Taste of one (not examinable here). Hoeffding: for iid \(X_i\in[a,b]\), \(\P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le2\exp\bigl(-\frac{2n\varepsilon^2}{(b-a)^2}\bigr)\). For fair coin flips and \(\varepsilon=0.1\): with \(n=100\), Chebyshev gives \(\frac{0.25/100}{0.01}=0.25\) and Hoeffding \(2e^{-2}\approx0.27\) — no better. With \(n=1000\): Chebyshev \(0.025\), Hoeffding \(2e^{-20}\approx4\cdot10^{-9}\). The exponential bound wins once \(n\) is large.

Exercise-sheet tasks

Sheet 8, Exercise 2 — server overload Sheet 8 · Ex 2

Requests per hour: \(N_A\) with mean and variance 50, \(N_B\) with mean and variance 100, independent; capacity \(C=200\); \(N_T=N_A+N_B\). (i) \(\E[N_T]\), \(\Var[N_T]\). (ii) Chebyshev bound on \(\P(N_T>C)\). (iii) Markov bound; compare. (iv) A suitable model for \(N_A,N_B\)? (v) Using \(X\sim\Poi(\lambda_1)\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\sim\Poi(\lambda_2)\Rightarrow X+Y\sim\Poi(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\), compute \(\P(N_T>C)\) exactly and discuss.

Solution

(i) Linearity: \(\E[N_T]=50+100=150\). Independence (Proposition 2.8(iv)): \(\Var[N_T]=50+100=150\).

(ii) Counts are integers, so \(\{N_T>200\}=\{N_T\ge201\}=\{N_T-150\ge51\}\subseteq\{|N_T-150|\ge51\}\). Chebyshev with \(\varepsilon=51\): \(\P(N_T>200)\le\frac{150}{51^2}=\frac{150}{2601}\approx0.0577\).

(iii) \(N_T\ge0\), so Markov: \(\P(N_T>200)\le\P(N_T\ge200)\le\frac{150}{200}=0.75\) (using \(\varepsilon=201\) gives \(0.746\)). Chebyshev is far sharper because it also uses the variance: the spread \(\sigma\approx12.2\) is small compared with the distance 51 to the capacity.

(iv) Poisson: counts of independent events in a fixed time window, and a Poisson variable has mean = variance, exactly as given. So \(N_A\sim\Poi(50)\), \(N_B\sim\Poi(100)\).

(v) \(N_T\sim\Poi(150)\) (proved in Sheet 8 Ex 1 with characteristic functions, §2.3), so \(\P(N_T>200)=1-\sum_{k=0}^{200}e^{-150}\frac{150^k}{k!}\approx4.2\cdot10^{-5}\) (computed numerically). That is more than a thousand times smaller than the Chebyshev bound.

Discussion (as in the official solution): bounds hold for every distribution with the given mean and variance, so they are safe but loose; the exact value depends on the Poisson assumption, which may underestimate the risk if requests arrive in bursts rather than independently. The official solution is correct.

Sheet 9, Exercise 2 (i), (iii) — insurance claims Sheet 9 · Ex 2

An insurer has \(n=10^4\) clients. Client \(i\) claims a random amount \(X_i\) per year; the \(X_i\) are iid with \(\mu=500\) and \(\sigma^2=800^2=640\,000\). Each client pays a premium [Prämie] of \(Z\) euros per year. \(S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is the total claimed. (i) Minimal \(Z\) for an expected profit of 500 000. (iii) With \(Z=550\), use Chebyshev to check whether the company is at least 95 % sure that premiums cover claims. (Parts (ii) and (iv) use the law of large numbers and the clt: §2.4.)

Solution

(i) Profit = premiums collected minus claims, \(nZ-S_n\). Its mean is \(nZ-\E[S_n]=nZ-n\mu=10^4Z-5\cdot10^6\) (linearity). Setting it to \(5\cdot10^5\): \(Z=\frac{5\cdot10^5+5\cdot10^6}{10^4}=550\).

(iii) A loss means \(S_n>nZ=5.5\cdot10^6\). \(\E[S_n]=5\cdot10^6\) and \(\Var[S_n]=n\sigma^2=6.4\cdot10^9\) (independence). One-sided to two-sided (primer box 3), then Chebyshev with \(\varepsilon=5\cdot10^5\):

\[ \P(S_n>5.5\cdot10^6)\le\P\bigl(|S_n-\E[S_n]|\ge5\cdot10^5\bigr)\le\frac{6.4\cdot10^9}{(5\cdot10^5)^2}=\frac{6.4\cdot10^9}{2.5\cdot10^{11}}=0.0256\le0.05 . \]

So yes: the probability of a loss is at most 2.56 %, and the 95 % requirement is met. (The clt approximation in (iv) gives about \(2\cdot10^{-10}\).) The official solution is correct.

Sheet 10, Exercise 4 — the best weights for an average Sheet 10 · Ex 4

iid \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) with unknown mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\) (dart distances). \(\hat\mu=\sum_i\lambda_iX_i\) with \(\lambda_i\ge0\), \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\) (a convex combination). (i) Show \(\hat\mu\) is unbiased. (ii) Prove \(\frac1n\sum_i\lambda_i^2\ge\frac1{n^2}\) (hint: Jensen for a suitable discrete random variable). (iii) Which \(\lambda_i\) minimise the mean squared error?

Solution

(i) Linearity: \(\E[\hat\mu]=\sum_i\lambda_i\mu=\mu\sum_i\lambda_i=\mu\). "Unbiased" means exactly \(\E[\hat\mu]=\mu\) (§3.2).

(ii) Let \(Z\) take the values \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\), each with probability \(\frac1n\) (a Laplace distribution on the list). Then \(\E[Z]=\frac1n\sum_i\lambda_i=\frac1n\) and \(\E[Z^2]=\frac1n\sum_i\lambda_i^2\). Jensen with the convex \(x\mapsto x^2\):

\[ \frac1n\sum_i\lambda_i^2=\E[Z^2]\ge(\E[Z])^2=\frac1{n^2}. \]

(iii) The mean squared error [mittlere quadratische Abweichung] is \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\mu]=\E[(\hat\mu-\mu)^2]\). By (i), \(\mu=\E[\hat\mu]\), so \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\mu]=\E[(\hat\mu-\E[\hat\mu])^2]=\Var[\hat\mu]\) (bias–variance decomposition, §3.2). Independence and Proposition 2.8(iii),(iv) (\(\Var[aY]=a^2\Var[Y]\); variances of independent summands add): \(\Var[\hat\mu]=\sum_i\lambda_i^2\sigma^2\ge\frac{\sigma^2}n\) by (ii). The choice \(\lambda_i=\frac1n\) gives exactly \(\frac{\sigma^2}n\), so the ordinary average is the best convex combination. Equality in Jensen for the strictly convex \(x^2\) forces \(Z\) to be constant, i.e. all \(\lambda_i\) equal — so, as long as \(\sigma>0\), it is the unique best choice (uniqueness added by me). (If \(\sigma=0\) every \(X_i\) equals \(\mu\) with probability 1, so every choice of weights has mean squared error 0 and nothing is to be optimised.)

The official solution is correct (its statement has a harmless typo, "\(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_1=1\)" for \(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i=1\)). The general lesson: Jensen with a uniform distribution over a finite list turns into an inequality between averages — a quick way to prove the power-mean-type inequalities that exams like.

Old-exam tasks

SoSe 2025, Problem 5c — the duck hunt with two hunters SoSe25 · P5c · 4 credits

Setting (parts (a), (b) are on §2.1). \(n\) hunters with perfect aim each shoot once at one of \(m\) ducks, chosen uniformly at random and independently. \(X\) is the number of surviving ducks. Part (b) gives \(\Var[X]=m\bigl(\frac{m-1}m\bigr)^n+m(m-1)\bigl(\frac{m-2}m\bigr)^n-m^2\bigl(\frac{m-1}m\bigr)^{2n}\).

Statement (c). Now \(n=2\) hunters. Find \(k\in\N\) as a function of \(m\) such that the number \(X\) of surviving ducks lies in \([\E[X]-k,\E[X]+k]\) with probability at least 90 %. Hint: rewrite so that Chebyshev applies.

Solution. \(\P(X\in[\E X-k,\E X+k])\ge0.9\) holds if \(\P(|X-\E X|>k)\le0.1\), which holds if \(\P(|X-\E X|\ge k)\le0.1\), which Chebyshev guarantees once \(\frac{\Var[X]}{k^2}\le0.1\), i.e. \(k^2\ge10\Var[X]\). With \(n=2\), part (b) gives

\[ \Var[X]=\frac{(m-1)^2}m+\frac{(m-1)(m-2)^2}m-\frac{(m-1)^4}{m^2}=\frac{m-1}{m^2}\bigl[m(m-1)+m(m-2)^2-(m-1)^3\bigr]=\frac{m-1}{m^2}, \]

because the bracket expands to \((m^2-m)+(m^3-4m^2+4m)-(m^3-3m^2+3m-1)=1\). Hence \(k=\Bigl\lceil\frac{\sqrt{10(m-1)}}m\Bigr\rceil\), rounding up so the inequality still holds.

What that number is. \(10(m-1)/m^2\le1\) iff \(m^2-10m+10\ge0\) iff \(m\ge9\), so the formula gives \(k=0\) for \(m=1\), \(k=2\) for \(2\le m\le8\), and \(k=1\) for \(m\ge9\). How loose Chebyshev is here: with two hunters at least \(m-2\) and at most \(m-1\) ducks survive, and \(\E[X]=\frac{(m-1)^2}m=m-2+\frac1m\). Both possible values lie within distance 1 of the mean, so \(k=1\) already works with probability 1 for every \(m\ge2\). The official answer is correct — it answers "find a \(k\)" with a valid one — but a sharper \(k\) exists. Small slip in the official solution: "at least 90 %" means \(\P(\text{outside})\le0.1\), but it writes "\(<0.1\)" and then sets \(\Var[X]/k^2=0.1\). The version above with "\(\le\)" is the consistent one; the final \(k\) is the same.

WiSe 25/26, Problem 4b — Chebyshev for an estimator WiSe25 · P4b · 3 credits

Setting. Rainfall amounts \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid with density \(p_\theta(x)=\frac1{\theta^2}xe^{-x/\theta}\) on \(x\ge0\); part (a) (maximum likelihood, §3.2) derives the estimator \(\hat\theta=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\). (b) Use Chebyshev to bound the probability that \(\hat\theta\) deviates from \(\theta\) by at least \(\varepsilon>0\). Hint: \(\E[X_i]=2\theta\), \(\Var[X_i]=2\theta^2\).

Solution. Linearity: \(\E[\hat\theta]=\frac1{2n}\cdot n\cdot2\theta=\theta\). Independence and scaling: \(\Var[\hat\theta]=\frac1{(2n)^2}\cdot n\cdot2\theta^2=\frac{\theta^2}{2n}\). Chebyshev (\(\P_\theta\) means: probability when the true parameter is \(\theta\)):

\[ \P_\theta\bigl(|\hat\theta-\theta|\ge\varepsilon\bigr)\le\frac{\theta^2}{2n\varepsilon^2}. \]

Where the hint comes from: the Gamma distribution [Gammaverteilung] \(\Gamma(\alpha,\beta)\) has density \(\frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta x}\) for \(x>0\) (Example 1.61(iii); here \(\Gamma(\alpha)\) is the Gamma function of Definition 1.60, with \(\Gamma(2)=1!=1\)). Putting \(\alpha=2\) and \(\beta=\frac1\theta\) turns this into \(\frac{(1/\theta)^2}{1}x\,e^{-x/\theta}=\frac1{\theta^2}xe^{-x/\theta}\), which is exactly \(p_\theta\). So \(X_i\sim\Gamma(2,\frac1\theta)\) and Lemma 2.27(iii) gives \(\E=\frac\alpha\beta=\frac{2}{1/\theta}=2\theta\) and \(\Var=\frac\alpha{\beta^2}=\frac2{(1/\theta)^2}=2\theta^2\). The bound shrinks like \(\frac1n\) — enough to show \(\hat\theta\to\theta\) in probability (consistency, §2.4 and §3.2). Parts (c), (d) compare with the clt (§2.4). The official solution is correct.

SoSe 2026, Problem 3 — Jensen's inequality SoSe26 · P3 · 5 credits

(a) State Jensen's inequality with all required assumptions. Official answer: \(X\) a real random variable with finite \(\E[X]\); \(g:\R\to\R\) convex; then \(\E[g(X)]\ge g(\E[X])\). One point each for "finite expectation", "convex \(g\)" and the correct inequality; the equality case and the concave version were not graded.

(b) If \(\E[X]\) and \(\E[e^X]\) are finite, show \(\E[X]\le\log\E[e^X]\). Solution. \(g(x)=e^x\) is convex (\(g''=e^x>0\)), so Jensen gives \(e^{\E[X]}\le\E[e^X]\). Since \(e^x>0\), also \(\E[e^X]>0\), so the logarithm is defined there; it is strictly increasing, and applying it to both sides keeps the direction: \(\E[X]=\log e^{\E[X]}\le\log\E[e^X]\).

Marks were given separately for "\(\log\) is increasing on \((0,\infty)\)" and "\(\E[e^X]>0\)" — say both explicitly. The official solution is correct.

SoSe 2026, Problem 4d — a Markov bound for a scaled random walk SoSe26 · P4d · 3 credits

Setting. \(Z_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{j=1}^nX_j\) with iid \(X_j=\pm1\) (probability \(\frac12\) each); part (c) (§2.1) gives \(\E[Z_n]=0\), \(\Var[Z_n]=1\). (d) For \(a>0\), use Markov to bound \(\P(|Z_n|\ge a)\), and use the clt to approximate it.

Solution. \(Z_n^2\ge0\), and \(|Z_n|\ge a\iff Z_n^2\ge a^2\) (both sides non-negative; squaring is increasing on \([0,\infty)\)). Markov for \(Z_n^2\) with \(\varepsilon=a^2\):

\[ \P(|Z_n|\ge a)=\P(Z_n^2\ge a^2)\le\frac{\E[Z_n^2]}{a^2}=\frac1{a^2}, \]

using \(\E[Z_n^2]=\Var[Z_n]+(\E[Z_n])^2=1\). By the clt, \(Z_n\) is approximately \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), so \(\P(|Z_n|\ge a)\approx2(1-\Phi(a))=2\Phi(-a)\) (§2.4). The factor 2 counts both tails, \(Z_n\ge a\) and \(Z_n\le-a\); they are equally likely because \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) is symmetric about 0.

This "Markov applied to \(Z^2\)" is Chebyshev. For \(a=2\): the bound is 0.25, the normal approximation 0.046. For \(a\le1\) the bound is \(\ge1\) and useless. The official solution is correct.

Summary sheet

The three inequalities

Markov
\(X\ge0\), \(\varepsilon>0\): \(\P(X\ge\varepsilon)\le\E[X]/\varepsilon\); general: \(\P(X\ge\varepsilon)\le\E[f(X)]/f(\varepsilon)\) for increasing \(f\ge0\)
Chebyshev
\(\P(|X-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/\varepsilon^2\); \(\P(|X-\mu|\ge k\sigma)\le1/k^2\)
Jensen
\(g\) convex: \(\E[g(X)]\ge g(\E[X])\); concave: \(\le\)
one-sided
\(\P(X\ge\mu+\varepsilon)\le\P(|X-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\)
integers
\(\{N>200\}=\{N\ge201\}\) for integer-valued \(N\)

Recipe for a Chebyshev problem

  1. Compute \(\E\) and \(\Var\) of the quantity (linearity; independence for the variance of sums).
  2. Rewrite the event as "distance from the mean at least \(\varepsilon\)" — enlarge a one-sided event to a two-sided one if needed.
  3. Plug in; for "find \(k\) / \(n\) such that probability \(\ge1-\alpha\)", solve \(\Var/\varepsilon^2\le\alpha\) and round in the safe direction.

Traps

  • Markov needs \(X\ge0\) (apply it to \(|X|\), \(X^2\), \(e^{X}\)… otherwise).
  • A bound \(\ge1\) is true but useless: Markov only helps for \(\varepsilon>\E[X]\), Chebyshev for \(\varepsilon>\sigma\).
  • These are upper bounds, not approximations; the clt gives approximations, not bounds.
  • Jensen's direction: convex \(\Rightarrow\) \(\E[g(X)]\) is the larger side (think \(\E[X^2]\ge(\E X)^2\)).
  • When stating Jensen in an exam: "\(\E[X]\) finite" and "\(g\) convex" are both graded.

Exam focus

Chebyshev appears in almost every exam, usually as the "bound" half of a "bound versus clt approximation" comparison (WiSe25 P4b–d, SoSe26 P4d, Sheet 9 Ex 2(iii)–(iv)) or as "find \(k\)" (SoSe25 P5c). Jensen appeared as a 5-credit definition-plus-application problem (SoSe26 P3).

Self-test

Section 2.3 · Lectures 8–9 (10 and 17 June 2026)

Computations with distributions

Rechnen mit Verteilungen

What this page covers Script §2.3, pp. 73–78

Everything from Definition 2.46 to Remark 2.54. The script's section goal: "We introduce and get used to a set of tools that are useful for performing computations with distributions, including characteristic functions (cf), transformations of distributions, and explicit computation rules for special distributions (e.g., Gaussians)."

Worked in place: Sheet 7 Ex 2 and 5, Sheet 8 Ex 1 and 5, Sheet 9 Ex 5, and the old-exam tasks SoSe26 P1c, P4a, P4b (plus the characteristic-function route to SoSe26 P4c). WiSe25 P3a is re-solved here with Proposition 2.51 as a cross-check of §1.3.

Background you need: complex numbers (primer below), and matrices, determinants, inverses, positive definiteness and the multivariable change of variables — all on the new background page B5.

The big picture

§2.1 summarised a distribution by a few numbers. This page is about computing with whole distributions. Three typical questions:

  • What is the distribution of a sum? Two independent Poisson counts: is the total Poisson again? Adding densities directly means a convolution integral (Sheet 7 Ex 2). The characteristic function turns "sum of independent variables" into "product of functions", which is much easier.
  • What is the density of \(g(X)\)? If you know \(p_X\) and apply a smooth invertible \(g\), the change-of-variables formula (Proposition 2.51) gives \(p_{g(X)}\) directly: take \(p_X\) at the pre-image and correct by how much \(g\) stretches space.
  • How do Gaussians behave? Sums, linear maps, marginals and conditionals of Gaussians are again Gaussian (Lemma 2.53), so every computation reduces to linear algebra with the mean vector and the covariance matrix.

In words: a characteristic function is a fingerprint of a distribution that multiplies under independent sums; the change-of-variables formula moves densities through maps; Gaussians are the family closed under everything linear.

Primer: complex numbers and \(e^{it}\) My addition

Cross-references

Complex numbers from scratch: Analysis: complex numbers; Euler's formula with a widget: Analysis 5.3. Taylor expansion: Analysis 10.1. Complex numbers as this course uses them (Euler, derivatives in \(t\), the complex limit \((1+z_n/n)^n\to e^z\)): B1. Differentiating under an integral sign: Analysis 9.2 treats only a continuous integrand on a bounded rectangle; for integrals over all of \(\R\) and expectations the justification is dominated convergence (B4, and B1). Matrices and change of variables: B5.

What you need about complex numbers

  • \(i\) is a number with \(i^2=-1\). A complex number is \(z=a+bi\) with real part \(a\) and imaginary part \(b\); picture it as the point \((a,b)\) in the plane. Add and multiply as usual, replacing \(i^2\) by \(-1\).
  • Modulus \(|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) (distance from 0); conjugate \(\bar z=a-bi\) (mirror image); \(z\) is real iff \(z=\bar z\).
  • Euler's formula: \(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\) — the point at angle \(\theta\) on the unit circle. Hence \(|e^{i\theta}|=\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta}=1\), \(\overline{e^{i\theta}}=e^{-i\theta}\), and \(e^{i\alpha}e^{i\beta}=e^{i(\alpha+\beta)}\).
  • Derivatives of complex-valued functions of a real \(t\) (B1). A function \(f(t)=u(t)+i\,v(t)\) with real \(u,v\) is differentiated part by part: \(f'(t):=u'(t)+i\,v'(t)\) — \(i\) is just a constant. Sum rule, product rule, chain rule (with a real inner function) and Taylor expansion then hold exactly as for real functions: multiply everything out into its real and its imaginary part and apply the real rule to each part. Key example, for a real constant \(c\): by Euler \(e^{ict}=\cos(ct)+i\sin(ct)\), so \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}e^{ict}=-c\sin(ct)+ic\cos(ct)=ic\bigl(\cos(ct)+i\sin(ct)\bigr)=ic\,e^{ict}\) (in the middle step we wrote \(-c\sin(ct)=ic\cdot i\sin(ct)\), using \(i^2=-1\)). Repeating it \(n\) times: \(\frac{\mathrm d^n}{\mathrm dt^n}e^{ict}=(ic)^ne^{ict}\) — exactly the real rule \((e^{ct})'=ce^{ct}\) with \(c\) replaced by \(ic\). Its size: \(|ic\,e^{ict}|=|ic|\cdot|e^{ict}|=|c|\cdot1=|c|\), because \(ic=0+ci\) has modulus \(\sqrt{0^2+c^2}=|c|\) and \(|e^{ict}|=1\) by the bullet above. This bound is what makes the moment formula of Remark 2.47(iii) work.
  • Expectation of a complex random variable is taken part by part: \(\E[U+iV]:=\E[U]+i\E[V]\). Linearity, \(|\E[Z]|\le\E[|Z|]\) and "independent factors: \(\E[Z_1Z_2]=\E[Z_1]\E[Z_2]\)" carry over.
  • Small-\(o\) notation (Analysis 6.1): \(f(s)=o(s^2)\) means \(f(s)/s^2\to0\) as \(s\to0\) — "negligible compared with \(s^2\)".

Example. For \(X=\pm1\) with probability \(\frac12\) each: \(\E[e^{itX}]=\frac12e^{it}+\frac12e^{-it}=\frac12(\cos t+i\sin t)+\frac12(\cos t-i\sin t)=\cos t\).

Words and symbols used on this page My addition — one-line reminders

  • RVRV: a real-valued random variable [reellwertige Zufallsvariable]. \(\P\) is probability, \(\E\) the expectation [Erwartungswert], \(\Var\) the variance, \(\Cov\) the covariance (§2.1).
  • pmf \(p_X(x)=\P(X=x)\) for a discrete \(X\); pdf (density [Dichte]) \(p_X\) for a continuous \(X\), with \(\P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^bp_X(x)\,\mathrm dx\); cdf \(F_X(x)=\P(X\le x)\) (§1.3). The derivative of the cdf is the pdf: \(F_X'=p_X\).
  • Support \(S_X=\{x:p_X(x)>0\}\): the set of values where the density is positive.
  • \(X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\): \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent [unabhängig]. iid: independent and identically distributed (all have the same distribution).
  • \(X\sim\) "name": \(X\) has this distribution. \(\P_X\) is the distribution [Verteilung] of \(X\), i.e. \(\P_X(B)=\P(X\in B)\).
  • Gamma function \(\Gamma(\alpha)=\int_0^\infty u^{\alpha-1}e^{-u}\,\mathrm du\) for \(\alpha>0\) (for whole numbers \(\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!\)). Gamma distribution \(\Gamma(\alpha,\beta)\): density \(\frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta x}\) for \(x>0\) (shape \(\alpha\), rate \(\beta\)). \(\chi^2_k\) ("chi-squared with \(k\) degrees of freedom") is \(\Gamma(\frac k2,\frac12)\). The Cauchy distribution has density \(\frac1{\pi(1+x^2)}\); it has no mean. All from §1.3.
  • \(\varphi^{(n)}\): the \(n\)-th derivative of \(\varphi\). \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\): "\(X_n\) converges in distribution to \(X\)" — the cdfs of \(X_n\) approach the cdf of \(X\) at every point where the latter is continuous (Definition 2.56, §2.4).
  • Vectors, matrices, transpose \(A^\top\), inverse \(A^{-1}\), determinant \(\det A\) (also written \(|A|\)), the Jacobian matrix and the Cholesky factor: B5.

Characteristic functions

The idea. A pmf lists \(\P(X=x)\) for every \(x\). A characteristic function stores the same information in a different form: one complex number \(\E[e^{itX}]\) for every real \(t\). Nothing is lost: the distribution can be recovered from it (uniqueness). The new form has two advantages. First, it turns sums of independent variables into products. Second, its derivatives at \(t=0\) give the moments \(\E[X],\E[X^2],\dots\). It always exists, because \(e^{itX}\) always has size 1.

Definition 2.46 characteristic function Script 2.46

The characteristic function [charakteristische Funktion] of a real random variable \(X\) is

\[ \varphi_X(t)=\E\bigl[e^{itX}\bigr]=\E[\cos(tX)]+i\,\E[\sin(tX)],\qquad t\in\R . \]
  1. discrete \(X\) with pmf \(p_X\): \(\varphi_X(t)=\sum_xe^{itx}p_X(x)\);
  2. continuous \(X\) with pdf \(p_X\): \(\varphi_X(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{itx}p_X(x)\,\mathrm dx\).

Here \(i=\sqrt{-1}\) is the imaginary unit and \(t\) is a real number of our choice. It exists for every \(X\) and every \(t\), because \(|e^{itX}|=\sqrt{\cos^2(tX)+\sin^2(tX)}=1\): we take the expectation of a bounded function.

Small example (mine). \(X\sim\Ber(0.3)\), so \(X=0\) with probability 0.7 and \(X=1\) with probability 0.3. By (i), \(\varphi_X(t)=e^{it\cdot0}\cdot0.7+e^{it\cdot1}\cdot0.3=0.7+0.3e^{it}\). At \(t=\pi\): \(e^{i\pi}=\cos\pi+i\sin\pi=-1\), so \(\varphi_X(\pi)=0.7-0.3=0.4\).

Characteristic functions to know My table; Poisson is Sheet 8 Ex 1, Gamma is Example 2.50, normal is Example 2.48

Remark 2.47 properties of characteristic functions Script 2.47

  1. \(\varphi_X(0)=1\) and \(|\varphi_X(t)|\le1\).
  2. \(\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)\).
  3. Moments: \(\E[X^n]=i^{-n}\varphi_X^{(n)}(0)\) (if the moments exist). In particular \(\E[X]=-i\varphi_X'(0)\) and \(\E[X^2]=-\varphi_X''(0)\).
  4. Independent sums: if \(X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\), then \(\varphi_{X+Y}(t)=\varphi_X(t)\varphi_Y(t)\).
  5. Uniqueness: the characteristic function determines the distribution; there are explicit inversion formulas (e.g. Lévy's inversion theorem).
  6. Lévy's continuity theorem: \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\) (Definition 2.56) iff \(\varphi_{X_n}(t)\to\varphi_X(t)\) for every \(t\) ("pointwise"); the script adds "and \(\varphi_X\) is continuous at \(t=0\)" (see the note in the proof box). This is the engine of the proof of the central limit theorem.

In words: the cf starts at 1 and never leaves the unit disc; shifting \(X\) multiplies it by a factor, stretching \(X\) stretches its argument; derivatives at 0 give moments; independent sums give products; the cf identifies the distribution; and convergence of cfs means convergence in distribution.

Proofs of (i)–(iv) (i), (ii), (iv): Sheet 9 Ex 5 (iii): mine

(i) \(\varphi_X(0)=\E[e^0]=1\). And \(|\E[e^{itX}]|\le\E[|e^{itX}|]=\E[1]=1\) (the triangle inequality for integrals, i.e. Jensen with the convex \(|\cdot|\)).

(ii) \(\E[e^{it(aX+b)}]=\E[e^{itb}e^{i(at)X}]=e^{itb}\E[e^{i(at)X}]=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)\): \(e^{itb}\) is a constant and comes out of \(\E\).

(iv) \(e^{itX}\) and \(e^{itY}\) are functions of independent variables, hence independent, so \(\E[e^{itX}e^{itY}]=\E[e^{itX}]\E[e^{itY}]\) (Proposition 2.4(v), applied to real and imaginary parts). By induction the same holds for \(n\) independent summands.

(iii) For fixed \(x\), the primer rule with \(c=x\) gives \(\frac{\mathrm d^n}{\mathrm dt^n}e^{itx}=(ix)^ne^{itx}\). We want to pull \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\) inside \(\E\) ("differentiate under the expectation sign"). This is allowed when the derivative is bounded, for all \(t\) at once, by something with finite expectation — that is the dominated convergence theorem [Satz von der majorisierten Konvergenz] (B4; the rule for parameter integrals is in B1). Here the bound is simple: \(\bigl|\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}e^{itx}\bigr|=|ix\,e^{itx}|=|x|\) and, for the \(k\)-th derivative, \(|(ix)^ke^{itx}|=|x|^k\), which does not depend on \(t\). The bound we need for the \(k\)-th step is therefore the function \(x\mapsto|x|^k\), and its expectation is \(\E|X|^k\). So if \(\E|X|^n<\infty\) — which also makes \(\E|X|^k<\infty\) for every \(k\le n\), since \(|x|^k\le1+|x|^n\) (if \(|x|\le1\) then \(|x|^k\le1\); if \(|x|>1\) then \(|x|^k\le|x|^n\)) and the expectation of the right-hand side is \(1+\E|X|^n<\infty\) — we may differentiate \(n\) times under \(\E\): \(\varphi_X^{(n)}(t)=\E[(iX)^ne^{itX}]=i^n\E[X^ne^{itX}]\), and at \(t=0\) (where \(e^{0}=1\)): \(\varphi_X^{(n)}(0)=i^n\E[X^n]\). Multiply by \(i^{-n}\). (Analysis 9.2 only covers a continuous integrand on a bounded rectangle, so it does not by itself justify this step for an integral over all of \(\R\).)

(v), (vi) are deep theorems of Fourier analysis; the course uses them without proof.

On the script's wording of (vi): it says convergence in distribution holds iff the characteristic functions converge "and \(\varphi_X\) is continuous at 0". The standard statement has two halves: (a) \(X_n\xrightarrow dX\iff\varphi_{X_n}\to\varphi_X\) pointwise; (b) if \(\varphi_{X_n}\) converge pointwise to some function \(\varphi\) that is continuous at 0, then \(\varphi\) is the characteristic function of some \(X\) and \(X_n\xrightarrow dX\). The continuity condition belongs to (b).

Example of (iii) (mine). \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), \(\varphi(t)=e^{-t^2/2}\): \(\varphi'(t)=-te^{-t^2/2}\), \(\varphi''(t)=(t^2-1)e^{-t^2/2}\). So \(\E[Z]=-i\cdot0=0\) and \(\E[Z^2]=-\varphi''(0)=1\) ✓.

Example 2.48 characteristic function of the normal distribution Script 2.48

\[ X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\varphi_X(t)=\exp\Bigl(i\mu t-\tfrac12\sigma^2t^2\Bigr). \]
Derivation supplied by me — the script states the result

First \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) with density \(\phi(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}\). The imaginary part \(\int\sin(tx)\phi(x)\,\mathrm dx\) vanishes (odd integrand), so \(\varphi(t)=\int\cos(tx)\phi(x)\,\mathrm dx\). Now differentiate under the integral sign, using \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\cos(tx)=-x\sin(tx)\) (chain rule, \(x\) is a constant here).

Why this is allowed: the derivative of the integrand obeys \(|-x\sin(tx)\phi(x)|\le|x|\phi(x)\) for every \(t\), because \(|\sin|\le1\); and this bound, which no longer contains \(t\), has finite integral, \(\int|x|\phi(x)\,\mathrm dx=\E|Z|=2\int_0^\infty x\phi(x)\,\mathrm dx=2\bigl[-\phi(x)\bigr]_0^\infty =2\phi(0)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\sqrt{2/\pi}<\infty\) (the antiderivative \(-\phi\) of \(x\phi\) is justified in the next line; the factor 2 is because \(|x|\phi(x)\) is symmetric about 0). That is the dominating function required by dominated convergence, exactly as in the proof of Remark 2.47(iii) (B4, B1).

Then integrate by parts with \(u=\sin(tx)\), \(v'=x\phi(x)\), \(v=-\phi(x)\) (by the chain rule \(\phi'(x)=-x\phi(x)\), so \(-\phi\) is an antiderivative of \(x\phi\)). The boundary term vanishes because \(\phi(x)\to0\) as \(x\to\pm\infty\):

\[ \varphi'(t)=-\int x\sin(tx)\phi(x)\,\mathrm dx=-\Bigl(\bigl[-\sin(tx)\phi(x)\bigr]_{-\infty}^{\infty}+\int t\cos(tx)\phi(x)\,\mathrm dx\Bigr)=-t\,\varphi(t). \]

So \(\varphi'=-t\varphi\) with \(\varphi(0)=1\). The function \(e^{-t^2/2}\) solves this, and it is the only solution: \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\bigl(\varphi(t)e^{t^2/2}\bigr)=(\varphi'+t\varphi)e^{t^2/2}=0\), so \(\varphi(t)e^{t^2/2}\) is constant, equal to its value 1 at \(t=0\). Hence \(\varphi_Z(t)=e^{-t^2/2}\).

General case: \(X=\mu+\sigma Z\) (Example 2.52(iii)), and Remark 2.47(ii) gives \(\varphi_X(t)=e^{i\mu t}\varphi_Z(\sigma t)=e^{i\mu t-\sigma^2t^2/2}\).

Remark 2.49 moment generating functions Script 2.49

The moment generating function (MGF) is \(M_X(t)=\E[e^{tX}]\) for real \(t\) where it exists (typically near \(t=0\)). If it exists and is differentiable, \(\E[X^n]=M_X^{(n)}(0)\) — no powers of \(i\). Like cfs, \(M_{X+Y}=M_XM_Y\) for independent \(X,Y\), and an MGF that exists near 0 determines the distribution. But MGFs do not always exist (Cauchy: \(\E[e^{tX}]=\infty\) for every \(t\ne0\)), while the cf always does.

Script, paragraph after 2.49 Together with uniqueness and the continuity theorem, cfs are powerful "calculation tools". Results about distributions are proved with tools from (complex) analysis: derivatives, Taylor series, convergence of functions.

Example: \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) has \(M_Z(t)=e^{t^2/2}\) (same derivation with the sign flipped), so \(\E[Z^4]=M^{(4)}(0)=3\).

Widget — characteristic functions, and what independence does to them My addition

Real part (blue) and imaginary part (orange) of \(\varphi(t)\) for \(t\in[-8,8]\), for the sum \(S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n\) of \(n\) independent copies — so the curve shown is \(\varphi_X(t)^n\) (Remark 2.47(iv)). Symmetric distributions have a purely real cf (Sheet 9 Ex 5(iii)); the slope of the imaginary part at 0 is the mean.

Example 2.50 sums of independent random variables Script 2.50

(i) Poisson + Poisson. \(X_1\sim\Poi(\lambda_1)\perp\!\!\!\perp X_2\sim\Poi(\lambda_2)\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(X_1+X_2\sim\Poi(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\). Proof: Sheet 8 Ex 1 below.

(ii) Gamma + Gamma with the same rate. \(X_1\sim\Gamma(\alpha_1,\beta)\perp\!\!\!\perp X_2\sim\Gamma(\alpha_2,\beta)\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(X_1+X_2\sim\Gamma(\alpha_1+\alpha_2,\beta)\). First the cf of \(X\sim\Gamma(\alpha,\beta)\):

\[ \varphi_X(t)=\int_0^\infty e^{itx}\frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta x}\,\mathrm dx =\frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}e^{-(\beta-it)x}\,\mathrm dx . \]

(The two exponentials were combined: \(e^{itx}e^{-\beta x}=e^{-(\beta-it)x}\).) Substitute \(u=(\beta-it)x\), so \(x=\frac{u}{\beta-it}\) and \(\mathrm dx=\frac{\mathrm du}{\beta-it}\). The integral becomes

\[ \int_0^\infty\Bigl(\frac{u}{\beta-it}\Bigr)^{\alpha-1}e^{-u}\,\frac{\mathrm du}{\beta-it}=\frac{1}{(\beta-it)^\alpha}\int_0^\infty u^{\alpha-1}e^{-u}\,\mathrm du=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha)}{(\beta-it)^\alpha}, \]

using the definition of the Gamma function (§1.3). The \(\Gamma(\alpha)\) cancels, so \(\varphi_X(t)=\bigl(\frac{\beta}{\beta-it}\bigr)^\alpha=(1-it/\beta)^{-\alpha}\) (divide top and bottom by \(\beta\)). For the sum, Remark 2.47(iv):

\[ \varphi_{X_1+X_2}(t)=(1-it/\beta)^{-\alpha_1}(1-it/\beta)^{-\alpha_2}=(1-it/\beta)^{-(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)}, \]

the cf of \(\Gamma(\alpha_1+\alpha_2,\beta)\); by uniqueness (Remark 2.47(v)) that is the distribution of the sum. Since \(\Exp(\lambda)=\Gamma(1,\lambda)\) and \(\chi^2_k=\Gamma(\frac k2,\frac12)\): the sum of \(n\) iid \(\Exp(\lambda)\) is \(\Gamma(n,\lambda)\), and \(\chi^2_k+\chi^2_l=\chi^2_{k+l}\) for independent summands.

A caveat on the substitution. \(u=(\beta-it)x\) is a complex number, so the new path of integration is a ray in the complex plane, not \([0,\infty)\). That it gives the same value is a theorem of complex analysis (Cauchy's integral theorem), not covered by your Analysis course. For \(\alpha=1\) you can check it by hand: \(\int_0^\infty\beta e^{-(\beta-it)x}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{\beta}{\beta-it}\) because \(|e^{-(\beta-it)x}|=e^{-\beta x}\to0\).

Sheet 7, Exercise 2 — sums of independent variables by convolution Sheet 7 · Ex 2

\(X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\) with densities \(p_X,p_Y\). (i) Show \(p_{X+Y}(z)=\int_\R p_X(z-y)\,p_Y(y)\,\mathrm dy\) (the convolution \(p_X\star p_Y\)). (ii) \(X,Y\) iid \(\Exp(\lambda)\): density of \(X+Y\). (iii) \(X\sim\mathcal N(\mu_x,\sigma_x^2)\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\sim\mathcal N(\mu_y,\sigma_y^2)\): show \(X+Y\sim\mathcal N(\mu_x+\mu_y,\sigma_x^2+\sigma_y^2)\).

Solution

(i) The cdf method. With \(A_z=\{(x,y):x+y\le z\}\) and the product density (independence, Definition 1.77(iii)):

\[ F_{X+Y}(z)=\iint_{A_z}p_X(x)p_Y(y)\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy=\int_{-\infty}^\infty\Bigl(\int_{-\infty}^{z-y}p_X(x)\,\mathrm dx\Bigr)p_Y(y)\,\mathrm dy =\int_{-\infty}^{z}\Bigl(\int_{-\infty}^\infty p_X(u-y)p_Y(y)\,\mathrm dy\Bigr)\mathrm du . \]

(Inner substitution \(x=u-y\); then swap the order, Fubini.) So \(F_{X+Y}\) is the integral up to \(z\) of the bracket, which is therefore a density of \(X+Y\) (Lemma 1.49).

(ii) \(p_X(z-y)p_Y(y)=\lambda e^{-\lambda(z-y)}\lambda e^{-\lambda y}=\lambda^2e^{-\lambda z}\) where both factors are non-zero, i.e. \(0\le y\le z\). So for \(z\ge0\): \(p_{X+Y}(z)=\int_0^z\lambda^2e^{-\lambda z}\,\mathrm dy=\lambda^2ze^{-\lambda z}\), and 0 for \(z<0\): the \(\Gamma(2,\lambda)\) density, as Example 2.50(ii) predicts.

(iii) — the short way (mine). By Example 2.48 and Remark 2.47(iv), \(\varphi_{X+Y}(t)=e^{i\mu_xt-\sigma_x^2t^2/2}e^{i\mu_yt-\sigma_y^2t^2/2}=e^{i(\mu_x+\mu_y)t-(\sigma_x^2+\sigma_y^2)t^2/2}\), the cf of \(\mathcal N(\mu_x+\mu_y,\sigma_x^2+\sigma_y^2)\); uniqueness finishes.

(iii) — the long way (as the sheet asks), in shifted variables to keep it short. Write \(s^2:=\sigma_x^2+\sigma_y^2\), \(w:=z-\mu_x-\mu_y\), and substitute \(u:=x-\mu_x\) (a shift, so \(\mathrm dx=\mathrm du\)). Then \(z-x-\mu_y=w-u\). By (i), written with the integration variable called \(x\) (substitute \(y=z-x\) in the formula of (i); the order of the two factors does not matter),

\[ p_{X+Y}(z)=\int p_X(x)p_Y(z-x)\,\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_x\sigma_y}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{u^2}{2\sigma_x^2}-\frac{(w-u)^2}{2\sigma_y^2}\Bigr)\mathrm du . \]

Complete the square in \(u\). Put \(\tau^2:=\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2/s^2\) and \(m:=\sigma_x^2w/s^2\). Multiplying out and collecting powers of \(u\) gives

\[ \frac{u^2}{\sigma_x^2}+\frac{(w-u)^2}{\sigma_y^2}=\frac{(u-m)^2}{\tau^2}+\frac{w^2}{s^2} . \]

(Check: the \(u^2\)-coefficient is \(\frac1{\sigma_x^2}+\frac1{\sigma_y^2}=\frac{s^2}{\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2}=\frac1{\tau^2}\); the \(u\)-coefficient is \(-\frac{2w}{\sigma_y^2}=-\frac{2m}{\tau^2}\); the constant is \(\frac{w^2}{\sigma_y^2}-\frac{m^2}{\tau^2}=\frac{w^2}{\sigma_y^2}\bigl(1-\frac{\sigma_x^2}{s^2}\bigr)=\frac{w^2}{s^2}\).) The factor \(e^{-w^2/(2s^2)}\) does not depend on \(u\) and comes out of the integral. The rest is a normal density without its constant: \(\int e^{-(u-m)^2/(2\tau^2)}\,\mathrm du=\sqrt{2\pi}\,\tau\) (the \(\mathcal N(m,\tau^2)\) density \(\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}\tau}e^{-(u-m)^2/(2\tau^2)}\) integrates to 1 — see §1.3; the Gaussian integral behind it is computed in B5). So

\[ p_{X+Y}(z)=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\tau}{2\pi\sigma_x\sigma_y}e^{-w^2/(2s^2)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,s}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{(z-\mu_x-\mu_y)^2}{2s^2}\Bigr), \]

the \(\mathcal N(\mu_x+\mu_y,\sigma_x^2+\sigma_y^2)\) density (using \(\tau/(\sigma_x\sigma_y)=1/s\)).

Notes on the official solution: in (iii) the exponent is labelled \(-\frac{(z+(\mu_x+\mu_y))^2}{2\sigma_z^2}\); the sign must be \(z-(\mu_x+\mu_y)\) (the final line has the right distribution). Also, in the completing-the-square lines it twice writes \(\sigma_x^2(z-\mu_x)\) where \(\sigma_x^2(z-\mu_y)\) is meant (the line before has it right). The hint's set should be in \(\R^2\), not \(\R^n\). The answer in (ii) should add "and 0 for \(z<0\)".

Sheet 7 Ex 2: \(p_{X+Y}(z)=\int p_X(z-y)\,p_Y(y)\,\mathrm dy\). Top: \(p_Y(y)\) (blue) and the flipped, shifted \(p_X(z-y)\) (orange) as functions of \(y\); their product is shaded, and its area is \(p_{X+Y}(z)\). Bottom: the whole curve \(z\mapsto p_{X+Y}(z)\) with the current \(z\) marked. Slide \(z\) and watch the overlap build the curve.

Transformation of densities

The idea. Push the random point \(X\) through a map \(g\). Probability is conserved: the mass in a tiny interval \([x,x+\mathrm dx]\) moves to \([g(x),g(x)+g'(x)\mathrm dx]\). If \(g\) stretches the interval (\(|g'|>1\)), the same mass is spread thinner, so the density goes down by the stretch factor. That is all the formula says. It is the general version of the cdf method from §1.3.

A number example first (mine). \(X\sim\Unif(0,1)\) has density 1 on \((0,1)\). Let \(Y=2X+1\). The map doubles lengths and moves \((0,1)\) to \((1,3)\). The total mass 1 is now spread over an interval of length 2, so \(p_Y(y)=\frac12\) on \((1,3)\) and 0 elsewhere. The formula below gives the same: \(g^{-1}(y)=\frac{y-1}2\), its derivative is \(\frac12\), and \(p_X=1\) there.

Words in the statement. Strictly monotone: strictly increasing or strictly decreasing, so each \(y\) comes from at most one \(x\). Continuously differentiable: \(g'\) exists and is continuous. \(g^{-1}\) is the inverse map (\(g^{-1}(y)\) is the \(x\) with \(g(x)=y\)), and \(g(S_X)\) is the set of all values \(g(x)\) with \(x\in S_X\). In the vector version, bijective means every \(y\) comes from exactly one \(x\), and the Jacobian matrix \(J_g(x)\) is the matrix of all partial derivatives \(\partial g_i/\partial x_j\); \(|\det J_g|\) is the factor by which \(g\) stretches small volumes (B5). Strictly monotone functions and their inverses: Analysis 5.1; the chain rule and the derivative of an inverse function: Analysis 6.3.

Proposition 2.51 transformation of densities / change of variables Script 2.51

Let \(X\) be continuous with density \(p_X\), support \(S_X:=\{x:p_X(x)>0\}\), and \(g:\R\to\R\) continuously differentiable and strictly monotone on \(S_X\). For \(Y:=g(X)\):

\[ p_Y(y)=p_X\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr)\,\Bigl|\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dy}g^{-1}(y)\Bigr|\quad\text{for }y\in g(S_X),\qquad p_Y(y)=0\text{ otherwise}. \]

Vector version. For a random vector \(X\) in \(\R^n\) and \(g:\R^n\to\R^n\) continuously differentiable and bijective with \(\det J_g(x)\ne0\) on \(S_X\):

\[ p_Y(y)=p_X\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr)\,\bigl|\det J_{g^{-1}}(y)\bigr|=\frac{p_X(x)}{|\det J_g(x)|}\Bigg|_{x=g^{-1}(y)}\quad\text{for }y\in g(S_X). \]

Here \(J_{g^{-1}}(y)=\bigl[\frac{\partial g_i^{-1}}{\partial y_j}\bigr]_{i,j}\) is the Jacobian matrix of the inverse map \(g^{-1}\), built the same way as \(J_g\) but from the partial derivatives of \(g^{-1}\). The second equality uses \(J_{g^{-1}}(y)=[J_g(g^{-1}(y))]^{-1}\) and \(\det(A^{-1})=1/\det A\) (B5). Why that first identity holds (my addition; the script states it without proof): \(g(g^{-1}(y))=y\) for every \(y\); differentiating both sides with the multivariate chain rule gives \(J_g(g^{-1}(y))\cdot J_{g^{-1}}(y)=I\) (the identity matrix is the Jacobian of \(y\mapsto y\)), so \(J_{g^{-1}}(y)\) is the inverse matrix of \(J_g(g^{-1}(y))\) — the vector version of \((g^{-1})'(y)=1/g'(g^{-1}(y))\); details in B5.

Proof sketch for the scalar case Script — each step explained

\(g\) strictly increasing. Then \(g(X)\le y\iff X\le g^{-1}(y)\), so \(F_Y(y)=F_X(g^{-1}(y))\). Chain rule: \(p_Y(y)=F_Y'(y)=p_X(g^{-1}(y))\cdot\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dy}g^{-1}(y)\), and the derivative is positive (the inverse of an increasing function increases), so it equals its absolute value.

\(g\) strictly decreasing. Then \(g(X)\le y\iff X\ge g^{-1}(y)\), so \(F_Y(y)=1-\P(X<g^{-1}(y))=1-F_X(g^{-1}(y))\) (for continuous \(X\), \(\P(X=c)=0\)). Differentiating gives \(-p_X(g^{-1}(y))\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dy}g^{-1}(y)\), and now the derivative is negative, so again the result is \(p_X(g^{-1}(y))\bigl|\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dy}g^{-1}(y)\bigr|\).

Not monotone: split the support into pieces on which \(g\) is strictly monotone and add the contributions of all pre-images. Vector case: it is the transformation theorem for integrals (B5) applied to \(\P(Y\in B)=\P(X\in g^{-1}(B))=\int_{g^{-1}(B)}p_X\).

Recipe. (1) Find the support of \(Y\). (2) Solve \(y=g(x)\) for \(x=g^{-1}(y)\). (3) Differentiate \(g^{-1}\), take the absolute value (or the \(|\det|\) of the Jacobian). (4) Multiply. (5) Say "0 outside".

In words: the density of \(Y=g(X)\) at \(y\) is the density of \(X\) at the point that \(g\) sends to \(y\), divided by how much \(g\) stretches space there.

Example 2.52 affine transformations Script 2.52

(i) \(Y=aX+b\), \(a\ne0\): \(g^{-1}(y)=\frac{y-b}a\), derivative \(\frac1a\), so \(p_Y(y)=\frac1{|a|}p_X\bigl(\frac{y-b}a\bigr)\).

(ii) \(Y=AX+b\) with invertible \(A\in\R^{n\times n}\): \(J_g=A\), so \(p_Y(y)=\frac{p_X(A^{-1}(y-b))}{|\det A|}\).

(iii) \(X\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\Rightarrow Z:=\sigma X+\mu\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) for \(\sigma\ne0\); conversely \((Z-\mu)/\sigma\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\). (Plug the standard density into (i).)

Three more examples My addition

WiSe25 P3a again. \(U\sim\Unif(0,1)\), \(Y=-\ln(U)/\lambda\). \(g\) is decreasing on \((0,1)\) with \(g(0,1)=(0,\infty)\); \(g^{-1}(y)=e^{-\lambda y}\), \(\bigl|\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dy}g^{-1}\bigr|=\lambda e^{-\lambda y}\), \(p_U=1\) there. So \(p_Y(y)=\lambda e^{-\lambda y}\) for \(y>0\): \(\Exp(\lambda)\), as found with the cdf method on §1.3.

A non-monotone map: \(Y=X^2\) with \(X\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\). For \(y>0\) there are two pre-images \(\pm\sqrt y\), each with \(|\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dy}(\pm\sqrt y)|=\frac1{2\sqrt y}\). Add both: \(p_Y(y)=2\cdot\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-y/2}\cdot\frac1{2\sqrt y}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi y}}e^{-y/2}\) — the \(\chi^2_1\) density. Hence (Example 2.50) a sum of \(k\) squared independent standard normals is \(\chi^2_k\).

Box–Muller (two dimensions). \(U_1,U_2\) iid \(\Unif(0,1)\), \(R=\sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\), \(\Theta=2\pi U_2\). Then \(R\) has density \(re^{-r^2/2}\) on \(r>0\) (cdf method: \(\P(R\le r)=\P(U_1\ge e^{-r^2/2})=1-e^{-r^2/2}\)), \(\Theta\) is uniform on \((0,2\pi)\), independent. The polar map \((r,\theta)\mapsto(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\) has \(|\det J|=r\) (B5), so \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)=\frac{re^{-r^2/2}\cdot\frac1{2\pi}}{r}=\frac1{2\pi}e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}\): two independent standard normals. This answers Sheet 7 Ex 5(i).
