Pick the distribution of \(X\) and the map \(g\). The grey histogram shows 20 000 simulated values of \(Y=g(X)\); the blue curve is \(p_Y\) from Proposition 2.51 (with both branches added for \(x^2\) when \(X\) can be negative).

Computing with Gaussians

The idea. A multivariate Gaussian is a bell-shaped cloud in \(\R^d\) whose contour lines are ellipses (ellipsoids). It is completely described by two things: its centre \(\mu\) and its covariance matrix \(\Sigma\), which fixes the shape and orientation of the ellipses (B5). And every linear operation — shifting, rotating, projecting, adding, conditioning — keeps it Gaussian.

Lemma 2.53 (first part) the multivariate Gaussian density Script 2.53

The density of the multivariate Gaussian with mean \(\mu\in\R^d\) and covariance matrix \(\Sigma\in\R^{d\times d}\) is

\[ p(x)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}}\exp\Bigl(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\Bigr), \]

where \(|\Sigma|=\det\Sigma\); we write \(X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)\). A valid covariance matrix is symmetric (\(\Sigma^\top=\Sigma\): entry \((j,k)\) equals entry \((k,j)\), because \(\Cov[X_j,X_k]=\Cov[X_k,X_j]\)) and positive semi-definite (\(x^\top\Sigma x\ge0\) for all \(x\in\R^d\), written \(\Sigma\succeq0\); this holds because \(x^\top\Sigma x=\Var[x^\top X]\ge0\)). To get a density one assumes the stronger positive definite (\(x^\top\Sigma x>0\) for \(x\ne0\), written \(\Sigma\succ0\)); then \(\Sigma^{-1}\) exists.

Here \(x^\top\) turns the column vector \(x\) into a row, so \(x^\top\Sigma x=\sum_{j,k}x_j\Sigma_{jk}x_k\) is a single number (B5).

Reading it piece by piece (mine). For \(d=1\), \(\Sigma=\sigma^2\): the exponent is \(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\) and the constant \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\) — the familiar normal density. In general \((x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\) is a squared distance measured in the "units" of \(\Sigma\) (the Mahalanobis distance); \(|\Sigma|^{1/2}\) is the volume factor that makes the total integral 1.

Example (mine). \(d=2\), \(\mu=0\), \(\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_X^2&\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y\\\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y&\sigma_Y^2\end{pmatrix}\) with \(|\rho|<1\). Then \(|\Sigma|=\sigma_X^2\sigma_Y^2(1-\rho^2)\) and

\[ p(x,y)=\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_X\sigma_Y\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)}\Bigl[\frac{x^2}{\sigma_X^2}-\frac{2\rho xy}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}+\frac{y^2}{\sigma_Y^2}\Bigr]\Bigr). \]

Lemma 2.53 (second part) computation rules for Gaussians Script 2.53

Let \(Z=(X,Y)\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)\) with \(X\in\R^{d_X}\), \(Y\in\R^{d_Y}\), \(\mu=(\mu_X,\mu_Y)\) and

\[ \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma_{XX}&\Sigma_{XY}\\\Sigma_{XY}^\top&\Sigma_{YY}\end{pmatrix}. \]

So \(Z\) is the long vector \(X\) stacked on top of \(Y\), and \(d=d_X+d_Y\). The blocks are: \(\Sigma_{XX}\in\R^{d_X\times d_X}\) the covariances among the entries of \(X\), \(\Sigma_{YY}\in\R^{d_Y\times d_Y}\) those among the entries of \(Y\), and \(\Sigma_{XY}\in\R^{d_X\times d_Y}\) the covariances between an entry of \(X\) and an entry of \(Y\). The marginal distribution of \(X\) is the distribution of \(X\) alone (ignoring \(Y\)); the conditional distribution of \(X\) given \(Y=y\) is how \(X\) is distributed once we know \(Y=y\).

  1. \(X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\) iff \(\Sigma_{XY}=0\).
  2. \(AZ+b\sim\mathcal N(A\mu+b,\ A\Sigma A^\top)\) for \(A\in\R^{d\times d}\), \(b\in\R^d\) (assuming \(A\Sigma A^\top\succ0\)).
  3. Marginals: \(X\sim\mathcal N(\mu_X,\Sigma_{XX})\) and \(Y\sim\mathcal N(\mu_Y,\Sigma_{YY})\).
  4. Conditionals: \(X\mid Y=y\ \sim\ \mathcal N(\mu_{X|y},\Sigma_{X|y})\) with \(\mu_{X|y}=\mu_X+\Sigma_{XY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}(y-\mu_Y)\) and \(\Sigma_{X|y}=\Sigma_{XX}-\Sigma_{XY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\Sigma_{XY}^\top\).
  5. If \(d_X=d_Y\) and \(\Sigma_{XY}=0\) (so \(X,Y\) are independent), then \(aX+bY\sim\mathcal N(a\mu_X+b\mu_Y,\ a^2\Sigma_{XX}+b^2\Sigma_{YY})\) for \(a,b\in\R\).
  6. In general (any \(d_X,d_Y\), any \(\Sigma_{XY}\)), for \(A\in\R^{k\times d_X}\), \(B\in\R^{k\times d_Y}\), \(c\in\R^k\): \(AX+BY+c\sim\mathcal N\bigl(A\mu_X+B\mu_Y+c,\ A\Sigma_{XX}A^\top+B\Sigma_{XY}^\top A^\top+A\Sigma_{XY}B^\top+B\Sigma_{YY}B^\top\bigr)\) — possibly "degenerate" (covariance not positive definite).

Numbers (mine, with the matrix of Sheet 7 Ex 5): \(\mu=(1,2)\), \(\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\). Then \(X\sim\mathcal N(1,2)\); \(X\mid Y=y\sim\mathcal N\bigl(1+\tfrac12(y-2),\ 2-\tfrac12\bigr)\), so observing \(Y=4\) moves the mean of \(X\) to 2 and shrinks its variance from 2 to 1.5; \(X+Y\sim\mathcal N(3,\,2+2+2\cdot1)=\mathcal N(3,6)\) by (vi) with \(A=B=1\); and \(X,Y\) are dependent because \(\Sigma_{XY}=1\ne0\).

In words: for a Gaussian vector, independence is the same as zero covariance; and linear maps, dropping coordinates, conditioning and linear combinations all give Gaussians again. The new mean and covariance come from simple matrix formulas.

Proofs of (i)–(vi) a streamlined route of mine; the official Sheet 8 Ex 5 solution integrates directly and has several slips (listed below)

Step 0 (Sheet 8 Ex 5, preliminary: \(\E[X]=\mu\), \(\Cov=\Sigma\)) — building \(\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)\) from independent standard normals. Let \(W=(W_1,\dots,W_d)\) have iid \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) entries; its density is the product \((2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-w^\top w/2}\). Take the Cholesky factor \(\Sigma=LL^\top\) (B5); \(\det L=\sqrt{\det\Sigma}>0\), so \(L\) is invertible. Put \(Z:=\mu+LW\). Example 2.52(ii) gives

\[ p_Z(z)=\frac{p_W(L^{-1}(z-\mu))}{|\det L|}=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}}\exp\Bigl(-\tfrac12(z-\mu)^\top\underbrace{L^{-\top}L^{-1}}_{=(LL^\top)^{-1}=\Sigma^{-1}}(z-\mu)\Bigr) , \]

exactly the density of the lemma. Also \(\E[Z]=\mu+L\E[W]=\mu\) and \(\Cov[Z]=L\,\Cov[W]\,L^\top=LIL^\top=\Sigma\) (the matrix rule \(\Cov[AW]=A\Cov[W]A^\top\) is Sheet 6 Ex 1 entry by entry). So the parameters really are the mean and the covariance matrix. Any \(X\) with this density has the same distribution as \(Z\) (a density fixes the distribution), hence also \(\E[X]=\mu\) and \(\Cov[X]=\Sigma\). In block form this says \(\Cov[X]=\Sigma_{XX}\), \(\Cov[X,Y]=\Sigma_{XY}\), \(\Cov[Y]=\Sigma_{YY}\) — the facts the official solution proves first.

The official route for \(\E[X]=\mu\), for comparison: write \(\E[X]=\int x\,p(x)\,\mathrm dx\) and substitute \(u=x-\mu\), so \(x=\mu+u\). This splits into \(\mu\int p=\mu\cdot1\) plus \(\int u\,c\,e^{-u^\top\Sigma^{-1}u/2}\,\mathrm du\), and the last integral is 0: replacing \(u\) by \(-u\) leaves the exponential unchanged but flips the sign of \(u\), so the integral equals its own negative.

(ii) [Sheet 8 Ex 5(ii)] For invertible \(A\), Example 2.52(ii) gives \(p_{AZ+b}(y)=p_Z(A^{-1}(y-b))/|\det A|\). In the exponent, \(A^{-1}(y-b)-\mu=A^{-1}\bigl(y-(A\mu+b)\bigr)\), so the quadratic form becomes \((y-(A\mu+b))^\top A^{-\top}\Sigma^{-1}A^{-1}(y-(A\mu+b))\) and \(A^{-\top}\Sigma^{-1}A^{-1}=(A\Sigma A^\top)^{-1}\). The constant: \(|\Sigma|^{1/2}|\det A|=(\det A\det\Sigma\det A^\top)^{1/2}=|A\Sigma A^\top|^{1/2}\). That is the \(\mathcal N(A\mu+b,A\Sigma A^\top)\) density.

(i) [Sheet 8 Ex 5(i)] "\(\Rightarrow\)": independence gives zero covariance entry by entry (Proposition 2.12(v)). "\(\Leftarrow\)": if \(\Sigma_{XY}=0\), \(\Sigma\) is block-diagonal, so \(\Sigma^{-1}\) is block-diagonal with blocks \(\Sigma_{XX}^{-1},\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\) and \(|\Sigma|=|\Sigma_{XX}||\Sigma_{YY}|\) (B5). The quadratic form splits into an \(x\)-part plus a \(y\)-part, so \(p_Z(x,y)\) is the product of the \(\mathcal N(\mu_X,\Sigma_{XX})\) density in \(x\) and the \(\mathcal N(\mu_Y,\Sigma_{YY})\) density in \(y\). A joint density that factorises into densities means independence with those marginals (Definition 1.77(iii), Theorem 1.68).

(iii) and (iv) [Sheet 8 Ex 5(iii), (iv)] — decorrelate first. Let \(B:=\Sigma_{XY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\) and \(V:=X-BY\). The map \((X,Y)\mapsto(V,Y)\) is linear with matrix \(M=\begin{pmatrix}I&-B\\0&I\end{pmatrix}\), which is invertible (block-triangular, \(\det M=1\)). By (ii), \((V,Y)\) is Gaussian with covariance \(M\Sigma M^\top\), whose blocks are (bilinearity)

\[ \Cov[V,Y]=\Sigma_{XY}-B\Sigma_{YY}=0,\qquad \Cov[V]=\Sigma_{XX}-B\Sigma_{XY}^\top-\Sigma_{XY}B^\top+B\Sigma_{YY}B^\top=\Sigma_{XX}-\Sigma_{XY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\Sigma_{XY}^\top=:S , \]

and \(\E[V]=\mu_X-B\mu_Y\). By (i), \(V\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\), with \(Y\sim\mathcal N(\mu_Y,\Sigma_{YY})\) — that is (iii) for \(Y\); swapping the roles of \(X\) and \(Y\) gives (iii) for \(X\). For (iv): \(X=V+BY\) with \(V\) independent of \(Y\). Given \(Y=y\), \(X\) is therefore \(V+By\), i.e. \(\mathcal N(\mu_X-B\mu_Y+By,\ S)=\mathcal N(\mu_X+\Sigma_{XY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}(y-\mu_Y),\ S)\). (Formally: \(p_{X|Y=y}(x)=p_{V,Y}(x-By,y)/p_Y(y)=p_V(x-By)\), using \(\det M=1\).) \(S\) is called the Schur complement (the name for the matrix \(\Sigma_{XX}-\Sigma_{XY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\Sigma_{XY}^\top\)) (B5); it is positive definite because \(M\Sigma M^\top\) is.

(vi) and (v) [Sheet 8 Ex 5(vi), (v)]. \(AX+BY+c=CZ+c\) with \(C=[A\ B]\in\R^{k\times d}\). If \(C\) has full row rank (its \(k\) rows are linearly independent: no row of \(C\) is a linear combination of the other rows — and then, because \(\Sigma\succ0\), equivalently \(C\Sigma C^\top\succ0\); rank, linear independence and extending rows to an invertible matrix: B5), add \(d-k\) further rows, each not a combination of the rows chosen so far (always possible in \(\R^d\)), to get an invertible \(d\times d\) matrix whose first \(k\) rows are \(C\); by (ii) the transformed vector is Gaussian, and by (iii) its first \(k\) coordinates, \(CZ+c\), are \(\mathcal N(C\mu+c,C\Sigma C^\top)\). Multiplying out in blocks, \(C\Sigma C^\top=A\Sigma_{XX}A^\top+A\Sigma_{XY}B^\top+B\Sigma_{XY}^\top A^\top+B\Sigma_{YY}B^\top\), which is (vi). (v) is \(A=aI\), \(B=bI\), \(\Sigma_{XY}=0\). If \(C\) does not have full row rank, the result is a degenerate Gaussian without a density; the cf \(e^{it^\top(C\mu+c)-t^\top C\Sigma C^\top t/2}\) still identifies it. (Here the cf of a random vector \(V\in\R^k\) is \(\varphi_V(t)=\E\bigl[e^{i\,t^\top V}\bigr]\) for \(t\in\R^k\), where \(t^\top V=t_1V_1+\dots+t_kV_k\) is a real number — the same definition as 2.46 with the product \(tX\) replaced by this sum. The script defines the cf only for real \(X\); this remark is my addition and not needed for exams.)

Widget — a two-dimensional Gaussian and its conditionals My addition

Contours at 1, 2, 3 "Mahalanobis units" and 300 samples of \((X,Y)\) with \(\mu=0\). The horizontal line is \(Y=y_0\); the orange bar is the conditional distribution of \(X\) given \(Y=y_0\): centred at \(\rho\frac{\sigma_X}{\sigma_Y}y_0\) with standard deviation \(\sigma_X\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\) (Lemma 2.53(iv) in two dimensions).

Remark 2.54 why Gaussians are so useful Script 2.54 · start of Lecture 9

Lemma 2.53 says: (i) for jointly Gaussian variables, uncorrelated and independent are the same; (ii)–(vi) Gaussians are closed under affine maps, marginalisation, conditioning and linear combinations. Since a Gaussian is fixed by its mean vector and covariance matrix, "every computation with Gaussian distributions just becomes linear algebra". Together with their maximum-entropy property and the central limit theorem (§2.4), this is why they are everywhere: Gaussian processes (regression), normalising flows and diffusion models (generative modelling), Gaussian splatting (computer vision).

Warning: (i) needs joint Gaussianity. Two variables can each be \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), uncorrelated, and still dependent: \(X\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), \(S=\pm1\) a fair sign independent of \(X\), \(Y=SX\). Then \(Y\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), \(\Cov[X,Y]=\E[S]\E[X^2]=0\), but \(|Y|=|X|\). The pair \((X,Y)\) is not jointly Gaussian (\(X+Y\) is 0 with probability \(\frac12\)).

Exercise-sheet tasks

Sheet 7 Ex 2 is worked above, right after Example 2.50.

Sheet 7, Exercise 5 (bonus) — sampling from a 2D Gaussian Sheet 7 · Ex 5

Sample from \(\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)\) with \(\mu=(1,2)\), \(\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\). (i) Derive a transformation that samples \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). (ii) Code: use \(AZ+b\sim\mathcal N(A\mu+b,A\Sigma A^\top)\) (hint: Cholesky).

Solution mine — the official solution is empty

(i) Inverse transform sampling needs \(\Phi^{-1}\), the inverse of the standard normal cdf. It exists because \(\Phi\) is continuous and strictly increasing, and by the quantile transformation (Proposition 2.23) \(\Phi^{-1}(U)\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) for \(U\sim\Unif(0,1)\). But \(\Phi^{-1}\) has no closed form; libraries evaluate it numerically. A closed-form alternative is Box–Muller (derived above): \(X=\sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\cos(2\pi U_2)\) and \(Y=\sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\sin(2\pi U_2)\) are two independent \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) values from two uniforms.

(ii) With \(W=(W_1,W_2)\) iid \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) and the Cholesky factor \(L=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt2&0\\1/\sqrt2&\sqrt{3/2}\end{pmatrix}\) (B5), set \(Z=\mu+LW\). By Lemma 2.53(ii), \(Z\sim\mathcal N(\mu,LL^\top)=\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)\). Concretely: \(Z_1=1+\sqrt2W_1\), \(Z_2=2+\frac{W_1}{\sqrt2}+\sqrt{\tfrac32}W_2\). Check: \(\Var[Z_1]=2\), \(\Var[Z_2]=\frac12+\frac32=2\), \(\Cov[Z_1,Z_2]=\sqrt2\cdot\frac1{\sqrt2}=1\) ✓.

The sheet's hint writes "\(AZ+b\sim\mathcal N(A\mu+b,A\Sigma A^\top)\) where \(Z\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)\)", reusing \(\mu,\Sigma\) for the input; for the sampling task the input is \(W\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\).

Sheet 8, Exercise 1 — the sum of independent Poissons is Poisson Sheet 8 · Ex 1

\(X\sim\Poi(\lambda_1)\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\sim\Poi(\lambda_2)\). Show \(X+Y\sim\Poi(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\) using characteristic functions.

Solution

\(\varphi_X(t)=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{itk}e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}=e^{-\lambda}\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(\lambda e^{it})^k}{k!}=e^{-\lambda}e^{\lambda e^{it}}=\exp\bigl(\lambda(e^{it}-1)\bigr)\), using \(e^{itk}\lambda^k=(\lambda e^{it})^k\) and the exponential series \(e^w=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{w^k}{k!}\) together with \(e^{w+z}=e^we^z\) (both valid for complex \(w,z\): Analysis 3.4 defines \(\exp\) on \(\mathbb C\) and proves this). By Remark 2.47(iv), \(\varphi_{X+Y}(t)=e^{\lambda_1(e^{it}-1)}e^{\lambda_2(e^{it}-1)}=e^{(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)(e^{it}-1)}\), the cf of \(\Poi(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\); uniqueness (2.47(v)) finishes.

A check without cfs (discrete convolution): \(\P(X+Y=n)=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{e^{-\lambda_1}\lambda_1^k}{k!}\frac{e^{-\lambda_2}\lambda_2^{n-k}}{(n-k)!} =\frac{e^{-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)}}{n!}\sum_k\binom nk\lambda_1^k\lambda_2^{n-k}=\frac{e^{-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)^n}{n!}\) by the binomial theorem. The official solution is correct (it switches between \(X,Y\) and \(X_1,X_2\)). Used in Sheet 8 Ex 2(v) on §2.2.

Sheet 8, Exercise 5 — prove the Gaussian computation rules Sheet 8 · Ex 5

The statement is Lemma 2.53 (i)–(vi) verbatim. All proofs are in the proof box "Proofs of (i)–(vi)" of Lemma 2.53 above (open it), by a shorter route than the official one. Each part is labelled there with "[Sheet 8 Ex 5 (…)]". Where to find what:

Sheet 8 Ex 5 — part by part Sheet 8 · Ex 5

  • Preliminary (\(\E[X]=\mu\), \(\Cov[Z]=\Sigma\) with the blocks \(\Sigma_{XX},\Sigma_{XY},\Sigma_{YY}\)): Step 0. Idea: \(Z=\mu+LW\) with \(W\) standard normal and \(\Sigma=LL^\top\); then \(\E[Z]=\mu\), \(\Cov[Z]=LL^\top=\Sigma\).
  • (ii) affine maps: change of variables (Example 2.52(ii)) and the matrix identity \(A^{-\top}\Sigma^{-1}A^{-1}=(A\Sigma A^\top)^{-1}\). The official solution adds an aside: "if \(A\) is not injective, use the pseudo-inverse \(A^\dagger\) (the inverse of \(A\) restricted to the orthogonal complement of its kernel)". This guide deliberately avoids the pseudo-inverse: it only ever applies (ii) to invertible square matrices, and handles non-square \(A\) by completing it to an invertible matrix in (vi) (rank: B5). You do not need the pseudo-inverse for this course.
  • (i) independence \(\iff\Sigma_{XY}=0\): with \(\Sigma_{XY}=0\) the density factorises into an \(x\)-part times a \(y\)-part.
  • (iii) marginals and (iv) conditionals: subtract \(BY\) from \(X\) (with \(B=\Sigma_{XY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\)) to get \(V\) independent of \(Y\); then read off.
  • (vi) \(AX+BY+c\): complete \([A\ B]\) to an invertible matrix, apply (ii), then (iii). (v) is the special case \(A=aI\), \(B=bI\), \(\Sigma_{XY}=0\); in one dimension it is also Sheet 7 Ex 2(iii) with \(aX\), \(bY\) in place of \(X\), \(Y\) (the official solution does it this way).

Slips in the official solution of Sheet 8 Ex 5 checked by me

  • Twice it writes \(\Sigma^{-1}=U\Lambda U^\top\); correct is \(\Sigma^{-1}=U\Lambda^{-1}U^\top\) (the decomposition \(U\Lambda^{-1/2}\Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top\) written next to it is right). An integral limit reads \(\int_\infty^\infty\) instead of \(\int_{-\infty}^\infty\).
  • (i) uses \(\Sigma^{XX},\Sigma^{YY}\) without defining them; they must be the blocks of \(\Sigma^{-1}\) (which, when \(\Sigma_{XY}=0\), equal \(\Sigma_{XX}^{-1},\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\)).
  • (ii) the final exponent has \((A\Sigma A^\top)\) where \((A\Sigma A^\top)^{-1}\) is needed.
  • (iii) applies (ii), which was proved for invertible square \(A\), to \(A=[I_{d_X},0]^\top\) — that matrix is not square (and the transpose is the wrong way round). The gap is exactly why my proof decorrelates with an invertible block-triangular map first.
  • (v) the exponent is labelled \(-(z+(\mu_x+\mu_y))^2/(2\sigma_z^2)\); the sign should be minus. As in Sheet 7 Ex 2(iii), it twice writes \(z-\mu_x\) where \(z-\mu_y\) is meant.
  • (vi) the final line reads \(\mathcal N(a\mu_X+b\mu_Y,\ a^2\sigma_X^2+b^2\sigma_Y^2,\ a^2\sigma_X^2+b^2\sigma_Y^2+2ab\sigma_X\sigma_Y)\). The line above it expands to \(a^2\sigma_X^2+b^2\sigma_Y^2+2ab\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y\) — the \(\rho\) is missing, and there is a stray third entry. Correct: \(aX+bY\sim\mathcal N(a\mu_X+b\mu_Y,\ a^2\sigma_X^2+b^2\sigma_Y^2+2ab\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y)\), which also follows from Proposition 2.12(vi).
  • Preliminary part (\(\E[X]=\mu\)): the substitution is written \(v=uU\Lambda^{-1/2}\) (wrong order for column vectors; it should be \(v=\Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top u\)), and the antiderivative of \(v e^{-v^2/2}\) is written without its minus sign (\(-e^{-v^2/2}\) is correct). Neither changes the result 0.
  • Preliminary part (\(\Cov[Z]=\Sigma\)): after substituting \(u=B(z-\mu)\) the volume factor is written \(|B|\,\mathrm du\); correct is \(\mathrm dz=|\det B|^{-1}\mathrm du=|\Sigma|^{1/2}\mathrm du\). Only with \(|B|^{-1}\) does the constant \(1/\sqrt{(2\pi)^d|\Sigma|}\) cancel to \(1/\sqrt{(2\pi)^d}\).
  • The sheet calls a valid covariance matrix positive definite; the script (Lemma 2.53) says positive semi-definite in general and assumes definite only to get a density.

Sheet 9, Exercise 5 (bonus) — basic properties of \(\varphi_X\) Sheet 9 · Ex 5

Show (i) \(|\varphi_X|\le1\), \(\varphi_X(0)=1\); (ii) \(\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{ibt}\varphi_X(at)\); (iii) \(\P_X=\P_{-X}\) iff \(\varphi_X\) is real-valued; (iv) \(\varphi_{X_1+\dots+X_n}=\varphi_{X_1}\cdots\varphi_{X_n}\) for independent \(X_i\).

Solution

(i), (ii), (iv) are the proofs in the Remark 2.47 box above.

(iii) By (ii) with \(a=-1,b=0\), \(\varphi_{-X}(t)=\varphi_X(-t)\). And \(\varphi_X(-t)=\E[\cos(tX)-i\sin(tX)]=\overline{\varphi_X(t)}\) (cos is even, \(\cos(-u)=\cos u\); sin is odd, \(\sin(-u)=-\sin u\); both are stated in Analysis 5.3, in the box on Euler's formula). So

  • "\(\Rightarrow\)": \(\P_X=\P_{-X}\) gives \(\varphi_X=\varphi_{-X}=\overline{\varphi_X}\), i.e. \(\varphi_X\) is real.
  • "\(\Leftarrow\)": \(\varphi_X\) real gives \(\varphi_X(t)=\overline{\varphi_X(t)}=\varphi_{-X}(t)\) for all \(t\); by uniqueness (Remark 2.47(v)) \(\P_X=\P_{-X}\).

The official solution states the "iff" in one chain but does not mention that the backward direction needs the uniqueness theorem — equal characteristic functions only give equal distributions because of it. Otherwise correct. In words: a distribution is symmetric about 0 exactly when its cf has no imaginary part (check with the widget above).

Old-exam tasks

SoSe 2026, Problem 1c — a cf of a sum SoSe26 · P1c · 1 credit

Statement. \(X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\) with \(\varphi_X(t)=\varphi_Y(t)=\cos t\). Then \(\varphi_{2X+Y}(t)=\cos(2t)\cos(t)\)?

Official answer: True. By Remark 2.47(iv) and (ii): \(\varphi_{2X+Y}(t)=\varphi_{2X}(t)\varphi_Y(t)=\varphi_X(2t)\varphi_Y(t)=\cos(2t)\cos t\). Correct.

SoSe 2026, Problem 4a–c — a scaled random walk via cfs SoSe26 · P4a, P4b, (P4c) · 1 + 3 (+ 2) credits

Setting. \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) iid with \(\P(X_j=\pm1)=\frac12\); \(Z_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{j=1}^nX_j\).

(a) \(\varphi_{X_1}(t)=\frac12e^{it}+\frac12e^{-it}=\cos t\) (Euler's formula; the hint gives it).

(b) \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t)=\E\bigl[\prod_je^{i(t/\sqrt n)X_j}\bigr]=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t/\sqrt n)=\cos^n(t/\sqrt n)\): independence turns the expectation of the product into the product of expectations, and each factor is \(\varphi_{X_1}\) at \(t/\sqrt n\). Points: scaling \(t/\sqrt n\), product by independence, final form.

(c) via the cf (the direct route is on §2.1). Write \(f(t)=\cos^n(t/\sqrt n)\). \(f'(t)=-\sqrt n\cos^{n-1}(t/\sqrt n)\sin(t/\sqrt n)\), so \(f'(0)=0\) and \(\E[Z_n]=-if'(0)=0\). For \(f''(0)\), differentiate \(f'(t)=-\sqrt n\,c^{n-1}s\) once more with the product and chain rules (Analysis 6.3), where \(c=\cos(t/\sqrt n)\), \(s=\sin(t/\sqrt n)\), \(c'=-s/\sqrt n\), \(s'=c/\sqrt n\): \(f''(t)=-\sqrt n\bigl((n-1)c^{n-2}\cdot(-\tfrac{s}{\sqrt n})\cdot s+c^{n-1}\cdot\tfrac{c}{\sqrt n}\bigr)=(n-1)c^{n-2}s^2-c^n\). At \(t=0\): \(c=1\), \(s=0\), so \(f''(0)=-1\). Hence \(\E[Z_n^2]=i^{-2}f''(0)=-f''(0)=1\) and \(\Var[Z_n]=\E[Z_n^2]-\E[Z_n]^2=1\). The official solution states \(\varphi''_{Z_n}(0)=-1\) without the computation; the lines above supply it. Its moment formulas \(\E[Z_n]=\frac1i\varphi'(0)\), \(\E[Z_n^2]=\frac1{i^2}\varphi''(0)\) are Remark 2.47(iii) and correct.

(c) directly (the official first route): \(\E[X_j]=\frac12\cdot1+\frac12\cdot(-1)=0\) and \(\Var[X_j]=\E[X_j^2]-0=1\). Linearity gives \(\E[Z_n]=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_j\E[X_j]=0\); independence gives \(\Var[Z_n]=\frac1n\sum_j\Var[X_j]=1\) (the factor \(\frac1{\sqrt n}\) comes out squared). Grading: 1 point each for mean and variance, by either route.

Part (d) (Markov bound and the clt) is on §2.2 and §2.4. Note that \(\cos^n(t/\sqrt n)\to e^{-t^2/2}\) — the clt for coin flips in one line.

Traps

  • \(\varphi_{X+Y}=\varphi_X\varphi_Y\) needs independence; \(\varphi_{2X}(t)=\varphi_X(2t)\), not \(\varphi_X(t)^2\).
  • In the change-of-variables formula: the derivative of the inverse, in absolute value, and "0 outside".

Exam focus

So far cfs appear as short computations (SoSe26 P1c, P4a–b: 5 credits), always "product by independence, then rescale the argument". Change of variables appears inside density problems (WiSe25 P3, SoSe25 P3, via either method). Gaussian rules are the working tool of §3 (confidence intervals, tests) rather than a separate exam question in the three exams we have.

Section 2.4 · Lecture 9 (17 June 2026)

Convergence of random variables and limit theorems

Konvergenz von Zufallsvariablen und Grenzwertsätze

What this page covers Script §2.4, pp. 78–83

This page covers everything from Remark 2.55 to Remark 2.65. The script states the goal of the section like this: "Introduce different ways in which a sequence of RVs can converge to another RVs or a constant, and then state and discuss the foundational limit theorems of probability: the laws of large numbers (lln) and the central limit theorem (clt)."

So there are three parts: (1) three ways a sequence of random variables can converge, and how they relate; (2) the weak and the strong law of large numbers; (3) the central limit theorem.

Worked in place: Sheet 8 Ex 4 (Monte Carlo), Sheet 9 Ex 1, 2(ii), 2(iv), 3, 4, and the old-exam tasks WiSe25 P1d, P2a, P2b, P4c, P4d, SoSe25 P2a, P2b, SoSe26 P1d, P2a and the clt part of SoSe26 P4d. This is the most examined page of the course. WiSe25 and SoSe25 each asked for a definition and a theorem statement from it; SoSe26 asked true/false items and a clt approximation instead.

The big picture

Toss a fair coin again and again. After \(n\) tosses, let \(\bar X_n\) be the fraction of heads so far (number of heads divided by \(n\)). At first \(\bar X_n\) jumps around. Then it settles near \(\frac12\). Two questions make this precise.

  • In what sense does \(\bar X_n\) "go to" \(\frac12\)? \(\bar X_n\) is random, so the school definition of a limit does not apply directly. We need new definitions, and there are several of different strength:
    • almost surely: for almost every infinite sequence of tosses, the numbers \(\bar X_n\) converge;
    • in probability: a big deviation from \(\frac12\) becomes unlikely;
    • in distribution: only the histograms (the shapes of the distributions) approach each other.
    The laws of large numbers say that \(\bar X_n\) goes to the true mean in the first two senses.
  • How big is the remaining error for large \(n\)? The central limit theorem answers this. The error \(\bar X_n-\mu\) (where \(\mu\) is the true mean, here \(\frac12\)) is roughly of size \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) (where \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of one toss, here \(\frac12\)). Rescaled by that factor, the error looks normally distributed (bell-shaped). This holds whatever the distribution of a single toss is.

Numbers (my example). Take 100 fair tosses. One toss has mean \(\mu=\frac12\) and standard deviation \(\sigma=\frac12\). So \(\bar X_{100}\) has standard deviation \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{100}}=\frac{0.5}{10}=0.05\). The value 0.6 lies \(\frac{0.6-0.5}{0.05}=2\) standard deviations above the mean. The clt then says \(\P(\bar X_{100}\ge0.6)\approx1-\Phi(2)\approx0.023\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cdf (primer box 2). With a continuity correction (see the recipe below) one gets \(0.029\); the exact binomial value is \(0.028\). With 10 000 tosses the standard deviation is \(\frac{0.5}{100}=0.005\), and 0.6 is \(\frac{0.1}{0.005}=20\) standard deviations away — practically impossible.

In words: averages of many independent measurements settle at the true mean (lln). The way they scatter around it is a bell curve whose width shrinks like \(1/\sqrt n\) (clt).

Cross-references

Convergence of real sequences (the ε–\(n_0\) definition): Analysis 2.1. \((1+\frac xn)^n\to e^x\) for every real \(x\): Analysis 6.3 (Lemma 6.24) (Analysis 2.2 only does \(x=1\), Euler's number); the complex version is proved in step (vi) of the CLT proof below and in B1. Convergent sequences are bounded: Analysis 2.1. Accumulation points, lim sup and lim inf: Analysis 4.3 (with Bolzano–Weierstrass). Continuity at a point and the sequence criterion (\(x_n\to x\Rightarrow f(x_n)\to f(x)\)): Analysis 4.1, which also proves that \(\exp\) is continuous on the complex numbers; the complex exponential series and the rule \(e^{u}e^{v}=e^{u+v}\): Analysis 3.4. Triangle inequality: Analysis 1.3. Landau symbols \(o(\cdot)\): Analysis 6.1. Taylor expansion: Analysis 10.1. Characteristic functions: §2.3. Chebyshev: §2.2. Markov: §2.2. 0. Words and symbols used on this page

  • Probability space \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\): \(\Omega\) is the set of all possible outcomes, a single outcome is written \(\omega\); \(\Aa\) is the collection of events (subsets of \(\Omega\) we can assign probabilities to); \(\P\) assigns each event its probability.
  • Random variable [Zufallsvariable] (RV): a function \(X:\Omega\to\R\) that turns each outcome \(\omega\) into a number \(X(\omega)\) (§1.3). The script writes "RVRV" for a real-valued random variable.
  • Sequence of random variables \((X_n)_{n\in\N}\): one random variable \(X_1,X_2,X_3,\dots\) for every natural number \(n\). For a fixed outcome \(\omega\), the values \(X_1(\omega),X_2(\omega),\dots\) form an ordinary sequence of numbers.
  • iid: "independent and identically distributed" — the variables do not influence each other (§1.4) and all have the same distribution.
  • Mean and variance: \(\mu=\E[X_i]\) is the expected value, \(\sigma^2=\Var[X_i]\) the variance, \(\sigma\) the standard deviation (§2.1).
  • Covariance [Kovarianz] \(\Cov[X,Y]=\E\bigl[(X-\E[X])(Y-\E[Y])\bigr]\) (Definition 2.9, §2.1): how strongly \(X\) and \(Y\) deviate from their means in the same direction. Uncorrelated means \(\Cov[X,Y]=0\).
  • Sum and sample mean: \(S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n\) and \(\bar X_n=\frac{S_n}n\).
  • cdf \(F_X(x)=\P(X\le x)\) (§1.1), and characteristic function (cf) \(\varphi_X(t)=\E[e^{itX}]\) (§2.3). Both describe the distribution of \(X\) completely.
  • Indicator \(\one_A\): equals 1 on the set \(A\) and 0 outside it.
  • \(\varepsilon\) (epsilon) always stands for a small positive number, a "tolerance".
  • Null set: an event of probability 0. Almost surely (a.s.) [fast sicher]: "outside a null set", i.e. with probability 1.

1. Three facts about probabilities of events that you will need

  • Union bound (σ-subadditivity, Proposition 1.19(vi)): \(\P(A\cup B)\le\P(A)+\P(B)\), and more generally \(\P(\bigcup_kA_k)\le\sum_k\P(A_k)\) for countably many events. Consequence: a countable union of null sets is a null set (a sum of zeros is zero).
  • Continuity from above (Proposition 1.19(v)): if the events shrink, \(B_1\supseteq B_2\supseteq\dots\), then \(\P(B_n)\to\P(\bigcap_nB_n)\), the probability of the part common to all of them. (Proposition 1.19(v) also requires the first set to have finite measure; for a probability measure that is automatic, since \(\P(B_1)\le1\).)
  • Splitting an inequality: if \(|a+b|\ge\varepsilon\), then \(|a|\ge\frac\varepsilon2\) or \(|b|\ge\frac\varepsilon2\). Reason: if both were smaller than \(\frac\varepsilon2\), the triangle inequality \(|a+b|\le|a|+|b|\) (Analysis 1.3) would give \(|a+b|<\varepsilon\). As events: \(\{|U+V|\ge\varepsilon\}\subseteq\{|U|\ge\frac\varepsilon2\}\cup\{|V|\ge\frac\varepsilon2\}\). This is the standard move in Sheet 9 Ex 3.

2. The standard normal cdf \(\Phi\) and how to read it

\(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) means: \(Z\) is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance 1 ("standard normal"). Its cdf is written \(\Phi(z)=\P(Z\le z)\). There is no closed formula for \(\Phi\). Exams give values or let you leave \(\Phi(\cdot)\) in the answer.

The bell curve is symmetric around 0, so \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\). Hence \(\P(|Z|\ge a)=\P(Z\le-a)+\P(Z\ge a)=2(1-\Phi(a))=2\Phi(-a)\). Values worth knowing:

\(z\)11.6451.9622.52.5763
\(\Phi(z)\)0.8410.9500.9750.9770.9940.9950.9987

For \(X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), standardise first (Example 2.52(iii)): \(\P(X\le x)=\Phi\bigl(\frac{x-\mu}\sigma\bigr)\).

3. lim inf and lim sup of a sequence of numbers

Take a bounded sequence of real numbers \((a_n)\). An accumulation point is a value that the sequence comes arbitrarily close to again and again. \(\limsup_na_n\) is the largest and \(\liminf_na_n\) the smallest accumulation point. The sequence converges exactly when the two agree.

Useful trick: suppose \(c\le\liminf a_n\le\limsup a_n\le d\), and you can make \(c\) and \(d\) as close to a number \(L\) as you like. Then lim inf and lim sup are both \(L\), so \(a_n\to L\). (Used in the proof that convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution.)

Modes of convergence

Remark 2.55 why sequences Script 2.55

In probability and statistics we often ask: what happens to a sequence of random variables as it gets longer? The concentration inequalities of §2.2 already gave a first answer for sums and means: the average of many observations gets closer to the true mean of the underlying process.

In such settings the variables in the sequence are usually independent observations — the data points of a dataset, as in Remark 1.80. The lln and the clt continue this theme. But first we must say precisely what "getting closer" means for random variables. That is Definition 2.56.

After that, the laws of large numbers and the central limit theorem state that and how the means of iid sequences get closer and closer to their mean (in probability or almost surely).

Definition 2.56 modes of convergence Script 2.56

Setup. Let \((X_n)_{n\in\N}\) be a sequence of real random variables and \(X\) another real random variable (\(X\) may also be a constant). All of them are defined on the same probability space \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\).

  1. In probability [stochastische Konvergenz], written \(X_n\xrightarrow{\P}X\), if for every \(\varepsilon>0\): \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\P(|X_n-X|\ge\varepsilon)=0 .\] Intuition: for large \(n\) it is very unlikely that \(X_n\) is far from \(X\).
  2. Almost surely [fast sicher], written \(X_n\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}X\) or \(X_n\to X\) a.s., if \[\P\bigl(\{\omega\in\Omega\mid\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n(\omega)=X(\omega)\}\bigr)=1 .\] Intuition: for almost every outcome \(\omega\), the sequence of numbers \(X_n(\omega)\) converges to the number \(X(\omega)\).
  3. In distribution (also: weakly) [Konvergenz in Verteilung], written \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\) or \(X_n\Rightarrow X\), if \[\lim_{n\to\infty}F_{X_n}(x)=F_X(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in\R\text{ at which }F_X\text{ is continuous.}\] Intuition: the overall shape of the distribution of \(X_n\) approaches the shape of the distribution of \(X\). Equivalently (Lévy's continuity theorem, Remark 2.47(vi)): \(\varphi_{X_n}(t)\to\varphi_X(t)\) for all \(t\in\R\).

How to read each definition (mine).

  • (i): fix \(\varepsilon\). For each \(n\), compute the number \(p_n=\P(|X_n-X|\ge\varepsilon)\). Ask that \(p_n\to0\), as an ordinary sequence of numbers.
  • (ii): fix an outcome \(\omega\). You get a sequence of numbers \(X_n(\omega)\). Ask that it converges to \(X(\omega)\). This must work for all \(\omega\) except a null set.
  • (iii): no \(\omega\) appears at all — only the cdfs, which are ordinary functions.

Why "at continuity points"? (my example) Let \(X_n=\frac1n\) (a constant) and \(X=0\). In any reasonable sense \(X_n\to0\). Now look at the cdfs at \(x=0\): \(F_{X_n}(0)=\P(\frac1n\le0)=0\) for every \(n\), while \(F_0(0)=\P(0\le0)=1\). So the cdfs fail to converge at \(x=0\) — exactly the point where \(F_0\) jumps from 0 to 1. At every other \(x\) they do converge. Ignoring jump points makes the definition give the sensible answer. (A cdf \(F\) is continuous at \(x\) when \(F(x_n)\to F(x)\) for every sequence \(x_n\to x\) — no jump there; Analysis 4.1.)

Remark 2.57 relations between the modes Script 2.57

\[ X_n\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}X\ \Longrightarrow\ X_n\xrightarrow{\P}X\ \Longrightarrow\ X_n\xrightarrow{d}X . \]

In words: almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability, which implies convergence in distribution.

The reverse implications fail in general (Examples 2.58 and 2.59 below). Two partial reverses hold:

  • If \(X_n\xrightarrow\P X\), then some subsequence of \((X_n)\) converges almost surely to \(X\).
  • If \(X_n\xrightarrow dc\) for a constant \(c\in\R\), then also \(X_n\xrightarrow\P c\).
Proofs of the three implications supplied by me — the script states them

a.s. ⟹ in probability. Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Let \(B_n=\bigcup_{m\ge n}\{|X_m-X|\ge\varepsilon\}\): the event "some term from index \(n\) on is at least \(\varepsilon\) away from \(X\)".

  • The \(B_n\) shrink as \(n\) grows (fewer indices \(m\) are allowed).
  • If \(\omega\) lies in every \(B_n\), then \(|X_m(\omega)-X(\omega)|\ge\varepsilon\) for infinitely many \(m\). So \(X_m(\omega)\) does not converge to \(X(\omega)\). By assumption, such \(\omega\) form a null set: \(\P(\bigcap_nB_n)=0\).
  • Continuity from above (primer box 1) gives \(\P(B_n)\to0\).
  • \(\{|X_n-X|\ge\varepsilon\}\subseteq B_n\) (take \(m=n\)), so \(\P(|X_n-X|\ge\varepsilon)\le\P(B_n)\to0\).

In probability ⟹ in distribution. Let \(x\) be a point where \(F_X\) is continuous, and \(\varepsilon>0\).

  • Upper bound: if \(X_n\le x\) and \(|X_n-X|<\varepsilon\), then \(X<x+\varepsilon\). So \(\{X_n\le x\}\subseteq\{X\le x+\varepsilon\}\cup\{|X_n-X|\ge\varepsilon\}\). The union bound gives \(F_{X_n}(x)\le F_X(x+\varepsilon)+\P(|X_n-X|\ge\varepsilon)\).
  • Lower bound: if \(X\le x-\varepsilon\) and \(|X_n-X|<\varepsilon\), then \(X_n<x\). So \(\{X\le x-\varepsilon\}\subseteq\{X_n\le x\}\cup\{|X_n-X|\ge\varepsilon\}\), which gives \(F_X(x-\varepsilon)\le F_{X_n}(x)+\P(|X_n-X|\ge\varepsilon)\).
  • Let \(n\to\infty\). The probabilities \(\P(|X_n-X|\ge\varepsilon)\) go to 0, so \(F_X(x-\varepsilon)\le\liminf_n F_{X_n}(x)\le\limsup_n F_{X_n}(x)\le F_X(x+\varepsilon)\).
  • Now let \(\varepsilon\to0\). Because \(F_X\) is continuous at \(x\), both bounds tend to \(F_X(x)\). By primer box 3, \(F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x)\).

In distribution to a constant ⟹ in probability. The constant \(c\) has cdf \(F_c(x)=0\) for \(x<c\) and \(F_c(x)=1\) for \(x\ge c\). Its only jump is at \(c\), so every \(x\ne c\) is a continuity point. If \(|X_n-c|\ge\varepsilon\), then either \(X_n\le c-\varepsilon\) or \(X_n\ge c+\varepsilon\) (and then certainly \(X_n>c+\frac\varepsilon2\)). Hence \[\P(|X_n-c|\ge\varepsilon)\le F_{X_n}(c-\varepsilon)+1-F_{X_n}(c+\tfrac\varepsilon2)\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}0+1-1=0 .\]

The subsequence statement needs the Borel–Cantelli lemma; it is not proved here.

Example 2.58 in probability does not imply almost surely: the travelling bump Script 2.58

Setup. The probability space is \(([0,1],\mathcal B|_{[0,1]},\lambda|_{[0,1]})\): outcomes are points \(\omega\in[0,1]\), and the probability of an interval is its length (the uniform distribution on \([0,1]\); \(\mathcal B\) are the Borel sets, \(\lambda\) is length, B4).

The sequence. Write each \(n\) as \(n=2^k+j\) with \(0\le j<2^k\) (\(j,k\in\N\)), and set \(X_n=\one_{[j/2^k,\,(j+1)/2^k]}\). Concretely:

  • \(X_1\) (\(k=0\)) is the indicator of \([0,1]\);
  • \(X_2,X_3\) (\(k=1\)) are the indicators of the two halves \([0,\frac12]\), \([\frac12,1]\);
  • \(X_4,\dots,X_7\) (\(k=2\)) are the indicators of the four quarters; and so on.

So in round \(k\) a "bump" of width \(2^{-k}\) sweeps once across \([0,1]\), and each round it gets narrower.

  • In probability to 0: take \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\). Since \(X_n\) only takes the values 0 and 1, \(\P(|X_n-0|\ge\varepsilon)=\P(X_n=1)\). This is the length of the bump, \(2^{-k}\). As \(n\to\infty\) also \(k\to\infty\), so \(\P(X_n=1)\to0\). Hence \(X_n\xrightarrow\P0\).
  • Not almost surely: fix any \(\omega\). In every round \(k\) the bump passes over \(\omega\), so \(X_n(\omega)=1\) for at least one \(n\) in every round — infinitely many \(n\) in total. Also \(X_n(\omega)=0\) for infinitely many \(n\). So the number sequence \(X_n(\omega)\) does not converge (certainly not to 0), for any \(\omega\). Thus \(\P(\lim_nX_n=0)=0\ne1\).

Detail: the script says "for each \(k\) there is exactly one \(j\)" with \(\omega\) in the interval. At dyadic endpoints like \(\omega=\frac12\) there are two, because the closed intervals overlap. The argument only needs "at least one", and that holds. The widget shows the bump and the sequence \(X_n(\omega)\).

In words: the chance of being hit at step \(n\) goes to 0, but every single point is still hit again in every round. "Rarely wrong at each time" is weaker than "eventually always right".

Widget — the travelling bump My addition

Top: the interval where \(X_n=1\) for the current \(n\). Bottom: the sequence \(X_1(\omega),X_2(\omega),\dots\) for your chosen \(\omega\) — it keeps returning to 1 in every round, although the probability of 1 (the bump's width) goes to 0.

Example 2.59 in distribution does not imply in probability Script 2.59

Let \(U\sim\Ber(0.5)\) (a fair 0/1 coin). Define \(X_n:=U\) for every \(n\), and \(Y:=1-U\).

  • In distribution: \(Y\) is also 0 or 1 with probability \(\frac12\) each, so \(Y\sim\Ber(0.5)\). Hence \(F_{X_n}=F_Y=F_{\Ber(0.5)}\) for all \(n\), and \(X_n\xrightarrow dY\) trivially.
  • Not in probability: \(|X_n-Y|=|U-(1-U)|=|2U-1|\). Since \(U\in\{0,1\}\), this is \(|-1|=1\) or \(|1|=1\). So \(\P(|X_n-Y|=1)=1\) for all \(n\). In particular \(\P(|X_n-Y|\ge\frac12)=1\not\to0\).

In words: convergence in distribution compares only the shapes of the distributions. \(X_n\) and \(Y\) have the same shape, but they are never close — in fact they always disagree.

Remark 2.60 what kind of "closeness" each mode means Script 2.60

  • Almost sure convergence and convergence in probability are strong notions. They compare \(X_n\) and \(X\) on the same probability space \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\), that is, on the same "outcome label" of the actual random experiment. For a given outcome, the variables really end up taking similar values. This only makes sense if they "measure the exact same process".
    • Almost surely: for almost every specific \(\omega\), the real numbers \(X_n(\omega)\) converge to the real number \(X(\omega)\). This is a direct, pointwise relationship on the sample space.
    • In probability: slightly weaker. For large \(n\), \(X_n(\omega)\) is very likely close to \(X(\omega)\).
    Both say that \(X_n\) and \(X\) are "coupled" — they live on the same space and their values become similar.
  • Convergence in distribution is much weaker. Only the cdfs \(F_{X_n}\) converge to \(F_X\) (at continuity points). \(X_n\) and \(X\) need not even be defined on the same probability space, and the values \(X_n(\omega)\) and \(X(\omega)\) can be entirely unrelated. One \(X_i\) could be measurements in a physics lab, another a count of microbes in a river, and \(X\) some property of galaxies. All that matters is that their "probabilistic shapes" (distributions) become similar.

This distinction matters for the clt, which is a statement about convergence in distribution. The standardised sum \(Z_n\) does not become equal to a standard normal \(Z\) pointwise; only its distribution increasingly resembles that of \(Z\).

The laws of large numbers

Theorem 2.61 weak law of large numbers (wlln) Script 2.61

Assumptions. \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are real random variables that are

  • identically distributed,
  • with finite mean \(\E[X_i]=\mu<\infty\),
  • and pairwise uncorrelated (\(\Cov[X_i,X_j]=0\) for \(i\ne j\)).

Conclusion. The sample mean \(\bar X_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) converges in probability to \(\mu\): \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow\P\mu\).

Proof with finite variance Script — each step explained

Assume in addition \(\Var[X_i]=\sigma^2<\infty\).

Step 1 (mean). By linearity of expectation, \(\E[\bar X_n]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\E[X_i]=\frac1n\cdot n\mu=\mu\).

Step 2 (variance). A constant factor comes out squared (Proposition 2.8(iii)), and for uncorrelated variables the variance of a sum is the sum of the variances (Proposition 2.12(vi), all covariances are 0): \[\Var[\bar X_n]=\Var\Bigl[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\Bigr]=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\Var[X_i]=\frac1{n^2}\cdot n\sigma^2=\frac{\sigma^2}n .\]

Step 3 (Chebyshev). Chebyshev's inequality (Theorem 2.40) says \(\P(|Y-\E[Y]|\ge\varepsilon)\le\Var[Y]/\varepsilon^2\). With \(Y=\bar X_n\), for any \(\varepsilon>0\):

\[ \P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\frac{\Var[\bar X_n]}{\varepsilon^2}=\frac{\sigma^2/n}{\varepsilon^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}0 . \]

That is exactly Definition 2.56(i) with \(X=\mu\).

Further remarks from the script.

  • The wlln holds even if only the mean is finite (the variance may be infinite), but the proof is more involved.
  • Convergence is slower when the variances can vary, especially when they become large or infinite. (The bound \(\frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}\) shows this: a larger \(\sigma^2\) needs a larger \(n\).)
  • The wlln also holds when \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are iid, since independent variables are pairwise uncorrelated (Proposition 2.12(v)).

My notes on the statement. (1) "Pairwise uncorrelated" only makes sense when the variances are finite (a covariance needs \(\E[X_i^2]<\infty\)). So the proof above covers exactly the uncorrelated case. The version with "only the mean finite" is true for iid variables (more generally, pairwise independent and identically distributed ones) and needs a different proof. (2) The script's proof says "since the \(X_i\) are iid", but only uncorrelatedness is used. (3) The Chebyshev bound also gives a rate: the probability of an \(\varepsilon\)-deviation is at most \(\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)\).

Theorem 2.62 strong law of large numbers (slln) Script 2.62

Assumptions. \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are iid real random variables with finite mean \(\E[X_i]=\mu<\infty\).

Conclusion. The sample mean \(\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) converges almost surely: \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\mu\).

The script gives no proof (see Remark 2.63). The theorem is examined as a statement: WiSe25 P2a asked for it "with all required assumptions" — iid, finite mean, almost sure convergence of the sample mean.

Compare with the wlln: the slln needs the stronger assumption (iid instead of pairwise uncorrelated) and gives the stronger conclusion (a.s. instead of in probability).

Remark 2.63 wlln versus slln Script 2.63

  • The slln implies the wlln (because a.s. ⟹ in probability, Remark 2.57). It says more: the sample mean \(\bar X_n\) converges to \(\mu\) for almost every sequence of outcomes — not just that large deviations become unlikely.
  • The proof of the slln is more complex, especially without assuming finite variance. It typically uses the Borel–Cantelli lemmas to show that large deviations from the mean occur only finitely often. (The first Borel–Cantelli lemma says: if the probabilities of events \(A_1,A_2,\dots\) have a finite sum, then almost surely only finitely many of the \(A_n\) happen. It is not proved in this course.)
  • The Wikipedia article on the law of large numbers gives structured overviews of how the proofs work. In particular, the wlln can be proven elegantly with characteristic functions and Lévy's continuity theorem.
  • The laws of large numbers are fundamental in statistics: they justify using sample averages to estimate population means. This can hardly be overstated. We want to reason about a whole distribution ("all humans", "any conditions I could ever encounter"), but we only have a fixed, finite number of observations (data). Without the llns (or the clt, or concentration inequalities), we would have no reason to believe that the average of the data has anything to do with the true mean.
  • For both the wlln and the slln there are many variants that relax some assumptions while adding others.
  • What the llns do not tell us: how \(\bar X_n\) is distributed around \(\mu\) for large but finite \(n\), and how fast it converges. That is what the clt addresses.

Widget — running averages My addition

Five independent sample paths of \(\bar X_n\) for \(n=1,\dots,2000\) (log-scaled horizontal axis), with the band \(\mu\pm\varepsilon\). The lln says the paths enter the band and stay there. For the Cauchy distribution there is no mean — watch the paths jump forever.

The central limit theorem

Idea first (mine). The lln says \(\bar X_n-\mu\to0\). Multiply this shrinking error by the growing factor \(\sqrt n/\sigma\). The result neither shrinks to 0 nor blows up: it keeps mean 0 and variance 1. The clt says its distribution approaches the standard normal bell curve.

Theorem 2.64 central limit theorem (clt) [zentraler Grenzwertsatz] Script 2.64

Assumptions. \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are iid real random variables with finite mean \(\E[X_i]=\mu\) and finite, non-zero variance \(\Var[X_i]=\sigma^2\in\R_{>0}\).

Notation. \(S_n:=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) is the sum and \(\bar X_n=S_n/n\) the sample mean. The standardised sum (or standardised mean) is

\[ Z_n=\frac{S_n-\E[S_n]}{\sqrt{\Var[S_n]}}=\frac{S_n-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}. \]

Conclusion. \(Z_n\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1)\).

The quantity \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) sets the "asymptotic standard deviation" of \(\bar X_n\) as \(n\to\infty\). It is called the standard error [Standardfehler].

Why the three forms of \(Z_n\) are the same number: \(\E[S_n]=n\mu\) by linearity; \(\Var[S_n]=n\sigma^2\) because the \(X_i\) are independent, so \(\sqrt{\Var[S_n]}=\sigma\sqrt n\). Dividing numerator and denominator by \(n\) turns \(\frac{S_n-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}\) into \(\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\). Note that \(Z_n\) has mean 0 and variance 1 for every \(n\); the theorem is about its shape.

Proof idea with characteristic functions Script — each step explained

The proof uses characteristic functions and Lévy's continuity theorem. \(o(s^2)\) means "a term that, divided by \(s^2\), goes to 0 as \(s\to0\)" (Landau symbol).

(i) Standardise each summand: \(Y_i=(X_i-\mu)/\sigma\). These are iid with \(\E[Y_i]=0\) and \(\Var[Y_i]=1\). Then \(\sum_iY_i=\frac{S_n-n\mu}\sigma\), so \(Z_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i\).

(ii) \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t)=\E[e^{itZ_n}]=\E\bigl[\exp\bigl(\frac{it}{\sqrt n}\sum Y_i\bigr)\bigr]=\varphi_{Y_1}\bigl(\frac t{\sqrt n}\bigr)^n\). Reason: the exponential of a sum is a product of exponentials; independence turns the expectation of the product into the product of expectations (Remark 2.47(iv)); scaling by \(\frac1{\sqrt n}\) replaces \(t\) by \(\frac t{\sqrt n}\) (Remark 2.47(ii)); identical distribution makes all \(n\) factors equal.

(iii) Taylor-expand \(\varphi=\varphi_{Y_1}\) around \(s=0\) to second order: \(\varphi(s)=\varphi(0)+s\varphi'(0)+\frac{s^2}2\varphi''(0)+o(s^2)\). By Remark 2.47(i),(iii): \(\varphi(0)=1\), \(\varphi'(0)=i\E[Y_1]=0\), \(\varphi''(0)=i^2\E[Y_1^2]=-\Var[Y_1]=-1\). So \(\varphi_{Y_1}(s)=1-\frac{s^2}2+o(s^2)\).

(iv) Substitute \(s=t/\sqrt n\): \(\varphi_{Y_1}(t/\sqrt n)=1-\frac{t^2}{2n}+o\bigl(\frac{t^2}n\bigr)\).

(v) Therefore \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t)=\bigl(1-\frac{t^2}{2n}+o(\frac{t^2}n)\bigr)^n\).

(vi) Write the bracket as \(1+\frac{z_n}n\) with \(z_n=-\frac{t^2}2+n\cdot o(\frac{t^2}n)\to-\frac{t^2}2\). (Why the last term vanishes, for fixed \(t\ne0\): \(n\cdot o(\frac{t^2}n)=t^2\cdot\frac{o(t^2/n)}{t^2/n}\), and the fraction tends to 0 by the meaning of \(o(\cdot)\), because \(\frac{t^2}n\to0\). For \(t=0\) there is nothing to show.) The fact "\(z_n\to z\Rightarrow(1+\frac{z_n}n)^n\to e^z\)" (the complex-number version of \((1+\frac xn)^n\to e^x\), Analysis 6.3, Lemma 6.24; proof just below) gives \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t)\to e^{-t^2/2}\). This is the cf of \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) (Example 2.48).

Why the Taylor step (iii) is allowed for a complex \(\varphi\). Here \(\varphi=\varphi_{Y_1}\) is a function of the real variable \(s\) whose values are complex numbers. Split it into real and imaginary part, \(\varphi=u+iv\), where \(u=\operatorname{Re}\varphi\) and \(v=\operatorname{Im}\varphi\) are ordinary real-valued functions of \(s\). Such a function is differentiated part by part, \(\varphi'=u'+iv'\) (§2.3 primer, B1), so \(u\) and \(v\) are twice differentiable at 0 exactly when \(\varphi\) is. Apply the real Taylor formula (Analysis 10.1) to \(u\) and to \(v\) separately and add the two expansions; the parts reassemble into \(\varphi(0)+s\varphi'(0)+\frac{s^2}2\varphi''(0)\). The two remainders combine into one remainder that is again \(o(s^2)\): call them \(r_u(s)\) and \(r_v(s)\), so \(r_u(s)/s^2\to0\) and \(r_v(s)/s^2\to0\). The combined remainder is \(r_u(s)+ir_v(s)\), and the triangle inequality together with \(|i|=1\) gives \(\bigl|r_u(s)+ir_v(s)\bigr|\le|r_u(s)|+|r_v(s)|\). Divide this by \(s^2\): the right-hand side tends to 0, so the left-hand side does too. That is exactly what \(o(s^2)\) means.

Proof of the complex limit. Neither the script nor the Analysis guide proves this version: the Analysis proof of \((1+\frac xn)^n\to e^x\) takes a logarithm, and the logarithm has no single continuous extension to the complex numbers. Numbers first: for \(z_n=z=-\frac12\) and \(n=10\), \((1-0.05)^{10}\approx0.5987\) while \(e^{-1/2}\approx0.6065\) — a gap of about \(0.0078\); at \(n=100\), \((1-0.005)^{100}\approx0.6058\), a gap of about \(0.00076\). Ten times larger \(n\), roughly ten times smaller gap: the gap shrinks like \(\frac1n\), and that is what the proof shows.

Let \(z_n\to z\) be complex numbers. (For complex numbers, \(z_n\to z\) means \(|z_n-z|\to0\), where \(|u+iv|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}\) is the distance from 0 in the plane, B1.) A convergent sequence is bounded, so there is a number \(C\ge0\) with \(|z_n|\le C\) for all \(n\) (Analysis 2.1 states this for real sequences; the proof given there uses nothing but the absolute value, so it works word for word with the complex modulus \(|\cdot|\)). Now fix \(n\) and put \(w=\frac{z_n}n\) (so \(|w|\le\frac Cn\)), \(a=1+w\) and \(b=e^{w}\). All three depend on \(n\); the notation suppresses that to keep the formulas short.

  1. \(b^n\to e^z\). \(b^n=(e^{w})^n=e^{nw}\): apply the rule \(e^{u}e^{v}=e^{u+v}\), which holds for all complex \(u,v\) (Analysis 3.4, functional equation), \(n-1\) times. And \(nw=n\cdot\frac{z_n}n=z_n\), so \(b^n=e^{z_n}\). Finally \(e^{z_n}\to e^z\), because \(\exp\) is continuous on all of \(\mathbb C\) (Analysis 4.1, Lemma 4.4) and continuity means exactly that \(z_n\to z\) forces \(e^{z_n}\to e^{z}\).
  2. An algebra identity. \(a^n-b^n=(a-b)\bigl(a^{n-1}+a^{n-2}b+\dots+ab^{n-2}+b^{n-1}\bigr)\) — multiply out: all middle terms cancel in pairs (for \(n=2\): \((a-b)(a+b)=a^2-b^2\)). The bracket has \(n\) terms \(a^{n-1-k}b^{k}\), \(k=0,\dots,n-1\), and each has modulus \(|a|^{n-1-k}|b|^{k}\le M^{n-1}\) with \(M=\max(|a|,|b|)\). Bounding the sum of the \(n\) terms by the triangle inequality gives \(|a^n-b^n|\le n\,|a-b|\,M^{n-1}\).
  3. \(M^{n-1}\) stays bounded. \(|a|=|1+w|\le1+|w|\le e^{|w|}\) (triangle inequality; and \(e^{x}=1+x+\frac{x^2}2+\dots\ge1+x\) for \(x\ge0\), since all the dropped terms are \(\ge0\)). \(|b|=|e^w|\le e^{|w|}\) (from the series: \(|\sum\frac{w^k}{k!}|\le\sum\frac{|w|^k}{k!}\); this is Analysis 3.4, property \(|e^{z}|\le e^{|z|}\)). Both \(|a|\) and \(|b|\) are therefore at most \(e^{|w|}\), so \(M=\max(|a|,|b|)\le e^{|w|}\) and \(M^{n-1}\le e^{(n-1)|w|}\le e^{n|w|}\le e^{n\cdot C/n}=e^C\), using \(|w|\le\frac Cn\) in the last step.
  4. \(a\) and \(b\) are very close. \(b-a=e^w-1-w=\frac{w^2}{2!}+\frac{w^3}{3!}+\dots\), so \(|a-b|\le|w|^2\bigl(\frac1{2!}+\frac{|w|}{3!}+\frac{|w|^2}{4!}+\dots\bigr)\le|w|^2e^{|w|}\le\frac{C^2}{n^2}e^C\) (each \(\frac1{(k+2)!}\le\frac1{k!}\), and \(|w|\le\frac Cn\le C\)).
  5. Put together. Feed the bounds of steps 4 and 3 into step 2: \(|a^n-b^n|\le n\cdot\frac{C^2}{n^2}e^C\cdot e^C=\frac{C^2e^{2C}}n\to0\), since \(C\) does not depend on \(n\). By the triangle inequality, \(|a^n-e^z|\le|a^n-b^n|+|b^n-e^z|\to0+0\), i.e. \((1+\frac{z_n}n)^n\to e^z\). \(\square\)

In words: \(1+\frac{z_n}n\) and \(e^{z_n/n}\) differ only by a term of size about \(\frac1{n^2}\); raising both to the \(n\)-th power multiplies that gap by at most about \(n\), so the gap is of size \(\frac1n\) and disappears, and \((e^{z_n/n})^n=e^{z_n}\) tends to \(e^z\).

(vii) Lévy's continuity theorem (Remark 2.47(vi)): the cfs converge to the cf of \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), so \(Z_n\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,1)\).

Where the assumptions were used: finite variance for the second-order Taylor expansion (step iii); \(\sigma>0\) to divide by it (step i); independence and identical distribution for the \(n\)-th power (step ii). For coin flips \(\pm1\), step (ii) is exactly SoSe26 P4b, which asks for \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t)=\cos^n(t/\sqrt n)\); steps (iii)–(vi) then show that this tends to \(e^{-t^2/2}\) (the exam did not ask for the limit).

Widget — the central limit theorem at work My addition

20 000 simulated values of the standardised sum \(Z_n\) for the chosen distribution of a single \(X_i\), with the \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) density on top. Skewed or discrete starting points need a larger \(n\) before the bell appears; the readout compares \(\P(Z_n\le1)\) with \(\Phi(1)=0.841\).

Remark 2.65 significance of the clt Script 2.65

  • Why it matters. The clt is one of the most remarkable results in probability theory. The sum (or average) of many iid random variables is approximately normal, whatever the distribution of a single one (as long as mean and variance are finite). This is why the normal distribution appears so often in nature and in statistics.
  • Other ways to write it. The clt implies \(\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\) (multiply \(Z_n\) by the constant \(\sigma\)). It is often read as \[S_n\approx\mathcal N(n\mu,n\sigma^2)\qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad\bar X_n\approx\mathcal N\Bigl(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}n\Bigr),\] where "\(\approx\)" means "approximately distributed like". In words: for large \(n\), the sum is approximately Gaussian with mean \(n\mu\) and variance \(n\sigma^2\), and the sample mean is approximately Gaussian with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2/n\).
    Sometimes the clt is sloppily written as \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)\). This is mathematically incorrect: convergence in distribution needs a fixed target, so the right-hand side must not depend on \(n\). Also, as \(n\to\infty\), \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)\) degenerates to a point mass at \(\mu\) — and that is what the llns already say.
  • Statistics. These approximations are the basis of many inference procedures, such as confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for means (§3.3, §3.4). For example, when a plot shows the standard error as an uncertainty interval, it implicitly invokes the clt: it assumes the plotted quantity is Gaussian and shows the scaled standard deviation as a meaningful measure of that Gaussian's spread. The \(\sqrt n\) rate of convergence is a key insight — statisticians are "obsessed with \(\sqrt n\)-rates" in all kinds of tasks.
  • Beyond iid. Theorem 2.64 assumes iid variables, but the clt holds much more generally. The Lindeberg–Feller clt covers sums of independent but not identically distributed variables, provided no single variable contributes too much to the total variance (formalised by the Lindeberg condition). There are also versions for certain dependent variables (e.g. martingales, mixing sequences — special kinds of dependent sequences that this course does not cover). This broad applicability underlines how fundamental the normal distribution is.
  • A caution. The clt is often invoked as a blanket justification whenever one would like something to be Gaussian (because that is convenient for computations). "There are many unmeasured additive influences on our outcome whose sum, mumble mumble, clt, mumble… so Gaussian noise is reasonable."
  • Visualisations. The script points to a visualisation on Moodle and several online ones for building intuition. On this page, use the widget above.

Recipe: a normal approximation with the clt My addition

  1. Identify \(S_n=\sum X_i\) (or \(\bar X_n\)) with iid summands. Compute \(\mu=\E[X_i]\) and \(\sigma^2=\Var[X_i]\).
  2. Standardise the event (subtract \(n\mu\), divide by \(\sigma\sqrt n\) on both sides): \(\P(S_n\le s)=\P\bigl(Z_n\le\frac{s-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}\bigr)\approx\Phi\bigl(\frac{s-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}\bigr)\).
  3. For "\(>\)" use \(1-\Phi(\cdot)\); for two-sided events \(\P(|Z_n|\ge a)\approx2\Phi(-a)\).
  4. Write "approximately, by the clt". It is an approximation, not a bound (contrast Chebyshev, §2.2).
  5. Optional: for integer-valued \(S_n\), a continuity correction (replace \(s\) by \(s+\frac12\)) improves accuracy. Example: 100 fair coins, \(\P(S\ge60)=\P(S>59.5)\approx1-\Phi\bigl(\frac{59.5-50}5\bigr)=1-\Phi(1.9)=0.0287\), versus the exact \(0.0284\); without the correction \(1-\Phi(2)=0.0228\).

Exercise-sheet tasks

Sheet 8, Exercise 4 (optional, coding) — Monte Carlo integration Sheet 8 · Ex 4

Idea. By the lln, the mean of a random variable \(Y\) can be estimated by averaging iid samples: \(\E[Y]\approx\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i\). Apply this to \(Y=f(X)\) with \(X\) uniform on a bounded region \(U\subsetneq\R^d\). The mean of \(f(X)\) is \(\frac1{\lambda^d(U)}\int_Uf(x)\,\mathrm dx\), where \(\lambda^d(U)\) is the area/volume of \(U\). So for iid \(X_1,\dots,X_n\sim\Unif(U)\) with observed values \(x_1,\dots,x_n\): \(\hat I_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(x_i)\approx\frac1{\lambda^d(U)}\int_Uf(x)\,\mathrm dx\).

Task. Approximate the integral of \(f(x)=10-x_1^2-x_2^2\) over the unit disc \(D_2=\{x\in\R^2\mid x_1^2+x_2^2<1\}\): (i) draw \(n\) samples uniformly and independently inside \(D_2\) (not in \((-1,1)^2\)); (ii) use them to estimate the area of \(D_2\), which is \(\pi\); (iii) approximate \(\int_{D_2}f\) and compare with the true value.

Solution

(i) Rejection sampling: draw \((u_1,u_2)\) uniformly in the square \([-1,1]^2\). Keep the point if \(u_1^2+u_2^2<1\), otherwise discard it. The kept points are uniform on \(D_2\).

(ii) Apply the lln to the indicator "point was kept". Its mean is \(\frac{\text{area}(D_2)}{\text{area}([-1,1]^2)}=\frac\pi4\). So the fraction of kept points estimates \(\frac\pi4\), and \(\hat\pi=4\times\)(fraction kept).

(iii) With \(m\) kept points \(x_i\): \(\widehat I=\hat\pi\cdot\frac1m\sum_{\text{kept}}f(x_i)\) (area times average value). True value, using polar coordinates \(x=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\), where the area element is \(r\,\mathrm dr\,\mathrm d\theta\) (B5) and \(x_1^2+x_2^2=r^2\):

\[ \int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^1(10-r^2)\,r\,\mathrm dr\,\mathrm d\theta=2\pi\int_0^1(10r-r^3)\,\mathrm dr=2\pi\Bigl[5r^2-\frac{r^4}4\Bigr]_0^1=2\pi\cdot\frac{19}4=\frac{19\pi}2\approx29.85 . \]

Note on the official solution: it writes the antiderivative as \(5r^2-\frac{r^3}3\) and the result as \(2\pi\cdot\frac{14}3\approx29.34\) (and \(2\pi\cdot\frac{14}3\) is in fact \(\approx29.32\)). That drops the Jacobian factor \(r\) from the \(r^2\) term (the integrand is \(10r-r^3\), not \(10r-r^2\)). The correct value is \(\frac{19\pi}2\approx29.85\); the widget below confirms it numerically. By the clt, the Monte Carlo error shrinks like \(1/\sqrt n\).

Widget — Sheet 8 Ex 4 in the browser My addition

Points uniform in the square; blue ones fell into the disc. The estimates of \(\pi\) and of \(\int_D(10-x_1^2-x_2^2)=\frac{19\pi}2\approx29.845\) improve as \(n\) grows.

Sheet 9, Exercise 1 — heavy planes Sheet 9 · Ex 1

A plane carries at most 100 passengers and has fuel for at most 8 t. For a fully booked flight, \(X_i\) is the weight of passenger \(i\) in kg. (i) Give one convincing argument for or against modelling the \(X_i\) as independent. From now on assume they are iid with \(\E[X_i]=75\) and \(\sigma[X_i]=20\). (ii) Can you compute the exact probability that 8 t is exceeded? (iii) Approximate it with the clt. (iv) The profit is 3 € per passenger; going over capacity costs 3000 € per flight. Is the plane profitable on average (always fully booked)?

Solution

(i) For independence: passengers are diverse and fly for all kinds of reasons; there is no reason one person's weight should depend on another's. Even if a route connects countries whose average weight is above or below the global mean, the individual weights can still be iid from that route's weight distribution. Against: families and groups book together, and people who live together share eating and activity habits, so their weights are dependent. A plane carrying the Japan Sumo Association or the Austrian State Ballet makes a big difference.

(ii) No. Let \(S_{100}=\sum_{j=1}^{100}X_j\) be the total weight. To compute \(\P(S_{100}>8000)\) exactly we need the full distribution of the \(X_i\). Mean and standard deviation alone do not determine it: a heavily skewed weight distribution with the same mean and variance gives a different probability.

(iii) \(\E[S_{100}]=100\cdot75=7500\) (linearity). \(\Var[S_{100}]=100\cdot20^2=40\,000\) (independence), so \(\sigma[S_{100}]=200\). By the clt, standardise: \(\P(S_{100}>8000)=\P\bigl(\frac{S_{100}-7500}{200}>\frac{8000-7500}{200}\bigr)\approx1-\Phi(2.5)\approx0.0062\).

(iv) Revenue per full flight: \(100\cdot3=300\) €. Expected extra cost: \(3000\cdot\P(\text{overload})\approx3000\cdot0.0062\approx18.6\) €. Expected profit per flight (linearity of expectation) \(\approx300-18.6=281.4\) € \(>0\): profitable. The official solution is correct.

For comparison: Chebyshev (§2.2) only guarantees \(\P(S_{100}\ge8000)\le\P(|S_{100}-7500|\ge500)\le\frac{40\,000}{500^2}=0.16\). That would allow an expected cost of up to 480 €, and the flight might be unprofitable. The clt's extra assumption (approximate normality) is what makes the flight look safe.

Sheet 9, Exercise 2 (ii), (iv) — insurance claims Sheet 9 · Ex 2

An insurer has \(n=10^4\) clients with iid yearly claims \(X_i\): mean \(\mu=500\), variance \(\sigma^2=800^2\). The premium per client is \(Z=550\). (Parts (i) and (iii) — the premium 550 and the Chebyshev bound 0.0256 — are on §2.2.) (ii) What does the wlln say about the average claim \(\bar X_n=S_n/n\) as \(n\) becomes very large? (iv) Approximate \(\P(S_n>nZ)\) with the clt, compare with Chebyshev, and say which you would trust.

Solution

(ii) The wlln gives \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow\P500\) as \(n\to\infty\). With many clients, the average claim per client is very likely close to 500.

(iv) \(\E[S_n]=n\mu=5\cdot10^6\), \(\Var[S_n]=n\sigma^2=6.4\cdot10^9\), \(\sigma[S_n]=\sqrt n\,\sigma=100\cdot800=8\cdot10^4\). The total premium is \(nZ=5.5\cdot10^6\). Standardise: \(\P(S_n>5.5\cdot10^6)\approx1-\Phi\bigl(\frac{5.5\cdot10^6-5\cdot10^6}{8\cdot10^4}\bigr)=1-\Phi(6.25)\approx2\cdot10^{-10}\). The official solution puts this in perspective: about one loss year in the age of the universe.

Which to trust? Chebyshev's 2.56 % is a guaranteed upper bound. It holds for any claim distribution with this mean and variance. The clt value is an approximation: \(S_n\) is only normal in the limit \(n\to\infty\). For finite \(n\) its quality depends on the claim distribution — especially in the far tail (6 standard deviations!). For heavily skewed claims it can badly underestimate the risk. If the normal approximation is good, the clt uses much more information and is much more precise. The official solution makes the same points ("you decide!") and is correct.

Sheet 9, Exercise 3 — rules for convergence in probability Sheet 9 · Ex 3

Show: (i) \(X_n\xrightarrow\P X\) and \(Y_n\xrightarrow\P Y\) ⟹ \(X_n+Y_n\xrightarrow\P X+Y\). (ii) \(\E|X_n-X|\to0\) ⟹ \(X_n\xrightarrow\P X\). (iii) \(X_n\xrightarrow\P X\) and \(X_n\xrightarrow\P Y\) ⟹ \(\P(X=Y)=1\). (iv) \(\E|X_n-X|\to0\) and \(\E|X_n-Y|\to0\) ⟹ \(\P(X=Y)=1\).

Solution

(i) Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Write \((X_n+Y_n)-(X+Y)=(X_n-X)+(Y_n-Y)\). By primer box 1, \(\{|(X_n+Y_n)-(X+Y)|\ge\varepsilon\}\subseteq\{|X_n-X|\ge\frac\varepsilon2\}\cup\{|Y_n-Y|\ge\frac\varepsilon2\}\). The union bound gives \(\P(|(X_n+Y_n)-(X+Y)|\ge\varepsilon)\le\P(|X_n-X|\ge\frac\varepsilon2)+\P(|Y_n-Y|\ge\frac\varepsilon2)\). Both terms go to 0 by assumption (use Definition 2.56(i) with \(\frac\varepsilon2\)). Probabilities are \(\ge0\), so the limit is 0.

(ii) Markov's inequality (Theorem 2.38) for the non-negative variable \(|X_n-X|\): \(\P(|X_n-X|\ge\varepsilon)\le\frac{\E|X_n-X|}\varepsilon\to0\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). (The mode "\(\E|X_n-X|\to0\)" is called convergence "in \(L^1\)" or "in mean".)

(iii) For every \(n\), the triangle inequality gives \(|X-Y|\le|X-X_n|+|X_n-Y|\). So, as in (i), \(\P(|X-Y|\ge\varepsilon)\le\P(|X_n-X|\ge\frac\varepsilon2)+\P(|X_n-Y|\ge\frac\varepsilon2)\). The left side does not depend on \(n\); the right side tends to 0. Hence \(\P(|X-Y|\ge\varepsilon)=0\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\). Finally, \(X\ne Y\) means \(|X-Y|\ge\frac1k\) for some \(k\in\N\) (if the number \(d=|X-Y|\) is positive, the Archimedean property supplies a \(k\in\N\) with \(\frac1k<d\), and then \(|X-Y|=d\ge\frac1k\) — Analysis 1.2), so \(\{X\ne Y\}=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\{|X-Y|\ge\frac1k\}\). This is a countable union of null sets, so \(\P(X\ne Y)\le\sum_k0=0\) (σ-subadditivity), i.e. \(\P(X=Y)=1\).

(iv) By (ii), both assumptions give convergence in probability: \(X_n\xrightarrow\P X\) and \(X_n\xrightarrow\P Y\). Then (iii) applies. The official solution is correct.

(iii) says limits in probability are unique almost surely. That is the best one can hope for: changing \(X\) on a null set changes no probability.

Sheet 9, Exercise 4 — convergence of normal random variables Sheet 9 · Ex 4

Let \(X_n\sim\mathcal N(\mu_n,\sigma_n^2)\) for each \(n\). (i) If \(\mu_n\to\mu\in\R\) and \(\sigma_n^2\to\sigma^2>0\), then \(X_n\xrightarrow dX\) with \(X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\). (ii) If \(\mu_n\to\mu\) and \(\sigma_n^2\to0\), then \(X_n\xrightarrow\P\mu\). (Hint: the cf of \(\mathcal N(m,s^2)\) is \(\varphi(t)=\exp(imt-\frac12s^2t^2)\).)

Solution

(i) \(\varphi_{X_n}(t)=e^{i\mu_nt-\sigma_n^2t^2/2}\). Fix \(t\). The exponent is the complex number \(i\mu_nt-\frac12\sigma_n^2t^2\); since \(\mu_n\to\mu\) and \(\sigma_n^2\to\sigma^2\), its imaginary part \(\mu_nt\) and its real part \(-\frac12\sigma_n^2t^2\) converge, so the exponent converges to \(i\mu t-\frac12\sigma^2t^2\). The exponential function is defined for complex arguments by its series (Analysis 3.4) and is continuous on all of \(\mathbb C\) (Analysis 4.1, Lemma 4.4) — continuity of a function \(f\) at a point means precisely that \(x_n\to x\) implies \(f(x_n)\to f(x)\). Hence \(\varphi_{X_n}(t)\to e^{i\mu t-\sigma^2t^2/2}\). This is the cf of \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), and it is continuous at \(t=0\) (the extra condition in Lévy's continuity theorem, Remark 2.47(vi)). So Lévy's theorem gives \(X_n\xrightarrow dX\).

(ii) Route 1 (Chebyshev). \(\P(|X_n-\mu_n|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma_n^2/\varepsilon^2\to0\), so \(X_n-\mu_n\xrightarrow\P0\). The numbers \(\mu_n-\mu\to0\); viewed as constant random variables they also converge in probability to 0. Since \(X_n-\mu=(X_n-\mu_n)+(\mu_n-\mu)\), Sheet 9 Ex 3(i) gives \(X_n-\mu\xrightarrow\P0\), i.e. \(X_n\xrightarrow\P\mu\).

Route 2 (cfs). As in (i), \(\varphi_{X_n}(t)\to e^{i\mu t}\), the cf of the constant \(\mu\) (continuous at 0). So \(X_n\xrightarrow d\mu\). Convergence in distribution to a constant implies convergence in probability (Remark 2.57).

The official solution is correct. One small point in its alternative route: it writes "from part (i), \(X_n\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(\mu,0)\)", but part (i) assumed \(\sigma^2>0\). Route 2 above avoids this by redoing the cf limit directly with \(\sigma^2=0\).

Old-exam tasks

WiSe 25/26, Problem 2 — definitions WiSe25 · P2a, P2b · 6 credits

(a) State the strong law of large numbers with all required assumptions. Answer: Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be a sequence of iid real random variables with finite mean \(\E[X_i]=\mu<\infty\). Let \(\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) be the sample mean. Then \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\mu\).

(b) Give the full definition (including setup/assumptions) of the type of convergence in the slln. Answer: Let \((X_n)_{n\in\N}\) be a sequence of real random variables and \(X\) another real random variable, all defined on the same probability space \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\). Then \(X_n\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}X\) if \(\P(\{\omega\in\Omega\mid\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n(\omega)=X(\omega)\})=1\).

Both official answers are correct and match Theorem 2.62 and Definition 2.56(ii) word for word. The "setup" credit goes to "on the same probability space".

SoSe 2025, Problem 2 — definitions SoSe25 · P2a, P2b · 6 credits

(a) State the clt with all required assumptions. Answer: Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be iid real random variables with finite mean \(\E[X_i]=\mu\) and finite, non-zero variance \(\Var[X_i]=\sigma^2\in\R_{>0}\). Then \(Z_n=\frac{S_n-\E[S_n]}{\sqrt{\Var[S_n]}}=\frac{S_n-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,1)\); equivalently \(\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\).

(b) Give the full general definition of the type of convergence in the clt. Answer: Definition 2.56(iii), including "for every \(x\in\R\) at which \(F_X\) is continuous". Pointwise convergence of the cfs was also accepted.

The official solution also accepted "\(S_n\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(n\mu,n\sigma^2)\)" and "\(\bar X_n\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)\)", while noting that they are mathematically incorrect (Remark 2.65). Do not rely on that leniency. One small inconsistency: the official (b) requires \(X_n\) and \(X\) on the same probability space. Convergence in distribution does not need that (Remark 2.60) — harmless, but not "general".

WiSe 25/26, Problem 1d — the lln needs independence WiSe25 · P1d · 3 credits

Statement. For \(X_1,X_2,\dots\sim\Poi(2)\), the sample mean satisfies \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow\P2\). True or false?

Official answer: False — the statement says nothing about independence. Counterexample: \(X_i:=X_1\) for all \(i\). Then \(\bar X_n=\frac1n\cdot nX_1=X_1\) for every \(n\). For any \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\P(|X_1-2|\ge\varepsilon)>0\), since a Poisson variable takes every value \(k\in\N_0\) with positive probability (for small \(\varepsilon\), e.g. \(\P(|X_1-2|\ge\varepsilon)\ge\P(X_1=0)=e^{-2}\)). This probability does not depend on \(n\), so it does not tend to 0. Correct.

The official statement is printed as "\(\lim_{n\to\infty}\bar X_n\xrightarrow\P2\)" — the "lim" is redundant notation; read it as \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow\P2\). With "iid" (or even "pairwise uncorrelated") added, the statement is true by the wlln. Reading assumptions carefully is the whole point of such items.

WiSe 25/26, Problem 4c, 4d — clt versus Chebyshev for an estimator WiSe25 · P4c, P4d · 3 + 1 credits

Setting (part b is on §2.2). Rainfall amounts \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are iid with \(\E[X_i]=2\theta\) and \(\Var[X_i]=2\theta^2\). The estimator is \(\hat\theta=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\). Then \(\E[\hat\theta]=\frac1{2n}\cdot n\cdot2\theta=\theta\) and \(\Var[\hat\theta]=\frac1{(2n)^2}\cdot n\cdot2\theta^2=\frac{\theta^2}{2n}\).

(c) Use the clt to approximate the distribution of \(\hat\theta\) by a Gaussian, and approximate \(\P(|\hat\theta-\theta|\ge\varepsilon)\) in terms of \(\Phi\). Answer: \(\hat\theta\) is \(\frac12\bar X_n\), so its standardisation equals \(Z_n\) for the \(X_i\): \(\frac{\hat\theta-\theta}{\sqrt{\Var[\hat\theta]}}=\frac{\hat\theta-\theta}{\theta/\sqrt{2n}}\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,1)\). Hence \(\hat\theta\approx\mathcal N(\theta,\frac{\theta^2}{2n})\) and

\[\P(|\hat\theta-\theta|\ge\varepsilon)=\P\Bigl(\Bigl|\frac{\hat\theta-\theta}{\theta/\sqrt{2n}}\Bigr|\ge\frac{\varepsilon\sqrt{2n}}\theta\Bigr)\approx2\Phi\Bigl(-\frac{\sqrt{2n}\,\varepsilon}\theta\Bigr).\]

(d) Compare (b) and (c). Answer: Chebyshev gives a guaranteed bound \(\frac{\theta^2}{2n\varepsilon^2}\) that uses only the variance and decays like \(\frac1n\). The clt gives an approximation that decays exponentially fast in \(n\) (roughly like \(e^{-n\varepsilon^2/\theta^2}\), because \(\Phi(-a)\) behaves like \(e^{-a^2/2}\)). Guaranteed but loose versus sharp but approximate.

The official (d) calls the clt result "stricter". Careful wording: it is not a bound at all, so it cannot be "stricter" in the sense of a guarantee — it is sharper as an estimate. Otherwise correct.

SoSe 2026, Problem 1d — in probability implies in distribution SoSe26 · P1d · 1 credit

Statement. Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be random variables on a common probability space and \(c\in\R\). If \(X_n\xrightarrow\P c\), then \(X_n\xrightarrow dc\). Official: True (Remark 2.57: in probability ⟹ in distribution). Correct. For a constant limit the converse also holds.

SoSe 2026, Problem 2a — convergence does not carry expectations along SoSe26 · P2a · 3 credits

Statement. \(X_n\xrightarrow dX\) on a common probability space, and all expectations \(\E[X_n]\), \(\E[X]\) exist and are finite ⟹ \(\lim_n\E[X_n]=\E[X]\)?

Official answer: False. Let \(U\sim\Unif(0,1)\), \(X_n:=n\one_{\{U\le1/n\}}\) and \(X:=0\). Then \(\P(X_n=n)=\frac1n\) and \(\P(X_n=0)=1-\frac1n\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(n\ge\varepsilon\), \(\P(|X_n|\ge\varepsilon)=\frac1n\to0\). So \(X_n\xrightarrow\P0\), and therefore \(X_n\xrightarrow d0\) (Remark 2.57). But \(\E[X_n]=n\cdot\frac1n+0=1\) for every \(n\), while \(\E[X]=0\). Correct.

The probability \(\frac1n\) sits on the ever larger value \(n\): rare but huge values keep the mean at 1. In fact \(X_n(\omega)\to0\) for every \(\omega\) with \(U(\omega)>0\), so even almost sure convergence does not help. This is the "escaping mass" phenomenon of B4, where the dominated convergence theorem says which extra assumption fixes it.

SoSe 2026, Problem 4d (clt part) — approximating \(\P(|Z_n|\ge a)\) SoSe26 · P4d

Setting. \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) iid with \(\P(X_j=1)=\P(X_j=-1)=\frac12\), and \(Z_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{j=1}^nX_j\). For \(a>0\), use the clt to approximate \(\P(|Z_n|\ge a)\). (The Markov bound \(1/a^2\) is on §2.2.)

Answer. Each \(X_j\) has \(\mu=\frac12\cdot1+\frac12\cdot(-1)=0\) and \(\sigma^2=\E[X_j^2]-0^2=1\). So \(Z_n=\frac{S_n-n\cdot0}{1\cdot\sqrt n}\) is exactly the standardised sum of Theorem 2.64, and \(Z_n\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,1)\). Hence, for large \(n\), \(\P(|Z_n|\ge a)\approx2(1-\Phi(a))=2\Phi(-a)\). The official solution is correct.

For \(a=2\): the clt gives \(2(1-0.977)\approx0.046\), while the Markov bound gives only \(\frac14=0.25\).

Summary sheet

Definitions (learn them word for word — they are examined)

Setup: \((X_n)_{n\in\N}\) and \(X\) real random variables on the same probability space \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\).

in probability
\(\forall\varepsilon>0:\ \P(|X_n-X|\ge\varepsilon)\to0\)
almost surely
\(\P(\{\omega:X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)\})=1\)
in distribution
\(F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x)\) at every continuity point \(x\) of \(F_X\) (⟺ cfs converge)
relations
a.s. ⟹ P ⟹ d; d to a constant ⟹ P; P ⟹ a.s. along a subsequence

Theorems

wlln
identically distributed, finite mean (and variance), pairwise uncorrelated: \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow\P\mu\)
slln
iid, finite mean: \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\mu\)
clt
iid, finite mean, finite variance \(>0\): \(\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,1)\)
approximation
\(\P(S_n\le s)\approx\Phi\bigl(\frac{s-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}\bigr)\); standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt n\)

Counterexamples to know

  • P but not a.s.: the travelling bump (Example 2.58).
  • d but not P: \(X_n=U\), \(Y=1-U\) (Example 2.59).
  • Convergence without convergence of means: \(n\one_{\{U\le1/n\}}\) (SoSe26 P2a).
  • lln fails without independence: \(X_i=X_1\) (WiSe25 P1d); lln fails without a mean: Cauchy.

Traps

  • "\(\bar X_n\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)\)" is wrong notation: the limit cannot depend on \(n\).
  • Forgetting "iid", "finite variance", "non-zero variance" or "same probability space" costs points.
  • The clt gives approximations, Chebyshev gives bounds.

Exam focus

WiSe25 and SoSe25: one definition (a.s. or in distribution, 3 credits) and one theorem statement (slln or clt, 3 credits). True/false items on the relations or on missing assumptions (WiSe25 P1d, SoSe26 P1d, P2a), and a "Chebyshev versus clt" computation (WiSe25 P4, SoSe26 P4, Sheet 9 Ex 1–2).
