Statistical models and basic concepts

Statistische Modelle und Grundbegriffe

What this page covers Script Ch. 3 intro and §3.1, pp. 84–92

This is the entry page of Part 3, statistical inference [statistische Inferenz]. It covers the chapter introduction (Overview 3.1, Example 3.2, Overview 3.3) and then all of §3.1, from Definition 3.4 to Remark 3.16, including the unnumbered remark on "inference" in statistics versus machine learning. The script's section goal: "Introduce the fundamental concepts of statistical inference, including statistical models, statistics, parameters of interest, and parameter identifiability."

The page has four parts: (1) what statistics wants and how it differs from probability; (2) the statistical model — the list of distributions we consider possible; (3) statistics (numbers computed from data), parameters of interest and identifiability; (4) the likelihood function, the bridge from data back to parameters.

Worked in place: the identifiability part of SoSe26 P5a (randomized response), solved again with Definition 3.11 (the conditional-probability side is on §1.4). From the sheets: the likelihood of Sheet 10 Ex 2(i) (the mle parts (ii)–(iii) are on §3.2) and Sheet 10 Ex 5(i)–(ii) (toaster box: distribution and statistical model; the estimator part (iii) is on §3.2). The true/false and definition problems of all three old exams were checked: none asks about §3.1 alone. SoSe25 P1b and SoSe26 P1e are on §3.2 and SoSe25 P1c on §3.3.

The big picture

Probability (Parts 1 and 2 of this course) works in one direction. Someone hands you the model — "this coin shows heads with probability \(p=0.5\)" — and you compute how likely various data are. Statistics works in the opposite direction. Someone hands you data — "I tossed this coin 10 times and got 7 heads" — and you ask which model produced it.

Numbers (my example). Write \(K\) for the number of heads in 10 independent tosses of a coin with heads probability \(p\). Then \(K\sim\Bin(10,p)\) (binomial distribution, §1.2), which means \[\P(K=k)=\binom{10}{k}p^k(1-p)^{10-k},\qquad k=0,1,\dots,10 .\] Here \(\binom{10}{k}\) ("10 choose \(k\)") counts the orders in which \(k\) heads can appear among 10 tosses (B3); \(\binom{10}{7}=120\).

  • Probability direction (\(p\) fixed, data vary). Take \(p=0.5\). Then \(\P(K=7)=120\cdot0.5^{10}=\frac{120}{1024}\approx0.117\). Doing this for every \(k=0,\dots,10\) gives a table of 11 probabilities that add up to 1: the distribution of the data.
  • Statistics direction (data fixed, \(p\) varies). We saw \(k=7\). Keep 7 fixed and try different \(p\):
    \(p\)0.30.50.60.70.80.9
    \(120\,p^7(1-p)^3\)0.0090.1170.2150.2670.2010.057
    The value \(p=0.7\) makes the observed data most probable. A fair coin (\(p=0.5\)) is less good at explaining "7 of 10", but far from impossible. \(p=0.3\) explains the data badly. This function of \(p\) is the likelihood (Definition 3.13 below).

Same formula, read in two directions. Everything in Part 3 is about the second reading: which parameter values fit the data (estimation, §3.2), is a specific value like \(p=0.5\) believable (testing, §3.3), and what range of values is plausible (interval estimation, §3.4). Before any of that we need a precise language: what the "possible models" are (statistical model), what we compute from data (statistic), what we want to learn (parameter of interest), whether the data can reveal it at all (identifiability), and how well a parameter fits the data (likelihood).

In words: probability goes from a known model to probabilities of data; statistics goes from observed data back to an unknown model. This page sets up the vocabulary for the way back.

Primer: what you need from earlier My addition

Cross-references

The natural logarithm and its rules: Analysis 5.2. Maxima of a function: Analysis 7.1. Injective maps and inverses: Analysis 5.1 and B2. Indexed families \((A_i)_{i\in I}\): B2. σ-algebras and measurable spaces: §1.1, §1.1. Measurable functions: B4. Named distributions: §1.2 (discrete) and §1.3 (continuous). Product spaces: §1.4. Independence: §1.4. Sample mean and the law of large numbers: §2.4.

0. Words and symbols used on this page

  • Measurable space \((\Omega,\Aa)\): \(\Omega\) is the set of possible outcomes; \(\Aa\) is a σ-algebra on \(\Omega\) — the collection of subsets ("events") we are allowed to give probabilities to (§1.1). \(\pow(\Omega)\) is the power set, the collection of all subsets; it is used when \(\Omega\) is finite or countable. \(\mathcal B\) is the Borel σ-algebra on \(\R\) (generated by the intervals), used when \(\Omega=\R\); \(\mathcal B^n\) is its version on \(\R^n\). \(\mathcal B|_\Omega\) means "the Borel sets that lie inside \(\Omega\)".
  • Probability distribution (probability measure) \(\P\) on \((\Omega,\Aa)\): a rule that gives each event \(A\in\Aa\) a number \(\P(A)\in[0,1]\), with \(\P(\Omega)=1\) and additivity over disjoint events (§1.1).
  • pmf and pdf. For a discrete distribution the pmf (probability mass function) is \(p(x)=\P(X=x)\). For a continuous one the pdf (density [Dichte]) \(p(x)\) satisfies \(\P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^bp(x)\,\mathrm dx\) (§1.3).
  • Named distributions: \(\Ber(p)\) — 1 with probability \(p\), else 0; its pmf can be written \(p^x(1-p)^{1-x}\) for \(x\in\{0,1\}\) (put in \(x=1\) and \(x=0\) to check). \(\Bin(m,p)\) — number of 1s in \(m\) independent \(\Ber(p)\) trials. \(\Poi(\lambda)\) — counts with mean \(\lambda\). \(\Unif(a,b)\) — uniform on an interval. \(\Exp(\lambda)\) — waiting times, pdf \(\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x\ge0\). \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) — normal with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\).
  • Indexed family \((P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}\): one object \(P_\theta\) for each index \(\theta\) in an index set \(\Theta\) (B2). \(\theta\) is the Greek letter theta, \(\Theta\) its capital.
  • \(\R_{>0}\) are the positive reals, \(\R_{\ge0}\) the non-negative reals, \(\N=\{0,1,2,\dots\}\) (the script counts 0 as natural, Convention 1.1), \(\N_{>0}=\{1,2,\dots\}\). \(\R^k\) is the set of lists of \(k\) real numbers.
  • iid: independent and identically distributed. RVRV: real-valued random variable (script abbreviation).
  • \(\prod_{i=1}^na_i=a_1\cdot a_2\cdots a_n\) (product), \(\sum_{i=1}^na_i=a_1+\dots+a_n\) (sum).
  • Injective [injektiv]: a map \(f\) is injective if different inputs always give different outputs: \(a\ne b\Rightarrow f(a)\ne f(b)\). Equivalently \(f(a)=f(b)\Rightarrow a=b\).

1. Logarithm rules used on this page

\(\ln\) is the natural logarithm, defined for positive numbers (Analysis 5.2).

  • \(\ln(ab)=\ln a+\ln b\), so \(\ln\prod_ia_i=\sum_i\ln a_i\): products become sums.
  • \(\ln(a^r)=r\ln a\), and \(\ln(e^y)=y\).
  • \(\ln\) is strictly increasing: \(a<b\Rightarrow\ln a<\ln b\). So \(\ln\) never changes which of two positive numbers is bigger, and a function \(L>0\) and \(\ln L\) have their maxima at the same place.

Example: \(\ln(0.7^7\cdot0.3^3)=7\ln0.7+3\ln0.3\approx7\cdot(-0.357)+3\cdot(-1.204)=-6.109\).

From probability to statistics

Overview 3.1 from probability to statistics Script 3.1

In the previous chapters we assumed that we know the underlying probability distribution (for example \(X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with known \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\)). We then calculated probabilities of events or properties of random variables. This is often called deductive inference [deduktive Inferenz]: moving from general principles (the model) to specific outcomes (probabilities of data).

Statistical inference, in contrast, typically involves inductive inference [induktive Inferenz]: we observe data (samples) and want to make statements or draw conclusions about the underlying — often unknown — probability distribution, or its parameters, that generated the data. We aim to learn from data.

The script's figure, described in words: on the left, a box "general principles, (assumed) ground truth, population"; on the right, a box "specific instances, concrete manifestations, samples / data". An arrow from left to right is labelled "deductive inference (probability)"; an arrow from right to left is labelled "inductive inference (statistics)". Redrawn:

Why the words: deduction draws conclusions that follow with certainty from the premises (if \(p=0.5\), then \(\P(K=7)=0.117\), no doubt about it). Induction generalises from particular cases to a general rule, and can never be certain (7 heads of 10 does not prove anything about \(p\)). This is why statistical answers come with "confidence" and "significance" instead of certainty (Overview 3.3(iv)).

Example 3.2 what we want from statistical inference Script 3.2

The script lists ten questions that statistical inference should help to answer. My short comments (marked mine) say which later page takes up the question, and sometimes do a first rough calculation with tools from Part 2.

  1. Coin flips. We observe \(n\) coin flips \(x_1,\dots,x_n\in\{0,1\}\) (1 = heads). Questions: (a) what is the probability \(p\) of heads for this coin? (b) can we say — with confidence? — whether the coin is fair (\(p=0.5\))? That is, can we test the hypothesis that the coin is fair against the alternative that it is biased? (c) what is a plausible range of values for \(p\), and how confident are we in that range?
    mine These are exactly the three tasks of Part 3: (a) point estimation (§3.2), (b) hypothesis testing (§3.3), (c) interval estimation (§3.4).
  2. Hard drives. A producer of NVMe hard drives signs a contract with Apple promising that at most 1 in 10 000 drives fails within the first year. Apple orders 12 million drives, tracks 112 345 MacBooks sold in the first months, and receives 15 complaints about failed drives within one year. Can Apple sue?
    mine If the promise holds exactly (failure probability \(10^{-4}\)), the expected number of failures among 112 345 drives is \(112\,345\cdot10^{-4}\approx11.2\). With a Poisson approximation (many trials, tiny success probability — Poisson limit theorem, §1.2), seeing 15 or more failures has probability about 0.16 — not rare at all. So these numbers alone are weak evidence. Making this reasoning precise is a test (§3.3).
  3. Bottling machine. A machine for 0.33 l bottles is certified to be precise up to ±2 ml. After selling 345 234 bottles of beer you notice you brewed at least 500 l more than you apparently sold. Is the machine a major suspect? Would measuring the exact amount in the next 100 bottles help?
    mine 500 l = 500 000 ml spread over 345 234 bottles is about 1.45 ml per bottle. That is inside ±2 ml for each single bottle, but a systematic overfill of 1.45 ml on average would be a different claim from "random errors of at most 2 ml around 330 ml". Example 3.5(vii) builds models for this.
  4. Bertrand's paradox (§1.2). Someone drops Mikado sticks "randomly" on a circle drawn on a table 1000 times to get random chords; 281 land in the favourable region and 719 do not. Does this tell us whether \(P_1=\frac13\), \(P_2=\frac12\) or \(P_3=\frac14\) is "correct"?
    mine The observed fraction is 0.281. If the truth were \(\frac14\), the fraction of 1000 trials would have standard deviation \(\sqrt{0.25\cdot0.75/1000}\approx0.014\) (one trial is \(\Ber(0.25)\) with variance \(0.25\cdot0.75\); averaging 1000 independent trials divides the variance by 1000, and the standard deviation is the square root of the variance — central limit theorem [zentraler Grenzwertsatz], "clt", §2.4: the fraction of successes in many independent trials is approximately normal with this spread), so 0.281 is about 2.3 standard deviations away; from \(\frac13\) it is about 3.5 away, and from \(\frac12\) about 14. The data fit none of the three perfectly — perhaps the physical stick dropping is a fourth way of choosing a chord. The data speak about this experiment, not about which mathematical model is "correct".
  5. Clinical study. 46 participants get a new drug, 234 in the control group get the conventional treatment. 42 of 46 survive in the treatment group, 201 of 234 in the control group. Should the new drug replace the old one?
    mine Survival rates \(\frac{42}{46}\approx0.913\) versus \(\frac{201}{234}\approx0.859\). Whether a difference of about 5 percentage points with only 46 treated patients could be chance is a testing question (§3.3).
  6. Election survey. On a Thursday morning at Marienplatz 239 people are interviewed; the CSU gets an approval rate of 79 %. Can we conclude they will get at least 2/3 of the votes in the Bavarian state election [Landtagswahl] the following Sunday?
    mine The main problem is not the sample size but the sample: people at Marienplatz on a Thursday morning are not a random sample of Bavarian voters, and "approval" is not "vote". No formula can repair a sample that does not come from the population the model describes (a mis-specified model, Definition 3.4).
  7. Algorithms. You measure CPU execution times of two algorithms on benchmark tasks on your laptop. Can we decide whether one is "significantly" faster, or estimate the average difference in execution time?
    mine Estimating the difference is §3.2/§3.4; "significantly" is §3.3.
  8. Higgs boson. The discovery paper states: "Clear evidence for the production of a neutral boson with a measured mass of 126.0 ± 0.4(stat) ± 0.4(sys) GeV is presented. This observation, which has a significance of 5.9 standard deviations, corresponding to a background fluctuation probability of \(1.7\times10^{-9}\), is compatible with the production and decay of the Standard Model Higgs boson." Have we discovered the Higgs boson or not?
    mine "5.9 standard deviations" and "background fluctuation probability" are the language of tests and p-values (a p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as the data actually seen, computed under the assumption that the claim being tested is true; §3.3); "±0.4" is the language of interval estimates (§3.4).
  9. Gravitational waves. The first LIGO detection paper states (emphasis in the script): "The signal was observed with a matched-filter signal-to-noise ratio of 24 and a false alarm rate estimated to be less than 1 event per 203 000 years, equivalent to a significance greater than 5.1σ. The source lies at a luminosity distance of \(410^{+160}_{-180}\) Mpc corresponding to a redshift \(z=0.09^{+0.03}_{-0.04}\). In the source frame, the initial black hole masses are \(36^{+5}_{-4}M_\odot\) and \(29^{+4}_{-4}M_\odot\) […] All uncertainties define 90 % credible intervals." What does all that mean?
    mine A confidence interval [Konfidenzintervall] is a range computed from the data together with a level such as 90 %, in the sense that the procedure produces a range covering the truth in 90 % of repetitions (§3.4). The Bayesian approach instead treats the unknown parameter itself as random and gives it a distribution; its ranges are called credible intervals (§3.5). The asymmetric ranges like \({}^{+160}_{-180}\) show that the plausible region does not have to be symmetric around the estimate.
  10. Review sentiment. As a data scientist at Amazon you analyse the sentiment of (verified) reviews of office equipment. Reviews by buyers who self-identify as male are on average 0.21 % more critical than those by buyers who identify as female, and further tests call the difference statistically significant. What do you recommend to your manager?
    mine "Statistically significant" only means "unlikely to be pure chance"; with enough data even a tiny difference like 0.21 % becomes significant. Whether it matters is a separate question (Overview 3.3(v): the actual numbers play a big role).

The script adds: unfortunately we will not be able to answer all of these questions fully. The goal of the chapter is to give first glimpses of, and pointers to, how statistical inference approaches such questions.

Overview 3.3 how to approach this Script 3.3

Trying to tackle the questions of Example 3.2 brings out the following points.

  1. We still need modelling assumptions. First of all we must decide what not to model, and what we consider possible. We start from a "collection of possibilities": a statistical model — a set of distributions we deem possible, so that we can then decide how likely each of them is to be the ground truth given the data ("which is most likely?"). We usually assume, implicitly, that the true distribution is inside this collection — even though that itself is unlikely.
  2. Real models have many moving parts. In reality the statistical model is often built from many components. Think of all the ways "noise" or "randomness" can enter the final observation of the Higgs particle. Introductory examples usually hide this.
  3. The quantity of interest can be close to or far from the model. The heads probability \(p\) of a coin is literally the one parameter describing the distribution. The measured sentiment of written reviews is a complicated construction on top of the actual (random?) process of people expressing their impressions.
  4. No final answers. It feels "wrong" to give final answers to most such questions. One is almost forced to speak in "levels of confidence" rather than "certainties".
  5. The numbers matter. The actual numbers involved (sample sizes, effect sizes, error rates) play a big role.

Point (i) is the reason for Definition 3.4, point (iii) for Definition 3.9 (parameter of interest), and point (iv) for everything in §3.3–§3.4.

Statistical models

Section goal Script §3.1: introduce the fundamental concepts of statistical inference — statistical models, statistics, parameters of interest, and parameter identifiability.

Idea first (mine). In probability we had one probability space \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\). In statistics we do not know \(\P\). So we write down a whole list of candidate distributions, one for each value of an unknown label \(\theta\) (the parameter), all on the same \((\Omega,\Aa)\). For a coin: "\(\Ber(p)\) for some \(p\) between 0 and 1" is the list \(\{\Ber(0),\dots,\Ber(0.5),\dots,\Ber(1)\}\), labelled by \(p\). The data then help us decide which entry of the list is plausible.

Definition 3.4 statistical model [statistisches Modell] Script 3.4

Let \((\Omega,\Aa)\) be a measurable sample space and \(\Theta\) a non-empty index set, called the parameter space [Parameterraum]. For a family of probability distributions \(\mathcal P_\Theta:=(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}\) on \((\Omega,\Aa)\), we call \((\Omega,\Aa,\mathcal P_\Theta)\) a statistical model. Often we just call \(\mathcal P_\Theta\) the statistical model, when the sample space and σ-algebra are clear.

  • Well-specified / mis-specified. The model is well-specified [korrekt spezifiziert] if there is a \(\theta\in\Theta\) such that \(P_\theta\) is the true distribution of the random experiment; this \(\theta\) is then called the true parameter. In words: the ground truth is inside your space of possibilities. Otherwise the model is mis-specified [fehlspezifiziert].
  • Parametric / non-parametric. If \(\Theta\subseteq\R^k\) for some finite \(k\), the model is parametric. Otherwise it is non-parametric. The literature has different explicit definitions of "non-parametric"; a common one is "\(\Theta\) is infinite-dimensional" (for example the set of all continuous distributions). my addition "Infinite-dimensional" means: no fixed, finite list of numbers \((\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k)\) is enough to pin down every member of \(\Theta\) — for example the set of all continuous densities on \(\R\) cannot be described by 2, 10 or a million numbers, whereas every normal distribution is pinned down by the two numbers \((\mu,\sigma^2)\) (dimension is explained in B5, rank and dimension). Broadly, non-parametric models put very few or no restrictions on the distributions considered. This chapter focuses mainly on parametric models.
  • Notation. If a random variable \(X\) satisfies \(X\sim P_\theta\) for some \(\theta\in\Theta\), we say \(X\) follows (is distributed according to) \((\Omega,\Aa,\mathcal P_\Theta)\) and write, in abuse of notation, \(X\sim\mathcal P_\Theta\).

Reading each part (mine).

  • \((\Omega,\Aa)\) is fixed and known: it says what the data can look like (for a coin: \(\{0,1\}\)).
  • \(\Theta\) is the set of labels we consider possible. \(\theta\) may be a single number (\(p\)) or a list of numbers (\((\mu,\sigma^2)\)).
  • For each label \(\theta\), \(P_\theta\) is a complete probability distribution on \((\Omega,\Aa)\). If the model is well-specified, at least one of them is the true distribution; we do not know which. It need not be only one label: two different \(\theta\) can name the very same distribution, and then both of them are true parameters. Whether that can happen is exactly the question of identifiability (Definition 3.11 below); Example 3.12 is a model where it does happen.
  • "\(X\sim\mathcal P_\Theta\)" is an "abuse of notation" because \(\mathcal P_\Theta\) is a whole family, not a single distribution. It means "\(X\sim P_\theta\) for one \(\theta\) we do not know".

Small example. \(\Omega=\{0,1\}\), \(\Aa=\pow(\{0,1\})\), \(\Theta=[0,1]\), \(P_p=\Ber(p)\). If the coin really has heads probability 0.62, the model is well-specified with true parameter \(p=0.62\). The model \((\Ber(p))_{p\in\{0.5\}}\) ("the coin is fair") is mis-specified for that coin. Both are parametric (\(\Theta\subseteq\R^1\)).

Non-parametric example (mine): "all distributions on \(\R\) that have a density". No finite list of numbers can label all of them, so \(\Theta\) cannot be a subset of any \(\R^k\).

How it is used. Exercises often say "write down an adequate statistical model" (Sheet 10 Ex 5(ii), below): give \(\Omega\), \(\Aa\), and the family \((P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}\) with the parameter space stated explicitly. Exam problems start with "Let \((\R,\mathcal B,\mathcal P_\Theta)\) be a statistical model" (SoSe25 P1b, SoSe26 P1e).

Example 3.5 parametric models Script 3.5

Models for some of the situations in Example 3.2 and elsewhere. In each case: \(\Omega\) = possible values of one observation, \(\Aa\) = its σ-algebra, then the family.

  1. Coin flips: \(\bigl(\Omega=\{0,1\},\ \Aa=\pow(\{0,1\}),\ (\Ber(p))_{p\in[0,1]}\bigr)\). The parameter space is \(\Theta=[0,1]\), and we write \(p\) for \(\theta\).
  2. Gender of a consumer, coded 1 for female and 0 for male: again a Bernoulli model \(\bigl(\{0,1\},\pow(\{0,1\}),(\Ber(p))_{p\in[0,1]}\bigr)\).
  3. Defective screws in bags of 50: the number of defective screws in a bag, modelled binomially, \(\bigl(\{0,\dots,50\},\pow(\{0,\dots,50\}),(\Bin(50,p))_{p\in[0,1]}\bigr)\).
  4. Call centre: numbers of incoming calls in 20 consecutive 15-minute intervals, modelled by \(\bigl(\N,\pow(\N),(\Poi(\lambda))_{\lambda\in\R_{>0}}\bigr)\). (\(\N\) contains 0: an interval may have no calls.)
  5. Subway waiting time recorded every day for a year: \(\bigl(\R,\mathcal B,(\Unif(0,\theta))_{\theta\in\R_{>0}}\bigr)\) — the train comes at a uniformly random moment within a maximal waiting time \(\theta\).
  6. Light bulbs: lifetimes of 2000 newly installed bulbs over 5 years, \(\bigl(\R,\mathcal B,(\Exp(\lambda))_{\lambda\in\R_{>0}}\bigr)\).
  7. Bottling machine (Example 3.2(iii)). Reading "±2 ml" as a strict bound gives, for example, \[\bigl(\Omega=[328,332],\ \mathcal B|_\Omega,\ \Unif([328,332])\bigr),\] where \(|\Theta|=1\): only one distribution is allowed. Then there is nothing to infer about the distribution, and most interesting questions go back to probability theory, e.g. "what is the probability of overfilling by 500 l within \(n\) bottles?"
    Reading "±2 ml" instead as "deviations are (mumble, mumble, clt) normally distributed and stay within 330 ± 2 ml in most cases" gives \[\bigl(\Omega=\R,\ \mathcal B,\ (\mathcal N(330,\sigma^2))_{\sigma^2\in\R_{>0}}\bigr),\] and we try to infer from measurements what \(\sigma^2\) is (or in which range it likely lies) and how that relates to ±2 ml. The parameter space is \(\Theta=\R_{>0}\), the possible variances. This model assumes the average fill is exactly 330 ml. Dropping that assumption: \[\bigl(\Omega=\R,\ \mathcal B,\ (\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2))_{(\mu,\sigma^2)\in\R\times\R_{>0}}\bigr),\] with \(\Theta=\R\times\R_{>0}\) containing both mean and variance. Both normal models are "wrong" in that they allow negative amounts or 1 litre, which cannot fit in the bottle — yet they may be useful. The script asks: can you argue for and against the case that they are well-specified?
    My answer. Against: strictly, neither normal model can be well-specified: every normal distribution gives positive probability to impossible values (below 0 ml, above the bottle's volume), and the true distribution gives them probability 0. So no \(P_\theta\) equals the truth exactly. The first normal model also fails if the machine is systematically miscalibrated (true mean \(\ne330\)), which the brewer's 500 l suggest. For: the probability a normal distribution with \(\sigma\) of about 1 ml puts on impossible values is astronomically small (330 ml is hundreds of standard deviations from 0), so the model can be "well-specified up to negligible error", which is all we need in practice. The second normal model at least allows a shifted mean.
  8. Image generation by "diffusion". Start from a high-dimensional standard Gaussian \(\mathcal N(0,\mathbf 1_{n\times n})\) (mean 0, covariance the \(n\times n\) identity matrix, i.e. \(n\) independent \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) coordinates; identity matrix: B5; Gaussian vectors: §2.3), where \(n\) is large — 3 times the number of pixels, for the colours RGB. This is transformed by a complex neural net with weights (parameters) \(\theta\in\R^d\), where \(d\) is in the millions or billions. The final "image distribution" is obtained by (repeated) application of the change-of-variables formula for densities (§2.3). So images are modelled as \(f_\theta(X)\) for a standard Gaussian \(X\), where \(f_\theta\) represents the (repeated) application of the net, giving the statistical model \[\bigl(\Omega=\R^{n\times n},\ \mathcal B^{n\times n},\ (P_{f_\theta(X)})_{\theta\in\R^d}\bigr),\] where \(P_{f_\theta(X)}\) is the distribution of the random variable \(f_\theta(X)\). Training such a model can be seen as inferring the parameters \(\theta\in\Theta=\R^d\) that "best explain the observed images in the training set" (in practice: minimising a loss like the mean squared error [mittlerer quadratischer Fehler] — the average of the squared differences between what the net produces and what it should produce). The script's author does not think this justifies the slogan "machine learning / artificial intelligence is just statistics on steroids", but one can see where it comes from.
    My note on notation: the script writes \(X\in\mathcal N(0,\mathbf 1_{n\times n})\) — read "\(X\sim\)". Since the covariance matrix is \(n\times n\), \(X\) is a vector with \(n\) entries, so the natural sample space is \((\R^n,\mathcal B^n)\); the script's \(\R^{n\times n}\) looks like a slip. It changes nothing in the idea. Note this model is still parametric by Definition 3.4: \(d\) is huge but finite.
  9. Other ways to build models. Models can be constrained and defined in many ways. In graphical models one considers all distributions with certain properties with respect to a given graph. In latent variable models one specifies a distribution of hidden ("latent") variables and a conditional distribution of the observed variables given the latent ones; integrating out ("marginalising") the latent variables gives the allowed distributions of the observed variables. There are also autoregressive, hierarchical, generalised linear and many other models; all of them produce a certain set of distributions over the observed variables by defining or constraining mechanisms and assumptions.

Remark (unnumbered) "inference" in statistics versus machine learning Script, after 3.5

  • In statistics, inference means learning about unknown quantities — like parameters or properties of distributions — from observed data, typically through estimation and uncertainty quantification. The "inference targets" are properties of the population distribution.
  • In machine learning, inference often means applying a trained model to new inputs, i.e. producing new predictions. The "inference targets" are predictions for new inputs, or newly generated outputs (images, text, …) for generative models. Terms like "inference time" (= "test time", "deployment time") and "inference cost" (the cost of making predictions after training) come from this usage.
  • This causes confusion: what statisticians call inference amounts to "fitting the model" and "finding the best parameters" — which machine learning calls training. What machine learning calls inference, statistics calls prediction (a word machine learning also uses). So "inference" names different stages of the pipeline in the two fields.
  • This shows a key difference: statistics aims to infer properties of an unknown ground truth; machine learning aims to infer predictions on new inputs.

For this course: "inference" always has the statistics meaning — from data to the unknown \(\theta\).

Sheet 10, Exercise 5 — the toaster box: distribution, model, estimator Sheet 10 · Ex 5

Task. A box holds \(n\in\N_{>1}\) toasters (so \(n\ge2\)), of which a fixed number \(d\) are broken. You draw two toasters uniformly at random (without putting the first back). (i) What is the distribution \(P_d\) of the number of broken toasters among the two? (ii) \(d\) is unknown and is to be estimated from this sample of two: write down an adequate statistical model and explain it briefly. (iii) Give an unbiased estimator for \(d\) and justify it.

Relevant tools. Laplace (equally likely) counting: probability = favourable cases / all cases (§1.1); the binomial coefficient \(\binom m2=\frac{m(m-1)}2\) = number of ways to choose 2 objects out of \(m\) when the order does not matter (B3); Definition 3.4 for (ii); Definition 3.6 and the definition of unbiasedness (Definition 3.20(i), §3.2) for (iii). An estimator [Schätzer] is simply a statistic that we use as our guess for the unknown parameter (Definition 3.18, §3.2); it is called unbiased [erwartungstreu] if its expected value equals the true parameter, for every possible value of that parameter.

(i) The distribution. Two drawn toasters contain 0, 1 or 2 broken ones, so the outcome space is \(\Omega=\{0,1,2\}\) with \(\Aa=\pow(\Omega)\). Every unordered pair of toasters is equally likely, and there are \(\binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}2\) pairs.

  • 0 broken: both toasters come from the \(n-d\) working ones: \(\binom{n-d}2=\frac{(n-d)(n-d-1)}2\) pairs. Dividing by \(\frac{n(n-1)}2\) (the factors \(\frac12\) cancel): \(\ p_d(0)=\dfrac{(n-d)(n-d-1)}{n(n-1)}\).
  • 2 broken: both from the \(d\) broken ones: \(\binom d2=\frac{d(d-1)}2\) pairs, so \(\ p_d(2)=\dfrac{d(d-1)}{n(n-1)}\).
  • 1 broken: one of the \(d\) broken and one of the \(n-d\) working ones: \(d(n-d)\) pairs, so \(\ p_d(1)=\dfrac{d(n-d)}{n(n-1)/2}=\dfrac{2d(n-d)}{n(n-1)}\).

Check that they add up to 1. Numerator sum: \((n-d)(n-d-1)+2d(n-d)+d(d-1)\). Expand: \((n-d)^2-(n-d)+2dn-2d^2+d^2-d = n^2-2nd+d^2-n+d+2dn-2d^2+d^2-d = n^2-n=n(n-1)\). Divided by \(n(n-1)\) this is 1 ✓. (The official solution gets \(p_d(1)\) the other way round, as \(1-p_d(0)-p_d(2)=\frac{2(nd-d^2)}{n(n-1)}\); same result, since \(nd-d^2=d(n-d)\).) This is the hypergeometric distribution with 2 draws (§1.2).

Numbers (mine): \(n=5\), \(d=2\): \(p_2(0)=\frac{3\cdot2}{20}=0.3\), \(p_2(1)=\frac{2\cdot2\cdot3}{20}=0.6\), \(p_2(2)=\frac{2\cdot1}{20}=0.1\); sum 1 ✓.

(ii) An adequate statistical model (official answer, correct): \[\bigl(\{0,1,2\},\ \pow(\{0,1,2\}),\ (P_d)_{d\in\{0,\dots,n\}}\bigr).\] Reading it with Definition 3.4: the sample space \(\{0,1,2\}\) lists what we can observe (0, 1 or 2 broken among the two drawn); the σ-algebra is the power set because the space is finite; the unknown parameter is \(d\), and the parameter space is \(\Theta=\{0,\dots,n\}\) because there cannot be fewer than 0 or more than \(n\) broken toasters. \(n\) is known, so it is part of the model's description, not a parameter. The model is parametric (\(\Theta\subseteq\R^1\)) with a finite parameter space, and it is well-specified as long as the draw really is uniform.

Is \(d\) identifiable (Definition 3.11)? Yes. The mean of the observed count under \(P_d\) is \(0\cdot p_d(0)+1\cdot p_d(1)+2\cdot p_d(2)=\frac{2d(n-d)+2d(d-1)}{n(n-1)}=\frac{2d(n-1)}{n(n-1)}=\frac{2d}n\). If \(P_{d_1}=P_{d_2}\), the means agree, \(\frac{2d_1}n=\frac{2d_2}n\), so \(d_1=d_2\). (This is my addition; the sheet does not ask it.)

The official exercise statement writes \(d\in\{0,\dots,d\}\); that is a typo for \(\{0,\dots,n\}\), which the solution then uses.

(iii) An unbiased estimator. The answer is \(\hat d(\omega)=\frac{\omega n}{2}\): the fraction of broken toasters in the sample, \(\frac\omega2\), scaled up to all \(n\) toasters. Why it is unbiased (its mean is exactly \(d\) for every \(d\)), its variance, and a check of the official solution are worked out on §3.2, Sheet 10 Ex 5, where estimators are introduced.

Widget — a statistical model is a family: the toaster box My addition

Left: one member \(P_d\) of the model of Sheet 10 Ex 5 — the pmf of the number of broken toasters among two drawn, for the \(d\) you choose. Moving \(d\) walks through the whole family \((P_d)_{d\in\{0,\dots,n\}}\). Right: fix an observation \(\omega\) and read the same formula as a function of \(d\) — the likelihood \(L(d\mid\omega)=p_d(\omega)\) over the finite parameter space.

Statistics and parameters of interest

Idea first (mine). Once data \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) are in, we compute numbers from them: the average, the largest value, the spread. Such a recipe "data in, number out" is a statistic. The one rule: the recipe may use only the data, never the unknown \(\theta\) — otherwise you could not compute it.

Definition 3.6 statistic [Statistik] Script 3.6

Let \((\Omega,\Aa,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})\) be a statistical model and \((X_1,\dots,X_n)\) a random sample [Stichprobe], i.e. a random vector on the product space \((\Omega^n,\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\Aa)\). A statistic is a measurable function \[T:\Omega^n\to\R^k\qquad\text{for some }k\in\N_{>0},\] that does not depend on the unknown parameter \(\theta\). Its value \(t=T(x_1,\dots,x_n)\) is computed from a realised data sample \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\). The key property of a statistic is that it is an observable quantity once the data are collected.

Each part (mine).

  • \(\Omega^n\) is the set of lists \((x_1,\dots,x_n)\) of \(n\) possible observations; \(\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\Aa\) is the product σ-algebra on it (§1.4). So \((X_1,\dots,X_n)\) is simply "the whole data set before we look at it".
  • Capital vs small letters: \(X_i\) is the random variable (before the experiment), \(x_i\) its observed value (after). \(T(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) is a random variable; \(t=T(x_1,\dots,x_n)\) is a number.
  • Measurable (B4) is a technical condition that makes \(T(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) a random variable with a distribution. Every formula built from sums, products, max, min and continuous functions is measurable, so in practice you never have to check it.
  • \(k\) is the number of outputs: \(k=1\) for "the average", \(k=2\) for "average and variance together".
  • Not depending on \(\theta\) is the real content. Counterexample (mine): in the model \((\mathcal N(\mu,1))_{\mu\in\R}\), the quantity \(\bar X_n-\mu\) is not a statistic: to compute it you need the unknown \(\mu\).

Example 3.7 statistics Script 3.7

For a sample \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) of real random variables:

  1. the sample mean [Stichprobenmittel] \(\bar X_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) is a statistic;
  2. the sample variance [Stichprobenvarianz] \(S_n^2:=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\) is a statistic;
  3. the maximum \(X_{(n)}:=\max(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) is a statistic;
  4. \(T(X_1,\dots,X_n)=\pi\) (a constant) and \(T(X_1,\dots,X_n)=X_6\) are also statistics.

With numbers (mine). Sheet 10 Ex 1 uses bus waiting times (in minutes) \(x=(4,1,7,12,5,9,10,2)\), so \(n=8\).

  • \(\bar x=\frac{4+1+7+12+5+9+10+2}8=\frac{50}8=6.25\).
  • Deviations \(x_i-\bar x\): \(-2.25,-5.25,0.75,5.75,-1.25,2.75,3.75,-4.25\). Their squares add up to \(5.0625+27.5625+0.5625+33.0625+1.5625+7.5625+14.0625+18.0625=107.5\). So \(s^2=\frac{107.5}{8-1}\approx15.36\).
  • \(x_{(8)}=\max=12\). Also \(x_{(1)}=\min=1\), and the median (middle value of the sorted list \(1,2,4,5,7,9,10,12\): average of the two middle ones) is \(\frac{5+7}2=6\).
  • \(T=\pi\) gives 3.14159… whatever the data; \(T=X_6\) gives the sixth value, 9.

Why divide by \(n-1\) in \(S_n^2\) rather than \(n\)? With \(n-1\), the expected value of \(S_n^2\) is exactly the true variance (it is unbiased); this is shown in §3.2. The subscript "\((n)\)" in \(X_{(n)}\) means "the \(n\)-th smallest", i.e. the largest; \(X_{(1)}\) is the smallest. (iv) shows that a statistic does not have to be useful — it only has to be computable from the data. The widget below computes all of these for any list you type.

Widget — statistic calculator My addition

Type numbers separated by commas or spaces (or pick a preset). The dot plot shows the data with the mean (blue line) and the median (orange line). Try the preset with an outlier: the mean moves a lot, the median hardly.

Remark 3.8 the \(n\) is implicit Script 3.8

A given statistic is only defined for a fixed \(n\) (its domain is \(\Omega^n\)). Usually the number of samples \(n\) is left variable, and we assume we have a version of the statistic for every \(n\). For Example 3.7(i)–(iii) this is straightforward. We then just write \(T\), or \(T_n\) to make the dependence on \(n\) visible. Example 3.7(iv) shows that a statistic in general need not have "a version for every \(n\)". In practice we only consider statistics that have "a natural version for every \(n\)".

Concretely: \(T=X_6\) makes no sense for \(n=5\) data points — there is no sixth one. \(\bar X_n\) has one single formula that works for every \(n\); that is what "natural version for any \(n\)" means. This matters because statements like "\(\bar X_n\to\mu\) as \(n\to\infty\)" (law of large numbers, §2.4) talk about a whole sequence of statistics \(T_1,T_2,T_3,\dots\).

Definition 3.9 parameter of interest Script 3.9

Often we are not interested in the whole parameter \(\theta\in\Theta\), but in a specific function of it. A parameter of interest is a function \(\gamma:\Theta\to\R^k\). The goal of statistical inference is then to make statements about the value \(\gamma(\theta)\).

\(\gamma\) is the Greek letter gamma. Example: a lab only cares about the average fill of the bottling machine, not how much it varies; in the model \((\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2))\) it chooses \(\gamma(\mu,\sigma^2)=\mu\). The unknown \(\theta\) goes in, the number we care about comes out. It is the formal version of Overview 3.3(iii).

Example 3.10 parameters of interest in Gaussians Script 3.10

In the Gaussian model \(\bigl(\R,\mathcal B,(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2))_{\mu\in\R,\sigma^2\in\R_{>0}}\bigr)\) with \(\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)=(\mu,\sigma^2)\) we might be interested only in

  • the mean: \(\gamma(\theta)=\theta_1=\mu\);
  • the variance: \(\gamma(\theta)=\theta_2=\sigma^2\);
  • the coefficient of variation [Variationskoeffizient]: \(\gamma(\theta)=\sqrt{\theta_2}/\theta_1=\sigma/\mu\).

We will mostly take \(\gamma=\mathrm{id}\) (the identity map, \(\gamma(\theta)=\theta\)): the parameter of interest is all of \(\theta\).

Numbers: for \(\theta=(330,4)\) (mean 330 ml, variance 4 ml², so \(\sigma=2\) ml) the three parameters of interest are 330, 4 and \(2/330\approx0.006\). The coefficient of variation measures spread relative to size. Small detail: \(\sigma/\mu\) is undefined when \(\mu=0\), so strictly this \(\gamma\) is a function on \(\Theta=(\R\setminus\{0\})\times\R_{>0}\).

Identifiability

Idea first (mine). Data can only ever tell us about the distribution that produced them: with more and more data, the frequencies and averages settle at the true distribution's values (law of large numbers, §2.4). So if two different parameter values produce exactly the same distribution, no amount of data can tell them apart. A parameter is identifiable if this never happens.

Tiny example. A friend picks a whole number \(\theta\) and then reports \(X=\theta^2+\) noise, with the noise \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). If \(\theta=3\) or \(\theta=-3\), \(X\sim\mathcal N(9,1)\) in both cases. Even a million reports cannot reveal the sign of \(\theta\). But \(\theta^2\) (and \(|\theta|\)) can be learned.

Definition 3.11 identifiability [Identifizierbarkeit] Script 3.11

A parameter of interest \(\gamma(\theta)\) (which may be the full parameter \(\theta\)) is identifiable in a model \((\Omega,\Aa,\mathcal P_\Theta)\) if for all \(\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta\): \[\gamma(\theta_1)\ne\gamma(\theta_2)\ \Longrightarrow\ P_{\theta_1}\ne P_{\theta_2}.\] Equivalently: \(P_{\theta_1}=P_{\theta_2}\ \Longrightarrow\ \gamma(\theta_1)=\gamma(\theta_2)\). If a parameter of interest is not identifiable, it is impossible to determine its value uniquely even with an infinite amount of data, and we call it unidentifiable.

Each part (mine).

  • "\(\gamma(\theta_1)\ne\gamma(\theta_2)\Rightarrow P_{\theta_1}\ne P_{\theta_2}\)": whenever two parameters differ in the part we care about, their distributions differ somewhere — so the data can in principle distinguish them.
  • Why "equivalently". "\(A\Rightarrow B\)" is logically the same as "not \(B\Rightarrow\) not \(A\)" (the contrapositive). Here not \(B\) is "\(P_{\theta_1}=P_{\theta_2}\)" and not \(A\) is "\(\gamma(\theta_1)=\gamma(\theta_2)\)". The second form is usually easier to prove: assume two distributions are equal and derive that the \(\gamma\)-values are equal.
  • Full parameter (\(\gamma=\mathrm{id}\)): \(\theta\) is identifiable exactly when the map \(\theta\mapsto P_\theta\) is injective — different labels, different distributions.
  • \(P_{\theta_1}=P_{\theta_2}\) means equality as distributions: \(P_{\theta_1}(A)=P_{\theta_2}(A)\) for every event \(A\). For two pmfs it is enough that they agree at every point. For two densities it is enough that they agree outside a null set [Nullmenge] — a set of total length 0, such as a single point or a finite list of points (B4). Changing a density on such a set changes no integral, hence no probability, hence not the distribution.

Examples (mine).

  • Bernoulli, identifiable. In \((\Ber(p))_{p\in[0,1]}\): if \(\Ber(p_1)=\Ber(p_2)\), then in particular they give the event \(\{1\}\) the same probability, so \(p_1=p_2\).
  • Normal, identifiable. In \((\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2))\): if \(\mathcal N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)=\mathcal N(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)\), then their means and variances agree (the mean and variance are computed from the distribution alone), so \((\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)=(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)\).
  • Not identifiable. In \((\mathcal N(\theta^2,1))_{\theta\in\R}\), \(\theta=3\) and \(\theta=-3\) give the same distribution but \(3\ne-3\). The parameter of interest \(\gamma(\theta)=\theta^2\) is identifiable: equal distributions have equal means, and the mean is \(\theta^2\).
  • Over-parametrised Bernoulli. \((\Ber(ab))_{(a,b)\in[0,1]^2}\): \((a,b)=(0.5,0.6)\) and \((0.6,0.5)\) both give \(\Ber(0.3)\). Only the product \(ab\) is identifiable.

How it is used. Exam pattern (SoSe26 P5a, below): compute the distribution of the observation as a function of the parameter, then check whether that function is injective. If it is not, find two parameter values with the same distribution — that is the whole proof of non-identifiability.

Example 3.12 identifiability in Gaussians Script 3.12

Let \(X=A+B\), where \(A\sim\mathcal N(\mu_A,1)\) and \(B\sim\mathcal N(\mu_B,1)\) are independent. Then \(X\) follows the statistical model \(\mathcal P_\Theta=(\mathcal N(\theta_1+\theta_2,2))_{\theta\in\R^2}\) with \(\theta=(\mu_A,\mu_B)\). The parameter \(\theta\) is not identifiable: for example \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\) give the same distribution of \(X\). But the mean of \(X\), as parameter of interest \(\gamma(\theta)=\mu_A+\mu_B\), is identifiable.

Details supplied by me — the script states the facts

Why \(X\sim\mathcal N(\mu_A+\mu_B,2)\). A sum of independent normal random variables is normal, with the means added and the variances added (Lemma 2.53(v) with \(a=b=1\), §2.3). Means: \(\mu_A+\mu_B\). Variances: \(1+1=2\).

\(\theta\) not identifiable. \(\theta_1=(1,2)\) gives \(\mathcal N(1+2,2)=\mathcal N(3,2)\), and \(\theta_2=(2,1)\) gives \(\mathcal N(2+1,2)=\mathcal N(3,2)\). So \(P_{\theta_1}=P_{\theta_2}\) although \(\theta_1\ne\theta_2\): the condition of Definition 3.11 (with \(\gamma=\mathrm{id}\)) fails. In fact every \(\theta\) on the line \(\mu_A+\mu_B=3\), such as \((0,3)\), \((-10,13)\), \((1.5,1.5)\), gives the same distribution.

\(\gamma(\theta)=\mu_A+\mu_B\) identifiable. Use the second form of Definition 3.11. Suppose \(P_{\theta}=P_{\theta'}\), i.e. \(\mathcal N(\mu_A+\mu_B,2)=\mathcal N(\mu_A'+\mu_B',2)\). Equal distributions have equal means, so \(\mu_A+\mu_B=\mu_A'+\mu_B'\), i.e. \(\gamma(\theta)=\gamma(\theta')\).

In words: if you only see the total \(A+B\), you can learn the total mean, but not how it is split between \(A\) and \(B\). The widget lets you move \((\mu_A,\mu_B)\) and watch the distribution of \(X\) stay put along the line \(\mu_A+\mu_B=\) const.

Widget — identifiability in Example 3.12 My addition

Left: the parameter plane \((\mu_A,\mu_B)\) with your point and the whole line of parameters that give the same distribution of \(X\). Right: the densities of \(A\), \(B\) (faint) and \(X=A+B\) (bold). Press "slide along the line": \(\theta\) changes, the bold curve does not.

The likelihood function

Idea first (mine). Take the formula for "the probability (or density) of the data", \(p(x\mid\theta)\). In probability we fix \(\theta\) and let the data \(x\) vary. The likelihood does the opposite: it fixes the observed data \(x\) and lets \(\theta\) vary. It answers "how well does \(\theta\) explain what we saw?" — exactly the table in the big picture.

Definition 3.13 likelihood function [Likelihood-Funktion] Script 3.13

Let \((X_1,\dots,X_n)\) be a random sample from a statistical model \((\Omega,\Aa,\mathcal P_\Theta)\) in which every \(P_\theta\) has a pmf or density \(p_\theta(\cdot)=:p(\cdot\mid\theta)\). Given observed data \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\), the likelihood (function) is \[L(\cdot\mid x):\Theta\to\R_{\ge0},\qquad \theta\mapsto L(\theta\mid x):=p_\theta(x)=p(x\mid\theta)=p(x_1,\dots,x_n\mid\theta).\] If \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are iid, then \[L(\theta\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i\mid\theta).\] The log-likelihood function is \(\ell(\theta\mid x):=\ln\bigl(L(\theta\mid x)\bigr)\).

Each part (mine).

  • \(p(x_1,\dots,x_n\mid\theta)\) is the joint pmf/density of the whole sample under \(P_\theta\), evaluated at the observed values. For discrete data it is literally \(P_\theta(X_1=x_1,\dots,X_n=x_n)\), the probability of seeing exactly these data.
  • Why the product for iid data: for independent random variables the joint pmf (density) is the product of the single pmfs (densities) (§1.4); identically distributed means each factor uses the same \(p(\cdot\mid\theta)\).
  • The output is \(\ge0\) because pmfs and densities are. It can be larger than 1 for densities (a density is not a probability).
  • \(\ell\) is only defined where \(L>0\); where \(L=0\) one sets \(\ell=-\infty\) (my convention; the script does not discuss it).

Example: 10 coin tosses, 7 heads (the big picture). Model \((\Ber(p))_{p\in[0,1]}\), data a sequence \(x_1,\dots,x_{10}\in\{0,1\}\) with seven 1s. With the Bernoulli pmf \(p(x_i\mid p)=p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i}\): \[L(p\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^{10}p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i}=p^{\sum x_i}(1-p)^{10-\sum x_i}=p^7(1-p)^3,\] using \(a^ra^s=a^{r+s}\) to collect the powers. \(\ell(p\mid x)=7\ln p+3\ln(1-p)\). At \(p=0.7\): \(L=0.7^7\cdot0.3^3\approx0.00222\), \(\ell\approx-6.109\).

In the big picture I used \(120\,p^7(1-p)^3\), the probability of the count "7 heads" (any order). Here the data are the sequence, whose probability has no factor 120. The two likelihoods differ by the constant factor 120, which does not depend on \(p\) — so they rank all values of \(p\) the same way and have the same maximiser. Constant factors never matter for likelihood comparisons.

Short example: writing a likelihood Sheet 10 · Ex 2(i)

Task. \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid from \((\Exp(\lambda))_{\lambda\in\R_{>0}}\), with pdf \(p(x\mid\lambda)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x\ge0\). Write down \(L(\lambda\mid x)\) and \(\ell(\lambda\mid x)\).

Solution. iid, so Definition 3.13 gives a product; assume all \(x_i\ge0\) (otherwise a factor is 0 and \(L=0\)): \[L(\lambda\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^n\lambda e^{-\lambda x_i}=\lambda^n\exp\Bigl(-\lambda\sum_{i=1}^nx_i\Bigr),\] because the \(n\) factors \(\lambda\) give \(\lambda^n\), and \(e^ae^b=e^{a+b}\) turns the product of exponentials into one exponential of the sum. Taking \(\ln\) (primer box 1: \(\ln(ab)=\ln a+\ln b\), \(\ln\lambda^n=n\ln\lambda\), \(\ln e^y=y\)): \[\ell(\lambda\mid x)=n\ln\lambda-\lambda\sum_{i=1}^nx_i .\] This matches the official solution. Parts (ii)–(iii) — finding the \(\lambda\) that maximises \(\ell\) (the maximum likelihood estimator [Maximum-Likelihood-Schätzer], mle) and checking its bias — are worked on §3.2; Ex 1 and Ex 3 of Sheet 10 as well.

Sheet 10 Ex 1(i) is the warning case: for \(\Unif(0,\theta)\) the density \(\frac1\theta\one_{[0,\theta]}(x_i)\) contains an indicator (\(\one_A\) is 1 on \(A\), 0 outside), so \(L(\theta\mid x)=\theta^{-n}\) only when \(\theta\ge\max_ix_i\), and 0 otherwise. For the bus data (max 12) that is \(\theta^{-8}\) for \(\theta\ge12\) and 0 for \(\theta<12\). Forgetting the indicator is the classic mistake.

Remark 3.14 how to interpret the likelihood Script 3.14

  1. The likelihood measures how "likely" a parameter value \(\theta\) is to have produced the observed data \(x\). It is a function of \(\theta\) (not of \(x\)), and it is defined only for a given set of observations. It does not exist without reference to data; in particular it is not a property of the statistical model alone.
  2. Maximising \(L(\theta\mid x)\) over \(\theta\) amounts to "finding the model (parameter) that is most likely to have generated the data \(x\)". (This is the maximum likelihood estimator of §3.2.)
  3. The likelihood function is not a probability density for \(\theta\).
  4. It is one possible way to get from "given the probability distribution, what can we say about possible observations" (probability theory) to "given observed data, what can we say about the underlying distribution (parameter)" (statistical inference).
  5. The new (and in principle unnecessary) notation \(p(x\mid\theta)\), and \(L(\theta\mid x)\) or \(\ell(\theta\mid x)\), stresses that we "condition" on the parameter or on the data, respectively, which we treat as fixed. It just highlights what is fixed and what varies.
  6. Especially for iid random variables the log-likelihood is useful: it turns products into sums and constant pre-factors into constant summands. Since the logarithm is strictly monotonic, optimising \(L(\theta\mid x)\) over \(\theta\) is the same as optimising \(\ell(\theta\mid x)\), and the latter is often more convenient.

(iii) with numbers (mine). A probability density for \(p\in[0,1]\) must have area 1. Compute the area under \(L(p)=120p^7(1-p)^3\) from the big picture. Expand \((1-p)^3=1-3p+3p^2-p^3\) (binomial formula), so \(p^7(1-p)^3=p^7-3p^8+3p^9-p^{10}\), and integrate term by term with \(\int_0^1p^m\,\mathrm dp=\frac1{m+1}\): \[\int_0^1p^7(1-p)^3\,\mathrm dp=\frac18-\frac39+\frac3{10}-\frac1{11}=\frac1{1320},\qquad \int_0^1120\,p^7(1-p)^3\,\mathrm dp=\frac{120}{1320}=\frac1{11}\approx0.091\ne1 .\] (Check of \(\frac1{1320}\): over the common denominator 3960, \(\frac{495-1320+1188-360}{3960}=\frac3{3960}=\frac1{1320}\).) So the likelihood does not integrate to 1 over \(\theta\). Compare: for fixed \(p\), the 11 values \(\P(K=k)\), \(k=0,\dots,10\), do add up to 1 — the likelihood is a pmf in \(x\), not in \(\theta\). The widget "two directions" below shows both sums.

(i) with numbers. "How likely \(\theta\) is to have produced \(x\)" must be read as a comparison: \(L(0.7)/L(0.5)=0.267/0.117\approx2.3\) says the observed data are 2.3 times as probable under \(p=0.7\) as under \(p=0.5\). It does not say "\(p=0.7\) has probability 0.267". In the frequentist view of this course \(\theta\) is not random at all; giving \(\theta\) a probability distribution is the Bayesian approach (§3.5).

(vi), why the maximiser does not change (mine). Let \(L(\theta^*)\ge L(\theta)\) for all \(\theta\) (with \(L>0\)). Because \(\ln\) is increasing, \(\ln L(\theta^*)\ge\ln L(\theta)\) for all \(\theta\): \(\theta^*\) also maximises \(\ell\). Conversely, \(e^y\) is increasing too, so a maximiser of \(\ell\) maximises \(L=e^\ell\). The same argument works for minimisers. Note: the script's text says "minimizing \(L\) … is the same as minimizing \(\ell\)"; that is true, but in context (maximum likelihood) the relevant statement is maximising. I wrote "optimising" above to cover both.

In words: the likelihood is the probability of the data you actually saw, viewed as a function of the unknown parameter. Higher means "explains the data better". It is a score for comparing parameter values, not a probability of the parameter.

Widget — likelihood explorer My addition

Top: the data (dots) and the model \(p(\cdot\mid\theta)\) for your current \(\theta\). In the two normal presets the short orange bars are the factors \(p(x_i\mid\theta)\) whose product is \(L\); in the two Bernoulli presets the two blue bars are the pmf \(\Ber(p)\) and the dots below them are the zeros and ones of the sample. Bottom: the whole likelihood curve \(\theta\mapsto L(\theta\mid x)\) with your \(\theta\) (orange) and the best \(\theta\) (blue dashed). In the normal presets \(\sigma\) is known (\(\sigma^2=4\) for the data of Example 3.15, \(\sigma^2=1\) for the 8 values), so \(\theta=\mu\).

Example 3.15 likelihood for a normal distribution Script 3.15

Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be iid \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), so \(\theta=(\mu,\sigma^2)\). The pdf of a single observation is \[p(x_i\mid\mu,\sigma^2)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{(x_i-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr).\] The likelihood is \[L(\mu,\sigma^2\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^n(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{(x_i-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\exp\Bigl(-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2\Bigr).\] The log-likelihood is \[\ell(\mu,\sigma^2\mid x)=-\frac n2\ln(2\pi)-\frac n2\ln(\sigma^2)-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2 .\]

Every step (mine).

  • First equality: Definition 3.13 for iid data (product of the single densities).
  • Second equality: the constant factor \((2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\) appears \(n\) times, giving \(\bigl((2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\bigr)^n=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\). The exponentials combine by \(e^{a_1}\cdots e^{a_n}=e^{a_1+\dots+a_n}\), and the common factor \(-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\) is pulled out of the sum.
  • Log-likelihood: \(\ln\) of a product is the sum of the \(\ln\)s. \(\ln(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}=-\frac n2\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) =-\frac n2\ln(2\pi)-\frac n2\ln(\sigma^2)\), and \(\ln\) of the exponential is its exponent.

Numbers (mine). Data \(x=(2,4,6)\), \(n=3\), and \(\sigma^2=4\) known. Then \(-\frac32\ln(2\pi)-\frac32\ln4\approx-2.757-2.079=-4.836\), and

  • \(\mu=4\): \(\sum(x_i-4)^2=4+0+4=8\), so \(\ell=-4.836-\frac8{8}=-5.836\);
  • \(\mu=3\): \(\sum(x_i-3)^2=1+1+9=11\), so \(\ell=-4.836-\frac{11}8=-6.211\); \(\mu=5\) gives the same by symmetry.

Only the last term depends on \(\mu\), and it is largest when the sum of squares \(\sum(x_i-\mu)^2\) is smallest. For this data that happens at \(\mu=4=\bar x\) — the maximum likelihood estimate of \(\mu\) is the sample mean; the general proof is on §3.2. The first preset of the likelihood widget is exactly this data set.

Remark 3.16 revisiting the implicit \(n\) Script 3.16

Our definition of a statistical model contains no \(n\), yet statistics is all about inference from \(n\) observations \(x:=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\) for some \(n\in\N_{>0}\). In practice we mostly consider \(n\) iid real random variables \(X_1,\dots,X_n\). Two viewpoints are possible:

  • Viewpoint 1: each \(X_i\) follows (independently) a fixed statistical model \(X_i\sim(\R,\mathcal B,\mathcal P_\Theta)\), and they all share the same true parameter \(\theta\in\Theta\).
  • Viewpoint 2: the vector \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) follows a statistical model \((\R^n,\mathcal B^n,\mathcal P_\Theta)\).

The second is more general in several ways (it need not assume iid), but the first is often more intuitive when we really talk about iid samples — which we will almost all the time. So the script uses the first. Do not be surprised to see \(X\sim\mathcal P_\Theta\) where \(X\) already has \(n\) components.

Coin example in both views: (1) each toss \(X_i\sim(\{0,1\},\pow(\{0,1\}),(\Ber(p))_{p\in[0,1]})\), all with the same \(p\); (2) the whole sequence \(X\in\{0,1\}^{10}\) with the family of distributions on \(\{0,1\}^{10}\) whose pmfs are \(p_p(x)=p^{\sum x_i}(1-p)^{10-\sum x_i}\) — the probability that the ten tosses come out exactly as the list \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_{10})\). The likelihood in Definition 3.13 is this pmf of view (2) evaluated at the data.

Widget — probability versus statistics: two directions through one table My addition

The grid shows \(f(k,p)=\binom{10}{k}p^k(1-p)^{10-k}\) for \(k=0,\dots,10\) heads (columns) and \(p\) from 0 to 1 (rows); darker = larger. Probability fixes \(p\) and reads a row: the distribution of the data. Statistics fixes the observed \(k\) and reads a column: the likelihood curve of \(p\).

Exercise-sheet tasks

The Sheet 10 tasks that start by writing down a statistical model or a likelihood are solved above:

  • Sheet 10 · Ex 5 — toaster box, parts (i)–(ii): box after Example 3.5; part (iii) on §3.2.
  • Sheet 10 · Ex 2(i) — likelihood and log-likelihood for \(\Exp(\lambda)\) (box after Definition 3.13), with a note on the likelihood of Ex 1(i).

The maximum likelihood parts of Sheet 10 (Ex 1, Ex 2(ii)–(iii), Ex 3) are solved fully on §3.2.

Method to reuse: writing down a model and a likelihood My addition

  1. Sample space: what values can one observation take? That is \(\Omega\); use \(\pow(\Omega)\) if it is finite or countable, \(\mathcal B\) if it is \(\R\) or an interval.
  2. Family and parameter space: which distribution type, and which parameter values are possible? State \(\Theta\) explicitly (\([0,1]\), \(\R_{>0}\), \(\{0,\dots,n\}\), …).
  3. Likelihood: write the pmf/pdf of one observation, including indicator functions for its support; for iid data multiply over \(i=1,\dots,n\).
  4. Simplify: collect powers (\(\prod\lambda=\lambda^n\)), merge exponentials into one exponential of a sum, and state for which \(\theta\) the likelihood is 0.
  5. Log-likelihood: take \(\ln\), turning products into sums.

Old-exam tasks

SoSe 2026, Problem 5a — randomized response: identifiability SoSe26 · P5a · 3 credits

Setting. Each survey participant has a sensitive yes/no attribute \(A\sim\Ber(p)\), \(p\in[0,1]\) unknown. We do not observe \(A\). We observe a privacy-protected answer \(Y\in\{0,1\}\): with probability \(r\in(0,1]\) the participant answers truthfully (\(Y=A\)); with probability \(1-r\) the participant flips a fair coin, independently of \(A\), and reports it. \(r\) is known. We observe iid answers \(Y_1,\dots,Y_n\).

Task. Compute \(\P(Y=1)\) in terms of \(p\) and \(r\). Is \(p\) identifiable from the distribution of \(Y\)?

Step 1 — the distribution of \(Y\). By the law of total probability over the two mechanisms (worked step by step on §1.4): \[\P(Y=1)=r\cdot p+(1-r)\cdot\tfrac12=rp+\frac{1-r}2=:q(p).\] \(Y\) takes only the values 0 and 1, so \(Y\sim\Ber(q(p))\).

Step 2 — the statistical model. In the language of Definition 3.4 (viewpoint 1 of Remark 3.16), each answer follows \[\Bigl(\{0,1\},\ \pow(\{0,1\}),\ \bigl(\Ber(q(p))\bigr)_{p\in[0,1]}\Bigr),\qquad q(p)=rp+\tfrac{1-r}2,\ r\text{ fixed and known}.\] The parameter is \(\theta=p\), \(\Theta=[0,1]\), and \(P_p=\Ber(q(p))\).

Step 3 — identifiability via Definition 3.11. We use the second form: assume \(P_{p_1}=P_{p_2}\) and show \(p_1=p_2\).

  • \(P_{p_1}=P_{p_2}\) means \(\Ber(q(p_1))=\Ber(q(p_2))\). Two Bernoulli distributions are equal only if they give \(\{1\}\) the same probability, so \(q(p_1)=q(p_2)\).
  • Write it out: \(rp_1+\frac{1-r}2=rp_2+\frac{1-r}2\). Subtract \(\frac{1-r}2\) on both sides: \(rp_1=rp_2\).
  • Divide by \(r\), which is allowed because \(r>0\): \(p_1=p_2\).

So \(p\mapsto P_p\) is injective: \(p\) is identifiable. In words: different true "yes" rates always produce different answer rates, so the answers carry the information needed to recover \(p\), namely \(p=\bigl(q-\frac{1-r}2\bigr)/r\).

Numbers. \(r=0.5\): \(q(0.2)=0.1+0.25=0.35\) and \(q(0.4)=0.2+0.25=0.45\) — different, as predicted. Recovering: \((0.35-0.25)/0.5=0.2\) ✓.

Why the assumptions matter. If \(r=0\) (excluded by \(r\in(0,1]\)), \(q(p)=\frac12\) for every \(p\): all \(P_p\) are \(\Ber(\frac12)\), and \(p\) is unidentifiable — nobody answers truthfully, so the answers say nothing. If \(r\) were unknown, so that \(\theta=(p,r)\), then \(p\) would not be identifiable either (my extension): \(q=r(p-\frac12)+\frac12\), and \((p,r)=(1,0.2)\) and \((0.75,0.4)\) both give \(q=0.6\), so \(P_{(1,0.2)}=P_{(0.75,0.4)}=\Ber(0.6)\) although \(\gamma(\theta)=p\) differs (1 versus 0.75).

Verification of the official solution: correct. It states \(\P(Y=1)=rp+\frac{1-r}2\) and "since \(r>0\), the map \(p\mapsto q(p)\) is injective on \([0,1]\); thus \(p\) is identifiable". The one step it leaves implicit is why injectivity of \(p\mapsto q(p)\) is the same as injectivity of \(p\mapsto P_p\) (Definition 3.11): because \(\Ber(a)=\Ber(b)\) exactly when \(a=b\). Marking: 1.5 points for \(\P(Y=1)\), 1 for the injectivity argument, 0.5 for the conclusion. Part (b), the maximum likelihood estimator of \(p\), belongs to §3.2.

SoSe25 · P1b (true/false: a weighted average \(\frac13\hat\theta_1+\frac23\hat\theta_2\) of two unbiased estimators is unbiased) uses a statistical model, but it is about estimators, so it is solved on §3.2.

Other exam problems checked for this page. All true/false and definition problems of the three old exams (SoSe25 P1a–d, P2a–b; WiSe25 P1a–d, P2a–b; SoSe26 P1a–e, P2a–d) were read. Apart from SoSe25 P1b (pointer above), none is about statistical models, statistics, identifiability or the likelihood. Two further items live in Part 3 but belong to other pages: SoSe26 P1e (does the mle always have the smallest mean squared error?) on §3.2, and SoSe25 P1c (what a rejected test at level 5 % means) on §3.3. Summary sheet

The shift

Probability (deductive): known model → probabilities of data. Statistics (inductive): observed data → unknown model. Tasks: estimate (§3.2), test (§3.3), give ranges (§3.4).

Definitions

statistical model
\((\Omega,\Aa,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})\): measurable space plus a family of distributions indexed by the parameter space \(\Theta\ne\emptyset\)
well-/mis-specified
true distribution is / is not some \(P_\theta\); that \(\theta\) is the true parameter
parametric
\(\Theta\subseteq\R^k\), \(k\) finite; otherwise non-parametric (e.g. infinite-dimensional \(\Theta\))
statistic
measurable \(T:\Omega^n\to\R^k\) not depending on \(\theta\); observable once data are in
examples
\(\bar X_n\), \(S_n^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\), \(X_{(n)}=\max\), even constants; \(\bar X_n-\mu\) is not one
parameter of interest
\(\gamma:\Theta\to\R^k\); usually \(\gamma=\mathrm{id}\)
identifiable
\(P_{\theta_1}=P_{\theta_2}\Rightarrow\gamma(\theta_1)=\gamma(\theta_2)\); for \(\gamma=\mathrm{id}\): \(\theta\mapsto P_\theta\) injective
likelihood
\(L(\theta\mid x)=p(x\mid\theta)\), iid: \(\prod_ip(x_i\mid\theta)\); log-likelihood \(\ell=\ln L\)

Formulas

Bernoulli
\(L(p\mid x)=p^{\sum x_i}(1-p)^{n-\sum x_i}\)
Exponential
\(L=\lambda^ne^{-\lambda\sum x_i}\), \(\ell=n\ln\lambda-\lambda\sum x_i\)
Normal
\(\ell=-\frac n2\ln(2\pi)-\frac n2\ln\sigma^2-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum(x_i-\mu)^2\)
Uniform(0, θ)
\(L=\theta^{-n}\) for \(\theta\ge\max x_i\), else 0 (keep the indicator!)

Key facts and traps

  • The likelihood is a function of \(\theta\) for fixed data; it is not a density for \(\theta\) (area \(\frac1{11}\) in the 7-of-10 example).
  • \(\ln\) is strictly increasing: \(L\) and \(\ell\) have the same maximiser; constant factors do not matter.
  • Non-identifiable: two parameters, same distribution — no amount of data separates them (\(X=A+B\): only \(\mu_A+\mu_B\) is learnable).
  • To prove identifiability: assume \(P_{\theta_1}=P_{\theta_2}\), derive \(\gamma(\theta_1)=\gamma(\theta_2)\). To disprove: exhibit two parameters with the same distribution.

Exam focus

SoSe26 P5a: compute the distribution of the observation and check injectivity of the parameter map (3 credits). SoSe25 P1b: linear combinations with weights summing to 1 keep unbiasedness. Every mle problem (SoSe25 P4a, WiSe25 P4a, SoSe26 P5b, Sheet 10) starts by writing the likelihood correctly — that step is this page.

Section 3.2 · Lectures 10–12 (the exact lecture is unknown: the script marks no lecture numbers after Lecture 9)

Point estimation

Punktschätzung

What this page covers Script §3.2, pp. 92–99

Everything from Convention 3.17 to Overview 3.32. The script states the goal of the section like this: "One common goal of statistical inference is to provide a single 'best guess' for an unknown parameter of interest based on the observed data. This guess is called a point estimate."

There are three parts: (1) what an estimator [Schätzer] is (Definition 3.18, Example 3.19); (2) how to judge whether an estimator is good — bias, consistency, variance, mean squared error, asymptotic normality, efficiency (Definition 3.20 and Examples 3.21–3.25); (3) a general recipe for building estimators, the maximum likelihood estimator (Definition 3.27 to Example 3.31), and an outlook (Overview 3.32).

Worked in place: Sheet 10 Ex 1, 2, 3, 5 (Sheet 10 Ex 4 is on §2.2 and is linked where it fits; Sheet 9 has no estimation exercise), and the old-exam tasks SoSe25 P1b, P4a, P4b, P4c, WiSe25 P4a–d (estimation side), WiSe25 P5b, P5c, SoSe26 P1e, P5b, P5c. Every old exam so far had a "derive the mle" task worth about 3–4 credits; that does not guarantee the next one will.

The big picture

You wait for the subway every morning. The train comes at regular intervals, but you do not know the interval length \(\theta\) (in minutes). Arriving at a random moment, your waiting time is somewhere between 0 and \(\theta\), each value equally likely: a uniform distribution \(\Unif(0,\theta)\). On eight days you write down your waiting times (these are the numbers used in Sheet 10 Ex 1):

\[ x=(4,\ 1,\ 7,\ 12,\ 5,\ 9,\ 10,\ 2). \]

What is your single best guess for \(\theta\)? Three reasonable answers (my numbers):

  • Twice the average. The average waiting time of \(\Unif(0,\theta)\) is \(\frac\theta2\) (the middle of the interval). The average of the data is \(\frac{4+1+7+12+5+9+10+2}{8}=\frac{50}8=6.25\). So guess \(2\cdot6.25=12.5\).
  • The largest value. You waited 12 minutes once, so \(\theta\ge12\) for sure. Guess \(12\).
  • The largest value, a bit enlarged. The largest of 8 draws usually lies a little below \(\theta\). Correct for that: \(\frac{8+1}8\cdot12=13.5\).

Each rule is an estimator: a recipe that turns the data into a number. The number it produces for your particular data (12.5, 12 or 13.5) is an estimate. This page answers two questions:

  • How do we compare estimators? An estimator is itself random (other days give other data). We ask: is it right on average (bias)? How much does it scatter (variance)? How far off is it on average, in squared distance (mean squared error)? Does it become exact with lots of data (consistency)? For the subway, the third rule turns out best among the three (Example 3.24).
  • Is there a general recipe? Yes: choose the parameter value under which the observed data would have been most probable — the maximum likelihood estimator (mle). For the subway it gives the second rule, 12.

In words: an estimator is a formula that guesses an unknown parameter from data. We judge it by how its guesses are spread around the truth over many imagined repetitions of the experiment, and maximum likelihood is the standard way to find a good formula.

0. Words and symbols from §3.1 used on this page

  • Statistical model [statistisches Modell] \((\Omega,\Aa,\mathcal P_\Theta)\) (Definition 3.4, §3.1): a set \(\Omega\) of possible observations, a collection \(\Aa\) of events, and a whole family of probability distributions \(\mathcal P_\Theta=(\P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}\), one for each value of a parameter \(\theta\). \(\Theta\) (capital theta) is the parameter space, the set of allowed values. Example: \((\R,\mathcal B,(\Unif(0,\theta))_{\theta>0})\) for the subway, with \(\Theta=\R_{>0}=(0,\infty)\).
  • True parameter: the value \(\theta\) whose distribution \(\P_\theta\) really generated the data. It is unknown; estimating it is the whole point.
  • Sample: random variables \(X_1,\dots,X_n\), usually iid (independent and identically distributed, §1.4) with distribution \(\P_\theta\). The observed data (realisation) are the numbers \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\) that actually came out. Capital letters = random, small letters = observed numbers.
  • Statistic [Statistik] (Definition 3.6): any function \(T(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) of the sample that can be computed without knowing \(\theta\). Examples: the sample mean \(\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\), the maximum \(X_{(n)}=\max\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}\) (also written \(X_{\max}\)).
  • Parameter of interest \(\gamma(\theta)\) (Definition 3.9): the part or function of \(\theta\) we care about, e.g. only the mean \(\mu\) of a normal distribution \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\).
  • Identifiable (Definition 3.11): different values of \(\gamma(\theta)\) give different distributions — so infinitely much data would pin \(\gamma(\theta)\) down. If two parameter values give the same distribution, no estimator can tell them apart.
  • Likelihood [Likelihood] (Definition 3.13): for fixed observed data \(x\), the function \(L(\theta\mid x)=p(x_1,\dots,x_n\mid\theta)\) of \(\theta\), where \(p(\cdot\mid\theta)\) is the pmf (discrete case) or pdf (continuous case) under \(\P_\theta\). For iid data \(L(\theta\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i\mid\theta)\) (the symbol \(\prod\) means "product of"). The log-likelihood is \(\ell(\theta\mid x)=\ln L(\theta\mid x)\).
  • \(\E_\theta\), \(\Var_\theta\), \(\P_\theta\): expectation, variance, probability computed when \(\theta\) is the true parameter. The script usually drops the index \(\theta\).
  • Indicator \(\one_A(x)\) (the script writes \(\chi_A\)): equals 1 if \(x\in A\) and 0 otherwise. A product of indicators is the indicator of the intersection, \(\one_A\one_B=\one_{A\cap B}\) (B2).

1. Finding the maximum of a function with calculus

Maximum likelihood means: find the \(\theta\) where a function is largest. School calculus is the tool.

  • Derivative \(f'(t)\): the slope of the graph of \(f\) at \(t\) (Analysis 6.2). Rules used here: \((t^k)'=kt^{k-1}\); \((\ln t)'=\frac1t\) for \(t>0\); \((\frac1t)'=-\frac1{t^2}\); constants in front stay; the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives (Analysis 6.3).
  • At an interior maximum the slope is 0. If \(f\) is differentiable and has its largest value at a point \(t^*\) inside an open interval, then \(f'(t^*)=0\) (Analysis 7.1). Reason: to the left of the peak the graph cannot go down towards the peak, to the right it cannot go up, so the tangent is flat. Points with \(f'=0\) are called critical points.
  • \(f'=0\) is not enough. A critical point can also be a minimum or a flat step. Two checks:
    • Second-derivative check (Analysis 7.5): if \(f'(t^*)=0\) and \(f''(t^*)<0\) (the slope is decreasing — the graph bends downwards), then \(t^*\) is a local maximum.
    • Sign check (Analysis 7.3): if \(f'(t)>0\) for all \(t<t^*\) and \(f'(t)<0\) for all \(t>t^*\), then \(f\) increases up to \(t^*\) and decreases afterwards, so \(t^*\) is the global maximum (the largest value overall). This is the stronger statement and the one we really need.
  • Maxima at the edge or at a jump. If the function is not differentiable everywhere (the uniform likelihood jumps), or the maximum sits at the boundary of the allowed interval, \(f'=0\) finds nothing. Then argue directly with "increasing" or "decreasing" (Sheet 10 Ex 1 and 3).
  • Several parameters. For \(f(\mu,v)\), the partial derivative \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial\mu}\) is the ordinary derivative in \(\mu\) with \(v\) held fixed (Analysis 11.2). The gradient \(\nabla f\) is the vector of all partial derivatives; at an interior maximum it is the zero vector.

Tiny example. \(f(t)=6t-t^2\). \(f'(t)=6-2t=0\) gives \(t^*=3\). \(f''(t)=-2<0\): maximum. Sign check: \(f'(t)>0\) for \(t<3\) and \(<0\) for \(t>3\), so it is the global maximum, \(f(3)=9\).

2. Why we take the logarithm of the likelihood

The natural logarithm \(\ln\) is defined for positive numbers (Analysis 5.2). Three properties do all the work:

  • Products become sums: \(\ln(ab)=\ln a+\ln b\), hence \(\ln\prod_{i=1}^na_i=\sum_{i=1}^n\ln a_i\). Differentiating a sum term by term is much easier than differentiating a product of \(n\) factors.
  • Powers and exponentials simplify: \(\ln(a^k)=k\ln a\) and \(\ln(e^{s})=s\).
  • \(\ln\) is strictly increasing: \(a<b\Rightarrow\ln a<\ln b\). So \(L(\theta_1\mid x)<L(\theta_2\mid x)\) exactly when \(\ell(\theta_1\mid x)<\ell(\theta_2\mid x)\): the two functions go up and down at the same places and have their maximum at the same \(\theta\). (The maximum value differs; the location does not, and the location is all we want.)

Example. Three coin tosses give 1, 0, 1. Under \(\Ber(p)\), \(L(p)=p\cdot(1-p)\cdot p=p^2(1-p)\) and \(\ell(p)=2\ln p+\ln(1-p)\). At \(p=\frac23\): \(L=\frac49\cdot\frac13=\frac4{27}\approx0.148\) and \(\ell=\ln0.148\approx-1.91\). Both are largest at \(p=\frac23\) (derivation in Example 3.29(i) below).

Caution: \(\ln\) needs positive input. Where \(L(\theta\mid x)=0\) the logarithm is undefined (\(-\infty\)); such \(\theta\) are never the maximum anyway, but they must be excluded first (Sheet 10 Ex 1, 3).

3. Facts about expectation and variance used on this page

  • Linearity: \(\E[aX+bY+c]=a\E[X]+b\E[Y]+c\) (§2.1).
  • Variance \(\Var[X]=\E[(X-\E[X])^2]=\E[X^2]-(\E[X])^2\); \(\Var[aX+c]=a^2\Var[X]\); for independent \(X_i\): \(\Var[\sum X_i]=\sum\Var[X_i]\) (§2.1). Consequence for iid with variance \(\sigma^2\): \(\Var[\bar X_n]=\frac{\sigma^2}n\).
  • Expectation of a function (LOTUS): \(\E[g(X)]=\int g(t)\,p_X(t)\,\mathrm dt\) for a density \(p_X\).
  • Named distributions (§2.1): \(\Ber(p)\): mean \(p\), variance \(p(1-p)\); \(\Poi(\lambda)\): mean and variance \(\lambda\); \(\Exp(\lambda)\) (density \(\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\), \(x\ge0\)): mean \(\frac1\lambda\), variance \(\frac1{\lambda^2}\); \(\Unif(0,\theta)\): mean \(\frac\theta2\), variance \(\frac{\theta^2}{12}\); \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\): mean \(\mu\), variance \(\sigma^2\); Gamma \(\Gamma(\alpha,\beta)\) (density \(\frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta x}\), \(x>0\), §1.3): mean \(\frac\alpha\beta\), variance \(\frac\alpha{\beta^2}\).
  • Convergence in probability \(Y_n\xrightarrow{\P}c\): \(\P(|Y_n-c|\ge\varepsilon)\to0\) for every tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\); almost surely: \(Y_n(\omega)\to c\) for all outcomes \(\omega\) outside an event of probability 0 (§2.4); in distribution, \(Y_n\xrightarrow{d}Y\): the cdfs \(F_{Y_n}(x)\to F_Y(x)\) at every \(x\) where \(F_Y\) is continuous (same place). The lln says \(\bar X_n\to\mu\) in both senses for iid data with finite mean; the clt says \(\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\) is approximately standard normal for large \(n\).

Estimators and estimates

Convention 3.17 the standing assumptions Script 3.17

Throughout §3.2, \((\Omega,\Aa,\mathcal P_\Theta)\) is a parametric statistical model (the parameter is a list of finitely many numbers, \(\Theta\subseteq\R^k\)) and \(n\in\N_{>0}\) is the number of observations. We call the parameter of interest \(\theta\), but everything also works for a derived parameter of interest \(\gamma(\theta)\). Finally, \(\theta\) (or \(\gamma\)) is assumed to be identifiable.

Why identifiability is assumed: if two values \(\theta_1\ne\theta_2\) gave the same distribution of the data, the data could never distinguish them, and "estimating \(\theta\)" would have no correct answer. Example 3.12 (§3.1): from \(X=A+B\) you can estimate \(\mu_A+\mu_B\), but never \(\mu_A\) alone.

Definition 3.18 estimator and estimate Script 3.18

An estimator [Schätzer] for a parameter of interest \(\gamma\) is a statistic \(\hat\gamma=T(X_1,\dots,X_n)\). An estimate [Schätzwert] is the specific value \(\hat\gamma_{\text{obs}}:=\hat\gamma(x)=T(x_1,\dots,x_n)\) obtained by applying the estimator to a particular realisation \(x\) of the data.

As for statistics in general, we assume the estimator exists for every \(n\), and sometimes write \(\hat\gamma_n\) to show the dependence on \(n\). For the full parameter, \(\gamma(\theta)=\theta\), we write \(\hat\theta\).

Each part explained (mine).

  • The hat \(\hat{\ }\) is the universal sign for "an estimate of". \(\hat\theta\) is read "theta hat".
  • An estimator is a random variable: it is a function of the random sample \(X_1,\dots,X_n\). This is what makes it possible to talk about its mean, its variance, its distribution.
  • An estimate is a number: the estimator evaluated at the data you actually have.
  • Being a statistic means: the formula may not contain the unknown \(\theta\). "\(\hat\theta=\theta\)" is not an estimator. Beyond that, any statistic counts as an estimator — also silly ones. Quality is judged afterwards (Definition 3.20).

Example (mine): \(\hat\theta=2\bar X_n\) is an estimator for the subway interval; with the data of the big picture, the estimate is \(\hat\theta_{\text{obs}}=12.5\).

Example 3.19 can I win? Script 3.19

At the yearly CIT graduation celebration you can buy lottery tickets for a TUM hoodie. There are 10 winning tickets. To judge your chances you want the total number of tickets \(N\in\N_{>0}\). You buy a ticket and try to estimate \(N\) from its number.

Model. You draw the ticket yourself, so its number \(X\) is Laplace distributed (uniform on \(\{1,\dots,N\}\), each number with probability \(\frac1N\)): the model is \((\N_{>0},\pow(\N_{>0}),(\Lap[N])_{N\in\N})\) — here \(\pow(\N_{>0})\) is the power set (all subsets) and the parameter space is \(\Theta=\N\). You observe one number \(x\) (so \(n=1\), \(x=x_1\)).

Possible estimators, all valid:

  • \(\hat N(X)=X\): just the number you drew. But it seems unlikely you drew the very largest number.
  • \(\hat N(X)=X+15\) or \(\hat N(X)=\operatorname{round}(1.2X)\): a bit more than what you drew.
  • \(\hat N(X)=2X\): if you expect to have drawn a number "in the middle", double it.

Then you buy two more tickets and have \(x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\) (assume \(N\) is so large that these are still essentially independent draws from \(\Lap[N]\)). Is \(\hat N(x)=\max\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}\) reasonable? What about \(\max\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}\) + the empirical variance? Or \(\hat N(x)=1000\)?
