All of these are valid estimates (numbers plugged in) or estimators (random variables plugged in). We need ways to decide which are good.

A first quality check, done with Definition 3.20(i) below. For \(X\sim\Lap[N]\), \(\E[X]=\frac1N(1+2+\dots+N)=\frac1N\cdot\frac{N(N+1)}2=\frac{N+1}2\) (the sum formula \(1+\dots+N=\frac{N(N+1)}2\)). So:

  • \(\hat N=X\) has \(\E[\hat N]=\frac{N+1}2\): on average it guesses about half the true value.
  • \(\hat N=2X\) has \(\E[\hat N]=N+1\): on average one too many.
  • \(\hat N=2X-1\) has \(\E[\hat N]=2\cdot\frac{N+1}2-1=N\): right on average ("unbiased").
  • \(\hat N=1000\) is right on average only if \(N=1000\) — useless unless you already know the answer.
  • The maximum of three draws is always \(\le N\), so it underestimates on average; the maximum likelihood recipe below nevertheless picks exactly this estimator (\(L(N\mid x)=N^{-3}\) for \(N\ge\max x_i\) and 0 otherwise, which is largest at \(N=\max x_i\) — the same argument as in Sheet 10 Ex 1). The enlarged maximum repairs the bias, like \(\frac{n+1}n X_{(n)}\) in Example 3.24. (This is the famous "German tank problem" of statistics.)

Properties of estimators

Idea first (mine). Imagine repeating the whole experiment many times — new eight mornings of waiting, again and again. Each repetition gives a new estimate. You get a cloud of estimates on the number line, and the true \(\theta\) is somewhere. A good estimator has its cloud centred on \(\theta\) (small bias), narrow (small variance), and — combining both — close to \(\theta\) on average (small mean squared error). With more data, the cloud should shrink onto \(\theta\) (consistency). Think of darts: bias is aiming at the wrong spot, variance is a shaky hand.

Definition 3.20 properties of estimators Script 3.20

Let \(\hat\theta\) be an estimator for the parameter \(\theta\). Its quality can be assessed by several properties.

  1. Bias [Verzerrung]: \(\operatorname{bias}[\hat\theta]=\E[\hat\theta]-\theta\). The estimator is unbiased [erwartungstreu] if \(\operatorname{bias}[\hat\theta]=0\), i.e. \(\E[\hat\theta]=\theta\), for all \(\theta\in\Theta\). The script asks: what is the expectation over?
  2. Consistency [Konsistenz]: \(\hat\theta_n\) is consistent if \(\hat\theta_n\xrightarrow{\P}\theta\), and strongly consistent if \(\hat\theta_n\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\theta\).
  3. Variance: \(\Var[\hat\theta]=\E[(\hat\theta-\E[\hat\theta])^2]\). For a vector parameter \(\theta\) this becomes the covariance matrix \(\Cov[\hat\theta,\hat\theta]\) (the \(k\times k\) table whose entry \((i,j)\) is \(\Cov[\hat\theta_i,\hat\theta_j]=\E[(\hat\theta_i-\E\hat\theta_i)(\hat\theta_j-\E\hat\theta_j)]\); the diagonal holds the variances of the coordinates, §2.1).
  4. Mean squared error (mse) [mittlerer quadratischer Fehler]: \[ \operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta]=\E[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]=\Var[\hat\theta]+(\operatorname{bias}[\hat\theta])^2 . \] The equality is the bias–variance decomposition. For a vector parameter, \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta]=\E[\|\hat\theta-\theta\|_2^2]\), where \(\|v\|_2^2=v_1^2+\dots+v_k^2\) is the squared Euclidean length (length of a vector in \(\R^k\) by Pythagoras; more on lengths/norms: Analysis 1.3).
  5. Asymptotic normality: \(\hat\theta_n\) is asymptotically normal if, properly centred and scaled, its distribution converges to a normal one: there is a quantity \(V(\theta)\), the asymptotic variance, with \[ \sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,V(\theta)) . \] This is fundamental for approximate confidence intervals and tests with large samples (§3.3, §3.4), because it means \(\hat\theta_n\) is approximately \(\mathcal N(\theta,V(\theta)/n)\).
  6. Efficiency [Effizienz]: compares the variances of unbiased estimators. An estimator is a minimum variance unbiased estimator (mvue) if it has the smallest variance among all unbiased estimators.

Each part explained (mine).

  • (i) What is the expectation over? Over the random sample. \(\theta\) is fixed (the truth), the data \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are drawn from \(\P_\theta\), and \(\hat\theta=T(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) is averaged over all possible data sets. Precisely, \(\E[\hat\theta]=\E_\theta[T(X_1,\dots,X_n)]\), which in general depends on \(\theta\). So the bias is a function of \(\theta\), and "unbiased" demands it is zero for every possible true value — because we do not know which one is true. Example: the constant estimator \(\hat\theta=5\) has bias \(5-\theta\), which is 0 only when \(\theta=5\); it is not unbiased.
  • (ii) Consistency is a statement about the sequence \(\hat\theta_1,\hat\theta_2,\dots\) as the sample grows: for every tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\P_\theta(|\hat\theta_n-\theta|\ge\varepsilon)\to0\). Again this must hold for every \(\theta\in\Theta\).
  • (iii) Variance measures scatter around the estimator's own mean, not around the truth. A constant estimator has variance 0 and can still be terrible.
  • (iv) The mse measures scatter around the truth. It punishes both a wrong centre (bias) and a wide cloud (variance). Its square root has the units of \(\theta\) (the "root mean squared error").
  • (vi) Only unbiased estimators compete here; otherwise the constant estimator would always win with variance 0.
Proof of the bias–variance decomposition My proof — the script states it

Write \(m=\E[\hat\theta]\) (a fixed number). Add and subtract \(m\) inside the square:

\[ (\hat\theta-\theta)^2=\bigl((\hat\theta-m)+(m-\theta)\bigr)^2=(\hat\theta-m)^2+2(m-\theta)(\hat\theta-m)+(m-\theta)^2 , \]

by the binomial formula \((a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2\). Take expectations and use linearity; \(m-\theta\) is a constant, so it comes out of the expectation:

\[ \E[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]=\E[(\hat\theta-m)^2]+2(m-\theta)\,\E[\hat\theta-m]+(m-\theta)^2 . \]

The first term is \(\Var[\hat\theta]\) by definition (iii). In the middle, \(\E[\hat\theta-m]=\E[\hat\theta]-m=0\). The last term is \((\operatorname{bias}[\hat\theta])^2\) by definition (i). Hence \(\operatorname{mse}=\Var+\operatorname{bias}^2\). ∎

Numbers: an estimator with bias \(0.3\) and variance \(0.16\) has mse \(0.16+0.09=0.25\), i.e. a typical distance of \(\sqrt{0.25}=0.5\) from the truth.

The bias–variance tradeoff, as discussed in the script. The decomposition is often read as an inherent tradeoff. The argument: simple estimators or models (few parameters) often have large bias — they cannot fully capture \(\theta\); they "underfit" the data. Complex estimators or models (many parameters) can bring the bias down, but they increase the variance — they "move more to capture the observations"; they "overfit". This argument is plausible and nicely visualised in polynomial regression, but it does not necessarily hold, so there is no necessary tradeoff. Modern machine learning has shown that even extremely complex, overparameterised models can have low variance. One can reduce bias and variance, and thus the mse, simultaneously. In practice, especially in machine learning, one looks for an estimator that minimises the mse.

A simple case where both go down together: \(\bar X_n\) versus \(X_1\) for the mean. Both are unbiased, but \(\Var[\bar X_n]=\sigma^2/n\) is smaller — more data lowers variance without adding bias. The widget below shows genuine tradeoffs (dividing by \(n\) instead of \(n-1\)) and cases where one estimator wins on both counts.

A test for consistency: mse → 0 My addition — used again and again in exercises

Claim. If \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_n]\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\) (for every \(\theta\)), then \(\hat\theta_n\) is consistent. In particular: if \(\hat\theta_n\) is unbiased (or its bias tends to 0) and \(\Var[\hat\theta_n]\to0\), it is consistent.

Proof. Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). The event \(|\hat\theta_n-\theta|\ge\varepsilon\) is the same as \((\hat\theta_n-\theta)^2\ge\varepsilon^2\) (both sides are non-negative, so squaring keeps the order). Markov's inequality (§2.2: \(\P(Y\ge a)\le\E[Y]/a\) for \(Y\ge0\), \(a>0\)) with \(Y=(\hat\theta_n-\theta)^2\) gives

\[ \P(|\hat\theta_n-\theta|\ge\varepsilon)\le\frac{\E[(\hat\theta_n-\theta)^2]}{\varepsilon^2}=\frac{\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_n]}{\varepsilon^2}\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}0 . \]

By the bias–variance decomposition, \(\operatorname{mse}=\Var+\operatorname{bias}^2\to0\) when both parts go to 0. ∎

Warning. "Bias → 0" alone is not enough: \(X_1\) is unbiased for \(\mu\) and not consistent (Example 3.23). The variance must shrink too.

Example 3.21 properties of the sample mean Script 3.21

Setup. \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are iid real random variables with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2>0\). More precisely, \(X_1,\dots,X_n\sim\P_\theta\) iid, where \(\theta=(\mu,\sigma^2,\dots)\in\Theta\) is the true parameter, \(\mu\) is the mean and \(\sigma^2\) the variance of \(\P_\theta\). Neither \(\P_\theta\) nor any other distribution in the model needs to be Gaussian; \(\theta\) may contain further parameters describing other properties. The estimator is \(\hat\mu=\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum X_i\) for the parameter of interest \(\gamma(\theta)=\mu\).

  1. Unbiased: \(\E[\bar X_n]=\mu\). Reason: linearity, \(\E[\bar X_n]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\E[X_i]=\frac1n\cdot n\mu=\mu\).
  2. Strongly consistent: by the wlln and slln, \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow\P\mu\) and \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\mu\) (§2.4).
  3. Variance \(\Var[\bar X_n]=\sigma^2/n\), decreasing in \(n\) — as expected from the clt. Reason: primer box 3, \(\frac1{n^2}\cdot n\sigma^2\).
  4. mse: since \(\hat\mu\) is unbiased, \(\operatorname{mse}[\bar X_n]=\Var[\bar X_n]=\sigma^2/n\).
  5. Asymptotically normal with asymptotic variance \(V(\theta)=\sigma^2\), by the clt (§2.4: \(\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\)).
  6. Efficiency: \(\bar X_n\) is efficient (an mvue) for Gaussian models, but need not be for other distributions.

For (vi): the counterexample is Example 3.24. For \(\Unif(0,\theta)\), the mean is \(\mu=\frac\theta2\), and \(\frac{n+1}{2n}X_{(n)}\) is also unbiased for \(\mu\) with variance \(\frac14\cdot\frac{\theta^2}{n(n+2)}=\frac{\theta^2}{4n(n+2)}\), which is smaller than \(\Var[\bar X_n]=\frac{\theta^2}{12n}\) for every \(n\ge2\): dividing the two variances gives the factor \(\frac{\theta^2}{4n(n+2)}\big/\frac{\theta^2}{12n}=\frac{12n}{4n(n+2)}=\frac3{n+2}\), which is below 1 exactly when \(n>1\) (it equals \(\frac34\) at \(n=2\) and shrinks to 0 for large \(n\)). Related: among all weighted averages \(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_iX_i\) whose weights \(\lambda_i\) sum to 1 — all of them unbiased — the equal weights \(\frac1n\) give the smallest variance. That is Sheet 10 Ex 4, solved on §2.2. Its Jensen argument never uses the sign of the \(\lambda_i\) (the auxiliary random variable there may take negative values), so it covers every linear unbiased estimator, not only the convex combinations (\(\lambda_i\ge0\)) written down on the sheet: \(\bar X_n\) is the best linear unbiased estimator (a blue, Remark 3.26), even when it is not the best unbiased estimator overall.

Example 3.22 the sample variance Script 3.22

\(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). The sample variance [Stichprobenvarianz]

\[ S_n^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X_n)^2 \]

is an unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\): \(\E[S_n^2]=\sigma^2\). Dividing by \(n-1\) instead of \(n\) is called Bessel's correction. The "naive" estimator \(\hat\sigma^2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\) is biased: \(\E[\hat\sigma^2]=\frac{n-1}n\sigma^2<\sigma^2\). Both are consistent estimators of \(\sigma^2\).

Numbers with the subway data (\(n=8\), \(\bar x=6.25\)): the squared deviations \((x_i-6.25)^2\) add up to \(107.5\), so \(s^2=\frac{107.5}7\approx15.36\) and \(\hat\sigma^2=\frac{107.5}8\approx13.44\). Why \(\frac1n\) is too small: the deviations are measured from \(\bar X_n\), which is computed from the same data and therefore sits closer to the data than the true \(\mu\) does. The proof of \(\E[S_n^2]=\sigma^2\) is in Example 3.31(i) below.

Why both are consistent My proof — the script only states it

Step 1. From the identity in Example 3.31(i), divided by \(n\): \(\hat\sigma^2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)^2-(\bar X_n-\mu)^2\).

Step 2. The variables \(Y_i=(X_i-\mu)^2\) are iid with mean \(\E[Y_i]=\Var[X_i]=\sigma^2\). The lln for the \(Y_i\) (iid with finite mean, Theorem 2.62) gives \(\frac1n\sum Y_i\to\sigma^2\) almost surely.

Step 3. The lln for the \(X_i\) gives \(\bar X_n\to\mu\) almost surely, so \((\bar X_n-\mu)^2\to0\) almost surely (square of a sequence tending to 0).

Step 4. Outside a probability-0 event both limits hold at once (the union of two null sets is a null set), so by the ordinary limit rules for number sequences (Analysis 2.2, limit rules), \(\hat\sigma^2\to\sigma^2-0=\sigma^2\) almost surely: strongly consistent, hence consistent (a.s. ⟹ in probability, Remark 2.57).

Step 5. \(S_n^2=\frac n{n-1}\hat\sigma^2\) and the numbers \(\frac n{n-1}=\frac1{1-1/n}\to\frac1{1-0}=1\) (divide top and bottom by \(n\), then \(\frac1n\to0\) and the quotient rule for limits, Analysis 2.2), so \(S_n^2\to1\cdot\sigma^2\) almost surely as well. ∎

Example 3.23 biased but consistent, unbiased but not consistent Script 3.23

\(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2>0\). Bias and consistency are independent of each other:

  • Biased but consistent: \(\hat\mu_n=\bar X_n+\frac1n\). Then \(\E[\hat\mu_n]=\E[\bar X_n]+\frac1n=\mu+\frac1n\ne\mu\): biased. By the wlln (Theorem 2.61) \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow\P\mu\), and \(\frac1n\to0\) (Analysis 2.2, limit rules), so \(\hat\mu_n\) is consistent. (Precisely: \(\hat\mu_n-\mu=(\bar X_n-\mu)+\frac1n\), a sum of two sequences that go to 0 in probability — a constant sequence of numbers tending to 0 does so trivially — and Sheet 9 Ex 3(i) on §2.4 says sums preserve convergence in probability.)
  • Unbiased but not consistent: \(\tilde\mu_n=X_1\) (ignore all data except the first observation). Then \(\E[\tilde\mu_n]=\E[X_1]=\mu\): unbiased. But \(\P(|\tilde\mu_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)=\P(|X_1-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\) does not depend on \(n\), and since \(\Var[X_1]=\sigma^2>0\), \(X_1\) is not almost surely equal to the constant \(\mu\). So for some \(\varepsilon>0\) this probability is a fixed positive number, not tending to 0: not consistent.

Detail for the second bullet: if \(\P(|X_1-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)=0\) held for every \(\varepsilon>0\), then \(X_1=\mu\) almost surely (take \(\varepsilon=\frac1k\) for all \(k\) and use that a countable union of null sets is null), and then \(\Var[X_1]=0\) — contradiction. Concretely, for a fair die (\(\mu=3.5\)) and \(\varepsilon=1\): \(\P(|X_1-3.5|\ge1)=\P(X_1\in\{1,2,5,6\})=\frac46\) for every \(n\).

Widget — bias, variance and mse by simulation My addition

4000 simulated data sets of size \(n\) (seeded). Each gives one estimate; the histogram shows the cloud of estimates, the vertical line the true value (1). The readout compares the simulated bias, variance and mse with the exact formulas from Examples 3.24 and 3.31 — and checks that mse = bias² + variance. (The histogram only draws the plotted range; for very small \(n\) a few estimates of \(\sigma^2\) land to the right of it. They are still counted in the readout, which uses all 4000 values.)

Example 3.24 an mvue for the uniform distribution Script 3.24

An iid sample \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) from the model \((\R,\mathcal B,(\Unif(0,\theta))_{\theta>0})\), so \(\Theta=\R_{>0}\). This is the subway model of Example 3.5(v) (§3.1): we want the maximum waiting time \(\theta\), and we look for an estimator with good properties.

  1. Naive: twice the sample mean. \(\bar X_n\) is an unbiased, strongly consistent, asymptotically normal estimator of \(\E[X_i]=\theta/2\) (Example 3.21). By linearity, \(\hat\theta_1:=2\bar X_n\) has the same properties as an estimator of \(\theta\). Its variance: \[ \Var[\hat\theta_1]=\Var[2\bar X_n]=4\Var[\bar X_n]=\frac{4\Var[X_1]}n=\frac4n\cdot\frac{\theta^2}{12}=\frac{\theta^2}{3n} . \] (Steps: \(\Var[aX]=a^2\Var[X]\) with \(a=2\); \(\Var[\bar X_n]=\Var[X_1]/n\); \(\Var[X_1]=\theta^2/12\) for \(\Unif(0,\theta)\).)
  2. A "better" estimator: the rescaled maximum. In the exercises (Sheet 10 Ex 1, below) the maximum likelihood estimator is \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=X_{(n)}=\max\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}\), with \(\E[X_{(n)}]=\frac n{n+1}\theta\). So \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\) is biased. Rescaling gives an unbiased estimator \[ \hat\theta_2:=\frac{n+1}nX_{(n)},\qquad \E[\hat\theta_2]=\frac{n+1}n\cdot\frac n{n+1}\theta=\theta . \] For its variance we first need \(\Var[X_{(n)}]\). With the density \(p_{X_{(n)}}(y)=\frac{ny^{n-1}}{\theta^n}\) on \([0,\theta]\) (derived in Sheet 10 Ex 1; the integral uses the power rule \(\int y^m\,\mathrm dy=\frac{y^{m+1}}{m+1}\), Analysis 8.3): \[ \E[X_{(n)}^2]=\int_0^\theta y^2\,\frac{ny^{n-1}}{\theta^n}\,\mathrm dy=\frac n{\theta^n}\int_0^\theta y^{n+1}\,\mathrm dy=\frac n{\theta^n}\cdot\frac{\theta^{n+2}}{n+2}=\frac n{n+2}\theta^2 . \] So \[ \Var[X_{(n)}]=\E[X_{(n)}^2]-(\E[X_{(n)}])^2=\frac n{n+2}\theta^2-\Bigl(\frac n{n+1}\theta\Bigr)^2=\frac{n\theta^2}{(n+2)(n+1)^2}, \] and therefore \[ \Var[\hat\theta_2]=\frac{(n+1)^2}{n^2}\Var[X_{(n)}]=\frac{\theta^2}{n(n+2)} . \] For every \(n>1\) we have \(n(n+2)>3n\), so \(\Var[\hat\theta_2]<\Var[\hat\theta_1]\). Hence \(\hat\theta_1=2\bar X_n\) is unbiased but not the mvue. We say \(\hat\theta_2\) is more efficient than \(\hat\theta_1\).

In fact \(\hat\theta_2\) is the unique mvue for \(\theta\) (the script states this without proof). The sample mean is often "good", but sometimes not the "best".

Algebra filled in. The variance step: put both terms over the common denominator \((n+2)(n+1)^2\): \(\frac{n\theta^2[(n+1)^2-n(n+2)]}{(n+2)(n+1)^2}\), and \((n+1)^2-n(n+2)=n^2+2n+1-n^2-2n=1\). Then \(\frac{(n+1)^2}{n^2}\cdot\frac{n\theta^2}{(n+2)(n+1)^2}=\frac{\theta^2}{n(n+2)}\). The comparison: \(n(n+2)>3n\iff n+2>3\iff n>1\) (divide by \(n>0\)). For \(n=1\) the two estimators coincide (\(2X_1\)).

Numbers (\(\theta=1\)): for \(n=10\), \(\Var[\hat\theta_1]=\frac1{30}\approx0.0333\) and \(\Var[\hat\theta_2]=\frac1{120}\approx0.0083\) — four times smaller. The first shrinks like \(\frac1n\), the second like \(\frac1{n^2}\): far faster than the \(\frac1n\) rate of Example 3.21. For the subway data, \(\hat\theta_1=12.5\) and \(\hat\theta_2=\frac98\cdot12=13.5\).

The mse of the mle itself (useful for SoSe26 P1e below). By the bias–variance decomposition, with \(\operatorname{bias}[X_{(n)}]=\frac n{n+1}\theta-\theta=-\frac\theta{n+1}\): \[ \operatorname{mse}[X_{(n)}]=\frac{n\theta^2}{(n+2)(n+1)^2}+\frac{\theta^2}{(n+1)^2}=\frac{(n+n+2)\theta^2}{(n+2)(n+1)^2}=\frac{2\theta^2}{(n+1)(n+2)} . \] Compare \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_2]=\frac{\theta^2}{n(n+2)}\): the mle is worse whenever \(\frac2{n+1}>\frac1n\iff2n>n+1\iff n>1\). For \(n=2\): \(\frac16\theta^2\approx0.167\theta^2\) versus \(\frac18\theta^2=0.125\theta^2\).

In words: for the subway interval, "twice the average" and "the enlarged maximum" are both right on average, but the enlarged maximum scatters far less, so it is the better estimator; the plain maximum (the mle) is slightly too small on average.

Example 3.25 the James–Stein estimator Script 3.25

Setup. One observation \(X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,I_d)\) from a \(d\)-dimensional normal distribution: \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_d)\) with independent coordinates \(X_j\sim\mathcal N(\mu_j,1)\) (\(I_d\) is the \(d\times d\) identity matrix — 1 on the diagonal, 0 elsewhere, B5 — used as the covariance matrix; zero covariances mean independent coordinates for Gaussian vectors, §2.3). We want the unknown mean vector \(\mu\in\R^d\).

The standard estimator \(\hat\mu(X)=X\) (unbiased, and also the mle) has

\[ \operatorname{mse}[\hat\mu]=\E[\|X-\mu\|^2]=\sum_{j=1}^d\E[(X_j-\mu_j)^2]=\sum_{j=1}^d\Var[X_j]=d . \]

(The script writes "\(=\dots=d\)"; the filled-in steps: the squared length is the sum of squared coordinates, linearity of expectation, and each coordinate has mean \(\mu_j\) and variance 1.)

For dimensions \(d\ge3\), the biased James–Stein shrinkage estimator is

\[ \hat\mu_{\text{js}}=\Bigl(1-\frac{d-2}{\|X\|^2}\Bigr)X . \]

It shrinks the observation \(X\) towards the origin (multiplies it by a factor below 1). The remarkable result: it has uniformly lower risk than the mle, \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\mu_{\text{js}}]<d\) for all \(\mu\in\R^d\).

Small caveat on the word "shrinks" (my addition): the factor \(1-\frac{d-2}{\|X\|^2}\) is below 1, but it is negative when \(\|X\|^2<d-2\), so in that case the estimator does not stop at the origin — it flips to the opposite side. That is why statisticians usually use the "positive-part" version \(\max\bigl\{0,\,1-\frac{d-2}{\|X\|^2}\bigr\}X\), which has an even smaller mse. The script states the plain version; the conclusion \(\operatorname{mse}<d\) is true for both.

This is paradoxical: wherever the mean of the Gaussian really is, shrinking towards the origin improves the estimate. One can also show that shrinking in any other direction improves it as well — even more surprising. The script refers to the Wikipedia page for why this makes sense.

Numbers (my simulation, 200 000 repetitions, \(d=10\)): with \(\mu=0\) the James–Stein mse is \(\approx2.0\) (exactly 2 by a known formula), with \(\|\mu\|=3\) it is \(\approx6.0\), with \(\|\mu\|=10\) it is \(\approx9.4\) — always below the mle's 10, with the biggest gain near the origin. "Any other direction" is best read as: shrinking towards any fixed point \(\nu\), i.e. \(\nu+\bigl(1-\frac{d-2}{\|X-\nu\|^2}\bigr)(X-\nu)\), also beats \(X\). The lesson for this page: the mle, although unbiased here, does not have the smallest mse (SoSe26 P1e).

Maximum likelihood estimation

Remark 3.26 constructing estimators Script 3.26

So far it looked as if we must "come up with" estimators by hand and then check their properties. But there are general procedures to construct estimators with certain properties, and a large statistical literature on when and how one can obtain mvues or blues (best linear unbiased estimators — the smallest variance among unbiased estimators that are linear combinations \(\sum_ic_iX_i\) of the data) etc. So it is less guesswork than it seemed. Still, finding better estimators for very specific settings is an active research area. We now see one general procedure.

A blue you have already met: Sheet 10 Ex 4 (§2.2) shows that among all unbiased weighted averages \(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_iX_i\) (unbiased means \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\)), the plain mean \(\bar X_n\) has the smallest variance.

Definition 3.27 maximum likelihood estimation (mle) Script 3.27

The maximum likelihood estimator [Maximum-Likelihood-Schätzer] \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\) is the value of \(\theta\in\Theta\) that maximises the likelihood function \(L(\theta\mid x)\):

\[ \hat\theta_{\text{mle}}(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta\in\Theta}L(\theta\mid x)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta\in\Theta}\ell(\theta\mid x) . \]

Maximising the log-likelihood is often mathematically simpler. If \(\ell(\theta\mid x)\) is differentiable and the maximum lies in the interior of \(\Theta\), \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\) can often be found by solving the likelihood equation \(\nabla_\theta\,\ell(\theta\mid x)=0\) for \(\theta\).

"Interior" [Inneres] (my addition): a point of \(\Theta\) is an interior point if you can move a little in every direction and still stay inside \(\Theta\) — in \(\R\): a small interval \((\theta-\varepsilon,\theta+\varepsilon)\) around it lies in \(\Theta\); in \(\R^k\): a small ball around it does. Example: the interior of \(\Theta=[0,1]\) is \((0,1)\); the endpoints 0 and 1 are boundary points, and there the slope of \(\ell\) need not be 0 (see Sheet 10 Ex 1 below, where the maximum sits at the boundary). More: interior and boundary.

Each part explained (mine).

  • The idea. Look at the data you actually got. For each candidate \(\theta\), ask: "if this were the truth, how probable (or how dense) would exactly these data be?" That number is \(L(\theta\mid x)\). Pick the \(\theta\) that makes your data least surprising.
  • \(\operatorname{arg\,max}_{\theta\in\Theta}f(\theta)\) is the set of all \(\theta\) where \(f\) reaches its largest value (the "argument of the maximum", as opposed to the maximum value itself). It is written with "\(\in\)" because there may be several maximisers (then any one of them is an mle) — or none (then no mle exists).
  • The two arg max sets are equal because \(\ln\) is strictly increasing (primer box 2).
  • \(\nabla_\theta\ell\) is the gradient: for one parameter just the derivative \(\frac{\mathrm d\ell}{\mathrm d\theta}\), for several the vector of partial derivatives (primer box 1). The likelihood equation finds candidates; you still have to check that the candidate is the global maximum (second derivative or sign check), and remember cases where the maximum is at the edge of \(\Theta\) or where \(\ell\) is not differentiable (uniform model).
  • The estimate \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}(x)\) depends on the data; plugging in the random sample \(X\) instead of \(x\) gives the estimator \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}(X)\).

Small example (mine): the coin data 1, 0, 1 of primer box 2. Candidate values: \(L(0.5)=0.125\), \(L(\frac23)\approx0.148\), \(L(0.9)=0.081\). The maximiser is \(\hat p=\frac23\), the fraction of ones.

Recipe: deriving an mle in an exam My addition

  1. Write the likelihood for iid data: \(L(\theta\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i\mid\theta)\). Keep the indicator functions if the support depends on \(\theta\) (uniform-type models!).
  2. If \(L>0\) on the relevant \(\theta\)-range, take logs: \(\ell=\sum_i\ln p(x_i\mid\theta)\). Terms without \(\theta\) are constants and can be dropped.
  3. Differentiate in \(\theta\), set \(\ell'(\theta)=0\), solve.
  4. Check it is a maximum: \(\ell''<0\) at the candidate, or better the sign of \(\ell'\) on both sides (global maximum).
  5. If the support depends on \(\theta\): no derivative; find where \(L=0\), and where \(L\) is increasing/decreasing; the maximum is usually at the boundary (the sample max or min).
  6. Write the answer as an estimator with capital letters, e.g. \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}=\bar X_n\).

Widget — the log-likelihood and its slope My addition

The curve is \(\ell(\theta\mid x)\) for the data shown in the readout. Move the parameter: the short line is the tangent, its slope is \(\ell'(\theta)\). Where the slope is 0 sits the mle (dashed line). "Data ×4" repeats the same data four times: the maximiser stays put but the curve becomes sharper — more data, more certainty.

Example 3.28 mle for the Gaussian Script 3.28

From Example 3.15 (§3.1), for an iid sample \(X_1,\dots,X_n\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\):

\[ \ell(\mu,\sigma^2\mid x)=-\frac n2\ln(2\pi)-\frac n2\ln(\sigma^2)-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2 . \]

(Where it comes from: the density of one observation is \((2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\exp\bigl(-\frac{(x_i-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\bigr)\). Its log is \(-\frac12\ln(2\pi)-\frac12\ln\sigma^2-\frac{(x_i-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\) by the rules of primer box 2; sum over \(i\).)

We maximise over \(\theta=(\mu,\sigma^2)\). Derivative in \(\mu\) (with \(\sigma^2\) fixed). Only the last term contains \(\mu\); by the chain rule, \(\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu}(x_i-\mu)^2=2(x_i-\mu)\cdot(-1)\):

\[ \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mu}=-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n2(x_i-\mu)(-1)=\frac1{\sigma^2}\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^nx_i-n\mu\Bigr) . \]

Setting this to zero gives \(\sum x_i-n\mu=0\), so

\[ \hat\mu_{\text{mle}}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nx_i=\bar x_n . \]

Derivative in \(\sigma^2\). Treat \(v=\sigma^2\) as the variable (not \(\sigma\)!). \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dv}\ln v=\frac1v\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dv}\frac1v=-\frac1{v^2}\):

\[ \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\sigma^2}=-\frac n{2\sigma^2}+\frac1{2(\sigma^2)^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2 . \]

Setting it to zero (and multiplying by 2) gives \(-\frac n{\sigma^2}+\frac1{(\sigma^2)^2}\sum(x_i-\mu)^2=0\), so \(\sigma^2=\frac1n\sum(x_i-\mu)^2\). Plugging in \(\hat\mu_{\text{mle}}\) for \(\mu\):

\[ \hat\sigma^2_{\text{mle}}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x_n)^2 . \]

As noted before, \(\hat\mu_{\text{mle}}\) is unbiased (it is the sample mean), but \(\hat\sigma^2_{\text{mle}}\) is biased (Example 3.22).

Why this critical point is the global maximum My addition — the script only solves the equations

In \(\mu\). For any fixed \(v=\sigma^2\), \(\ell\) depends on \(\mu\) only through \(-\frac1{2v}\sum(x_i-\mu)^2\), a downward parabola in \(\mu\). Its peak is where the derivative vanishes, \(\mu=\bar x_n\) — the same for every \(v\). So \(\ell(\mu,v)\le\ell(\bar x_n,v)\) for all \(\mu\).

In \(v\). Write \(Q=\sum(x_i-\bar x_n)^2\) (assume \(Q>0\), i.e. not all data equal). Then \(f(v)=\ell(\bar x_n,v)=\text{const}-\frac n2\ln v-\frac Q{2v}\) and \(f'(v)=-\frac n{2v}+\frac Q{2v^2}=\frac{Q-nv}{2v^2}\). This is positive for \(v<\frac Qn\) and negative for \(v>\frac Qn\) (sign check, primer box 1): global maximum at \(\hat v=\frac Qn\).

Together: \(\ell(\mu,v)\le\ell(\bar x_n,v)\le\ell(\bar x_n,\hat v)\) for all \((\mu,v)\). This also justifies "plugging \(\hat\mu_{\text{mle}}\) in for \(\mu\)". ∎

Example 3.29 mles for common distributions Script 3.29

For an iid sample \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) from the respective distribution. In general, an mle need not have a closed-form expression; then it has to be computed numerically.

  1. Bernoulli \(\Ber(p)\): \(\hat p_{\text{mle}}(X)=\frac1n\sum X_i=\bar X_n\).
  2. Poisson \(\Poi(\lambda)\): \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}(X)=\bar X_n\). Derived in SoSe25 P4a below.
  3. Exponential \(\Exp(\lambda)\): \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}(X)=\frac1{\bar X_n}\). Derived in Sheet 10 Ex 2 below.
  4. Gaussian \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\): \(\hat\mu_{\text{mle}}(X)=\bar X_n\) and \(\hat\sigma^2_{\text{mle}}(X)=\frac1n\sum(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\) (Example 3.28).
  5. Uniform \(\Unif(0,\theta)\): \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}(X)=X_{(n)}=\max\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}\). Derived in Sheet 10 Ex 1 below.
Derivation of (i) My derivation

The pmf of \(\Ber(p)\) is \(p(x\mid p)=p^x(1-p)^{1-x}\) for \(x\in\{0,1\}\) (it gives \(p\) for \(x=1\) and \(1-p\) for \(x=0\)). Let \(k=\sum x_i\) be the number of ones. Then

\[ L(p\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^np^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i}=p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}, \]

because exponents add when multiplying equal bases. For \(0<p<1\): \(\ell(p)=k\ln p+(n-k)\ln(1-p)\), and by the chain rule \((\ln(1-p))'=\frac{-1}{1-p}\):

\[ \ell'(p)=\frac kp-\frac{n-k}{1-p}=\frac{k(1-p)-(n-k)p}{p(1-p)}=\frac{k-np}{p(1-p)} . \]

The denominator is positive, so \(\ell'(p)>0\) for \(p<\frac kn\) and \(\ell'(p)<0\) for \(p>\frac kn\): global maximum at \(\hat p=\frac kn=\bar x_n\). Edge cases: if \(k=0\), \(L(p)=(1-p)^n\) is largest at \(p=0=\bar x_n\); if \(k=n\), \(L(p)=p^n\) is largest at \(p=1=\bar x_n\). So the formula holds in all cases (with \(\Theta=[0,1]\)).

Properties of the mle

Remark 3.30 properties of mles Script 3.30

For finite \(n\) we cannot give many general guarantees for mles (see Example 3.24: the mle \(X_{(n)}\) is biased). But under fairly mild regularity conditions — which hold for most common models, and which we always assume — mles have desirable properties as \(n\to\infty\):

  1. Consistency: \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\xrightarrow\P\theta\).
  2. Asymptotic normality: \(\sqrt n(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}-\theta)\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,V(\theta))\), where \(V(\theta)=I(\theta)^{-1}\) and \(I(\theta)\) is the Fisher information (matrix) — an extremely important object in statistics which the course does not have time to cover (a glimpse is in Overview 3.32).
  3. Asymptotic efficiency: mles achieve the lowest possible variance among a large class of estimators as \(n\to\infty\).
  4. Invariance: if \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\) is the mle of \(\theta\) and \(g\) is a function, then \(g(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}})\) is the mle of \(g(\theta)\) (provided \(g\) does not reduce the dimensionality of \(\Theta\)). For instance, for a normal distribution the mle of the standard deviation \(\sigma\) is \(\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2_{\text{mle}}}\).

Reading note on \(V(\theta)\) versus \(I(\theta)\). Two things to keep apart.

  • Inverse, not the thing itself. The script's sentence "where \(V(\theta)=I(\theta)^{-1}\) is the Fisher information matrix" reads as if \(V(\theta)\) were the Fisher information. It is its inverse: \(I(\theta)\) is the Fisher information, and the asymptotic variance is \(V(\theta)=I(\theta)^{-1}\) (for a single parameter simply \(V=1/I\)). So a large Fisher information — much information about \(\theta\) in the data — means a small asymptotic variance, which is the sensible direction.
  • One observation or all \(n\)? The script writes \(I(\theta)\) with the log-likelihood \(\ell(\theta\mid x)\), which elsewhere in §3.1 means the log-likelihood of the whole sample, but describes it as the information "an observable random variable \(X\) carries", which points at a single observation. The two readings differ by the factor \(n\): for iid data the log-likelihoods add, so \(I_n(\theta)=n\,I_1(\theta)\), where \(I_1\) uses one observation. On this page I always write \(I_1(\theta)\) for the one-observation version. Both statements in the script are then correct with the reading that fits them: \(V(\theta)=I_1(\theta)^{-1}\) here in Remark 3.30(ii), and \(\Var[\hat\theta]\ge1/I_n(\theta)=1/(n\,I_1(\theta))\) for the Cramér–Rao bound in Overview 3.32 (an estimator built from all \(n\) observations cannot be bounded using the information in one of them). The two fit together: \(\Var[\hat\theta_n]\approx\frac{V(\theta)}n=\frac1{n\,I_1(\theta)}\).

Examples for (i) and (ii). Poisson: \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}=\bar X_n\to\lambda\) by the lln, and by the clt \(\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\lambda)\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,\lambda)\), so \(V(\lambda)=\lambda\) (SoSe25 P4c). Uniform: the regularity conditions fail (the support \([0,\theta]\) moves with \(\theta\)); \(X_{(n)}\) is still consistent (Sheet 10 Ex 1 below), but its error shrinks like \(\frac1n\), not like \(\frac1{\sqrt n}\). So \(\sqrt n(X_{(n)}-\theta)\to0\) (a useless, degenerate limit), and with the right scaling \(n(\theta-X_{(n)})\) the limit is an exponential distribution, not a normal one: from Sheet 10 Ex 1, \(\P(n(\theta-X_{(n)})>s)=\bigl(1-\frac s{n\theta}\bigr)^n\to e^{-s/\theta}\) for \(s\ge0\).

Why invariance holds for a one-to-one \(g\) My proof

Let \(g\) be a bijection from \(\Theta\) onto a set \(H\), and write \(\eta=g(\theta)\) (eta) for the new parameter. The same model, described by \(\eta\), has likelihood \(L^*(\eta\mid x)=L(g^{-1}(\eta)\mid x)\): the distribution labelled \(\eta\) is the one labelled \(\theta=g^{-1}(\eta)\). As \(\eta\) runs through \(H\), \(g^{-1}(\eta)\) runs through all of \(\Theta\), so \(L^*\) takes exactly the same values as \(L\), just relabelled. The largest value is reached at \(\eta\) with \(g^{-1}(\eta)=\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\), i.e. at \(\hat\eta=g(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}})\). ∎

Example: for \(\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^2}\) (a bijection of \((0,\infty)\)), the mle of \(\sigma\) is \(\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2_{\text{mle}}}\). For SoSe26 P5b below, \(g\) is the affine map \(p\mapsto rp+\frac{1-r}2\). The condition "does not reduce dimensionality" rules out things like \(g(\mu,\sigma^2)=\mu\); for such \(g\) the statement is usually taken as a definition of the mle of \(g(\theta)\).

In words: with lots of data, the mle homes in on the truth, its errors look normal and are as small as they can be; and to estimate a function of the parameter, you may simply apply that function to the mle. For small samples none of this is promised.

Example 3.31 variance estimation: unbiased versus mle Script 3.31

Continuing Example 3.22, compare \(S_n^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\) and \(\hat\sigma^2=\frac1n\sum(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\) as estimators of \(\sigma^2\). The first is unbiased in any model; the second is the mle in a Gaussian model. Both are estimators of \(\sigma^2\) in any model ("anything is a valid estimator").

(i) The expectation. A key algebraic identity (write \(X_i-\bar X_n=(X_i-\mu)-(\bar X_n-\mu)\)):

\[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X_n)^2&=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl((X_i-\mu)-(\bar X_n-\mu)\bigr)^2\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)^2-2(\bar X_n-\mu)\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)+n(\bar X_n-\mu)^2\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)^2-2n(\bar X_n-\mu)^2+n(\bar X_n-\mu)^2\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)^2-n(\bar X_n-\mu)^2 . \end{aligned} \]

Line by line: (1) insert \(\pm\mu\); (2) expand \((a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2\) inside the sum; the factor \(\bar X_n-\mu\) does not depend on \(i\), so it comes out of the sum, and \(\sum_{i=1}^nb^2=nb^2\); (3) \(\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)=\sum X_i-n\mu=n\bar X_n-n\mu=n(\bar X_n-\mu)\); (4) collect \(-2n+n=-n\).

Taking expectations and using linearity:

\[ \E\Bigl[\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\Bigr]=\sum_{i=1}^n\E[(X_i-\mu)^2]-n\E[(\bar X_n-\mu)^2]=\sum_{i=1}^n\Var[X_i]-n\Var[\bar X_n]=n\sigma^2-n\frac{\sigma^2}n=(n-1)\sigma^2 . \]

(\(\E[(X_i-\mu)^2]=\Var[X_i]\) because \(\mu=\E[X_i]\); \(\E[(\bar X_n-\mu)^2]=\Var[\bar X_n]\) because \(\mu=\E[\bar X_n]\). Only "iid with finite variance" is used — no normality.)

(ii) Bias. \(\E[\hat\sigma^2]=\frac1n\E\bigl[\sum(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\bigr]=\frac{n-1}n\sigma^2\): biased (bias \(-\frac{\sigma^2}n\)). \(\E[S_n^2]=\frac1{n-1}\E\bigl[\sum(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\bigr]=\sigma^2\): unbiased. This is where Bessel's correction comes from. Does this mean \(S_n^2\) is better?

(iii) mse for normal data. Now let \(X_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\). One can compute (the script skips it) \(\Var[S_n^2]=\frac{2\sigma^4}{n-1}\). Since \(S_n^2\) is unbiased,

\[ \operatorname{mse}[S_n^2]=\Var[S_n^2]=\frac{2\sigma^4}{n-1} . \]

For \(\hat\sigma^2\) (also skipped in the script):

\[ \operatorname{mse}[\hat\sigma^2]=\Var[\hat\sigma^2]+(\operatorname{bias}[\hat\sigma^2])^2=\frac{2(n-1)\sigma^4}{n^2}+\Bigl(-\frac{\sigma^2}n\Bigr)^2=\frac{(2n-1)\sigma^4}{n^2} . \]

Since \(\frac2{n-1}>\frac{2n-1}{n^2}\) for all \(n>1\), \(\hat\sigma^2\) has the better (smaller) mse. This is a classic example supporting the bias–variance tradeoff idea: accepting a small bias reduces the variance enough to improve the overall mse.

Checks. \(\Var[\hat\sigma^2]=\bigl(\frac{n-1}n\bigr)^2\Var[S_n^2]=\frac{(n-1)^2}{n^2}\cdot\frac{2\sigma^4}{n-1}=\frac{2(n-1)\sigma^4}{n^2}\) (since \(\hat\sigma^2=\frac{n-1}nS_n^2\)); adding \(\frac{\sigma^4}{n^2}\) gives \(\frac{(2n-2+1)\sigma^4}{n^2}\). The inequality: \(\frac2{n-1}>\frac{2n-1}{n^2}\iff2n^2>(2n-1)(n-1)=2n^2-3n+1\iff3n>1\). Numbers for \(n=5\), \(\sigma^2=1\): \(0.5\) versus \(0.36\). Even better is dividing by \(n+1\): mse \(\frac{2\sigma^4}{n+1}\), i.e. \(0.333\) for \(n=5\) — the smallest mse among all estimators of the form \(c\sum(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\) (proof below). Try all three in the widget above.

Proof of \(\Var[S_n^2]=\frac{2\sigma^4}{n-1}\) for normal data My proof — the script skips it

Shifting all \(X_i\) by the same constant does not change \(S_n^2\), so assume \(\mu=0\). Write \(\mu_4=\E[X_i^4]\) (the fourth moment), \(A=\sum_iX_i^2\), \(B=(\sum_iX_i)^2\). By the identity in (i) with \(\mu=0\): \(Q:=\sum(X_i-\bar X_n)^2=A-\frac Bn\).

Three expectations. Expand the products into sums over indices. A term \(\E[X_iX_jX_kX_l]\) vanishes whenever some index appears exactly once (independence splits off a factor \(\E[X_i]=0\)). The surviving terms:

  • \(\E[A^2]=\sum_i\E[X_i^4]+\sum_{i\ne j}\E[X_i^2]\E[X_j^2]=n\mu_4+n(n-1)\sigma^4\).
  • \(\E[AB]=\sum_i\sum_{j,k}\E[X_i^2X_jX_k]\): only \(j=k\) survives, giving \(\sum_i\sum_j\E[X_i^2X_j^2]=n\mu_4+n(n-1)\sigma^4\).
  • \(\E[B^2]=\sum_{i,j,k,l}\E[X_iX_jX_kX_l]\): all four indices equal (\(n\) terms, each \(\mu_4\)) or two different indices each appearing twice (\(3n(n-1)\) ordered tuples: 3 ways to pair up the four positions, \(n(n-1)\) ways to choose the two indices), so \(\E[B^2]=n\mu_4+3n(n-1)\sigma^4\).

Combine. \(\E[Q^2]=\E[A^2]-\frac2n\E[AB]+\frac1{n^2}\E[B^2] =\bigl(n\mu_4+n(n-1)\sigma^4\bigr)\frac{n-2}n+\frac{\mu_4+3(n-1)\sigma^4}n =\frac{(n-1)^2}n\mu_4+\frac{(n-1)(n^2-2n+3)}n\sigma^4\). With \(\E[Q]=(n-1)\sigma^2\) from (i):

\[ \Var[Q]=\E[Q^2]-(n-1)^2\sigma^4=\frac{(n-1)^2}n\mu_4-\frac{(n-1)(n-3)}n\sigma^4 ,\qquad \Var[S_n^2]=\frac{\Var[Q]}{(n-1)^2}=\frac{\mu_4}n-\frac{(n-3)\sigma^4}{n(n-1)} . \]

This holds for any iid data with finite fourth moment. For the normal distribution \(\mu_4=3\sigma^4\) (a standard fact, e.g. from the fourth derivative of the characteristic function \(e^{-\sigma^2t^2/2}\), §2.3), so \(\Var[S_n^2]=\frac{\sigma^4}n\bigl(3-\frac{n-3}{n-1}\bigr)=\frac{\sigma^4}n\cdot\frac{2n}{n-1}=\frac{2\sigma^4}{n-1}\). ∎

Best divisor. For an estimator \(cQ\): \(\operatorname{mse}(c)=c^2\E[Q^2]-2c\sigma^2\E[Q]+\sigma^4\), a parabola in \(c\) with minimum at \(c^*=\frac{\sigma^2\E[Q]}{\E[Q^2]}\). For normal data \(\E[Q^2]=\Var[Q]+(\E Q)^2=2(n-1)\sigma^4+(n-1)^2\sigma^4=(n-1)(n+1)\sigma^4\), so \(c^*=\frac{(n-1)\sigma^4}{(n-1)(n+1)\sigma^4}=\frac1{n+1}\), with mse \(\sigma^4\bigl(1-\frac{n-1}{n+1}\bigr)=\frac{2\sigma^4}{n+1}\).

In words: dividing the sum of squared deviations by \(n-1\) makes the variance estimate right on average; dividing by \(n\) (the Gaussian mle) makes it a little too small on average but less jumpy, and for normal data that trade makes its mean squared error smaller.

Widget — consistency: does the estimate settle? My addition

Five independent data streams from \(\mathcal N(1,1)\) (true \(\mu=1\), \(\sigma^2=1\)). For each stream the estimate is recomputed after every new observation, \(n=1,\dots,2000\) (log-scaled axis). Consistent estimators enter the band "truth \(\pm\varepsilon\)" and stay; \(X_1\) never moves.

Overview 3.32 outlook on point estimation Script 3.32

Maximum likelihood is a general principle for constructing estimators with good asymptotic properties. There is a rich classical theory for finding and evaluating estimators, especially optimal estimators for finite samples, which the course has no time to cover. It shows the limits of estimation and how to construct optimal estimators systematically. A brief glimpse of the central concepts:

  • Fisher information \[ I(\theta)=\E\Bigl[\Bigl(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\ell(\theta\mid X)\Bigr)^2\,\Big|\,\theta\Bigr]=-\E\Bigl[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\ell(\theta\mid X)\,\Big|\,\theta\Bigr] \] quantifies how much information an observable random variable \(X\) carries about the unknown \(\theta\). (The second equality needs regularity conditions.) So the Fisher information is the variance of the score \(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\ell(\theta\mid x)\), and can also be written as the negative expected second derivative (the Hessian matrix of second derivatives for vector \(\theta\), Analysis 11.3).
  • Cramér–Rao lower bound (crlb): for any unbiased estimator \(\hat\theta\), \(\Var[\hat\theta]\ge1/I(\theta)\). The Fisher information limits how precise an estimator can be. (Here \(I(\theta)\) is the Fisher information of the whole sample the estimator is built from; for iid data that is \(I_n(\theta)=n\,I_1(\theta)\), so the bound reads \(\Var[\hat\theta]\ge\frac1{n\,I_1(\theta)}\) and shrinks like \(\frac1n\) — see the reading note in Remark 3.30.)
  • Efficient estimator: an unbiased estimator whose variance attains the crlb; it is then an mvue. Every efficient estimator is an mvue, but an mvue may exist even if no estimator reaches the crlb (lots of room for research).
  • Sufficiency: a statistic \(T(X)\) is sufficient if it captures all information about \(\theta\) in the sample. The Rao–Blackwell theorem improves any unbiased estimator by conditioning it on a sufficient statistic (taking its conditional expectation given that statistic, §2.1), which often leads to an mvue.
  • blue: the mvue within the class of linear estimators. The Gauss–Markov theorem says the ordinary least squares estimator is the blue for linear regression models under certain assumptions.

    What is linear regression / least squares? (my addition; outlook, not examined) You observe pairs \((x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_n,y_n)\) — say hours studied \(x_i\) and exam points \(y_i\) — and model \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i\): a straight line with unknown intercept \(\beta_0\) and slope \(\beta_1\) (the parameters), plus random errors \(\varepsilon_i\) with mean 0. Ordinary least squares (OLS) [Methode der kleinsten Quadrate] estimates \(\beta_0,\beta_1\) by the line that makes the sum of squared vertical distances \(\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2\) as small as possible. Example: the points \((0,1),(1,2),(2,3)\) lie exactly on \(y=1+x\), so OLS gives \(\hat\beta_0=1,\hat\beta_1=1\) with sum of squares 0. The resulting estimators are linear in the \(y_i\), and Gauss–Markov says no other linear unbiased estimator has smaller variance (if the errors are uncorrelated with equal variance). The fitted slope equals \(\operatorname{Cov}/\operatorname{Var}\) of the data, the same quantity as in the covariance and correlation section §2.1.

The figure (a concept map, described in words). Arrows connect the concepts: Fisher information defines the Cramér–Rao lower bound; the crlb bounds the variance of unbiased estimators; a sufficient statistic is used by the Rao–Blackwell theorem, which improves unbiased estimators and constructs an mvue; the unbiased estimator with minimal variance is the mvue; an unbiased estimator attaining the crlb is an efficient estimator, and an efficient estimator is an mvue.

A worked number for the Poisson model. For one observation \(\ell(\lambda\mid x)=-\lambda+x\ln\lambda-\ln x!\), so \(\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\lambda}=-1+\frac x\lambda\) and \(\frac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial\lambda^2}=-\frac x{\lambda^2}\). Using the second form of the definition, \(I_1(\lambda)=-\E\bigl[-\frac X{\lambda^2}\bigr]=\frac{\E[X]}{\lambda^2}=\frac\lambda{\lambda^2}=\frac1\lambda\) (the Poisson mean is \(\lambda\)). For \(n\) iid observations the log-likelihoods add, so \(I_n(\lambda)=n\,I_1(\lambda)=\frac n\lambda\) and the crlb is \(\frac1{I_n(\lambda)}=\frac\lambda n\). Since \(\Var[\bar X_n]=\frac\lambda n\), the mle \(\bar X_n\) attains the bound: it is efficient, hence the mvue. And \(V(\lambda)=\lambda=I_1(\lambda)^{-1}\), matching Remark 3.30(ii). For the uniform model the regularity conditions fail (the support \([0,\theta]\) moves with \(\theta\), so one may not differentiate under the integral sign), and the crlb indeed does not apply: \(\Var[\hat\theta_2]=\frac{\theta^2}{n(n+2)}\) shrinks like \(\frac1{n^2}\), faster than any bound of the shape \(\frac{c(\theta)}n\).

In words: the Fisher information measures how sharply the log-likelihood peaks at the true \(\theta\) — a sharp peak means the data pin \(\theta\) down well. The Cramér–Rao bound turns this into a hard floor: no unbiased estimator can have a variance below \(1/I(\theta)\). An estimator that reaches the floor is called efficient and is then the best unbiased estimator (mvue); Rao–Blackwell is a recipe for improving an unbiased estimator towards that goal, and "blue" is the same idea restricted to estimators that are linear in the data.

Exercise-sheet tasks

Sheet 10, Exercise 1 — mle for the uniform distribution Sheet 10 · Ex 1

\(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid \(\Unif(0,\theta)\), \(\theta>0\) unknown, with pdf \(p(x_i\mid\theta)=\frac1\theta\one_{[0,\theta]}(x_i)\). (i) Write down the likelihood \(L(\theta\mid x)\), careful with the indicators. (ii) Find \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\) (hint: not differentiable — reason with monotonicity and where it is non-zero). (iii) Compute \(\E[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}]\) (hint: cdf, then pdf, then expectation). Is it unbiased?

Solution

(i) By independence the joint density is the product:

\[ L(\theta\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac1\theta\one_{[0,\theta]}(x_i)=\Bigl(\frac1\theta\Bigr)^n\prod_{i=1}^n\one_{[0,\theta]}(x_i) . \]

A product of indicators is 1 exactly when every factor is 1, i.e. when \(0\le x_i\le\theta\) for all \(i\). That is the same as \(x_{\min}:=\min_ix_i\ge0\) and \(x_{\max}:=\max_ix_i\le\theta\). The data come from \(\Unif(0,\theta)\), so all \(x_i\ge0\), and

\[ L(\theta\mid x)=\begin{cases}\theta^{-n}&\text{if }\theta\ge x_{\max},\\ 0&\text{if }\theta<x_{\max}.\end{cases} \]

(Assume \(x_{\max}>0\), which happens with probability 1.)

(ii) For \(\theta<x_{\max}\) the likelihood is 0: such a \(\theta\) cannot have produced an observation larger than itself. For \(\theta\ge x_{\max}\), \(\theta^{-n}\) is strictly decreasing in \(\theta\) (a larger interval spreads the probability thinner). So the maximum sits at the smallest allowed value: \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=x_{\max}\), as an estimator \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=X_{(n)}=\max\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}\). Setting \(\ell'=0\) would not work: \(\ell(\theta)=-n\ln\theta\) on \([x_{\max},\infty)\) has derivative \(-\frac n\theta\ne0\) everywhere; the maximum is at the boundary.

Bus example from the official solution: waiting times \((4,1,7,12,5,9,10,2)\) minutes give the estimate 12 minutes.

(iii) cdf of the maximum. \(X_{(n)}\le t\) holds exactly when every \(X_i\le t\). By independence, for \(0\le t\le\theta\):

\[ F_{X_{(n)}}(t)=\P(X_1\le t,\dots,X_n\le t)=\prod_{i=1}^n\P(X_i\le t)=\Bigl(\frac t\theta\Bigr)^n , \]

using the uniform cdf \(F_{X_i}(t)=\frac t\theta\) on \([0,\theta]\) (0 below, 1 above). pdf by differentiating the cdf (pdf \(=F'\), §1.3; power rule for derivatives, Analysis 6.2): \(p_{X_{(n)}}(t)=\frac{nt^{n-1}}{\theta^n}\) on \([0,\theta]\), 0 elsewhere. Expectation (antiderivative of \(t^n\) is \(\frac{t^{n+1}}{n+1}\), Analysis 8.3):

\[ \E[X_{(n)}]=\int_0^\theta t\cdot\frac{nt^{n-1}}{\theta^n}\,\mathrm dt=\frac n{\theta^n}\int_0^\theta t^n\,\mathrm dt=\frac n{\theta^n}\Bigl[\frac{t^{n+1}}{n+1}\Bigr]_0^\theta=\frac n{\theta^n}\cdot\frac{\theta^{n+1}}{n+1}=\frac n{n+1}\theta . \]

So \(\operatorname{bias}[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}]=\frac n{n+1}\theta-\theta=-\frac\theta{n+1}\ne0\): biased (it underestimates, because the maximum is always \(\le\theta\)). The bias tends to 0 as \(n\to\infty\): "asymptotically unbiased". The unbiased correction is \(\frac{n+1}nX_{(n)}\) (Example 3.24); for the bus data \(\frac98\cdot12=13.5\).

Consistency (not asked, but instructive): for \(0<\varepsilon<\theta\), \(\P(|X_{(n)}-\theta|\ge\varepsilon)=\P(X_{(n)}\le\theta-\varepsilon)=\bigl(\frac{\theta-\varepsilon}\theta\bigr)^n\to0\), since the base is below 1. So the mle is consistent. Verification: the official solution is correct. One subtle point it relies on: the pdf uses the closed interval \([0,\theta]\). With \((0,\theta)\) the likelihood at \(\theta=x_{\max}\) would be 0, and the supremum would not be attained — no mle in the strict sense. Densities can be changed at single points without changing the distribution, so this is a convention, but it matters for the argmax.

Method to reuse. When the support depends on \(\theta\): write the indicators, turn them into one condition on \(\theta\) (here \(\theta\ge x_{\max}\)), and maximise the remaining monotone function at the boundary. For the distribution of a maximum: \(\P(\max\le t)=\prod\P(X_i\le t)\); for a minimum: \(\P(\min>t)=\prod\P(X_i>t)\).

Widget — the uniform likelihood My addition

Top: the sample points on the time axis. Bottom: the likelihood \(L(\theta\mid x)\), scaled so that its peak is 1: it is 0 left of \(x_{\max}\), jumps up at \(x_{\max}\) and then decays like \(\theta^{-n}\). Move the candidate \(\theta\) to see its likelihood. The true \(\theta\) for random samples is 10.

Sheet 10, Exercise 2 — mle for the exponential distribution Sheet 10 · Ex 2

\(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid \(\Exp(\lambda)\), \(n\ge2\), rate \(\lambda>0\) unknown. (i) Write down \(L(\lambda\mid x)\) and \(\ell(\lambda\mid x)\). (ii) Find \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}\). (iii) Compute \(\E[\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}]\); is it unbiased? Hint: \(\Exp(\lambda)=\Gamma(1,\lambda)\), so \(S_n=\sum X_i\sim\Gamma(n,\lambda)\); \(\frac1{\bar X_n}=\frac n{S_n}\); for \(Y\sim\Gamma(\alpha,\beta)\) with \(\alpha>1\), \(\E[\frac1Y]=\frac\beta{\alpha-1}\).

Solution

(i) The pdf is \(p(x\mid\lambda)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x\ge0\). By independence (all \(x_i\ge0\)):

\[ L(\lambda\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^n\lambda e^{-\lambda x_i}=\lambda^n\exp\Bigl(-\lambda\sum_{i=1}^nx_i\Bigr),\qquad \ell(\lambda\mid x)=n\ln\lambda-\lambda\sum_{i=1}^nx_i , \]

using \(e^ae^b=e^{a+b}\), then \(\ln(\lambda^n)=n\ln\lambda\) and \(\ln(e^s)=s\).

(ii) \(\frac{\mathrm d\ell}{\mathrm d\lambda}=\frac n\lambda-\sum x_i=0\iff\lambda=\frac n{\sum x_i}=\frac1{\bar x_n}\). Second derivative \(\frac{\mathrm d^2\ell}{\mathrm d\lambda^2}=-\frac n{\lambda^2}<0\) for all \(\lambda>0\), so \(\ell\) bends downwards everywhere and the critical point is the global maximum (a function with negative second derivative on an interval has at most one critical point, and it is the global maximum; equivalently, \(\ell'\) is positive before and negative after). Hence \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}=\frac1{\bar X_n}\).

Sanity check: the mean of \(\Exp(\lambda)\) is \(\frac1\lambda\), so \(\bar X_n\approx\frac1\lambda\), i.e. \(\lambda\approx\frac1{\bar X_n}\). Light bulbs lasting \(1.2, 0.4, 2.5, 0.9, 1.6, 0.3, 3.1, 1.0\) years (sum 11) give \(\hat\lambda=\frac8{11}\approx0.73\) per year (preset in the log-likelihood widget).

(iii) \(\E[\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}]=\E[\frac n{S_n}]=n\E[\frac1{S_n}]\). With \(S_n\sim\Gamma(n,\lambda)\) and \(n>1\): \(\E[\frac1{S_n}]=\frac\lambda{n-1}\), so

\[ \E[\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}]=\frac n{n-1}\lambda,\qquad\operatorname{bias}[\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}]=\frac n{n-1}\lambda-\lambda=\frac\lambda{n-1}\ne0 . \]

The mle is biased (it overestimates). For \(n=1\), \(\E[\frac1{X_1}]=\int_0^\infty\frac1x\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\,\mathrm dx\) diverges (near \(x=0\) the integrand behaves like \(\frac\lambda x\), since \(e^{-\lambda x}\to1\), and \(\int_0^1\frac1x\,\mathrm dx=\infty\) — the benchmark improper integral, Analysis 9.1), so the expectation is \(+\infty\).

The two facts from the hint My proofs

\(S_n\sim\Gamma(n,\lambda)\). \(\Exp(\lambda)\) has density \(\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\), which is the \(\Gamma(1,\lambda)\) density \(\frac{\lambda^1}{\Gamma(1)}x^0e^{-\lambda x}\) (\(\Gamma(1)=1\)). Sums of independent Gammas with the same rate are Gamma with the shapes added (proved with characteristic functions on §2.3). So \(S_n\sim\Gamma(1+\dots+1,\lambda)=\Gamma(n,\lambda)\).

\(\E[1/Y]=\frac\beta{\alpha-1}\) for \(Y\sim\Gamma(\alpha,\beta)\), \(\alpha>1\). By LOTUS,

\[ \E\Bigl[\frac1Y\Bigr]=\int_0^\infty\frac1y\cdot\frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}y^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta y}\,\mathrm dy =\frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_0^\infty y^{(\alpha-1)-1}e^{-\beta y}\,\mathrm dy =\frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\cdot\frac{\Gamma(\alpha-1)}{\beta^{\alpha-1}}=\frac{\beta\,\Gamma(\alpha-1)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}=\frac\beta{\alpha-1} . \]

The middle integral is the \(\Gamma(\alpha-1,\beta)\) density without its constant, so it equals the reciprocal of that constant, \(\frac{\Gamma(\alpha-1)}{\beta^{\alpha-1}}\) (a density integrates to 1; needs \(\alpha-1>0\)). The last step uses \(\Gamma(\alpha)=(\alpha-1)\Gamma(\alpha-1)\) (§1.3).

The official solution — one wrong justification

It ends with "It is consistent as \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac n{n-1}\lambda=\lambda\)". That limit only shows the bias tends to 0 (asymptotic unbiasedness), which does not imply consistency: \(X_1\) is even exactly unbiased and not consistent (Example 3.23). The conclusion is true, with a correct reason: by the slln, \(\bar X_n\to\frac1\lambda\) almost surely; the function \(t\mapsto\frac1t\) is continuous at \(\frac1\lambda>0\) (continuity: Analysis 4.1), so \(\frac1{\bar X_n}\to\lambda\) almost surely (for each outcome in the probability-1 event, \(\bar X_n(\omega)\) is a number sequence tending to \(\frac1\lambda\ne0\), and the limit rule for quotients of number sequences, Analysis 2.2, gives \(\frac1{\bar X_n(\omega)}\to\lambda\)). Hence \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}\) is strongly consistent. (Alternatively: bias → 0 and variance → 0, then the mse test above.) Everything else in the official solution is correct.

An unbiased version: \(\frac{n-1}n\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}=\frac{n-1}{S_n}\) has expectation \(\frac{n-1}n\cdot\frac n{n-1}\lambda=\lambda\).

Method to reuse. Product → log → derivative → solve → sign of second derivative. For expectations of \(\frac1{S_n}\), identify the distribution of \(S_n\) and integrate against its density, spotting another density inside the integral.

Sheet 10, Exercise 3 — the density \(2c^2/x^3\) Sheet 10 · Ex 3

\(X\) has pdf \(p_X(x)=\frac{2c^2}{x^3}\) for \(x\ge c\) and 0 otherwise, with \(c>0\). (i) Show \(p_X\) is a valid pdf for all \(c>0\). (ii) Find the cdf. (iii) For iid \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) from this distribution, find the mle for \(c\) (hint: what if a sample value is below \(c\)?).

Solution

(i) A pdf must be \(\ge0\) and integrate to 1. Non-negative: for \(x\ge c>0\), \(2c^2>0\) and \(x^3>0\); elsewhere it is 0. Integral — an improper integral (Analysis 9.1): integrate up to \(a\), then let \(a\to\infty\). An antiderivative of \(x^{-3}\) is \(-\frac12x^{-2}\) (power rule \(\int x^m\,\mathrm dx=\frac{x^{m+1}}{m+1}\) with \(m=-3\), Analysis 8.3):

\[ \int_c^\infty\frac{2c^2}{x^3}\,\mathrm dx=2c^2\lim_{a\to\infty}\Bigl[-\frac1{2x^2}\Bigr]_c^a=2c^2\lim_{a\to\infty}\Bigl(-\frac1{2a^2}+\frac1{2c^2}\Bigr)=2c^2\cdot\frac1{2c^2}=1 . \]

(ii) \(F_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^xp_X(t)\,\mathrm dt\). For \(x<c\) the density is 0 there, so \(F_X(x)=0\). For \(x\ge c\):

\[ F_X(x)=\int_c^x\frac{2c^2}{t^3}\,\mathrm dt=2c^2\Bigl[-\frac1{2t^2}\Bigr]_c^x=2c^2\Bigl(\frac1{2c^2}-\frac1{2x^2}\Bigr)=1-\frac{c^2}{x^2} . \]

Check: \(F_X(c)=0\) and \(F_X(x)\to1\) as \(x\to\infty\).

(iii) With the support written as an indicator, \(p_X(x_i)=\frac{2c^2}{x_i^3}\one_{[c,\infty)}(x_i)\), and by independence

\[ L(c\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{2c^2}{x_i^3}\one_{[c,\infty)}(x_i)=\begin{cases}(2c^2)^n\prod_{i=1}^nx_i^{-3}&\text{if }c\le x_{\min},\\0&\text{if }c>x_{\min},\end{cases} \]

because all indicators equal 1 exactly when every \(x_i\ge c\), i.e. \(x_{\min}=\min_ix_i\ge c\). For fixed data, \(\prod x_i^{-3}\) is a positive constant, and \((2c^2)^n=2^nc^{2n}\) is strictly increasing in \(c>0\). So make \(c\) as large as possible without making \(L=0\): \(\hat c_{\text{mle}}=x_{\min}\), as an estimator \(\hat c_{\text{mle}}=\min\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}\).

Verification: the official solution is correct in all three parts. As in Ex 1, the closed interval \([c,\infty)\) makes the maximum attained at \(c=x_{\min}\).

Extra: is it unbiased? The mirror image of Ex 1. For \(t\ge c\): \(\P(\min_iX_i>t)=\prod_i\P(X_i>t)=\bigl(\frac{c^2}{t^2}\bigr)^n=\frac{c^{2n}}{t^{2n}}\). The density of the minimum is the derivative of \(1-\frac{c^{2n}}{t^{2n}}\), namely \(\frac{2nc^{2n}}{t^{2n+1}}\), and \(\E[\min X_i]=\int_c^\infty t\cdot\frac{2nc^{2n}}{t^{2n+1}}\,\mathrm dt=2nc^{2n}\cdot\frac{c^{1-2n}}{2n-1}=\frac{2n}{2n-1}c\). So the mle overestimates (the minimum is always \(\ge c\)), bias \(\frac c{2n-1}\to0\); \(\frac{2n-1}{2n}\min X_i\) is unbiased.

Method to reuse. "Support depends on the parameter" ⟹ mle is a sample extreme. If the likelihood decreases in the parameter on the allowed range, take the smallest allowed value (the sample maximum in Ex 1); if it increases, take the largest allowed value (the sample minimum here).

Sheet 10, Exercise 5 — how many toasters are broken? Sheet 10 · Ex 5

A box holds \(n\in\N_{>1}\) toasters; a fixed but unknown number \(d\) of them is broken. You draw two toasters uniformly at random (without putting the first one back). (i) What is the distribution \(P_d\) of the number of broken toasters among the two? (Hint: a distribution on a set with only 3 elements; give its pmf.) (ii) Now \(d\) is unknown and is to be estimated from this sample of two. Write down an adequate statistical model and explain it briefly. (iii) Give an unbiased estimator for \(d\) in this model and justify your choice.

Solution

Picture first (mine). Take \(n=10\) toasters, \(d=3\) of them broken. If both drawn toasters work, you would guess "few are broken"; if both are broken, "many". The exercise turns this gut feeling into an estimator and checks that it is right on average.

(i) The number of broken toasters among the two drawn ones can be 0, 1 or 2, so the sample space is \(\Omega=\{0,1,2\}\) with all subsets as events, \(\Aa=\pow(\Omega)\). Every pair of toasters is equally likely (a Laplace experiment, §1.1: probability = favourable cases / all cases). The draw is without replacement and the order does not matter, so the cases are the 2-element subsets of the \(n\) toasters. There are \(\binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}2\) of them (\(\binom nk\), "n choose k", is the number of ways to choose \(k\) of \(n\) objects, B3). Label the toasters \(1,\dots,n\) so that the broken ones are \(1,\dots,d\).

  • No broken one: both toasters come from the \(n-d\) working ones: \(\binom{n-d}2\) pairs, so \[ p_d(0)=\frac{\binom{n-d}2}{\binom n2}=\frac{(n-d)(n-d-1)/2}{n(n-1)/2}=\frac{(n-d)(n-d-1)}{n(n-1)} . \]
  • Two broken ones: both come from the \(d\) broken ones: \(\binom d2\) pairs, so \(p_d(2)=\frac{d(d-1)}{n(n-1)}\).
  • Exactly one broken one: the rest of the probability, \[ p_d(1)=1-p_d(0)-p_d(2)=\frac{n(n-1)-(n-d)(n-d-1)-d(d-1)}{n(n-1)}=\frac{2d(n-d)}{n(n-1)} . \] Algebra: \((n-d)(n-d-1)=n^2-2nd+d^2-n+d\) and \(d(d-1)=d^2-d\); subtracting both from \(n^2-n\) leaves \(2nd-2d^2=2d(n-d)\). Direct count as a check: one of the \(d\) broken times one of the \(n-d\) working toasters gives \(d(n-d)\) pairs, and \(\frac{d(n-d)}{n(n-1)/2}=\frac{2d(n-d)}{n(n-1)}\) ✓.

\(P_d\) is the distribution on \(\{0,1,2\}\) with this pmf. It is the hypergeometric distribution \(\Hyp(n,d,2)\) (§1.2) — in the script's order of arguments: \(n\) objects in total, \(d\) of them "marked" (here: broken), \(2\) of them drawn without replacement, and the value counts how many marked ones you drew. Numbers for \(n=10\), \(d=3\): \(p_3(0)=\frac{7\cdot6}{90}=\frac7{15}\), \(p_3(1)=\frac{2\cdot3\cdot7}{90}=\frac7{15}\), \(p_3(2)=\frac{3\cdot2}{90}=\frac1{15}\); they add up to 1 ✓.

(ii) An adequate statistical model (Definition 3.4, §3.1) is

\[ \bigl(\{0,1,2\},\ \pow(\{0,1,2\}),\ (P_d)_{d\in\{0,\dots,n\}}\bigr). \]

The observation is the number of broken toasters in the sample (0, 1 or 2). The unknown parameter is \(d\), and the parameter space is \(\Theta=\{0,1,\dots,n\}\): there cannot be fewer than 0 or more than \(n\) broken toasters. For each candidate value \(d\) the model contains the distribution \(P_d\) from (i). (More on this model: §3.1.)

(iii) Idea: the fraction of broken toasters in the sample, \(\frac\omega2\) (where \(\omega\in\{0,1,2\}\) is the observed number), should be about the fraction \(\frac dn\) in the whole box. Scale it up to all \(n\) toasters:

\[ \hat d:\{0,1,2\}\to\R,\qquad \omega\mapsto\hat d(\omega)=\frac{\omega\,n}2 . \]

It is a function of the data only (it does not use \(d\)); every map on the finite set \(\{0,1,2\}\) with the power set is measurable, so it is a statistic and hence an estimator (Definition 3.18). Unbiased: the expectation of a function of a discrete random variable is the sum of its values weighted by the pmf, so

\[ \E_d[\hat d]=\sum_{\omega=0}^2p_d(\omega)\,\hat d(\omega)=p_d(0)\cdot0+p_d(1)\cdot\frac n2+p_d(2)\cdot n =\frac n2\Bigl(\frac{2d(n-d)}{n(n-1)}+\frac{2d(d-1)}{n(n-1)}\Bigr) . \]

Take out the common factor \(\frac{2d}{n(n-1)}\) from the bracket: \(\frac n2\cdot\frac{2d}{n(n-1)}\bigl((n-d)+(d-1)\bigr) =\frac{d}{n-1}\cdot(n-1)=d\). This holds for every \(d\in\{0,\dots,n\}\), so \(\hat d\) is unbiased (Definition 3.20(i)). ∎

Numbers (\(n=10\), \(d=3\)): the estimate is 0, 5 or 10 with probabilities \(\frac7{15},\frac7{15},\frac1{15}\), and \(0\cdot\frac7{15}+5\cdot\frac7{15}+10\cdot\frac1{15}=\frac{45}{15}=3\) ✓. Note that the estimate is never 3 — unbiased only means "right on average over many repetitions".

How precise is it? (Not asked.) By the same sum, \(\E_d[\hat d^2]=p_d(1)\frac{n^2}4+p_d(2)n^2\), and \(\Var[\hat d]=\E[\hat d^2]-d^2\) simplifies to \(\Var[\hat d]=\operatorname{mse}[\hat d]=\frac{d(n-d)(n-2)}{2(n-1)}\) (checked exactly with fractions for all \(d\) and several \(n\)). For \(n=10\), \(d=3\): \(\frac{3\cdot7\cdot8}{18}=\frac{28}3\approx9.3\), a standard deviation of about 3 toasters — two toasters are very little data.

It is the only unbiased estimator. (Not asked.) Any estimator is a triple of values \(T(0),T(1),T(2)\). Unbiasedness means \(T(0)p_d(0)+T(1)p_d(1)+T(2)p_d(2)=d\) for all \(d\in\{0,\dots,n\}\). Multiply by \(n(n-1)\): both sides are polynomials in \(d\) of degree at most 2 that agree at the \(n+1\ge3\) points \(0,\dots,n\), so they are the same polynomial (two different polynomials of degree \(\le2\) agree in at most 2 points). \(d=0\) gives \(T(0)n(n-1)=0\), so \(T(0)=0\); comparing the \(d^2\)-coefficients gives \(-2T(1)+T(2)=0\); comparing the \(d\)-coefficients gives \(2nT(1)-T(2)=n(n-1)\). Hence \(T(1)=\frac n2\), \(T(2)=n\): exactly \(\hat d\).

Note on the official solution

The exercise statement says "\(d\in\{0,\dots,d\}\)"; this is a typo for \(d\in\{0,\dots,n\}\), which the solution then uses in (ii). The computations in (i) and (iii) are correct (checked above and with exact fractions).

Method to reuse. "Give an unbiased estimator": guess by matching fractions or means (here sample fraction \(\approx\) population fraction), then compute \(\E_\theta[\hat\theta]\) with the model's pmf and show it equals \(\theta\) for every \(\theta\in\Theta\).

Sheet 9. Sheet 10 Ex 1 is marked "repeated from sheet 9", but the Sheet 9 solutions uploaded to the project contain no estimation exercise (Sheet 9 covers the lln, the clt and convergence, §2.4). So nothing from Sheet 9 is missing on this page.

Sheet 10 Ex 4 (best weights for an average: unbiasedness and minimal mse of \(\sum\lambda_iX_i\)) is solved on §2.2, because its key step is Jensen's inequality. In the language of this page: a weighted average \(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_iX_i\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\mu\) exactly when \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), its mse is then its variance \(\sigma^2\sum_i\lambda_i^2\), and equal weights make that smallest — so \(\bar X_n\) is the blue (Remark 3.26). The sheet states the task for convex combinations (\(\lambda_i\ge0\)), but its Jensen step works for negative weights too, so the conclusion holds for all linear unbiased estimators.

Old-exam tasks

SoSe 2025, Problem 1b — a weighted average of unbiased estimators SoSe25 · P1b · 3 credits

Statement (true or false, with justification). Let \((\Omega,\Aa,\mathcal P_\Theta)\) be a statistical model and \(\hat\theta_1,\hat\theta_2\) unbiased estimators of \(\theta\). Then \(\frac13\hat\theta_1+\frac23\hat\theta_2\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\theta\) as well.

Answer: True (official answer, correct). Justification. Unbiased means \(\E_\theta[\hat\theta_1]=\theta\) and \(\E_\theta[\hat\theta_2]=\theta\) for every \(\theta\in\Theta\) (Definition 3.20(i)). By linearity of expectation (§2.1: constants come out, expectations of sums add),

\[ \E_\theta\Bigl[\tfrac13\hat\theta_1+\tfrac23\hat\theta_2\Bigr]=\tfrac13\E_\theta[\hat\theta_1]+\tfrac23\E_\theta[\hat\theta_2] =\tfrac13\theta+\tfrac23\theta=\theta\quad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta . \]

Also, the combination is again a function of the data only (both \(\hat\theta_i\) are statistics), so it is an estimator. ∎

What makes it work, and what does not matter. Only that the weights add up to 1: for weights \(a,b\), \(\E[a\hat\theta_1+b\hat\theta_2]=(a+b)\theta\), which equals \(\theta\) for all \(\theta\) exactly when \(a+b=1\). Counterexample for weights not adding to 1: \(\frac12\hat\theta_1+\frac12\cdot\frac12\hat\theta_2\) has expectation \(\frac34\theta\ne\theta\) (whenever \(\theta\ne0\)). Independence of \(\hat\theta_1,\hat\theta_2\) is not needed — linearity holds for any random variables with finite expectation. Independence would matter only for the variance of the combination; choosing the weights to make that variance small is Sheet 10 Ex 4 (§2.2). The same item is also on §2.1.

SoSe 2025, Problem 4a — mle for Poisson SoSe25 · P4a · 4 credits

Task. \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid \(\Poi(\lambda)\), \(\lambda>0\) unknown. Derive \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}\) explicitly. (Hint in the exam: the pmf is \(e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^x}{x!}\) on \(\N_0\), with mean and variance \(\lambda\); the derivative of \(\ln t\) is \(\frac1t\).)

Solution. Likelihood, by independence and \(e^ae^b=e^{a+b}\), \(\lambda^a\lambda^b=\lambda^{a+b}\):

\[ L(\lambda\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^ne^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^{x_i}}{x_i!}=\frac{e^{-n\lambda}\lambda^{\sum_ix_i}}{\prod_ix_i!} . \]

Log-likelihood (log of a quotient is the difference of logs):

\[ \ell(\lambda\mid x)=-n\lambda+\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^nx_i\Bigr)\ln\lambda-\ln\Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^nx_i!\Bigr) . \]

The last term does not contain \(\lambda\), so its derivative is 0:

\[ \frac{\mathrm d\ell}{\mathrm d\lambda}=-n+\frac1\lambda\sum_{i=1}^nx_i\overset!=0\iff\lambda=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nx_i=\bar x_n . \]

Second derivative \(\frac{\mathrm d^2\ell}{\mathrm d\lambda^2}=-\frac{\sum x_i}{\lambda^2}<0\), so this is a maximum (and, being negative for all \(\lambda>0\), the global one). Hence \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}=\bar X_n\).

Verification. The official solution is correct. One edge case it skips: "\(-\frac{\sum x_i}{\lambda^2}<0\)" needs \(\sum x_i>0\). If all observations are 0, \(\ell(\lambda)=-n\lambda\) is strictly decreasing on \((0,\infty)\) and has no maximum there — the mle would be \(\lambda=0\), which is outside \(\Theta\). This has probability \(e^{-n\lambda}\), tiny for large \(n\); a remark in the exam would be a bonus, not required. Example: calls in 8 intervals \(3,5,2,4,6,3,4,5\) give \(\hat\lambda=\frac{32}8=4\) (preset in the log-likelihood widget).

SoSe 2025, Problem 4b — is it unbiased? SoSe25 · P4b · 2 credits

Solution. Yes. \(\E[\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}]=\E[\bar X_n]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\E[X_i]=\frac1n\cdot n\lambda=\lambda\) for every \(\lambda>0\) (linearity; the Poisson mean is \(\lambda\)). mles are not unbiased in general (Sheet 10 Ex 1, 2), but this one is a sample mean, and sample means are unbiased for the mean (Example 3.21(i)). The official solution says the same and is correct.

SoSe 2025, Problem 4c — clt approximation of the mle SoSe25 · P4c · 2 credits

Task. Use the clt to find the approximate distribution of \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}\) for large \(n\).

Solution. The \(X_i\) are iid with \(\E[X_i]=\lambda\) and \(\Var[X_i]=\lambda\in(0,\infty)\), so the clt (§2.4) applies: \(\frac{\bar X_n-\lambda}{\sqrt{\lambda/n}}\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,1)\), equivalently \(\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\lambda)\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,\lambda)\). For large \(n\) this is read as

\[ \hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}=\bar X_n\ \approx\ \mathcal N\Bigl(\lambda,\frac\lambda n\Bigr) . \]

Verification. The official answer \(\bar X_n\approx\mathcal N(\lambda,\lambda/n)\) is correct as an approximation. Remember (Remark 2.65, §2.4) that "\(\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(\lambda,\lambda/n)\)" would be wrong notation — write "\(\approx\)" or the \(\sqrt n\) form. Numbers: \(\lambda=4\), \(n=100\) gives standard deviation \(\sqrt{0.04}=0.2\). In the language of Definition 3.20(v): the mle is asymptotically normal with \(V(\lambda)=\lambda\), matching Remark 3.30(ii). Part d (a test built on this) belongs to §3.3.

WiSe 25/26, Problem 4a — mle for the rainfall density \(\frac1{\theta^2}xe^{-x/\theta}\) WiSe25 · P4a · 4 credits

Task. Rainfall amounts \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid with density \(p_\theta(x)=\frac1{\theta^2}xe^{-x/\theta}\) on \(\R_{\ge0}\), \(\theta>0\). Show by a full derivation that \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\).

Solution. For data \(x\in\R_{\ge0}^n\) (with all \(x_i>0\), which has probability 1):

\[ L(\theta\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac1{\theta^2}x_ie^{-x_i/\theta}=\theta^{-2n}\Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^nx_i\Bigr)\exp\Bigl(-\frac1\theta\sum_{i=1}^nx_i\Bigr) . \]

Log-likelihood: \(\ln\theta^{-2n}=-2n\ln\theta\), \(\ln\prod x_i=\sum\ln x_i\) (a constant in \(\theta\)), \(\ln e^s=s\):

\[ \ell(\theta\mid x)=-2n\ln\theta-\frac1\theta\sum_{i=1}^nx_i+\sum_{i=1}^n\ln x_i . \]

Derivative, with \((\ln\theta)'=\frac1\theta\) and \((\frac1\theta)'=-\frac1{\theta^2}\); write \(s=\sum x_i>0\):

\[ \frac{\mathrm d\ell}{\mathrm d\theta}=-\frac{2n}\theta+\frac s{\theta^2}=\frac{-2n\theta+s}{\theta^2}\overset!=0\iff\theta=\frac s{2n}=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^nx_i . \]

Second-derivative check. \(\bigl(-\frac{2n}\theta\bigr)'=\frac{2n}{\theta^2}\) and \(\bigl(\frac s{\theta^2}\bigr)'=-\frac{2s}{\theta^3}\), so

\[ \frac{\mathrm d^2\ell}{\mathrm d\theta^2}=\frac{2n}{\theta^2}-\frac{2s}{\theta^3}=\frac2{\theta^3}(n\theta-s) . \]

At \(\hat\theta=\frac s{2n}\): \(n\hat\theta-s=\frac s2-s=-\frac s2<0\), and \(\frac2{\hat\theta^3}>0\), so \(\ell''(\hat\theta)<0\): a maximum. Hence \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\).

Verification and one gap. The official solution is correct and matches this line by line. Note that \(\ell''\) is not negative everywhere here (it is positive for \(\theta>\frac sn\)), so the second-derivative check alone only proves a local maximum. The global statement follows from the sign of \(\ell'=\frac{s-2n\theta}{\theta^2}\): positive for \(\theta<\hat\theta\), negative for \(\theta>\hat\theta\) (sign check, primer box 1). One extra line in the exam makes the argument complete. Plausibility: this density is \(\Gamma(2,\frac1\theta)\) with mean \(2\theta\), so \(\bar X_n\approx2\theta\), i.e. \(\theta\approx\frac{\bar X_n}2\) — exactly the mle. Parts b, c, d (Chebyshev and clt for this estimator) are also on §2.2 and §2.4; the estimation side is solved in the next box.

WiSe 25/26, Problem 4b–d — bias, variance, consistency and asymptotic normality of the rainfall mle WiSe25 · P4b WiSe25 · P4c WiSe25 · P4d · 3 + 3 + 1 credits

Tasks. For \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) from P4a: (b) use the Chebyshev inequality to bound the probability that the estimate deviates from the true \(\theta\) by at least \(\varepsilon>0\); (c) use the clt to approximate the distribution of \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\) by a Gaussian and approximate \(\P(|\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}-\theta|\ge\varepsilon)\) in terms of the standard normal cdf \(\Phi\); (d) comment on the key differences between (b) and (c). Hint for (b), (c): \(\E[X_i]=2\theta\), \(\Var[X_i]=2\theta^2\).

Step 1 — bias and variance (needed by both (b) and (c)). By linearity of expectation, \(\E[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}]=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n\E[X_i]=\frac1{2n}\cdot n\cdot2\theta=\theta\), for every \(\theta>0\): the mle is unbiased, bias 0. For the variance, a constant factor \(c\) comes out squared, \(\Var[cY]=c^2\Var[Y]\), and for independent \(X_i\) variances add (§2.1):

\[ \Var[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}]=\frac1{(2n)^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\Var[X_i]=\frac{n\cdot2\theta^2}{4n^2}=\frac{\theta^2}{2n} . \]

Because the bias is 0, the bias–variance decomposition (Definition 3.20(iv)) gives \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}]=\Var[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}]+0^2=\frac{\theta^2}{2n}\).

(b) Chebyshev. The Chebyshev inequality (§2.2) says \(\P(|Y-\E[Y]|\ge\varepsilon)\le\frac{\Var[Y]}{\varepsilon^2}\) for a random variable \(Y\) with finite variance and any \(\varepsilon>0\). With \(Y=\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\) and \(\E[Y]=\theta\) from Step 1:

\[ \P_\theta\bigl(|\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}-\theta|\ge\varepsilon\bigr)\le\frac{\theta^2}{2n\varepsilon^2} . \]

Consequence for estimation (mine; not asked): the right side tends to 0 as \(n\to\infty\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and every \(\theta\), so \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\xrightarrow\P\theta\): the estimator is consistent (Definition 3.20(ii)). This is the "mse \(\to0\)" test above in action; the lln gives even strong consistency, since \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=\frac12\bar X_n\to\frac12\cdot2\theta\) almost surely.

(c) clt. The \(X_i\) are iid with finite mean \(2\theta\) and finite, non-zero variance \(2\theta^2\), so the clt (§2.4) applies to their average. \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\) is the average divided by 2, so after standardising with the mean and variance from Step 1,

\[ \frac{\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}-\theta}{\sqrt{\Var[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}]}}=\frac{\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}-\theta}{\theta/\sqrt{2n}}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1), \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\approx\mathcal N\Bigl(\theta,\frac{\theta^2}{2n}\Bigr)\ \text{for large }n . \]

(The two fractions are the same because the standardisation of \(\frac12\bar X_n\) equals that of \(\bar X_n\): the factor \(\frac12\) cancels between numerator and denominator.) Write \(Z\) for a standard normal variable. The event \(|\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}-\theta|\ge\varepsilon\) is, after dividing by \(\theta/\sqrt{2n}>0\), the event \(|Z_n|\ge\frac{\sqrt{2n}\,\varepsilon}\theta\) for the standardised variable \(Z_n\approx Z\). The two tails \(Z\ge a\) and \(Z\le-a\) have the same probability \(\Phi(-a)\) by symmetry of \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), so

\[ \P_\theta\bigl(|\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}-\theta|\ge\varepsilon\bigr)\approx2\,\Phi\Bigl(-\frac{\sqrt{2n}\,\varepsilon}\theta\Bigr) . \]

In the language of this page: \(\sqrt n(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}-\theta)\xrightarrow d\mathcal N\bigl(0,\frac{\theta^2}2\bigr)\), so the mle is asymptotically normal with asymptotic variance \(V(\theta)=\frac{\theta^2}2\) (Definition 3.20(v), Remark 3.30(ii)).

(d) Differences. Chebyshev uses only the variance and is a guaranteed upper bound for every \(n\), but it can be loose and decays only like \(\frac1n\). The clt value is only an approximation (valid for large \(n\)), but it is usually much sharper and decays much faster (like the tail of a normal distribution, faster than any power of \(\frac1n\)). Numbers for \(\theta=1\), \(n=50\), \(\varepsilon=0.2\): Chebyshev gives \(\frac1{2\cdot50\cdot0.04}=0.25\); the clt gives \(2\Phi(-\sqrt{100}\cdot0.2)=2\Phi(-2)\approx0.0455\); a simulation with 200 000 repetitions gives \(\approx0.045\). The bound is true but more than five times too large.

Verification. The official solutions of (b), (c), (d) are correct and give the same formulas. Extra link to Overview 3.32: for one observation, \(\ell(\theta\mid x)=-2\ln\theta+\ln x-\frac x\theta\), so \(\frac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial\theta^2}=\frac2{\theta^2}-\frac{2x}{\theta^3}\) and \(I_1(\theta)=-\E\bigl[\frac2{\theta^2}-\frac{2X}{\theta^3}\bigr] =-\frac2{\theta^2}+\frac{2\cdot2\theta}{\theta^3}=\frac2{\theta^2}\). The Cramér–Rao bound for \(n\) observations is \(\frac1{nI_1(\theta)}=\frac{\theta^2}{2n}\) — exactly \(\Var[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}]\). So this mle is unbiased and attains the bound: it is efficient, hence the mvue; and \(V(\theta)=\frac{\theta^2}2=I_1(\theta)^{-1}\), as Remark 3.30(ii) predicts.

In words: the rainfall mle is right on average, its error shrinks like \(\theta/\sqrt{2n}\), it becomes exact as the data grow, and for large \(n\) its errors look normal. Chebyshev guarantees a bound; the clt gives a much smaller, approximate value.

WiSe 25/26, Problem 5b, 5c — the empirical cdf as an estimator WiSe25 · P5b WiSe25 · P5c · 2 + 2 credits

Setting. \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid with cdf \(F:=F_{X_1}\) (the cdf \(F(t)=\P(X_1\le t)\)). For a fixed \(t\in\R\), the empirical cdf [empirische Verteilungsfunktion] \(\hat F_n(t)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\chi_{(-\infty,t]}(X_i)\) is the fraction of data points \(\le t\) (\(\chi_A\) = indicator of \(A\), 1 inside and 0 outside).
