Part (a) shows \(n\hat F_n(t)\sim\Bin(n,F(t))\) (full solution on §2.1): each indicator is \(\Ber(F(t))\), and they are independent — \(\Bin(n,p)\) being the binomial distribution (§1.2), the number of successes in \(n\) independent trials each with success probability \(p\), with mean \(np\) and variance \(np(1-p)\). (b) Is \(\hat F_n(t)\) an unbiased estimator of \(F(t)\)? (c) Compute \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat F_n(t)]\).

(b) Yes. The mean of \(\Bin(n,p)\) is \(np\), so \(\E[n\hat F_n(t)]=nF(t)\), and dividing by the constant \(n\) (linearity) gives \(\E[\hat F_n(t)]=F(t)\), for every possible distribution of the data: unbiased.

(c) Because it is unbiased, mse = variance (bias–variance decomposition with bias 0). The variance of \(\Bin(n,p)\) is \(np(1-p)\), and \(\Var[\frac1nY]=\frac1{n^2}\Var[Y]\):

\[ \operatorname{mse}[\hat F_n(t)]=\Var[\hat F_n(t)]=\frac{nF(t)(1-F(t))}{n^2}=\frac{F(t)\bigl(1-F(t)\bigr)}n . \]

Estimation properties (not asked). The mse tends to 0, so \(\hat F_n(t)\) is consistent (mse test above); by the slln it is even strongly consistent, since it is the sample mean of the iid \(\Ber(F(t))\) indicators. By the clt it is asymptotically normal with \(V=F(t)(1-F(t))\) — the basis of the confidence interval in part (d) on §3.4. Numbers: \(n=100\), \(F(t)=0.3\): mse \(=\frac{0.21}{100}=0.0021\). The official solutions are correct.

SoSe 2026, Problem 1e — does the mle have the smallest mse? SoSe26 · P1e · 1 credit

Statement. Let \((\R,\mathcal B,\mathcal P_\Theta)\) be a statistical model, \(\hat\theta_n^{(\text{mle})}\) the mle for \(\theta\) and \(\hat\theta_n\) any other estimator. Then for every finite \(n\) and every \(\theta\in\Theta\), \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_n^{(\text{mle})}]\le\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_n]\). True or false?

Answer: False (official answer, correct). The good properties of the mle are asymptotic (Remark 3.30); for finite \(n\) there are no such guarantees. To refute a "for every" claim, one concrete case is enough:

  • Uniform (Example 3.24). \(\Unif(0,\theta)\) with \(\theta=1\), \(n=2\): the mle \(X_{(2)}\) has \(\operatorname{mse}=\frac{2}{3\cdot4}=\frac16\approx0.167\), while \(\frac32X_{(2)}\) has \(\operatorname{mse}=\frac1{2\cdot4}=0.125\). Smaller.
  • Normal mean, many dimensions (Example 3.25): James–Stein beats the mle \(X\) for every \(\mu\) when \(d\ge3\).
  • Trivial: the constant estimator \(\hat\theta\equiv\theta_0\) has mse 0 at \(\theta=\theta_0\), while the mle's mse there is positive (e.g. \(\frac\lambda n\) for Poisson). This alone refutes the "every \(\theta\)" claim.

Example 3.31 shows the other direction: there the mle \(\hat\sigma^2\) beats the unbiased \(S_n^2\). So the mle is sometimes better, sometimes worse at finite \(n\) — exactly why the statement is false.

SoSe 2026, Problem 5b — mle in randomized response SoSe26 · P5b · 3 credits

Setting. A sensitive attribute \(A\sim\Ber(p)\), \(p\in[0,1]\) unknown. With probability \(r\in(0,1]\) (known) a participant answers truthfully, otherwise reports a fair coin flip. Part (a): each answer is \(Y\sim\Ber(q)\) with \(q=q(p)=rp+\frac{1-r}2\), and \(p\) is identifiable because \(p\mapsto q(p)\) is injective for \(r>0\). We observe iid \(Y_1,\dots,Y_n\), \(\bar y_n=\frac1n\sum y_i\). Task (b): assuming \(\bar y_n\in\bigl[\frac{1-r}2,\frac{1+r}2\bigr]\), derive the mle for \(p\). (Hint: the Bernoulli mle is the sample mean.)

Solution. Step 1 — likelihood. With \(k=\sum y_i\), exactly as in Example 3.29(i), as a function of \(p\):

\[ L(p\mid y)=q(p)^{k}\bigl(1-q(p)\bigr)^{n-k},\qquad q(p)=rp+\tfrac{1-r}2 . \]

Step 2 — maximise in terms of \(q\). As \(p\) runs through \([0,1]\), \(q(p)\) runs through the interval \(\bigl[\frac{1-r}2,\frac{1+r}2\bigr]\) (plug in \(p=0\) and \(p=1\); the map is increasing and affine). The Bernoulli likelihood \(q^k(1-q)^{n-k}\) increases for \(q<\bar y_n\) and decreases for \(q>\bar y_n\) (Example 3.29(i)). By assumption \(\bar y_n\) lies in the reachable interval, so the best reachable \(q\) is \(\hat q=\bar y_n\).

Step 3 — translate back. Solve \(\bar y_n=r\hat p+\frac{1-r}2\) for \(\hat p\) (subtract \(\frac{1-r}2\), divide by \(r>0\)):

\[ \hat p_{\text{mle}}=\frac{\bar Y_n-\frac{1-r}2}r . \]

The assumption on \(\bar y_n\) makes this lie in \([0,1]\): \(\bar y_n\ge\frac{1-r}2\) gives \(\hat p\ge0\), and \(\bar y_n\le\frac{1+r}2\) gives \(\hat p\le\frac{r}{r}=1\). This is the invariance property (Remark 3.30(iv)) for the one-to-one map \(p\mapsto q(p)\).

Alternative by calculus (for \(\hat p\) inside \((0,1)\)): by the chain rule, \(\frac{\mathrm d\ell}{\mathrm dp}=\frac{\mathrm d\ell}{\mathrm dq}\cdot\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dp}=\frac{k-nq}{q(1-q)}\cdot r\), which is 0 exactly when \(q=\frac kn=\bar y_n\), positive before and negative after — same answer. Numbers (from part d of the same exam): \(r=\frac12\), 64 of 100 answers are 1, so \(\bar y=0.64\in[0.25,0.75]\) and \(\hat p=\frac{0.64-0.25}{0.5}=0.78\). If the assumption fails, e.g. \(\bar y_n<\frac{1-r}2\), the likelihood is decreasing on the whole reachable range and the mle is the boundary value \(\hat p=0\) (similarly \(\hat p=1\) above) — the unrestricted formula would give a negative "probability".

Verification. The official solution is correct; its step "the Bernoulli likelihood is maximised at \(\hat q=\bar y_n\)" silently needs \(\bar y_n\) to be a reachable \(q\), which is exactly the assumption given. Part (c) follows in the next box (also on §2.1); part (d) (a test) is on §3.3.

SoSe 2026, Problem 5c — randomized response: unbiasedness and variance SoSe26 · P5c · 2 credits

Task. Same setting as P5b: \(Y_1,\dots,Y_n\) iid \(\Ber(q)\) with \(q=q(p)=rp+\frac{1-r}2\), \(r\in(0,1]\) known. Show that \[ \hat p:=\frac{\bar Y_n-\frac{1-r}2}r \] is unbiased for \(p\) and compute \(\Var[\hat p]\).

Unbiased. Each \(Y_i\sim\Ber(q)\) has mean \(q\), so by linearity \(\E[\bar Y_n]=\frac1n\cdot nq=q\). Linearity again (a constant is subtracted, then everything is divided by the constant \(r\)):

\[ \E[\hat p]=\frac{\E[\bar Y_n]-\frac{1-r}2}r=\frac{q(p)-\frac{1-r}2}r=\frac{rp}r=p\qquad\text{for every }p\in[0,1] . \]

Variance. A \(\Ber(q)\) variable has variance \(q(1-q)\); for independent \(Y_i\), \(\Var[\bar Y_n]=\frac1{n^2}\cdot n\,q(1-q)=\frac{q(1-q)}n\). Subtracting a constant does not change a variance, and dividing by \(r\) multiplies it by \(\frac1{r^2}\) (\(\Var[aY+b]=a^2\Var[Y]\)):

\[ \Var[\hat p]=\frac1{r^2}\Var[\bar Y_n]=\frac{q(p)\bigl(1-q(p)\bigr)}{n\,r^2} . \]

Estimation view (not asked). Since \(\hat p\) is unbiased, \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat p]=\Var[\hat p]\to0\), so \(\hat p\) is consistent. The factor \(\frac1{r^2}\) is the price of privacy: with \(r=\frac12\) you need four times as many participants as with direct questions (\(r=1\)) for the same variance — in fact even more, because \(q(1-q)\) moves towards \(\frac14\). Numbers from part (d): \(r=\frac12\), \(n=100\), \(\bar y=0.64\) give \(\hat p=0.78\) and an estimated standard deviation \(\sqrt{0.64\cdot0.36/(100\cdot0.25)}\approx0.096\).

Subtle point: \(\hat p\) and the mle are not always the same. P5b assumed \(\bar y_n\in[\frac{1-r}2,\frac{1+r}2]\); then the mle equals \(\hat p\). Without that assumption the mle is \(\hat p\) cut off at 0 and 1 (see P5b), because \(\hat p\) itself can be negative or above 1 — for example \(r=\frac12\), \(n=4\), all answers 0 gives \(\hat p=\frac{0-0.25}{0.5}=-0.5\). So \(\hat p\) is unbiased but can leave \([0,1]\); the cut-off mle always lies in \([0,1]\) but is (slightly) biased near \(p=0\) and \(p=1\). This is another instance of "mles need not be unbiased". The official solution is correct for the task as posed.

Definitions

estimator / estimate
statistic \(\hat\theta=T(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) (random) / its value \(T(x_1,\dots,x_n)\) (a number)

\(\E[\hat\theta]-\theta\); unbiased: 0 for all \(\theta\in\Theta\)

Results to know

sample mean
unbiased, strongly consistent, \(\Var=\sigma^2/n\), asymptotically normal (\(V=\sigma^2\))
variance
\(\E[\frac1n\sum(X_i-\bar X)^2]=\frac{n-1}n\sigma^2\); \(S_n^2\) (divide by \(n-1\)) unbiased; normal data: mse \(\frac{2\sigma^4}{n-1}\) vs \(\frac{(2n-1)\sigma^4}{n^2}\)
uniform
\(\E[X_{(n)}]=\frac n{n+1}\theta\); \(\frac{n+1}nX_{(n)}\) is the mvue, \(\Var=\frac{\theta^2}{n(n+2)}\); \(\Var[2\bar X_n]=\frac{\theta^2}{3n}\)
consistency test
mse → 0 ⟹ consistent (Markov); bias → 0 alone is not enough
combinations
\(a\hat\theta_1+b\hat\theta_2\) unbiased for all θ iff \(a+b=1\) (linearity, no independence needed)
unbiased by scaling
toasters: \(\hat d=\frac{n}{2}\omega\); randomized response: \(\hat p=(\bar Y_n-\frac{1-r}2)/r\), \(\Var=\frac{q(1-q)}{nr^2}\); empirical cdf: mse \(\frac{F(t)(1-F(t))}n\)
rainfall mle
\(\frac1{2n}\sum X_i\): unbiased, \(\Var=\operatorname{mse}=\frac{\theta^2}{2n}\), \(V(\theta)=\frac{\theta^2}2\), attains the crlb
mle table
Ber, Poi: \(\bar X_n\); Exp: \(1/\bar X_n\); normal: \(\bar X_n\), \(\frac1n\sum(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\); Unif(0,θ): \(X_{(n)}\); \(2c^2/x^3\): \(\min X_i\); rainfall \(xe^{-x/\theta}/\theta^2\): \(\bar X_n/2\)
mle properties
asymptotic: consistent, asymptotically normal (\(V(\theta)=I_1(\theta)^{-1}\), the inverse Fisher information of one observation), asymptotically efficient; invariance \(g(\hat\theta)\); finite \(n\): no guarantees
outlook
Fisher information, crlb \(\Var[\hat\theta]\ge1/I_n(\theta)=\frac1{n\,I_1(\theta)}\), efficient ⟹ mvue, Rao–Blackwell, Gauss–Markov

Methods

  • mle: product → log → derivative = 0 → check maximum (second derivative or, better, sign of \(\ell'\)).
  • Support depends on \(\theta\): indicators → condition on \(\theta\) → monotone → boundary (sample max/min).
  • Distribution of \(\max\): \(\P(\max\le t)=\prod\P(X_i\le t)\); of \(\min\): \(\P(\min>t)=\prod\P(X_i>t)\).
  • Reparametrised model: maximise in the convenient parameter, translate back (invariance).

Traps

  • Asymptotically unbiased does not imply consistent (official Sheet 10 Ex 2 slip; \(X_1\) counterexample).
  • mle ≠ smallest mse at finite \(n\) (SoSe26 P1e).
  • \(\ell''<0\) at the critical point proves only a local maximum.
  • Differentiate in \(\sigma^2\), not \(\sigma\), when the parameter is \(\sigma^2\).

Exam focus

Every exam so far had an mle derivation (SoSe25 P4a Poisson, WiSe25 P4a rainfall, SoSe26 P5b randomized response), followed by unbiasedness/variance, a Chebyshev bound or a clt approximation of the same estimator. Short items so far: unbiasedness of a weighted combination (SoSe25 P1b), unbiasedness and mse of the empirical cdf (WiSe25 P5b, c), and a true/false item on finite-\(n\) optimality of the mle (SoSe26 P1e). This describes past exams only.

Hypothesis testing

Hypothesentests

What this page covers Script §3.3, pp. 100–110

This page covers everything from Overview 3.33 to Overview 3.53. The script states the goal of the section like this: "Hypothesis testing provides a formal framework for making decisions about claims on population (true) parameters based on sample data/observations. We formulate a 'null hypothesis' (H0), often representing a default state, no effect, or a statement to be falsified, and an 'alternative hypothesis' (H1), representing the claim we wish to support. Then we use the observed data to decide (ideally with high confidence) whether we can reject the null hypothesis."

There are four parts: (1) the building blocks of a test — hypotheses, test, rejection region, the two kinds of error, level, power (Overview 3.33 – Convention 3.37); (2) optimal tests and the Neyman–Pearson lemma (Definition 3.38 – Example 3.41); (3) how tests are built in practice, with the z-test, the t-test, the χ²-test and the two-sample t-test (Viewpoint 3.42 – Remark 3.47); (4) p-values, how they are misread, p-hacking, and an outlook (Definition 3.48 – Overview 3.53).

Worked in place: Sheet 11 Ex 1, 2, 3, 4 (Sheet 11 itself has no confidence-interval part; §3.4 re-reads Ex 1 and Ex 3 as intervals: Ex 1 as a ci, Ex 3 as a ci, and the test–interval duality Remark 3.59 is at §3.4), and the old-exam tasks SoSe25 P1c, SoSe25 P4d and SoSe26 P5d. The earlier parts of those exam problems (the maximum-likelihood estimator, abbreviated mle, and the central-limit-theorem approximation, abbreviated clt — SoSe25 P4a–c and SoSe26 P5b–c) are on §3.2; SoSe26 P5a is on §1.4.

The big picture

A friend hands you a coin and says "it is fair". You are suspicious. You toss it 100 times and count heads. How many heads would make you say "I do not believe you"?

Hypothesis testing turns this gut feeling into a rule. It works like a court of law:

  • The null hypothesis [Nullhypothese] \(H_0\) is the "defendant is innocent" statement — here "the coin is fair". We keep believing it unless the evidence is strong.
  • The alternative [Alternativhypothese] \(H_1\) is what we suspect — "the coin is not fair".
  • We compute how surprising the data would be if \(H_0\) were true. If the data would be very surprising, we reject \(H_0\) ("guilty"). Otherwise we do not reject it ("not proven guilty") — which is not the same as "proven innocent".

Numbers (my example). Let \(S\) be the number of heads in 100 tosses. If the coin is fair, one toss has mean \(\frac12\) and standard deviation \(\frac12\), so \(S\) has mean \(100\cdot\frac12=50\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{100}\cdot\frac12=5\). By the central limit theorem (clt, §2.4) \(S\) is roughly normally distributed. We measure the surprise by the number of standard deviations between the observed count and 50, the standardised value \(z=\frac{S-50}{5}\), and by the probability that a fair coin gives a result at least this far from 50 (the p-value, Definition 3.48 below):

heads observed\(z=\frac{S-50}5\)p-value (clt)p-value (exact binomial)verdict at "5 %"
5510.3170.368not surprising — do not reject
6020.0460.057borderline — the approximation says reject, the exact value says do not
6530.00270.0035very surprising — reject

The "5 %" is the significance level \(\alpha\) [Signifikanzniveau]: we decide in advance that we reject \(H_0\) whenever the data fall into a region that a fair coin would only produce with probability 5 %. Then, if the coin really is fair, we wrongly accuse it in only 5 % of all experiments. That wrong accusation is the type I error. The opposite mistake — not noticing that the coin is biased — is the type II error.

In words: a test asks "could the data plausibly have come from \(H_0\)?". If the answer is "only with a tiny probability", we reject \(H_0\). The small print (the row with 60 heads) shows that the answer depends on how well we know the distribution of our statistic under \(H_0\).

Cross-references

Natural logarithm and its monotonicity: Analysis 5.2. Antiderivatives (for integrating the exponential density): Analysis 8.3. The normal, \(t\) and \(\chi^2\) distributions: §1.3. Quantiles: §2.1. Affine maps of Gaussians (standardising): §2.3. The clt: §2.4. Bayes' theorem: §1.4. Measurable maps: B4. Statistical models, statistics and the likelihood: §3.1. Estimators, the sample variance, the mle: §3.2.

0. Words and symbols from §3.1 and §3.2 used on this page

  • Parameter space \(\Theta\) (Theta): the set of all parameter values we consider possible, e.g. \(\Theta=\R\) for an unknown mean. A single parameter value is written \(\theta\) (theta).
  • Statistical model \((\Omega,\Aa,\P_\Theta)\) (Definition 3.4, §3.1): a sample space \(\Omega\) of possible observations, its events \(\Aa\), and a whole family \(\P_\Theta=(\P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}\) of candidate distributions, one for each parameter value. The model is well-specified if one of the \(\P_\theta\) is the true distribution of the data; that \(\theta\) is the true parameter.
  • \(\P_\theta(\cdot)\) and \(\E_\theta[\cdot]\): probability and expectation computed as if \(\theta\) were the true parameter. Example: \(\P_{\mu_0}(\bar X_n>c)\) is "the probability that the sample mean exceeds \(c\), if the true mean is \(\mu_0\)".
  • Sample \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)\): the random data (before we look), usually iid (independent and identically distributed). The observed data are the numbers \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\). Capital letter = random, small letter = the value we actually saw. \(\Omega^n\) is the set of all possible data vectors of length \(n\).
  • Statistic (Definition 3.6): any function \(T(X)\) of the data alone, e.g. the sample mean \(\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) and the sample variance \(S_n^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\) (Example 3.7). \(S_n=\sqrt{S_n^2}\) is the sample standard deviation. Observed values are written \(\bar x_n\), \(s_n^2\), \(t_{\text{obs}}=T(x)\). A hat, as in \(\hat\theta\) or \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}\), marks an estimator of the quantity under the hat — a statistic used as a guess for it (§3.2).
  • Likelihood (Definition 3.13): \(L(\theta\mid x)=p(x\mid\theta)\), the probability mass function (pmf, for discrete data: \(p(x\mid\theta)=\P_\theta(X=x)\)) or density (for continuous data) of the observed data \(x\), read as a function of \(\theta\). For iid data it is the product \(\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i\mid\theta)\).
  • Indicator \(\one_R(t)\) (the Greek letter chi with the set \(R\) as index, as in the script): equals 1 if \(t\in R\) and 0 otherwise (B2). Its expectation is a probability: \(\E[\one_R(T)]=1\cdot\P(T\in R)+0\cdot\P(T\notin R)=\P(T\in R)\). This fact is used all the time below.
  • \(\sup\) (supremum): the smallest upper bound of a set of numbers. For a finite set, or when the largest value is attained, it is simply the maximum. Example: the set \(\{0.5,0.9,0.99,0.999,\dots\}\) has no largest element, but its supremum is 1. Full treatment: Analysis 1.2.
  • \(\Theta=\Theta_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}\Theta_1\) (the script writes a small circle over the union sign): \(\Theta\) is split into two parts with no overlap (\(\Theta_0\cap\Theta_1=\emptyset\)) that together give all of \(\Theta\) — a partition. \(|\Theta_0|\) is the number of elements of \(\Theta_0\).
  • Measurable map (B4): a technical condition which guarantees that \(\varphi(X)\) is again a random variable, so that \(\E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\) makes sense. Every formula-defined test on this page is measurable; you never have to check it in exercises.

1. The standard normal: \(\Phi\), standardising, and the upper quantiles \(z_\alpha\)

\(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) means \(Z\) is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance 1. Its cumulative distribution function [Verteilungsfunktion], abbreviated cdf — the function that returns, for each number \(z\), the probability of landing at or below \(z\) — is \(\Phi(z)=\P(Z\le z)\) (the area under the bell curve to the left of \(z\)). There is no closed formula; exams give values. The bell curve is symmetric about 0, so \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\).

Standardising (Example 2.52, §2.3): if \(Y\sim\mathcal N(m,s^2)\), then \(\frac{Y-m}{s}\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\). So \(\P(Y\le y)=\P\bigl(\frac{Y-m}s\le\frac{y-m}s\bigr)=\Phi\bigl(\frac{y-m}s\bigr)\). For iid \(X_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the sample mean is again normal, \(\bar X_n\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}n)\) (sums of independent Gaussians are Gaussian, §2.3; mean by linearity, variance \(\frac1{n^2}\cdot n\sigma^2\)). Hence

\[ \frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim\mathcal N(0,1). \]

\(\sigma/\sqrt n\) is the standard error of the sample mean.

Upper quantiles (the notation of this section). A \(q\)-quantile is a point below which probability \(q\) lies (Definition 2.20, §2.1). In testing, the script writes \(z_\alpha\) for the point with probability \(\alpha\) above it:

\[ \P(Z>z_\alpha)=\alpha,\qquad\text{i.e. }z_\alpha\text{ is the }(1-\alpha)\text{-quantile of }\mathcal N(0,1),\qquad \Phi(z_\alpha)=1-\alpha . \]

Watch the index: \(z_{0.05}\) is the 0.95-quantile. A two-sided test at level \(\alpha\) needs \(z_{\alpha/2}\): half of \(\alpha\) in each tail. The values you need (computed with Python/scipy):

\(\alpha\)0.100.050.0250.010.0050.0005
\(z_\alpha\)1.28161.64491.96002.32632.57583.2905
used forone-sided 10 %one-sided 5 %two-sided 5 %one-sided 1 %two-sided 1 %two-sided 0.1 %

Exam hints round these to 1.28, 1.64 (or 1.645), 1.96, 2.33, 2.576 and 3.29. Useful \(\Phi\) values: \(\Phi(1)=0.8413\), \(\Phi(2)=0.9772\), \(\Phi(3)=0.99865\), and \(1-\Phi(5)=2.87\cdot10^{-7}\).

A small \(\Phi\) table my addition, computed with Python/scipy (enough for this course's exercises; exams print the values they need):

\(z\)00.170.511.281.51.6451.9622.3262.52.5763
\(\Phi(z)\)0.50000.56750.69150.84130.89970.93320.95000.97500.97720.99000.99380.99500.99865

Negative \(z\). Tables list only \(z\ge0\). For negative arguments use the symmetry rule \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\). Why: the bell curve is a mirror image around 0, so the area to the left of \(-z\) equals the area to the right of \(+z\), and the area to the right of \(z\) is the total area 1 minus the area to its left, \(1-\Phi(z)\). Example: \(\Phi(-0.17)=1-\Phi(0.17)=1-0.5675=0.4325\) (used in Sheet 11 Ex 4 below).

In words: look up the positive value, and if your \(z\) was negative, take 1 minus it.

2. Student's \(t\) and the \(\chi^2\) distribution

Both are introduced in Script 1.61 (§1.3). What you need here:

  • \(\chi^2_k\) (chi-squared with \(k\) degrees of freedom): the distribution of \(Z_1^2+\dots+Z_k^2\) for independent standard normals \(Z_i\). It lives on \((0,\infty)\), has mean \(k\), and is skewed to the right.
  • \(t_\nu\) (Student's \(t\) with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom, Remark 1.62): the distribution of \(\frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/\nu}}\) with \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and \(V\sim\chi^2_\nu\) independent. It is a bell curve centred at 0, symmetric, but with heavier tails than \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). As \(\nu\to\infty\) it approaches \(\mathcal N(0,1)\).
  • Why the t appears in testing: if we do not know \(\sigma\) and replace it by the estimate \(S_n\), the standardised mean \(\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{S_n/\sqrt n}\) is no longer exactly normal: the random denominator adds extra spread. For Gaussian data it is exactly \(t_{n-1}\) (Example 3.45 below).

Upper quantiles are written like \(z_\alpha\): \(t_{\nu,\alpha}\) has probability \(\alpha\) above it, and \(\chi^2_{k,\alpha}\) likewise. Values (scipy):

\(\nu\)1259142999\(\infty\) (normal)
\(t_{\nu,0.025}\)12.7064.3032.5712.2622.1452.0451.9841.960
\(t_{\nu,0.05}\)6.3142.9202.0151.8331.7611.6991.6601.645

The \(t\) quantiles are larger than the normal ones: with an estimated \(\sigma\) you need stronger evidence before rejecting. The difference is large for small samples and vanishes for large ones.

3. Two algebra facts used in the Neyman–Pearson computations

  • \(\ln\) keeps inequalities: \(\ln\) is strictly increasing (Analysis 5.2), so for positive \(a,b\): \(a>b\iff\ln a>\ln b\). Also \(\ln(e^u)=u\).
  • Dividing by a negative number flips an inequality: \(-2x>6\iff x<-3\). Dividing by a positive number keeps it.

Building blocks of a test

Overview 3.33 hypothesis testing motivation Script 3.33

A statistical hypothesis is a claim about the parameters of a statistical model. We usually consider two competing claims that cannot both be true:

  • The null hypothesis \(H_0\): a statement of "no effect" or "no difference", often the default or status quo. Formally it is a subset \(\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta\) of the parameter space: "the true \(\theta\) lies in \(\Theta_0\)".
  • The alternative hypothesis \(H_1\) (or \(H_A\)): contradicts the null; it is the claim we want to find evidence for. It is a subset \(\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta\) with \(\Theta_0\cap\Theta_1=\emptyset\).

Given a sample \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)\sim\P_\Theta\), we want to decide whether the smaller model \((\Omega,\Aa,\P_{\Theta_0})\) is misspecified — whether we can conclude that the true parameter is not in \(\Theta_0\). Then we reject the null. This is a yes/no decision based only on the sample, so a test maps observed data \(x\) to \(\{0,1\}\) (reject or not).

How to design the rule. Take a real-valued statistic \(T(X)\) whose distribution we can work out (at least approximately) assuming the null is true. For the observed data we compute the number \(T(x)\), and we know which distribution it would come from if \(H_0\) held. If \(T(x)\) is exceedingly unlikely under that distribution (judged by a threshold fixed in advance), we reject the null.

In the coin example of the big picture: \(\Theta=[0,1]\) (the probability of heads), \(\Theta_0=\{0.5\}\), \(\Theta_1=[0,1]\setminus\{0.5\}\), \(T=\) number of heads, and under \(H_0\) we know \(T\sim\Bin(100,0.5)\approx\mathcal N(50,25)\).

Definition 3.34 building blocks and properties of hypothesis tests Script 3.34

Setup. \((\Omega,\Aa,\P_\Theta)\) is a statistical model and \(\Theta=\Theta_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}\Theta_1\) a partition of the parameter space.

  1. Simple vs composite. A hypothesis is simple [einfach] if it contains exactly one parameter, \(|\Theta_0|=1\) (or \(|\Theta_1|=1\)); its element is then called \(\theta_0\) (or \(\theta_1\)). Otherwise (\(|\Theta_{0}|>1\), resp. \(|\Theta_1|>1\)) it is composite [zusammengesetzt]. Composite hypotheses often have a special "boundary" value too, e.g. \(\Theta_0=\{\theta\in\Theta\mid\theta>\theta_0\}\).
  2. Which one is valid. For \(X\sim\P_\Theta\): the null \(H_0\) is valid if \((\Omega,\Aa,\P_{\Theta_0})\) is well-specified (the true parameter lies in \(\Theta_0\)). Otherwise the alternative \(H_1\) is valid.
  3. Test. A statistical test [Test] is a measurable map \(\varphi:\Omega^n\to[0,1]\), read as a decision rule for rejecting the null. If \(\varphi\) only takes the values 0 and 1, the test is non-randomized; otherwise it is randomized. The course focuses on non-randomized tests.
  4. Rejection region and errors. For a non-randomized test, \(\varphi(x)=1\) means "reject the null". The set \(\varphi^{-1}(\{1\})=\{x\in\Omega^n\mid\varphi(x)=1\}\) is the rejection region [Ablehnungsbereich / kritischer Bereich]. (\(\varphi^{-1}(\{1\})\) is the pre-image of \(\{1\}\): all data vectors the test sends to 1. It does not mean an inverse function — B2. The set-builder form after the equals sign says the same thing.)
    • Type I error [Fehler 1. Art]: rejecting \(H_0\) although it is true (\(\varphi(x)=1\) while \(\P_{\Theta_0}\) is well-specified).
    • Type II error [Fehler 2. Art]: not rejecting \(H_0\) although it is false (\(\varphi(x)=0\) while \(\P_{\Theta_1}\) is well-specified).
    true state \ decisionfail to reject \(H_0\)reject \(H_0\)
    \(H_0\) is truecorrect decisiontype I error
    \(H_1\) is truetype II errorcorrect decision
  5. Size and level. The significance level or size [Signifikanzniveau, Umfang] of \(\varphi\) is the largest probability of a type I error: \[ \alpha:=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\E_\theta[\varphi]. \] \(\varphi\) is a test at (significance) level \(\alpha\) for a given \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) if \(\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\E_\theta[\varphi]\le\alpha\).
  6. Power function. The power function [Gütefunktion] of the test is \[ G_\varphi:\Theta\to[0,1],\qquad\theta\mapsto\E_\theta[\varphi]. \] For \(\theta\in\Theta_1\), \(G_\varphi(\theta)\) is the power [Macht, Trennschärfe] of \(\varphi\) against the alternative \(\theta\): the probability that the alternative is recognised when it is true. The probability of a type II error at \(\theta\in\Theta_1\) is \(\beta(\theta):=1-G_\varphi(\theta)\).

How to read each part (mine).

  • Why \(\E_\theta[\varphi]\) is a probability. Write \(\varphi\) short for \(\varphi(X)\). For a non-randomized test \(\varphi(X)\) is 0 or 1, i.e. the indicator of "\(X\) in the rejection region". By the indicator fact (primer 0), \(\E_\theta[\varphi]=\P_\theta(\text{reject }H_0)\). So the power function is "probability of rejecting", as a function of the true parameter. On \(\Theta_0\) its values are type I error probabilities (we want them small); on \(\Theta_1\) its values are the power (we want it large). For a randomized test the same holds: by Remark 3.36(iv) we reject with probability \(\varphi(x)\) once the data \(x\) are seen, and averaging this over the data (law of total probability, §1.4) gives \(\P_\theta(\text{reject})=\E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\).
  • Why a supremum in (v). A composite null contains many parameter values, each with its own probability of wrongly rejecting. The size is the worst of them. "Level \(\alpha\)" is a promise: whatever \(\theta\in\Theta_0\) is true, we wrongly reject with probability at most \(\alpha\).
  • Size vs level. The script uses "significance level" for both. Strictly, the size is the number \(\sup_{\Theta_0}\E_\theta[\varphi]\), while "at level \(\alpha\)" only asks size \(\le\alpha\). A test of size 0.01 is also a test at level 0.05.

A small example with real numbers (mine). Toss a coin 10 times; \(S\) = number of heads, \(S\sim\Bin(10,p)\). Test \(H_0:p=0.5\) (simple) against \(H_1:p>0.5\) (composite) with the rule "reject if \(S\ge9\)". So \(\varphi(x)=\one_{\{9,10\}}(S)\), and the rejection region is "9 or 10 heads".

  • Size: \(G_\varphi(0.5)=\P_{0.5}(S\ge9)=\binom{10}9\frac1{2^{10}}+\binom{10}{10}\frac1{2^{10}}=\frac{10+1}{1024}=0.0107\). This is a test at level 0.05 (and even at level 0.011).
  • Power against \(p=0.8\): \(G_\varphi(0.8)=10\cdot0.8^9\cdot0.2+0.8^{10}=0.376\). So \(\beta(0.8)=1-0.376=0.624\): a coin with 80 % heads is missed 62 % of the time. Ten tosses are not much evidence.
  • Power against \(p=0.6\): \(G_\varphi(0.6)=0.046\), barely above the size.

How it is used. Exams ask you to state \(H_0\), \(H_1\), the test statistic, its distribution under \(H_0\), the rejection rule, the observed value and the decision (SoSe26 P5d below), or to compute \(\beta\) and the power (Sheet 11 Ex 4).

Example 3.35 hypotheses Script 3.35

  1. A coin with unknown probability of heads \(p\): is it fair? \(H_0:p=0.5\) (simple) versus \(H_1:p\ne0.5\) (composite).
  2. \(\mu\) is the average recovery time with a new drug; the current standard is \(\mu_0=10\) days. Is the new drug better? \(H_0:\mu\ge10\) (no improvement or worse) versus \(H_1:\mu<10\) (improvement). Both are composite. A simpler setup that is often used: \(H_0:\mu=10\) versus \(H_1:\mu<10\).

Note which claim goes where: the claim we want to show (the drug is better) is \(H_1\). The reason is the asymmetry of Remark 3.36: only a rejection is a strong statement, so we set things up so that rejecting \(H_0\) means "we found evidence for what we care about". In (ii), \(H_0:\mu\ge10\) and \(H_0:\mu=10\) lead to the same test, because the worst case over \(\mu\ge10\) is the boundary \(\mu=10\) (Viewpoint 3.42(iii)).

Remark 3.36 testing in practice Script 3.36

  1. Deliberate asymmetry. Type I and type II errors are not treated equally. We mainly want to detect "non-default situations", i.e. to detect when the null should be rejected. So in practice we first fix a desired level \(\alpha\) (which determines the rejection region), and then look for a test that (a) satisfies \(G_\varphi(\theta)\le\alpha\) for all \(\theta\in\Theta_0\) and (b) maximises \(G_\varphi(\theta)\) for all \(\theta\in\Theta_1\). We demand an upper bound on type I errors, and within that requirement minimise type II errors.
  2. Trade-off. For a fixed sample size \(n\), \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) pull against each other. A smaller \(\alpha\) generally makes the rejection region smaller: more extreme observations are needed to reject. Being more conservative in this way increases the type II error \(\beta(\theta)\) for at least some alternatives, i.e. lowers the power against them. (Try it in the z-test widget below: move \(\alpha\) and watch \(\beta\).)
  3. Not rejecting is not accepting. Failing to reject the null does not mean accepting it or having strong evidence for it. Absence of evidence against the null is not evidence for the null. A test can have weak power regardless of its level.
  4. Randomized tests. When \(\varphi(x)\in(0,1)\), one rejects with probability \(\varphi(x)\): the decision is a single draw of a \(\Ber(\varphi(x))\) random variable. Randomized tests matter in the theory of "uniformly most powerful" tests (Definition 3.38).

Why one would ever randomize (my example, continuing the 10-toss test). With a discrete statistic you often cannot hit a level exactly: "reject if \(S\ge9\)" has size 0.0107, and "reject if \(S\ge8\)" has size \(\frac{56}{1024}=0.0547>0.05\). The randomized test "reject if \(S\ge9\); if \(S=8\), reject with probability \(\gamma\)" has size \(0.0107+\gamma\cdot\frac{45}{1024}\). Setting this equal to 0.05 gives \(\gamma=0.893\), and the power at \(p=0.8\) rises from 0.376 to 0.646. In practice nobody flips an extra coin to decide a medical study — but the theory needs such tests to make "most powerful at exactly level \(\alpha\)" always possible.

Convention 3.37 Script 3.37

From now on we always have a statistical model \((\Omega,\Aa,\P_\Theta)\), a partition \(\Theta=\Theta_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}\Theta_1\) into the null hypothesis \(H_0:\Theta_0\) and the alternative \(H_1:\Theta_1\), and a test \(\varphi\) of \(H_0\) against \(H_1\).

Optimal tests and the Neyman–Pearson lemma

Idea first (mine). Remark 3.36(i) says: among all tests whose type I error is at most \(\alpha\), find the one that detects the alternative most often. The next two definitions name the ideal (a test that is best against every alternative at once) and a minimal sanity requirement (never be worse than guessing). The Neyman–Pearson lemma then solves the problem completely in the simplest case: one null value against one alternative value.

Definition 3.38 uniformly most powerful test (ump) Script 3.38

Let \(\alpha\in[0,1]\). A test \(\varphi\) at level \(\alpha\) is (uniformly) most powerful [gleichmäßig bester Test] at level \(\alpha\) if for every other test \(\psi\) of \(H_0\) against \(H_1\) at level \(\alpha\):

\[ G_\varphi(\theta)\ge G_\psi(\theta)\qquad\text{for all }\theta\in\Theta_1 . \]

"Uniformly" means: the same test \(\varphi\) beats every competitor at every alternative \(\theta\). That is a lot to ask; often one test is best against small effects and another against large ones, and then no ump exists (Overview 3.53(i)). When \(\Theta_1\) has only one element, "uniformly" adds nothing and one just says "most powerful". (The script's definition does not repeat that \(\varphi\) itself must be at level \(\alpha\); this is meant.)

Definition 3.39 unbiased test Script 3.39

Let \(\alpha\in[0,1]\). \(\varphi\) is unbiased [unverfälscht] at level \(\alpha\) if

\[ G_\varphi(\theta_0)\le\alpha\le G_\varphi(\theta_1)\qquad\text{for all }\theta_0\in\Theta_0,\ \theta_1\in\Theta_1 . \]

Intuition (mine): the test rejects at least as often when \(H_1\) is true as when \(H_0\) is true. A biased test would reject a true null more often than some false one — worse than a coin flip that rejects with probability \(\alpha\) regardless of the data.

Counterexample (mine). Test \(H_0:\mu=\mu_0\) against the two-sided \(H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0\), but use the one-sided rule "reject if \(\frac{\bar X_n-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}>z_\alpha\)" (Example 3.41). If the true mean is one standard error below \(\mu_0\), the standardised mean is \(\mathcal N(-1,1)\), and the power is \(\P(Z-1>1.645)=1-\Phi(2.645)=0.004<0.05\). So this test is not unbiased for the two-sided alternative. The two-sided z-test (Example 3.44) is unbiased; the power widget below shows both curves.

Theorem 3.40 Neyman–Pearson lemma (1932) Script 3.40

Assumptions. A binary statistical model \((\Omega,\Aa,(\P_{\theta_0},\P_{\theta_1}))\) — only two candidate distributions. We test the simple null \(H_0:\{\theta_0\}\) against the simple alternative \(H_1:\{\theta_1\}\). \(L(\theta\mid x)\) is the likelihood (pmf or density of the data under \(\theta\)). A level \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) is given.

Conclusion. The most powerful test at level \(\alpha\) is the likelihood ratio test (lrt) [Likelihood-Quotienten-Test], which rejects \(H_0\) if and only if

\[ \frac{L(\theta_1\mid x)}{L(\theta_0\mid x)}>k , \]

where the constant \(k\) is chosen such that the test has size \(\alpha\) (the script adds: "implying that such a test exists").

Intuition (mine). We have a "budget" of \(\alpha\) probability under \(H_0\) to spend on the rejection region. Each possible data point \(x\) costs \(L(\theta_0\mid x)\) (its probability under \(H_0\)) and earns \(L(\theta_1\mid x)\) (its probability under \(H_1\), which counts towards the power). The best buy is to put into the rejection region the data points with the best earnings-per-cost ratio \(\frac{L(\theta_1\mid x)}{L(\theta_0\mid x)}\), starting with the best, until the budget \(\alpha\) is used up. The cut-off ratio is \(k\).

Why the assumptions matter. Both hypotheses must be simple: with several alternative values, the best region could depend on which alternative we aim at (then there may be no ump). "Size exactly \(\alpha\)" is essential in the proof; for discrete data such a \(k\) may not exist without randomizing (Remark 3.36(iv)) — so the script's "implying that such a test exists" really needs either continuous data or randomized tests.

Proof (for densities, non-randomized) My proof — the script states the lemma without proof

Write \(p_0(x)=L(\theta_0\mid x)\) and \(p_1(x)=L(\theta_1\mid x)\) for the densities of the data under the two hypotheses (for discrete data replace integrals by sums). Let \(\varphi(x)=1\) if \(p_1(x)>k\,p_0(x)\) and \(\varphi(x)=0\) otherwise, with \(k\ge0\) chosen so that \(\E_{\theta_0}[\varphi]=\alpha\). Let \(\psi\) be any test with values in \([0,1]\) and \(\E_{\theta_0}[\psi]\le\alpha\). We show \(\E_{\theta_1}[\varphi]\ge\E_{\theta_1}[\psi]\).

Step 1 (a pointwise inequality). For every \(x\): \[ \bigl(\varphi(x)-\psi(x)\bigr)\bigl(p_1(x)-k\,p_0(x)\bigr)\ge0 . \] Reason, case by case:

  • If \(p_1(x)>kp_0(x)\): then \(\varphi(x)=1\), and \(\psi(x)\le1\), so the first bracket is \(\ge0\); the second is \(>0\). Product \(\ge0\).
  • If \(p_1(x)\le kp_0(x)\): then \(\varphi(x)=0\), and \(\psi(x)\ge0\), so the first bracket is \(\le0\); the second is \(\le0\). Product of two non-positive numbers \(\ge0\).

Step 2 (integrate). Integrating a non-negative function gives a non-negative number: \[ 0\le\int(\varphi-\psi)(p_1-kp_0)\,\mathrm dx=\underbrace{\int\varphi p_1-\int\psi p_1}_{\E_{\theta_1}[\varphi]-\E_{\theta_1}[\psi]}-k\underbrace{\Bigl(\int\varphi p_0-\int\psi p_0\Bigr)}_{\E_{\theta_0}[\varphi]-\E_{\theta_0}[\psi]} . \] (Expanding the product and using linearity of the integral; \(\int\varphi p_1\,\mathrm dx\) is the expectation of \(\varphi(X)\) when \(X\) has density \(p_1\).)

Step 3 (use the sizes). Rearranging: \(\E_{\theta_1}[\varphi]-\E_{\theta_1}[\psi]\ge k\bigl(\E_{\theta_0}[\varphi]-\E_{\theta_0}[\psi]\bigr)=k\bigl(\alpha-\E_{\theta_0}[\psi]\bigr)\ge0\), because \(k\ge0\) and \(\E_{\theta_0}[\psi]\le\alpha\). So \(G_\varphi(\theta_1)\ge G_\psi(\theta_1)\): no test at level \(\alpha\) has more power. ∎

Where the assumptions were used: size exactly \(\alpha\) in step 3 (if \(\varphi\) had size below \(\alpha\), a competitor could spend the rest of the budget and win); simple hypotheses so that there is a single \(p_0\) and a single \(p_1\). (Why \(k\ge0\): for \(k<0\) every \(x\) would satisfy \(p_1>kp_0\), and the test would always reject, with size 1.)

Widget — Neyman–Pearson in action My addition

Setting of Sheet 11 Ex 2 with \(\lambda_0=1\): one observation \(X\), grey curve = density under \(H_0\) (\(\Exp(1)\)), blue curve = density under \(H_1\) (\(\Exp(\lambda_1)\)). Choose a rejection region; every choice below has the same size \(\alpha\) (orange area under the grey curve). The blue area under the blue curve over the same region is the power. The likelihood-ratio region "\(x<c\)" always wins — that is Theorem 3.40.

Example 3.41 testing the mean of a Gaussian Script 3.41

Setting. \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with unknown mean and known variance \(\sigma^2\); so \(\theta=\mu\in\Theta=\R\). Test the simple \(H_0:\{\mu_0\}\) against the simple \(H_1:\{\mu_1\}\), with \(\mu_1>\mu_0\) for concreteness.

Step 1: the likelihood ratio. The likelihood of iid normal data is \(L(\mu\mid x)=\prod_i\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(x_i-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\exp\bigl(-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2\bigr)\) (product of exponentials = exponential of the sum). In the ratio the constant \((2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\) cancels:

\[ \Lambda(x):=\frac{\exp\bigl(-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum(x_i-\mu_1)^2\bigr)}{\exp\bigl(-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum(x_i-\mu_0)^2\bigr)} =\exp\Bigl(\frac1{2\sigma^2}\Bigl[\sum(x_i-\mu_0)^2-\sum(x_i-\mu_1)^2\Bigr]\Bigr) =\exp\Bigl(\frac1{2\sigma^2}\Bigl[2(\mu_1-\mu_0)\sum x_i+n(\mu_0^2-\mu_1^2)\Bigr]\Bigr). \]

The last step: expand \((x_i-\mu)^2=x_i^2-2\mu x_i+\mu^2\). In the difference the \(x_i^2\) cancel, leaving \(\sum(-2\mu_0x_i+\mu_0^2)-\sum(-2\mu_1x_i+\mu_1^2)=2(\mu_1-\mu_0)\sum x_i+n(\mu_0^2-\mu_1^2)\).

Step 2: simplify the rule. Reject if \(\Lambda(x)>k\). Since \(\ln\) is strictly increasing (primer 3), this is equivalent to

\[ \frac1{2\sigma^2}\Bigl[2(\mu_1-\mu_0)\sum x_i+n(\mu_0^2-\mu_1^2)\Bigr]>\ln k . \]

With \(\mu_1>\mu_0\), rearrange to isolate \(\bar x_n=\frac1n\sum x_i\): the rule becomes \(\bar x_n>c\) for a constant \(c\) depending on \(k\). Explicitly (mine): multiply by \(2\sigma^2\), add \(n(\mu_1^2-\mu_0^2)\), divide by the positive number \(2n(\mu_1-\mu_0)\), and use \(\mu_1^2-\mu_0^2=(\mu_1-\mu_0)(\mu_1+\mu_0)\): \(c=\frac{\sigma^2\ln k}{n(\mu_1-\mu_0)}+\frac{\mu_0+\mu_1}2\). So the most powerful test depends on the data only through the sample mean.

Step 3: choose \(c\) for size \(\alpha\). We need \(\P_{\mu_0}(\bar X_n>c)=\alpha\). Under \(H_0\), \(\bar X_n\sim\mathcal N(\mu_0,\sigma^2/n)\), so \(Z=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) (primer 1), and we need

\[ \P\Bigl(Z>\frac{c-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\Bigr)=\alpha\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{c-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}=z_\alpha\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=\mu_0+z_\alpha\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}, \]

where \(z_\alpha\) satisfies \(\P(Z\ge z_\alpha)=\alpha\): the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of the standard normal. The script notes that this is a common convention in testing: \(t_\alpha\) denotes the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of a random variable \(T\).

Result. Reject \(H_0\) whenever \(\bar x_n>\mu_0+z_\alpha\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\). This is the one-sided z-test. (If \(\mu_1<\mu_0\), dividing by the negative \(\mu_1-\mu_0\) flips the inequality, and the region is \(\bar x_n<c'\).)

Numbers (mine): \(\mu_0=0\), \(\mu_1=1\), \(\sigma=1\), \(n=4\), \(\alpha=0.05\). Standard error \(\frac1{\sqrt4}=0.5\), so \(c=0+1.645\cdot0.5=0.822\). Power: \(\P_{\mu_1}(\bar X_4>0.822)=\P\bigl(Z>\frac{0.822-1}{0.5}\bigr)=\P(Z>-0.355)=0.639\).

Two notes. (1) The script calls this test "the ump". For a simple alternative "most powerful" is the right word. But notice that \(c\) does not depend on \(\mu_1\): the same test is most powerful against every \(\mu_1>\mu_0\), so it is indeed uniformly most powerful for \(H_0:\mu=\mu_0\) against \(H_1:\mu>\mu_0\) (and, since its power function increases in \(\mu\), also for \(H_0:\mu\le\mu_0\)). (2) The statistic \(\bar X_n\) arose automatically from the likelihood ratio — this is how Neyman–Pearson constructs tests (Viewpoint 3.42).

In words: for normal data with known variance, the best test of "mean \(\mu_0\)" against "a larger mean" rejects when the sample mean is more than \(z_\alpha\) standard errors above \(\mu_0\).

Constructing tests in practice

Viewpoint 3.42 constructing tests in practice Script 3.42

So far Theorem 3.40 is our only way of constructing tests, and Example 3.41 showed how it works. Viewing a test as a map \(\varphi:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}\) (\(\mathcal X\) = the set of possible data sets, \(\Omega^n\) above) is good for theory, but in practice nobody writes down \(\varphi\) directly. Instead, one follows the steps extracted from Example 3.41:

  1. Choose a real-valued test statistic [Teststatistik] \(T:\mathcal X\to\R\) — any statistic. For a mean, the sample mean is a good start; for a variance, a sample variance. It can get more sophisticated. The goal: reduce the high-dimensional sample \(x\) to a single number \(T(x)\).
  2. Know its null distribution. Choose \(T\) such that you can (approximately) derive the distribution of \(T(X)\) if the null were true. In Example 3.41, \(T_n(X)=\bar X_n\sim\mathcal N(\mu_0,\sigma^2/n)\) under the null. In other settings, invoke the clt for an approximate normal distribution, or find other ways to approximate the distribution of \(T(X)\) for \(X\sim\P_{\theta_0}\) (\(\theta_0\in\Theta_0\)).
  3. Define the rejection region \(R\) via quantiles of \(T(X)\) under the null. E.g. reject if the observed \(t_{\text{obs}}=T(x)>t_\alpha\) (the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of \(T(X)\)). Or reject outside the \(\alpha/2\)- and \((1-\alpha/2)\)-quantiles (two tails). The value \(t_\alpha\) is the critical value [kritischer Wert] and the rejection region the critical region. For a composite null (\(|\Theta_0|>1\)) there is no single null distribution; since \(\alpha=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}G_\varphi(\theta)\), the supremum determines \(R\). In many settings where \(\Theta\subset\R\) is an interval, \(G_\varphi\) is monotone in \(\theta\) and only one boundary value of \(\Theta_0\) matters — the null boundary.
  4. Final test: \[ \varphi(x)=\one_R(T(x))=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }T(x)\in R\ \text{(reject }H_0),\\0&\text{if }T(x)\notin R\ \text{(don't reject }H_0).\end{cases} \]

The central tasks: choose a good statistic \(T(X)\), and find \(R\) from the distribution of \(T(X)\) under the null so that the test has size \(\alpha\).

Why the boundary is the worst case, in the one-sided z-test with \(H_0:\mu\le\mu_0\): the rule is \(\bar x_n>c\), and \(\P_\mu(\bar X_n>c)\) grows as \(\mu\) grows (the whole bell curve moves right). So over \(\mu\le\mu_0\) the largest rejection probability occurs at \(\mu=\mu_0\). Choosing \(c\) for \(\mu_0\) gives level \(\alpha\) for the whole composite null. This is the argument behind "under \(H_0\) boundary" in Example 3.46.

Definition 3.43 one-sided and two-sided tests Script 3.43

Let \(\Theta\subset\R\).

  • A one-sided (one-tailed) test [einseitiger Test] is used for directional hypotheses such as \(H_1:\theta>\theta_0\) or \(H_1:\theta<\theta_0\). The rejection region lies entirely in one tail of the distribution of the test statistic.
  • A two-sided (two-tailed) test [zweiseitiger Test] is used for non-directional hypotheses such as \(H_1:\theta\ne\theta_0\). The rejection region is split between the two tails.

For a given \(\alpha\), a one-sided test is more powerful for detecting an effect in the specified direction, but has no power to detect an effect in the opposite direction.

Why: the one-sided test puts all of \(\alpha\) in one tail, so its cut-off is lower (1.645 instead of 1.96 at \(\alpha=0.05\)) — easier to exceed. The price is the "wrong" tail: an effect in the other direction is never detected (the biased-test counterexample under Definition 3.39). Choose the direction before seeing the data; choosing it afterwards secretly doubles \(\alpha\).

Example 3.44 z-test for a normal mean (again) Script 3.44

\(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma^2\) known. Test \(H_0:\mu=\mu_0\) versus \(H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0\). Following Example 3.41, the test statistic is the standardised sample mean

\[ Z=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n} . \]

Under \(H_0\), \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\). We reject \(H_0\) when the observed \(z_{\text{obs}}\) is "too far in either tail of \(\mathcal N(0,1)\)": for a fixed level \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), reject if \(|z_{\text{obs}}|>z_{\alpha/2}\), the \((1-\alpha/2)\)-quantile of \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). For \(\alpha=0.05\): \(z_{\alpha/2}\approx1.96\), so reject if \(|z_{\text{obs}}|>1.96\).

Check of the size: \(\P_{\mu_0}(|Z|>z_{\alpha/2})=\P(Z>z_{\alpha/2})+\P(Z<-z_{\alpha/2})=\frac\alpha2+\frac\alpha2=\alpha\) (symmetry of the bell curve). Power function (mine): if the true mean is \(\mu\), then \(Z\sim\mathcal N(\delta,1)\) with \(\delta=\frac{\mu-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\) (the shift in standard-error units). Hence \(G(\mu)=\P(Z>z_{\alpha/2})+\P(Z<-z_{\alpha/2})=1-\Phi(z_{\alpha/2}-\delta)+\Phi(-z_{\alpha/2}-\delta)\). For the one-sided version \(G(\mu)=1-\Phi(z_\alpha-\delta)\). Both formulas are what the two widgets below draw.

Widget — the z-test and its two errors My addition

Setting of Sheet 11 Ex 4: data \(\mathcal N(\mu,9)\), \(\mu_0=10\). Grey curve: distribution of \(\bar X_n\) if \(H_0\) is true. Blue curve: distribution of \(\bar X_n\) if the true mean is \(\mu_1\). Orange area = type I error (\(\alpha\)): \(H_0\) true, but \(\bar X_n\) lands in the rejection region. Blue shaded area = type II error (\(\beta\)): \(\mu_1\) true, but \(\bar X_n\) lands outside the rejection region. Defaults reproduce Sheet 11 Ex 4.

Widget — power functions and sample size My addition

\(G(\mu)=\P_\mu(\text{reject }H_0)\) for the z-test with \(\mu_0=10\), \(\sigma=3\), for four sample sizes. On the null side the curves stay at or below \(\alpha\) (dashed line); on the alternative side they rise towards 1, faster for larger \(n\). The third button keeps the same rule, and therefore draws the same curves as the first — what changes is the alternative it is judged against: with \(H_1:\mu\ne10\) the region \(\mu<10\) now belongs to \(\Theta_1\), and there the curve falls below \(\alpha\) instead of rising above it. That makes the test biased (Definition 3.39), and the readout reports the power at \(\mu=9\) to show how small it is. The readout also does the power analysis of Overview 3.53(ii).

Example 3.45 one-sample t-test for a mean Script 3.45

If \(\sigma^2\) in Example 3.44 is unknown, estimate it by the sample variance \(S_n^2\). The test statistic becomes

\[ T=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu_0}{S_n/\sqrt n}. \]

Under \(H_0\), \(T\) follows Student's \(t\)-distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom, \(T\sim t_{n-1}\) (primer 2). The rejection region of the two-sided test is \(|t_{\text{obs}}|>t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\), the \((1-\alpha/2)\)-quantile of \(t_{n-1}\).

Why \(T\sim t_{n-1}\) (sketch) My addition — the script states it without proof

Write \(T=\dfrac{\frac{\bar X_n-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}}{\sqrt{\frac{(n-1)S_n^2/\sigma^2}{n-1}}}\) (divide numerator and denominator by \(\sigma/\sqrt n\); the \(\sigma\)'s cancel, so \(T\) does not depend on the unknown \(\sigma\)). For iid Gaussian data, three facts hold (the last two are a standard theorem, often called Cochran's or Student's theorem, not proved in this course):

  • the numerator is \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) under \(H_0\) (primer 1);
  • \(V=(n-1)S_n^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-1}\) — one degree of freedom is "used up" by estimating the mean with \(\bar X_n\);
  • \(\bar X_n\) and \(S_n^2\) are independent.

So \(T=Z/\sqrt{V/(n-1)}\) with independent \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), \(V\sim\chi^2_{n-1}\): by Remark 1.62 this is \(t_{n-1}\).

Example 3.46 common Gaussian tests Script 3.46

\(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). A subscript denotes the upper \(\alpha\)-quantile (the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile): \(z_\alpha\) is the value with \(\P(Z>z_\alpha)=\alpha\) for \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), and likewise \(t_{\nu,\alpha}\), \(\chi^2_{k,\alpha}\). "Under \(H_0\) boundary" means: the distribution holds at the boundary value of the composite null (Viewpoint 3.42(iii)).

  1. One-sided z-test for the mean, \(\sigma^2\) known. \(H_0:\mu\le\mu_0\) against \(H_1:\mu>\mu_0\). Statistic \(Z=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) (under \(H_0\) boundary). Reject if \(z_{\text{obs}}>z_\alpha\).
  2. Two-sided z-test, \(\sigma^2\) known. \(H_0:\mu=\mu_0\) against \(H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0\). Same \(Z\); reject if \(|z_{\text{obs}}|>z_{\alpha/2}\).
  3. One-sided t-test, \(\sigma^2\) unknown. \(H_0:\mu\le\mu_0\) against \(H_1:\mu>\mu_0\). Statistic \(T=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu_0}{S_n/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}\) (under \(H_0\) boundary), \(S_n\) the sample standard deviation. Reject if \(t_{\text{obs}}>t_{n-1,\alpha}\).
  4. Two-sided t-test, \(\sigma^2\) unknown. \(H_0:\mu=\mu_0\) against \(H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0\). Same \(T\); reject if \(|t_{\text{obs}}|>t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\).
  5. One-sided χ²-test for the variance, \(\mu\) unknown. \(H_0:\sigma^2\le\sigma_0^2\) against \(H_1:\sigma^2>\sigma_0^2\). Statistic \(C=\frac{(n-1)S_n^2}{\sigma_0^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}\) (under \(H_0\) boundary). Reject if \(c_{\text{obs}}>\chi^2_{n-1,\alpha}\). For the left-sided test (\(H_1:\sigma^2<\sigma_0^2\)) reject if \(c_{\text{obs}}<\chi^2_{n-1,1-\alpha}\).
  6. Two-sided χ²-test for the variance, \(\mu\) unknown. \(H_0:\sigma^2=\sigma_0^2\) against \(H_1:\sigma^2\ne\sigma_0^2\). Same \(C\); reject if \(c_{\text{obs}}<\chi^2_{n-1,1-\alpha/2}\) or \(c_{\text{obs}}>\chi^2_{n-1,\alpha/2}\). (The \(\chi^2\) distribution is not symmetric, so the two cut-offs are not mirror images.)
  7. Two-sample t-test for means, unknown but equal variances. \(X_1,\dots,X_{n_X}\) and \(Y_1,\dots,Y_{n_Y}\) are two independent iid samples from \(\mathcal N(\mu_X,\sigma^2)\) and \(\mathcal N(\mu_Y,\sigma^2)\). \(H_0:\mu_X=\mu_Y\) against \(H_1:\mu_X\ne\mu_Y\). Statistic \[ T=\frac{\bar X_{n_X}-\bar Y_{n_Y}}{S_p\sqrt{\frac1{n_X}+\frac1{n_Y}}}\sim t_{n_X+n_Y-2}\ \ (\text{under }H_0),\qquad S_p^2=\frac{(n_X-1)S_{n_X}^2+(n_Y-1)S_{n_Y}^2}{n_X+n_Y-2}, \] where \(S_p^2\) is the pooled sample variance (a weighted average of the two sample variances). Reject if \(|t_{\text{obs}}|>t_{n_X+n_Y-2,\alpha/2}\).

Beyond Gaussian data. For many of these tests we only need the null distribution of the statistic. By the clt (§2.4), for large \(n\) we can relax the assumptions to \(X_i\) iid with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2>0\) (not necessarily normal): then \(\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\) is approximately \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), and the same tests can still be used approximately. (The script prints \(\bar X_n-\mu/(\sigma/\sqrt n)\); the brackets around \(\bar X_n-\mu\) are meant.) This is how SoSe25 P4d and SoSe26 P5d below work.

Overview of the standard tests (the script's table). One- and two-sided versions use the same statistics and null distributions; only the rejection region moves to one or both tails.

name\(H_0\)statisticnull distr.
single mean \(\mu\)
z-test (\(\sigma^2\) known)\(\mu=\mu_0\)\(Z=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\)\(\mathcal N(0,1)\)
t-test (\(\sigma^2\) unknown)\(\mu=\mu_0\)\(T=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu_0}{S_n/\sqrt n}\)\(t_{n-1}\)
single variance \(\sigma^2\)
χ²-test (\(\mu\) unknown)\(\sigma^2=\sigma_0^2\)\(C=\frac{(n-1)S_n^2}{\sigma_0^2}\)\(\chi^2_{n-1}\)
comparing means \(\mu_X,\mu_Y\)
two-sample t-test (equal variances)\(\mu_X=\mu_Y\)\(T=\frac{\bar X-\bar Y}{S_p\sqrt{\frac1{n_X}+\frac1{n_Y}}}\)\(t_{n_X+n_Y-2}\)

Two worked numbers for (v) and (vii) (mine).

  • (v): 10 bottles with sample variance \(s_{10}^2=4\,\text{ml}^2\) (the brewery of Sheet 11 Ex 3). Is the filling machine less precise than the specification \(\sigma_0^2=1\)? \(H_0:\sigma^2\le1\), \(H_1:\sigma^2>1\), \(c_{\text{obs}}=\frac{9\cdot4}1=36>\chi^2_{9,0.05}=16.92\): reject at level 0.05.
  • (vii): \(n_X=n_Y=8\), \(\bar x=10.2\), \(\bar y=9.0\), \(s_X^2=1.5\), \(s_Y^2=2.1\). Pooled: \(s_p^2=\frac{7\cdot1.5+7\cdot2.1}{14}=1.8\), \(s_p=1.342\). Then \(t_{\text{obs}}=\frac{1.2}{1.342\cdot\sqrt{1/8+1/8}}=\frac{1.2}{0.671}=1.79<t_{14,0.025}=2.145\): do not reject at level 0.05.

How to recognise which test (mine): what is tested (mean or variance; one sample or two)? Is \(\sigma\) known (z) or estimated from the data (t)? Is \(H_1\) directional (one tail) or not (two tails)? Exams give the needed quantile in a hint — the quantile named in the hint often tells you which test is expected.

Remark 3.47 the testing zoo Script 3.47

There is a large zoo of statistical tests for different questions, distributional assumptions and prior knowledge. Many flowcharts and guides online say which test to use when. Many of these tests are robust approximations, and they all have different gotchas — which you can now understand.

The script's figure (a flowchart titled "What statistical test should I do?", credited to @statsandr), described in words as far as the text of the figure can be read. It branches first on how many variables:

  • One variable. Qualitative: 2 groups → one-proportion test; more than 2 groups → chi-square goodness-of-fit test. Quantitative: parametric → one-sample Student's t-test (Example 3.45); nonparametric → one-sample Wilcoxon test.
  • Two variables.
    • Two quantitative: parametric → Pearson correlation; nonparametric → Spearman's rank correlation.
    • Two qualitative: with 2 groups for each variable → for independent samples, Fisher's exact test (expected frequencies below 5) or the chi-square test of independence (at least 5); for paired samples, McNemar's test. With more than 2 groups for at least one variable → chi-square test of independence (independent samples) or Cochran's Q test (paired samples).
    • One quantitative and one qualitative → depends on the number of groups to compare. 2 groups, independent samples: Student's t-test for 2 independent samples (equal variances, Example 3.46(vii)), Welch's t-test (unequal variances), Mann–Whitney U test (nonparametric). 2 groups, paired samples: Student's t-test for paired samples, or the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. More than 2 groups, independent: one-way ANOVA (analysis of variance; equal variances), Welch's ANOVA (unequal), Kruskal–Wallis test (nonparametric). More than 2 groups, paired: repeated-measures ANOVA, or the Friedman test.
  • More than two variables. Quantitative dependent variable → multiple linear regression. Qualitative dependent variable → binary logistic regression (2 groups) or multinomial logistic regression (more than 2).

"Parametric" means the test assumes a specific family of distributions (usually Gaussian); "nonparametric" tests use ranks or counts and make weaker assumptions. None of the names beyond Example 3.46 are needed for this course; the point is that each box is a Viewpoint-3.42 recipe with its own statistic and null distribution.

p-values

Idea first (mine). A test only says "reject" or "not". But \(z_{\text{obs}}=2.0\) and \(z_{\text{obs}}=5.0\) are very different amounts of surprise. The p-value reports how surprising the observed statistic is under \(H_0\) — and you can then compare it with any \(\alpha\) you like.

Definition 3.48 p-value Script 3.48

Viewpoint 3.42 and Definition 3.43 lead to the p-value [p-Wert]: the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one computed from the sample. The direction of "extreme" is determined by the alternative \(H_1\). For an observed statistic \(t_{\text{obs}}\):

  • if \(H_1:\theta>\theta_0\): p-value \(=\P_{\theta_0}(T(X)\ge t_{\text{obs}})\);
  • if \(H_1:\theta<\theta_0\): p-value \(=\P_{\theta_0}(T(X)\le t_{\text{obs}})\);
  • if \(H_1:\theta\ne\theta_0\): p-value \(=\P_{\theta_0}(T(X)\text{ as or more extreme than }t_{\text{obs}})\).

The test is then \(\varphi(x)=1\) if the p-value is less than or equal to the chosen level \(\alpha\in[0,1]\).

Reading it (mine).

  • Two-sided, symmetric null distribution (z- and t-tests): "as or more extreme" means "at least as far from 0", so p-value \(=\P_{\theta_0}(|T|\ge|t_{\text{obs}}|)=2\bigl(1-F(|t_{\text{obs}}|)\bigr)\), with \(F\) the null cdf. For the z-test: \(2(1-\Phi(|z_{\text{obs}}|))\).
  • Why "p ≤ α" is the same test as "\(t_{\text{obs}}\) beyond the critical value" (one-sided, continuous \(T\)): \(\P_{\theta_0}(T\ge t)\) decreases as \(t\) increases, and equals \(\alpha\) exactly at \(t=t_\alpha\). So p-value \(\le\alpha\iff t_{\text{obs}}\ge t_\alpha\). (Whether the boundary itself counts — "\(>\)" in Example 3.44, "\(\le\)" here — has probability 0 for continuous statistics and does not matter.)
  • Example: the light bulbs of Sheet 11 Ex 1 give \(z_{\text{obs}}=2\), two-sided, so p-value \(=2(1-\Phi(2))=2\cdot0.02275=0.0455\). Rejected at \(\alpha=0.05\), not at \(\alpha=0.01\) or 0.001. The p-value is the smallest level at which the data would still lead to rejection.
  • What the p-value is NOT: the probability that \(H_0\) is true. See Caveat 3.50.

Widget — the p-value as a tail area My addition

The curve is the null distribution of the statistic. The shaded tail(s) beyond the observed value have total area = p-value. The dashed line(s) mark the critical value(s) for the chosen \(\alpha\); the p-value is \(\le\alpha\) exactly when the observed value lies beyond them. The chips load the exercises of this page.

Viewpoint 3.49 falsification vs confirmation Script 3.49

The logic of hypothesis testing is rooted in the philosophy of falsification, popularised by Karl Popper. We cannot prove a scientific theory (or \(H_0\)) true, because we can never observe all possible instances. But we can find evidence that falsifies it. Hypothesis testing adopts this principle: we never "accept" \(H_0\). We either find enough evidence to "reject" it in favour of \(H_1\), or we "fail to reject" it because the evidence is insufficient. This distinction is crucial: failing to find evidence against a claim is not the same as finding evidence for it.

Classic picture: "all swans are white" cannot be proven by counting white swans, but one black swan refutes it. In the coin example, 52 heads in 100 tosses does not show the coin is fair — a coin with \(p=0.52\) would produce such data just as easily.

Caveat 3.50 p-value misinterpretations Script 3.50

The p-value is one of the most misinterpreted concepts in statistics.

  • It is not the probability that the null is true: p-value \(\ne\P(H_0\text{ is true}\mid\text{data})\). This is a very common mistake. The p-value is calculated assuming \(H_0\) is true.
  • A large p-value (e.g. \(p>0.05\)) does not mean \(H_0\) is true. It only means the data are not inconsistent with \(H_0\). It could also mean the test had low power to detect a true effect.
  • Statistical significance does not imply practical significance. A tiny effect can be statistically significant with a large enough sample, yet irrelevant in practice.
  • Thresholds as rituals. In practice, instead of comparing the p-value with a pre-chosen \(\alpha\), people report p-values and call a result "statistically significant" if \(p\le0.05\), or "highly statistically significant" if \(p\le0.001\) (default values the community has converged on). This suggests the p-value is a continuous indicator of "how true the claim is". It is not.
  • Other fields are much stricter. In physics a discovery is often considered real at "5σ" or "6σ": the statistic lies more than 5 or 6 standard deviations out in the normal distribution, a p-value close to \(2.86\cdot10^{-7}\). Genome-wide association studies commonly use thresholds of \(5\cdot10^{-8}\).

The American Statistical Association (ASA) published a statement in 2016 to address the widespread misuse of p-values. In another statement they wrote: "We conclude, based on our review of the articles in this special issue and the broader literature, that it is time to stop using the term 'statistically significant' entirely. Nor should variants such as 'significantly different,' 'p ≤ 0.05,' and 'nonsignificant' survive, whether expressed in words, by asterisks in a table, or in some other way."

Numbers and sources. The 5σ value is the one-sided tail \(1-\Phi(5)=2.87\cdot10^{-7}\) (the script's \(2.86\cdot10^{-7}\) is this number truncated; two-sided it would be \(5.7\cdot10^{-7}\)); 6σ gives \(1-\Phi(6)=9.9\cdot10^{-10}\). The quoted passage is from the editorial "Moving to a World Beyond 'p < 0.05'" (Wasserstein, Schirm, Lazar) that opened a 2019 special issue of The American Statistician. The 2016 ASA statement lists six principles: p-values can indicate how incompatible the data are with a specified model; they do not measure the probability that the hypothesis is true or that the data arose by chance alone; conclusions should not rest only on whether a p-value passes a threshold; proper inference needs full reporting and transparency; a p-value does not measure the size of an effect or its importance; by itself a p-value is not a good measure of evidence.

Why \(\P(\text{data}\mid H_0)\ne\P(H_0\mid\text{data})\), with numbers. Suppose 90 % of the hypotheses a lab tests are in fact true nulls, the tests have level 0.05 and power 0.5. By Bayes' theorem (§1.4), among the rejections the fraction of true nulls is \(\frac{0.9\cdot0.05}{0.9\cdot0.05+0.1\cdot0.5}=\frac{0.045}{0.095}=0.47\). Nearly half of the "discoveries" are false, although every test had level 5 %. The p-value alone cannot tell you this; it needs the prior share of true nulls (the Bayesian view, §3.5).

Remark 3.51 p-hacking and the replication crisis Script 3.51

p-hacking (or data dredging) is re-analysing data in many different ways until a statistically significant result appears: trying different tests, removing "outliers", or testing many different hypotheses. This dramatically increases the rate of false positives and has contributed to the replication crisis in many fields: published findings fail to be replicated by independent researchers. Preregistering study designs and analysis plans is one proposed remedy.

The arithmetic (mine). Run \(k\) independent tests, each at level 0.05, when every null is true. Each test avoids a false alarm with probability 0.95, so by independence (multiply) all \(k\) avoid it with probability \(0.95^k\), and at least one false alarm happens with probability \(1-0.95^k\): 0.05 (\(k=1\)), 0.226 (\(k=5\)), 0.401 (\(k=10\)), 0.642 (\(k=20\)), 0.923 (\(k=50\)). Twenty tries give a "significant" result about two times in three, with no effect at all. The Bonferroni correction (Overview 3.53(iv)) tests each at level \(\alpha/k\). Then the chance of at least one false alarm is at most \(k\cdot\frac\alpha k=\alpha\), by the union bound [σ-Subadditivität]: for any events, \(\P(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_k)\le\P(A_1)+\dots+\P(A_k)\) (the probability of "at least one" never exceeds the sum of the single probabilities, because overlaps are counted at most once on the left and at least once on the right; Proposition 1.19(vi), §1.1). Here \(A_j\) = "test \(j\) gives a false alarm", each with probability \(\frac\alpha k\). The union bound needs no independence.

Widget — p-hacking under a true null My addition

400 simulated "studies". Each study runs \(k\) independent two-sided z-tests on fresh data (10 observations from \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) each, testing \(\mu=0\) — so every null is true). A dot turns orange if the study found at least one "significant" result. Compare the simulated fraction with \(1-(1-\alpha')^k\), where \(\alpha'\) is the per-test level.

Remark 3.52 summary: how to build a hypothesis test Script 3.52

  1. Formulate \(H_0\) and \(H_1\) from the research question. This includes statistical modelling (writing down your model).
  2. Choose a test statistic \(T(X)\) that is expected to behave differently under \(H_0\) and \(H_1\). Often it is based on an estimator of the parameter of interest.
  3. Find the sampling distribution of \(T(X)\) assuming \(H_0\) is true — the most critical and often most difficult step.
    • For some models (like the Gaussian) the exact distribution is known.
    • For large samples it can often be approximated with the clt.
    • Otherwise, simulation methods (like permutation tests or bootstrapping) can approximate the null distribution.

    The two simulation methods in one line each (not examined): a permutation test compares two groups by shuffling the group labels many times — if \(H_0\) "no difference" holds, the labels do not matter, so the shuffled data show how the statistic varies under \(H_0\); bootstrapping draws many new samples of size \(n\) with replacement from the observed data and recomputes the statistic on each, to imitate "fresh data".

  4. Specify \(\alpha\) and determine the rejection region \(R\) from the null distribution of \(T(X)\).
  5. Collect data, compute \(t_{\text{obs}}\), and decide: reject \(H_0\) if \(t_{\text{obs}}\in R\).

This is exactly the list of items an exam asks for (SoSe26 P5d: "state the test statistic, its approximate distribution at the null boundary, the rejection rule, the observed value, and the conclusion") — one point each. Always add the one-sentence conclusion in words ("we reject \(H_0\) at level 0.05; the data give evidence that …").

Overview 3.53 outlook on hypothesis testing Script 3.53

  1. The Neyman–Pearson lemma constructs most powerful tests for simple hypotheses. For composite hypotheses umps rarely exist, except for simple one-sided examples in exponential families and similar cases. In many real settings, the quality of tests is judged empirically, in simulation studies that mimic the expected data. (An exponential family [Exponentialfamilie] is, roughly, a model whose density has the form \(h(x)\,e^{\eta(\theta)T(x)-A(\theta)}\) — normal, exponential, Poisson, Bernoulli and binomial all do. Example 3.41 and Sheet 11 Ex 2 are such one-sided cases: the Neyman–Pearson region did not depend on the particular alternative, so one test was best against all of them. For the two-sided \(H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0\) no ump exists: the one-sided test "\(z>z_\alpha\)" is most powerful against every \(\mu>\mu_0\) but useless against \(\mu<\mu_0\), and the mirror test "\(z<-z_\alpha\)" is the other way round, so neither beats the other everywhere on \(\Theta_1\). The power widget's third button draws the first of the two: its curve rises above \(\alpha\) only to the right of \(\mu_0\) and sinks below \(\alpha\) to the left; the mirror test's curve is that same curve reflected at \(\mu_0\).)
  2. When tests are used to decide on a change — switching to a new medication, introducing a new design on a large online platform — high power matters. Especially for studies on humans, one performs a power analysis up front to determine the sample size \(n\) needed for a desired power (at fixed size \(\alpha\)). Example (mine): in the setting of Sheet 11 Ex 4 (\(\sigma=3\), \(\mu_0=10\), one-sided, \(\alpha=0.01\)), what \(n\) gives power 0.8 against \(\mu_a=11.5\)? Power \(=1-\Phi\bigl(z_\alpha-\frac{\mu_a-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\bigr)\ge0.8\) means \(z_\alpha-\frac{1.5\sqrt n}{3}\le-z_{0.2}\), i.e. \(\sqrt n\ge\frac{3(z_{0.01}+z_{0.2})}{1.5}=2(2.326+0.842)=6.34\), so \(n\ge40.1\): 41 observations instead of 25 (which gave power 0.57). For power 0.9: \(n\ge52.1\), i.e. 53.
  3. This section covered the frequentist (Neyman–Pearson) approach, dominant in many sciences. Other approaches exist. Bayesian hypothesis testing uses no p-values; it computes the Bayes factor, the ratio of the marginal likelihood of the data under \(H_1\) to that under \(H_0\). This allows quantifying evidence for \(H_0\) or \(H_1\). (Priors and posteriors: §3.5.) The marginal likelihood under a hypothesis is the likelihood \(L(\theta\mid x)\) averaged over the parameter values in that hypothesis, weighted by a prior distribution on them. For two simple hypotheses there is nothing to average, and the Bayes factor is exactly the Neyman–Pearson ratio \(\frac{L(\theta_1\mid x)}{L(\theta_0\mid x)}\) — but it is read as "how many times better \(H_1\) explains the data", not compared with a cut-off chosen for size \(\alpha\).
  4. Multiple testing is a crucial issue: when many hypotheses are tested simultaneously (genomics, online A/B testing), the probability of at least one type I error inflates dramatically. Procedures like the Bonferroni correction or methods controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) are essential. (See the arithmetic under Remark 3.51 and the widget above.) Bonferroni: test each of \(k\) hypotheses at level \(\alpha/k\). The FDR is the expected fraction of false discoveries among all rejections — in the lab example under Caveat 3.50 that fraction was 47 %; FDR methods (e.g. Benjamini–Hochberg) keep it below a chosen bound and are less strict than Bonferroni.
  5. The framework — especially tests for simple hypotheses like the z- and t-test — is the foundation for more complex models: analysis of variance (ANOVA), chi-squared tests, regression analysis, where hypotheses concern model parameters or their relationships.

Exercise-sheet tasks

Sheet 11, Exercise 1 — has the light-bulb lifetime changed? Sheet 11 · Ex 1

Historical mean lifetime \(\mu_0=1200\) h, known standard deviation \(\sigma=150\) h. A new process; a sample of \(n=36\) bulbs has \(\bar x_{36}=1250\) h. Lifetimes are normal. (i) State \(H_0\) and \(H_1\). (ii) Compute the test statistic. (iii) Reject at \(\alpha=0.05\)? At \(\alpha=0.001\)? What does that mean for the confidence you should have in the rejection?

Solution

Relevant tools: two-sided z-test (Example 3.44, Example 3.46(ii)), since \(\sigma\) is known and the data are normal; Definition 3.34(v) for the meaning of \(\alpha\).

(i) "Has changed" has no direction, so the test is two-sided: \(H_0:\mu=1200\) against \(H_1:\mu\ne1200\).

(ii) \(Z=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\), which is \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) under \(H_0\) (primer 1). Standard error \(\frac{150}{\sqrt{36}}=\frac{150}6=25\). So \(z_{\text{obs}}=\frac{1250-1200}{25}=\frac{50}{25}=2\).

(iii) Reject if \(|z_{\text{obs}}|>z_{\alpha/2}\).

  • \(\alpha=0.05\): \(z_{0.025}=1.96\), and \(2>1.96\): reject.
  • \(\alpha=0.001\): \(z_{0.0005}=3.29\), and \(2<3.29\): do not reject.
  • p-value (mine): \(2(1-\Phi(2))=0.0455\). The data lead to rejection exactly at levels \(\alpha\ge0.0455\).

What it means. \(\alpha=\E_{\mu_0}[\varphi]\) is a probability over repeating the whole procedure on new data sets drawn under the null: if \(H_0\) were true, a level-0.05 test would wrongly reject in 5 % of repetitions. It is a property of the procedure, not a probability statement about this one data set, and not "95 % confidence that the lifetime changed". We do not know whether the null is true; if it is false, \(\alpha\) does not describe any real probability of this situation at all. That the result flips between \(\alpha=0.05\) and \(\alpha=0.001\) says: the evidence is moderate — enough for the conventional 5 % rule, far from overwhelming.

Verification. The official solution is correct. Small differences: it writes the rule as \(|z_{\text{obs}}|\ge z_{\alpha/2}\) where the script uses "\(>\)" (irrelevant for a continuous statistic, see Definition 3.48), and "\(z_{\alpha/2}\approx3.29\)" is \(z_{0.0005}=3.2905\) — correct.

Same data as an interval. The 95 % confidence interval \(1250\pm1.96\cdot25=[1201.0,\,1299.0]\) does not contain 1200 — the same verdict as the level-0.05 test, by the duality of Remark 3.59. Worked out on §3.4.

Method to reuse: known \(\sigma\) + normal data (or large \(n\)) → z-test. Standard error first, then \(z_{\text{obs}}\), then compare with the right quantile (\(z_{\alpha/2}\) for two-sided). When asked "what does it mean", answer: \(\alpha\) is the long-run type I error rate of the procedure under \(H_0\).

Sheet 11, Exercise 2 — Neyman–Pearson test for an exponential sample Sheet 11 · Ex 2

One observation \(X\sim\Exp(\lambda)\). Test \(H_0:\{\lambda_0\}\) against \(H_1:\{\lambda_1\}\) with \(\lambda_1>\lambda_0>0\). (i) Write down \(\Lambda(x)=\frac{L(\lambda_1\mid x)}{L(\lambda_0\mid x)}\). (ii) The most powerful test rejects if \(\Lambda(x)>k'\); show this is equivalent to \(x<c\) or \(x>c\) for a constant \(c\), and decide which. (iii) Find \(c\) for level \(\alpha\). (iv) What is the power?

Solution

Relevant tools: Neyman–Pearson lemma (Theorem 3.40); the exponential density \(p(x\mid\lambda)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x\ge0\) (§1.3), mean \(\frac1\lambda\); primer 3.

(i) With one observation the likelihood is the density: \(L(\lambda\mid x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\). So \[ \Lambda(x)=\frac{\lambda_1e^{-\lambda_1x}}{\lambda_0e^{-\lambda_0x}}=\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_0}e^{-(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)x}\qquad(x\ge0), \] using \(\frac{e^a}{e^b}=e^{a-b}\) with \(a-b=-\lambda_1x+\lambda_0x\).

(ii) \(\Lambda(x)>k'\) (with \(k'>0\)). Multiply by the positive \(\frac{\lambda_0}{\lambda_1}\): \(e^{-(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)x}>k''\) with \(k'':=k'\frac{\lambda_0}{\lambda_1}>0\). Take \(\ln\) (strictly increasing, so the inequality stays): \(-(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)x>\ln k''\). Since \(\lambda_1>\lambda_0\), the number \(-(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)\) is negative; dividing by it flips the inequality: \[ x<-\frac{\ln k''}{\lambda_1-\lambda_0}=:c . \] So the region is of the form \(x<c\). Intuition: a larger rate \(\lambda_1\) means faster decay and smaller typical values (mean \(\frac1{\lambda_1}<\frac1{\lambda_0}\)), so small observations speak for \(H_1\). For a non-trivial test we need \(c>0\) (otherwise \(\P_{\lambda_0}(X<c)=0\)), which happens exactly when \(\ln k''<0\), i.e. \(0<k''<1\).

(iii) The size is the probability of rejecting under \(H_0\): with the antiderivative \(-e^{-\lambda_0x}\) of \(\lambda_0e^{-\lambda_0x}\) (Analysis 8.3), \[ \alpha=\P_{\lambda_0}(X<c)=\int_0^c\lambda_0e^{-\lambda_0x}\,\mathrm dx=\bigl[-e^{-\lambda_0x}\bigr]_0^c=1-e^{-\lambda_0c}. \] Solve: \(e^{-\lambda_0c}=1-\alpha\), so \(-\lambda_0c=\ln(1-\alpha)\) and \[ c=-\frac{\ln(1-\alpha)}{\lambda_0}. \] Since \(0<1-\alpha<1\), \(\ln(1-\alpha)<0\), so \(c>0\). The test rejects \(H_0\) if \(x<-\frac{\ln(1-\alpha)}{\lambda_0}\). (Note: \(c\) is the \(\alpha\)-quantile of \(\Exp(\lambda_0)\) — the lower tail, because small values are "extreme" here.)

(iv) The power is the probability of rejecting under \(H_1\): \[ G_\varphi(\lambda_1)=\P_{\lambda_1}(X<c)=1-e^{-\lambda_1c}=1-e^{\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_0}\ln(1-\alpha)}=1-\bigl(e^{\ln(1-\alpha)}\bigr)^{\lambda_1/\lambda_0}=1-(1-\alpha)^{\lambda_1/\lambda_0}. \] (Substituting \(c\): \(-\lambda_1c=\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_0}\ln(1-\alpha)\); then \(e^{ab}=(e^a)^b\).)

Numbers and checks. \(\lambda_0=1\), \(\lambda_1=2\), \(\alpha=0.05\): \(c=-\ln0.95=0.0513\), power \(1-0.95^2=0.0975\). Only about 10 %: one observation is weak evidence. (The Neyman–Pearson widget shows exactly this case at its defaults, and that other regions of the same size have even less power: right tail \(0.05^2=0.0025\), middle interval \(0.525^2-0.475^2=0.05\).) Checks: (a) since \(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_0}>1\) and \(0<1-\alpha<1\), \((1-\alpha)^{\lambda_1/\lambda_0}<1-\alpha\), so the power exceeds \(\alpha\) — the test is unbiased (Definition 3.39); (b) \(c\) does not depend on \(\lambda_1\), so the same test is most powerful against every \(\lambda_1>\lambda_0\) — a ump for \(H_1:\lambda>\lambda_0\), as in Example 3.41.

Verification. The official solution is correct in every step.

Method to reuse: (1) write \(\Lambda\) and cancel; (2) take \(\ln\) and isolate the statistic, watching the sign when dividing; (3) the direction of the region comes out of the algebra — check it with intuition; (4) set \(\P_{\theta_0}(\text{region})=\alpha\) and solve for \(c\); (5) power = same probability under \(\theta_1\).

Sheet 11, Exercise 3 — one-sample t-test: does the brewery fill 330 ml? Sheet 11 · Ex 3

A brewery claims its bottles contain exactly 330 ml. A student measures \(n=10\) bottles: \(\bar x_{10}=328.5\) ml, sample variance \(s_{10}^2=4\) ml². The content is normal. (i) State the hypotheses for "the true mean differs from 330 ml". (ii) Which test? State the statistic and its null distribution. (iii) Test at \(\alpha=0.05\). Reject the claim? (Hint: \(t_{9,0.025}\approx2.262\).)

Solution

Relevant tools: two-sided one-sample t-test (Example 3.45, Example 3.46(iv)): normal data, \(\sigma^2\) unknown (only the sample variance is given).

(i) \(H_0:\mu=330\) (the claim) against \(H_1:\mu\ne330\). Two-sided, because "differs" has no direction.
