(ii) One-sample t-test. \(T=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu_0}{S_n/\sqrt n}\) with \(\mu_0=330\) and \(S_n=\sqrt{S_n^2}\). Under \(H_0\), \(T\sim t_{n-1}=t_9\).

(iii) \(s_{10}=\sqrt4=2\); standard error \(\frac2{\sqrt{10}}=\frac2{3.1623}=0.6325\). So \(t_{\text{obs}}=\frac{328.5-330}{0.6325}=\frac{-1.5}{0.6325}=-2.372\). Reject if \(|t_{\text{obs}}|>t_{9,0.025}=2.262\). Since \(2.372>2.262\): reject \(H_0\). At the 5 % level the data give evidence that the mean content is not 330 ml (here: less).

Extras. p-value \(=2\,\P(t_9\ge2.372)=0.042\) — just below 0.05, so the conclusion is fragile. Had we wrongly used the normal quantile 1.96, we would compute \(p=0.018\) and overstate the evidence: with only 10 observations, the estimated \(\sigma\) adds real uncertainty. Also note that the data point in a direction (under-filling) that matters to customers — but since \(H_1\) was two-sided, we may only conclude "different"; choosing a one-sided test after seeing the data would be p-hacking.

Verification. The official solution is correct. It rounds the standard error to 0.632 and reports \(t_{\text{obs}}\approx-2.373\); with more digits \(t_{\text{obs}}=-2.3717\). The decision is unaffected.

Same data as an interval. The 95 % t-interval \(328.5\pm2.262\cdot0.6325=[327.07,\,329.93]\) just misses 330 — matching the narrow rejection (Remark 3.59). Worked out on §3.4.

Method to reuse: sample variance given, \(\sigma\) not → t-test with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom. Take the square root of \(s^2\) before dividing by \(\sqrt n\).

Sheet 11, Exercise 4 — type II error and power of a z-test Sheet 11 · Ex 4

Normal data with known \(\sigma^2=9\), \(n=25\). Test \(H_0:\mu\le10\) against \(H_1:\mu>10\) at \(\alpha=0.01\). (i) Determine the rejection region (\(z_{0.01}\approx2.33\)). (ii) Compute the type II error probability \(\beta\) if the true mean is \(\mu_a=11.5\). (iii) What is the power against \(\mu_a=11.5\)?

Solution

Relevant tools: one-sided z-test (Example 3.46(i)); null boundary (Viewpoint 3.42(iii)); type II error and power (Definition 3.34(vi)); standardising (primer 1).

(i) At the null boundary \(\mu_0=10\): \(Z=\frac{\bar X_{25}-10}{3/\sqrt{25}}=\frac{\bar X_{25}-10}{0.6}\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\). Reject if \(z_{\text{obs}}>2.33\). In terms of the sample mean (multiply by 0.6, add 10): \[ \bar X_{25}>10+2.33\cdot0.6=10+1.398=11.398 . \] Because the rejection probability increases in \(\mu\), every \(\mu\le10\) gives type I error at most 0.01.

(ii) A type II error happens if we do not reject although \(\mu=11.5\): \(\beta=\P_{11.5}(\bar X_{25}\le11.398)\). Under \(\mu=11.5\), \(\bar X_{25}\sim\mathcal N(11.5,\frac9{25})=\mathcal N(11.5,0.36)\), standard deviation 0.6. Standardise with the true mean 11.5: \[ \beta=\P\Bigl(\frac{\bar X_{25}-11.5}{0.6}\le\frac{11.398-11.5}{0.6}\Bigr)=\P(Z'\le-0.17)=\Phi(-0.17)=1-\Phi(0.17)=1-0.5675=0.4325, \] with \(Z'\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\). (Here \(\frac{11.398-11.5}{0.6}=\frac{-0.102}{0.6}=-0.17\); the value \(\Phi(0.17)=0.5675\) comes from the \(\Phi\) table, and the symmetry rule \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\) handles the minus sign.) About 43 %.

(iii) Power \(=1-\beta=0.5675\), about 57 %: a true mean of 11.5 is detected only slightly more often than a coin flip.

Note on the official solution. It writes \(\beta\) = "\(P(\text{fail to reject }H_0\mid\mu=\mu_a)\)" (in quotation marks). In this frequentist setting \(\mu\) is a fixed number, not a random variable, so there is no event "\(\mu=\mu_a\)" to condition on; the correct notation is \(\P_{\mu_a}(\bar X_{25}\le11.398)\) — "computed as if the true mean were \(\mu_a\)", which the solution then uses. The quotation marks show the authors know this; in an exam write \(\P_{\mu_a}\).

Verification. The numbers are correct. With the unrounded quantile \(z_{0.01}=2.3263\) the cut-off is 11.396, \(\beta=\Phi(-0.174)=0.431\) and power 0.569 — the widget above uses these exact values. The power analysis under Overview 3.53(ii) shows that \(n=41\) would be needed for power 0.8.

Method to reuse: (1) find the cut-off for \(\bar X\) using the null mean; (2) compute the probability of landing on the non-rejection side using the alternative mean. Two different standardisations — the most common mistake is to use \(\mu_0\) in step 2.

Old-exam tasks

Hypothesis testing appeared in SoSe 2025 (a true/false item and the last part of Problem 4) and in SoSe 2026 (the last part of Problem 5). In both cases the test came at the end of a longer problem whose earlier parts built the estimator and its clt approximation. That is a pattern of these two exams, not a prediction.

SoSe 2025, Problem 1c — what does a rejection at level 5 % say? SoSe25 · P1c · 3 credits

Statement. From a large batch of switches you take a random subsample of size \(n\) and run a suitable test at \(\alpha=0.05\) of \(H_0\): "the proportion of defective switches in the batch is at most what the manufacturer claimed" against \(H_1\): "the proportion is larger". The test rejects \(H_0\). "You can therefore conclude that the probability that the entire batch conforms to the claimed proportion is at most 5 %." True or false?

Answer: False. Reasons, step by step:

  • What \(\alpha\) is. By Definition 3.34(v), \(\alpha\ge\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\P_\theta(\text{reject})\). It is a probability of rejecting, computed assuming \(H_0\): "if the batch conforms, this procedure rejects in at most 5 % of repeated samples". It describes the procedure.
  • What the statement claims. It claims \(\P(H_0\text{ true}\mid\text{rejected})\le0.05\) — a probability of the hypothesis, given the data. That is the reverse conditional (Caveat 3.50, first bullet).
  • Why that probability does not exist here. In the frequentist framework, the batch's defect proportion is a fixed, unknown number. The batch either conforms or it does not; there is nothing random about it, so "the probability that the batch conforms" is not defined by the test.
  • Even with a prior it is not 5 %. If we added a prior probability for "batch conforms" (Bayesian view, §3.5), Bayes' theorem would give \(\P(H_0\mid\text{reject})\), and it depends on the prior and the power. With the numbers under Caveat 3.50 (90 % of batches conform, power 0.5) it would be 47 %, not \(\le5\) %.

The official answer ("False. The significance level makes claims about the procedure, not probabilities of the true parameter (or how it manifests in a given batch).") is correct. A correct statement would be: "If the batch conforms, the probability that this procedure rejects is at most 5 %." For full credit give the direction of conditioning explicitly.

SoSe 2025, Problem 4d — approximate one-sided test for a Poisson rate SoSe25 · P4d · 4 credits

Setting. \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid \(\Poi(\lambda)\) (mean and variance \(\lambda\)). Earlier parts (on §3.2): (a) \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}=\bar X_n\); (b) it is unbiased; (c) by the clt, \(\bar X_n\approx\mathcal N(\lambda,\lambda/n)\). Now: defects per batch are Poisson; historically \(\lambda_0=4\). After a process change, \(n=100\) batches give \(\bar x_{100}=5\). Construct an approximate test of whether the mean number of defects has increased, at \(\alpha=0.05\) (hint \(z_{0.05}\approx1.64\)). Reject?

Solution (Remark 3.52, step by step).

  1. Hypotheses: \(H_0:\lambda=4\) (or \(H_0:\lambda\le4\); both work) against \(H_1:\lambda>4\). One-sided: only an increase matters.
  2. Statistic: based on the estimator \(\bar X_n\). Under \(H_0\) its mean is 4 and its variance \(\frac4n\) (Poisson: variance = mean; divided by \(n\) for a mean of iid variables). Standardise: \(Z=\frac{\bar X_n-4}{\sqrt{4/n}}=\frac{\bar X_n-4}{\sqrt{4/100}}=\frac{\bar X_n-4}{0.2}\).
  3. Null distribution: by the clt (§2.4), approximately \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) under \(H_0\) (at the null boundary).
  4. Rejection rule: reject if \(z_{\text{obs}}>z_{0.05}\approx1.64\).
  5. Observed value and decision: \(z_{\text{obs}}=\frac{5-4}{0.2}=5>1.64\). Reject \(H_0\): the data give strong evidence that the defect rate increased.

Verification and extras. The official solution is correct (the hint's 1.64 is \(z_{0.05}=1.6449\) rounded; irrelevant here since \(z_{\text{obs}}=5\)). (1) It uses the null variance \(\lambda_0/n\) — the natural choice, because the null distribution is computed assuming \(H_0\). Plugging in the estimate instead (\(\sqrt{5/100}\)) gives \(z=4.47\): same decision. (2) For the composite \(H_0:\lambda\le4\), the rule "\(\bar x>4+1.64\cdot0.2=4.33\)" has its largest rejection probability at \(\lambda=4\) (larger rates push the sample mean up), so the boundary gives the size. (3) p-value: \(1-\Phi(5)=2.9\cdot10^{-7}\). Exactly, \(\sum X_i\sim\Poi(400)\) under \(H_0\) (sums of independent Poissons, §2.3), and \(\P(\sum X_i\ge500)=8.1\cdot10^{-7}\): the clt tail is off by a factor of about 3 this far out, but both are tiny and the decision is the same.

SoSe 2026, Problem 5d — testing a sensitive proportion with randomized response SoSe26 · P5d · 5 credits

Setting. Each participant has a sensitive attribute \(A\sim\Ber(p)\), \(p\) unknown. With probability \(r\) they answer truthfully, otherwise they report a fair coin flip. Part (a) (on §1.4) gave \(q(p):=\P(Y=1)=rp+\frac{1-r}2\); parts (b), (c) (on §3.2) gave the mle \(\hat p=\frac{\bar Y_n-(1-r)/2}r\). Now \(r=\frac12\), \(n=100\) iid responses, 64 of them equal 1. Do more than 60 % have the attribute? Formulate the hypotheses and perform an approximate test at \(\alpha=0.05\) (\(z_{0.05}\approx1.64\)): statistic, its approximate distribution at the null boundary, rejection rule, observed value, conclusion.

Solution.

  1. Hypotheses (1 point): the claim to show goes into \(H_1\): \(H_0:p\le0.6\) against \(H_1:p>0.6\). One-sided.
  2. Null boundary (1 point): with \(r=\frac12\), \(q(p)=\frac12p+\frac14\), which increases in \(p\). So "large \(p\)" means "many ones", and the worst case of the null is its boundary \(p_0=0.6\), where \(q_0=q(0.6)=0.3+0.25=0.55\). Each \(Y_i\sim\Ber(0.55)\) there, so \(\E[\bar Y_{100}]=0.55\) and \(\Var[\bar Y_{100}]=\frac{0.55\cdot0.45}{100}=0.002475\) (Bernoulli variance \(q(1-q)\), divided by \(n\)).
  3. Statistic and null distribution (1 point): \(Z=\frac{\bar Y_{100}-0.55}{\sqrt{0.55\cdot0.45/100}}\), approximately \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) at the null boundary by the clt.
  4. Rejection rule and observed value (1 point): reject if \(z_{\text{obs}}>z_{0.05}\approx1.64\). Observed \(\bar y_{100}=\frac{64}{100}=0.64\), standard error \(\sqrt{0.002475}=0.04975\), so \(z_{\text{obs}}=\frac{0.64-0.55}{0.04975}=\frac{0.09}{0.04975}=1.81\).
  5. Conclusion (1 point): \(1.81>1.64\), so reject \(H_0\) at (approximate) level 0.05. The data give evidence that more than 60 % of the population have the attribute.

Why the null boundary gives level α for all of \(H_0\). The rule is \(\bar y>c\) with \(c=0.55+1.64\cdot0.04975=0.632\). For \(p<0.6\), \(q(p)<0.55\), and a Bernoulli mean with a smaller success probability exceeds \(c\) less often. So the rejection probability over \(H_0\) is largest at \(p=0.6\), where it is (approximately) 0.05.

Verification and extras. The official solution is correct (\(z_{\text{obs}}=1.809\)). Remarks: (1) the cut-off 0.632 means the test rejects for 64 or more ones out of 100 — the observed 64 is the smallest count that rejects, so the result is borderline; p-value \(1-\Phi(1.81)=0.035\). The exact binomial p-value \(\P(\Bin(100,0.55)\ge64)=0.043\) is also below 0.05, so the decision stands. (2) The same test can be written with the estimator: \(\hat p=\frac{0.64-0.25}{0.5}=0.78\), and \(\frac{\hat p-0.6}{\sqrt{\Var_{0.6}[\hat p]}}=\frac{0.18}{2\cdot0.04975}=1.81\) — identical, since \(\hat p\) is an affine function of \(\bar Y\) (standardisation removes the \(a\) and \(b\) of \(a\bar Y+b\), up to the sign of \(a\)). (3) The privacy mechanism costs power: the standard error of \(\hat p\) is \(2\cdot0.04975=0.0995\) instead of \(\sqrt{0.6\cdot0.4/100}=0.049\) for direct answers.

Summary sheet

Definitions

hypotheses
\(\Theta=\Theta_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}\Theta_1\); \(H_0:\theta\in\Theta_0\), \(H_1:\theta\in\Theta_1\); simple = one element, composite = more
test
\(\varphi:\Omega^n\to[0,1]\); non-randomized: values in \(\{0,1\}\), 1 = reject; rejection region \(\varphi^{-1}(\{1\})\)
errors
type I: reject a true \(H_0\); type II: keep a false \(H_0\)
power function
\(G_\varphi(\theta)=\E_\theta[\varphi]=\P_\theta(\text{reject})\); power at \(\theta\in\Theta_1\); \(\beta(\theta)=1-G_\varphi(\theta)\)
size / level
size \(=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\E_\theta[\varphi]\); level \(\alpha\) if size \(\le\alpha\)
ump
level \(\alpha\) and \(G_\varphi\ge G_\psi\) on \(\Theta_1\) for every level-\(\alpha\) test \(\psi\)
unbiased
\(G_\varphi\le\alpha\) on \(\Theta_0\) and \(G_\varphi\ge\alpha\) on \(\Theta_1\)
p-value
\(\P_{\theta_0}(T\text{ at least as extreme as }t_{\text{obs}})\), direction from \(H_1\); reject iff p \(\le\alpha\)

Results

Neyman–Pearson
simple vs simple: reject iff \(\frac{L(\theta_1\mid x)}{L(\theta_0\mid x)}>k\), \(k\) chosen for size \(\alpha\) — most powerful
Gaussian mean
lrt ⟹ reject iff \(\bar x_n>\mu_0+z_\alpha\sigma/\sqrt n\) (one-sided z-test; ump for \(\mu>\mu_0\))
z-test
\(Z=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\); one-sided \(z>z_\alpha\), two-sided \(|z|>z_{\alpha/2}\)
t-test
\(T=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu_0}{S_n/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}\); \(t>t_{n-1,\alpha}\) or \(|t|>t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\)
χ²-test
\(C=\frac{(n-1)S_n^2}{\sigma_0^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}\); right: \(c>\chi^2_{n-1,\alpha}\); left: \(c<\chi^2_{n-1,1-\alpha}\)
two-sample t
\(T=\frac{\bar X-\bar Y}{S_p\sqrt{1/n_X+1/n_Y}}\sim t_{n_X+n_Y-2}\), \(S_p^2\) pooled
approximate
large \(n\), any iid data with finite variance: z-test via the clt
power (z)
one-sided \(G(\mu)=1-\Phi(z_\alpha-\delta)\), \(\delta=\frac{\mu-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\); \(n\ge\bigl(\frac{(z_\alpha+z_\beta)\sigma}{\mu_a-\mu_0}\bigr)^2\) for power \(1-\beta\)
quantiles
\(z_{0.1}=1.28\), \(z_{0.05}=1.645\), \(z_{0.025}=1.96\), \(z_{0.01}=2.33\), \(z_{0.005}=2.576\)

Method (Remark 3.52)

Hypotheses (claim to show in \(H_1\)) → statistic → its distribution under \(H_0\) (at the null boundary) → rejection rule from \(\alpha\) → observed value → decision + one sentence in words.

Traps

  • \(\alpha\) and the p-value are probabilities assuming \(H_0\), never "the probability that \(H_0\) is true" (SoSe25 P1c).
  • Not rejecting ≠ accepting \(H_0\); low power can hide real effects.
  • \(z_\alpha\) is the upper quantile; two-sided tests need \(z_{\alpha/2}\).
  • In power computations standardise the cut-off with the alternative mean.
  • Unknown \(\sigma\) → t-quantiles, not normal ones (Sheet 11 Ex 3).
  • Choosing the direction or the test after seeing the data, or running many tests, inflates type I errors (\(1-0.95^k\)).

Exam focus

SoSe25 and SoSe26 each ended an estimation problem with an approximate one-sided z-test (P4d: Poisson, \(z=5\); P5d: randomized response, \(z=1.81\)) and SoSe25 had a true/false item on interpreting \(\alpha\). Sheet 11 adds the t-test, the Neyman–Pearson derivation and type II error/power computations. Other question types are possible.

Section 3.4 · Lectures 10–12 (the script marks no lecture numbers after Lecture 9, so the exact lecture is not known)

Interval estimation

Intervallschätzung (Konfidenzintervalle)

What this page covers Script §3.4, pp. 110–111

Everything from the section goal and Definition 3.54 to Remark 3.59: the definition of a confidence interval (Definition 3.54), how to interpret it (Remark 3.55), the three standard intervals — normal mean with known variance (Example 3.56), normal mean with unknown variance (Example 3.57), a proportion (Example 3.58, the Wald interval) — and the duality between confidence intervals and tests (Remark 3.59).

The section is short, so this page adds a lot of my own material (marked): every interval is derived step by step from a pivot, the duality is proved, the quantiles \(z_{\alpha/2}\) and \(t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\) get a recomputed table, and there is a sample-size calculation.

Worked in place: no sheet exercise asks for a confidence interval, so Sheet 11 Ex 1 and Ex 3 are redone as confidence intervals and Sheet 11 Ex 4 as a one-sided confidence bound (the tests themselves are solved on §3.3); Sheet 10 Ex 1 (uniform distribution) and Sheet 11 Ex 2 (exponential) get exact confidence intervals from non-normal pivots; and there is a note on the "confidence level" of Sheet 5 Ex 1. The only old-exam part that asks for a confidence interval is WiSe25 P5d, fully solved. The true/false item SoSe25 P1c is about the same interpretation question as Remark 3.55 and is discussed here too. As practice, the estimators of WiSe25 P4 (rainfall), SoSe25 P4 (Poisson defects) and SoSe26 P5 (randomized response) are turned into confidence intervals — those exams did not ask for this; it is my addition. No definitions item of the three exams concerns §3.4.

The big picture

An estimator (§3.2) gives one number as a guess for an unknown quantity: "the average lifetime of the new light bulbs is about 1250 hours". But how sure are we? Would 1240 hours also be believable? 1100? A single number does not say.

A confidence interval [Konfidenzintervall] answers with a range instead: "the mean lifetime is between 1201 and 1299 hours, at 95 % confidence". Its width shows how uncertain the guess is.

The picture to keep in mind: ring toss. The unknown parameter is a peg fixed in the ground. We cannot see it. Each time we collect data and compute an interval, we throw a ring. Some rings land around the peg, some miss. A "95 % confidence interval" is a way of throwing that puts the ring around the peg in 95 % of throws. The peg never moves; the rings are what is random.

Numbers (my example). A scale has measurement noise with standard deviation \(\sigma=2\) g. You weigh an object \(n=4\) times and get the average \(\bar x=50.3\) g. The average of 4 measurements has standard deviation \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}=\frac22=1\) g. For a normal distribution, 95 % of the probability lies within 1.96 standard deviations of the mean. So the average lands within \(1.96\cdot1=1.96\) g of the true mass \(\mu\) with probability 95 %. Turned around: the interval \(50.3\pm1.96=[48.34,\,52.26]\) is a 95 % confidence interval for \(\mu\). If you measured 16 times instead, the standard deviation of the average would be \(\frac2{\sqrt{16}}=0.5\) g, and the interval half as wide.

In words: a confidence interval is "estimate ± (a quantile) × (the estimate's standard deviation)". The 95 % describes how often the method catches the true value, not a probability for one particular interval.

Cross-references

Rules for inequalities (adding, multiplying by positive and negative numbers): stated and explained in primer box 2 below; the order axioms [Anordnungsaxiome] they come from: Analysis 1.1, ordering (that section lists only the axioms, not these rules). Solving \(F(x)=q\) numerically by bisection: Analysis 4: bisection. The clt: §2.4. Standardising a normal variable and sums of normals: §2.3. Quantiles: §2.1. Student's t distribution: §1.3. Statistical models: §3.1; estimators: §3.2; tests: §3.3.

0. Words and symbols used on this page

  • Statistical model (Definition 3.4, §3.1): a family of probability distributions \((\P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}\). \(\theta\) (theta) is the unknown parameter, \(\Theta\) (capital theta) the set of all values it could have (the parameter space). \(\P_\theta\) means "probability computed as if the true parameter were \(\theta\)". Example: data \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with unknown \(\mu\); then \(\theta=\mu\) and \(\Theta=\R\).
  • Parameter of interest (Definition 3.9): a function \(\gamma:\Theta\to\R\) (gamma) of the parameter — the number we actually want to know. Often simply \(\gamma(\theta)=\theta\). If \(\theta=(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then \(\gamma(\theta)=\mu\) picks out the mean.
  • Sample \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)\): the data before we look at them, as random variables; usually iid (independent and identically distributed, §1.4). Lower-case \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\) are the observed numbers.
  • Sample mean \(\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) and sample variance \(S_n^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\) (Example 3.7). \(S_n=\sqrt{S_n^2}\) is the sample standard deviation. Their observed values are written \(\bar x_n\), \(s_n\).
  • Normal distribution \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\): mean \(\mu\), variance \(\sigma^2\), bell-shaped density. \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) is the standard normal, with cdf \(\Phi(z)=\P(Z\le z)\). If \(X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then \(\frac{X-\mu}\sigma\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) (Example 2.52). If \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are iid \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then \(\bar X_n\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}n)\) exactly (sums of independent normals are normal, Lemma 2.53, §2.3; the mean and variance follow from linearity and independence).
  • Standard error [Standardfehler]: the standard deviation of an estimator, here \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\) for \(\bar X_n\) (Theorem 2.64, §2.4).
  • Central limit theorem (clt, §2.4): for iid \(X_i\) with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\in(0,\infty)\), \(\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\) is approximately \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) for large \(n\).
  • Bernoulli \(\Ber(p)\): the value 1 with probability \(p\), else 0. Mean \(p\), variance \(p(1-p)\). \(\chi_A\) (the script's indicator, also written \(\one_A\)) is 1 on the set \(A\), 0 outside.
  • Test (§3.3): a rule that looks at the data and either rejects a null hypothesis \(H_0\) or does not. Level (significance level) \(\alpha\): the probability of rejecting \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is true is at most \(\alpha\). The z-test (Example 3.44) and t-test (Example 3.45) for \(H_0:\mu=\mu_0\) are the ones used here.
  • Other distributions used in the extensions (§1.3): \(\mathrm{Unif}(0,\theta)\) — every value in \([0,\theta]\) equally likely, cdf \(x/\theta\) there; \(\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)\) — waiting time with cdf \(1-e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x\ge0\); \(\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\) — counts \(k=0,1,2,\dots\) with mean and variance \(\lambda\).
  • Maximum likelihood estimator (mle) [Maximum-Likelihood-Schätzer] (§3.2): the parameter value under which the observed data are most probable; written \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\). A hat \(\hat{\ }\) on a symbol always means "estimate of".
  • Law of large numbers (lln, §2.4): \(\bar X_n\) gets close to \(\mu\) as \(n\) grows. Chebyshev's inequality (§2.2): for any random variable \(Y\) with finite variance and any \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\P(|Y-\E[Y]|\ge\varepsilon)\le\frac{\Var[Y]}{\varepsilon^2}\) — always true, but often loose.
  • Bayes' rule (Theorem 1.70, §1.4): \(\P(A\mid B)=\frac{\P(B\mid A)\P(A)}{\P(B)}\), used once in SoSe25 P1c.
  • \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) (alpha) is a small number such as 0.05; \(1-\alpha\) such as 0.95 is the confidence level. "\(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\)" turns it into a percentage: \(\alpha=0.05\) gives 95 %.

1. Critical values: the quantiles \(z_{\alpha/2}\) and \(t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\)

Quantile (§2.1): for a continuous, strictly increasing cdf \(F\), the \(q\)-quantile is the number \(x\) with \(F(x)=q\) — the point with probability \(q\) to its left.

The course's subscript convention (Example 3.46): a subscript gives the probability to the right. So \(z_a\) is the value with \(\P(Z>z_a)=a\), i.e. the \((1-a)\)-quantile of \(\mathcal N(0,1)\): \(\Phi(z_a)=1-a\). In particular \(z_{\alpha/2}\) has probability \(\frac\alpha2\) to its right. By the symmetry of the bell curve, \(-z_{\alpha/2}\) has probability \(\frac\alpha2\) to its left, so exactly \(1-\alpha\) lies between them. Example: \(\alpha=0.05\): \(\Phi(z_{0.025})=0.975\), \(z_{0.025}\approx1.96\).

In the same way, \(t_{\nu,a}\) is the value with probability \(a\) to its right under Student's \(t_\nu\) distribution (§1.3: a symmetric bell-shaped density with heavier tails than the normal; \(\nu\) (nu) is the number of "degrees of freedom" [Freiheitsgrade]).

Values recomputed by me with scipy:

\(\alpha\)0.200.100.050.010.001
confidence \(1-\alpha\)80 %90 %95 %99 %99.9 %
\(z_{\alpha/2}\)1.2821.6451.9602.5763.291
\(\nu=n-1\)123459192999\(\infty\)
\(t_{\nu,0.05}\) (90 %)6.3142.9202.3532.1322.0151.8331.7291.6991.6601.645

Read the table like this: the t values are always larger than the z value in the same row, much larger for small \(\nu\), and they approach it as \(\nu\to\infty\) (last column). Sheet 11 Ex 3 uses \(t_{9,0.025}\approx2.262\). Exams give the value you need or let you leave the symbol in the answer.

2. Moving things around inside a double inequality

All derivations below turn "\(-c\le\text{something with }\mu\le c\)" into "\(\text{lower}\le\mu\le\text{upper}\)". Only three rules are used, and each is applied to both inequalities at once. my addition They follow from the order axioms of the real numbers (Analysis 1.1, ordering, which states the axioms but not these rules); the one-line reasons are given with each rule:

  1. Adding the same number \(b\) to all three parts keeps the directions: \(a\le y\le c\iff a+b\le y+b\le c+b\).
  2. Multiplying all three parts by a positive number keeps the directions. (Reason: \(a\le y\) means \(y-a\ge0\); a positive number \(s\) times a non-negative number is non-negative, so \(sy-sa=s(y-a)\ge0\), i.e. \(sa\le sy\).)
  3. Multiplying by \(-1\) reverses both directions: \(a\le y\le c\iff -c\le -y\le -a\). (Reason: add \(-a-y\) to both sides of \(a\le y\) using rule 1: \(a+(-a-y)\le y+(-a-y)\), i.e. \(-y\le-a\). Example: \(2\le3\) but \(-3\le-2\).)

Each rule is an "if and only if", so the event before and the event after contain exactly the same outcomes. Hence they have the same probability. That is the whole trick behind "rearranging the inequality for \(\mu\)".

Confidence intervals

Section goal Script §3.4

A point estimate gives a single "best guess" for a parameter, but it says nothing about how uncertain that guess is. An interval estimate, such as a confidence interval, gives a range of plausible values for an unknown parameter, together with a level of confidence.

Definition 3.54 confidence interval [Konfidenzintervall] Script 3.54

Let \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). A \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) confidence interval (ci) for a parameter of interest \(\gamma(\theta)\in\R\) is an interval with random endpoints \((L(X),U(X))\), computed from the sample \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)\), such that

\[ \P_\theta\bigl(L(X)\le\gamma(\theta)\le U(X)\bigr)\ \ge\ 1-\alpha\qquad\text{for all }\theta\in\Theta . \]

The value \(1-\alpha\) is the confidence level [Konfidenzniveau]. The key point: the interval is random, while the parameter is treated as a fixed, unknown constant.

Each part explained (mine).

  • \(L\) and \(U\) ("lower" and "upper") are statistics: formulas that take the data and return a number, like \(L(X)=\bar X_n-1.96\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\). They may not contain the unknown \(\theta\) — otherwise we could not compute them from the data.
  • Because \(X\) is random, \(L(X)\) and \(U(X)\) are random variables. The event \(\{L(X)\le\gamma(\theta)\le U(X)\}\) means "the random interval covers the fixed number \(\gamma(\theta)\)". Its probability is called the coverage probability [Überdeckungswahrscheinlichkeit].
  • "\(\ge1-\alpha\) for all \(\theta\in\Theta\)": we do not know the true \(\theta\), so the guarantee has to hold whichever \(\theta\) is true. The coverage may be bigger than \(1-\alpha\) for some \(\theta\) ("conservative"); in the normal examples below it is exactly \(1-\alpha\).
  • After the data are in, we plug in the observed \(x\) and get two numbers \(L(x)\), \(U(x)\). The script uses the word "confidence interval" both for the random interval (the method) and for this computed interval (its result).
  • The script writes \((L,U)\) with round brackets but uses \(\le\) in the probability. For the continuous distributions below the endpoints are hit with probability 0, so open or closed makes no difference.

Simple example (mine): the scale from the big picture. \(L(X)=\bar X_4-1.96\), \(U(X)=\bar X_4+1.96\) with \(\bar X_4\sim\mathcal N(\mu,1)\). Coverage \(=\P(|\bar X_4-\mu|\le1.96)=0.95\) for every \(\mu\) (derived in Example 3.56 below). Counterexample: \(L=U=\bar X_4\) (a "zero-width interval") has coverage \(\P(\bar X_4=\mu)=0\): it is a point estimate, not a ci at any level. At the other extreme, \(L=-\infty\), \(U=\infty\) has coverage 1 but is useless. A good ci is as short as possible while keeping the coverage.

In exercises and exams: you are asked to "give a \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) ci", and the answer is a formula "estimate \(\pm\) quantile \(\times\) standard error" together with the reason why its coverage is (approximately) \(1-\alpha\) (WiSe25 P5d below).

Remark 3.55 interpretation of confidence intervals Script 3.55

The frequentist interpretation of a 95 % confidence interval: if we repeated our sampling procedure a large number of times, each time constructing a 95 % confidence interval, then about 95 % of these randomly generated intervals would contain the true, fixed parameter value.

It is incorrect to say that for a specific, calculated interval there is a 95 % probability that the true parameter lies within it. Once calculated, the interval is fixed, and the true parameter is either in it or not. The probability statement applies to the procedure, not to a particular outcome.

Remark 3.55 with numbers, and the common misreadings My addition

Before and after the data. Light bulbs (Sheet 11 Ex 1): \(n=36\), \(\sigma=150\), so the standard error is \(\frac{150}{\sqrt{36}}=25\) hours.

  • Before sampling: \(\P_\mu\bigl(\bar X_{36}-49\le\mu\le\bar X_{36}+49\bigr)=0.95\) for every \(\mu\) (\(1.96\cdot25=49\)). This is a true probability statement about the random \(\bar X_{36}\).
  • After sampling, \(\bar x_{36}=1250\), and the interval is \([1201,1299]\). The statement "\(\P(1201\le\mu\le1299)=0.95\)" is meaningless in the frequentist model: \(1201\), \(1299\) and \(\mu\) are all fixed numbers. The inequality is simply true or false — probability 1 or 0 — and we do not know which.

How many intervals miss? Each of \(100\) independent 95 % intervals misses with probability 0.05, so the number of misses is \(\Bin(100,0.05)\): on average 5, but exactly 5 only with probability 0.18, and anything from 1 to 9 misses happens with probability 0.97. The first widget below shows this.

Common misreadings — all wrong:

  1. "There is a 95 % probability that \(\mu\) lies in \([1201,1299]\)." (Remark 3.55 — the parameter is not random. A statement of this form is what a Bayesian credible interval gives, §3.5, Definition 3.64 and Remark 3.65.)
  2. "95 % of the data lie in the interval." No: the interval is about the mean, and it shrinks like \(\frac1{\sqrt n}\); the spread of individual bulbs (\(\sigma=150\)) does not shrink. Here the interval is only 98 hours wide, while single bulbs vary by hundreds of hours.
  3. "If I repeat the experiment, the new mean will lie in my interval with probability 95 %." No: both the old interval and the new mean are random. The difference of two independent sample means has standard deviation \(\sqrt2\cdot25\), so the probability is \(\P(|Z|\le1.96/\sqrt2)=2\Phi(1.386)-1\approx0.83\).
  4. "The true value is more likely near the centre of the interval." Not a frequentist statement at all — \(\mu\) has no distribution here.
  5. "A 99 % interval is better than a 95 % one." It covers more often, but it is wider (\(2.576\) instead of \(1.96\) standard errors). Confidence and precision trade off; only more data (larger \(n\)) buys both.

In words: "95 %" is the hit rate of the ring-throwing method. Any one ring either surrounds the peg or not.

Confidence interval versus credible interval — a preview My addition

The sentence that Remark 3.55 forbids — "given my data, \(\mu\) lies in this interval with probability 95 %" — is exactly what a Bayesian credible interval [Kredibilitätsintervall] says (Definition 3.64). That is possible there because the Bayesian model gives the parameter itself a probability distribution (a prior, updated to a posterior). The script contrasts the two in Remark 3.65 on §3.5:

  • confidence interval: the interval is random, the parameter fixed; "95 %" is a property of the method over repeated samples;
  • credible interval: the data are fixed (observed), the parameter is random; "95 %" is a probability for this one interval, but it depends on the chosen prior.

With a lot of data the two often give nearly the same numbers, but they still answer different questions.

Widget — coverage: 100 intervals from 100 samples My addition

Each horizontal bar is the interval computed from one simulated sample of size \(n\) from \(\mathcal N(10,2^2)\); the vertical line is the true \(\mu=10\). Bars that miss it are drawn in the exam colour. Compare the three methods at small \(n\): the known-\(\sigma\) z interval and the t interval hit about \(1-\alpha\) of the time; the "z interval with estimated \(\sigma\)" (plugging \(S_n\) into the z formula) is too narrow and misses too often.

The mean of a normal distribution: z and t intervals

Example 3.56 ci for a normal mean, known variance Script 3.56

Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be iid \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma^2\) known. The quantity

\[ Z=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\ \sim\ \mathcal N(0,1) \]

is a pivotal quantity [Pivot], because its distribution does not depend on the unknown parameter \(\mu\). We can find a critical value \(z_{\alpha/2}\) such that \(\P(-z_{\alpha/2}\le Z\le z_{\alpha/2})=1-\alpha\). Rearranging the inequality for \(\mu\) yields

\[ \P\Bigl(\bar X_n-z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\ \le\ \mu\ \le\ \bar X_n+z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\Bigr)=1-\alpha . \]

Thus the \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) ci for \(\mu\) is \(\bar X_n\pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\).

What is a pivot? (mine) A pivot is a formula that involves both the data and the unknown parameter, but whose distribution is completely known. \(\bar X_n\) alone is not a pivot: its distribution \(\mathcal N(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}n)\) depends on the unknown \(\mu\). Subtracting \(\mu\) and dividing by the standard error removes that dependence. Because we know the pivot's distribution, we can write down an event of probability \(1-\alpha\) for it — and then solve that event for the parameter.

Derivation, every step steps filled in by me

Step 1: \(Z\) really is \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). \(\bar X_n\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}n)\) exactly (primer box 0: a sum of independent normals is normal; \(\E[\bar X_n]=\mu\) by linearity; \(\Var[\bar X_n]=\frac1{n^2}\cdot n\sigma^2=\frac{\sigma^2}n\) by independence). Standardising a normal variable (subtract its mean, divide by its standard deviation \(\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\)) gives \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) (Example 2.52).

Step 2: choose the critical value. For a continuous distribution, \(\P(-z\le Z\le z)=\Phi(z)-\Phi(-z)\). By symmetry \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\), so this equals \(2\Phi(z)-1\). Setting \(2\Phi(z)-1=1-\alpha\) and solving: \(2\Phi(z)=2-\alpha\), so \(\Phi(z)=1-\frac\alpha2\). That is the definition of \(z_{\alpha/2}\) (primer box 1).

Step 3: write the event. \(\P\Bigl(-z_{\alpha/2}\le\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\le z_{\alpha/2}\Bigr)=1-\alpha\).

Step 4: multiply by the positive number \(\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\) (primer box 2, rule 2): \(-z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\le\bar X_n-\mu\le z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\).

Step 5: subtract \(\bar X_n\) from all three parts (rule 1): \(-\bar X_n-z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\le-\mu\le-\bar X_n+z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\).

Step 6: multiply by \(-1\), which reverses both inequalities (rule 3): \(\bar X_n+z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\ge\mu\ge\bar X_n-z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\). Read from right to left, this is \(\bar X_n-z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\le\mu\le\bar X_n+z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\).

Step 7: same event, same probability. Steps 4–6 were "if and only if" transformations, so the event in step 6 contains exactly the same outcomes as the event in step 3. Its probability is \(1-\alpha\), for every \(\mu\). So Definition 3.54 holds with \(L=\bar X_n-z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\) and \(U=\bar X_n+z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\), with equality instead of \(\ge\). \(L\) and \(U\) contain no \(\mu\), so they are computable. ∎

Numbers (mine): \(n=25\), \(\sigma=3\), observed \(\bar x_{25}=11\), \(\alpha=0.05\). Standard error \(\frac3{\sqrt{25}}=0.6\); half-width \(1.96\cdot0.6=1.176\); interval \([9.824,\,12.176]\).

Three things that control the width \(2z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\) (mine): more confidence (smaller \(\alpha\)) → larger \(z_{\alpha/2}\) → wider; noisier data (larger \(\sigma\)) → wider; more data → narrower, but only like \(\frac1{\sqrt n}\): to halve the width you need four times as many observations.

Recipe: a confidence interval from a pivot My addition

  1. Find a pivot \(Q(X,\gamma)\): a formula in the data and the parameter whose distribution is known and does not depend on any unknown parameter (exactly, or approximately by the clt).
  2. Take its quantiles: find \(a,b\) with \(\P(a\le Q\le b)=1-\alpha\). For a symmetric pivot, \(a=-b\) and \(b\) is the upper \(\frac\alpha2\) point (\(z_{\alpha/2}\), \(t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\)).
  3. Solve the double inequality \(a\le Q\le b\) for the parameter, one "if and only if" step at a time (primer box 2).
  4. Read off \(L\) and \(U\). Check they contain no unknown quantity. Plug in the data.
  5. State the level, and say "approximate" whenever step 1 used the clt.

Example 3.57 ci for a normal mean, unknown variance Script 3.57

If \(\sigma^2\) is unknown, we use the pivotal quantity

\[ T=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{S_n/\sqrt n}, \]

which follows a Student's t-distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom (§1.3). The \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) ci for \(\mu\) is

\[ \bar X_n\pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\frac{S_n}{\sqrt n}, \]

where \(t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\) is the critical value from the \(t_{n-1}\) distribution. The t-distribution has heavier tails than the normal, accounting for the extra uncertainty of estimating \(\sigma^2\).

Why a new pivot? (mine) The z interval needs \(\sigma\). If \(\sigma\) is unknown, the endpoints \(\bar X_n\pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\) cannot be computed. The natural idea is to replace \(\sigma\) by its estimate \(S_n\). But then the denominator is random too: sometimes \(S_n\) comes out too small, and the ratio becomes larger than a standard normal would. So \(T\) is not \(\mathcal N(0,1)\); it is more spread out. William Gosset ("Student", 1908) computed its exact distribution.

Why \(T\sim t_{n-1}\) explained by me — the script states it without proof

For iid \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) data, two facts hold (Student's theorem; their proofs use linear algebra beyond this course, so I only state them):

  • (a) \(\bar X_n\) and \(S_n^2\) are independent;
  • (b) \(V:=\frac{(n-1)S_n^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}\) (the chi-squared distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom, §1.3).

Remark 1.62 says: if \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and \(V\sim\chi^2_\nu\) are independent, then \(\frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/\nu}}\sim t_\nu\). Take \(Z=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\) (standard normal by Example 3.56), \(V\) from (b) and \(\nu=n-1\); by (a) they are independent. Now simplify:

\[ \frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/(n-1)}}=\frac{\dfrac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}}{\sqrt{\dfrac{(n-1)S_n^2}{\sigma^2(n-1)}}}=\frac{\dfrac{(\bar X_n-\mu)\sqrt n}{\sigma}}{\dfrac{S_n}{\sigma}}=\frac{(\bar X_n-\mu)\sqrt n}{S_n}=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{S_n/\sqrt n}=T . \]

(Middle steps: \((n-1)\) cancels; \(\sqrt{S_n^2/\sigma^2}=S_n/\sigma\) because both are positive; dividing by \(\frac{S_n}\sigma\) is multiplying by \(\frac\sigma{S_n}\), and \(\sigma\) cancels.) The unknown \(\sigma\) has disappeared — that is why \(T\) is a pivot. Only \(n-1\) (not \(n\)) degrees of freedom remain, because \(S_n^2\) measures spread around \(\bar X_n\), which already "used up" one piece of information.

Derivation of the interval steps filled in by me

Exactly as in Example 3.56, with \(t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\) instead of \(z_{\alpha/2}\) and \(S_n\) instead of \(\sigma\). The \(t_{n-1}\) density is symmetric about 0, so \(\P(-t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\le T\le t_{n-1,\alpha/2})=1-2\cdot\frac\alpha2=1-\alpha\). Multiply by \(\frac{S_n}{\sqrt n}>0\), subtract \(\bar X_n\), multiply by \(-1\): \(\bar X_n-t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\frac{S_n}{\sqrt n}\le\mu\le\bar X_n+t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\frac{S_n}{\sqrt n}\), with probability exactly \(1-\alpha\) for every \(\mu\) and every \(\sigma\). Here \(\theta=(\mu,\sigma^2)\) and \(\gamma(\theta)=\mu\); \(\sigma\) is a "nuisance parameter" the interval does not need to know. ∎

Numbers (mine): five measurements \(9.8,\ 10.4,\ 10.1,\ 9.6,\ 10.6\). Then \(\bar x_5=\frac{50.5}5=10.1\). Deviations from 10.1: \(-0.3,\,0.3,\,0,\,-0.5,\,0.5\); their squares sum to \(0.09+0.09+0+0.25+0.25=0.68\), so \(s_5^2=\frac{0.68}4=0.17\), \(s_5=0.412\), and \(\frac{s_5}{\sqrt5}=0.184\). With \(t_{4,0.025}=2.776\): half-width \(2.776\cdot0.184=0.512\), interval \([9.588,\,10.612]\). Using 1.96 instead would give \([9.739,\,10.461]\) — narrower, but its true coverage for \(n=5\) is only \(\P(|T_4|\le1.96)\approx0.878\), not 0.95 (widget above, method "z with S").

For large \(n\) the difference fades: \(t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\to z_{\alpha/2}\) (last column of the table), and the "z with S" coverage is 0.935 for \(n=20\), 0.947 for \(n=100\). This is also why, for large samples of non-normal data, "estimate \(\pm z_{\alpha/2}\cdot\)estimated standard error" is the standard approximate interval — Example 3.58 is one.

A proportion: the Wald interval

Example 3.58 ci for a proportion Script 3.58

Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be iid \(\Ber(p)\) and \(\hat p=\bar X_n\) (the fraction of ones). For large \(n\), the clt implies that \(\dfrac{\hat p-p}{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}}\) is approximately distributed like \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). Replacing the unknown \(p\) in the standard error with its estimate \(\hat p\) gives the Wald interval, an approximate \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) ci for \(p\):

\[ \hat p\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}n}. \]

This approximation performs poorly for small \(n\) or when \(p\) is near 0 or 1. Other methods like the Wilson score interval or the Clopper–Pearson interval have better coverage in those cases.

Derivation, every step steps filled in by me

Step 1 (clt). One \(X_i\sim\Ber(p)\) has mean \(p\) and variance \(p(1-p)\). If \(0<p<1\), the variance is positive and finite, so the clt (Theorem 2.64) applies with \(\mu=p\), \(\sigma=\sqrt{p(1-p)}\): \(\frac{\hat p-p}{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}}\approx\mathcal N(0,1)\). So \(\P\Bigl(-z_{\alpha/2}\le\frac{\hat p-p}{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}}\le z_{\alpha/2}\Bigr)\approx1-\alpha\).

Step 2 (the problem). Solving this for \(p\) is awkward, because \(p\) appears in the denominator too.

Step 3 (plug in). Replace \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\) by \(\widehat{\mathrm{se}}=\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}\). By the lln (§2.4) \(\hat p\to p\), so the ratio of the two standard errors tends to 1 and the approximation stays valid for large \(n\). (The theorem that makes "tends to 1 does not spoil a limit in distribution" precise is called Slutsky's lemma; it is not in the script.)

Step 4 (solve). Now \(\widehat{\mathrm{se}}\) is a positive number that does not contain \(p\). Multiply by it, subtract \(\hat p\), multiply by \(-1\) (primer box 2): \(\hat p-z_{\alpha/2}\widehat{\mathrm{se}}\le p\le\hat p+z_{\alpha/2}\widehat{\mathrm{se}}\), with probability \(\approx1-\alpha\). ∎

Numbers (mine): a poll of \(n=400\) people, 220 say yes, so \(\hat p=0.55\). \(\widehat{\mathrm{se}}=\sqrt{0.55\cdot0.45/400}=0.0249\); half-width \(1.96\cdot0.0249=0.049\); 95 % interval \([0.501,\,0.599]\). ("The margin of error is ±4.9 percentage points.")

Why "poorly near 0 or 1" (my examples, exact binomial computations):

  • If \(\hat p=0\) (no successes at all), then \(\widehat{\mathrm{se}}=0\) and the Wald interval is the single point \(\{0\}\) — it claims certainty from, say, 20 observations.
  • The interval can stick out of \([0,1]\): \(n=50\), \(\hat p=0.02\) gives a lower end of \(-0.019\).
  • The real coverage of the nominal 95 % Wald interval is 0.876 for \(n=20,\ p=0.1\); 0.877 for \(n=100,\ p=0.05\); only 0.395 for \(n=50,\ p=0.01\). For \(n=100,\ p=0.3\) it is 0.950 — fine.

Wilson's fix, briefly. Instead of plugging in \(\hat p\) (step 3), solve step 1's inequality \((\hat p-p)^2\le z^2\frac{p(1-p)}n\) for \(p\) exactly; it is a quadratic inequality in \(p\), and its solution set is an interval that always lies inside \([0,1]\) and never has zero width. For \(n=20\), \(\hat p=0\) it gives \([0,\,0.161]\). Clopper–Pearson instead inverts exact binomial tests (the duality of Remark 3.59). Neither is examined; the widget shows Wilson for comparison.

Widget — the Wald interval for a proportion My addition

Top: the interval \(\hat p\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}\) on \([0,1]\) (blue), with the Wilson interval underneath (grey) for comparison. Bottom: the half-width as a function of \(n\) for your \(\hat p\) — it falls like \(1/\sqrt n\). The readout gives the exact coverage the Wald method would have if the true \(p\) were your \(\hat p\).

Planning: how large must \(n\) be? My addition

The half-width ("margin of error") of the z interval is \(E=z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\). To guarantee a half-width of at most \(E\), solve \(z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\le E\) for \(n\): multiply by \(\sqrt n>0\) and divide by \(E>0\) to get \(\sqrt n\ge\frac{z_{\alpha/2}\sigma}E\); both sides are positive, so squaring keeps the direction:

\[ n\ \ge\ \Bigl(\frac{z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma}{E}\Bigr)^2 , \]

rounded up to the next integer.

  • Light bulbs, \(\sigma=150\), want \(E=25\) hours at 95 %: \(n\ge(1.96\cdot150/25)^2=11.76^2=138.3\), so \(n=139\). For \(E=10\): \(n\ge864.3\), so \(n=865\). Dividing \(E\) by 2.5 multiplies \(n\) by \(2.5^2=6.25\).
  • Proportion: \(\sigma=\sqrt{p(1-p)}\) is unknown before the study, but \(p(1-p)\le\frac14\) (a parabola with its top at \(p=\frac12\)). Worst case \(\sigma=\frac12\): for \(E=0.03\) (±3 points) at 95 %, \(n\ge(1.96\cdot0.5/0.03)^2=1067.1\), so \(n=1068\) — the familiar "about 1000 people" of opinion polls.

This is the interval version of the "power analysis up front" mentioned in Overview 3.53(ii).

Widget — sample-size calculator My addition

Required \(n=\lceil(z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/E)^2\rceil\) (the ceiling \(\lceil\cdot\rceil\) rounds up). The curve shows required \(n\) against the desired half-width \(E\) (logarithmic vertical axis); the dot is your choice.

Duality between confidence intervals and tests

Remark 3.59 duality between cis and hypothesis tests Script 3.59

There is a direct correspondence between two-sided hypothesis tests and confidence intervals. A \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) confidence interval for a parameter \(\theta\) consists of all values \(\theta_0\) for which the null hypothesis \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) would not be rejected at significance level \(\alpha\). Conversely, if a test rejects \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\), then \(\theta_0\) does not lie in the \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) ci. This duality gives two perspectives on the same inferential problem.

The concrete case first (mine). The two-sided z-test (Example 3.44) rejects \(H_0:\mu=\mu_0\) when \(|z_{\text{obs}}|>z_{\alpha/2}\), with \(z_{\text{obs}}=\frac{\bar x_n-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\). So

\[ \text{not rejected}\iff\Bigl|\frac{\bar x_n-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\Bigr|\le z_{\alpha/2}\iff|\bar x_n-\mu_0|\le z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\iff\mu_0\in\Bigl[\bar x_n-z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n},\ \bar x_n+z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\Bigr]. \]

(First step: multiply by \(\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}>0\). Second step: \(|d|\le c\) means \(-c\le d\le c\), and solving that for \(\mu_0\) is the same computation as steps 4–6 of Example 3.56.) The right-hand set is exactly the z interval of Example 3.56. The same computation with \(t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\) and \(s_n\) links the t-test (Example 3.45) to the t interval (Example 3.57).

Proof of the general duality My proof — the script states the remark without proof

Setup. For each candidate value \(\theta_0\in\Theta\), let \(\varphi_{\theta_0}\) be a test of \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) of level \(\alpha\): \(\P_{\theta_0}(\varphi_{\theta_0}\text{ rejects})\le\alpha\). Write \(A(\theta_0)\) for its acceptance region: the set of data \(x\) for which it does not reject. Then the level condition reads \(\P_{\theta_0}(X\in A(\theta_0))\ge1-\alpha\).

Tests → confidence set. Define, for observed data \(x\), \(C(x):=\{\theta_0\in\Theta:\ x\in A(\theta_0)\}\) — all parameter values that the data do not reject. Fix any true parameter \(\theta\). For every outcome, "\(\theta\in C(X)\)" holds exactly when "\(X\in A(\theta)\)" holds (definition of \(C\), with \(\theta_0=\theta\)). Two descriptions of the same event have the same probability, so

\[ \P_\theta\bigl(\theta\in C(X)\bigr)=\P_\theta\bigl(X\in A(\theta)\bigr)\ge1-\alpha . \]

This holds for every \(\theta\in\Theta\), which is Definition 3.54 (whenever \(C(x)\) is an interval — true for the z- and t-tests, as computed above).

Confidence interval → tests. Conversely, let \([L(X),U(X)]\) be a \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) ci. For each \(\theta_0\) define the test "reject \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) if \(\theta_0\notin[L(X),U(X)]\)". If \(H_0\) is true, i.e. \(\theta=\theta_0\), its rejection probability is \(\P_{\theta_0}(\theta_0\notin[L,U])=1-\P_{\theta_0}(\theta_0\in[L,U])\le1-(1-\alpha)=\alpha\). So it has level \(\alpha\). ∎

Two small conditions hide in the remark: (1) the ci and the test must be built from the same pivot and the same \(\alpha\) (a 95 % interval matches a two-sided test at \(\alpha=0.05\)); (2) the boundary conventions must match — the script's z-test rejects on "\(>\)" and the interval is closed, so a \(\mu_0\) exactly on the boundary is "not rejected" and "inside". For continuous data this boundary case has probability 0.

How it is used (mine): a ci answers every two-sided test at once. From one interval you can read off the decision for any \(\mu_0\): reject exactly the values outside. It also shows more than a single test decision — how far from \(\mu_0\) the plausible values are, which is the "practical significance" point of Caveat 3.50.

In words: the confidence interval is the list of all parameter values the data cannot reject. "Rejected at level \(\alpha\)" = "outside the \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) interval".

One-sided confidence bounds — the partners of one-sided tests My addition

Remark 3.59 speaks about two-sided tests. A one-sided test (Definition 3.43, e.g. \(H_0:\mu\le\mu_0\) against \(H_1:\mu>\mu_0\)) has a partner too: a one-sided confidence bound [einseitige Konfidenzschranke], an interval of the form \([L(X),\infty)\).

Construction (normal data, \(\sigma\) known). All of the probability \(\alpha\) is put into one tail: \(\P_\mu\bigl(\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\le z_\alpha\bigr)=1-\alpha\), where \(z_\alpha\) (not \(z_{\alpha/2}\)) has probability \(\alpha\) to its right. Multiply by \(\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}>0\) and rearrange (primer box 2): \(\bar X_n-\mu\le z_\alpha\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\iff\mu\ge\bar X_n-z_\alpha\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\). So

\[ \P_\mu\Bigl(\mu\in\Bigl[\bar X_n-z_\alpha\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n},\ \infty\Bigr)\Bigr)=1-\alpha\quad\text{for every }\mu . \]

Duality. The one-sided z-test (Example 3.46(i)) rejects \(H_0:\mu\le\mu_0\) when \(\frac{\bar x_n-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}>z_\alpha\), i.e. when \(\mu_0<\bar x_n-z_\alpha\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\): exactly when \(\mu_0\) lies below the lower bound. (Same algebra as above, with \(\mu_0\) in place of \(\mu\).)

Sheet 11 Ex 4 as a bound Sheet 11 · Ex 4: \(\sigma=3\), \(n=25\), standard error \(0.6\), \(\alpha=0.01\), \(z_{0.01}\approx2.33\). The 99 % lower confidence bound is \(\bar x_{25}-2.33\cdot0.6=\bar x_{25}-1.398\). It lies above \(\mu_0=10\) exactly when \(\bar x_{25}>11.398\) — the sheet's rejection region, found on §3.3.

Trap: a two-sided 95 % interval uses \(z_{0.025}=1.96\); a one-sided 95 % bound uses \(z_{0.05}\approx1.645\). The SoSe26 P5 extension below shows a case where the one-sided test rejects but the two-sided 95 % interval still contains the null value — no contradiction, because they are partners of different tests.

Widget — one picture for all tests and the interval My addition

Sheet 11 Ex 1 setting: standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt n=150/6=25\). Horizontal axis: candidate \(\mu_0\). Vertical axis: sample mean \(\bar x\). The shaded band is the set of all \((\mu_0,\bar x)\) where the z-test does not reject (\(|\bar x-\mu_0|\le z_{\alpha/2}\cdot25\)). Read it vertically at your \(\mu_0\): the acceptance region of that test. Read it horizontally at your observed \(\bar x\): the confidence interval.

Exercise-sheet tasks

No exercise sheet asks for a confidence interval directly (I checked Sheets 9, 10 and 11 line by line). Sheet 11 is about tests; its tests are solved on §3.3. Below I redo their data as confidence intervals and check that the decisions agree, as Remark 3.59 promises (Ex 4 is done as a one-sided bound in the box above). Sheet 10 is about estimators (solved on §3.2); its Ex 1 gives a nice exact interval that is not of the form "estimate ± quantile × standard error".

Sheet 11, Exercise 1 — light bulbs, as a confidence interval Sheet 11 · Ex 1 my addition

Data. Normal lifetimes, known \(\sigma=150\) hours, \(n=36\), observed \(\bar x_{36}=1250\). The sheet tests \(H_0:\mu=1200\) against \(H_1:\mu\ne1200\) and finds \(z_{\text{obs}}=\frac{1250-1200}{150/6}=\frac{50}{25}=2\): rejected at \(\alpha=0.05\) (\(2>1.96\)), not rejected at \(\alpha=0.001\) (\(2<3.29\)).

The same data as confidence intervals

Which interval? Normal data, \(\sigma\) known → Example 3.56: \(\bar x_n\pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\), with standard error \(\frac{150}{\sqrt{36}}=\frac{150}6=25\).

95 % (\(\alpha=0.05\)): half-width \(1.96\cdot25=49\). Interval \([1250-49,\ 1250+49]=[1201,\,1299]\). The null value 1200 lies outside (just below 1201). Duality: reject \(H_0\) at 5 % — the same decision as the test.

99.9 % (\(\alpha=0.001\)): \(z_{0.0005}=3.291\), half-width \(3.291\cdot25=82.3\). Interval \([1167.7,\,1332.3]\). Now 1200 lies inside: do not reject at 0.1 % — again the same decision.

Why they must agree: \(1200\notin[1201,1299]\iff|1250-1200|>49\iff\frac{50}{25}>1.96\iff|z_{\text{obs}}|>z_{0.025}\) — the chain in Remark 3.59.

What the interval adds: the test only says "changed". The interval says "the new mean is somewhere between about 1201 and 1299 hours" — an improvement of anywhere from 1 to 99 hours, which a manager can judge for practical relevance.

Part (iii) of the sheet asks what the level means "for the confidence you should have". The official answer (the level is a long-run frequency over repeated datasets under \(H_0\), not a probability about this dataset) is correct and is the testing version of Remark 3.55. One convention difference: the sheet rejects when \(|z_{\text{obs}}|\ge z_{\alpha/2}\), the script (Example 3.44) when \(|z_{\text{obs}}|>z_{\alpha/2}\); for continuous data this changes nothing.

Sheet 11, Exercise 3 — beer bottles, as a confidence interval Sheet 11 · Ex 3 my addition

Data. Normal contents, \(\sigma\) unknown, \(n=10\), \(\bar x_{10}=328.5\) ml, \(s_{10}^2=4\) ml², so \(s_{10}=2\). The sheet tests \(H_0:\mu=330\) against \(H_1:\mu\ne330\) with the t-test, gets \(t_{\text{obs}}\approx-2.37\), and rejects at \(\alpha=0.05\) because \(2.37>t_{9,0.025}\approx2.262\).

The same data as a confidence interval

Which interval? Normal data, \(\sigma\) unknown → Example 3.57: \(\bar x_n\pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\frac{s_n}{\sqrt n}\) with \(n-1=9\) degrees of freedom.

Standard error: \(\frac{s_{10}}{\sqrt{10}}=\frac2{3.1623}=0.6325\) ml.

Half-width: \(t_{9,0.025}\cdot0.6325=2.262\cdot0.6325=1.431\) ml.

95 % interval: \([328.5-1.431,\ 328.5+1.431]=[327.07,\,329.93]\) ml.

Duality check: the claimed 330 ml lies outside (above 329.93), so the t-test at 5 % rejects — the sheet's decision. It is a close call: 330 misses the interval by only 0.07 ml, matching \(|t_{\text{obs}}|=2.372\) being only a little above 2.262. (The two-sided p-value is \(0.042\), just under 0.05.)

What the interval adds: the plausible mean contents are 327.1–329.9 ml, i.e. the bottles are short by between 0.07 and 2.9 ml on average.

Checking the official solution: correct. One rounding detail: it gives \(t_{\text{obs}}\approx-2.373\); more precisely \(-1.5/0.63246=-2.3717\approx-2.372\). This does not affect the decision.

Sheet 10, Exercise 1 extended — an exact ci for the uniform \(\theta\) Sheet 10 · Ex 1 my extension

Data from the sheet. \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid \(\mathrm{Unif}(0,\theta)\), \(\theta>0\) unknown. The sheet finds the mle \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=X_{\max}=\max\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}\) and, in part (iii), its cdf \(F_{X_{\max}}(t)=(t/\theta)^n\) for \(0\le t\le\theta\) (solved on §3.2). Its bus example: waiting times \(4,1,7,12,5,9,10,2\), so \(n=8\), \(x_{\max}=12\) minutes. The sheet stops there; here is a 95 % confidence interval for \(\theta\).

Solution with a non-normal pivot

Step 1: find a pivot. Put \(Q:=X_{\max}/\theta\). For \(0\le u\le1\): \(\P_\theta(Q\le u)=\P_\theta(X_{\max}\le u\theta)=\bigl(\frac{u\theta}\theta\bigr)^n=u^n\) (the sheet's cdf at \(t=u\theta\)). The \(\theta\) cancels, so the distribution of \(Q\) is the same for every \(\theta\): \(Q\) is a pivot. Also \(Q\le1\) always, because no observation can exceed \(\theta\).

Step 2: an event of probability \(1-\alpha\). Take \(\P(a\le Q\le1)=1-a^n\) (cdf at 1 minus cdf at \(a\)). Setting \(1-a^n=1-\alpha\) gives \(a^n=\alpha\), so \(a=\alpha^{1/n}\).

Step 3: solve for \(\theta\). \(a\le\frac{X_{\max}}\theta\le1\). Multiply by \(\theta>0\) (keeps directions): \(a\theta\le X_{\max}\le\theta\). The right inequality says \(\theta\ge X_{\max}\); dividing the left one by \(a>0\) says \(\theta\le X_{\max}/a\). Hence

\[ \P_\theta\Bigl(X_{\max}\ \le\ \theta\ \le\ X_{\max}\,\alpha^{-1/n}\Bigr)=1-\alpha\quad\text{for every }\theta>0 , \]

an exact \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) ci in the sense of Definition 3.54 — no clt needed.

Numbers: \(n=8\), \(\alpha=0.05\): \(\alpha^{1/8}=0.05^{0.125}=0.6877\), so \(\alpha^{-1/8}=1.4542\). Interval \([12,\ 12\cdot1.4542]=[12,\,17.45]\) minutes. (A simulation with \(10^5\) samples, \(\theta=5\), gave coverage 0.951.)

What to notice: the interval is not symmetric around the estimate; it starts exactly at the mle. That makes sense: \(\theta\) can never be smaller than the largest observation, so values below 12 are impossible, not just implausible. The recipe (pivot → quantiles → solve) is the same as in Example 3.56; only the pivot's distribution changed.

Sheet 11, Exercise 2 extended — a ci from one exponential observation Sheet 11 · Ex 2 my extension

Setting from the sheet. One observation \(X\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)\), cdf \(\P_\lambda(X\le x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x\ge0\). The sheet builds the Neyman–Pearson test of \(\lambda_0\) against \(\lambda_1>\lambda_0\), which rejects when \(x<-\frac{\ln(1-\alpha)}{\lambda_0}\) (solved on §3.3).

Solution

Pivot. \(Q:=\lambda X\). For \(u\ge0\): \(\P_\lambda(\lambda X\le u)=\P_\lambda(X\le u/\lambda)=1-e^{-\lambda\cdot u/\lambda}=1-e^{-u}\): an \(\mathrm{Exp}(1)\) distribution, the same for every \(\lambda\).

Two-sided interval. Cut \(\frac\alpha2\) off each tail: \(a=-\ln(1-\frac\alpha2)\) (so that \(1-e^{-a}=\frac\alpha2\)) and \(b=-\ln\frac\alpha2\) (so that \(1-e^{-b}=1-\frac\alpha2\)). Then \(\P(a\le\lambda X\le b)=(1-\frac\alpha2)-\frac\alpha2=1-\alpha\). Divide by \(X>0\) (keeps directions): \(\bigl[\frac aX,\ \frac bX\bigr]\) is an exact \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) ci for \(\lambda\). For \(\alpha=0.05\): \(a=0.0253\), \(b=3.689\); with the observation \(x=2\) the interval is \([0.0127,\,1.844]\) — very wide, as it must be with a single data point.

Duality with the sheet's one-sided test. \(\P_\lambda\bigl(\lambda X\ge-\ln(1-\alpha)\bigr)=e^{\ln(1-\alpha)}=1-\alpha\), so \(\bigl[-\frac{\ln(1-\alpha)}X,\ \infty\bigr)\) is a \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) lower confidence bound for \(\lambda\). The sheet's test rejects \(\lambda_0\) when \(x<-\frac{\ln(1-\alpha)}{\lambda_0}\), i.e. (multiply by \(\lambda_0/x>0\)) when \(\lambda_0<-\frac{\ln(1-\alpha)}x\): exactly when \(\lambda_0\) lies below the lower bound — the one-sided duality of the box above.

"Confidence level" in Sheet 5 Ex 1 is not a confidence interval Sheet 5 · Ex 1 my note

Sheet 5 Ex 1 (solved on §1.3) defines the "Value at Risk at confidence level \(\alpha\)" as the loss \(L\) with \(\P(R\le-L)=\alpha\) — a quantile of a fully known return distribution. Nothing is estimated and nothing is random about \(L\). In the sense of Definition 3.54, a confidence level belongs to a random interval built from data to catch an unknown parameter. Same words, different concept.

Old-exam tasks

I read all three exams in full (every true/false and definitions item included). Only one part asks for a confidence interval: WiSe25 P5d. One true/false item, SoSe25 P1c, tests exactly the misreading that Remark 3.55 warns about (there for a test instead of an interval). Three further problems — WiSe25 P4, SoSe25 P4, SoSe26 P5 — build an estimator and its clt approximation, which are the ingredients of a confidence interval; the exams did not ask for one, so the intervals below are my practice extensions. Past exams do not predict the next one.

WiSe 25/26, Problem 5d — an approximate ci for a cdf value WiSe25 · P5d · 2 credits

Context (parts a–c are solved on §2.1). \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are iid real random variables with cdf \(F_{X_1}\). Fix \(t\in\R\). The empirical cdf [empirische Verteilungsfunktion] is \(\hat F_n(t):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\chi_{(-\infty,t]}(X_i)\) — the fraction of data points \(\le t\). Parts (a)–(c) showed: \(n\hat F_n(t)\sim\Bin(n,F_{X_1}(t))\); \(\hat F_n(t)\) is unbiased; \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat F_n(t)]=\frac{F_{X_1}(t)(1-F_{X_1}(t))}n\). Here \(\operatorname{mse}\) is the mean squared error [mittlerer quadratischer Fehler] of an estimator \(\hat\theta\), \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta]=\E[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]=\Var[\hat\theta]+(\operatorname{bias}[\hat\theta])^2\) (Definition 3.20(iv), §3.2): the average squared distance between the estimate and the truth. For an unbiased estimator, which \(\hat F_n(t)\) is by part (b), the bias is 0 and the mse is just the variance.

Task. Give an approximate \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) confidence interval for \(F_{X_1}(t)\), for \(\alpha\in(0,1)\).

Solution.

  1. Recognise a proportion. Put \(Y_i:=\chi_{(-\infty,t]}(X_i)\). Each \(Y_i\) is 1 if \(X_i\le t\) and 0 otherwise, so \(Y_i\sim\Ber(p)\) with \(p:=\P(X_i\le t)=F_{X_1}(t)\) (definition of the cdf). The \(Y_i\) are iid, because they are the same function applied to iid \(X_i\). And \(\hat F_n(t)=\bar Y_n=:\hat p\). So we are exactly in Example 3.58 with the unknown proportion \(p=F_{X_1}(t)\).
  2. Pivot via the clt. Assume \(0<p<1\), so that \(\Var[Y_i]=p(1-p)>0\). The clt gives \(\dfrac{\hat F_n(t)-F_{X_1}(t)}{\sqrt{F_{X_1}(t)(1-F_{X_1}(t))/n}}\approx\mathcal N(0,1)\) for large \(n\). (The denominator is the square root of the mse from part (c) — the standard error.)
  3. Plug in and solve (Example 3.58, steps 3–4). Replace \(F_{X_1}(t)\) in the standard error by \(\hat F_n(t)\) and solve for \(F_{X_1}(t)\):
\[ \hat F_n(t)\ \pm\ z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat F_n(t)\bigl(1-\hat F_n(t)\bigr)}{n}}, \]

where \(z_{\alpha/2}\) is the \((1-\frac\alpha2)\)-quantile of \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), i.e. \(\Phi(z_{\alpha/2})=1-\frac\alpha2\). Its coverage \(\P\bigl(F_{X_1}(t)\in\text{interval}\bigr)\) tends to \(1-\alpha\) as \(n\to\infty\).

Numbers (mine): \(n=100\), 30 data points \(\le t\), \(\alpha=0.05\): \(\hat F_{100}(t)=0.3\), standard error \(\sqrt{0.3\cdot0.7/100}=0.0458\), half-width \(1.96\cdot0.0458=0.090\), interval \([0.210,\,0.390]\).

Checking the official solution: it gives exactly this Wald interval, with the same reduction to \(Y_i\sim\Ber(p)\). Correct. Two small points: the task writes "100(1 − α) confidence interval" without "%", and the official answer does not say what \(z_{\alpha/2}\) is — in an exam, define it (one line) and say "approximate, by the clt", to be safe.

Two alternatives worth knowing (not asked). (1) Without plugging in: since \(p(1-p)\le\frac14\), the interval \(\hat F_n(t)\pm\frac{z_{\alpha/2}}{2\sqrt n}\) is also approximately valid and never too narrow; for the numbers above it is \(0.3\pm0.098\). (2) A guaranteed (non-approximate) interval via Chebyshev (§2.2): by part (c), \(\Var[\hat F_n(t)]\le\frac1{4n}\), so \(\P(|\hat F_n(t)-F_{X_1}(t)|\ge\varepsilon)\le\frac1{4n\varepsilon^2}\). Setting this equal to \(\alpha\) gives \(\varepsilon=\frac1{2\sqrt{n\alpha}}\), and \(\hat F_n(t)\pm\frac1{2\sqrt{n\alpha}}\) is a true \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) ci in the sense of Definition 3.54, for every \(n\). Price: for \(n=100\), \(\alpha=0.05\) the half-width is \(0.224\) instead of \(0.090\). This is the "guaranteed but loose versus sharp but approximate" trade-off of WiSe25 P4d (§2.4).

In words: the empirical cdf at \(t\) is just the proportion of data below \(t\), so its confidence interval is the proportion interval of Example 3.58.

SoSe 2025, Problem 1c — "at most 5 % probability that the batch conforms"? SoSe25 · P1c · 3 credits

Statement. From a large batch of switches you test a random subsample at level \(\alpha=0.05\): \(H_0\): "the defect proportion is at most what the manufacturer claimed" against \(H_1\): "it is larger". The test rejects. Claim: "the probability that the entire batch conforms to the claimed proportion is at most 5 %". True or false? (Full test-side discussion on §3.3.)

Answer: false.

  1. What \(\alpha\) really says. The level is \(\P_\theta(\text{reject})\le0.05\) for every \(\theta\) in \(H_0\): a probability about the procedure, computed assuming \(H_0\) is true (Definition 3.34, §3.3).
  2. What the claim says. "\(\P(H_0\text{ is true})\le0.05\)" — a probability about the fixed, unknown defect proportion of this batch. In the frequentist model the parameter is not random, so this is either 0 or 1 and the test does not tell us which. This is the same mistake as reading "95 % probability that \(\mu\) lies in [1201, 1299]" into a confidence interval (Remark 3.55).
  3. Even with a probability for \(H_0\), 5 % is wrong (my illustration). Suppose 90 % of batches conform, the test has level 0.05 and power 0.8 against bad batches. Then by Bayes' rule \(\P(H_0\text{ true}\mid\text{reject})=\frac{0.9\cdot0.05}{0.9\cdot0.05+0.1\cdot0.8}=\frac{0.045}{0.125}=0.36\) — far above 5 %. Such a statement needs a prior, i.e. the Bayesian view of §3.5.

Checking the official solution: "False. The significance level makes claims about the procedure, not probabilities of the true parameter." Correct, but short for 3 credits; in an exam add point 1 (what \(\alpha\) is) explicitly.

Practice: exam estimators turned into confidence intervals my extensions

The next three problems were asked as estimation and testing problems. None of them asked for a confidence interval; I add one to each because every ingredient is already there (an estimator, its variance, a clt approximation). Parts asked in the exams are solved on §3.2, §3.3 and §2.4.

WiSe 25/26, Problem 4 (rainfall) as a confidence interval WiSe25 · P4 my extension

What the exam gives. iid \(X_i\) with density \(p_\theta(x)=\frac1{\theta^2}xe^{-x/\theta}\) (\(x\ge0\)), \(\theta>0\); mle \(\hat\theta=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) (P4a); \(\E[\hat\theta]=\theta\), \(\Var[\hat\theta]=\frac{\theta^2}{2n}\); Chebyshev \(\P_\theta(|\hat\theta-\theta|\ge\varepsilon)\le\frac{\theta^2}{2n\varepsilon^2}\) (P4b); clt: \(\frac{\hat\theta-\theta}{\theta/\sqrt{2n}}\approx\mathcal N(0,1)\) (P4c).

(i) Approximate ci from the clt. Put \(c:=\frac{z_{\alpha/2}}{\sqrt{2n}}\). Then \(\P_\theta\bigl(|\hat\theta-\theta|\le c\,\theta\bigr)\approx1-\alpha\). Here the standard error \(\theta/\sqrt{2n}\) contains the unknown \(\theta\), but the inequality can still be solved exactly, because \(\theta>0\):

  • \(|\hat\theta-\theta|\le c\theta\iff-c\theta\le\hat\theta-\theta\le c\theta\) (definition of the absolute value);
  • add \(\theta\) to all three parts: \(\theta(1-c)\le\hat\theta\le\theta(1+c)\);
  • right part: divide by \(1+c>0\): \(\theta\ge\frac{\hat\theta}{1+c}\). Left part: if \(c<1\), divide by \(1-c>0\): \(\theta\le\frac{\hat\theta}{1-c}\).

So \(\Bigl[\frac{\hat\theta}{1+c},\ \frac{\hat\theta}{1-c}\Bigr]\) is an approximate \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) ci (valid once \(2n>z_{\alpha/2}^2\)). The plug-in (Wald-type) alternative replaces \(\theta\) by \(\hat\theta\) in the standard error: \(\hat\theta\bigl(1\pm c\bigr)\).

Numbers: \(n=50\), observed \(\hat\theta=3\), \(\alpha=0.05\): \(c=\frac{1.96}{10}=0.196\). Solved interval \(\bigl[\frac3{1.196},\frac3{0.804}\bigr]=[2.508,\,3.731]\); plug-in \([2.412,\,3.588]\). (Simulated coverage of the solved interval at \(n=50\): 0.950.)

(ii) Guaranteed ci from Chebyshev. In P4b take \(\varepsilon=k\theta\): the bound becomes \(\frac{\theta^2}{2nk^2\theta^2}=\frac1{2nk^2}\). Setting it equal to \(\alpha\) gives \(k=\frac1{\sqrt{2n\alpha}}\). Then \(\P_\theta(|\hat\theta-\theta|<k\theta)\ge1-\alpha\) for every \(\theta\) and every \(n\), and the same algebra as in (i) gives the guaranteed-level (conservative) ci \(\bigl(\frac{\hat\theta}{1+k},\frac{\hat\theta}{1-k}\bigr)\), provided \(k<1\), i.e. \(n>\frac1{2\alpha}\). "Guaranteed-level" means what Definition 3.54 asks for, coverage \(\ge1-\alpha\), with no clt approximation anywhere — not coverage equal to \(1-\alpha\). Chebyshev's bound is usually far from tight, so the real coverage here is close to 1 (a simulation at \(n=50\), \(\theta=3\) gave 1.000 out of \(2\cdot10^5\) samples), which is exactly why the interval is so wide. Numbers: \(k=\frac1{\sqrt5}=0.447\), interval \((2.073,\,5.427)\) — much wider.

Link to P4d: that part asked for the difference between b) and c): "Chebyshev is a guarantee that may be loose, clt is approximate but typically much sharper". The two intervals show it in one picture: \((2.07,5.43)\) guaranteed versus \([2.51,3.73]\) approximate.

SoSe 2025, Problem 4 (Poisson defects) as a confidence interval SoSe25 · P4 my extension

What the exam gives. iid \(X_i\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)\) (mean and variance \(\lambda\)); mle \(\hat\lambda=\bar X_n\) (P4a), unbiased (P4b), and \(\bar X_n\approx\mathcal N(\lambda,\lambda/n)\) by the clt (P4c). P4d: \(n=100\), \(\bar x_{100}=5\), one-sided test of \(H_0:\lambda=4\) against \(H_1:\lambda>4\) at 5 %, \(z_{\text{obs}}=\frac{5-4}{\sqrt{4/100}}=5>1.64\): reject.

Two-sided Wald interval (Example 3.58's idea: plug \(\hat\lambda\) into the standard error \(\sqrt{\lambda/n}\)): \(\bar x\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\bar x/n}=5\pm1.96\cdot\sqrt{0.05}=5\pm1.96\cdot0.2236=[4.562,\,5.438]\).

One-sided bound, the partner of P4d's test (box one-sided bounds): \(5-z_{0.05}\cdot0.2236=5-1.645\cdot0.2236=4.632\). The null value 4 lies below it, matching the rejection. (The exam's hint rounds \(z_{0.05}\) to 1.64, which gives 4.633 — the same conclusion. I use the four-digit value 1.645 here and below so that the two computations in this box match.)

A subtlety. The exam's test divides by the standard error under \(H_0\), \(\sqrt{4/100}=0.2\); the Wald bound divides by the estimated one, \(\sqrt{5/100}=0.2236\). So the Wald bound is not exactly the set of values the exam's test accepts. Inverting the exam's test exactly means collecting all \(\lambda_0\) with \(\frac{5-\lambda_0}{\sqrt{\lambda_0/100}}\le1.645\); solving numerically gives \(\lambda_0\ge4.645\). Both versions lead to the same decision here.

Trap — do not put the null standard error into a confidence bound. A tempting but wrong answer here is \(5-1.645\cdot0.2=4.671\), taking the \(0.2\) from the exam's test statistic. It is wrong because \(0.2=\sqrt{4/100}\) is the standard error computed at the particular null value \(\lambda_0=4\). Definition 3.54 requires the endpoint \(L(X)\) to be a statistic — a formula in the data alone — and a formula that still contains \(\lambda_0\) is not one; it would give a different "interval" for every value you happened to test. The two honest repairs are the ones above: estimate the standard error from the data (\(\sqrt{5/100}=0.2236\), giving 4.632), or invert the test exactly and let \(\lambda_0\) appear on both sides (giving 4.645).

SoSe 2026, Problem 5 (randomized response) as a confidence interval SoSe26 · P5 my extension

What the exam gives. Answers \(Y_i\) iid \(\Ber(q)\) with \(q=q(p)=rp+\frac{1-r}2\) (P5a); \(\hat p=\frac{\bar Y_n-\frac{1-r}2}r\), unbiased, \(\Var[\hat p]=\frac{q(1-q)}{r^2n}\) (P5c). P5d: \(r=\frac12\), \(n=100\), 64 answers are 1, test of \(H_0:p\le0.6\) against \(H_1:p>0.6\): \(z_{\text{obs}}=\frac{0.64-0.55}{\sqrt{0.55\cdot0.45/100}}\approx1.81>1.64\), reject.

Wald-type interval. By the clt, \(\hat p\) is approximately normal with standard error \(\frac1r\sqrt{q(1-q)/n}\); plug in \(\hat q=\bar y_n\): \(\widehat{\mathrm{se}}=\frac{\sqrt{0.64\cdot0.36/100}}{0.5}=\frac{0.048}{0.5}=0.096\). Estimate \(\hat p=\frac{0.64-0.25}{0.5}=0.78\).

  • Two-sided 95 %: \(0.78\pm1.96\cdot0.096=[0.592,\,0.968]\). It contains 0.6.
  • One-sided 95 % lower bound: \(0.78-1.645\cdot0.096=0.622\). It lies above 0.6.

Is that a contradiction with the rejection? No. The exam's test is one-sided at 5 %; its partner is the one-sided 95 % bound (0.622 > 0.6: reject — agrees). The two-sided 95 % interval is the partner of the two-sided test at 5 %, which would not reject. The randomization costs precision, for two reasons at once. First, dividing by \(r=\frac12\) multiplies the standard error by \(\frac1r=2\). Second, the coin flip pulls \(q=rp+\frac{1-r}2\) towards \(\frac12\), where \(q(1-q)\) is largest, so the thing being multiplied is bigger too. Together: here \(\widehat{\mathrm{se}}=0.096\), while asking the question directly would give \(\sqrt{0.78\cdot0.22/100}=0.0414\) — a factor \(2.3\), not just 2. (Inverting the exam's own test statistic exactly gives the bound 0.617 instead of 0.622 — the same small null-versus-estimated standard error difference as in SoSe25 P4.)

Summary sheet

Definition

ci (Def 3.54)
random \(L(X),U(X)\) with \(\P_\theta(L(X)\le\gamma(\theta)\le U(X))\ge1-\alpha\) for all \(\theta\in\Theta\); \(1-\alpha\) = confidence level
meaning (Rem 3.55)
in repeated sampling, about \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) of the intervals contain the fixed parameter; a computed interval contains it or not — no 95 % "for this interval"
pivot
formula in data and parameter with a known distribution free of unknowns
\(z_{a}\), \(t_{\nu,a}\)
upper-\(a\) points: \(\P(Z>z_a)=a\); \(z_{0.05}=1.645\), \(z_{0.025}=1.96\), \(z_{0.005}=2.576\); \(t_{9,0.025}=2.262\)

Standard intervals

normal, σ known (3.56)
\(\bar X_n\pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\) — exact
normal, σ unknown (3.57)
\(\bar X_n\pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\frac{S_n}{\sqrt n}\) — exact; \(T\sim t_{n-1}\), heavier tails
proportion (3.58)
Wald: \(\hat p\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}\) — approximate (clt); bad for small \(n\) or \(p\) near 0, 1
cdf value (WiSe25 P5d)
\(\hat F_n(t)\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\hat F_n(t)(1-\hat F_n(t))/n}\)
sample size
\(n\ge(z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/E)^2\); width \(\propto1/\sqrt n\) ("\(\propto\)" = "is proportional to": the width is a fixed multiple of \(1/\sqrt n\), so quadrupling \(n\) halves it)
one-sided bound
\([\bar X_n-z_\alpha\sigma/\sqrt n,\infty)\) — uses \(z_\alpha\), partner of the one-sided test
non-normal pivots
uniform: \(X_{\max}/\theta\) gives \([X_{\max},X_{\max}\alpha^{-1/n}]\); exponential: \(\lambda X\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)\) gives \([-\ln(1-\frac\alpha2)/X,\,-\ln\frac\alpha2/X]\)
Chebyshev ci
guaranteed level for every \(n\), but much wider than the clt interval (WiSe25 P4, P5d)

Duality (Rem 3.59)

ci = all \(\theta_0\) not rejected by the two-sided level-\(\alpha\) test; test rejects \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) ⟺ \(\theta_0\notin\) ci. Proof: \(\{\theta\in C(X)\}=\{X\in A(\theta)\}\).

Method

Pivot → \(\P(-c\le Q\le c)=1-\alpha\) → solve for the parameter (multiply by positive, add, multiply by \(-1\) flips) → plug in data.

Traps

  • "95 % probability that μ is in [1201, 1299]" — wrong (Remark 3.55).
  • Using \(z\) instead of \(t\) when \(\sigma\) is estimated from a small sample: too narrow (coverage 0.88 at \(n=5\)).
  • Forgetting "approximate" for clt-based intervals; forgetting to define \(z_{\alpha/2}\).
  • A 95 % ci matches a two-sided test at \(\alpha=0.05\), not a one-sided one (SoSe26 P5 extension).
  • "Rejected at 5 %, so \(H_0\) has probability at most 5 %" — wrong for the same reason as Remark 3.55 (SoSe25 P1c).
  • A confidence bound uses the estimated standard error, a test may use the one under \(H_0\) (SoSe25 P4).

Exam focus

WiSe25 P5d (2 credits): a Wald interval for a probability, at the end of an estimator problem. SoSe25 P1c: the interpretation of a level, same logic as Remark 3.55. Sheet 11 shows the tests whose duals are the z and t intervals and the one-sided bound. Past exams are not a prediction.

Self-test

Section 3.5 · The last section of the script, marked there as a "philosophical interlude" (the script marks no lecture numbers after Lecture 9)

Bayesian vs. frequentist inference

Bayes'sche vs. frequentistische Inferenz

What this page covers Script §3.5, pp. 111–113

This page covers everything from Overview 3.60 to Viewpoint 3.66: the two schools of statistics (3.60), the Bayesian statistical model with its prior (3.61), the posterior obtained with Bayes' rule (3.62), Bayesian point estimators — posterior mean, posterior median and map estimate (3.63), the credible interval (3.64), how it differs from a confidence interval (3.65), and the philosophical divide together with the practical agreement of both schools for large samples (3.66).

The script frames the whole section as a "philosophical interlude" and gives no worked example. No exercise sheet and none of the three old exams asks about this section. (One exam task, WiSe25 P6b, is a discrete Bayes' rule computation; it is solved on §1.4 and read in prior/posterior language below.) So the worked examples on this page are all mine: the Beta–Bernoulli model from start to finish, the Normal–Normal model, what happens for large samples, and a table of "which interval means what".

The big picture

You find a strange coin. Is it fair? You toss it 10 times and see 7 heads. What can you say about its probability \(\theta\) (theta) of heads?

  • The frequentist answer (everything in §3.1–§3.4). \(\theta\) is a fixed number that we do not know. It is not random, so we never write "the probability that \(\theta>0.5\)". What is random is the data. We judge methods by how they behave over many imagined repetitions of the experiment: the estimate \(\hat\theta=\frac7{10}\) (the maximum likelihood estimator, §3.2), a test (§3.3), a 95 % confidence interval (§3.4) that "catches the true \(\theta\) in 95 % of repetitions".
  • The Bayesian answer (this page). Our knowledge about \(\theta\) is uncertain, and uncertainty is described by a probability distribution. Before the data we write down a prior distribution for \(\theta\) (our belief). After the data we update it with Bayes' rule to a posterior distribution. From the posterior we can read off statements like "given the data, \(\theta\) lies between 0.39 and 0.86 with probability 95 %" or "\(\P(\theta>0.5\mid\text{data})=0.87\)" (both statements use the prior \(\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)\) of the worked example below).

A tiny example with real numbers (my example). Suppose the coin can only be of two kinds: fair (\(\theta=0.5\)) or bent (\(\theta=0.8\)).
