Before tossing, you think both are equally likely: prior \(\pi(0.5)=\pi(0.8)=\frac12\). (The letter \(\pi\) is used here and throughout this page as the name of the prior function, never as the number 3.14….) You toss 10 times and see a particular sequence with 7 heads and 3 tails. The tosses are independent, so the probability of that exact sequence is a product of 7 factors \(\theta\) and 3 factors \(1-\theta\):

  • if fair: \(0.5^{7}\cdot0.5^{3}=0.5^{10}\approx0.000977\);
  • if bent: \(0.8^{7}\cdot0.2^{3}\approx0.2097\cdot0.008\approx0.001678\).

Bayes' rule (Theorem 1.70(iii), §1.4) with the two cases "fair" and "bent" as the partition gives

\[ \P(\text{bent}\mid\text{data})=\frac{0.001678\cdot\frac12}{0.000977\cdot\frac12+0.001678\cdot\frac12}=\frac{0.001678}{0.002655}\approx0.632 . \]

So the data moved your belief in "bent" from 50 % to 63 %. That is all Bayesian inference is: Bayes' rule applied to the unknown parameter. The only new difficulty on this page is that \(\theta\) usually can be any number in \([0,1]\), not just one of two values, so sums become integrals and probabilities become densities.

In words: frequentists put probability on the data and keep the parameter fixed; Bayesians put probability on the parameter too and update it with the data. With lots of data both usually end up with similar numbers, but the sentences that describe those numbers mean different things.

Primer My addition

Cross-references

Integrals: Analysis 8.1; improper integrals: Analysis 9.1; finding a maximum by setting the derivative to 0: Analysis 7.1; logarithm rules: Analysis 5.2. Densities: §1.3. Gamma and Beta functions: §1.3. Bayes' rule: §1.4. Quantiles and "mean minimises squared error, median minimises absolute error": §2.1. Mean and variance of the Beta distribution: §2.1. Likelihood: §3.1; mle: §3.2; confidence intervals: §3.4.

0. Words and symbols used on this page

  • Parameter \(\theta\) and parameter space \(\Theta\) (capital theta): the unknown number (or vector) that picks one distribution out of a family, and the set of all allowed values. Coin: \(\Theta=[0,1]\). (Definition 3.4, §3.1.)
  • Data \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\): the observed values of the random sample \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)\). Capital \(X\) is random, small \(x\) is the fixed observed outcome.
  • pmf, pdf, cdf. A pmf (probability mass function) [Zähldichte] lists \(\P(X=v)\) for each possible value \(v\) of a random variable that takes only separate values — a coin, a count. A pdf (probability density function, "density", see the bullet further down) does the same job for a random variable that can take any value in an interval. A cdf (cumulative distribution function) [Verteilungsfunktion] is \(F(c)=\P(X\le c)\), "how much probability sits at or below \(c\)".
  • iid: independent and identically distributed — the \(X_i\) do not influence each other and all follow the same distribution (Definition 1.79, §1.4).
  • Likelihood [Likelihood-Funktion] \(p(x\mid\theta)=L(\theta\mid x)\): the pmf or density of the data when the parameter is \(\theta\) (Definition 3.13, §3.1). For iid data it is the product \(\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i\mid\theta)\). Read as a function of \(\theta\) with \(x\) held fixed.
  • mle \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\): the \(\theta\) that makes \(L(\theta\mid x)\) largest (Definition 3.27, §3.2). For coin tosses with \(k\) heads in \(n\) tosses, \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=\frac kn\).
  • Confidence interval (ci) [Konfidenzintervall]: an interval \((L(X),U(X))\) computed from the random sample such that \(\P_\theta(L(X)\le\theta\le U(X))\ge1-\alpha\) for every \(\theta\) (Definition 3.54, §3.4; the script states it for a general parameter of interest \(\gamma(\theta)\), and this page only ever needs the case \(\gamma(\theta)=\theta\)). \(\alpha\) is a small number such as 0.05, and \(1-\alpha\) the confidence level.
  • \(z_{\alpha/2}\): the number with \(\P(-z_{\alpha/2}\le Z\le z_{\alpha/2})=1-\alpha\) for a standard normal \(Z\). For \(\alpha=0.05\): \(z_{0.025}\approx1.96\).
  • \(\arg\max_\theta f(\theta)\): the place \(\theta\) where \(f\) is largest (not the largest value itself).
  • Density (pdf): a function \(p\ge0\) with \(\int p=1\); probabilities are areas under it: \(\P(a\le Y\le b)=\int_a^bp(y)\,\mathrm dy\) (§1.3).
  • Mode: the place where a density (or pmf) is highest.
  • \(q\)-quantile: a point \(x_q\) with probability \(q\) at or to its left (Definition 2.20, §2.1). For the continuous distributions on this page (Beta, normal) the cdf is continuous and strictly increasing, so \(x_q\) is the unique solution of \(F(x_q)=q\). The median is the 0.5-quantile.

1. Bayes' rule, from events to densities

Discrete version (Theorem 1.70(iii), §1.4). If the cases \(B_1,B_2,\dots\) split up the whole sample space, then

\[ \P(B_i\mid A)=\frac{\P(A\mid B_i)\,\P(B_i)}{\sum_j\P(A\mid B_j)\,\P(B_j)} . \]

Read \(B_i\) as "the parameter has value \(\theta_i\)" and \(A\) as "we observed the data \(x\)". Then \(\P(B_i)\) is the prior, \(\P(A\mid B_i)\) the likelihood, and \(\P(B_i\mid A)\) the posterior.

Density version (my derivation). When \(\theta\) can be any number in an interval, we describe our belief by a density \(\pi(\theta)\). Treat the pair (parameter, data) as a random vector with joint density "prior times likelihood": \(p(x,\theta)=p(x\mid\theta)\,\pi(\theta)\). This is the continuous analogue of \(\P(A\cap B_i)=\P(A\mid B_i)\P(B_i)\) (Definition 1.69). The conditional density of \(\theta\) given the data is the joint density divided by the marginal density of the data (Definition 1.78(ii), §1.4). The marginal density of the data is obtained by integrating the joint density over \(\theta\) (the continuous analogue of the law of total probability):

\[ \pi(\theta\mid x)=\frac{p(x,\theta)}{p(x)}=\frac{p(x\mid\theta)\,\pi(\theta)}{\int_\Theta p(x\mid\vartheta)\,\pi(\vartheta)\,\mathrm d\vartheta}. \]

(\(\vartheta\) is just another name for the integration variable, so that it is not confused with the \(\theta\) on the left.) Compare the two formulas term by term: sum becomes integral, probabilities become densities. Nothing else changes.

A mixed case, and why it is still fine. In the coin example below the parameter \(\theta\) is continuous but the data \(x\) are discrete, so \(p(x\mid\theta)\) is a pmf in \(x\) and \(\pi(\theta)\) is a density in \(\theta\) — strictly speaking Definition 1.78(ii), which assumes both variables continuous, does not apply word for word. The formula above is still correct, and it is the one the script writes in Definition 3.62: for each fixed \(x\) the function \(\theta\mapsto p(x\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)\) is non-negative and, divided by its own integral \(p(x)\), integrates to 1, so it is a density in \(\theta\). Checking that this density really is "the conditional distribution of \(\theta\) given \(X=x\)" needs measure theory that this course does not develop; the script does not do it either.

2. "Proportional to", the symbol \(\propto\)

\(f(\theta)\propto g(\theta)\) means: there is a number \(c>0\) that does not depend on \(\theta\) with \(f(\theta)=c\cdot g(\theta)\) for all \(\theta\). Example: \(6\theta^2\propto\theta^2\) (here \(c=6\)).

Why this is useful. If \(f\) is a density and \(f\propto g\), then \(c\) is determined by the requirement that \(f\) integrates to 1: \(1=\int f=c\int g\), so \(c=1/\int g\). So you may throw away every factor that does not contain \(\theta\), work with the simpler \(g\) (the kernel [Kern]), and put the constant back at the end. Very often you do not even need to compute \(\int g\): if \(g\) is the kernel of a named density, the constant is that density's constant. Example: if \(f(\theta)\propto\theta^8(1-\theta)^4\) on \([0,1]\), then \(f\) must be the \(\mathrm{Beta}(9,5)\) density (box 3), because that is the only density on \([0,1]\) with this kernel.

Caution. "Does not depend on \(\theta\)" is the only condition. The factor may depend on the data \(x\) — for the posterior it always does.

3. The Beta distribution from scratch

Picture. The Beta distribution is a flexible family of densities on the interval \([0,1]\). It is the natural way to describe uncertainty about an unknown probability or proportion, because its values always lie between 0 and 1.

Definition (the script gives it as Example 1.61(vii), §1.3). For \(\alpha,\beta>0\), the \(\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)\) density is

\[ p(\theta)=\frac{\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)}\quad\text{for }\theta\in[0,1],\qquad p(\theta)=0\text{ otherwise}. \]

The Beta function \(B(\alpha,\beta)=\int_0^1t^{\alpha-1}(1-t)^{\beta-1}\,\mathrm dt=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}\) (Definition 1.60, §1.3) is exactly the area under the numerator, so dividing by it makes the total area 1. \(\Gamma\) is the Gamma function, with \(\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!\) for whole numbers \(n\ge1\) and \(\Gamma(s+1)=s\,\Gamma(s)\).

Shapes. \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\): \(p(\theta)=1\), the uniform distribution ("every \(\theta\) equally plausible"). \(\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)=6\theta(1-\theta)\): a hump centred at \(\frac12\), zero at the ends. Larger \(\alpha\) pushes mass towards 1, larger \(\beta\) towards 0; larger \(\alpha+\beta\) makes the hump narrower.

Numbers (mine; the mean and variance are also on §2.1). For \(Y\sim\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)\):

  • Mean \(\E[Y]=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\). Proof: \(\E[Y]=\int_0^1\theta\frac{\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)}\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{B(\alpha+1,\beta)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}\), since the integral is the Beta function with \(\alpha+1\) in place of \(\alpha\). Write both with Gamma functions: \(\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+1)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta+1)}\cdot\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}\). Use \(\Gamma(\alpha+1)=\alpha\Gamma(\alpha)\) and \(\Gamma(\alpha+\beta+1)=(\alpha+\beta)\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)\) and cancel: \(\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\).
  • Variance \(\Var[Y]=\frac{\alpha\beta}{(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)}\) (same trick with \(B(\alpha+2,\beta)\)).
  • Mode (for \(\alpha,\beta>1\)) \(\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha+\beta-2}\). Proof: maximise the logarithm of the density, \((\alpha-1)\ln\theta+(\beta-1)\ln(1-\theta)-\ln B(\alpha,\beta)\) (the logarithm is increasing, so it has its maximum at the same place, Analysis 5.2). Derivative: \(\frac{\alpha-1}\theta-\frac{\beta-1}{1-\theta}=0\). Multiply by \(\theta(1-\theta)\): \((\alpha-1)(1-\theta)=(\beta-1)\theta\), so \(\alpha-1=\theta(\alpha+\beta-2)\). If \(\alpha\le1\) or \(\beta\le1\), this interior formula does not apply and the density is highest at an end point instead: at \(\theta=0\) when \(\alpha\le1\) and \(\beta\ge1\), at \(\theta=1\) when \(\alpha\ge1\) and \(\beta\le1\), at both ends when \(\alpha<1\) and \(\beta<1\). The single exception is \(\alpha=\beta=1\), where the density is flat and every point is a maximum.
  • Quantiles and median: there is no closed formula. One computes them numerically (software, or the widgets below). Exams would have to give them to you.

Two schools of thought

Overview 3.60 two schools of thought Script 3.60

The methods discussed so far — mle, hypothesis testing with confidence levels or p-values, and confidence intervals — belong to the frequentist school of statistics [frequentistische Statistik]. This school treats parameters as fixed, unknown constants and defines probability as the long-run frequency of outcomes in (hypothetical) repeated experiments.

Bayesian inference [Bayes'sche Inferenz] offers an alternative perspective. It treats parameters as random variables about which we can have beliefs that are updated with data.

What "long-run frequency" means, concretely: "the probability of heads is 0.5" means "if you toss this coin again and again, the fraction of heads approaches 0.5" — exactly what the law of large numbers (§2.4) guarantees. On that reading a fixed number like \(\theta\) cannot have a probability: it is not the outcome of a repeatable experiment. The Bayesian reading of probability as "degree of belief" allows it. Both readings obey the same axioms of a probability measure (§1.1), so all the mathematics of Chapters 1–2 applies to both. The script already discussed these interpretations in an earlier philosophical interlude, Remark 1.30 (§1.1).

The Bayesian model: prior and posterior

Definition 3.61 Bayesian statistical model Script 3.61

A (parametric) Bayesian statistical model has two constituents.

  1. A likelihood \(p(x\mid\theta)\), which is the same as in the frequentist model. It describes the data-generating process for a given parameter \(\theta\).
  2. A prior distribution [Priori-Verteilung, A-priori-Verteilung] \(\pi(\theta)\), which represents our belief about the parameter \(\theta\) before observing the data. It is a probability distribution over the parameter space \(\Theta\).

Each part explained (mine).

  • (i) is nothing new: it is the statistical model of Definition 3.4 (a family of distributions \(\P_\theta\)), written through its pmf or density. The frequentist stops here.
  • (ii) is the new ingredient. \(\pi\) is a pmf (if \(\Theta\) is finite or countable) or a density (if \(\Theta\) is an interval). The letter \(\pi\) here is a function name, not the number 3.14….
  • Together, (i) and (ii) define one joint distribution of the pair (parameter, data): first draw \(\theta\) from \(\pi\), then draw the data from \(p(\cdot\mid\theta)\). That is why Bayes' rule becomes available.

Example (mine). Coin tosses \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid \(\Ber(\theta)\), \(\Theta=[0,1]\). (i) \(p(x\mid\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n\theta^{x_i}(1-\theta)^{1-x_i}\). (ii) Prior \(\pi=\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)\), i.e. \(\pi(\theta)=6\theta(1-\theta)\): "the coin is probably not extremely biased".

Where does a prior come from? (mine) From earlier studies ("similar coins had \(\theta\) between 0.4 and 0.6"), from expert knowledge, or from a deliberate choice to say as little as possible — a non-informative (flat, vague) prior such as \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\), the uniform density. The choice of prior is the most criticised part of Bayesian statistics: two people with different priors get different posteriors from the same data. The widget "prior washes out" below shows how much that matters.

Definition 3.62 posterior distribution Script 3.62

Using Bayes' rule, the prior belief is updated with the observed data \(x\) to form the posterior distribution [Posteriori-Verteilung, A-posteriori-Verteilung] \(\pi(\theta\mid x)\):

\[ \pi(\theta\mid x)=\frac{p(x\mid\theta)\,\pi(\theta)}{p(x)}=\frac{\text{likelihood}\times\text{prior}}{\text{evidence}} . \]

The denominator \(p(x)=\int_\Theta p(x\mid\theta)\,\pi(\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta\) is the marginal likelihood (the evidence) of the data and acts as a normalising constant. The posterior \(\pi(\theta\mid x)\) encapsulates all our knowledge about \(\theta\) after seeing the data. We often work with the unnormalised posterior

\[ \pi(\theta\mid x)\propto p(x\mid\theta)\,\pi(\theta). \]

Each part explained (mine).

  • The formula is Bayes' rule for densities (primer box 1). If \(\Theta\) is discrete, the integral is a sum.
  • Evidence \(p(x)\): "how probable were these data, averaged over all parameter values, weighted by the prior". It is one number (for fixed data) and does not contain \(\theta\).
  • \(\propto\) (primer box 2): because \(p(x)\) does not contain \(\theta\), the posterior is "likelihood times prior, rescaled to area 1". In practice you compute the product, drop every factor without \(\theta\), recognise the kernel, and read off the posterior.
  • "All our knowledge": in the Bayesian view, every answer — an estimate, an interval, the probability of a hypothesis — is computed from the posterior. Definitions 3.63 and 3.64 are two examples.

Note the change of roles compared to Remark 3.14(iii) (§3.1): there the script stresses that the likelihood \(\theta\mapsto L(\theta\mid x)\) is not a density in \(\theta\). Multiplying it by a prior and normalising turns it into one — the posterior.

Worked example: the Beta–Bernoulli model, step by step My example

Setup. Data \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\) from iid \(\Ber(\theta)\) tosses (1 = heads). Let \(k=x_1+\dots+x_n\) be the number of heads. Prior \(\theta\sim\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)\) with numbers \(a,b>0\) you choose.

Step 1 — likelihood. One toss has pmf \(p(x_i\mid\theta)=\theta^{x_i}(1-\theta)^{1-x_i}\) (this is \(\theta\) if \(x_i=1\) and \(1-\theta\) if \(x_i=0\)). Independence lets us multiply (§1.4), and the exponents add up (power rule \(\theta^u\theta^v=\theta^{u+v}\)):

\[ p(x\mid\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n\theta^{x_i}(1-\theta)^{1-x_i}=\theta^{\sum x_i}(1-\theta)^{\sum(1-x_i)}=\theta^{k}(1-\theta)^{n-k}. \]

Step 2 — prior. \(\pi(\theta)=\frac{1}{B(a,b)}\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}\) on \([0,1]\).

Step 3 — multiply. Again by the power rule,

\[ p(x\mid\theta)\,\pi(\theta)=\frac1{B(a,b)}\,\theta^{a+k-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-k-1}. \]

Step 4 — drop constants. \(\frac1{B(a,b)}\) does not contain \(\theta\), so

\[ \pi(\theta\mid x)\propto\theta^{(a+k)-1}(1-\theta)^{(b+n-k)-1}\qquad(\theta\in[0,1]). \]

Step 5 — recognise the kernel. This is the kernel of \(\mathrm{Beta}(a+k,\,b+n-k)\) (primer box 3 with \(\alpha=a+k\), \(\beta=b+n-k\)). By primer box 2 the posterior is that density:

\[ \boxed{\;\theta\mid x\ \sim\ \mathrm{Beta}(a+k,\;b+n-k)\;} \]

Step 6 (optional) — the evidence. The integral of the product in step 3 is \(p(x)=\frac{1}{B(a,b)}\int_0^1\theta^{a+k-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-k-1}\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{B(a+k,\,b+n-k)}{B(a,b)}\). Dividing the product by it gives exactly the \(\mathrm{Beta}(a+k,b+n-k)\) density, as the shortcut predicted.

Numbers. Prior \(\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)\), data \(k=7\) heads in \(n=10\) tosses. Posterior \(\mathrm{Beta}(2+7,\;2+3)=\mathrm{Beta}(9,5)\). Evidence \(p(x)=B(9,5)/B(2,2)\approx0.000932\). A useful by-product: \(\P(\theta>0.5\mid x)=\int_{0.5}^1\pi(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm d\theta\approx0.867\) (computed numerically) — a sentence that has no meaning in frequentist statistics.

Reading the result. The prior's \(a\) and \(b\) behave like heads and tails you had "already seen" before the experiment: the update just adds the real heads to \(a\) and the real tails to \(b\). \(a+b\) is the prior sample size — how many tosses the prior belief is worth. A prior whose posterior belongs to the same family as the prior is called conjugate [konjugiert]: the Beta family is conjugate for Bernoulli (and binomial) data.

Two more facts. (1) Beta–Binomial. Often only the count is reported: \(K\sim\Bin(n,\theta)\), the number of heads in \(n\) tosses, with pmf \(\P(K=k\mid\theta)=\binom nk\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}\) (\(\binom nk\) = number of ways to choose which \(k\) of the \(n\) tosses are heads). Using this as the likelihood instead of the probability of the exact sequence gives the same posterior \(\mathrm{Beta}(a+k,b+n-k)\): \(\binom nk\) has no \(\theta\) and is dropped in step 4 like \(\frac1{B(a,b)}\). Only the evidence changes, by the factor \(\binom nk\). (That is also why the orange "likelihood" curve in the widget below is the same for both readings: rescaled to area 1, the two differ by nothing.) (2) Updating toss by toss (each posterior becomes the prior for the next toss) gives the same final posterior as updating once with all the data: each toss just adds 1 to \(a\) or to \(b\) — the + heads and + tails buttons of the widget below do exactly this, and you can watch the posterior agree with the one-shot update.

In words: with a Beta prior and coin-toss data, Bayesian updating is counting: add the heads to \(a\), add the tails to \(b\).

Bayesian point estimators

Idea first. The posterior is a whole distribution. Sometimes you must report one number. Which single number summarises a distribution best depends on how you measure the cost of being wrong — exactly the question of Remark 2.22(v) on §2.1, now applied to the posterior.

Definition 3.63 Bayesian point estimators Script 3.63

Point estimates for \(\theta\) can be derived from the posterior distribution in different ways. Common choices:

  • Posterior mean [Posteriori-Erwartungswert] \(\hat\theta_{\text{mean}}=\E[\theta\mid x]=\int\theta\,\pi(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm d\theta\). It minimises the posterior expected squared error.
  • Posterior median \(\hat\theta_{\text{med}}\): the value with \(\P(\theta\le\hat\theta_{\text{med}}\mid x)=0.5\). It minimises the posterior expected absolute error.
  • Maximum a posteriori (map) estimate \(\hat\theta_{\text{map}}=\arg\max_\theta\pi(\theta\mid x)=\arg\max_\theta p(x\mid\theta)\,\pi(\theta)\), the mode of the posterior. This is perhaps the most common choice of point estimator derived from Bayesian inference, and it is akin to the mle when no prior is considered.

Each part explained (mine).

  • \(\E[\theta\mid x]\) is the ordinary expected value (§2.1) of a random variable whose density is the posterior.
  • "Posterior expected squared error" of a guess \(c\) means \(\E[(\theta-c)^2\mid x]=\int(\theta-c)^2\pi(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm d\theta\): how far off \(c\) is on average, measured by the square and averaged with the posterior as weight. Similarly the absolute error \(\E[|\theta-c|\mid x]\).
  • Why the two \(\arg\max\) in the map line agree: \(\pi(\theta\mid x)=p(x\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)/p(x)\), and dividing by the positive constant \(p(x)\) does not move the place of the maximum. So the map never needs the evidence.
Why the mean and the median minimise these errors §3.5 states it without proof; the argument is the script's own from Remark 2.22(v), retold

This is Remark 2.22(v) (§2.1) applied to a random variable \(Y\) that has the posterior as its distribution. For the squared error, expand and use linearity of expectation:

\[ \E[(Y-c)^2]=\E\bigl[\bigl((Y-\E Y)+(\E Y-c)\bigr)^2\bigr]=\Var[Y]+2(\E Y-c)\underbrace{\E[Y-\E Y]}_{=0}+(\E Y-c)^2=\Var[Y]+(\E Y-c)^2 . \]

The first term does not depend on \(c\); the second is \(\ge0\) and equals 0 exactly for \(c=\E Y\). So \(c=\E[\theta\mid x]\) is the unique minimiser, and the smallest possible value is the posterior variance.

For the absolute error, with posterior cdf \(F\): \(g(c)=\E|Y-c|=\int_{-\infty}^c(c-t)\pi(t\mid x)\,\mathrm dt+\int_c^\infty(t-c)\pi(t\mid x)\,\mathrm dt\). Differentiate in \(c\) with the Leibniz integral rule (the script uses the same rule in Remark 2.22(v)): the derivative of \(\int_{-\infty}^c h(c,t)\,\mathrm dt\) is "integrand at the upper limit, \(h(c,c)\)" plus "\(\int_{-\infty}^c\frac{\partial h}{\partial c}\,\mathrm dt\)". Here \(h(c,t)=(c-t)\pi(t\mid x)\), so \(h(c,c)=0\) and \(\frac{\partial h}{\partial c}=\pi(t\mid x)\): the first integral has derivative \(\int_{-\infty}^c\pi(t\mid x)\,\mathrm dt=F(c)\). In the same way the second has derivative \(-\int_c^\infty\pi(t\mid x)\,\mathrm dt=-(1-F(c))\). Together \(g'(c)=F(c)-(1-F(c))=2F(c)-1\). This is negative while \(F(c)<\frac12\) and positive once \(F(c)>\frac12\), so \(g\) is smallest where \(F(c)=\frac12\): at the median. ∎

Worked example: the three estimators for the Beta–Bernoulli model My example

Posterior \(\mathrm{Beta}(a+k,\,b+n-k)\). Insert \(\alpha=a+k\), \(\beta=b+n-k\) (so \(\alpha+\beta=a+b+n\)) into primer box 3:

  • Posterior mean \(\displaystyle\hat\theta_{\text{mean}}=\frac{a+k}{a+b+n}\).
  • map (if \(a+k>1\) and \(b+n-k>1\)) \(\displaystyle\hat\theta_{\text{map}}=\frac{a+k-1}{a+b+n-2}\).
  • Posterior median: no closed formula; computed numerically.

The posterior mean is a weighted average. Split the fraction into two parts and multiply and divide each by a suitable number:

\[ \frac{a+k}{a+b+n}=\frac{a}{a+b+n}+\frac{k}{a+b+n}=\underbrace{\frac{a+b}{a+b+n}}_{w_{\text{prior}}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{a}{a+b}}_{\text{prior mean}}+\underbrace{\frac{n}{a+b+n}}_{w_{\text{data}}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac kn}_{\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}} . \]

(Check: in the first product \(a+b\) cancels and leaves \(\frac a{a+b+n}\); in the second \(n\) cancels and leaves \(\frac k{a+b+n}\).) The weights are positive and add up to \(\frac{a+b+n}{a+b+n}=1\). So the posterior mean lies between the prior mean and the mle, and the data get the weight \(\frac{n}{a+b+n}\): the more data, the closer to the mle. Bayesian estimates are "shrunk" towards the prior mean.

Numbers (prior \(\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)\), 7 heads in 10, posterior \(\mathrm{Beta}(9,5)\)):

quantityformulavalue
prior mean\(\frac{2}{4}\)0.5
mle\(\frac{7}{10}\)0.7
weight of the data\(\frac{10}{14}\)0.714
posterior mean\(\frac{9}{14}=0.286\cdot0.5+0.714\cdot0.7\)0.643
posterior mediannumerical0.650
map\(\frac{8}{12}\)0.667

map with a flat prior equals the mle (the connection to §3.2). Take the uniform prior \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\), \(\pi(\theta)=1\) on \([0,1]\). Then \(p(x\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)=p(x\mid\theta)=L(\theta\mid x)\), so \(\arg\max_\theta p(x\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)=\arg\max_\theta L(\theta\mid x)=\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\). The formula agrees: \(\frac{1+k-1}{2+n-2}=\frac kn\). This holds in general whenever the prior is constant on \(\Theta\): a constant factor does not move the maximum. That is what the script means by "akin to the mle when not considering a prior". With a non-flat prior, the map maximises \(\ln L(\theta\mid x)+\ln\pi(\theta)\) (logarithm rule \(\ln(uv)=\ln u+\ln v\)): the log-likelihood plus a "penalty" that pulls towards values the prior likes.

With the flat prior, the posterior mean is \(\frac{k+1}{n+2}\) (Laplace's "rule of succession"): after 3 heads in 3 tosses the mle says \(\theta=1\) ("tails is impossible"), the posterior mean says \(\frac45\). The prior protects against over-confident estimates from very little data.

Credible intervals

Definition 3.64 credible interval Script 3.64

A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) credible interval [Glaubwürdigkeitsintervall, Kredibilitätsintervall] for a parameter \(\theta\) is an interval \((l,u)\) such that

\[ \P(l\le\theta\le u\mid x)=\int_l^u\pi(\theta\mid x)\,\mathrm d\theta=1-\alpha . \]

Unlike frequentist confidence intervals, the boundaries \(l,u\) are fixed numbers, and we now indeed interpret the credible interval as the range in which the true parameter lies with probability \(1-\alpha\), given the data and the model. A common choice is the equal-tailed interval, whose lower and upper bounds are the \(\frac\alpha2\) and \(1-\frac\alpha2\) quantiles of the posterior distribution. This is in line with the posterior representing our final beliefs about the true parameter value.

Each part explained (mine).

  • The probability is computed with the posterior: it is the area under \(\pi(\cdot\mid x)\) between \(l\) and \(u\). The data \(x\) are fixed (already observed); \(\theta\) is the random quantity.
  • Many intervals have posterior probability \(1-\alpha\) (slide a window along the density). "Equal-tailed" picks the one that leaves \(\frac\alpha2\) of the posterior on each side: \(l\) is the \(\frac\alpha2\)-quantile, \(u\) the \((1-\frac\alpha2)\)-quantile. (Another common choice, not in the script, is the highest posterior density interval, the shortest one.)
  • The script's "ture" is a typo for "true".

Worked example: 95 % credible interval versus the Wald confidence interval My example

Credible interval. Posterior \(\mathrm{Beta}(9,5)\), \(\alpha=0.05\). The 0.025- and 0.975-quantiles of \(\mathrm{Beta}(9,5)\) (computed numerically) are 0.386 and 0.861. So

\[ \P(0.386\le\theta\le0.861\mid x)=0.95 . \]

Wald confidence interval (Example 3.58, §3.4) for the same data: \(\hat p=\frac7{10}=0.7\), standard error \(\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}=\sqrt{0.7\cdot0.3/10}=\sqrt{0.021}\approx0.145\), so

\[ \hat p\pm z_{0.025}\sqrt{\tfrac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}n}=0.7\pm1.96\cdot0.145=0.7\pm0.284=(0.416,\;0.984). \]

Comparison.

  • The credible interval is pulled towards \(\frac12\) by the prior (and by the skewness of the posterior — it is not symmetric: \(\mathrm{Beta}(9,5)\) has a longer tail towards 0 than towards 1, which is why its mean 0.643 sits below its peak 0.667); the Wald interval is symmetric around the mle 0.7 and reaches almost to 1.
  • With the flat prior \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\) the posterior is \(\mathrm{Beta}(8,4)\) and the credible interval is \((0.390,\,0.891)\): still not equal to the Wald interval, because \(n=10\) is small and the Wald interval rests on a normal approximation (the central limit theorem [zentraler Grenzwertsatz], §2.4, abbreviated clt) that is poor here. The script warns about this in Example 3.58. In fact, for \(\theta=0.7\) and \(n=10\) the Wald interval covers the true value only with probability about 84 % instead of 95 % (my exact computation by summing binomial probabilities).
  • With more data they agree: for 70 heads in 100 tosses, credible (prior \(\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)\)) \((0.601,\,0.777)\), Wald \((0.610,\,0.790)\); for 700 in 1000: \((0.670,\,0.727)\) versus \((0.672,\,0.728)\).

In words: the credible interval is "cut off 2.5 % of the posterior on each side". For small samples it can differ noticeably from the confidence interval; for large samples the numbers nearly coincide — but the sentences that go with them do not (Remark 3.65).

Widget — the Beta–Bernoulli updater My addition

Choose a prior \(\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)\) and data (\(k\) heads in \(n\) tosses), or add tosses one at a time. Grey dashed: prior. Orange: likelihood, rescaled to area 1. Blue: posterior \(\mathrm{Beta}(a+k,b+n-k)\), with the 95 % credible interval shaded. Under the axis: the credible interval (blue) and the Wald confidence interval (orange).

Remark 3.65 confidence vs. credible intervals Script 3.65

The interpretation of a credible interval is direct and intuitive: "Given the data, there is a 95 % probability that the true parameter \(\theta\) lies in this specific interval." This is fundamentally different from the frequentist confidence interval, where the probability statement is about the procedure of generating intervals, not about a specific interval covering the fixed parameter. The confidence interval is a statement about the data, while the credible interval is a statement about the parameter.

The fact that it is a common pitfall to interpret frequentist confidence intervals as if they were Bayesian credible intervals often fuels arguments that we should just always use Bayesian analysis and credible intervals instead of frequentist methods.

Unpacking "a statement about the data". In Definition 3.54 the probability \(\P_\theta(L(X)\le\theta\le U(X))\) is taken over the random sample \(X\), with \(\theta\) held fixed: before the experiment, the random interval will catch \(\theta\) with probability at least 95 %. Once you plug in the observed \(x\), the interval \((L(x),U(x))\) is two fixed numbers and \(\theta\) is a fixed number, so "\(\theta\) is inside" is simply true or false — no probability is left (Remark 3.55). In Definition 3.64 the probability is taken over \(\theta\) (with the posterior), with the data held fixed. So the random object is different in the two definitions: the interval in one, the parameter in the other.

Which interval means what — a comparison table My addition

95 % confidence interval (Def. 3.54)95 % credible interval (Def. 3.64)
What is randomthe interval (its end points are functions of the random sample \(X\))the parameter \(\theta\) (described by the posterior)
What is fixedthe true \(\theta\)the observed data \(x\), and therefore \(l,u\)
The probability statement\(\P_\theta(L(X)\le\theta\le U(X))\ge0.95\) for every \(\theta\)\(\P(l\le\theta\le u\mid x)=0.95\)
"95 %" refers tothe long-run share of repetitions in which the procedure succeedsthe degree of belief in this one interval
Needs a prior?noyes — different priors give different intervals
Guaranteecoverage in repeated sampling, whatever \(\theta\) is (exact or approximate)coherence with the stated beliefs; no coverage guarantee in general
Coin, 7 heads in 10Wald: \((0.416,\,0.984)\)prior \(\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)\): \((0.386,\,0.861)\); flat prior: \((0.390,\,0.891)\)

Wrong sentence"\(\theta\) lies in \((0.416,0.984)\) with probability 95 %.""95 % of repeated experiments would give an interval containing \(\theta\)." (not guaranteed)

Widget — two meanings of "95 %" My addition

Frequentist view: the true \(\theta\) is fixed (vertical line) and each repetition of the experiment (\(n=30\) tosses) gives a new Wald interval; roughly 95 % of them catch \(\theta\) — the readout gives the exact long-run share, which is a little below 95 % because the Wald interval is only approximate. Bayesian view: the data are fixed (18 heads in 30, flat prior) and the uncertainty is about \(\theta\); the dots are 300 draws from the posterior and about 95 % of them fall inside the one fixed credible interval.

A second worked model: Normal data, Normal prior

Worked example: the posterior of a normal mean with known \(\sigma\) My example

Setup. \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) iid \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with known standard deviation \(\sigma\) and unknown mean \(\mu\) (the parameter, \(\Theta=\R\)). Prior \(\mu\sim\mathcal N(m_0,\tau^2)\): "I think \(\mu\) is about \(m_0\), give or take \(\tau\)". \(\bar x=\frac1n\sum x_i\) is the observed sample mean.

Precision [Präzision] means 1/variance. Big precision = small spread = much information. Write \(\lambda_0=\frac1{\tau^2}\) (precision of the prior) and \(\lambda_n=\frac n{\sigma^2}\) (precision of the data: the sample mean has variance \(\frac{\sigma^2}n\)).

Step 1 — likelihood as a function of \(\mu\). The normal density is \(\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(x_i-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\). Multiply over \(i\) (independence) and use \(e^ue^v=e^{u+v}\): \(p(x\mid\mu)\propto\exp\bigl(-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2\bigr)\). Now split each term as \(x_i-\mu=(x_i-\bar x)+(\bar x-\mu)\) and expand the square:

\[ \sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2+2(\bar x-\mu)\underbrace{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)}_{=\,n\bar x-n\bar x\,=\,0}+n(\bar x-\mu)^2 . \]

The first sum does not contain \(\mu\), so its factor \(e^{-\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\) is a constant and can be dropped: \(p(x\mid\mu)\propto\exp\bigl(-\frac{\lambda_n}2(\mu-\bar x)^2\bigr)\).

Step 2 — times the prior. \(\pi(\mu)\propto\exp\bigl(-\frac{\lambda_0}2(\mu-m_0)^2\bigr)\). The product has exponent \(-\frac12\bigl[\lambda_0(\mu-m_0)^2+\lambda_n(\mu-\bar x)^2\bigr]\).

Step 3 — complete the square. Expand: \(\lambda_0(\mu^2-2\mu m_0+m_0^2)+\lambda_n(\mu^2-2\mu\bar x+\bar x^2)=(\lambda_0+\lambda_n)\mu^2-2(\lambda_0m_0+\lambda_n\bar x)\mu+\text{const}\). With \(\lambda_1:=\lambda_0+\lambda_n\) and \(m_1:=\frac{\lambda_0m_0+\lambda_n\bar x}{\lambda_1}\) this equals \(\lambda_1(\mu-m_1)^2+\text{const}\) (expand \(\lambda_1(\mu-m_1)^2=\lambda_1\mu^2-2\lambda_1m_1\mu+\lambda_1m_1^2\) and compare the \(\mu^2\) and \(\mu\) terms). The constants drop out under \(\propto\):

\[ \pi(\mu\mid x)\propto\exp\Bigl(-\frac{\lambda_1}2(\mu-m_1)^2\Bigr),\qquad\text{so}\qquad \boxed{\;\mu\mid x\sim\mathcal N\Bigl(m_1,\ \frac1{\lambda_0+\lambda_n}\Bigr)\;} \]

because this is the kernel of the normal density with mean \(m_1\) and variance \(1/\lambda_1\).

Reading the result.

  • Posterior mean = precision-weighted average: \(m_1=\frac{\lambda_0}{\lambda_0+\lambda_n}m_0+\frac{\lambda_n}{\lambda_0+\lambda_n}\bar x\). Whoever is more precise gets more weight. It is also the posterior median and the map (a normal density is symmetric with its peak at the mean).
  • Precisions add: \(\lambda_1=\lambda_0+\lambda_n\). The posterior is always narrower than both the prior and the data alone.
  • 95 % equal-tailed credible interval: \(m_1\pm1.96/\sqrt{\lambda_1}\).

Numbers. Heights in cm, \(\sigma=8\). Prior \(\mathcal N(170,10^2)\), so \(\lambda_0=\frac1{100}=0.01\). Data: \(n=4\) people with \(\bar x=178\), so \(\lambda_4=\frac4{64}=0.0625\).

  • Weights: prior \(\frac{0.01}{0.0725}\approx0.138\), data \(\frac{0.0625}{0.0725}\approx0.862\).
  • Posterior mean \(0.138\cdot170+0.862\cdot178\approx176.9\); posterior variance \(\frac1{0.0725}\approx13.79\), so the posterior standard deviation (sd, the square root of the variance) is \(\sqrt{13.79}\approx3.71\).
  • 95 % credible interval \(176.9\pm1.96\cdot3.71=(169.6,\;184.2)\). Frequentist ci (Example 3.56, §3.4): \(178\pm1.96\cdot\frac8{\sqrt4}=(170.2,\;185.8)\).
  • With \(n=16\) (same \(\bar x\)): data weight 0.962, credible \((173.8,181.5)\) vs. ci \((174.1,181.9)\). With \(n=100\): data weight 0.994, credible \((176.4,179.5)\) vs. ci \((176.4,179.6)\).

In words: for normal data and a normal prior, the posterior is normal; its centre is a weighted average of prior guess and sample mean, with weights proportional to how precise each is.

Widget — Normal prior, normal data My addition

\(\sigma=8\) is known. Grey dashed: prior \(\mathcal N(m_0,\tau^2)\). Orange: likelihood of \(\mu\), i.e. the \(\mathcal N(\bar x,\sigma^2/n)\) curve. Blue: posterior. The bar on top shows the weights of prior and data in the posterior mean.

The philosophical divide and the practical convergence

Viewpoint 3.66 the philosophical divide and practical convergence Script 3.66

The core philosophical difference lies in the definition of probability and the nature of parameters.

  • Frequentists view parameters as fixed constants and probability as a long-run frequency.
  • Bayesians view parameters as random variables representing states of knowledge, and probability as a degree of belief.

In practice, for large sample sizes and under non-informative priors, Bayesian and frequentist results are often numerically similar. For example, the credible interval for a normal mean with a flat prior is identical to the frequentist confidence interval. However, the interpretations remain distinct. The choice between approaches often depends on the specific problem, the prior knowledge available, and the desired interpretation of the results.

Specifically, frequentist inference typically has the goal of building methods with frequency guarantees (in repeated sampling), whereas Bayesian inference aims at analysing degrees of belief. The script points to a stackexchange answer that formulates this divide well, and to a paper on common fallacies around confidence intervals (the links are not visible in the text version of the script; a well-known paper on exactly this topic is Morey et al. 2016, "The fallacy of placing confidence in confidence intervals" — my guess, not confirmed by the script).

Proof of the script's example: flat prior ⟹ credible interval = confidence interval My proof

Normal data with known \(\sigma\), as in the Normal–Normal example above. "Flat prior" means \(\pi(\mu)=\text{const}\) on all of \(\R\). Then the posterior is proportional to the likelihood alone. By step 1 of the example, \(\pi(\mu\mid x)\propto\exp\bigl(-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}(\mu-\bar x)^2\bigr)\), the kernel of \(\mathcal N(\bar x,\sigma^2/n)\). (Equivalently: let \(\tau\to\infty\) in the example; then \(\lambda_0=1/\tau^2\to0\), \(m_1\to\bar x\) and \(1/\lambda_1\to\sigma^2/n\).)

The equal-tailed \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) credible interval of \(\mathcal N(\bar x,\sigma^2/n)\) is \(\bar x\pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac\sigma{\sqrt n}\) (standardise: the quantiles of \(\mathcal N(m,s^2)\) are \(m\) plus \(s\) times the standard normal quantiles). That is exactly the ci of Example 3.56. ∎

A subtlety the script skips. A constant function on \(\R\) has infinite area, so a "flat prior" on \(\R\) is not a probability distribution — it violates Definition 3.61(ii). Such improper priors are nevertheless used, because the posterior (likelihood times constant, normalised) is a proper density. On a bounded parameter space such as \([0,1]\), the flat prior \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\) is a genuine distribution.

Why the prior "washes out" for large \(n\). In both worked models the weight of the data is \(\frac{n}{a+b+n}\) (Beta–Bernoulli) or \(\frac{n/\sigma^2}{1/\tau^2+n/\sigma^2}\) (Normal–Normal). Both tend to 1 as \(n\to\infty\), for every fixed prior. The posterior variance shrinks like \(\frac1n\) — for the Beta posterior, \(\Var=\frac{\alpha\beta}{(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)}\approx\frac{\hat\theta(1-\hat\theta)}{n}\) — which is exactly the squared standard error that the frequentist Wald interval uses. So posterior mean \(\approx\) mle and posterior sd \(\approx\) standard error, and credible and confidence intervals nearly coincide. The general version of this fact is the Bernstein–von Mises theorem (beyond this course). Two caveats: a prior that gives probability 0 to the true value can never recover (the posterior is 0 wherever the prior is 0), and for small \(n\) the prior matters a lot.

In words: the two schools disagree on what probability is, not on arithmetic; with a lot of data and a mild prior they produce nearly the same numbers, which they then describe in different sentences.

Widget — the prior washes out My addition

Three people with very different priors watch the same seeded sequence of tosses of a coin with true \(\theta\). Flat: \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\). Optimist: \(\mathrm{Beta}(20,5)\), prior mean \(\frac{20}{25}=0.8\). Pessimist: \(\mathrm{Beta}(2,20)\), prior mean \(\frac{2}{22}\approx0.09\). As \(n\) grows, their posteriors merge around the truth.

Further reading from the script's bibliography Script p. 114

The bibliography lists Georgii (2015, Stochastik, German), Klenke (2013, Probability Theory), Siegel (2017, Counterexamples in Probability and Statistics), Hennig–Osborne–Kersting (2022, Probabilistic Numerics) and Jaynes (2003, Probability Theory: The Logic of Science).

Which of them is relevant here is my own comment, not the script's: Jaynes is the classic book-length argument for the Bayesian view of probability as degree of belief, and Hennig–Osborne–Kersting use Bayesian reasoning for numerical computation.

Exercise-sheet tasks

No exercise sheet has a task on §3.5 (I searched all sheets, in particular the statistics Sheets 10 and 11, for priors, posteriors, Bayesian estimators and credible intervals; there are none). The closest relative is Sheet 7 Ex 4 (trout or salmon), worked on §2.1. There the words "prior probabilities" \(\P(Y=0)=\P(Y=1)=\frac12\) and "likelihood densities" \(p(x\mid Y)\) already appear, with the class label \(Y\) playing the role of the unknown parameter. The probability \(\P(Y=1\mid X=x)=\frac{2x\cdot\frac12}{(2-2x)\frac12+2x\cdot\frac12}=x\) is the posterior of the label (my reading), and "classify as salmon when this posterior exceeds \(\frac12\)", i.e. when \(x>\frac12\), is a map decision.

Old-exam tasks

None of the three old exams (WiSe 25/26, SoSe 2025, SoSe 2026) asks about priors, posteriors, Bayesian estimators or credible intervals — this includes every true/false item and every definitions item, which I checked one by one. (The only interval question, WiSe25 P5d, asks for a frequentist Wald confidence interval and is solved on §3.4.) Do not conclude from this that the topic cannot be examined — the script marks it as an interlude, but it is part of the script. The one related exam task is placed elsewhere:

WiSe 25/26, Problem 6b — Bayes on the schedule, read as a prior-to-posterior update WiSe25 · P6b · 2 credits

Setting (from part a). You beat the strong player S with probability \(p\) and the weak player W with probability \(q\), where \(0<p<q<1\); matches are independent; you win the tournament if you win two consecutive matches out of three. A fair coin decides between the schedules SWS and WSW. You are told only that you won. How probable is it that the schedule was SWS?

The full solution is on §1.4. In the language of this page: the unknown "parameter" is the schedule (SWS or WSW); the fair coin gives the prior \(\pi(\text{SWS})=\pi(\text{WSW})=\frac12\); the likelihood of the observation "won" is \(pq(2-p)\) under SWS and \(pq(2-q)\) under WSW; the posterior is

\[ \pi(\text{SWS}\mid\text{won})=\frac{pq(2-p)\cdot\frac12}{pq(2-p)\cdot\frac12+pq(2-q)\cdot\frac12}=\frac{2-p}{4-p-q}, \]

which agrees with the official answer (the evidence is \(\P(\text{won})=\frac12pq(4-p-q)\)). Since \(p<q\), the posterior exceeds \(\frac12\): winning makes the better schedule SWS more believable, so the map "estimate" of the schedule is SWS. (my reading; the official solution is correct)

Summary sheet

The two schools (Overview 3.60, Viewpoint 3.66)

frequentist
\(\theta\) fixed unknown constant; probability = long-run frequency; methods judged by guarantees over repeated sampling (mle, tests, cis)
Bayesian
\(\theta\) random, describing knowledge; probability = degree of belief; everything is read off the posterior

Definitions

model (3.61)
likelihood \(p(x\mid\theta)\) + prior \(\pi(\theta)\) on \(\Theta\)
posterior (3.62)
\(\pi(\theta\mid x)=\frac{p(x\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)}{p(x)}\propto p(x\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)\); evidence \(p(x)=\int_\Theta p(x\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta\)
posterior mean (3.63)
\(\E[\theta\mid x]\); minimises posterior expected squared error
posterior median
\(\P(\theta\le\hat\theta_{\text{med}}\mid x)=0.5\); minimises posterior expected absolute error
map
\(\arg\max_\theta p(x\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)\), the posterior mode; flat prior ⟹ map = mle
credible interval (3.64)
\(\P(l\le\theta\le u\mid x)=1-\alpha\); equal-tailed: \(\frac\alpha2\)- and \((1-\frac\alpha2)\)-quantiles of the posterior

Formulas (my worked models)

Beta–Bernoulli
prior \(\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)\), \(k\) heads in \(n\): posterior \(\mathrm{Beta}(a+k,b+n-k)\); mean \(\frac{a+k}{a+b+n}=\frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\cdot\frac a{a+b}+\frac n{a+b+n}\cdot\frac kn\); map \(\frac{a+k-1}{a+b+n-2}\)
Normal–Normal
prior \(\mathcal N(m_0,\tau^2)\), \(\sigma\) known: posterior \(\mathcal N\bigl(\frac{\lambda_0m_0+\lambda_n\bar x}{\lambda_0+\lambda_n},\frac1{\lambda_0+\lambda_n}\bigr)\), \(\lambda_0=\frac1{\tau^2}\), \(\lambda_n=\frac n{\sigma^2}\)
flat prior, normal mean
credible interval \(=\bar x\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n=\) ci of Example 3.56

Methods

  • Posterior: multiply likelihood and prior, drop every factor without \(\theta\), recognise the kernel.
  • Large \(n\): data weight \(\to1\), posterior mean \(\to\) mle, credible interval \(\approx\) confidence interval.

Traps

  • "The true \(\theta\) lies in this 95 % confidence interval with probability 95 %" is wrong (Remark 3.55, 3.65).
  • The likelihood is not a density in \(\theta\); the posterior is.
  • The evidence \(p(x)\) does not depend on \(\theta\) — it is never needed for the map.

Exam focus

No old exam or sheet asks about §3.5. If it is examined, the natural questions are the definitions (3.61–3.64), the difference between confidence and credible intervals (3.65), and a conjugate update such as Beta–Bernoulli.

How the exam is built WiSe 25/26 · SoSe 2025 · SoSe 2026 cover pages

The format, from the three cover pages. All three papers are written in 120 minutes. The permitted aids [Hilfsmittel] are printed identically on all three: one single sheet of A4 paper with handwritten notes on both sides, and one analogue dictionary English ↔ native language without notes. Nothing else. No formula sheet is handed out, no calculator is allowed, and no statistical tables (no table of \(\Phi\), no table of quantiles) are supplied. Writing in red or green, or in pencil, is forbidden; electronic devices go into the bag; detaching pages is forbidden.

One more sentence is printed on all three: "Answers are only accepted if the solution approach is documented. Give a reason for each answer unless explicitly stated otherwise in the respective subproblem." In the three papers so far, that exception was used exactly once — SoSe 2026 Problem 1, which says "No justification is required".

A word on the naming. The file called "WiSe25" is the retake of the winter-semester 2025/26 run, written on 2 October 2025. Chronologically it is the second of the three, sitting between SoSe 2025 and SoSe 2026. This guide calls it WiSe 25/26 throughout.

Three habits hold in all three papers.

  1. The paper opens with a true/false block (Problem 1 every time).
  2. Somewhere on the paper you are asked to state a named result with all its assumptions, worth 3 to 6 credits of pure recall.
  3. The paper closes with a long applied story problem worth 10 to 13 credits, chaining three to five subchapters of the script.

And here is where the three papers disagree — honestly.

  • Position 2. Twice "Definitions" (6 credits, two recall parts); once (SoSe 2026) a second true/false block worth 12 credits, with the recall moved to Problem 3a.
  • Position 3. Twice a block literally titled "Density computations" (11 and 9 credits); once (SoSe 2026) Jensen's inequality for 5 credits — and that paper has no density block anywhere. That is a real disagreement, not noise.
  • Position 6. Exists once, on the retake only ("Strategic tennis matches", 10 credits). It is also the only place inclusion–exclusion (Theorem 1.22) has ever appeared.
  • The true/false format. Twice 4 items × 3 credits with justification; once 5 items × 1 credit with no justification plus a separate justified block.
  • The credit total fell 59 → 51 → 44. Two steps down is a direction, not a law.

The standing warning

Three papers is a tiny sample: two endterms and one retake, and the retake looked visibly different from its own endterm — different problem count, different credit total, different topic mix. Everything on this page is "what has been asked", never "what will be asked". Nothing here licenses skipping a topic. A topic that has never appeared in three papers is not a safe topic; it is an untested one.

How to use this page. The page is organised by problem position, because that is the one thing the three papers share. For each position you get: what that slot has actually been, what a full-credit answer contains, and then a drill bank — every past task of that type, solved in full, plus new tasks written in the same style and marked as mine. Work a block, hide the solutions, and answer on paper first; the credits on each drill tell you roughly how much writing the examiner expects. Where a published official solution is wrong, incomplete or sloppy, the drill says so and gives the repair.

The point of rank 1. Expectation, variance and covariance (§2.1) is the heaviest topic by a wide margin — 38 of 154 credits, a quarter of everything — and yet it has never been a problem of its own. There has never been a problem titled "Expectation" or "Variance". It is the engine inside the other problems: it is how you answer a true/false item about covariance (SoSe26 P1a, P1b, P2c, P2d), how you price the mean and variance of an estimator before Chebyshev or the clt can be applied (WiSe25 P4b/c, SoSe26 P4c), and how the long story problem is solved at all (SoSe25 P5a/P5b, the duck hunt). If you can compute \(\E\), \(\Var\) and \(\Cov\) quickly and correctly — linearity, \(\Var[aX+b]=a^2\Var[X]\), bilinearity of covariance, \(\Var[X]=\E[X^2]-\E[X]^2\) — you are touching a quarter of the marks no matter which problems appear.

In words: §2.1 is not a chapter you revise once and tick off. It is the arithmetic the whole exam is written in.

What has never been examined in these three papers — and why that is not permission to skip it

None of the following appeared anywhere in WiSe 25/26, SoSe 2025 or SoSe 2026:

  • §1.1–§1.2: urn models (Lemma 1.36) and combinatorial counting; the Poisson limit theorem (Theorem 1.42); Vitali sets (Theorems 1.27, 1.28).
  • §1.3: Radon–Nikodym (Theorem 1.48); the hypergeometric, geometric, negative-binomial, Beta, \(\chi^2\) and Student-\(t\) distributions.
  • §2.1–§2.3: the quantile transformation (Proposition 2.23); partial correlation (Definition 2.16); moment generating functions (Remark 2.49); the computation rules for multivariate Gaussians (Lemma 2.53).
  • §2.4: the weak law of large numbers stated as such (Theorem 2.61) — although its assumption list is exactly the point of WiSe25 P1d, so the theorem is examined through the back door.
  • §3.3–§3.4: uniformly most powerful and unbiased tests (Definitions 3.38, 3.39); the Neyman–Pearson lemma (Theorem 3.40); \(p\)-values computed numerically (Definition 3.48); \(t\)-tests and \(t\)-intervals (Examples 3.45, 3.46(iii), 3.57).
  • Whole units: §3.5 in its entirety (Bayesian models, posteriors, credible intervals); the whole of Chapter 0; Appendix A.1.

Read that list as "untested", not as "safe". Three papers cannot cover a two-chapter-plus script, and an examiner who notices that a topic has been quiet for three rounds has a reason to use it. The Neyman–Pearson lemma is a numbered theorem with a proof in the script and a full exercise sheet behind it; nothing about its absence from three papers makes it unexaminable. Use the ranking to decide what to drill hardest, never to decide what to not read.

Problem 1 — the true/false block

This is the one stable fixture of the three papers: all three open with a problem titled True or false. Counting SoSe 2026's second block (its Problem 2, which is also true/false), the true/false material is worth 12 + 12 + 17 = 41 credits across the three papers — the largest single task type on any of them.

The two variants, and what a justification must contain

Variant A — with justification (WiSe25 P1, SoSe25 P1, SoSe26 P2). The printed instruction asks you to decide whether each statement is true or false, to mark your answer unambiguously, and to provide a justification — which it says may be a proof, a counterexample, or an explanation via known results. Three credits per item.

Variant B — mark only (SoSe 2026 Problem 1). The instruction printed is "For the following statements, mark exactly one answer. No justification is required." Five items, one credit each, two boxes (True / False) to tick. This is the highest credits-per-minute block on any of the three papers: five credits with no writing at all. It is also the only place on any of the three papers where the standing "give a reason for each answer" instruction is switched off.

What a justification must contain to score. SoSe 2026 is the only one of the three whose official solution prints its marking scheme, and it is worth reading literally:

  • P2a: "1 point for false; 2 points for a valid sequence for the counterexample."
  • P2b: "1 point for false; 2 points for a valid counterexample and identification of a failed σ-algebra property."
  • P2c: "1 point for false; 1 point for a valid example satisfying the conditional-expectation identity; 1 point for demonstrating dependence."
  • P2d: "1 point for true; 1 point for using independence to obtain zero covariance; 1 point for expanding the covariance and concluding equality of the variances."

Three things follow, and they are worth more than any single fact on this page.

  1. The bare verdict is worth 1 credit. In every one of the four SoSe26 items, the word "true" or "false" alone earns one of the three credits. Never leave a true/false item blank, and write the verdict word first, on its own, before you start justifying. Even a guess is worth a third of the item.
  2. A counterexample scores only if it is checked in both directions. P2c splits its remaining two credits into "an example satisfying the hypothesis" and "demonstrating that the conclusion fails". So a counterexample has to do two jobs out loud: show the hypothesis holds for your example, and show the conclusion fails for it — both with actual numbers.
  3. Naming the broken property is part of the credit. P2b does not pay for "this is not a σ-algebra"; it pays for "this is not a σ-algebra because it contains \(\{a\}\) but not its complement \(\{b\}\)", which is axiom (ii) of Definition 1.6. Whenever a definition has numbered clauses, say which clause breaks.

The method for any true/false item, in four moves my distillation from the three official solutions

  1. Read the quantifier. Words like "for any", "for all", "then it already holds" mean the claim is universal, and one witness kills it. Words like "there exists" would need a proof of existence — no item on the three papers has been of that shape so far.
  2. Compare the hypotheses printed with the hypotheses the result needs. Write the named result from the script next to the statement and look for the gap. Missing independence, missing finiteness, missing non-degeneracy — the counterexample almost always lives exactly in that gap. WiSe25 P1d omits "independent"; SoSe26 P2a omits any control on the tails.
  3. If true: name the script item (Theorem 2.35, Proposition 2.12(iii)(v), Remark 2.57, …) and write the one or two lines it needs. Naming is not decoration — it is what "explanation via known results" means in the printed instruction.
  4. If false: build the smallest counterexample and verify both halves with numbers.

The counterexample habit. The three papers keep reusing a very small toolbox. Learn these five machines and most false items become mechanical:

  • A finite \(\Omega\) with 2 to 4 points and an explicit pmf (probability mass function — the list of probabilities of the individual outcomes, Definition 1.34). Used by SoSe25 P1a (\(\Omega\) with 2 points), WiSe25 P1c (4 points), SoSe26 P2b (3 points).
  • \(X_i := X_1\) for every \(i\) — keeps the marginal distribution exactly as stated and destroys independence. This is WiSe25 P1d's official counterexample.
  • \(X_n := n\cdot\one_{\{U\le 1/n\}}\) with \(U\sim\Unif(0,1)\) — a spike that gets taller and rarer. It converges to \(0\) in every mode, yet \(\E[X_n]=1\) for every \(n\). This is SoSe26 P2a.
  • \(X\) uniform on \(\{-1,0,1\}\) with \(Y:=X^2\) — uncorrelated, satisfies \(\E[X\mid Y]=\E[X]\), and is very much not independent. This is SoSe26 P2c.
  • A count that is not a power of two. A σ-algebra on a finite \(\Omega\) always has \(2^k\) elements for some \(k\) (its atoms partition \(\Omega\), and every union of atoms is in it). So a listed collection of size 5, 6 or 7 cannot be one — a five-second check before you hunt for the missing complement. WiSe25 P1a's collection has 5 elements.

The drills below are grouped by topic so you can attack one area at a time. Every past item from the three papers is here, with its exam, part and credits, and every one I wrote myself is chipped my addition. Hide the solution, write your verdict word and your justification on paper, then open it.

Drills — σ-algebras and measures (§1.1)

Is this collection a σ-algebra? WiSe25 · P1a · 3 credits

Statement. On \(\Omega=\{\circ,\triangle,\star\}\), the set \(\{\emptyset,\{\circ\},\{\star\},\{\circ,\star\},\Omega\}\) is a σ-algebra. True or false?

Solution

Verdict: False.

The definition being tested. Definition 1.6: a collection \(\Aa\subseteq\pow(\Omega)\) (a set of subsets of \(\Omega\); \(\pow(\Omega)\) is the power set, the collection of all subsets) is a σ-algebra [σ-Algebra] on \(\Omega\) if (i) \(\Omega\in\Aa\); (ii) for every \(A\in\Aa\) also the complement \(A^c=\Omega\setminus A\) is in \(\Aa\); (iii) for every sequence \((A_i)_{i\in\N}\) in \(\Aa\), the union \(\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i\) is in \(\Aa\).

Which clause breaks. Clause (ii). The set \(\{\circ\}\) is in the collection, but its complement is \[ \Omega\setminus\{\circ\}=\{\triangle,\star\}, \] and \(\{\triangle,\star\}\) is not one of the five listed sets. So the collection is not closed under complements and is not a σ-algebra.

The five-second check. The collection has \(5\) elements. A σ-algebra on a finite \(\Omega\) always has \(2^k\) elements for some \(k\in\N\), and \(5\) is not a power of \(2\), so it cannot be one. This is a good alarm bell, but write the concrete missing complement as well: the marking scheme of the comparable SoSe26 P2b pays explicitly for "identification of a failed σ-algebra property".

What earns the 3 credits: the word "false" (1), a concrete set whose complement is missing (1), and naming the axiom — closure under complements, Definition 1.6(ii) (1).

Do two measures agreeing on a generator agree everywhere? WiSe25 · P1c · 3 credits

Statement. Let \(\Omega\) be a set, \(L\subseteq\pow(\Omega)\), and let \(S\) be the σ-algebra \[ S=\bigcap\{A \mid A\text{ is a σ-algebra on }\Omega\text{ and }L\subseteq A\} \] (the intersection of all σ-algebras on \(\Omega\) that contain \(L\); this is a σ-algebra by Proposition 1.7, and it is written \(\sigma(L)\) in Lemma 1.8). Then for any two probability measures \(\P_1,\P_2\) on \((\Omega,S)\) with \(\P_1(L)=\P_2(L)\) for all \(L\in L\), it already holds that \(\P_1=\P_2\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: False.

Words first. A probability measure [Wahrscheinlichkeitsmaß] \(\P\) on \((\Omega,S)\) assigns to each set in \(S\) a number in \([0,1]\), with \(\P(\Omega)=1\) and countable additivity (Definition 1.20). A generator \(L\) of \(S\) is any collection with \(\sigma(L)=S\) (Lemma 1.8). The claim is that knowing a measure on a generator pins it down on the whole σ-algebra.

The official counterexample. Take \(\Omega=\{1,2,3,4\}\) and \(L=\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\}\}\). Then \(\sigma(L)=\pow(\Omega)\) (all \(16\) subsets), so \(S=\pow(\Omega)\) and every single outcome is measurable. Define two measures through their pmfs: \[ p_1(1)=\tfrac13,\quad p_1(2)=\tfrac13,\quad p_1(3)=\tfrac13,\quad p_1(4)=0, \] \[ p_2(1)=\tfrac16,\quad p_2(2)=\tfrac12,\quad p_2(3)=\tfrac16,\quad p_2(4)=\tfrac16. \] Both are pmfs: each is non-negative and \(\tfrac13+\tfrac13+\tfrac13+0=1\) and \(\tfrac16+\tfrac12+\tfrac16+\tfrac16=1\). By Lemma 1.35 each pmf defines a probability measure on \(\pow(\Omega)\) through \(\P(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}p(\omega)\).

Both halves checked with numbers. On the generator: \[ \P_1(\{1,2\})=\tfrac13+\tfrac13=\tfrac23,\qquad \P_2(\{1,2\})=\tfrac16+\tfrac12=\tfrac16+\tfrac36=\tfrac46=\tfrac23, \] \[ \P_1(\{2,3\})=\tfrac13+\tfrac13=\tfrac23,\qquad \P_2(\{2,3\})=\tfrac12+\tfrac16=\tfrac36+\tfrac16=\tfrac46=\tfrac23. \] So the hypothesis holds. But \(\P_1(\{4\})=0\neq\tfrac16=\P_2(\{4\})\), so \(\P_1\neq\P_2\) and the conclusion fails.

Why it fails — the idea worth carrying. Uniqueness does hold if the generator is closed under finite intersections (a π-system). Here \(\{1,2\}\cap\{2,3\}=\{2\}\), which is not in \(L\) — and \(\{2\}\) is exactly the set the two measures disagree on (\(p_1(2)=\tfrac13\), \(p_2(2)=\tfrac12\)). The gap in the hypothesis is the counterexample.

Note on the published solution. The PDF renders the shared value \(\tfrac23\) as "32". That is a typesetting slip in the rendering, not a mathematical error; the value is \(2/3\), as the arithmetic above shows.

Is the forward image of a σ-algebra a σ-algebra? SoSe26 · P2b · 3 credits

Statement. Let \(\Omega,\Omega'\) be sets, \(\Aa\) a σ-algebra on \(\Omega\), and \(f:\Omega\to\Omega'\) an arbitrary function. Then \(f(\Aa):=\{f(A)\mid A\in\Aa\}\) is a σ-algebra on \(\Omega'\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: False.

Notation. \(f(A)=\{f(\omega)\mid\omega\in A\}\) is the forward image [Bild] of \(A\): everything \(f\) actually hits when it is fed the points of \(A\). Contrast this with the pre-image [Urbild] \(f^{-1}(A')=\{\omega\in\Omega\mid f(\omega)\in A'\}\), which is what Definition 1.50 uses to define measurable maps. Pre-images of a σ-algebra always form a σ-algebra; forward images need not. That asymmetry is the whole item.

The official counterexample. \(\Omega=\{1,2,3\}\), \(\Omega'=\{a,b\}\), with \(f(1)=f(2)=a\) and \(f(3)=b\), and \[ \Aa=\{\emptyset,\{1,3\},\{2\},\Omega\}. \] Check the hypothesis: \(\Aa\) really is a σ-algebra on \(\Omega\). (i) \(\Omega\in\Aa\). (ii) complements: \(\emptyset^c=\Omega\in\Aa\), \(\{1,3\}^c=\{2\}\in\Aa\), \(\{2\}^c=\{1,3\}\in\Aa\), \(\Omega^c=\emptyset\in\Aa\). (iii) unions: \(\{1,3\}\cup\{2\}=\Omega\in\Aa\), and every other union is one of the four sets again. So \(\Aa\) is a σ-algebra with \(4=2^2\) elements.

Compute the forward images: \[ f(\emptyset)=\emptyset,\quad f(\{1,3\})=\{a,b\},\quad f(\{2\})=\{a\},\quad f(\Omega)=\{a,b\}, \] so \(f(\Aa)=\{\emptyset,\{a\},\{a,b\}\}\).

Check the conclusion fails, naming the axiom: \(\{a\}\in f(\Aa)\), but its complement in \(\Omega'\) is \(\{a\}^c=\{b\}\), and \(\{b\}\notin f(\Aa)\). Closure under complements, Definition 1.6(ii), fails. (The alarm bell again: \(|f(\Aa)|=3\), not a power of \(2\).)

Why \(f\) is chosen surjective. \(f\) hits both \(a\) and \(b\), so \(f(\Omega)=\Omega'\) and the objection "but the image is too small" is closed off. The failure is not about missing the top set; it is about complements.

The printed marking scheme: "1 point for false; 2 points for a valid counterexample and identification of a failed σ-algebra property." Writing the counterexample without the sentence "\(\{b\}\) is missing, so axiom (ii) fails" does not get the two points.

Is the union of two σ-algebras a σ-algebra? my addition · 3 credits

Statement. Let \(\Aa_1\) and \(\Aa_2\) be σ-algebras on the same set \(\Omega\). Then \(\Aa_1\cup\Aa_2\) is a σ-algebra on \(\Omega\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: False.

Where the trap is. Proposition 1.7 says the intersection of any family of σ-algebras on \(\Omega\) is again a σ-algebra — that is exactly what makes Lemma 1.8's \(\sigma(E)\) well defined. It is tempting to assume the union behaves the same way. It does not.

Counterexample. Take \(\Omega=\{1,2,3\}\) and, using Example 1.9(iii) (\(\sigma(\{A\})=\{\emptyset,\Omega,A,A^c\}\)), \[ \Aa_1=\{\emptyset,\{1\},\{2,3\},\Omega\},\qquad \Aa_2=\{\emptyset,\{2\},\{1,3\},\Omega\}. \] Hypothesis holds: both are σ-algebras — each contains \(\Omega\), each is closed under complements by construction (\(\{1\}^c=\{2,3\}\), \(\{2\}^c=\{1,3\}\)), and every union of their members is again a member (for instance \(\{1\}\cup\{2,3\}=\Omega\)). Each has \(4=2^2\) elements.

Conclusion fails: the union is \[ \Aa_1\cup\Aa_2=\{\emptyset,\{1\},\{2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\},\Omega\}, \] which has \(6\) elements — not a power of \(2\), so it cannot be a σ-algebra. Concretely, the axiom that breaks is (iii), closure under unions: \(\{1\}\in\Aa_1\cup\Aa_2\) and \(\{2\}\in\Aa_1\cup\Aa_2\), but \[ \{1\}\cup\{2\}=\{1,2\}\notin\Aa_1\cup\Aa_2 . \] (Equivalently, by (ii): \(\{1,2\}=\{3\}^c\) and \(\{3\}\) is not in the union either.)

In words: intersecting σ-algebras keeps only sets that both systems can measure, and that is safe. Taking the union throws two incompatible systems into one bag, and the bag is no longer closed under combining its sets.

What earns the 3 credits: "false" (1); two explicit σ-algebras with the hypothesis verified (1); a concrete pair of sets whose union is missing, with the axiom named (1).

Drills — conditional probability, independence, Bayes (§1.4)

Is \(\P(A\mid B)=\P(B\mid A)\)? SoSe25 · P1a · 3 credits

Statement. Let \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\) be a probability space and \(A,B\in\Aa\) with \(\P(A)>0\) and \(\P(B)>0\). Then \(\P(A\mid B)=\P(B\mid A)\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: False.

The definition. Definition 1.69: for events \(A,B\) with \(\P(B)>0\), \(\P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{\P(A\cap B)}{\P(B)}\). The two conditional probabilities share the numerator \(\P(A\cap B)\) but divide by different numbers, so they agree only when \(\P(A)=\P(B)\).

The official counterexample. \(\Omega=\{0,1\}\), \(\Aa=\pow(\Omega)\), \(\P\) the Laplace (uniform) distribution, so \(\P(\{0\})=\P(\{1\})=\tfrac12\). Take \(A=\{0,1\}=\Omega\) and \(B=\{0\}\). Then \(\P(A)=1>0\) and \(\P(B)=\tfrac12>0\), so the hypothesis holds. Also \(A\cap B=\{0\}\), so \(\P(A\cap B)=\tfrac12\), and \[ \P(A\mid B)=\frac{1/2}{1/2}=1,\qquad \P(B\mid A)=\frac{1/2}{1}=\frac12 . \] Since \(1\neq\tfrac12\), the conclusion fails.

The right relation. What is true is Bayes' rule (Theorem 1.70(iii)), which in its two-event form reads \[ \P(A\mid B)=\frac{\P(B\mid A)\,\P(A)}{\P(B)} . \] The two conditionals differ by the factor \(\P(A)/\P(B)\); they coincide exactly when \(\P(A)=\P(B)\). Confusing the two directions is the "prosecutor's fallacy" and it is the same error as SoSe25 P1c's misreading of a significance level.

What earns the 3 credits: "false" (1); a concrete space with both probabilities positive (1); the two numbers computed and compared (1).

The cdf of a ratio of two exponentials SoSe25 · P1d · 3 credits

Statement. Let \(X,Y\) be iid (independent and identically distributed, Definition 1.79) following \(\Exp(\lambda)\) for \(\lambda>0\). Then the cdf of the ratio \(X/Y\) is \[ F_{X/Y}(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{t}{1+t} & t>0,\\[2pt] 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases} \] True or false? Hint printed on the exam: the pdf of the exponential distribution is \(p_{\Exp(\lambda)}(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x\ge0\) (and \(0\) otherwise); note that \(F_{X/Y}(t)=\P(X<t\cdot Y)\).

Solution

Verdict: True.

Words first. The cdf [Verteilungsfunktion] of a random variable \(Z\) is \(F_Z(t)=\P(Z\le t)\) (Definition 1.56). Since \(X\) and \(Y\) are exponential they are almost surely positive, so \(X/Y>0\) almost surely; therefore \(\P(X/Y\le t)=0\) for \(t\le0\), which settles the second branch immediately.

The joint density. \(X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\) means the joint pdf factorises (Definition 1.77(iii)): for \(x,y\ge0\), \[ p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_X(x)\,p_Y(y)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\cdot\lambda e^{-\lambda y}, \] and \(0\) elsewhere. This is the only place independence is used.

The computation, for \(t>0\). Using the hint's rewriting \(\{X/Y\le t\}=\{X<tY\}\) up to a null set (dividing by the positive \(Y\)), we integrate the joint density over the region \(\{0\le x<ty,\ y\ge0\}\), doing the inner integral in \(x\) first: \[ F_{X/Y}(t)=\int_0^\infty\Bigl(\int_0^{ty}\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\,dx\Bigr)\lambda e^{-\lambda y}\,dy . \] The inner integral is a standard antiderivative: \(\int_0^{c}\lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx= \bigl[-e^{-\lambda x}\bigr]_0^{c}=1-e^{-\lambda c}\) with \(c=ty\). So \[ F_{X/Y}(t)=\int_0^\infty\bigl(1-e^{-\lambda ty}\bigr)\lambda e^{-\lambda y}\,dy =\int_0^\infty\lambda e^{-\lambda y}dy-\lambda\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda(t+1)y}\,dy . \] The first integral is \(1\) (the exponential density integrates to \(1\)). For the second, with \(\lambda(t+1)>0\), \[ \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda(t+1)y}\,dy=\Bigl[\frac{-1}{\lambda(t+1)}e^{-\lambda(t+1)y}\Bigr]_0^\infty =\frac{1}{\lambda(t+1)} . \] Hence \[ F_{X/Y}(t)=1-\lambda\cdot\frac{1}{\lambda(t+1)}=1-\frac1{t+1}=\frac{t+1-1}{t+1}=\frac{t}{t+1}, \] which is the claimed formula. The \(\lambda\) cancels — the distribution of the ratio does not depend on the rate, which makes sense because scaling both \(X\) and \(Y\) by the same factor leaves \(X/Y\) unchanged.

Sanity checks. \(F(t)\to0\) as \(t\downarrow0\) and \(F(t)\to1\) as \(t\to\infty\), and \(F\) is increasing since \(F'(t)=\frac{1}{(1+t)^2}>0\) — the three properties a cdf must have (Lemma 1.24).

What earns the 3 credits: "true" (1); setting up the correct double integral from the factorised joint density (1); carrying the integration through to \(t/(1+t)\) and handling \(t\le0\) (1).

Are disjoint events independent? my addition · 2 credits

Statement. Let \(A,B\in\Aa\) be disjoint events (\(A\cap B=\emptyset\)) with \(\P(A)>0\) and \(\P(B)>0\). Then \(A\) and \(B\) are independent. True or false?

Solution

Verdict: False. In fact the hypothesis makes independence impossible.

The definition. Definition 1.74: events \(A,B\) are independent [unabhängig] if \(\P(A\cap B)=\P(A)\P(B)\).

The argument. Disjointness gives \(A\cap B=\emptyset\), so \(\P(A\cap B)=\P(\emptyset)=0\). But \(\P(A)>0\) and \(\P(B)>0\) give \(\P(A)\P(B)>0\), because a product of two strictly positive numbers is strictly positive. So \[ \P(A\cap B)=0\ \neq\ \P(A)\P(B)>0, \] and the defining equation fails. No example is even needed — the hypothesis contradicts the conclusion in general. If you want one anyway: a fair coin, \(A=\{\text{heads}\}\), \(B=\{\text{tails}\}\), then \(\P(A\cap B)=0\) while \(\P(A)\P(B)=\tfrac14\).

In words: "disjoint" and "independent" are near-opposites. Disjoint means knowing \(A\) happened tells you \(B\) definitely did not — the strongest possible dependence. Independent means knowing \(A\) happened tells you nothing about \(B\).

What earns the 2 credits: "false" (1); the comparison \(0\neq\P(A)\P(B)>0\) with Definition 1.74 named (1).

Does positive relevance run both ways? my addition · 3 credits

Statement. Let \(A,B\in\Aa\) with \(\P(A)>0\) and \(\P(B)>0\). If \(\P(A\mid B)>\P(A)\), then \(\P(B\mid A)>\P(B)\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: True. (This one is a deliberate companion to SoSe25 P1a above: the values of the two conditionals need not agree, but the direction of the effect always does.)

Proof, one equivalence at a time. By Definition 1.69, \(\P(A\mid B)=\frac{\P(A\cap B)}{\P(B)}\). Since \(\P(B)>0\), multiplying the assumed inequality \(\frac{\P(A\cap B)}{\P(B)}>\P(A)\) by the positive number \(\P(B)\) preserves the direction and gives \[ \P(A\cap B)>\P(A)\,\P(B). \tag{$\ast$} \] Now run the same step backwards on the other side. Since \(\P(A)>0\), dividing \((\ast)\) by the positive number \(\P(A)\) preserves the direction: \[ \frac{\P(A\cap B)}{\P(A)}>\P(B), \] and the left-hand side is exactly \(\P(B\mid A)\) by Definition 1.69. So \(\P(B\mid A)>\P(B)\).

Where the symmetry comes from. Both statements are disguised versions of the single symmetric inequality \((\ast)\), \(\P(A\cap B)>\P(A)\P(B)\) — "\(A\) and \(B\) co-occur more often than independence would predict". Swapping \(A\) and \(B\) changes nothing in \((\ast)\).

In words: if \(B\) is evidence for \(A\), then \(A\) is evidence for \(B\) — always, and by the same "excess" \(\P(A\cap B)-\P(A)\P(B)\). What does not transfer is the size of the two conditional probabilities.

What earns the 3 credits: "true" (1); reducing the hypothesis to \((\ast)\) using \(\P(B)>0\) (1); reading \((\ast)\) back as \(\P(B\mid A)>\P(B)\) using \(\P(A)>0\) (1). Both positivity assumptions must be used out loud — they are what make the multiplications legal.

Drills — expectation, variance, covariance, conditional expectation (§2.1)

The ladder these items live on

Almost every §2.1 true/false item is a question about one chain of implications, and it is worth memorising the chain with the information that no arrow reverses:

\[ X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y \;\Longrightarrow\; \E[X\mid Y]=\E[X] \;\Longrightarrow\; \Cov[X,Y]=0 . \]

Left to right: independence gives \(\E[XY]=\E[X]\E[Y]\) (Proposition 2.4(v)) and hence zero covariance (Proposition 2.12(v)); conditioning on \(Y\) tells you nothing, so \(\E[X\mid Y]=\E[X]\). Right to left: neither arrow reverses in general — Proposition 2.12(v) says so explicitly for the second one, and SoSe26 P2c is the exam item for the first one. The single exception the exams have used: for a pair of Bernoulli variables, zero covariance does give independence (SoSe26 P1b). Two items on the same page test the rule and its exception, on purpose; answering "false" to both from reflex costs a credit.

\(\Var[Y]\ge\E[\Var[Y\mid X]]\)? WiSe25 · P1b · 3 credits

Statement. Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two random variables on a shared probability space such that all required expectations and variances exist. Then \(\Var[Y]\ge\E[\Var[Y\mid X]]\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: True.

The objects. \(\Var[Y\mid X]\) is the conditional variance (Definition 2.34): for each value \(x\), \(\Var[Y\mid X=x]\) is the variance of \(Y\) computed inside the conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X=x\); as \(x\) ranges over the values of \(X\) this becomes a random variable \(\Var[Y\mid X]\), exactly as \(\E[Y\mid X]\) does in Definition 2.30. So \(\E[\Var[Y\mid X]]\) is "the average leftover spread of \(Y\) once \(X\) is known".

The named result. Theorem 2.35, the law of total variance [Varianzzerlegung]: \[ \Var[Y]=\E\bigl[\Var[Y\mid X]\bigr]+\Var\bigl[\E[Y\mid X]\bigr] . \] One line finishes it. The second summand is a variance, and by Proposition 2.8(i) every variance is non-negative: \(\Var[\E[Y\mid X]]\ge0\). Subtracting a non-negative number from \(\Var[Y]\) cannot increase it, so \[ \Var[Y]=\E[\Var[Y\mid X]]+\underbrace{\Var[\E[Y\mid X]]}_{\ge0}\ \ge\ \E[\Var[Y\mid X]] . \]

When is it an equality? Exactly when \(\Var[\E[Y\mid X]]=0\), which by Proposition 2.8(i) means \(\E[Y\mid X]\) is almost surely constant — that is, knowing \(X\) never shifts the mean of \(Y\).

In words: conditioning on more information can only shrink the average remaining variance. Total spread = average leftover spread + spread of the conditional means, and the second term cannot be negative.

What earns the 3 credits: "true" (1); quoting Theorem 2.35 correctly (1); the sentence that the second summand is non-negative because variances are (1). This is a "cite and do one line" item — no example is wanted.

Are \(X\) and \(1-X\) uncorrelated? SoSe26 · P1a · 1 credit (mark only)

Statement. Let \(X\sim\Ber(p)\) and set \(Y:=1-X\). If \(p=1/2\), then \(X\) and \(Y\) are uncorrelated. True or false? (No justification was required on the exam.)

Solution

Verdict: False.

What "uncorrelated" means. \(X\) and \(Y\) are uncorrelated [unkorreliert] if \(\Cov[X,Y]=0\), where \(\Cov[X,Y]=\E[(X-\E[X])(Y-\E[Y])]\) (Definition 2.9); equivalently the correlation coefficient \(\rho[X,Y]=\frac{\Cov[X,Y]}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}\) of Definition 2.13 is \(0\), which needs \(\sigma_X,\sigma_Y>0\).

The computation, in two steps. By bilinearity of covariance (Proposition 2.12(iii)) and covariance with a constant being \(0\) (Proposition 2.12(iv)), \[ \Cov[X,\,1-X]=\Cov[X,1]-\Cov[X,X]=0-\Var[X]=-\Var[X], \] where \(\Cov[X,X]=\Var[X]\) is Proposition 2.12(ii). For \(X\sim\Ber(p)\), Lemma 2.26(iii) gives \(\Var[X]=p(1-p)\), so at \(p=\tfrac12\) \[ \Cov[X,Y]=-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=-\tfrac14\ \neq\ 0 . \] They are not uncorrelated; in fact \(\rho[X,Y]=\frac{-1/4}{(1/2)(1/2)}=-1\), perfect negative correlation.

In words: \(Y\) is \(X\) flipped. Knowing one gives the other exactly, so they are as correlated as two variables can be. The value \(p=\tfrac12\) is a red herring: it maximises \(\Var[X]\) and so makes the covariance as far from \(0\) as it can be, but for any \(p\in(0,1)\) the answer is still "false".

Why this is placed next to P1b. The pair is designed so that a student who answers "false" by reflex to anything mentioning Bernoulli and covariance gets P1a right and P1b wrong. Compute, do not pattern-match.

For Bernoulli variables, does zero covariance give independence? SoSe26 · P1b · 1 credit (mark only)

Statement. For any two Bernoulli random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), \(\Cov[X,Y]=0\) implies \(X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\). True or false? (No justification was required on the exam.)

Solution

Verdict: True. This is the one place where the arrow in Proposition 2.12(v) does turn around — and the reason is that a Bernoulli pair has so few joint probabilities that one equation pins them all down.

Proof supplied by me; the exam required no justification, and the script states only the general "converse fails" warning. Let \(X\sim\Ber(p)\) and \(Y\sim\Ber(q)\), so both take only the values \(0\) and \(1\), with \(\P(X=1)=p\), \(\P(Y=1)=q\). Write \(r:=\P(X=1,Y=1)\).

Step 1 — turn the covariance into \(r\). Since \(XY\) takes the value \(1\) exactly on the event \(\{X=1,Y=1\}\) and \(0\) elsewhere, \(\E[XY]=1\cdot r+0=r\). Also \(\E[X]=p\) and \(\E[Y]=q\) (Lemma 2.26(iii)). The computational formula for covariance (Remark 2.10) gives \[ \Cov[X,Y]=\E[XY]-\E[X]\E[Y]=r-pq . \] So the hypothesis \(\Cov[X,Y]=0\) says exactly \(r=pq\).

Step 2 — the other three joint probabilities follow. The events \(\{Y=1\}\) and \(\{Y=0\}\) partition the space, so by additivity (Proposition 1.19) \[ \P(X=1,Y=0)=\P(X=1)-\P(X=1,Y=1)=p-pq=p(1-q), \] \[ \P(X=0,Y=1)=\P(Y=1)-\P(X=1,Y=1)=q-pq=(1-p)q, \] \[ \P(X=0,Y=0)=1-\bigl[pq+p(1-q)+(1-p)q\bigr]=1-p-q+pq=(1-p)(1-q), \] where the last line multiplies out: \((1-p)(1-q)=1-p-q+pq\).
