Step 3 — read off independence. All four joint probabilities factorise as \(\P(X=x,Y=y)=\P(X=x)\P(Y=y)\), which is exactly Definition 1.77(ii), the factorisation of the pmf for discrete variables. Hence \(X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\).

Why the general converse still fails. The proof used that each variable has only two values, so that one number \(r\) determines the whole joint pmf. With three values the joint pmf has more free parameters than the covariance can control — which is exactly what SoSe26 P2c exploits with \(X\) uniform on \(\{-1,0,1\}\).

Does \(\E[X\mid Y]=\E[X]\) imply independence? SoSe26 · P2c · 3 credits

Statement. Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be integrable random variables. If \(\E[X\mid Y]=\E[X]\) then \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent. True or false?

Solution

Verdict: False.

Reading the statement. "Integrable" means the expectations exist and are finite (Definition 2.1). \(\E[X\mid Y]\) is the random variable of Definition 2.30: it takes the value \(\E[X\mid Y=y]\) when \(Y=y\). The claim "\(\E[X\mid Y]=\E[X]\)" says this random variable is the constant \(\E[X]\) — learning \(Y\) never moves the mean of \(X\).

The official counterexample. Let \(X\) be uniform on \(\{-1,0,1\}\), so \(\P(X=-1)=\P(X=0)=\P(X=1)=\tfrac13\), and set \(Y:=X^2\).

First half — the hypothesis holds. By Definition 2.1(i), \(\E[X]=(-1)\tfrac13+0\cdot\tfrac13+1\cdot\tfrac13=0\). The variable \(Y=X^2\) takes the value \(0\) (when \(X=0\), probability \(\tfrac13\)) and \(1\) (when \(X=\pm1\), probability \(\tfrac23\)). Condition on each (Definition 2.28):

  • Given \(Y=0\): then \(X^2=0\), so \(X=0\) with conditional probability \(1\), hence \(\E[X\mid Y=0]=0\).
  • Given \(Y=1\): then \(X\in\{-1,1\}\), and by symmetry each has conditional probability \(\frac{1/3}{2/3}=\tfrac12\), hence \(\E[X\mid Y=1]=(-1)\tfrac12+1\cdot\tfrac12=0\).

So \(\E[X\mid Y]\) equals \(0\) whatever \(Y\) is, i.e. \(\E[X\mid Y]=0=\E[X]\). The hypothesis holds.

Second half — the conclusion fails. Independence would require the joint pmf to factorise (Definition 1.77(ii)). Test one cell: \[ \P(X=0,\,Y=0)=\P(X=0)=\tfrac13,\qquad \P(X=0)\,\P(Y=0)=\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac13=\tfrac19, \] and \(\tfrac13\neq\tfrac19\). So \(X\) and \(Y\) are dependent. (They are also uncorrelated: \(\E[XY]=\E[X^3]=(-1)\tfrac13+0+1\cdot\tfrac13=0=\E[X]\E[Y]\) — the same example sits at the bottom of the ladder too.)

In words: \(Y=X^2\) tells you the size of \(X\) but nothing about its sign, so the conditional mean never budges from \(0\) even though \(Y\) reveals a great deal about \(X\). Constant conditional mean is far weaker than "no information".

The printed marking scheme: "1 point for false; 1 point for a valid example satisfying the conditional-expectation identity; 1 point for demonstrating dependence." All three jobs must appear separately on the page.

Does \(X+Y\perp\!\!\!\perp X-Y\) force equal variances? SoSe26 · P2d · 3 credits

Statement. Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables with finite variance. If \(X+Y\) and \(X-Y\) are independent, then \(\Var[X]=\Var[Y]\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: True.

Step 1 — independence gives zero covariance. By Proposition 2.12(v), if \(U\perp\!\!\!\perp V\) then \(\Cov[U,V]=0\). With \(U=X+Y\) and \(V=X-Y\) (both have finite variance because \(X,Y\) do, so the covariance exists), \[ \Cov[X+Y,\;X-Y]=0 . \]

Step 2 — expand by bilinearity. Proposition 2.12(iii) says covariance is linear in each slot separately, and \(X-Y=1\cdot X+(-1)\cdot Y\). Expanding both slots: \[ \Cov[X+Y,\,X-Y]=\Cov[X,X]-\Cov[X,Y]+\Cov[Y,X]-\Cov[Y,Y] . \] By symmetry (Proposition 2.12(i)) \(\Cov[X,Y]=\Cov[Y,X]\), so those two middle terms cancel. By Proposition 2.12(ii), \(\Cov[X,X]=\Var[X]\) and \(\Cov[Y,Y]=\Var[Y]\). Therefore \[ \Cov[X+Y,\,X-Y]=\Var[X]-\Var[Y] . \]

Step 3 — combine. Steps 1 and 2 give \(\Var[X]-\Var[Y]=0\), i.e. \(\Var[X]=\Var[Y]\).

In words: the sum and the difference are uncorrelated exactly when the two variables have the same spread. Independence is a stronger assumption than needed here — plain uncorrelatedness of \(X+Y\) and \(X-Y\) already forces equal variances, which is worth saying in the answer.

The printed marking scheme: "1 point for true; 1 point for using independence to obtain zero covariance; 1 point for expanding the covariance and concluding equality of the variances." Note that the middle credit is for the sentence "independent \(\Rightarrow\) covariance \(0\), by Proposition 2.12(v)" — jumping straight to the expansion loses it.

Is \(\Var[X-Y]=\Var[X]-\Var[Y]\)? my addition · 3 credits

Statement. For any two random variables \(X,Y\) with finite variance, \(\Var[X-Y]=\Var[X]-\Var[Y]\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: False.

What is actually true. Proposition 2.12(vi) gives the general formula \(\Var[X+Y]=\Var[X]+\Var[Y]+2\Cov[X,Y]\). Applying it to \(X+(-Y)\), and using \(\Var[-Y]=(-1)^2\Var[Y]=\Var[Y]\) (Proposition 2.8(iii)) together with \(\Cov[X,-Y]=-\Cov[X,Y]\) (Proposition 2.12(iii)): \[ \Var[X-Y]=\Var[X]+\Var[Y]-2\Cov[X,Y] . \] Variances add, never subtract; only the covariance term changes sign.

Counterexample with numbers. Let \(X\sim\Ber(\tfrac12)\) and set \(Y:=-X\). Both have finite variance, so the hypothesis holds. By Lemma 2.26(iii), \(\Var[X]=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac14\), and by Proposition 2.8(iii), \(\Var[Y]=\Var[-X]=(-1)^2\Var[X]=\tfrac14\). Now \[ X-Y=X-(-X)=2X,\qquad \Var[X-Y]=\Var[2X]=2^2\Var[X]=4\cdot\tfrac14=1, \] again by Proposition 2.8(iii). But the claimed right-hand side is \(\Var[X]-\Var[Y]=\tfrac14-\tfrac14=0\). Since \(1\neq0\), the conclusion fails.

A second reason the claim cannot hold in general: its right-hand side can be negative (take any \(X,Y\) with \(\Var[Y]>\Var[X]\)), while the left-hand side is a variance and so is \(\ge0\) by Proposition 2.8(i). A formula that can produce a negative variance is wrong on sight.

What earns the 3 credits: "false" (1); the correct identity with the \(-2\Cov\) term, named from Proposition 2.12(vi) (1); a concrete pair with both sides computed (1).

Is \(\E[\E[X\mid Y]]=\E[X]\)? my addition · 2 credits

Statement. For any two random variables \(X,Y\) for which the relevant expectations exist, \(\E\bigl[\E[X\mid Y]\bigr]=\E[X]\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: True. This is Theorem 2.32 verbatim — the law of total expectation, also called the tower property [Turmregel] or iterated expectation: \(\E[Y]=\E[\E[Y\mid X]]\), with the roles of the two letters swapped relative to the script's phrasing.

Why it is not circular. The two \(\E\) signs are expectations over different things. The inner \(\E[X\mid Y]\) averages \(X\) within each value of \(Y\); by Definition 2.30 the result is a random variable \(h(Y)\), where \(h(y)=\E[X\mid Y=y]\). The outer \(\E\) then averages \(h(Y)\) over the distribution of \(Y\). Splitting the average into groups and then averaging the group averages — weighted by how likely each group is — returns the overall average.

A concrete check with numbers my example. Let \(Y\) be the result of a fair coin, \(\P(Y=0)=\P(Y=1)=\tfrac12\), and let \(X\) be \(0\) or \(10\) with \(\P(X=10\mid Y=0)=0.2\) and \(\P(X=10\mid Y=1)=0.8\). Then \(\E[X\mid Y=0]=10\cdot0.2=2\) and \(\E[X\mid Y=1]=10\cdot0.8=8\), so \(\E[X\mid Y]\) is the random variable taking values \(2\) and \(8\), each with probability \(\tfrac12\), and \[ \E[\E[X\mid Y]]=\tfrac12\cdot2+\tfrac12\cdot8=5 . \] Directly: \(\P(X=10)=\tfrac12\cdot0.2+\tfrac12\cdot0.8=0.5\) by the law of total probability (Theorem 1.70(ii)), so \(\E[X]=10\cdot0.5=5\). The two agree.

What earns the 2 credits: "true" (1); naming Theorem 2.32 and saying which average is taken over what (1). No example is needed for a "true" item that is a named theorem, but the numbers above are how you check yourself under time pressure.

Uncorrelated and the product rule my addition · 2 credits

Statement. If \(X\) and \(Y\) are uncorrelated (and all relevant expectations exist), then \(\E[XY]=\E[X]\E[Y]\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: True — and this is the item that catches people who have learned "uncorrelated is weaker than independent" as a slogan and then refuse to grant anything at all to uncorrelatedness.

One line. "Uncorrelated" means \(\Cov[X,Y]=0\) (Definition 2.9 together with Definition 2.13). The computational formula for covariance (Remark 2.10) says \[ \Cov[X,Y]=\E[XY]-\E[X]\E[Y] . \] Setting the left-hand side to \(0\) and adding \(\E[X]\E[Y]\) to both sides gives \(\E[XY]=\E[X]\E[Y]\).

What is not implied. Independence would give much more: \(\E[g(X)h(Y)]=\E[g(X)]\E[h(Y)]\) for all well-behaved functions \(g,h\), not just for \(g(x)=x\), \(h(y)=y\). That is precisely where the counterexample of SoSe26 P2c lives: with \(X\) uniform on \(\{-1,0,1\}\) and \(Y=X^2\) we have \(\E[XY]=\E[X]\E[Y]\), but taking \(g(x)=x^2\) breaks the product rule, since \(\E[X^2Y]=\E[X^4]=\tfrac23\) while \(\E[X^2]\E[Y]=\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac23=\tfrac49\).

In words: uncorrelated is exactly "the product rule holds for the variables themselves". Independent is "the product rule holds for every function of them".

What earns the 2 credits: "true" (1); the one-line rearrangement of Remark 2.10 (1).

Drills — Markov, Chebyshev, Jensen (§2.2)

No true/false item on the three papers has been about an inequality from §2.2 — the inequalities appear as computation tasks instead (WiSe25 P4b, SoSe25 P5c, SoSe26 P3b and P4d). Since §2.2 is rank 5 by credits and appears in all three papers, the two items below are mine, written to test the hypotheses rather than the algebra.

Markov without non-negativity my addition · 3 credits

Statement. For every random variable \(X\) with finite mean and every \(\epsilon>0\), \[ \P(X\ge\epsilon)\le\frac{\E[X]}{\epsilon} . \] True or false?

Solution

Verdict: False. The inequality as printed drops the hypothesis that makes it work.

What the script actually says. Theorem 2.38 (Markov's inequality [Markow-Ungleichung]) is stated for a monotonically increasing \(f:S_X\to\R_{\ge0}\) in the form \(\P(X\ge\epsilon)\le\frac{1}{f(\epsilon)}\E[f(X)]\), and then records the familiar special case: let \(X\) be a non-negative random variable (that is, \(\P(X\ge0)=1\)); then for any constant \(\epsilon>0\), \(\P(X\ge\epsilon)\le\frac{\E[X]}{\epsilon}\). Non-negativity is not decoration.

Counterexample with numbers. Let \(X\) be the constant \(-1\) — that is, \(\P(X=-1)=1\). Its mean is finite: \(\E[X]=-1\) by Definition 2.1(i). Take \(\epsilon=1>0\). Then \[ \P(X\ge1)=0,\qquad \frac{\E[X]}{\epsilon}=\frac{-1}{1}=-1 , \] and the claimed inequality reads \(0\le-1\), which is plainly false.

A non-degenerate counterexample, in case a constant feels like cheating: let \(X\) take the value \(-10\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) and the value \(2\) with probability \(\tfrac12\). Then \(\E[X]=\tfrac12(-10)+\tfrac12(2)=-4\). With \(\epsilon=2\): \(\P(X\ge2)=\tfrac12\) while \(\frac{\E[X]}{\epsilon}=\frac{-4}{2}=-2\), and \(\tfrac12\le-2\) is false.

The structural reason. A probability is always in \([0,1]\); the right-hand side \(\E[X]/\epsilon\) is negative as soon as \(\E[X]<0\). So the claim cannot survive any variable with a negative mean. Non-negativity of \(X\) is exactly what forces \(\E[X]\ge0\) (Proposition 2.4(iii)) and makes the bound meaningful.

The repair used on the exams. When you need to bound \(\P(|Z|\ge a)\) — an event about a variable that can be negative — you first square it: \(|Z|\ge a\iff Z^2\ge a^2\), and \(Z^2\) is non-negative, so Markov applies and gives \(\P(|Z|\ge a)\le\E[Z^2]/a^2\). That is exactly the move in SoSe26 P4d, and it is also how Theorem 2.40 (Chebyshev) is derived from Theorem 2.38.

What earns the 3 credits: "false" (1); naming the missing non-negativity hypothesis from Theorem 2.38 (1); a concrete variable with both sides evaluated (1).

\(\E[X^2]\ge(\E[X])^2\) my addition · 2 credits

Statement. For every random variable \(X\) whose mean and second moment are finite, \(\E[X^2]\ge(\E[X])^2\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: True, and there are two one-line proofs. Give either.

Route 1 — Jensen (Theorem 2.42). Jensen's inequality says: if \(\E[X]\) is finite and \(g:\R\to\R\) is convex [konvex] — meaning \(g(tx_1+(1-t)x_2)\le tg(x_1)+(1-t)g(x_2)\) for all \(x_1,x_2\in\R\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), i.e. the chord never dips below the graph — then \(\E[g(X)]\ge g(\E[X])\). Take \(g(x)=x^2\), which is convex because \(g''(x)=2>0\) everywhere. Then \(\E[X^2]\ge(\E[X])^2\) immediately.

Route 2 — the variance is non-negative. Remark 2.6 gives the computational formula \(\Var[X]=\E[X^2]-(\E[X])^2\), and Proposition 2.8(i) says \(\Var[X]\ge0\). Adding \((\E[X])^2\) to both sides of \(\E[X^2]-(\E[X])^2\ge0\) gives the claim.

When is it an equality? By Proposition 2.8(i), \(\Var[X]=0\) exactly when \(\P(X=\E[X])=1\), i.e. \(X\) is almost surely constant. Theorem 2.42's equality clause says the same thing from the Jensen side, because \(x\mapsto x^2\) is strictly convex.

In words: squaring and averaging gives at least as much as averaging and squaring, and the gap between the two is exactly the variance.

What earns the 2 credits: "true" (1); either named route written out (1). Route 2 is safer under time pressure because it needs no convexity check.

Drills — characteristic functions (§2.3)

The cf of \(2X+Y\) SoSe26 · P1c · 1 credit (mark only)

Statement. Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be independent random variables with \(\phi_X(t)=\phi_Y(t)=\cos(t)\) for all \(t\in\R\). Then \[ \phi_{2X+Y}(t)=\cos(2t)\cos(t) \] for all \(t\in\R\). True or false? (No justification was required on the exam.)

Solution

Verdict: True.

What a cf is. The characteristic function [charakteristische Funktion] of a random variable \(X\) is \(\phi_X(t)=\E[e^{itX}]\) (Definition 2.46), where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\) and, by Euler's formula, \(e^{iu}=\cos u+i\sin u\). It always exists, because \(|e^{itX}|=1\). A cf of \(\cos t\) is the cf of the symmetric sign variable \(\P(X=1)=\P(X=-1)=\tfrac12\), since \(\tfrac12e^{it}+\tfrac12e^{-it}=\cos t\) — this is exactly the variable of SoSe26 P4a.

Two rules, applied in order (both from Remark 2.47).

  1. Independence turns a sum into a product (Remark 2.47(iv)): if \(U\perp\!\!\!\perp V\) then \(\phi_{U+V}(t)=\phi_U(t)\phi_V(t)\). Here \(2X\) is a function of \(X\) alone and \(Y\) is independent of \(X\), so \(2X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\) and \[ \phi_{2X+Y}(t)=\phi_{2X}(t)\,\phi_Y(t). \]
  2. Affine scaling (Remark 2.47(ii)): \(\phi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\phi_X(at)\). With \(a=2\), \(b=0\): \(\phi_{2X}(t)=\phi_X(2t)=\cos(2t)\).

Putting the two together: \(\phi_{2X+Y}(t)=\cos(2t)\cdot\cos(t)\), which is the claim.

The classic wrong turn is \(\phi_{2X}(t)=\phi_X(t)^2=\cos^2 t\), which confuses \(2X\) (one variable doubled) with \(X_1+X_2\) (two independent copies added). Those are different random variables: \(2X\) takes values in \(\{-2,2\}\), while \(X_1+X_2\) takes values in \(\{-2,0,2\}\). The scaling rule is Remark 2.47(ii); the power rule is Remark 2.47(iv).

Drills — convergence, lln and clt (§2.4)

The second ladder, and the one place it turns around

Remark 2.57: \(X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}X\Rightarrow X_n\xrightarrow{\P}X\Rightarrow X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\). In words: almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution. The reverse implications fail in general (Examples 2.58 and 2.59). Remark 2.57 records one reversal: if \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}c\) for a constant \(c\in\R\), then also \(X_n\xrightarrow{\P}c\). So for a constant limit, "in distribution" and "in probability" are the same thing.

Poisson sample mean without independence WiSe25 · P1d · 3 credits

Statement. For \(X_1,X_2,\dots\sim\Poi(2)\) we have for the sample mean \(\bar X_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) that \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{\P}2\). True or false?

Note on the printed statement. The exam prints it as "\(\lim_{n\to\infty}\bar X_n\xrightarrow{\P}2\)". The "\(\lim\)" is redundant notation — the arrow \(\xrightarrow{\P}\) already contains the limit. Read the statement as \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{\P}2\).

Solution

Verdict: False.

Where the gap is. The notation "\(X_1,X_2,\dots\sim\Poi(2)\)" says the \(X_i\) are identically distributed (Definition 1.54) — each one is Poisson with parameter \(2\) — and nothing more. It does not say iid (Definition 1.79), which additionally demands independence. Both laws of large numbers need something beyond identical distribution: Theorem 2.61 (wlln) needs the \(X_i\) to be pairwise uncorrelated; Theorem 2.62 (slln) needs them iid. Reading "iid" into a statement that does not say it is the single most examined reflex error on these papers.

The official counterexample. Set \(X_i:=X_1\) for every \(i\in\N_{>0}\) — one Poisson draw, repeated forever.

  • Hypothesis holds: every \(X_i\) has exactly the \(\Poi(2)\) distribution, since it is \(X_1\).
  • Conclusion fails: \(\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_1=\frac1n\cdot nX_1=X_1\) for every \(n\). So the sequence \(\bar X_n\) does not move at all, and for any \(\epsilon>0\), \[ \P(|\bar X_n-2|\ge\epsilon)=\P(|X_1-2|\ge\epsilon), \] a number that does not depend on \(n\) and therefore cannot tend to \(0\) unless it is already \(0\). It is not \(0\): the \(\Poi(2)\) pmf is \(\P(X_1=k)=e^{-2}2^k/k!>0\) for every \(k\in\N\), so for example \(\P(X_1=0)=e^{-2}\approx0.1353>0\), and the value \(0\) is at distance \(2\ge\epsilon\) from \(2\) whenever \(\epsilon\le2\). Hence \(\P(|\bar X_n-2|\ge\epsilon)\ge e^{-2}>0\) for all \(n\), and Definition 2.56(i) fails.

The repair. Add one word. With \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) iid \(\Poi(2)\), the mean is \(\E[X_i]=2<\infty\) (Lemma 2.26(vii)), Theorem 2.62 gives \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}2\), and Remark 2.57 then gives \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{\P}2\). The statement becomes true.

What earns the 3 credits: "false" (1); naming the missing independence assumption (1); the explicit counterexample \(X_i:=X_1\) with the probability shown not to vanish (1).

In probability to a constant, hence in distribution SoSe26 · P1d · 1 credit (mark only)

Statement. Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be a sequence of random variables on a common probability space and let \(c\in\R\). If \(X_n\xrightarrow{\P}c\), then \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}c\). True or false? (No justification was required on the exam.)

Solution

Verdict: True.

Why. This is the second arrow of Remark 2.57, which holds for any limit variable \(X\), constant or not: \(X_n\xrightarrow{\P}X\Rightarrow X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\). Nothing special about the constant is needed for this direction.

The two definitions, so the statement is readable (Definition 2.56). \(X_n\xrightarrow{\P}X\) ("in probability" [in Wahrscheinlichkeit]) means: for every \(\epsilon>0\), \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\P(|X_n-X|\ge\epsilon)=0\). \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\) ("in distribution" [in Verteilung]) means: \(\lim_{n\to\infty}F_{X_n}(x)=F_X(x)\) for every \(x\in\R\) at which \(F_X\) is continuous.

What makes the constant case special is the converse, which Remark 2.57 also records: if \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}c\) for a constant \(c\), then \(X_n\xrightarrow{\P}c\) as well. So for a constant limit the two modes are equivalent — whereas for a genuinely random limit the converse fails (Example 2.59: \(U\sim\Ber(0.5)\), \(X_n:=U\), \(X:=1-U\); then \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\) because both are \(\Ber(0.5)\), but \(|X_n-X|=1\) always, so there is no convergence in probability).

A small correction to how this item is sometimes summarised. The statement as printed on the exam is the forward direction \(\xrightarrow{\P}\Rightarrow\xrightarrow{d}\), which is the general ladder and needs no constant. The constant only matters for the converse. Both directions are true here, so the answer is "true" either way — but be clear which one you are citing.

Does convergence in distribution carry the expectations along? SoSe26 · P2a · 3 credits

Statement. Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) and \(X\) be random variables on a common probability space such that \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\). If all expectations \(\E[X_n]\) and \(\E[X]\) exist and are finite, then \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\E[X_n]=\E[X]\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: False.

The official counterexample. Let \(U\sim\Unif(0,1)\) — the uniform distribution on the interval \((0,1)\), so \(\P(U\le u)=u\) for \(u\in[0,1]\) — and define \[ X_n:=n\cdot\one_{\{U\le1/n\}},\qquad X:=0 , \] where \(\one_A\) is the indicator [Indikatorfunktion] of the event \(A\): it equals \(1\) if \(A\) occurs and \(0\) otherwise. All of these live on the one probability space carrying \(U\), as the statement requires.

The distribution of \(X_n\). The event \(\{U\le1/n\}\) has probability \(1/n\), so \[ \P(X_n=n)=\frac1n,\qquad \P(X_n=0)=1-\frac1n . \] A tall, rare spike: height \(n\), probability \(1/n\).

First half — the hypothesis holds. For every \(\epsilon>0\) and all \(n\) large enough that \(n>\epsilon\), the only way \(|X_n|\ge\epsilon\) is \(X_n=n\), so \[ \P(|X_n|\ge\epsilon)=\frac1n\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0 , \] which is Definition 2.56(i): \(X_n\xrightarrow{\P}0\). By Remark 2.57, convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution, so \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}0=X\). All the expectations exist and are finite, as we now compute.

Second half — the conclusion fails. By Definition 2.1(i), \[ \E[X_n]=n\cdot\frac1n+0\cdot\Bigl(1-\frac1n\Bigr)=1 \quad\text{for every }n , \] so \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\E[X_n]=1\). But \(\E[X]=\E[0]=0\). Since \(1\neq0\), the claim is false.

In words: convergence in distribution is about where the bulk of the probability sits, and the bulk of \(X_n\) does go to \(0\). The mean, however, is a weighted average in which a vanishing probability \(1/n\) is multiplied by an exploding value \(n\); the product stays at \(1\) and the mass that escapes to infinity carries the whole expectation with it. A mode of convergence that ignores tails cannot control a quantity that is all about tails.

The printed marking scheme: "1 point for false; 2 points for a valid sequence for the counterexample." Note that the two points are for the sequence, so the definition of \(X_n\) plus the two computations (\(\P(|X_n|\ge\epsilon)\to0\) and \(\E[X_n]=1\)) is what must be on the page.

Keep this machine. \(X_n=n\cdot\one_{\{U\le1/n\}}\) is the standard device for "convergence without convergence of means". Memorise it; it costs two lines and answers a whole family of items.

Is the limit in distribution unique? my addition · 3 credits

Statement. Let \((X_n)_{n\in\N}\), \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables on a common probability space with \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\) and \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}Y\). Then \(X=Y\) almost surely, i.e. \(\P(X=Y)=1\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: False.

Where the gap is. Definition 2.56(iii) only constrains the cdfs: \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\) means \(F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x)\) at every continuity point of \(F_X\). So the two hypotheses together force \(F_X=F_Y\) — the limits have the same distribution. They say nothing about the two variables agreeing outcome by outcome, and "almost surely equal" is a statement about outcomes.

Counterexample with numbers. Let \(X\sim\Ber(\tfrac12)\), so \(\P(X=0)=\P(X=1)=\tfrac12\), and set \(Y:=1-X\). Then \(Y\) is also \(\Ber(\tfrac12)\): \(\P(Y=1)=\P(X=0)=\tfrac12\). Define the constant sequence \(X_n:=X\) for all \(n\).

  • Hypotheses hold: \(F_{X_n}=F_X\) for every \(n\), so trivially \(F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x)\) everywhere, giving \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\). And since \(X\) and \(Y\) have the same distribution, \(F_{X_n}=F_X=F_Y\), so \(F_{X_n}(x)\to F_Y(x)\) as well, giving \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}Y\).
  • Conclusion fails: \(X=Y\) would mean \(X=1-X\), i.e. \(X=\tfrac12\), which \(X\) never is. So \(\P(X=Y)=0\), not \(1\) — as far from almost-sure equality as possible.

The correct statement. The limit in distribution is unique as a distribution: if \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\) and \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}Y\) then \(F_X=F_Y\), so \(X\) and \(Y\) are identically distributed (Corollary 1.57). For convergence in probability the stronger conclusion does hold — if \(X_n\xrightarrow{\P}X\) and \(X_n\xrightarrow{\P}Y\), then \(\P(X=Y)=1\) — which is a clean way to see that the three modes really are different.

In words: convergence in distribution only sees the shape of the distribution, never which outcome goes with which. Two variables can have identical shapes and still disagree on every single outcome.

What earns the 3 credits: "false" (1); a pair \(X,Y\) with the same cdf and an explicit sequence satisfying both hypotheses (1); showing \(\P(X=Y)\ne1\) with numbers, plus the sentence that what is unique is the distribution (1).

iid with finite mean, no variance assumed my addition · 3 credits

Statement. Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be iid random variables with finite mean \(\E[X_i]=\mu<\infty\), and let \(\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\). Then \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{\P}\mu\), even if the variance of the \(X_i\) is infinite. True or false?

Solution

Verdict: True. (This is deliberately the mirror image of WiSe25 P1d: there the independence was missing and the answer was "false"; here everything the theorem needs is present, and the extra clause about the variance is a distractor.)

Route 1 — the strong law plus the ladder. Theorem 2.62 (slln) assumes exactly: a sequence of iid random variables with finite mean \(\E[X_i]=\mu<\infty\). No variance assumption appears in it. Its conclusion is \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}\mu\). Remark 2.57 then gives \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{\P}\mu\), because almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability.

Route 2 — the weak law directly. Theorem 2.61 (wlln) assumes: identically distributed, finite mean, and pairwise uncorrelated. Our \(X_i\) are iid, hence in particular pairwise independent, hence pairwise uncorrelated by Proposition 2.12(v). So Theorem 2.61 applies directly and gives \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{\P}\mu\) with no variance assumption either.

Where the confusion usually comes from. The script's proof sketch of Theorem 2.61 adds "if we additionally assume that the \(X_i\) have finite variance \(\sigma^2<\infty\)", because that makes the Chebyshev argument work in two lines. A hypothesis used in one convenient proof is not a hypothesis of the theorem. Read the theorem statement, not the proof sketch. (Contrast the clt, Theorem 2.64, which genuinely does require finite and non-zero variance — there the variance is in the statement, because the standardisation divides by \(\sigma\).)

In words: to make the sample mean settle down you need independence and a mean to settle down to. You need a finite variance only to say how fast (Chebyshev) or in what shape (the clt).

What earns the 3 credits: "true" (1); naming Theorem 2.62 or 2.61 with its exact assumption list (1); the sentence that no variance assumption is part of that list, plus the Remark 2.57 step if you went through the strong law (1).

Drills — estimators, mle, and what a level means (§3.1–§3.3)

A weighted average of two unbiased estimators SoSe25 · P1b · 3 credits

Statement. Let \((\Omega,\Aa,\P_\Theta)\) be a statistical model and let \(\hat\theta_1,\hat\theta_2\) be unbiased estimators of \(\theta\) in \(\P_\Theta\). Then \(\tfrac13\hat\theta_1+\tfrac23\hat\theta_2\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\theta\) as well. True or false?

Solution

Verdict: True.

The definition. An estimator [Schätzer] \(\hat\theta\) is a statistic used as a guess for \(\theta\) (Definition 3.18). It is unbiased [erwartungstreu] if \(\operatorname{bias}[\hat\theta]=\E[\hat\theta]-\theta=0\), i.e. \(\E[\hat\theta]=\theta\) for all \(\theta\in\Theta\) (Definition 3.20(i)). The expectation is taken under \(\P_\theta\), the distribution that the parameter value \(\theta\) says the data have.

One line of linearity. By Proposition 2.4(i), \(\E[aX+bY]=a\E[X]+b\E[Y]\). With \(a=\tfrac13\), \(b=\tfrac23\): \[ \E\Bigl[\tfrac13\hat\theta_1+\tfrac23\hat\theta_2\Bigr] =\tfrac13\E[\hat\theta_1]+\tfrac23\E[\hat\theta_2] =\tfrac13\theta+\tfrac23\theta =\Bigl(\tfrac13+\tfrac23\Bigr)\theta=\theta . \] So the combination is unbiased.

What makes it work — and what is not needed. The only facts used are linearity of expectation and that the two weights sum to \(1\). No independence between \(\hat\theta_1\) and \(\hat\theta_2\) is required, because linearity of expectation never requires it (Proposition 2.4(i) holds for any two variables on the same space). This matters: the same statement about the variance of the combination would be false without independence.

The general rule to carry away. Any convex combination — weights \(w_1,\dots,w_k\ge0\) with \(\sum_i w_i=1\) — of unbiased estimators is unbiased, by the same computation. Weights that do not sum to \(1\) break it: \(\tfrac13\hat\theta_1+\tfrac13\hat\theta_2\) has expectation \(\tfrac23\theta\) and bias \(-\tfrac13\theta\).

What earns the 3 credits: "true" (1); the linearity computation written out (1); the sentence that the weights sum to \(1\), and that Definition 3.20(i) is the definition being verified (1).

What does a rejection at level 5 % say? SoSe25 · P1c · 3 credits

Statement. Upon receiving a large batch of switches, you take a subsample (uniformly at random) of size \(n\). You run a suitable hypothesis test at significance level \(\alpha=0.05\) of \(H_0\): "the proportion of defective switches in the batch is at most what the manufacturer claimed" versus \(H_1\): "the proportion of defective switches is larger". The test rejects \(H_0\) at level \(\alpha=0.05\). You can therefore conclude that the probability that the entire batch conforms to the claimed proportion is at most 5 %. True or false?

Solution

Verdict: False.

What \(\alpha\) actually is. Definition 3.34(v): the significance level [Signifikanzniveau] of a test \(\varphi\) is \[ \alpha\ \ge\ \sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\E_\theta[\varphi] , \] where \(\Theta_0\) is the set of parameter values making \(H_0\) true and \(\E_\theta[\varphi]\) is the probability of rejecting when \(\theta\) is the true parameter. So \(\alpha\) bounds \[ \P(\text{reject}\mid H_0\text{ true}) . \] It is a property of the procedure: "if the batch conforms, this procedure raises a false alarm in at most 5 % of repeated samples".

What the statement claims instead. It claims \[ \P(H_0\text{ true}\mid\text{we rejected})\le0.05 , \] which is the reverse conditional. As SoSe25 P1a showed with numbers, \(\P(A\mid B)\) and \(\P(B\mid A)\) are different quantities, related by Bayes' rule (Theorem 1.70(iii)) through the factor \(\P(A)/\P(B)\).

Worse: in this framework the claimed quantity is not even defined. In the frequentist model of §3.3 the true parameter \(\theta\) is a fixed unknown constant, not a random variable. So "the probability that the batch conforms" has no meaning here: the batch either conforms or it does not. Attaching a probability to a hypothesis requires a prior distribution over \(\theta\) — that is the Bayesian machinery of §3.5 (Definition 3.61, Definition 3.62), which this model does not have.

The same error in another costume. Remark 3.55 warns against reading a 95 % confidence interval as "\(\mu\) lies in this interval with probability 95 %". Identical mistake: the randomness is in the interval (or in the decision), never in the parameter.

In words: the 5 % is a promise about how often the method cries wolf when there is no wolf. It is not a probability that there is no wolf.

What earns the 3 credits: "false" (1); stating what \(\alpha\) bounds, with Definition 3.34(v) (1); saying that the statement is the reverse conditional, and that \(\theta\) is not random in this model (1).

Is the mle optimal at finite \(n\)? SoSe26 · P1e · 1 credit (mark only)

Statement. Let \((\R,\mathcal B,\P_\Theta)\) be a statistical model. Let \(\hat\theta_n^{(\mathrm{mle})}\) be the maximum likelihood estimator for \(\theta\) and let \(\hat\theta_n\) be any other estimator for \(\theta\). Then, for every finite \(n\) and every \(\theta\in\Theta\), \[ \operatorname{mse}\bigl[\hat\theta_n^{(\mathrm{mle})}\bigr]\le\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_n] . \] True or false? (No justification was required on the exam.)

Solution

Verdict: False.

The words. The mean squared error [mittlerer quadratischer Fehler] of an estimator is \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta]=\E[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2] =\Var[\hat\theta]+(\operatorname{bias}[\hat\theta])^2\) (Definition 3.20(iv), the bias–variance decomposition). The mle \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{mle}}\) is the value of \(\theta\) maximising the likelihood \(L(\theta\mid x)\) (Definition 3.27).

Why the claim fails. Remark 3.30 lists what the mle is good at — consistency, asymptotic normality, asymptotic efficiency, invariance — and every one of these is a statement about \(n\to\infty\). The script says so directly: "in general, we cannot give many guarantees for mle for finite \(n\)", pointing at Example 3.24. There is no finite-sample optimality claim anywhere.

A concrete counterexample supplied by me; the exam needed none. Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be iid \(\mathcal N(\theta,1)\). The mle is \(\hat\theta^{(\mathrm{mle})}_n=\bar X_n\) (Example 3.28), which is unbiased with variance \(\frac1n\), so \[ \operatorname{mse}[\bar X_n]=\Var[\bar X_n]+0^2=\frac1n . \] Now take the shrunken competitor \(\hat\theta_n:=\tfrac12\bar X_n\). By Proposition 2.4(i), \(\E[\hat\theta_n]=\tfrac12\theta\), so \(\operatorname{bias}=\tfrac12\theta-\theta=-\tfrac\theta2\); by Proposition 2.8(iii), \(\Var[\hat\theta_n]=\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)^2\cdot\frac1n=\frac1{4n}\). Hence \[ \operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_n]=\frac1{4n}+\frac{\theta^2}{4} . \] At \(\theta=0\) this is \(\frac1{4n}\), which is a quarter of the mle's \(\frac1n\). So the claim "for every finite \(n\) and every \(\theta\in\Theta\)" is refuted by a single parameter value.

Reading the quantifier. The statement is universal in three things at once — every competing estimator, every finite \(n\), every \(\theta\). One competitor at one \(\theta\) destroys it. This is also why the shrunken estimator is not a "better estimator" in any useful sense: it wins only near \(\theta=0\) and loses badly for large \(|\theta|\). The honest summary is that no estimator dominates everywhere, which is the point Example 3.24 and Example 3.25 (James–Stein) make in the script.

Does unbiased beat biased? my addition · 3 credits

Statement. If \(\hat\theta_1\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\theta\) and \(\hat\theta_2\) is a biased one, then \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_1]\le\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_2]\) for every \(\theta\in\Theta\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: False.

The decomposition that settles it. Definition 3.20(iv): \[ \operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta]=\Var[\hat\theta]+\bigl(\operatorname{bias}[\hat\theta]\bigr)^2 . \] Being unbiased zeroes the second term only. It says nothing at all about the first, so a biased estimator with a much smaller variance can have the smaller mse.

Counterexample with numbers. Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be iid \(\mathcal N(\theta,1)\) with \(\Theta=\R\), and take \[ \hat\theta_1=\bar X_n \quad\text{(unbiased)},\qquad \hat\theta_2=\tfrac12\bar X_n\quad\text{(biased)} . \] Hypothesis holds: \(\E[\bar X_n]=\theta\) by Proposition 2.4(i), so \(\hat\theta_1\) is unbiased; \(\E[\hat\theta_2]=\tfrac\theta2\ne\theta\) for \(\theta\ne0\), so \(\hat\theta_2\) is biased. Now the two mse's. \(\Var[\bar X_n]=\frac1n\) (constants come out squared, Proposition 2.8(iii), and independent variances add, Proposition 2.8(iv): \(\frac1{n^2}\cdot n\cdot1=\frac1n\)). So \[ \operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_1]=\frac1n+0=\frac1n,\qquad \operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_2]=\frac{1}{4n}+\frac{\theta^2}{4} . \] Conclusion fails whenever \(\frac1{4n}+\frac{\theta^2}4<\frac1n\), i.e. \(\frac{\theta^2}{4}<\frac{3}{4n}\), i.e. \(\theta^2<\frac3n\). For instance at \(\theta=0\): \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_2]=\frac1{4n}<\frac1n=\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_1]\).

Reading the quantifier. The claim says "for every \(\theta\)", so one parameter value is enough to refute it. And that is the honest picture: for \(|\theta|>\sqrt{3/n}\) the unbiased estimator wins again. Neither dominates.

In words: unbiasedness is one of two ingredients of the mse, not a guarantee about the mse. Trading a little bias for a lot less variance can be a good deal — this is the whole content of the bias–variance decomposition, and it is why Definition 3.20(iv) is stated as a sum of two terms.

What earns the 3 credits: "false" (1); the bias–variance decomposition quoted as the reason a biased estimator can win (1); an explicit pair with both mse's computed and a \(\theta\) where the inequality reverses (1).

The mle of a transformed parameter my addition · 2 credits

Statement. Let \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{mle}}\) be the maximum likelihood estimator of \(\theta\) and let \(g\) be a function that does not reduce the dimension of the parameter space. Then \(g(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{mle}})\) is the maximum likelihood estimator of \(g(\theta)\). True or false?

Solution

Verdict: True. This is the invariance [Invarianz] property of the mle, Remark 3.30(iv), stated in the script in exactly this form, with the example that for a normal distribution the mle of the standard deviation \(\sigma\) is \(\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{mle}}}\).

Why it is plausible, in one sentence. For an invertible \(g\), maximising the likelihood over \(\theta\) and then applying \(g\), or re-parametrising by \(\eta=g(\theta)\) and maximising over \(\eta\), search the same set of candidate distributions in a different labelling — and a maximum does not care what you call the point where it sits. Formally: if \(L(\theta\mid x)\le L(\hat\theta\mid x)\) for all \(\theta\), then writing \(\tilde L(\eta\mid x):=L(g^{-1}(\eta)\mid x)\) gives \(\tilde L(\eta\mid x)\le\tilde L(g(\hat\theta)\mid x)\) for all \(\eta\), so \(g(\hat\theta)\) maximises the re-parametrised likelihood.

Why the proviso is there. If \(g\) is not injective — say \(\Theta=\R\) and \(g(\theta)=\theta^2\), which sends \(\pm2\) to the same value — several \(\theta\) share one \(g(\theta)\) and the re-parametrisation is no longer a relabelling. The script covers this by the parenthetical "provided \(g\) does not reduce the dimensionality of \(\Theta\)"; the standard fix in the literature is to define the likelihood of \(\eta\) as the largest likelihood over all \(\theta\) with \(g(\theta)=\eta\), under which invariance holds in general. On an exam, quote Remark 3.30(iv) as printed and note the proviso.

Where you would use it. SoSe26 P5b is invariance in action, run backwards: the mle of the Bernoulli parameter \(q\) is \(\hat q=\bar Y_n\), and since \(q(p)=rp+\frac{1-r}2\) is an invertible affine map for \(r\ne0\), the mle of \(p\) is obtained by inverting it, \(\hat p=\frac{\bar Y_n-(1-r)/2}{r}\), rather than by differentiating a likelihood in \(p\).

What earns the 2 credits: "true" (1); naming Remark 3.30(iv) and stating the proviso on \(g\) (1).

Drill bank summary — 29 items

Past exam items, all of them: WiSe25 P1a–d (4 × 3 cr); SoSe25 P1a–d (4 × 3 cr); SoSe26 P1a–e (5 × 1 cr, mark only); SoSe26 P2a–d (4 × 3 cr). That is 17 items, 41 credits — every true/false credit ever set on the three papers. My additions: 12 more, chipped my addition, weighted towards the heavy topics of the ranking (§2.1 three items, §2.4 two, §3.2 two, §2.2 two, §1.4 two, §1.1 one).

A timing target. On the justified format you have roughly two minutes per item (12 credits out of 59 in 120 minutes is about 24 minutes for four items). Practise to that clock: verdict word in ten seconds, named result or counterexample in the next ninety, both halves checked in the last twenty.

Problem 2 — state a definition or theorem exactly

Somewhere on every one of the three papers there is a block of pure recall: write down a named result, with all its assumptions, in the script's own notation. No computation, no example, no application — the credits are for reproducing a statement correctly. It is the cheapest block on the paper if you have prepared it and the most annoying if you have not, because there is nothing to derive your way out of.

 WiSe 25/26SoSe 2025SoSe 2026
whereProblem 2, titled "Definitions"Problem 2, titled "Definitions" Problem 3a, inside the problem titled "Jensen's inequality"
credits6 (3 + 3)6 (3 + 3)3 (of the problem's 5)
(a)state the strong law of large numbers with all required assumptions (Theorem 2.62)state the central limit theorem with all required assumptions (Theorem 2.64)state Jensen's inequality with all required assumptions (Theorem 2.42)
(b)the full definition, including the set-up, of the type of convergence in the slln — almost sure convergence (Definition 2.56(ii)) the full general definition of the type of convergence in the clt — convergence in distribution (Definition 2.56(iii)) — (P3b is an application, not recall)

In the two papers where this block is a problem of its own it has exactly the same shape: (a) a limit theorem, (b) the mode of convergence that theorem uses. SoSe 2026 kept the recall but moved it inside a topic problem and dropped the paired convergence definition. Across all three papers, recall is worth 15 credits.

What "with all assumptions" means, and how assumptions are marked

SoSe 2026 P3a is the only recall item on the three papers whose marking scheme is printed, and it is itemised per assumption:

The printed scheme for SoSe26 P3a SoSe26 · P3a · 3 credits

"1 point for \(X\) with finite expectation; 1 point for \(g:\R\to\R\) convex; 1 point for the correct inequality. The parenthetical additions are not graded."

Read that literally. Two of the three credits are for the two hypotheses. Only one is for the conclusion. A student who writes "\(\E[g(X)]\ge g(\E[X])\)" and nothing else collects one credit out of three, even though the formula is right.

So a full-credit recall answer has four parts, in this order.

  1. Set the stage. Say what objects exist and where they live. "Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be a sequence of iid real random variables"; "Let \((X_n)_{n\in\N}\) be a sequence of random variables and let \(X\) be another random variable, all defined on the same probability space \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\)". The official solutions to WiSe25 P2b and SoSe25 P2b both open with that sentence, and the question asks for "the full definition including the set-up/assumptions".
  2. List every finiteness and regularity assumption separately, on its own line. Finite mean. Finite and non-zero variance. \(g\) convex, from \(\R\) to \(\R\). Independence, and whether it is full independence or only pairwise uncorrelatedness. One line per assumption, because that is how they are counted.
  3. State the conclusion in the script's own notation, and name the mode of convergence on the arrow: \(\xrightarrow{a.s.}\), \(\xrightarrow{\P}\), \(\xrightarrow{d}\).
  4. For a mode of convergence, include the exceptional-set clause. It is the part people drop and it is exactly what is being tested: "\(\P(\{\omega\in\Omega\mid\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n(\omega)=X(\omega)\})=1\)" for almost sure convergence (Definition 2.56(ii)), and "for every \(x\in\R\) at which \(F_X\) is continuous" for convergence in distribution (Definition 2.56(iii)).

Two traps this block has actually set

1. Do not add unasked extras. SoSe26 P3a's scheme says "the parenthetical additions are not graded" — the equality case and the concave version earned nothing. They cost nothing either, unless you get one of them wrong, in which case you have handed the corrector a mistake for free. Write what was asked.

2. Do not rely on the SoSe25 leniency. The official solution to SoSe25 P2a accepts four versions of the clt and then admits in a printed bracket: "[We'll count all of these as correct even though the ones for \(S_n\) and \(\bar X_n\) are mathematically incorrect.]" The two wrong ones are \(S_n\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(n\mu,n\sigma^2)\) and \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n})\): a limit law cannot depend on \(n\), because the limit is what is left after \(n\) has gone to infinity. That was leniency by one corrector on one paper. Write the standardised version, \(Z_n=\frac{S_n-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1)\), which is correct and is what Theorem 2.64 says.

The drills below are prompts. Cover the solution, write the full statement on paper as you would in the exam, then compare word by word with the model answer — which uses the script's numbering and wording. Three of them have been asked; the rest are results of the same kind and weight that a paper could ask for in the same slot.

State it — the limit theorems (§2.4)

State the strong law of large numbers with all required assumptions WiSe25 · P2a · 3 credits

Model answer

Assumptions (Theorem 2.62):

  • \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) is a sequence of iid random variables (independent and identically distributed, Definition 1.79);
  • with finite mean \(\E[X_i]=\mu<\infty\).

Notation. \(\bar X_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) is the sample mean.

Conclusion. \[ \bar X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}\mu . \]

In words: for iid observations with a finite mean, the sample average converges to the true mean for almost every possible infinite sequence of outcomes.

Marking anatomy (by analogy with the SoSe26 P3a scheme): one credit for "iid", one for "finite mean", one for the conclusion with the \(a.s.\) arrow named. Writing \(\xrightarrow{\P}\) instead of \(\xrightarrow{a.s.}\) turns the strong law into the weak law and loses the third credit. There is no variance assumption — adding "finite variance" is an unasked extra that is also wrong as a description of the theorem.

State the weak law of large numbers with all required assumptions my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Assumptions (Theorem 2.61):

  • \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) is a sequence of identically distributed random variables (Definition 1.54) — note: not "iid";
  • with finite mean \(\E[X_i]=\mu<\infty\);
  • that are pairwise uncorrelated, i.e. \(\Cov[X_i,X_j]=0\) for all \(i\ne j\).

Conclusion. With \(\bar X_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\), \[ \bar X_n\xrightarrow{\P}\mu . \]

In words: for identically distributed, pairwise uncorrelated observations with a finite mean, the probability that the sample average is further than any fixed \(\epsilon\) from the true mean tends to \(0\).

Why this one is worth preparing even though it has never been asked directly: its assumption list is precisely the content of WiSe25 P1d (3 credits), and Remark 2.63 compares it with the slln. The differences to memorise: the slln needs full iid and delivers the stronger \(a.s.\) mode; the wlln needs only pairwise uncorrelated and delivers the weaker \(\P\) mode. Neither needs a finite variance — that assumption appears only in the script's proof sketch of Theorem 2.61, not in its statement.

State the central limit theorem with all required assumptions SoSe25 · P2a · 3 credits

Model answer

Assumptions (Theorem 2.64):

  • \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) is a sequence of iid random variables;
  • with finite mean \(\E[X_i]=\mu\);
  • and finite, non-zero variance \(\Var[X_i]=\sigma^2\in\R_{>0}\).

Notation. \(S_n:=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) is the sum and \(\bar X_n=S_n/n\) the sample mean. Consider the standardised sum \[ Z_n=\frac{S_n-\E[S_n]}{\sqrt{\Var[S_n]}}=\frac{S_n-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}=\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} . \] (The three expressions are the same number: \(\E[S_n]=n\mu\) by linearity, Proposition 2.4(i), and \(\Var[S_n]=n\sigma^2\) by independence, Proposition 2.8(iv), so \(\sqrt{\Var[S_n]}=\sigma\sqrt n\); dividing numerator and denominator of the middle expression by \(n\) gives the right-hand one.)

Conclusion. \[ Z_n\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1) . \]

In words: however the individual \(X_i\) are distributed, once you centre the sum at its mean and divide by its standard deviation, the resulting quantity looks more and more like a standard normal.

The non-zero variance matters because the standardisation divides by \(\sigma\): with \(\sigma=0\) every \(X_i\) is the constant \(\mu\) (Proposition 2.8(i)) and \(Z_n\) is not defined. That is why the script writes \(\sigma^2\in\R_{>0}\) and not merely \(\sigma^2<\infty\).

Write the standardised version. See the warning box above: the official SoSe25 solution also accepted \(S_n\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(n\mu,n\sigma^2)\) and \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)\) while admitting in print that both are mathematically incorrect, because a limit cannot depend on \(n\). A fourth accepted version is correct: \(\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\).

State it — the modes of convergence (§2.4)

Give the full definition, including the set-up, of almost sure convergence WiSe25 · P2b · 3 credits

Model answer

Set-up (Definition 2.56): let \((X_n)_{n\in\N}\) be a sequence of random variables and let \(X\) be another random variable (which may also be a constant), all defined on the same probability space \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\).

Definition (ii). The sequence \((X_n)_{n\in\N}\) converges almost surely [fast sicher] to \(X\), written \(X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}X\) or \(X_n\to X\) a.s., if \[ \P\Bigl(\bigl\{\omega\in\Omega \;\bigm|\; \lim_{n\to\infty}X_n(\omega)=X(\omega)\bigr\}\Bigr)=1 . \]

In words: collect all the outcomes \(\omega\) for which the ordinary sequence of numbers \(X_1(\omega),X_2(\omega),\dots\) converges to the number \(X(\omega)\). Almost sure convergence says that this set of outcomes has probability \(1\) — the sequence converges pointwise except possibly on a set we never see.

The two things that are marked and are easy to drop. (1) The common probability space: the definition compares \(X_n(\omega)\) with \(X(\omega)\) at the same \(\omega\), so both must be functions on the same \(\Omega\). (2) The exceptional-set clause, i.e. the probability of the convergence set being \(1\) rather than the convergence happening for every \(\omega\). Writing "\(\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n=X\)" without the \(\P(\cdot)=1\) wrapper is not this definition.

Give the full general definition of convergence in distribution SoSe25 · P2b · 3 credits

Model answer

Set-up (Definition 2.56): let \((X_n)_{n\in\N}\) be a sequence of random variables and let \(X\) be another random variable.

Definition (iii). \((X_n)_{n\in\N}\) converges in distribution (or converges weakly) [in Verteilung] to \(X\), written \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\) or \(X_n\Rightarrow X\), if \[ \lim_{n\to\infty}F_{X_n}(x)=F_X(x) \] for every \(x\in\R\) at which \(F_X\) is continuous. Here \(F_Z(x)=\P(Z\le x)\) is the cdf of \(Z\) (Definition 1.56). Equivalently (also Definition 2.56(iii)): \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi_{X_n}(t)=\phi_X(t)\) for all \(t\in\R\), where \(\phi\) is the characteristic function of Definition 2.46.

In words: the shape of the distribution of \(X_n\) settles down to the shape of the distribution of \(X\). Nothing is claimed about the individual outcomes.

The continuity clause is the marked part. Without it the definition would be wrong. Example: \(X_n:=\frac1n\) (a constant) and \(X:=0\). Then \(F_{X_n}(0)=\P(\frac1n\le0)=0\) for every \(n\), while \(F_X(0)=\P(0\le0)=1\), so the cdfs do not converge at \(x=0\) — and \(x=0\) is exactly where \(F_X\) jumps, hence is not a continuity point. Everywhere else they do converge, so \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}0\) as it should.

Where the official solution goes slightly beyond the question. The published SoSe25 P2b answer demands that \((X_n)\) and \(X\) live on the same probability space. Convergence in distribution does not need that — it is a statement about cdfs only, and the variables may be defined on completely different spaces. The script's Definition 2.56 does set up all three modes on a common space at once, so quoting it that way is safe; it is just not a requirement of this particular mode, and the question asked for the "full general definition". Say the clause if you are quoting Definition 2.56's set-up, but know that it is not what makes this mode work.

Give the full definition of convergence in probability my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Set-up (Definition 2.56): let \((X_n)_{n\in\N}\) be a sequence of random variables and let \(X\) be another random variable (possibly a constant), all defined on the same probability space \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\).

Definition (i). \((X_n)_{n\in\N}\) converges in probability [in Wahrscheinlichkeit] to \(X\), written \(X_n\xrightarrow{\P}X\), if for every \(\epsilon>0\) \[ \lim_{n\to\infty}\P\bigl(|X_n-X|\ge\epsilon\bigr)=0 . \]

In words: for large \(n\) it is very unlikely that \(X_n\) is far from \(X\). "Far" is measured by a tolerance \(\epsilon\) that you are allowed to choose as small as you like, and the probability of exceeding it must vanish for each such choice.

The two marked details. (1) The quantifier "for every \(\epsilon>0\)" comes before the limit — a single \(\epsilon\) is not enough. (2) The probability is of the event \(\{|X_n-X|\ge\epsilon\}\), which requires \(X_n\) and \(X\) on a common space so that the difference is a random variable at all. This is the mode that appears in the wlln (Theorem 2.61) and in the definition of a consistent estimator (Definition 3.20(ii)).

State the relations between the three modes of convergence my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Remark 2.57. For random variables \((X_n)_{n\in\N}\) and \(X\) on a common probability space, \[ X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}X \;\Longrightarrow\; X_n\xrightarrow{\P}X \;\Longrightarrow\; X_n\xrightarrow{d}X . \] In words: almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution.

The three things Remark 2.57 adds, which are the examinable part.

  • The opposite implications generally do not hold. Example 2.58 (the "travelling bump" on \([0,1]\)) converges in probability but not almost surely; Example 2.59 (\(U\sim\Ber(0.5)\), \(X_n:=U\), \(X:=1-U\)) converges in distribution but not in probability.
  • A subsequence survives: whenever \(X_n\xrightarrow{\P}X\), there exists a subsequence of \((X_n)\) that converges to \(X\) almost surely.
  • Constant limits are special: if \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}c\) for some \(c\in\R\), then also \(X_n\xrightarrow{\P}c\). So for a constant limit the two modes coincide. This is the fact behind SoSe26 P1d.

Why this is worth having on the A4 sheet: a convergence-mode question appears in all three papers (WiSe25 P1d and P2b; SoSe25 P2b; SoSe26 P1d and P2a), and the ladder plus its two exceptions answers most of them in one line.

State it — the three inequalities (§2.2)

State Jensen's inequality with all required assumptions SoSe26 · P3a · 3 credits

Model answer

Assumptions (Theorem 2.42):

  • Let \(X\) be a random variable such that \(\E[X]\) is finite.
  • Let \(g:\R\to\R\) be a convex function — that is, for all \(x_1,x_2\in\R\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \(g(tx_1+(1-t)x_2)\le t\,g(x_1)+(1-t)\,g(x_2)\).

Conclusion. \[ \E[g(X)]\ge g(\E[X]) . \]

In words: for a convex function, applying the function and then averaging gives at least as much as averaging and then applying the function.

The printed marking scheme: "1 point for \(X\) with finite expectation; 1 point for \(g:\R\to\R\) convex; 1 point for the correct inequality." Two credits out of three are for the two hypotheses — write them as two separate lines.

What the script adds and the scheme explicitly does not grade: if \(g\) is strictly convex, equality holds if and only if \(X=\E[X]\) with probability \(1\) (i.e. \(X\) is constant); if \(g\) is concave, the inequality reverses to \(\E[g(X)]\le g(\E[X])\). The published scheme says "the parenthetical additions are not graded", so these earn nothing — include them only if you are certain of them.

Getting the direction right under pressure. Test with \(g(x)=x^2\), which is convex: Jensen gives \(\E[X^2]\ge(\E[X])^2\), which is true because the difference is \(\Var[X]\ge0\) (Remark 2.6 and Proposition 2.8(i)). If your version of the inequality contradicts that, you have written it backwards.

State Markov's inequality with all required assumptions my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

The script's general form (Theorem 2.38). Let \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\) be a probability space, let \(X:\Omega\to\R\) be a random variable, and let \(f:S_X\to\R_{\ge0}\) be monotonically increasing, where \(S_X=\operatorname{im}(X)=X(\Omega)\subseteq\R\) is the set of values \(X\) can take. Then for each \(\epsilon\in\R\) with \(f(\epsilon)>0\), \[ \P(X\ge\epsilon)\le\frac{1}{f(\epsilon)}\,\E[f(X)] . \]

The special case everyone uses, which the script states immediately after: let \(X\) be a non-negative random variable, i.e. \(\P(X\ge0)=1\). Then for any constant \(\epsilon>0\), \[ \P(X\ge\epsilon)\le\frac{\E[X]}{\epsilon} . \]

In words: a non-negative quantity cannot be far above its mean very often, because the rare large values already have to be paid for inside the average.

Assumptions worth one credit each: \(X\) non-negative (or, in the general form, \(f\) monotonically increasing into \(\R_{\ge0}\)); \(\epsilon>0\) (or \(f(\epsilon)>0\)); the expectation exists. Dropping non-negativity makes the statement false — see the drill "Markov without non-negativity" above, where the bound goes negative.

Where it has been used: SoSe26 P4d (3 credits), where the event \(\{|Z_n|\ge a\}\) is first rewritten as \(\{Z_n^2\ge a^2\}\) so that a non-negative variable is being bounded, giving \(\P(|Z_n|\ge a)\le\E[Z_n^2]/a^2\).

State Chebyshev's inequality with all required assumptions my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Assumptions (Theorem 2.40): let \(X\) be a random variable with finite mean \(\E[X]\) and finite variance \(\Var[X]>0\). Let \(\epsilon>0\).

Conclusion. \[ \P\bigl(|X-\E[X]|\ge\epsilon\bigr)\le\frac{\Var[X]}{\epsilon^2} . \]

In words: the probability of being at least \(\epsilon\) away from the mean is at most the variance divided by \(\epsilon^2\). Doubling the tolerance quarters the bound.

How it follows from Markov (the script's proof, worth knowing because it shows what the assumptions are for): put \(f(x)=x^2\) in Theorem 2.38 to get \(\P(|X|\ge\epsilon)\le\epsilon^{-2}\E[X^2]\), then substitute \(Y:=X-\E[X]\), so that \(\P(|X-\E[X]|\ge\epsilon)\le\epsilon^{-2}\E[(X-\E[X])^2]=\epsilon^{-2}\Var[X]\), the last equality being Definition 2.5.

Compared with Markov: Chebyshev needs more information (both mean and variance) and in exchange gives a bound that decays like \(1/\epsilon^2\) rather than \(1/\epsilon\), so it is usually tighter. This comparison is itself a credit — WiSe25 P4d is one whole credit for saying that Chebyshev is a valid but loose guarantee while the clt is only approximate but far sharper.

Where it has been used: WiSe25 P4b (3 credits) and SoSe25 P5c (4 credits). The second one shows the standard rearrangement: "\(X\) lies in \([\E[X]\pm k]\) with probability at least 90 %" becomes \(\P(|X-\E[X]|>k)\le0.1\), and then \(\Var[X]/k^2=0.1\) is solved for \(k\).

State it — definitions from Chapters 1 and 2

Define a σ-algebra my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Definition 1.6. Let \(\Omega\) be a set and \(\pow(\Omega)\) its power set (the collection of all subsets of \(\Omega\)). We call \(\Aa\subseteq\pow(\Omega)\) a σ-algebra on \(\Omega\) if

  1. \(\Omega\in\Aa\);
  2. for each \(A\in\Aa\) we have \(A^c\in\Aa\) (closure under complements, where \(A^c=\Omega\setminus A\));
  3. for each sequence \((A_i)_{i\in\N}\) in \(\Aa\) we have \(\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i\in\Aa\) (closure under countable unions).

In words: a σ-algebra is a list of the subsets we are allowed to assign a probability to, and the list must be closed under the operations "not" and "at least one of countably many".

Immediate consequences worth one line (Corollary 1.10): \(\emptyset=\Omega^c\in\Aa\), and \(\Aa\) is also closed under countable intersections, differences and symmetric differences — these follow from (i)–(iii) via de Morgan's laws (Lemma 1.3).

Why this one is on the list: σ-algebra axioms have carried 6 credits of true/false material (WiSe25 P1a, SoSe26 P2b), and both marking notes reward naming the failing axiom by number. You cannot name a numbered axiom you have not memorised in numbered form.

State the law of total probability and Bayes' rule my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Prerequisite definition (Definition 1.69): for events \(A,B\in\Aa\) with \(\P(B)>0\), the conditional probability [bedingte Wahrscheinlichkeit] of \(A\) given \(B\) is \(\P(A\mid B)=\frac{\P(A\cap B)}{\P(B)}\).

Theorem 1.70(ii) — law of total probability. Let \(B\in\Aa\) with \(\P(B)>0\), let \(I\) be a countable index set, and let \(\{B_i\mid i\in I\}\subseteq\Aa\) be a measurable partition of \(B\), i.e. \(\bigcup_{i\in I}B_i=B\) and \(B_i\cap B_j=\emptyset\) for all \(i\ne j\). Then for all \(A\in\Aa\), \[ \P(A\cap B)=\sum_{i\in I}\P(A\mid B_i)\,\P(B_i) . \] (Taking \(B=\Omega\) gives the familiar form \(\P(A)=\sum_i\P(A\mid B_i)\P(B_i)\).)

Theorem 1.70(iii) — Bayes' rule. For each \(A\in\Aa\) with \(\P(A)>0\) and every measurable partition \(\{B_i\mid i\in I\}\) of \(\Omega\) with \(\P(B_i)>0\) for all \(i\), \[ \P(B_i\mid A)=\frac{\P(A\mid B_i)\,\P(B_i)}{\sum_{j\in I}\P(A\mid B_j)\,\P(B_j)}\qquad\text{for all }i\in I . \]

In words: total probability says "split the world into cases, price the event inside each case, and weight by how likely each case is". Bayes says "to reverse a conditional, multiply by the prior and divide by the total probability you just computed".

The assumptions that are marked: the \(B_i\) must be disjoint and must cover; every conditioning event must have strictly positive probability, otherwise Definition 1.69 does not apply.

Where it has been used: WiSe25 P6a and P6b (6 credits), SoSe26 P5a (3 credits).

State the inclusion–exclusion principle my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Theorem 1.22. Let \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\) be a probability space and let \(A_1,\dots,A_n\in\Aa\) be any finite collection of events, \(n\in\N_{>0}\). Then \[ \P\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^nA_i\Bigr)=\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^{k-1}\!\!\sum_{1\le i_1<\dots<i_k\le n}\!\! \P\bigl(A_{i_1}\cap\dots\cap A_{i_k}\bigr) . \]

Unpacking the double sum. The outer sum runs over the size \(k\) of the intersections; the inner sum runs over all choices of \(k\) distinct indices in increasing order. The sign \((-1)^{k-1}\) is \(+\) for odd \(k\) and \(-\) for even \(k\). For \(n=3\) it reads \[ \P(A_1\cup A_2\cup A_3)=\P(A_1)+\P(A_2)+\P(A_3)-\P(A_1\cap A_2)-\P(A_1\cap A_3)-\P(A_2\cap A_3)+\P(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3). \]

In words: add the single probabilities, subtract the overlaps you double-counted, add back the triple overlaps you over-subtracted, and so on with alternating signs.

No assumptions beyond measurability. There is no independence assumption — that is exactly why the formula is needed when the events overlap in a structured way.

Where it has been used: WiSe25 P6c (4 credits), the only appearance in the three papers.

Two typesetting slips in that official solution. It writes "\(\P(E_{13}\cup E_{14}\cup E_{14})\)", where the last term should be \(E_{24}\); and the bracket opened after the minus sign closes only after the triple-intersection term, so as printed the triple term is subtracted instead of added. The following line has the signs right and the final answer \(p(2q+p-2pq)\) is correct, but do not copy the typeset line.

Define independence of random variables my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Definition 1.77. There are three equivalent-in-practice formulations; give the one matching the kind of variables in the question.

  1. General (via cdfs). A family \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) of real-valued random variables is independent if for each finite subset \(J\subseteq I\) and all \(x_j\in\R\) (\(j\in J\)), \[ \P\Bigl(\bigcap_{j\in J}\{X_j\le x_j\}\Bigr)=\prod_{j\in J}\P(X_j\le x_j) . \] For \(I=[n]\) this is equivalent to the cdf factorising: \(F_{(X_1,\dots,X_n)}(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{i\in[n]}F_{X_i}(x_i)\) for all \(x\in\R^n\).
  2. Discrete (via pmfs). \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) taking values in discrete sets are independent if the pmf factorises: \(p_{(X_1,\dots,X_n)}(s)=\prod_{i\in[n]}p_{X_i}(s_i)\) for all \(s\in\prod_{i\in[n]}\Omega_i\).
  3. Continuous (via pdfs). For a continuous random vector, \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are independent if the pdf factorises: \(p_X(x)=\prod_{i\in[n]}p_{X_i}(x_i)\) for Lebesgue-almost all \(x\in\R^n\) (i.e. everywhere except on a set of Lebesgue measure zero).

The clause that is easy to drop: "for each finite subset \(J\)". Independence of an infinite family is defined through its finite sub-families, never through an infinite product.

And the related definition (Definition 1.79): a sequence or collection of random variables is iid [uiv, unabhängig und identisch verteilt] if it is independent and all members have the same distribution. Both halves are needed, and forgetting that "\(X_1,X_2,\dots\sim\Poi(2)\)" gives only the second half is exactly the trap of WiSe25 P1d.

State the law of total expectation and the law of total variance my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Prerequisite (Definition 2.30): \(\E[Y\mid X]\) is the random variable \(h(X)\), where \(h(x)=\E[Y\mid X=x]\) is the conditional expectation of Definition 2.28. Similarly \(\Var[Y\mid X]\) is the random variable built from \(\Var[Y\mid X=x]\) (Definition 2.34).

Theorem 2.32 — law of total expectation (also: tower property, iterated expectation). For any two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), assuming the relevant expectations exist, \[ \E[Y]=\E\bigl[\E[Y\mid X]\bigr] . \]

Theorem 2.35 — law of total variance. For any two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), assuming the relevant expectations and variances exist, \[ \Var[Y]=\E\bigl[\Var[Y\mid X]\bigr]+\Var\bigl[\E[Y\mid X]\bigr] . \] The script's own restatement: "the total variance is the expected conditional variance plus the variance of the conditional expectation".

In words: to get the overall mean, average the group means. To get the overall spread, add the average within-group spread to the spread between the group means.

The assumption to state: existence of the relevant expectations and variances — that is all the script asks for. No independence, no finiteness of anything else.

Where it has been used: WiSe25 P1b (3 credits) is Theorem 2.35 plus the single observation that a variance is non-negative.

Define the characteristic function and state its main properties my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Definition 2.46. Let \(X\) be a random variable. Its characteristic function (cf), denoted \(\phi_X(t)\), is \[ \phi_X(t)=\E\bigl[e^{itX}\bigr]=\E\bigl[\cos(tX)+i\sin(tX)\bigr],\qquad t\in\R, \] where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\). For discrete \(X\) with pmf \(p_X\): \(\phi_X(t)=\sum_xe^{itx}p_X(x)\); for continuous \(X\) with pdf \(p_X\): \(\phi_X(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{itx}p_X(x)\,dx\).

No assumptions are needed. The script notes that the cf always exists, for every random variable and every \(t\), because \(|e^{itX}|=\sqrt{\cos^2(tX)+\sin^2(tX)}=1\), so the expectation is of a bounded function. That is worth saying: it is the one place in the course where a transform needs no integrability hypothesis at all.

Properties (Remark 2.47), the examinable ones:

  1. \(\phi_X(0)=1\) and \(|\phi_X(t)|\le1\);
  2. affine scaling: \(\phi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\phi_X(at)\);
  3. moments from derivatives: \(\E[X^n]=i^{-n}\phi_X^{(n)}(0)\), if the moments exist;
  4. independence: if \(X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\), then \(\phi_{X+Y}(t)=\phi_X(t)\phi_Y(t)\);
  5. uniqueness: the cf determines the distribution;
  6. Lévy's continuity theorem: \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\) if and only if \(\phi_{X_n}(t)\to\phi_X(t)\) pointwise for all \(t\) and \(\phi_X\) is continuous at \(t=0\).

Where they have been used: SoSe26 P1c (1 credit, properties (ii) and (iv)), P4a (1 credit, the definition plus Euler's formula), P4b (3 credits, (ii) and (iv) combined into \(\phi_{Z_n}(t)=\phi_{X_1}(t/\sqrt n)^n\)), P4c (2 credits, property (iii) as an accepted alternative route to mean and variance).

State the change-of-variables formula for densities my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Proposition 2.51. Assumptions:

  • \(X\) is a continuous random variable with density \(p_X\);
  • \(g:\R\to\R\) is continuously differentiable and strictly monotonic on the support \(S_X:=\{x\in\R\mid p_X(x)>0\}\) of \(X\);
  • \(Y:=g(X)\).

Conclusion. The pdf of \(Y\) is \[ p_Y(y)=p_X\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr)\,\Bigl|\tfrac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\Bigr|\qquad\text{for }y\in g(S_X), \] and \(p_Y(y)=0\) for \(y\notin g(S_X)\).

In words: to find the density of a transformed variable, evaluate the old density at the point that \(g\) came from, and multiply by how much \(g^{-1}\) stretches or compresses the axis there. The absolute value is there because a density can never be negative, even when \(g\) is decreasing.

The two assumptions that are the whole content: strict monotonicity (so that \(g^{-1}\) exists on the relevant range) and continuous differentiability (so that the derivative of \(g^{-1}\) exists and is continuous). Without monotonicity the formula needs a sum over all pre-images.

The support clause is separately worth credit. WiSe25 P3a prints "Be sure to correctly specify the support of \(X\)", and the statement "\(p_Y(y)=0\) off \(g(S_X)\)" is part of the answer, not an afterthought.

Where it has been used: SoSe25 P3d (3 credits) — where the exam supplied the formula as a hint, which tells you the examiner does not regard it as recall — and WiSe25 P3a (4 credits), where the cdf route was used instead.

State it — definitions from Chapter 3

Define bias, variance and mean squared error of an estimator my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Set-up (Definition 3.18): an estimator \(\hat\theta\) for a parameter \(\theta\) is a statistic — a function of the sample \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) alone — used as a guess for \(\theta\). All expectations below are under \(\P_\theta\).

Definition 3.20.

  • (i) Bias. \(\operatorname{bias}[\hat\theta]=\E[\hat\theta]-\theta\). The estimator is unbiased if \(\operatorname{bias}[\hat\theta]=0\), i.e. \(\E[\hat\theta]=\theta\) for all \(\theta\in\Theta\).
  • (ii) Consistency. \(\hat\theta_n\) is consistent if \(\hat\theta_n\xrightarrow{\P}\theta\), and strongly consistent if \(\hat\theta_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}\theta\).
  • (iii) Variance. \(\Var[\hat\theta]=\E[(\hat\theta-\E[\hat\theta])^2]\).
  • (iv) Mean squared error. \[ \operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta]=\E\bigl[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2\bigr] =\Var[\hat\theta]+\bigl(\operatorname{bias}[\hat\theta]\bigr)^2 , \] the bias–variance decomposition.

The distinction that is marked: \(\Var[\hat\theta]\) measures spread around \(\E[\hat\theta]\) (wherever that is), while \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta]\) measures spread around the true \(\theta\). They agree exactly when the estimator is unbiased — the sentence "since the estimator is unbiased, \(\operatorname{mse}=\Var\)" is what WiSe25 P5c and SoSe25 P4b turn on.

The quantifier in (i) is part of the definition: unbiasedness must hold for every \(\theta\in\Theta\), not just for the true one — an estimator that happens to be right on average at one parameter value is not unbiased.

Define the likelihood function and the maximum likelihood estimator my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Definition 3.13 — likelihood. Let \((X_1,\dots,X_n)\) be a random sample from a statistical model \((\Omega,\Aa,\P_\Theta)\) in which every \(\P_\theta\) has a pmf or density \(p_\theta(\cdot)=p(\cdot\mid\theta)\). Given observed data \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\), the likelihood function [Likelihood-Funktion] is \[ L(\cdot\mid x):\Theta\to\R_{\ge0},\qquad \theta\mapsto L(\theta\mid x):=p_\theta(x)=p(x_1,\dots,x_n\mid\theta) . \] If \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are iid, then \(L(\theta\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i\mid\theta)\). The log-likelihood is \(\ell(\theta\mid x):=\ln\bigl(L(\theta\mid x)\bigr)\).

Definition 3.27 — mle. The maximum likelihood estimator \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{mle}}\) is the value of \(\theta\in\Theta\) maximising the likelihood: \[ \hat\theta_{\mathrm{mle}}(x)\in\arg\max_{\theta\in\Theta}L(\theta\mid x)=\arg\max_{\theta\in\Theta}\ell(\theta\mid x) . \] If \(\ell\) is differentiable and the maximum lies in the interior of \(\Theta\), it can often be found by solving the likelihood equation \(\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta\mid x)=0\).

The two details that are marked. (1) The likelihood is a function of \(\theta\), for fixed observed data — Remark 3.14 stresses this, and it is why \(L\) does not exist without data. (2) The product form needs the iid assumption; without it the joint density does not factorise. (3) Maximising \(\ell\) and maximising \(L\) give the same argmax because \(\ln\) is strictly increasing on \((0,\infty)\) — that sentence is itself worth a credit in SoSe26 P3b's marking scheme, in a different context.

Where it has been used: WiSe25 P4a (4 credits), SoSe25 P4a (4 credits), SoSe26 P5b (3 credits) — an mle derivation appears in all three papers.

Define the significance level of a test, and the two error types my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Set-up (Definition 3.34): let \((\Omega,\Aa,\P_\Theta)\) be a statistical model and let \(\Theta=\Theta_0\,\dot\cup\,\Theta_1\) be a partition of the parameter space into disjoint pieces whose union is \(\Theta\). A statistical test is a measurable map \(\varphi:\Omega^n\to[0,1]\); for a non-randomized test, \(\varphi(x)=1\) is read as rejecting the null hypothesis, and \(\varphi^{-1}(\{1\})\) is the rejection region.

The two errors (Definition 3.34(iv)). A type I error is rejecting \(H_0\) when it is true. A type II error is failing to reject \(H_0\) when it is false.

Definition 3.34(v) — significance level. The significance level (or size) of a test \(\varphi\) is the maximum probability of a type I error, \[ \alpha:=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\E_\theta[\varphi] , \] and \(\varphi\) is called a test at level \(\alpha\) if \(\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\E_\theta[\varphi]\le\alpha\).

Definition 3.34(vi) — power. The power function is \(G_\varphi:\Theta\to[0,1]\), \(\theta\mapsto\E_\theta[\varphi]\). For \(\theta\in\Theta_1\), \(G_\varphi(\theta)\) is the power against \(\theta\), and the probability of a type II error at \(\theta\) is \(\beta(\theta)=1-G_\varphi(\theta)\).

The three words that carry the credits: the supremum is over \(\Theta_0\) (the null set, not the whole parameter space); \(\E_\theta\) is computed as if \(\theta\) were true; and the whole quantity is a property of the procedure, not of the data. SoSe25 P1c is 3 credits for exactly that last point.

Related: Definition 3.43 distinguishes a one-sided test (directional alternative, \(H_1:\theta>\theta_0\) or \(H_1:\theta<\theta_0\), rejection region in one tail) from a two-sided test (\(H_1:\theta\ne\theta_0\), region split between both tails). Both tests ever set on these papers were one-sided.

Define a confidence interval, and say what it does not mean my addition · 3 credits

Model answer

Definition 3.54. A \(100(1-\alpha)\,\%\) confidence interval [Konfidenzintervall] for a parameter of interest \(\gamma(\theta)\in\R\) is an interval with random endpoints \((L(X),U(X))\), computed from the sample \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)\), such that \[ \P_\theta\bigl(L(X)\le\gamma(\theta)\le U(X)\bigr)\ge1-\alpha\qquad\text{for all }\theta\in\Theta . \] The value \(1-\alpha\) is the confidence level.

The sentence the script itself stresses: "the interval is random, while the parameter is treated as a fixed, unknown constant". The "\(\ge\)" and the "for all \(\theta\)" are both part of the definition and both are markable.

What it does not mean (Remark 3.55). It is not "the probability that \(\theta\) lies in this interval is \(95\,\%\)". Once the data are observed, \(L(x)\) and \(U(x)\) are numbers and \(\theta\) is a number; either \(\theta\) is between them or it is not, and no probability is involved. The correct reading is frequentist: if the whole sampling procedure were repeated many times, about \(95\,\%\) of the intervals produced would contain the true fixed \(\theta\). Misreading this is the same error as SoSe25 P1c's misreading of \(\alpha\).

Where it has been used: WiSe25 P5d (2 credits), the Wald interval of Example 3.58, \(\hat p\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}\), with \(z_{\alpha/2}\) left symbolic.

Recall bank summary — 21 statements

Asked so far: the slln (WiSe25 P2a), almost sure convergence (WiSe25 P2b), the clt (SoSe25 P2a), convergence in distribution (SoSe25 P2b), Jensen (SoSe26 P3a) — 15 credits across the three papers. Written by me in the same slot's style: the wlln, convergence in probability, the relations between the modes, Markov, Chebyshev, the σ-algebra axioms, total probability and Bayes, inclusion–exclusion, independence of random variables, the laws of total expectation and total variance, characteristic functions, the change-of-variables formula, bias/variance/mse, likelihood and mle, the significance level, and the confidence interval.

How to drill this bank. Recall is the only part of the exam where repetition beats understanding: write each statement out by hand, close the page, write it again, and compare. Since no formula sheet is handed out and the only aid is your own A4 sheet, everything in this bank either lives on that sheet or lives in your memory. Three of these twenty-one have been asked; which three come next is not knowable, so prepare the shape — set-up, assumptions one per line, conclusion with the mode named — rather than betting on a particular theorem.

The density problem

Two of the three papers put a block literally titled "Density computations" in position 3. It is the most mechanical block on the paper: there is one chain of steps, the chain is always the same, and every link of it is worth credits on its own. If you can run the chain without hesitating you collect nine to eleven credits in about fifteen minutes.

What this slot has been WiSe25 · P3 (11 cr) · SoSe25 · P3 (9 cr) · SoSe26: none

PaperTitle as printedCreditsWhat the parts asked
WiSe 25/26 (retake)Density computations11 (a) 4 — density of \(X=-\frac1\lambda\ln U\) with its support; (b) 4 — a conditional probability \(\P(X\ge10\mid X\ge5)\); (c) 3 — evaluate \(\int_0^1\ln u\,du\) backwards from \(\E[X]\)
SoSe 2025Density computations9 (a) 2 — normalising constant; (b) 2 — cdf; (c) 2 — mean and median; (d) 3 — density of \(Y=\ln X\)
SoSe 2026— (no density block anywhere on the paper)0 Position 3 was "Jensen's inequality", 5 credits. Densities did not appear in any other problem either.

Say this honestly to yourself. The newest of the three papers, SoSe 2026, contains no density computation at all. That is a real disagreement between the papers, not noise. So this block is "asked in 2 of 3 papers so far", and — as everywhere on this page — three papers do not predict the fourth. What makes the chain worth drilling anyway is that its individual steps (normalise, integrate to a cdf, differentiate back, transform) are the same steps used inside the estimation problems, which did appear on all three.

Words and symbols used in this block My addition

  • Probability density function [Wahrscheinlichkeitsdichte], abbreviated pdf, written \(p_X\) (Definition 1.45, §1.3): a function \(p_X:\R\to\R_{\ge0}\) with \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p_X(x)\,dx=1\), whose integral over a set gives the probability of landing in that set: \(\P(X\in[a,b])=\int_a^b p_X(x)\,dx\). A density is not a probability: \(p_X(x)\) may be larger than 1, and \(\P(X=x)=0\) for every single point \(x\).
  • Support [Träger] \(S_X:=\{x\in\R\mid p_X(x)>0\}\) (the notation of Proposition 2.51): the set where the density is not zero — where the random variable can actually land. Outside it you must write "\(p_X(x)=0\) otherwise"; both density problems marked this separately.
  • Cumulative distribution function [Verteilungsfunktion], abbreviated cdf, written \(F_X\) (Definition 1.56): \(F_X(x):=\P(X\le x)\).
