Lemma 1.49 says the two are linked by \(F_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}p_X(t)\,dt\) and \(p_X=F_X'\) — in words, the cdf is the integral of the density and the density is the derivative of the cdf.
  • Expectation [Erwartungswert] \(\E[X]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x\,p_X(x)\,dx\) (Definition 2.1(ii), §2.1): the average value of \(X\), weighted by the density.
  • Median [Median] and \(q\)-quantile [Quantil] (Definition 2.20, §2.1): a number \(x_q\) with \(\P(X\le x_q)\ge q\) and \(\P(X\ge x_q)\ge 1-q\). When \(F_X\) is continuous and strictly increasing on the support, \(x_q\) is the unique solution of \(F_X(x_q)=q\). The median is \(x_{1/2}\).
  • Law of the unconscious statistician, abbreviated lotus (Lemma 2.2): for a function \(g\), \(\E[g(X)]=\int g(x)p_X(x)\,dx\). You may compute the expectation of \(g(X)\) with the density of \(X\); you never need the density of \(g(X)\) for this.
  • \(\Unif(0,1)\): the uniform distribution [Gleichverteilung] on \((0,1)\), density \(p_U(u)=1\) for \(u\in(0,1)\) and 0 otherwise. \(\Exp(\lambda)\): the exponential distribution, density \(\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x\ge0\), mean \(1/\lambda\), variance \(1/\lambda^2\) (Lemma 2.27, §1.3).

The standard chain, step by step

Every density problem the course has set is a walk along the same six links. Some papers ask for links 1–3, some for links 1, 2 and 5. Learn the whole chain; then each part is one link.

Method — the density chain My addition, distilled from the two official solutions

  1. Normalise. A density must integrate to 1 over its stated support only: \(\int_{S}p(x)\,dx=1\). Solve that single equation for the unknown constant. Then check \(p\ge0\) on the support with the constant you found — SoSe25's official solution writes this check out, so it is worth saying. Script Def 1.45
  2. Integrate to the cdf. \(F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}p(t)\,dt\). Write all three branches: \(0\) below the support, the formula on the support, \(1\) above it. Full credit in SoSe25 P3b needs all three. Two sanity checks that cost one second each: \(F\) at the left end of the support must be 0, and at the right end must be 1. Script Lem 1.49(i), Def 1.56
  3. Median and quantiles. Solve \(F(x_q)=q\) on the support and throw away roots outside it. A quadratic will often produce a second, negative root; discarding it with one word ("outside the support") is part of the answer. Script Def 2.20
  4. Mean (and, if asked, variance). \(\E[X]=\int_S x\,p(x)\,dx\), and \(\Var[X]=\E[X^2]-\E[X]^2\) with \(\E[X^2]=\int_S x^2p(x)\,dx\) (Proposition 2.8(i), §2.1). The mean and the median are different numbers unless the density is symmetric — an examiner can ask for both precisely to see whether you know that. Script Def 2.1(ii), Prop 2.8(i)
  5. Transform: the density of \(Y=g(X)\). Two routes, both accepted for full marks:
    • Change of variables (Proposition 2.51): if \(g\) is continuously differentiable and strictly monotonic on the support \(S_X\), then \[p_Y(y)=p_X\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr)\Bigl|\tfrac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\Bigr|\quad\text{for }y\in g(S_X), \qquad p_Y(y)=0\text{ otherwise.}\] The absolute value is what makes a decreasing \(g\) come out with a positive density.
    • cdf route: \(F_Y(y)=\P(g(X)\le y)\); rearrange the inequality into one about \(X\) (flipping it if \(g\) is decreasing), read off \(F_X\), then differentiate. This route is the only one available when \(g\) is not strictly monotonic, for instance \(g(x)=|x-1|\) or \(g(x)=x^2\) on a support straddling 0.
  6. Push the support through \(g\) first, and say so. WiSe25 P3a prints "Be sure to correctly specify the support of \(X\)" and marks it. Do step 6 before step 5: knowing that \(y\) ranges over \(g(S_X)\) tells you which branch of an inverse to take and stops sign errors. Finish with the free check \(\int p_Y(y)\,dy=1\).

In words: fix the constant by making the area 1; sweep the area from the left to get the cdf; cut the cdf at height \(q\) to get quantiles; weight by \(x\) to get the mean; and to move to \(g(X)\), first move the support, then either divide by \(|g'|\) (via the inverse) or chase the inequality through the cdf.

Four traps this block sets My addition

  • Integrating over all of \(\R\) instead of the support. \(\int_0^2 \frac{x}{c}dx=1\) gives \(c=2\); \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\) gives nonsense. The support is in the problem statement — copy it into the integral limits before anything else.
  • Forgetting the absolute value in Proposition 2.51. For \(x=-\frac1\lambda\ln u\) the inverse is \(u=e^{-\lambda x}\) with \(\frac{d}{dx}e^{-\lambda x}=-\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\), which is negative. Its absolute value \(\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) is the density. Without the bars you produce a negative "density".
  • Using Proposition 2.51 when \(g\) is not strictly monotonic on the support. The proposition's hypothesis is not decoration: \(g^{-1}\) has to exist. Check monotonicity out loud, and switch to the cdf route when it fails.
  • Answering with a formula but no support. "\(p_Y(y)=\frac{e^{2y}}{2}\)" is only half the answer; the other half is "for \(y\le\ln 2\), and \(0\) otherwise".

Drill bank — eleven density problems

Drills D1–D7 are the seven sub-parts that have actually been set, each with the credits printed on the paper. Drills D8–D11 are four I wrote in the same style, on four different kinds of density: piecewise linear, triangular, power law, and exponential-type. Work each one with paper only — no calculator is allowed in the exam — then open the solution.

Drill D1 — density of a transformed uniform WiSe25 · P3a · 4 credits

Let \(U\sim\Unif(0,1)\) and fix \(\lambda>0\). Set \(X=g(U)=-\frac1\lambda\ln(U)\). Derive the pdf \(p_X\) of \(X\). Be sure to specify the support of \(X\) correctly.

Solution (4 credits: inverse and its derivative, absolute value, support, final formula)

Step 1 — the density we start from. \(U\sim\Unif(0,1)\) means \(p_U(u)=1\) for \(u\in(0,1)\) and \(p_U(u)=0\) otherwise. So the support is \(S_U=(0,1)\).

Step 2 — push the support through \(g\) (method step 6, done first). The natural logarithm \(\ln\) maps \((0,1)\) onto \((-\infty,0)\): \(\ln u\) is negative for \(0<u<1\), it tends to \(-\infty\) as \(u\downarrow0\) and to \(0\) as \(u\uparrow1\) (Analysis 5.2). Multiplying by \(-\frac1\lambda<0\) flips that interval to \((0,\infty)\). Therefore \[S_X=g(S_U)=(0,\infty).\] The official solution writes \(x\in\R_{\ge0}\); the endpoint 0 has probability 0 either way, so both are accepted.

Step 3 — is \(g\) strictly monotonic there? \(g(u)=-\frac1\lambda\ln u\) has derivative \(g'(u)=-\frac{1}{\lambda u}\), which is strictly negative for \(u\in(0,1)\). So \(g\) is strictly decreasing and continuously differentiable on \(S_U\). Proposition 2.51 applies.

Step 4 — invert. From \(x=-\frac1\lambda\ln u\) multiply both sides by \(-\lambda\): \(-\lambda x=\ln u\). Apply \(\exp\) to both sides (the inverse of \(\ln\)): \(u=e^{-\lambda x}\). So \(g^{-1}(x)=e^{-\lambda x}\).

Step 5 — differentiate the inverse and take the absolute value. By the chain rule, \(\frac{d}{dx}e^{-\lambda x}=-\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\). This is negative, so \(\bigl|\frac{d}{dx}g^{-1}(x)\bigr|=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\).

Step 6 — assemble. Proposition 2.51 gives, for \(x>0\), \[p_X(x)=p_U\bigl(g^{-1}(x)\bigr)\cdot\Bigl|\tfrac{d}{dx}g^{-1}(x)\Bigr| =\underbrace{1}_{\text{because }e^{-\lambda x}\in(0,1)}\cdot\;\lambda e^{-\lambda x}=\lambda e^{-\lambda x},\] and \(p_X(x)=0\) for \(x\le0\). The factor \(p_U(e^{-\lambda x})\) equals 1 exactly because \(x>0\) forces \(e^{-\lambda x}\in(0,1)\), which is where \(p_U\) is 1 — this is the place where the support work pays off.

Answer. \(X\sim\Exp(\lambda)\): \(p_X(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x\ge0\), and \(0\) otherwise.

Free check. \(\int_0^\infty\lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx=\bigl[-e^{-\lambda x}\bigr]_0^\infty=0-(-1)=1\).

What this drill is really teaching. This is the inverse transform construction: feeding a uniform random number through \(F^{-1}\) produces a variable with cdf \(F\). It is how a computer simulates an exponential variable. The guide works the same task from the \(\Exp\) side at §1.3.

Drill D2 — a conditional probability on the exponential WiSe25 · P3b · 4 credits

Use \(X\) from Drill D1 to model the response time (in hours) of your professor to Moodle posts. The probability that you wait at least 5 hours is \(p\in(0,1)\). Given that you have already waited 5 hours, what is the probability that you will wait at least 5 more? The exam's hint: if you could not solve (a), you may assume \(F_X(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x>0\) and 0 otherwise.

Solution (4 credits: tail formula, definition of conditional probability, the intersection step, the answer)

Step 1 — the tail probability. \(\P(X\ge x)=1-\P(X<x)=1-F_X(x)=1-(1-e^{-\lambda x})=e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x\ge0\). (For a continuous variable \(\P(X<x)=\P(X\le x)\), because a single point has probability 0.) In particular \(p=\P(X\ge5)=e^{-5\lambda}\).

Step 2 — the conditional probability. Definition 1.69 (§1.4): for events \(A,B\) with \(\P(B)>0\), \(\P(A\mid B)=\frac{\P(A\cap B)}{\P(B)}\). Here \(A=\{X\ge10\}\) and \(B=\{X\ge5\}\).

Step 3 — the intersection. If \(X\ge10\) then automatically \(X\ge5\), so \(\{X\ge10\}\subseteq\{X\ge5\}\) and therefore \(\{X\ge10\}\cap\{X\ge5\}=\{X\ge10\}\). This is the step that is worth a credit and that people skip.

Step 4 — divide. \[\P(X\ge10\mid X\ge5)=\frac{\P(X\ge10)}{\P(X\ge5)}=\frac{e^{-10\lambda}}{e^{-5\lambda}}=e^{-10\lambda+5\lambda} =e^{-5\lambda}=\P(X\ge5)=p.\] The middle equality is the exponent rule \(\frac{e^{a}}{e^{b}}=e^{a-b}\).

Answer. \(p\). Having waited 5 hours tells you nothing: the remaining wait has the same distribution as a fresh wait.

The official solution's primary route is not supported by the script

The printed solution's first argument is "the exponential distribution is memoryless". The word memoryless does not occur anywhere in the lecture script — the property is never defined or proved there. The official "Alternative", which is exactly Steps 1–4 above, uses nothing but Definition 1.69 and the cdf. Write the alternative. It is four lines and it stands on material the course actually gives you. The guide proves the memorylessness property itself, so you can cite it if you want, at §1.4.

Why 4 credits for four lines. Note the hint: "if you could not solve (a), you may assume the cdf". This part was designed to be reachable even if you failed the harder part (a). Items like this are the best credits-per-minute on the whole paper — never leave one blank.

Drill D3 — evaluate an integral backwards WiSe25 · P3c · 3 credits

With \(X=-\frac1\lambda\ln U\), \(U\sim\Unif(0,1)\), you are given \(\E[X]=\frac1\lambda\). Use these facts to compute \(\int_0^1\ln(u)\,du\) without integrating directly (in particular without integration by parts).

Solution (3 credits: naming lotus, setting up the integral, solving for the unknown integral)

Step 1 — name the tool. The law of the unconscious statistician, lotus (Lemma 2.2, §2.1), says that for a function \(g\) and a continuous variable \(U\) with density \(p_U\), \[\E[g(U)]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}g(u)\,p_U(u)\,du .\] In words: to average \(g(U)\) you weight \(g\) by the density of \(U\); you do not need the density of \(g(U)\).

Step 2 — apply it with \(g(u)=-\frac1\lambda\ln u\) and \(p_U=1\) on \((0,1)\). \[\frac1\lambda=\E[X]=\E[g(U)]=\int_0^1\Bigl(-\frac1\lambda\ln u\Bigr)\cdot 1\,du =-\frac1\lambda\int_0^1\ln(u)\,du,\] where the constant \(-\frac1\lambda\) comes out of the integral by linearity of the integral.

Step 3 — solve for the unknown integral. Multiply both sides by \(-\lambda\): \[-1=\int_0^1\ln(u)\,du .\]

Answer. \(\int_0^1\ln(u)\,du=-1\).

Sanity check (not required, but free). \(\ln u\) is negative on \((0,1)\), so the integral must be negative. It is. And the direct antiderivative \(u\ln u-u\) gives \([u\ln u-u]_0^1=(0-1)-0=-1\) (using \(u\ln u\to0\) as \(u\downarrow0\)) — the same number, obtained the forbidden way.

The general move. An expectation you know + lotus = an integral you did not want to do. The guide works this one in §2.1 at §2.1. It is worth practising in the other direction too: any time an exam hands you \(\E[X]\) "for free", ask what integral that fact evaluates.

Drill D4 — the normalising constant SoSe25 · P3a · 2 credits

Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable with \(p_X(x)=\frac{x}{c}\) for \(x\in[0,2]\) and \(p_X(x)=0\) otherwise, for some \(c\in\R\). Find \(c\) so that \(p_X\) is a valid pdf.

Solution (2 credits: the equation \(\int p=1\) on the support; solving it, plus the non-negativity check)

Step 1 — write the defining equation. Definition 1.45: a pdf integrates to 1. The density is 0 outside \([0,2]\), so the integral over \(\R\) is the integral over \([0,2]\): \[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p_X(x)\,dx=\int_0^2\frac{x}{c}\,dx\stackrel{!}{=}1 .\] (The symbol \(\stackrel{!}{=}\) means "we demand that this equals".)

Step 2 — integrate. The antiderivative of \(x\) is \(\frac{x^2}{2}\), and \(\frac1c\) is a constant that comes out: \[\frac1c\Bigl[\frac{x^2}{2}\Bigr]_0^2=\frac1c\Bigl(\frac{4}{2}-\frac{0}{2}\Bigr)=\frac{2}{c}.\]

Step 3 — solve. \(\frac2c=1\Rightarrow c=2\). So \(p_X(x)=\frac{x}{2}\) on \([0,2]\).

Step 4 — the check the official solution writes out. A pdf must also be non-negative. On \([0,2]\) we have \(x\ge0\) and \(c=2>0\), so \(p_X(x)=\frac x2\ge0\). Both conditions hold, so \(p_X\) is a valid pdf.

Answer. \(c=2\).

Why the sign check matters. The equation \(\int_0^2\frac xc dx=1\) has exactly one solution here, but for a density like \(p(x)=c(1-x^2)\) on \([-2,2]\) the normalising equation can be solved by a \(c\) that makes the density negative somewhere. Then no valid pdf of that shape exists. One sentence buys the credit.

Drill D5 — the cdf, all three branches SoSe25 · P3b · 2 credits

For the \(X\) of Drill D4 (density \(\frac x2\) on \([0,2]\)), determine the cdf \(F_X\).

Solution (2 credits: the middle branch; the two outer branches)

Step 1 — the definition. Lemma 1.49(i): \(F_X(x)=\P(X\le x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}p_X(t)\,dt\).

Branch 1: \(x<0\). On \((-\infty,x]\) the density is identically 0, so \(F_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}0\,dt=0\).

Branch 2: \(0\le x\le2\). The density is 0 on \((-\infty,0)\) and \(\frac t2\) on \([0,x]\), so \[F_X(x)=\int_0^{x}\frac{t}{2}\,dt=\Bigl[\frac{t^2}{4}\Bigr]_0^{x}=\frac{x^2}{4}.\]

Branch 3: \(x>2\). Beyond 2 the density is 0 again, so nothing is added: \(F_X(x)=\int_0^{2}\frac t2dt=\frac{2^2}{4}=1\).

Answer. \[F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<0,\\[2pt]\dfrac{x^2}{4},&0\le x\le2,\\[4pt]1,&x>2.\end{cases}\]

Two free checks. Continuity at the joins: \(\frac{0^2}{4}=0\) matches branch 1, and \(\frac{2^2}{4}=1\) matches branch 3. Differentiating the middle branch gives \(\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x^2}{4}=\frac{2x}{4}=\frac x2=p_X(x)\), which is Lemma 1.49(ii) run backwards.

Full credit needs all three branches. Answering only "\(F_X(x)=x^2/4\)" describes a function that is negative before 0 and larger than 1 after 2 — impossible for a cdf, which is always in \([0,1]\).

Drill D6 — mean and median SoSe25 · P3c · 2 credits

For the same \(X\), calculate the mean and the median.

Solution (2 credits: the mean; the median)

Mean. Definition 2.1(ii): \[\E[X]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x\,p_X(x)\,dx=\int_0^2 x\cdot\frac{x}{2}\,dx=\int_0^2\frac{x^2}{2}\,dx =\Bigl[\frac{x^3}{6}\Bigr]_0^2=\frac{8}{6}=\frac43\approx 1.333 .\] (Antiderivative of \(x^2\) is \(\frac{x^3}{3}\); dividing by the 2 gives \(\frac{x^3}{6}\).)

Median. Definition 2.20: solve \(F_X(m)=\frac12\). Here \(F_X\) is continuous and strictly increasing on \([0,2]\), so the solution is unique: \[\frac{m^2}{4}=\frac12\;\Longrightarrow\;m^2=2\;\Longrightarrow\;m=\pm\sqrt2 .\] The root \(-\sqrt2\) lies outside the support \([0,2]\) and is discarded. So \(m=\sqrt2\approx1.414\).

Answer. \(\E[X]=\frac43\approx1.333\), median \(=\sqrt2\approx1.414\).

In words: the median (1.414) sits to the right of the mean (1.333). The density \(\frac x2\) grows towards 2, so the mass is packed on the right; the long empty stretch near 0 pulls the mean down more than it pulls the median, because the mean weights how far a point is, while the median only counts how many points lie on each side.

The reusable point. Mean and median coincide only for a symmetric density. Whenever an exam asks for both in one breath, it is checking that you do not compute one and write it twice.

Drill D7 — the density of \(Y=\ln X\) SoSe25 · P3d · 3 credits

For the same \(X\) (density \(\frac x2\) on \([0,2]\)), let \(Y=\ln(X)\). Determine the pdf of \(Y\). The exam's hint: you may use the change of variables formula \(p_Y(y)=p_X(g^{-1}(y))\bigl|\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\bigr|\).

Solution (3 credits: the support; the inverse and its derivative; the assembled density)

Step 1 — the support, first. \(X\) lives on \([0,2]\) (more precisely on \((0,2]\), since \(x=0\) has density 0 and probability 0). \(\ln\) is strictly increasing and maps \((0,2]\) onto \((-\infty,\ln 2]\). So \[S_Y=(-\infty,\ln 2],\qquad \ln 2\approx 0.6931 .\]

Step 2 — monotonicity. \(g(x)=\ln x\) has \(g'(x)=\frac1x>0\) on \((0,2]\): strictly increasing and continuously differentiable. Proposition 2.51 applies.

Step 3 — invert. \(y=\ln x\iff x=e^{y}\), so \(g^{-1}(y)=e^{y}\), and \(\frac{d}{dy}e^{y}=e^{y}\), which is positive, so the absolute value changes nothing: \(\bigl|\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\bigr|=e^{y}\).

Step 4 — assemble. For \(y\le\ln2\), \(g^{-1}(y)=e^y\in(0,2]\) lies in the support of \(X\), so \(p_X(e^y)=\frac{e^y}{2}\) and \[p_Y(y)=p_X(e^{y})\cdot e^{y}=\frac{e^{y}}{2}\cdot e^{y}=\frac{e^{2y}}{2},\] using \(e^y\cdot e^y=e^{2y}\).

Answer. \(p_Y(y)=\frac{e^{2y}}{2}\) for \(y\le\ln 2\), and \(p_Y(y)=0\) otherwise.

Free check. \(\int_{-\infty}^{\ln2}\frac{e^{2y}}{2}dy=\Bigl[\frac{e^{2y}}{4}\Bigr]_{-\infty}^{\ln2} =\frac{e^{2\ln2}}{4}-0=\frac{4}{4}=1\), using \(e^{2\ln 2}=(e^{\ln2})^2=2^2=4\).

A wording slip in the official solution

It writes "the support of \(X\) is \([0,2]\), so the support of \(Y\) is \((-\infty,\ln2]\)". Strictly, \(\ln 0\) is not defined, so the map is only defined on \((0,2]\). The conclusion is unaffected because \(\P(X=0)=0\) for a continuous variable, but if you write \((0,2]\) you are being more careful than the model answer, not less.

Drill D8 — a piecewise-linear (trapezoidal) density, full chain My problem, written in the style of SoSe25 P3 · 10 credits

Let \(X\) have density \(p_X(x)=c\,(1+x)\) for \(x\in[0,2]\) and \(p_X(x)=0\) otherwise.

  1. (2 cr) Find \(c\).
  2. (2 cr) Determine the cdf \(F_X\), all branches.
  3. (2 cr) Compute the median and the \(0.9\)-quantile.
  4. (2 cr) Compute \(\E[X]\) and \(\Var[X]\).
  5. (2 cr) Determine the density of \(Y=X^2\), with its support.
Solution

(i) Normalising constant. \[\int_0^2 c(1+x)\,dx=c\Bigl[x+\frac{x^2}{2}\Bigr]_0^2=c\Bigl(2+\frac42\Bigr)=c\,(2+2)=4c\stackrel{!}{=}1 \;\Longrightarrow\;c=\frac14 .\] Non-negativity: on \([0,2]\), \(1+x\ge1>0\) and \(c=\frac14>0\), so \(p_X\ge0\). Valid pdf.

(ii) cdf. For \(0\le x\le2\), \[F_X(x)=\int_0^{x}\frac{1+t}{4}\,dt=\frac14\Bigl[t+\frac{t^2}{2}\Bigr]_0^{x}=\frac{x+\frac{x^2}{2}}{4} =\frac{2x+x^2}{8}.\] (The last step multiplies numerator and denominator by 2.) Hence \[F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<0,\\[2pt]\dfrac{2x+x^2}{8},&0\le x\le 2,\\[4pt]1,&x>2.\end{cases}\] Check: \(F_X(0)=0\) and \(F_X(2)=\frac{4+4}{8}=1\).

(iii) Quantiles. Solve \(\frac{2m+m^2}{8}=q\), i.e. \(m^2+2m-8q=0\). The quadratic formula \(m=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\) with \(a=1,b=2,c=-8q\) gives \[m=\frac{-2\pm\sqrt{4+32q}}{2}=-1\pm\sqrt{1+8q}.\] The minus sign gives a negative number, outside \([0,2]\); discard it. So \(x_q=-1+\sqrt{1+8q}\).

  • Median \(q=\frac12\): \(x_{1/2}=-1+\sqrt{5}=1.236\) (4 significant digits: \(1.236\)).
  • \(q=0.9\): \(x_{0.9}=-1+\sqrt{1+7.2}=-1+\sqrt{8.2}=1.864\).

Both lie in \([0,2]\), as they must.

(iv) Mean and variance. \[\E[X]=\int_0^2 x\cdot\frac{1+x}{4}dx=\frac14\int_0^2(x+x^2)dx=\frac14\Bigl[\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^3}{3}\Bigr]_0^2 =\frac14\Bigl(2+\frac83\Bigr)=\frac14\cdot\frac{14}{3}=\frac{7}{6}\approx1.167 .\] \[\E[X^2]=\frac14\int_0^2(x^2+x^3)dx=\frac14\Bigl[\frac{x^3}{3}+\frac{x^4}{4}\Bigr]_0^2 =\frac14\Bigl(\frac83+4\Bigr)=\frac14\cdot\frac{20}{3}=\frac{5}{3}\approx1.667 .\] By Proposition 2.8(i), \(\Var[X]=\E[X^2]-\E[X]^2=\frac53-\frac{49}{36}=\frac{60-49}{36}=\frac{11}{36}\approx0.3056\).

The median \(1.236\) is again to the right of the mean \(1.167\), for the same reason as in Drill D6: the density rises towards 2.

(v) The density of \(Y=X^2\).

Support first. \(g(x)=x^2\) maps \([0,2]\) onto \([0,4]\), so \(S_Y=[0,4]\).

Monotonicity. \(g'(x)=2x>0\) for \(x\in(0,2]\): strictly increasing on the support. (Note that \(x\mapsto x^2\) would not be monotonic on a support like \([-1,2]\); here it is, because the support sits entirely on the non-negative half-line. Checking this is exactly the hypothesis of Proposition 2.51.)

Invert. \(y=x^2\) with \(x\ge0\) gives \(g^{-1}(y)=\sqrt y\), and \(\frac{d}{dy}\sqrt y=\frac{1}{2\sqrt y}>0\).

Assemble. For \(y\in(0,4]\), \[p_Y(y)=p_X(\sqrt y)\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt y}=\frac{1+\sqrt y}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt y} =\frac{1+\sqrt y}{8\sqrt y},\] and \(p_Y(y)=0\) otherwise.

Check. \(\int_0^4\frac{1+\sqrt y}{8\sqrt y}dy=\frac18\int_0^4\bigl(y^{-1/2}+1\bigr)dy =\frac18\bigl[2\sqrt y+y\bigr]_0^4=\frac18(4+4)=1\).

A second, independent check: by lotus, \(\E[Y]=\E[X^2]=\frac53\), and integrating \(\int_0^4 y\,p_Y(y)\,dy\) gives \(\frac53\) as well.

What earns the credits. (i) the equation \(\int_S p=1\) plus the sign check; (ii) all three branches; (iii) discarding the negative root in one named sentence; (iv) using \(\Var=\E[X^2]-\E[X]^2\) rather than \(\int(x-\E X)^2p\,dx\), which is longer; (v) the support \([0,4]\) written down before anything else, and the absolute value of the derivative written even though it is positive here.

Drill D9 — a triangular density and a non-monotone transform My problem · 10 credits

Let \(X\) have the "tent" density \[p_X(x)=\begin{cases}c\,x,&0\le x\le1,\\ c\,(2-x),&1<x\le2,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]

  1. (2 cr) Find \(c\).
  2. (3 cr) Determine \(F_X\) on all branches, and the \(0.25\)-quantile.
  3. (2 cr) Give \(\E[X]\) and the median with a one-line reason, then compute \(\Var[X]\).
  4. (3 cr) Let \(Y=|X-1|\) (the distance from the peak). Determine \(p_Y\). Explain first why Proposition 2.51 cannot be used.
Solution

(i) The two pieces are triangles. Integrate each: \[\int_0^1 cx\,dx=c\Bigl[\frac{x^2}{2}\Bigr]_0^1=\frac c2,\qquad \int_1^2 c(2-x)\,dx=c\Bigl[2x-\frac{x^2}{2}\Bigr]_1^2=c\Bigl((4-2)-\bigl(2-\tfrac12\bigr)\Bigr)=\frac c2 .\] Total \(\frac c2+\frac c2=c\stackrel{!}{=}1\), so \(c=1\). Non-negativity: \(x\ge0\) on \([0,1]\) and \(2-x\ge0\) on \([1,2]\). Valid pdf.

(ii) cdf. For \(0\le x\le1\): \(F_X(x)=\int_0^x t\,dt=\frac{x^2}{2}\). At \(x=1\) this is \(\frac12\).
For \(1<x\le2\): start from the value already accumulated and add the second piece, \[F_X(x)=\frac12+\int_1^{x}(2-t)\,dt=\frac12+\Bigl[2t-\frac{t^2}{2}\Bigr]_1^{x} =\frac12+\Bigl(2x-\frac{x^2}{2}\Bigr)-\Bigl(2-\frac12\Bigr)=2x-\frac{x^2}{2}-1 .\] Check: at \(x=1\) this gives \(2-\frac12-1=\frac12\) (matches), at \(x=2\) it gives \(4-2-1=1\) (matches). \[F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<0,\\[2pt]\dfrac{x^2}{2},&0\le x\le1,\\[4pt]2x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}-1,&1<x\le2,\\[4pt]1,&x>2.\end{cases}\] \(0.25\)-quantile: since \(F_X(1)=\frac12>0.25\), the answer lies in the first branch. Solve \(\frac{x^2}{2}=0.25\Rightarrow x^2=0.5\Rightarrow x=\sqrt{0.5}=0.7071\) (the negative root is outside the support).

(iii) Mean, median, variance. The density is symmetric about \(x=1\): substituting \(x\mapsto 2-x\) turns \(x\) into \(2-x\) and \(2-x\) into \(x\), which swaps the two pieces. For a density symmetric about a point \(a\), both the mean and the median equal \(a\). So \(\E[X]=1\) and the median is \(1\). (The median also follows directly: \(F_X(1)=\frac12\).)

For the variance, use symmetry again: \(\Var[X]=\E[(X-1)^2]\) because \(\E[X]=1\), and by lotus \[\E[(X-1)^2]=\int_0^1(x-1)^2x\,dx+\int_1^2(x-1)^2(2-x)\,dx=2\int_0^1(x-1)^2x\,dx,\] the two integrals being equal by the symmetry. Now \(\int_0^1(x^2-2x+1)x\,dx=\int_0^1(x^3-2x^2+x)dx=\frac14-\frac23+\frac12=\frac{3-8+6}{12}=\frac1{12}\). Hence \(\Var[X]=2\cdot\frac1{12}=\frac16\approx0.1667\).

(iv) The density of \(Y=|X-1|\).

Why Proposition 2.51 does not apply. Its hypothesis is that \(g\) be strictly monotonic on the support. Here \(g(x)=|x-1|\) is strictly decreasing on \([0,1]\) and strictly increasing on \([1,2]\); it takes the same value at \(x=1-y\) and \(x=1+y\). So \(g^{-1}\) does not exist as a function and the formula is unusable. Use the cdf route.

Support. \(|x-1|\) ranges over \([0,1]\) as \(x\) ranges over \([0,2]\), so \(S_Y=[0,1]\).

cdf route. For \(0\le y\le1\), \[F_Y(y)=\P(|X-1|\le y)=\P(1-y\le X\le 1+y)=F_X(1+y)-F_X(1-y),\] the last equality because \(\P(a\le X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a)\) for a continuous variable (single points have probability 0). Now \(1+y\in[1,2]\) uses the third branch and \(1-y\in[0,1]\) the second: \[F_X(1+y)=2(1+y)-\frac{(1+y)^2}{2}-1,\qquad F_X(1-y)=\frac{(1-y)^2}{2}.\] Subtract, expanding \((1\pm y)^2=1\pm2y+y^2\): \[F_Y(y)=2+2y-\frac{1+2y+y^2}{2}-1-\frac{1-2y+y^2}{2} =1+2y-\frac{(1+2y+y^2)+(1-2y+y^2)}{2}=1+2y-\frac{2+2y^2}{2}=2y-y^2 .\] Check: \(F_Y(0)=0\), \(F_Y(1)=2-1=1\).

Differentiate (Lemma 1.49(ii)): \(p_Y(y)=\frac{d}{dy}(2y-y^2)=2-2y\) for \(y\in[0,1]\), and 0 otherwise.

Check. \(\int_0^1(2-2y)dy=[2y-y^2]_0^1=1\). And \(\E[Y]=\int_0^1y(2-2y)dy=[y^2-\frac23y^3]_0^1=\frac13\approx0.3333\).

In words: folding a symmetric tent in half at its peak gives a right triangle that is highest at 0 — the distance from the peak is most likely to be small.

Why this drill exists. Both past transformation tasks had a monotone \(g\) and handed you the change-of-variables formula. The hypothesis "strictly monotonic" was therefore never tested. A single absolute value or square is all it takes to break it, and the cdf route is the fix. Say the sentence "\(g\) is not injective on the support, so Proposition 2.51 does not apply" out loud — it is a marked step in any reasonable scheme.

Drill D10 — a power-law density with an infinite variance My problem · 10 credits

Let \(X\) have density \(p_X(x)=\dfrac{c}{x^{3}}\) for \(x\ge1\) and \(0\) otherwise.

  1. (2 cr) Find \(c\).
  2. (2 cr) Determine \(F_X\); compute the median and the \(0.9\)-quantile.
  3. (3 cr) Compute \(\E[X]\). Then decide whether \(\Var[X]\) is finite, with a reason.
  4. (3 cr) Determine the density of \(Y=\ln X\) and name the resulting distribution.
Solution

(i) The support is unbounded, so the integral is improper — it is a limit: \[\int_1^{\infty}\frac{c}{x^3}dx=c\lim_{b\to\infty}\Bigl[-\frac{1}{2x^{2}}\Bigr]_1^{b} =c\lim_{b\to\infty}\Bigl(\frac12-\frac{1}{2b^{2}}\Bigr)=\frac c2\stackrel{!}{=}1\;\Longrightarrow\;c=2 .\] (The antiderivative of \(x^{-3}\) is \(\frac{x^{-2}}{-2}=-\frac{1}{2x^2}\), and \(\frac1{2b^2}\to0\).) Non-negativity: \(2/x^3>0\) for \(x\ge1\). Valid pdf.

(ii) For \(x\ge1\): \(F_X(x)=\int_1^{x}\frac{2}{t^{3}}dt=\Bigl[-\frac{1}{t^{2}}\Bigr]_1^{x}=1-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\), and \(F_X(x)=0\) for \(x<1\). (There is no third branch: the support is unbounded, and \(F_X(x)\to1\) as \(x\to\infty\).)

Quantiles: \(1-\frac1{x_q^2}=q\iff x_q^{2}=\frac{1}{1-q}\iff x_q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-q}}\).

  • Median: \(x_{1/2}=\frac1{\sqrt{0.5}}=\sqrt2=1.414\).
  • \(0.9\)-quantile: \(x_{0.9}=\frac1{\sqrt{0.1}}=\sqrt{10}=3.162\).

(iii) Mean, and the variance question. \[\E[X]=\int_1^{\infty}x\cdot\frac{2}{x^{3}}dx=\int_1^{\infty}\frac{2}{x^{2}}dx =2\lim_{b\to\infty}\Bigl[-\frac1x\Bigr]_1^{b}=2\,(0+1)=2 .\] For the second moment, \[\E[X^{2}]=\int_1^{\infty}x^{2}\cdot\frac{2}{x^{3}}dx=\int_1^{\infty}\frac{2}{x}dx =2\lim_{b\to\infty}\bigl[\ln x\bigr]_1^{b}=2\lim_{b\to\infty}\ln b=+\infty .\] The integral \(\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{x}\) diverges (Analysis 8.3). So \(\E[X^{2}]\) is infinite and therefore \(\Var[X]=\E[X^2]-\E[X]^2\) is not finite.

Why this matters beyond this drill

Every limit theorem of §2.4 and every inequality of §2.2 that uses a variance has "finite variance" in its hypothesis list. This \(X\) has a perfectly finite mean but no variance, so Chebyshev's inequality and the central limit theorem cannot be applied to it, while the strong law of large numbers (Theorem 2.62, which only needs a finite mean) still can. That distinction is exactly what Problem 1-style true/false items probe. See §2.2 and §2.4.

(iv) The density of \(Y=\ln X\).

Support. \(\ln\) maps \([1,\infty)\) onto \([0,\infty)\), so \(S_Y=[0,\infty)\).

Monotonicity. \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln x=\frac1x>0\) on \([1,\infty)\): strictly increasing. Proposition 2.51 applies.

Invert and differentiate. \(g^{-1}(y)=e^{y}\), \(\bigl|\frac{d}{dy}e^{y}\bigr|=e^{y}\).

Assemble. For \(y\ge0\), \[p_Y(y)=p_X(e^{y})\cdot e^{y}=\frac{2}{(e^{y})^{3}}\cdot e^{y}=2e^{-3y}e^{y}=2e^{-2y},\] using \((e^y)^3=e^{3y}\) and \(e^{-3y}e^{y}=e^{-2y}\). And \(p_Y(y)=0\) for \(y<0\).

Answer. \(Y=\ln X\sim\Exp(2)\): the exponential distribution with rate \(\lambda=2\). Its mean is \(\frac1\lambda=\frac12\) and its variance \(\frac1{\lambda^{2}}=\frac14\) (Lemma 2.27).

Check. \(\int_0^{\infty}2e^{-2y}dy=[-e^{-2y}]_0^{\infty}=1\).

Two things to take away. First, a transform can turn a variable with no variance into one with every moment finite — taking a logarithm tames a heavy tail. Second, this is Drill D1 run in reverse: there a uniform became exponential, here a power law becomes exponential. Exponentiating an \(\Exp(2)\) variable gives this \(X\) back.

Drill D11 — a shifted exponential, and the transform back to uniform My problem · 11 credits

A machine needs a fixed 2 minutes of set-up and then a random amount of extra time. Model the total time by \(X\) with density \(p_X(x)=c\,e^{-x/3}\) for \(x\ge2\) and \(0\) otherwise.

  1. (2 cr) Find \(c\) and write \(p_X\) in the tidiest form you can.
  2. (2 cr) Determine \(F_X\) and the median.
  3. (2 cr) Compute \(\E[X]\) and \(\Var[X]\).
  4. (2 cr) Compute \(\P(X\ge8\mid X\ge5)\).
  5. (3 cr) Determine the density of \(Y=e^{-(X-2)/3}\), with its support, and name the distribution.
Solution

(i) \[\int_2^{\infty}c\,e^{-x/3}dx=c\lim_{b\to\infty}\bigl[-3e^{-x/3}\bigr]_2^{b}=c\,\bigl(0+3e^{-2/3}\bigr) =3c\,e^{-2/3}\stackrel{!}{=}1\;\Longrightarrow\;c=\frac{e^{2/3}}{3}\approx 0.6494 .\] (The antiderivative of \(e^{-x/3}\) is \(-3e^{-x/3}\), because differentiating it gives \(-3\cdot(-\frac13)e^{-x/3}=e^{-x/3}\).) Substituting back, \[p_X(x)=\frac{e^{2/3}}{3}e^{-x/3}=\frac13\,e^{-(x-2)/3}\quad (x\ge2),\] using \(e^{2/3}e^{-x/3}=e^{-(x-2)/3}\). So \(X\) is an \(\Exp(\frac13)\) variable shifted right by 2.

(ii) For \(x\ge2\), \(F_X(x)=\int_2^{x}\frac13e^{-(t-2)/3}dt=\bigl[-e^{-(t-2)/3}\bigr]_2^{x}=1-e^{-(x-2)/3}\); and \(F_X(x)=0\) for \(x<2\).

Median: \(1-e^{-(m-2)/3}=\frac12\iff e^{-(m-2)/3}=\frac12\). Take \(\ln\) of both sides: \(-\frac{m-2}{3}=\ln\frac12=-\ln2\), so \(m=2+3\ln2\approx 4.079\).

(iii) Write \(X=2+W\) with \(W\sim\Exp(\frac13)\) (the shift). By linearity (Proposition 2.4(i)) and Lemma 2.27, \(\E[W]=\frac{1}{1/3}=3\) and \(\Var[W]=\frac{1}{(1/3)^{2}}=9\). Hence \[\E[X]=2+\E[W]=5,\qquad \Var[X]=\Var[2+W]=\Var[W]=9,\] the last step by Proposition 2.8(iii): adding a constant shifts a variable without spreading it, \(\Var[aX+b]=a^{2}\Var[X]\) with \(a=1\). The standard deviation is \(\sqrt9=3\).

If you prefer the direct route: \(\E[X]=\int_2^\infty x\cdot\frac13e^{-(x-2)/3}dx=5\) by substitution \(w=x-2\), and the same substitution gives \(\Var[X]=9\).

(iv) Tail: \(\P(X\ge x)=1-F_X(x)=e^{-(x-2)/3}\) for \(x\ge2\). Since \(\{X\ge8\}\subseteq\{X\ge5\}\), \[\P(X\ge8\mid X\ge5)=\frac{\P(X\ge8)}{\P(X\ge5)}=\frac{e^{-6/3}}{e^{-3/3}}=\frac{e^{-2}}{e^{-1}}=e^{-1} \approx 0.3679 .\] That is the same as \(\P(X\ge5)\) computed from the shifted start: \(\P(X\ge2+3)=e^{-1}\). The shift does not spoil the "no memory" behaviour once you are past the 2-minute set-up.

(v) The density of \(Y=e^{-(X-2)/3}\).

Support first. As \(x\) runs from 2 to \(\infty\), \(-(x-2)/3\) runs from 0 down to \(-\infty\), so \(e^{-(x-2)/3}\) runs from 1 down to 0. Hence \(S_Y=(0,1]\).

Monotonicity. \(g(x)=e^{-(x-2)/3}\) has \(g'(x)=-\frac13e^{-(x-2)/3}<0\): strictly decreasing and continuously differentiable on \([2,\infty)\). Proposition 2.51 applies — and the absolute value will do real work.

Invert. \(y=e^{-(x-2)/3}\Rightarrow \ln y=-\frac{x-2}{3}\Rightarrow x=2-3\ln y\). So \(g^{-1}(y)=2-3\ln y\), and \(\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)=-\frac3y\), whose absolute value is \(\frac3y\) (positive, since \(y>0\)).

Assemble. For \(y\in(0,1]\), \[p_Y(y)=p_X(2-3\ln y)\cdot\frac3y=\frac13e^{-\frac{(2-3\ln y)-2}{3}}\cdot\frac3y =\frac13e^{\ln y}\cdot\frac3y=\frac13\cdot y\cdot\frac3y=1 .\] Step by step: the exponent is \(-\frac{-3\ln y}{3}=\ln y\); then \(e^{\ln y}=y\); then the \(y\) cancels the \(\frac1y\) and the 3 cancels the \(\frac13\).

Answer. \(p_Y(y)=1\) for \(y\in(0,1]\) and 0 otherwise, that is \(Y\sim\Unif(0,1)\).

This is Drill D1 read backwards. Drill D1 fed a uniform through \(-\frac1\lambda\ln u\) to manufacture an exponential; here an exponential is fed through its own survival function \(x\mapsto\P(X\ge x)\) and a uniform comes out. That is a general fact (the "probability integral transform"): if \(F\) is a continuous cdf then \(F(X)\sim\Unif(0,1)\), and here \(Y=1-F_X(X)\), which is uniform for the same reason. The script's Proposition 2.23 is the statement in the other direction; the exams have never asked for it, but the computation above is exactly the kind they have asked for, with a decreasing \(g\) so that the absolute-value bars matter.

What to have automatic before the exam My addition

  • \(\int_S p=1\) with the limits copied from the support, plus the sentence "and \(p\ge0\) there".
  • The three-branch cdf template, and the two free checks \(F(\text{left end})=0\), \(F(\text{right end})=1\).
  • \(F(x_q)=q\), and one word for why the second root is discarded.
  • \(\E[X]=\int xp\), \(\E[X^2]=\int x^2p\), \(\Var=\E[X^2]-\E[X]^2\).
  • Proposition 2.51 with the monotonicity check and with the absolute value; the cdf route as the fallback when monotonicity fails.
  • The support of the transform, written before the formula.
  • The four standard antiderivatives that have actually been needed: \(x\mapsto\frac{x^{2}}2\), \(x^{2}\mapsto\frac{x^{3}}3\), \(e^{ax}\mapsto\frac{e^{ax}}{a}\), \(x^{-1}\mapsto\ln x\).

The estimation, inequality and limit-theorem chain

This is the part of the paper where §3.1–§3.2 (models and estimators), §2.2 (the inequalities) and §2.4 (the limit theorems) are used together on one model. All three papers so far contain such a chain, each worth 9 to 12 credits, and each ends with a statement about a tail — a probability of being far from the target — which is either bounded (Markov, Chebyshev) or approximated (central limit theorem, abbreviated clt). The content differed every time; the shape did not.

What this slot has been WiSe25 · P4 (11 cr) · SoSe25 · P4 (12 cr) · SoSe26 · P4 (9 cr) + P3 (5 cr)

PaperTitle as printedCrThe chain
WiSe 25/26Rainfall11 (a) 4 derive the mle for \(p_\theta(x)=\theta^{-2}xe^{-x/\theta}\) → (b) 3 Chebyshev bound on \(\P(|\hat\theta-\theta|\ge\epsilon)\) → (c) 3 the same probability by the clt, in terms of \(\Phi\) → (d) 1 compare (b) and (c) in words
SoSe 2025Estimating and testing12 (a) 4 derive the mle for \(\Poi(\lambda)\) → (b) 2 is it unbiased → (c) 2 its approximate law by the clt → (d) 4 a one-sided approximate z-test at \(\alpha=0.05\)
SoSe 2026Characteristic functions and tail bounds9 (a) 1 the characteristic function of \(\P(X=\pm1)=\frac12\) → (b) 3 the characteristic function of \(Z_n=n^{-1/2}\sum X_j\) → (c) 2 \(\E[Z_n]\), \(\Var[Z_n]\) → (d) 3 a Markov bound for \(\P(|Z_n|\ge a)\) plus the clt approximation of the same
SoSe 2026Jensen's inequality (in position 3)5 (a) 3 state Jensen with all assumptions → (b) 2 deduce \(\E[X]\le\log\E[e^{X}]\)

How to read this table. Two of the three papers put a maximum-likelihood derivation here; the third put it in the last problem instead. All three finish with a tail bound or a tail approximation. That is what "has been asked" — and three papers, one of which is a retake with a visibly different shape, do not tell you what the fourth will contain.

Words and symbols used in this block My addition

  • Sample: random variables \(X_1,\dots,X_n\), usually iid [unabhängig und identisch verteilt] — independent and identically distributed. Capital letters are random; the observed numbers are \(x_1,\dots,x_n\). \(\bar X_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\) is the sample mean.
  • Likelihood [Likelihood] (Definition 3.13, §3.1): for iid data, \(L(\theta\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p_\theta(x_i)\) — the density or probability of the data you actually saw, read as a function of the unknown parameter \(\theta\). Log-likelihood \(\ell(\theta\mid x)=\ln L(\theta\mid x)\).
  • Maximum likelihood estimator [Maximum-Likelihood-Schätzer], abbreviated mle (Definition 3.27, §3.2): \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=\arg\max_{\theta\in\Theta}L(\theta\mid x)\) — the parameter value under which the observed data were most likely. \(\arg\max\) means "the argument at which the maximum is attained".
  • Estimator [Schätzer] \(\hat\theta\): any function of the data used as a guess for \(\theta\). Bias [Verzerrung] \(\operatorname{bias}[\hat\theta]=\E_\theta[\hat\theta]-\theta\); unbiased means bias \(=0\); mean squared error \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta]=\E_\theta[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]\) (Definition 3.20, §3.2). The decomposition \(\operatorname{mse}=\Var[\hat\theta]+\operatorname{bias}[\hat\theta]^2\) is the single most-used identity in this block.
  • Consistent [konsistent]: \(\hat\theta_n\xrightarrow{\ \P\ }\theta\), the estimator gets arbitrarily close to the truth in probability as \(n\) grows.
  • Convergence in probability \(\xrightarrow{\P}\) (Definition 2.56(i)): \(\P(|X_n-X|>\epsilon)\to0\) for every \(\epsilon>0\). Almost surely \(\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\) (2.56(ii)): \(\P(\{\omega:\lim_nX_n(\omega)=X(\omega)\})=1\). In distribution \(\xrightarrow{d}\) (2.56(iii)): \(F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x)\) at every \(x\) where \(F_X\) is continuous. See §2.4.
  • Markov (Theorem 2.38): for \(X\ge0\) and \(\epsilon>0\), \(\P(X\ge\epsilon)\le\frac{\E[X]}{\epsilon}\). Chebyshev (Theorem 2.40): \(\P(|X-\E[X]|\ge\epsilon)\le\frac{\Var[X]}{\epsilon^{2}}\). Jensen (Theorem 2.42): for \(g:\R\to\R\) convex and \(\E[X]\) finite, \(\E[g(X)]\ge g(\E[X])\). See §2.2.
  • Characteristic function [charakteristische Funktion], abbreviated cf (Definition 2.46): \(\varphi_X(t)=\E[e^{itX}]\), where \(i\) is the imaginary unit with \(i^{2}=-1\). Euler's formula \(e^{iu}=\cos u+i\sin u\) turns it into ordinary trigonometry for discrete variables. See §2.3.
  • clt (Theorem 2.64): for \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) iid with finite mean \(\mu\) and finite, non-zero variance \(\sigma^{2}\), \(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1)\). \(\Phi\) is the cdf of \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), and \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\) by symmetry. See §2.4.
  • \(\operatorname{mse}\), \(\operatorname{bias}\): written in upright letters, as in the script.

The five recipes this block runs on

Recipe A — derive a maximum likelihood estimator Script Def 3.13, Def 3.27

  1. Write the likelihood as a product: \(L(\theta\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p_\theta(x_i)\). Collect the powers of \(\theta\) and merge the exponentials: \(\prod e^{-x_i/\theta}=e^{-\frac1\theta\sum x_i}\).
  2. Take logs: \(\ell=\ln L\). Logs turn products into sums, and \(\ln\) is strictly increasing, so the maximiser is unchanged — say that sentence, it is the justification for the whole step. Drop additive terms that contain no \(\theta\) (such as \(\sum\ln x_i\) or \(-\ln\prod x_i!\)) and say you are dropping them and why.
  3. Differentiate and set to zero: solve \(\frac{d\ell}{d\theta}=0\) for \(\theta\). Call the solution \(\hat\theta\).
  4. Prove it is a maximum, and a global one. Both official solutions do a second-derivative check. The cleanest complete argument is the sign of \(\ell'\): if \(\ell'>0\) to the left of \(\hat\theta\) and \(\ell'<0\) to the right, then \(\ell\) rises then falls, so \(\hat\theta\) is the global maximum on the parameter set.
  5. If the derivative route cannot work, say so and argue directly. When the parameter appears in the support (as in \(\Unif(0,\theta)\)), \(L\) is discontinuous and \(\frac{d\ell}{d\theta}=0\) has no useful solution; you must read the maximum off the shape of \(L\). This has not been examined yet, and it is the one gap in the two examined mle tasks — Drill E5 below covers it.
  6. If the model is a reparametrisation, find the mle of the easy parameter and then invert the known map (the mle is invariant under a bijective reparametrisation). Check that the result lies in the parameter set.

Recipe B — bias, variance, mse, consistency Script Def 3.20, Prop 2.4(i), Prop 2.8(iii)(iv)

  1. Write the estimator as \(c\sum_iX_i\) or as \(\bar Y_n\) after a linear map.
  2. Mean: constants come out, then linearity (Proposition 2.4(i)): \(\E[\sum X_i]=\sum\E[X_i]\). No independence is needed here — say so, because it is often the difference between a correct and a hand-waving answer.
  3. Variance: constants come out squared (Proposition 2.8(iii), \(\Var[aX]=a^{2}\Var[X]\)), then variances of independent summands add (Proposition 2.8(iv)). Independence is needed here and only here — name it.
  4. mse: \(\operatorname{mse}=\Var+\operatorname{bias}^{2}\). If the bias is 0, then \(\operatorname{mse}=\Var\), one line.
  5. Consistency, the cheap route: if \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_n]\to0\) then \(\hat\theta_n\xrightarrow{\P}\theta\). Reason: Markov applied to the non-negative variable \((\hat\theta_n-\theta)^{2}\) gives \(\P(|\hat\theta_n-\theta|\ge\epsilon)=\P((\hat\theta_n-\theta)^{2}\ge\epsilon^{2}) \le\frac{\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta_n]}{\epsilon^{2}}\to0\). Three lines, and it works for biased estimators too.
  6. If the estimator is a count divided by \(n\), recognise the \(\Bin(n,p)\) behind it and reuse \(\E=np\), \(\Var=np(1-p)\) (Lemma 2.26(iv)) instead of re-deriving.

Recipe C — bound a tail with Markov or Chebyshev Script Thm 2.38, Thm 2.40

  1. Reshape the event. Chebyshev wants \(\{|Y-\E[Y]|\ge\epsilon\}\); Markov wants a non-negative variable over a threshold. For \(\P(|Z|\ge a)\) with \(\E[Z]=0\) the official move is \(\{|Z|\ge a\}=\{Z^{2}\ge a^{2}\}\) followed by Markov on \(Z^{2}\). For "\(X\) lies in \([\E[X]\pm k]\) with probability at least \(90\%\)" the move is \(\P(X\notin[\E X\pm k])\le0.1\iff\P(|X-\E X|>k)\le0.1\).
  2. Compute \(\E[Y]\) and \(\Var[Y]\) (or \(\E[Z^{2}]=\Var[Z]+\E[Z]^{2}\)) as a separate labelled step.
  3. Apply the theorem by name and number.
  4. If a value is wanted, set the bound equal to the allowed failure probability and solve; round in the direction that keeps the inequality true, and say which direction that is and why.

Recipe D — approximate the same tail with the clt Script Thm 2.64

  1. Check the hypotheses out loud: iid, finite mean, finite and non-zero variance.
  2. Standardise: \(\frac{\hat\theta-\E[\hat\theta]}{\sqrt{\Var[\hat\theta]}}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1)\), so for large \(n\), \(\hat\theta\) is approximately \(\mathcal N(\theta,\Var[\hat\theta])\).
  3. Two-sided tail: \(\P(|\hat\theta-\theta|\ge\epsilon)\approx2\Phi\!\left(-\frac{\epsilon}{\text{sd}}\right) =2\Bigl(1-\Phi\bigl(\tfrac{\epsilon}{\text{sd}}\bigr)\Bigr)\), where sd \(=\sqrt{\Var[\hat\theta]}\). Leave \(\Phi\) symbolic. No table has ever been supplied and none is needed.
  4. Use the word approximation. A whole credit (WiSe25 P4d) was for saying that Chebyshev is a valid but loose guarantee decaying like \(1/n\), whereas the clt is only approximate but far sharper.

Recipe E — compute a characteristic function Script Def 2.46, Rem 2.47

  1. Definition: \(\varphi_X(t)=\E[e^{itX}]\). For a finite discrete \(X\), this is the finite sum \(\sum_x e^{itx}\P(X=x)\); Euler's formula \(e^{iu}=\cos u+i\sin u\) then tidies it. (Simplifying to a cosine was explicitly not required for the credit in SoSe26 P4a.)
  2. Affine maps (Remark 2.47(ii)): \(\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)\).
  3. Independence turns sums into products (Remark 2.47(iv)): \(\varphi_{X+Y}=\varphi_X\varphi_Y\); for an iid sum, \(\varphi_{S_n}(t)=\varphi_{X_1}(t)^{n}\).
  4. Combine for a scaled sum: \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t)=\varphi_{X_1}\!\bigl(\tfrac{t}{\sqrt n}\bigr)^{n}\).
  5. Moments from derivatives at 0 (Remark 2.47(iii)): \(\E[X^{k}]=i^{-k}\varphi_X^{(k)}(0)\).

Drill bank — ten chains

Drills E1–E4 are the four past chains, part by part, with the credits printed on the papers. Drills E5–E10 are six I wrote to cover what the past four leave untested: an mle where differentiating fails, a case where the mle is beaten at finite \(n\), Chebyshev against the clt on the same numbers, a different characteristic function, a Jensen argument that is not the exam's, and a convergence-ladder decision.

Drill E1 — Rainfall: mle → Chebyshev → clt → compare WiSe25 · P4a–d · 11 credits

Rainfall in a fixed timespan is modelled by \(p_\theta:\R_{\ge0}\to\R\), \(p_\theta(x)=\frac{1}{\theta^{2}}x\,e^{-x/\theta}\), with \(\theta>0\) unknown. Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be iid with this density.

  1. (4 cr) Show by a full derivation that \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\).
  2. (3 cr) Use Chebyshev to bound \(\P_\theta(|\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}-\theta|\ge\epsilon)\). Hint given on the exam: \(\E[X_i]=2\theta\), \(\Var[X_i]=2\theta^{2}\).
  3. (3 cr) Use the clt to approximate the same probability in terms of \(\Phi\).
  4. (1 cr) Comment on the key differences between (b) and (c).
Solution

(a) The mle. For \(x\in\R_{\ge0}^{n}\), \[L(\theta\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\theta^{2}}x_ie^{-x_i/\theta} =\theta^{-2n}\Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i\Bigr)\exp\Bigl(-\frac1\theta\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\Bigr).\] Three separate algebra facts were used: \(\prod\frac1{\theta^2}=\theta^{-2n}\) (\(n\) equal factors); the \(x_i\) collect into one product; and \(\prod e^{-x_i/\theta}=e^{-\sum x_i/\theta}\) (multiplying powers of \(e\) adds exponents).

Take the logarithm. \(\ln\) is strictly increasing on \((0,\infty)\), so it does not move the maximiser. Writing \(s:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\), \[\ell(\theta\mid x)=-2n\ln\theta-\frac{s}{\theta}+\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln x_i}_{\text{no }\theta\text{ in it}} .\] The last term does not depend on \(\theta\), so it shifts \(\ell\) up or down by a constant and cannot move the maximiser; drop it.

Differentiate with respect to \(\theta\), using \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\ln\theta=\frac1\theta\) and \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\theta^{-1}=-\theta^{-2}\): \[\frac{d\ell}{d\theta}=-\frac{2n}{\theta}+\frac{s}{\theta^{2}}=\frac{-2n\theta+s}{\theta^{2}} \stackrel{!}{=}0\;\Longrightarrow\;s=2n\theta\;\Longrightarrow\;\hat\theta=\frac{s}{2n}=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i .\] (The denominator \(\theta^{2}\) is never zero for \(\theta>0\), so only the numerator matters.)

The official maximum check is incomplete — add one line

The printed solution computes \(\ell''(\theta)=\frac{2n}{\theta^{2}}-\frac{2s}{\theta^{3}} =\frac{2}{\theta^{3}}(n\theta-s)\) and evaluates it at \(\hat\theta\): \(n\hat\theta-s=\frac s2-s=-\frac s2<0\), so \(\ell''(\hat\theta)<0\). That proves a local maximum only — indeed \(\ell''(\theta)>0\) for \(\theta>s/n\), so \(\ell\) is convex far out to the right. The complete argument is the sign of the first derivative: from \(\ell'=\frac{s-2n\theta}{\theta^{2}}\), the numerator is positive exactly for \(\theta<\hat\theta\) and negative exactly for \(\theta>\hat\theta\), while \(\theta^{2}>0\) always. So \(\ell\) strictly increases up to \(\hat\theta\) and strictly decreases after it: \(\hat\theta\) is the global maximum on \((0,\infty)\). One extra line. Write it.

(b) Chebyshev. First the two moments of the estimator, using the hint \(\E[X_i]=2\theta\), \(\Var[X_i]=2\theta^{2}\): \[\E[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}]=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\E[X_i]=\frac{1}{2n}\cdot n\cdot2\theta=\theta \quad\text{(linearity, Prop 2.4(i); no independence needed),}\] \[\Var[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}]=\frac{1}{(2n)^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Var[X_i]=\frac{1}{4n^{2}}\cdot n\cdot2\theta^{2} =\frac{\theta^{2}}{2n}\quad\text{(Prop 2.8(iii) for the square, Prop 2.8(iv) for the sum — here independence is used).}\] So the estimator is unbiased. Chebyshev (Theorem 2.40) with \(Y=\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\) and \(\E[Y]=\theta\): \[\P_\theta\bigl(|\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}-\theta|\ge\epsilon\bigr)\le\frac{\Var[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}]}{\epsilon^{2}} =\frac{\theta^{2}}{2n\epsilon^{2}} .\]

(c) clt. Hypotheses of Theorem 2.64: the \(X_i\) are iid, \(\E[X_i]=2\theta\) is finite, and \(\Var[X_i]=2\theta^{2}\) is finite and non-zero (because \(\theta>0\)). Therefore \[\frac{\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}-\theta}{\sqrt{\Var[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}]}} =\frac{\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}-\theta}{\theta/\sqrt{2n}}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1),\] i.e. \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\) is approximately \(\mathcal N\bigl(\theta,\frac{\theta^{2}}{2n}\bigr)\). Hence \[\P_\theta\bigl(|\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}-\theta|\ge\epsilon\bigr) =\P\Bigl(\Bigl|\tfrac{\hat\theta-\theta}{\theta/\sqrt{2n}}\Bigr|\ge\tfrac{\epsilon\sqrt{2n}}{\theta}\Bigr) \approx 2\Phi\Bigl(-\frac{\sqrt{2n}\,\epsilon}{\theta}\Bigr),\] using \(\P(|Z|\ge a)=2\P(Z\le-a)=2\Phi(-a)\) for a standard normal \(Z\), by symmetry of the bell curve.

(d) The comparison (1 credit, purely verbal). Chebyshev is an exact guarantee valid for every \(n\) and every distribution with a finite variance, but it decays only like \(\frac1n\) and is usually loose. The clt expression is only an approximation, valid for large \(n\), but it decays far faster (the normal tail falls off like \(e^{-z^{2}/2}\)), so it is much sharper. A numerical illustration is Drill E7 below.

Note on the form of the answer. \(2\Phi(-\sqrt{2n}\,\epsilon/\theta)\) still contains the unknown \(\theta\). That is what was asked, and it is not a number. Do not "improve" the answer by substituting \(\hat\theta\) for \(\theta\) unless the question asks for that. The guide works this chain on the chapter pages: the mle and the moments at §3.2, the Chebyshev step at §2.2, the clt step at §2.4.

Drill E2 — Poisson: mle → unbiased → clt → z-test SoSe25 · P4a–d · 12 credits

Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be iid \(\Poi(\lambda)\), \(\lambda>0\) unknown. Hints given on the exam: the pmf is \(p(x)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{x}}{x!}\) with mean and variance \(\lambda\); the derivative of \(\ln t\) is \(1/t\); and \(z_{0.05}\approx1.64\).

  1. (4 cr) Explicitly derive \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}\).
  2. (2 cr) Is \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}\) unbiased?
  3. (2 cr) Give its approximate distribution for large \(n\) by the clt.
  4. (4 cr) With \(\lambda_0=4\), \(n=100\), \(\bar x=5\), \(\alpha=0.05\): construct an approximate test and decide.
Solution

(a) With \(s:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\), \[L(\lambda\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{x_i}}{x_i!} =\frac{e^{-n\lambda}\lambda^{s}}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_i!},\] because \(n\) factors \(e^{-\lambda}\) multiply to \(e^{-n\lambda}\) and \(\prod\lambda^{x_i}=\lambda^{\sum x_i}\).

Log-likelihood (dropping \(-\ln\prod x_i!\), which contains no \(\lambda\)): \(\ell(\lambda)=-n\lambda+s\ln\lambda\). Differentiate: \[\frac{d\ell}{d\lambda}=-n+\frac{s}{\lambda}\stackrel{!}{=}0\;\Longrightarrow\;\lambda=\frac{s}{n}=\bar x_n .\] Maximum check: \(\frac{d^{2}\ell}{d\lambda^{2}}=-\frac{s}{\lambda^{2}}<0\) whenever \(s>0\), so \(\ell\) is strictly concave and \(\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}=\bar X_n\) is the global maximum.

A hidden condition in the official maximum check

"\(\frac{d^{2}\ell}{d\lambda^{2}}=-\frac{\sum x_i}{\lambda^{2}}<0\)" silently assumes \(\sum x_i>0\). If every observation is 0 then \(\ell(\lambda)=-n\lambda\), which is strictly decreasing on \((0,\infty)\) and has no interior maximum: the likelihood is maximised at the boundary \(\lambda\downarrow0\), which is outside the parameter set \((0,\infty)\). The event has probability \(e^{-n\lambda}\), tiny but positive. Writing "for \(\sum x_i>0\)" costs one clause.

(b) Unbiasedness. \(\E[\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}]=\E[\bar X_n]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\E[X_i] =\frac1n\cdot n\lambda=\lambda\) by linearity (Proposition 2.4(i)) and \(\E[X_i]=\lambda\) (Lemma 2.26(vii)). The bias is \(\lambda-\lambda=0\): unbiased.

(c) clt. The \(X_i\) are iid with finite mean \(\lambda\) and finite non-zero variance \(\lambda\), so Theorem 2.64 applies. \(\Var[\bar X_n]=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\cdot n\lambda=\frac\lambda n\), hence \[\frac{\bar X_n-\lambda}{\sqrt{\lambda/n}}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1), \qquad\text{i.e. }\;\hat\lambda_{\text{mle}}\ \text{is approximately}\ \mathcal N\Bigl(\lambda,\frac{\lambda}{n}\Bigr).\]

What the official solution admitted about the neighbouring Problem 2a

On the same paper, the model answer to P2a (state the clt) printed the note: "We'll count all of these as correct even though the ones for \(S_n\) and \(\bar X_n\) are mathematically incorrect." Writing "\(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(\lambda,\lambda/n)\)" is wrong as a convergence statement, because a limit law cannot depend on \(n\). The correct sentence is either the standardised limit above, or the word approximately for finite \(n\), as written here. Do not rely on the leniency.

(d) The test. The question is whether the rate has increased above 4 — directional wording, so the test is one-sided (Definition 3.43): \[H_0:\lambda\le4\qquad\text{against}\qquad H_1:\lambda>4 .\] At the null boundary \(\lambda_0=4\): \(\E[\bar X_{100}]=4\) and \(\Var[\bar X_{100}]=\frac{4}{100}=0.04\), so the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{0.04}=0.2\). By the clt the statistic \[Z=\frac{\bar X_n-\lambda_0}{\sqrt{\lambda_0/n}}=\frac{\bar X_{100}-4}{0.2}\] is approximately \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) under the null boundary. Rejection rule for a one-sided test at level \(\alpha=0.05\): reject \(H_0\) if \(z_{\text{obs}}>z_{0.05}\approx1.64\). Observed value: \[z_{\text{obs}}=\frac{5-4}{0.2}=5 .\] Since \(5>1.64\) we reject \(H_0\) at the approximate level 0.05: the data give evidence that \(\lambda>4\).

Two traps in one part. First, the variance is evaluated at the null boundary \(\lambda_0=4\), not at the observed \(\bar x=5\). Second, the cut-off is \(z_{0.05}=1.64\) and not \(z_{0.025}=1.96\), because the alternative is one-sided. Both tests ever set on these papers were one-sided. The test itself is worked in full at §3.3.

Drill E3 — Characteristic functions and tail bounds SoSe26 · P4a–d · 9 credits

Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be iid with \(\P(X_j=1)=\P(X_j=-1)=\frac12\), and set \(Z_n:=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_j\). Hints on the exam: Euler's formula \(e^{iu}=\cos u+i\sin u\); and "if you could not solve (c), you may use \(\E[Z_n^{2}]=1\)".

  1. (1 cr) Compute \(\varphi_{X_1}(t)\).
  2. (3 cr) Compute \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t)\).
  3. (2 cr) Compute \(\E[Z_n]\) and \(\Var[Z_n]\).
  4. (3 cr) For \(a>0\), bound \(\P(|Z_n|\ge a)\) with Markov, and approximate it with the clt.
Solution

(a) By Definition 2.46, and because \(X_1\) takes only the two values \(\pm1\), \[\varphi_{X_1}(t)=\E[e^{itX_1}]=e^{it\cdot1}\cdot\tfrac12+e^{it\cdot(-1)}\cdot\tfrac12 =\tfrac12e^{it}+\tfrac12e^{-it}=\cos t,\] the last step by Euler: \(e^{it}=\cos t+i\sin t\) and \(e^{-it}=\cos t-i\sin t\); adding them the sine terms cancel and the cosines double, so the half-sum is \(\cos t\). (The official note says that simplifying to \(\cos t\) was not required for the credit.)

(b) Write \(Z_n=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_jX_j\). Then \[\varphi_{Z_n}(t)=\E\Bigl[\exp\Bigl(it\tfrac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_j\Bigr)\Bigr] =\E\Bigl[\prod_{j=1}^{n}\exp\Bigl(i\tfrac{t}{\sqrt n}X_j\Bigr)\Bigr] =\prod_{j=1}^{n}\E\Bigl[\exp\Bigl(i\tfrac{t}{\sqrt n}X_j\Bigr)\Bigr] =\varphi_{X_1}\!\Bigl(\tfrac{t}{\sqrt n}\Bigr)^{n}=\cos^{n}\!\Bigl(\tfrac{t}{\sqrt n}\Bigr).\] The first equality turns a sum in the exponent into a product (\(e^{a+b}=e^ae^b\)); the second pulls the expectation inside the product, which is legitimate because the \(X_j\) are independent (Remark 2.47(iv)) — name that; the third uses that they are identically distributed, so every factor is the same function evaluated at \(t/\sqrt n\).

The marking split this into 1 credit for the \(t/\sqrt n\) scaling, 1 for using independence to get a product, 1 for the final expression — and it grants follow-through credit: a wrong (a) carried forward correctly here loses nothing.

(c) Directly: \(\E[X_j]=1\cdot\frac12+(-1)\cdot\frac12=0\), and since \(X_j^{2}=1\) always, \(\E[X_j^{2}]=1\), so \(\Var[X_j]=\E[X_j^{2}]-\E[X_j]^{2}=1-0=1\). Then \[\E[Z_n]=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\E[X_j]=0,\qquad \Var[Z_n]=\frac{1}{(\sqrt n)^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\Var[X_j]=\frac1n\cdot n=1 .\] (Variance: constants come out squared, Proposition 2.8(iii); independent variances add, 2.8(iv).)

The official alternative route is stated without its computation

The model answer offers "\(\varphi'_{Z_n}(0)=0\), \(\varphi''_{Z_n}(0)=-1\)" and then Remark 2.47(iii). It does not show the differentiation. If you take that route you should: with \(f(t)=\cos^{n}(t/\sqrt n)\), \(f'(t)=-\sqrt n\cos^{n-1}(t/\sqrt n)\sin(t/\sqrt n)\), which is 0 at \(t=0\) because \(\sin 0=0\); and differentiating once more and setting \(t=0\) (where \(\cos0=1\), \(\sin0=0\)) leaves \(f''(0)=-\cos^{n-1}(0)=-1\). Then \(\E[Z_n]=i^{-1}f'(0)=0\) and \(\E[Z_n^{2}]=i^{-2}f''(0)=-(-1)=1\). The direct route in (c) above is shorter and scores the same — the official note says so.

(d) Markov. \(Z_n\) itself can be negative, so Markov cannot be applied to it. But \(Z_n^{2}\ge0\) always, and squaring is order-preserving on non-negative numbers, so \(\{|Z_n|\ge a\}=\{Z_n^{2}\ge a^{2}\}\). Theorem 2.38 gives \[\P(|Z_n|\ge a)=\P(Z_n^{2}\ge a^{2})\le\frac{\E[Z_n^{2}]}{a^{2}}=\frac{1}{a^{2}},\] where \(\E[Z_n^{2}]=\Var[Z_n]+\E[Z_n]^{2}=1+0=1\).

clt. The \(X_j\) are iid with mean 0 and variance 1 (both finite, the variance non-zero), so Theorem 2.64 gives \(Z_n\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1)\). Hence for large \(n\) \[\P(|Z_n|\ge a)\approx\P(|Z|\ge a)=2\bigl(1-\Phi(a)\bigr)=2\Phi(-a).\]

Two bounds, one picture. The Markov bound \(1/a^{2}\) is valid for every \(n\) and needs only the second moment. The clt value \(2\Phi(-a)\) needs \(n\) large but is dramatically smaller: at \(a=3\), \(1/a^{2}=0.1111\) while \(2\Phi(-3)=0.002700\) — a factor of about 41. At \(a=4\): \(0.0625\) against \(2\Phi(-4)=6.334\cdot10^{-5}\), a factor of about 987. Applying Markov to \(Z_n^2\) here is exactly Chebyshev in disguise, since \(\E[Z_n]=0\). The guide works this problem at §2.3 and §2.2.

Drill E4 — Jensen stated and applied SoSe26 · P3a–b · 5 credits

  1. (3 cr) State Jensen's inequality with all required assumptions.
  2. (2 cr) Let \(X\) be such that \(\E[X]\) and \(\E[e^{X}]\) exist and are finite. Show \(\E[X]\le\log\bigl(\E[e^{X}]\bigr)\).
Solution, with the official credit split

(a) Theorem 2.42 (Jensen's inequality). Let \(X\) be a real random variable such that \(\E[X]\) is finite. Let \(g:\R\to\R\) be a convex function. Then \[\E[g(X)]\ge g(\E[X]).\]

The official credit split was: 1 credit for "\(X\) with finite expectation", 1 for "\(g:\R\to\R\) convex", 1 for the correct inequality direction. Three assumptions, three credits — this is a pure recall item and the marking is per clause. The parenthetical extras in the model answer (the equality case for strictly convex \(g\), and the reversed inequality for concave \(g\)) were explicitly not graded.

What "convex" means [konvex]: for all \(x,y\in\R\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \(g(tx+(1-t)y)\le t\,g(x)+(1-t)g(y)\) — the chord between two points of the graph lies on or above the graph. For twice differentiable \(g\) this is the same as \(g''\ge0\).

(b) The function \(g(x)=e^{x}\) is convex on \(\R\), because \(g''(x)=e^{x}>0\) everywhere. So Jensen with this \(g\) gives \[e^{\E[X]}=g(\E[X])\le\E[g(X)]=\E[e^{X}].\] Now apply \(\log\) to both sides. Two facts are needed, and the official scheme marks them separately:

  • \(\log\) is strictly increasing on \((0,\infty)\), so applying it to both sides of an inequality preserves the direction;
  • \(e^{X}>0\) pointwise, hence \(\E[e^{X}]>0\), so the logarithm of the right-hand side is defined. (The left-hand side \(e^{\E[X]}\) is positive for the same reason.)

Therefore \(\log\bigl(e^{\E[X]}\bigr)\le\log\bigl(\E[e^{X}]\bigr)\), and since \(\log(e^{a})=a\), this reads \(\E[X]\le\log\bigl(\E[e^{X}]\bigr)\), as required.

What the marking scheme reveals. "Marks were given separately for '\(\log\) is increasing on \((0,\infty)\)' and '\(\E[e^{X}]>0\)'." Steps that feel too small to mention are exactly the ones being counted. Say them. Worked also at §2.2.

Drill E5 — an mle where differentiating fails: \(\Unif(0,\theta)\) My problem · 12 credits

Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be iid \(\Unif(0,\theta)\), that is with density \(p_\theta(x)=\frac1\theta\) for \(x\in[0,\theta]\) and 0 otherwise, with \(\theta>0\) unknown.

  1. (3 cr) Show that the likelihood cannot be maximised by setting a derivative to zero, and derive \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=\max\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}\).
  2. (3 cr) Given that \(M_n:=\max_iX_i\) has cdf \(F_{M_n}(m)=(m/\theta)^{n}\) on \([0,\theta]\), compute \(\E[M_n]\) and \(\Var[M_n]\), and give the bias and the mse of \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\).
  3. (2 cr) Construct an unbiased estimator from \(M_n\) and compute its mse.
  4. (2 cr) Compare all of this with the "moment" estimator \(\tilde\theta_n=2\bar X_n\) at \(n=10\).
  5. (2 cr) Show directly that \(M_n\xrightarrow{\P}\theta\), i.e. that the mle is consistent.
Solution

(a) Why the derivative route breaks, and what to do instead. The likelihood is \[L(\theta\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p_\theta(x_i) =\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{\theta^{n}},&\text{if }x_i\in[0,\theta]\text{ for every }i,\\[6pt] 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\] The condition "\(x_i\le\theta\) for every \(i\)" is the same as "\(\max_ix_i\le\theta\)". So, as a function of \(\theta\), \(L\) is zero for \(\theta<\max_ix_i\), then jumps to \(\frac{1}{\theta^{n}}\) at \(\theta=\max_ix_i\), and then decreases (because \(\theta^{-n}\) is decreasing in \(\theta\) for \(\theta>0\)).

A function with a jump is not differentiable there, and where it is differentiable its derivative \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\theta^{-n}=-n\theta^{-n-1}\) is never zero. So the equation \(\frac{d\ell}{d\theta}=0\) has no solution and Recipe A step 3 is unusable. This is the case flagged in Recipe A step 5.

Read the maximum off the shape instead: \(L\) is 0 below \(\max_ix_i\) and strictly decreasing above it, so the largest value of \(L\) is attained exactly at \[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=\max\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}=:m_n .\] Note what this says: the mle can never exceed the largest observation, so it always underestimates \(\theta\) — a bias is built in.

(b) Moments of the maximum. Differentiating the given cdf (Lemma 1.49(ii)) gives the density of \(M_n\) on \([0,\theta]\): \(p_{M_n}(m)=\frac{d}{dm}\frac{m^{n}}{\theta^{n}}=\frac{n\,m^{n-1}}{\theta^{n}}\). (Where the cdf comes from, in one line: \(\{M_n\le m\}\) means every \(X_i\le m\), and by independence that has probability \(\prod_i\P(X_i\le m)=(m/\theta)^{n}\).) Then \[\E[M_n]=\int_0^{\theta}m\cdot\frac{nm^{n-1}}{\theta^{n}}dm=\frac{n}{\theta^{n}}\Bigl[\frac{m^{n+1}}{n+1}\Bigr]_0^{\theta} =\frac{n}{n+1}\theta,\] \[\E[M_n^{2}]=\frac{n}{\theta^{n}}\Bigl[\frac{m^{n+2}}{n+2}\Bigr]_0^{\theta}=\frac{n}{n+2}\theta^{2},\qquad \Var[M_n]=\frac{n}{n+2}\theta^{2}-\frac{n^{2}}{(n+1)^{2}}\theta^{2} =\frac{n\,\theta^{2}}{(n+1)^{2}(n+2)} .\] (The last simplification: put over the common denominator \((n+1)^2(n+2)\); the numerator is \(n(n+1)^{2}-n^{2}(n+2)=n\bigl[(n^{2}+2n+1)-(n^{2}+2n)\bigr]=n\).)

Bias: \(\operatorname{bias}[M_n]=\frac{n}{n+1}\theta-\theta=-\frac{\theta}{n+1}<0\) — negative, as predicted. mse: \[\operatorname{mse}[M_n]=\Var[M_n]+\operatorname{bias}^{2} =\frac{n\theta^{2}}{(n+1)^{2}(n+2)}+\frac{\theta^{2}}{(n+1)^{2}} =\frac{\theta^{2}\bigl(n+(n+2)\bigr)}{(n+1)^{2}(n+2)}=\frac{2\theta^{2}}{(n+1)(n+2)},\] where the last step cancels one factor \((n+1)\) from \(2n+2=2(n+1)\).

(c) An unbiased version. Since \(\E[M_n]=\frac{n}{n+1}\theta\), multiplying by the reciprocal constant fixes the mean: put \(\hat\theta^{\,*}:=\frac{n+1}{n}M_n\). Then \(\E[\hat\theta^{\,*}]=\frac{n+1}{n}\cdot\frac{n}{n+1}\theta=\theta\): unbiased. Its variance, by Proposition 2.8(iii) (constants come out squared), \[\Var[\hat\theta^{\,*}]=\Bigl(\frac{n+1}{n}\Bigr)^{2}\frac{n\theta^{2}}{(n+1)^{2}(n+2)} =\frac{\theta^{2}}{n(n+2)},\] and since the bias is 0, \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat\theta^{\,*}]=\frac{\theta^{2}}{n(n+2)}\).

(d) Numbers at \(n=10\) (all in units of \(\theta^{2}\)):

estimatorbiasvariancemse at \(n=10\)
\(M_n\) (the mle)\(-\theta/(n+1)\)\(\theta^{2}n/((n+1)^{2}(n+2))\)\(2\theta^{2}/132=0.01515\,\theta^{2}\)
\(\frac{n+1}{n}M_n\)0\(\theta^{2}/(n(n+2))\)\(\theta^{2}/120=0.008333\,\theta^{2}\)
\(2\bar X_n\)0\(\theta^{2}/(3n)\)\(\theta^{2}/30=0.03333\,\theta^{2}\)

For \(2\bar X_n\): \(\E[X_i]=\frac\theta2\) so \(\E[2\bar X_n]=\theta\) (unbiased), and \(\Var[X_i]=\frac{\theta^{2}}{12}\) (Lemma 2.27), so \(\Var[2\bar X_n]=4\cdot\frac{1}{n^{2}}\cdot n\cdot\frac{\theta^{2}}{12}=\frac{\theta^{2}}{3n}\).

In words: the corrected maximum is about four times more accurate than the sample-mean estimator here, and about 1.8 times more accurate than the raw mle. Its mse shrinks like \(1/n^{2}\), while the sample-mean estimator's shrinks only like \(1/n\).

(e) Consistency. Definition 2.56(i) asks for \(\P(|M_n-\theta|>\epsilon)\to0\) for every \(\epsilon>0\). Fix \(0<\epsilon<\theta\). Since \(M_n\le\theta\) always, the event \(\{|M_n-\theta|>\epsilon\}\) is exactly \(\{M_n<\theta-\epsilon\}\). So \[\P(|M_n-\theta|>\epsilon)=\P(M_n<\theta-\epsilon)\le F_{M_n}(\theta-\epsilon) =\Bigl(\frac{\theta-\epsilon}{\theta}\Bigr)^{n}=\Bigl(1-\frac{\epsilon}{\theta}\Bigr)^{n}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0,\] because \(0\le1-\frac\epsilon\theta<1\) and \(q^{n}\to0\) for \(|q|<1\) (Analysis 2.1). For \(\epsilon\ge\theta\) the probability is 0 outright. Hence \(M_n\xrightarrow{\P}\theta\): the mle is consistent.

Numerically, with \(\epsilon=0.1\theta\) and \(n=10\): \(0.9^{10}=0.3487\); at \(n=50\): \(0.9^{50}=0.005154\). The convergence is geometric, far faster than the \(1/n\) that Chebyshev would give for a sample mean.

Why this drill matters. Both examined mle tasks had a smooth interior maximum, so they never tested whether you know why the derivative trick works. If a parameter sits in the support of the density, it does not. And note part (d): the maximum likelihood estimator \(M_n\) is beaten at every finite \(n\) by \(\frac{n+1}{n}M_n\). That is exactly the content of the true/false item SoSe26 P1e, whose answer is "false" — the mle has no finite-sample optimality guarantee (Remark 3.30, §3.2).

Drill E6 — bias, variance, mse and when a biased estimator wins My problem · 10 credits

Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be iid \(\Ber(p)\), \(p\in[0,1]\) unknown, and write \(S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\). Consider \[\hat p=\bar X_n=\frac{S}{n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad \tilde p=\frac{S+1}{n+2}.\]

  1. (2 cr) Compute \(\E[\hat p]\), \(\Var[\hat p]\), \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat p]\).
  2. (3 cr) Compute \(\E[\tilde p]\), its bias, \(\Var[\tilde p]\) and \(\operatorname{mse}[\tilde p]\).
  3. (3 cr) At \(n=10\), decide which estimator has the smaller mse at \(p=0.5\), at \(p=0.2\) and at \(p=0.9\). What do you conclude?
  4. (2 cr) Show that both estimators are consistent.
Solution

(a) \(S\sim\Bin(n,p)\) (a sum of \(n\) independent \(\Ber(p)\) variables), so \(\E[S]=np\) and \(\Var[S]=np(1-p)\) (Lemma 2.26(iv)). Hence \[\E[\hat p]=\frac{np}{n}=p\ \ (\text{unbiased}),\qquad \Var[\hat p]=\frac{1}{n^{2}}np(1-p)=\frac{p(1-p)}{n},\qquad \operatorname{mse}[\hat p]=\Var[\hat p]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n},\] the last equality because the bias is 0 (Definition 3.20(iv)).

(b) \(\tilde p=\frac{S+1}{n+2}\) is an affine function of \(S\): \(\tilde p=aS+b\) with \(a=\frac{1}{n+2}\), \(b=\frac{1}{n+2}\). So by linearity and Proposition 2.8(iii), \[\E[\tilde p]=\frac{np+1}{n+2},\qquad \operatorname{bias}[\tilde p]=\frac{np+1}{n+2}-p=\frac{np+1-p(n+2)}{n+2}=\frac{1-2p}{n+2},\] \[\Var[\tilde p]=\frac{1}{(n+2)^{2}}\Var[S]=\frac{np(1-p)}{(n+2)^{2}},\qquad \operatorname{mse}[\tilde p]=\frac{np(1-p)}{(n+2)^{2}}+\frac{(1-2p)^{2}}{(n+2)^{2}} .\] (Adding the constant \(b\) does not change the variance.) The bias vanishes exactly at \(p=\frac12\).

(c) Numbers at \(n=10\), so \((n+2)^{2}=144\):

\(p\)\(\operatorname{mse}[\hat p]=\frac{p(1-p)}{10}\)bias\([\tilde p]\)\(\Var[\tilde p]\)\(\operatorname{mse}[\tilde p]\)winner
0.50.0250000.017360.01736\(\tilde p\)
0.20.01600\(+0.05000\)0.011110.01361\(\tilde p\)
0.90.009000\(-0.06667\)0.0062500.01069\(\hat p\)

Sample computation for \(p=0.9\): \(\Var[\tilde p]=\frac{10\cdot0.9\cdot0.1}{144}=\frac{0.9}{144}=0.006250\); bias \(=\frac{1-1.8}{12}=-\frac{0.8}{12}=-0.06667\), squared \(=0.004444\); sum \(=0.01069\), against \(\frac{0.09}{10}=0.009000\) for \(\hat p\).

Conclusion. Neither estimator is uniformly better. The biased \(\tilde p\) wins in the middle of the range, where its smaller variance more than pays for its small bias; the unbiased \(\hat p\) wins near the ends, where \(\tilde p\)'s bias is largest. Unbiasedness is not a guarantee of accuracy: the mse is the quantity that measures accuracy, and it trades bias against variance.

(d) Consistency. Use Recipe B step 5. For \(\hat p\): \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat p]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}\le\frac{1}{4n}\to0\) (the maximum of \(p(1-p)\) on \([0,1]\) is \(\frac14\), attained at \(p=\frac12\)), so by Markov applied to \((\hat p-p)^{2}\), \[\P(|\hat p-p|\ge\epsilon)\le\frac{\operatorname{mse}[\hat p]}{\epsilon^{2}}\le\frac{1}{4n\epsilon^{2}}\to0 .\] For \(\tilde p\): \(\Var[\tilde p]\le\frac{n/4}{(n+2)^{2}}\to0\) and \(\operatorname{bias}[\tilde p]=\frac{1-2p}{n+2}\to0\), so \(\operatorname{mse}[\tilde p]\to0\) and the same Markov argument applies. Both are consistent.

Where you have seen this before. SoSe25 P1b asked whether \(\frac13\hat\theta_1 +\frac23\hat\theta_2\) is unbiased when both parts are (answer: true, by linearity); SoSe26 P1e asked whether the mle always has the smallest mse (answer: false). This drill is the computation behind both. The \(\frac{S+1}{n+2}\) estimator is the Laplace rule-of-succession estimator and also the posterior mean under a uniform prior — the Bayesian view of §3.5, which no exam has ever touched.

Drill E7 — Chebyshev against the clt on the same number My problem · 9 credits

Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be iid \(\Ber(\frac12)\) (fair coin tosses coded 0/1) and \(\bar X_n\) the sample mean. Consider \(\P\bigl(|\bar X_n-\tfrac12|\ge0.1\bigr)\).

  1. (2 cr) Bound it with Chebyshev for general \(n\), then evaluate at \(n=100\) and \(n=400\).
  2. (3 cr) Approximate it with the clt, first symbolically in terms of \(\Phi\), then at \(n=100\) and \(n=400\) using \(\Phi(2)=0.9772\), \(\Phi(4)=0.99997\).
  3. (2 cr) The exact values are \(0.05689\) at \(n=100\) and \(7.427\cdot10^{-5}\) at \(n=400\). Comment.
  4. (2 cr) How large must \(n\) be for the Chebyshev bound alone to guarantee \(\P(|\bar X_n-\frac12|\ge0.1)\le0.05\)?
Solution

Preliminaries. \(\E[X_i]=\frac12\) and \(\Var[X_i]=\frac12\bigl(1-\frac12\bigr)=\frac14\) (Lemma 2.26(iii) for \(\Ber(p)\)). Hence \(\E[\bar X_n]=\frac12\) and \(\Var[\bar X_n]=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\cdot n\cdot\frac14=\frac{1}{4n}\).

(a) Chebyshev (Theorem 2.40) with \(\epsilon=0.1\): \[\P\Bigl(\bigl|\bar X_n-\tfrac12\bigr|\ge0.1\Bigr)\le\frac{\Var[\bar X_n]}{0.1^{2}} =\frac{1/(4n)}{0.01}=\frac{25}{n}.\] At \(n=100\): \(\frac{25}{100}=0.2500\). At \(n=400\): \(\frac{25}{400}=0.06250\).

(b) clt (Theorem 2.64; the \(X_i\) are iid, mean \(\frac12\) finite, variance \(\frac14\) finite and non-zero). The standard deviation of \(\bar X_n\) is \(\sqrt{\frac{1}{4n}}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt n}\), so \[\P\Bigl(\bigl|\bar X_n-\tfrac12\bigr|\ge0.1\Bigr) =\P\Bigl(\Bigl|\frac{\bar X_n-\frac12}{1/(2\sqrt n)}\Bigr|\ge\frac{0.1}{1/(2\sqrt n)}\Bigr) \approx2\Phi\bigl(-0.2\sqrt n\bigr),\] because \(\frac{0.1}{1/(2\sqrt n)}=0.1\cdot2\sqrt n=0.2\sqrt n\).

At \(n=100\): \(0.2\sqrt{100}=2\), so the approximation is \(2\Phi(-2)=2(1-\Phi(2))=2(1-0.9772)=0.04550\). At \(n=400\): \(0.2\sqrt{400}=4\), giving \(2\Phi(-4)=2(1-0.99997)=6.334\cdot10^{-5}\).

(c) The comparison.

\(n\)Chebyshev boundclt approximationexactChebyshev / exact
1000.25000.045500.056894.4
4000.06250\(6.334\cdot10^{-5}\)\(7.427\cdot10^{-5}\)842

Three observations, and they are the whole point of WiSe25 P4d:

  • Chebyshev is always a valid upper bound — the exact value never exceeds it — but it is loose, and it gets relatively worse as \(n\) grows: it decays like \(\frac{1}{n}\), while the true probability decays roughly like \(e^{-2n\epsilon^{2}}\).
  • The clt figure is not a bound. At \(n=100\) it is 0.04550 against a true 0.05689 — it understates the truth by about 20 %. If you need a guarantee, Chebyshev is the honest tool; if you need a realistic number, the clt is.
  • The clt approximation improves as \(n\) grows: at \(n=400\) the relative error is down to about 15 %, and it keeps shrinking. (The remaining gap here is mostly the "lattice" effect of a discrete count being approximated by a continuous curve.)

(d) Solve \(\frac{25}{n}\le0.05\): \(n\ge\frac{25}{0.05}=500\). So Chebyshev alone needs \(n\ge500\). The clt approximation, by contrast, crosses 0.05 when \(2\Phi(-0.2\sqrt n)\le0.05\), i.e. \(0.2\sqrt n\ge z_{0.025}=1.96\), i.e. \(n\ge\bigl(\frac{1.96}{0.2}\bigr)^{2}=96.04\), so \(n\ge97\). The exact probability first falls below 0.05 at \(n=92\) and then oscillates around the threshold for a while (it is a sum of binomial point masses, so it jumps as the cut-off \(0.4n\) crosses an integer: \(0.05044\) at \(n=105\), \(0.04087\) at \(n=106\)), settling below it for good from \(n=106\) on. Chebyshev therefore asks for roughly five times more data than is really needed. That is the price of a bound that has to hold for every distribution with that variance.

Exam form. On the exam you would leave the answers as \(\frac{25}{n}\) and \(2\Phi(-0.2\sqrt n)\); no \(\Phi\) table has ever been supplied. The numerical columns here exist only so you can see the sizes once, in advance.

Drill E8 — a characteristic function you have not seen My problem · 9 credits

Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be iid with \(\P(X_j=-1)=\P(X_j=0)=\P(X_j=1)=\frac13\).

  1. (2 cr) Compute \(\varphi_{X_1}(t)\) and simplify it with Euler's formula.
  2. (2 cr) Compute \(\E[X_1]\) and \(\Var[X_1]\) from \(\varphi_{X_1}\), using \(\E[X^{k}]=i^{-k}\varphi^{(k)}(0)\).
  3. (2 cr) Let \(Y=2X_1+1\). Compute \(\varphi_Y(t)\).
  4. (3 cr) Let \(S_n=\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_j\) and \(Z_n=\frac{S_n}{\sqrt{2n/3}}\). Compute \(\varphi_{Z_n}\) and state what the clt says about \(Z_n\).
Solution

(a) By Definition 2.46, \[\varphi_{X_1}(t)=\E[e^{itX_1}]=\tfrac13e^{-it}+\tfrac13e^{i\cdot0}+\tfrac13e^{it} =\tfrac13\bigl(1+e^{it}+e^{-it}\bigr)=\frac{1+2\cos t}{3},\] using \(e^{0}=1\) and, as in Drill E3, \(e^{it}+e^{-it}=2\cos t\) from Euler's formula.

(b) Differentiate \(\varphi(t)=\frac{1+2\cos t}{3}\): \(\varphi'(t)=-\frac{2\sin t}{3}\) and \(\varphi''(t)=-\frac{2\cos t}{3}\). At \(t=0\), with \(\sin0=0\) and \(\cos0=1\): \(\varphi'(0)=0\), \(\varphi''(0)=-\frac23\). By Remark 2.47(iii), \[\E[X_1]=i^{-1}\varphi'(0)=0,\qquad \E[X_1^{2}]=i^{-2}\varphi''(0)=(-1)\cdot\Bigl(-\frac23\Bigr)=\frac23,\] using \(i^{-2}=\frac{1}{i^{2}}=\frac{1}{-1}=-1\). Hence \(\Var[X_1]=\frac23-0^{2}=\frac23\).

Cross-check directly, which is always worth ten seconds: \(\E[X_1]=\frac13(-1+0+1)=0\) and \(\E[X_1^{2}]=\frac13(1+0+1)=\frac23\). Same answers.

(c) Remark 2.47(ii) says \(\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)\). With \(a=2\), \(b=1\), \[\varphi_{Y}(t)=e^{it}\,\varphi_{X_1}(2t)=e^{it}\cdot\frac{1+2\cos(2t)}{3}.\] (Sanity check at \(t=0\): every characteristic function must satisfy \(\varphi(0)=\E[e^{0}]=1\). Here \(e^{0}\cdot\frac{1+2}{3}=1\). )

(d) First the scaling constant: \(\Var[S_n]=n\Var[X_1]=\frac{2n}{3}\) by independence, and \(\E[S_n]=0\), so \(Z_n=\frac{S_n}{\sqrt{2n/3}}\) is exactly the standardised sum. Writing \(\sigma_n:=\sqrt{2n/3}\) and using Remark 2.47(ii) then (iv), \[\varphi_{Z_n}(t)=\varphi_{S_n}\!\Bigl(\frac{t}{\sigma_n}\Bigr) =\varphi_{X_1}\!\Bigl(\frac{t}{\sigma_n}\Bigr)^{n} =\left(\frac{1+2\cos\bigl(t\sqrt{3/(2n)}\bigr)}{3}\right)^{\!n},\] where the middle equality uses that the \(X_j\) are independent and identically distributed, so the characteristic function of the sum is the product of \(n\) identical factors.

What the clt says. The \(X_j\) are iid with finite mean 0 and finite non-zero variance \(\frac23\), so Theorem 2.64 gives \(Z_n\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1)\). Since the characteristic function of \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) is \(e^{-t^{2}/2}\), this says \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t)\to e^{-t^{2}/2}\) for every \(t\). A numerical check at \(t=1\): \(n=5\) gives \(0.5987\), \(n=50\) gives \(0.6058\), \(n=500\) gives \(0.6065\), against \(e^{-1/2}=0.6065\).

What is genuinely new here compared with SoSe26 P4. That problem had a symmetric two-point variable with \(\Var=1\), so the scaling was the plain \(\sqrt n\) and the characteristic function came out as \(\cos^{n}(t/\sqrt n)\). Here the variance is \(\frac23\ne1\), so you must divide by \(\sigma\sqrt n\) and not by \(\sqrt n\) — the step where the standardisation actually bites. Part (c) adds the affine rule, which was tested separately in SoSe26 P1c. See §2.3.

Drill E9 — three Jensen arguments, and one place where the script's version is too narrow My problem · 9 credits

  1. (2 cr) Use Jensen with \(g(x)=x^{2}\) to prove \(\Var[X]\ge0\).
  2. (2 cr) Use Jensen to prove \(|\E[X]|\le\E[|X|]\).
  3. (2 cr) Show \(\E[e^{-X}]\ge e^{-\E[X]}\), and say what this means for the average of \(e^{-X}\) over a population.
  4. (3 cr) Show \(\E\bigl[\frac1X\bigr]\ge\frac{1}{\E[X]}\) for a strictly positive \(X\), and explain exactly which hypothesis of Theorem 2.42 this argument stretches.
Solution

(a) \(g(x)=x^{2}\) is convex on \(\R\) (\(g''(x)=2>0\)) and maps \(\R\) into \(\R\), so Theorem 2.42 applies whenever \(\E[X]\) is finite: \[\E[X^{2}]=\E[g(X)]\ge g(\E[X])=(\E[X])^{2}.\] Subtracting \((\E[X])^{2}\) from both sides and using \(\Var[X]=\E[X^{2}]-(\E[X])^{2}\) (Proposition 2.8(i)) gives \(\Var[X]\ge0\).

(b) \(g(x)=|x|\) is convex on \(\R\): its graph is a V, and the chord between any two points lies on or above it. (It is not differentiable at 0, but convexity does not require differentiability.) Jensen gives \(\E[|X|]\ge|\E[X]|\), which is the statement, read right to left.

(c) \(g(x)=e^{-x}\) has \(g''(x)=e^{-x}>0\), so it is convex on \(\R\). Jensen: \(\E[e^{-X}]\ge e^{-\E[X]}\).

In words: if \(X\) is the time until an event and you are interested in the average of the decaying quantity \(e^{-X}\), that average is always at least as large as the value you would get by plugging in the average time. Averaging the outputs of a convex function gives more than the function of the average input — the spread of \(X\) can only push the average up.

(d) Let \(X>0\) with \(\E[X]\) finite and \(\E[\frac1X]\) finite. On \((0,\infty)\) the function \(g(x)=\frac1x\) has \(g'(x)=-\frac1{x^{2}}\) and \(g''(x)=\frac{2}{x^{3}}>0\), so it is convex there. Jensen then reads \[\E\Bigl[\frac1X\Bigr]\ge\frac{1}{\E[X]}.\] In words: the average of reciprocals is at least the reciprocal of the average — the harmonic mean never exceeds the arithmetic mean.
