Numerical check. Let \(X\) take the values 1 and 2 with probability \(\frac12\) each. Then \(\E[X]=1.5\) and \(\E[\frac1X]=\frac12(1+\frac12)=0.7500\), while \(\frac1{\E[X]}=\frac{1}{1.5}=0.6667\). Indeed \(0.7500\ge0.6667\). With three values \(1,2,3\) each of probability \(\frac13\): \(\E[\frac1X]=\frac13(1+0.5+0.3333)=0.6111\ge\frac12=0.5000\).

Which hypothesis this stretches, and how to be safe

Theorem 2.42 as the script states it requires \(g:\R\to\R\) — a convex function defined on all of \(\R\). The map \(x\mapsto\frac1x\) is not defined at 0 and is not convex on \(\R\setminus\{0\}\) taken as a whole (on the negative half-line it is concave). So the theorem as printed does not literally cover part (d).

The honest way to write it in an exam: say "\(X>0\) almost surely, so the distribution of \(X\) lives in the interval \((0,\infty)\), on which \(g(x)=1/x\) is convex; Jensen's inequality holds in this form for a convex function on an interval containing the support of \(X\)." That sentence names the gap and closes it. The same caveat applies to \(g=\ln\) (concave on \((0,\infty)\), giving \(\E[\ln X]\le\ln\E[X]\)), which is the version people use most often.

Parts (a)–(c) need no such caveat: \(x^{2}\), \(|x|\) and \(e^{-x}\) are convex on all of \(\R\), so they fit Theorem 2.42 exactly as printed. In an exam, prefer those.

How Jensen is examined. Once, so far: SoSe26 P3, 5 credits, 3 of them for the bare statement. The pattern of the application half is always the same — name the function, show it is convex (usually by \(g''\ge0\)), apply the inequality, then do one monotone operation to both sides. Do not skip the "\(g''>0\)" line: the marking scheme counted it.

Drill E10 — placing five claims on the convergence ladder My problem · 10 credits

For each of the following, decide in which of the three modes of Definition 2.56 the sequence converges, and to what. Justify each answer. (2 credits each.)

  1. \(U\sim\Unif(0,1)\) is one fixed random variable, and \(X_n:=\one_{\{U\le1/n\}}\) (the indicator that is 1 when \(U\le\frac1n\) and 0 otherwise).
  2. \(Y_n:=n\cdot\one_{\{U\le1/n\}}\), with the same \(U\).
  3. \(W_n\sim\mathcal N\bigl(0,\frac1n\bigr)\), independent of each other.
  4. \(V_1,V_2,\dots\) iid \(\Unif(0,1)\). Does \(V_n\) converge in distribution? In probability?
  5. \(T_n\xrightarrow{d}5\) (the constant 5). Does \(T_n\xrightarrow{\P}5\) follow?
Solution

The ladder first (Remark 2.57): \(\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\Rightarrow\xrightarrow{\P} \Rightarrow\xrightarrow{d}\), and no arrow reverses in general. The one exception, which is exactly item (v), is that convergence in distribution to a constant does imply convergence in probability to that constant.

(i) Fix an outcome \(\omega\) with \(U(\omega)>0\). Since \(\frac1n\to0\), there is an \(N\) with \(\frac1N<U(\omega)\), and from then on \(X_n(\omega)=0\). So \(X_n(\omega)\to0\) for every \(\omega\) in the set \(\{U>0\}\), which has probability \(\P(U>0)=1\) (a single point has probability 0 for a continuous variable). By Definition 2.56(ii), \(X_n\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}0\), and therefore also in probability and in distribution.

(ii) The same argument applies pointwise: for \(\omega\) with \(U(\omega)>0\) we eventually have \(Y_n(\omega)=n\cdot0=0\). So \(Y_n\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}0\), hence in probability and in distribution. But \(\E[Y_n]=n\cdot\P(U\le\frac1n)=n\cdot\frac1n=1\) for every \(n\), so \(\E[Y_n]\to1\ne0=\E[0]\). Convergence in any of the three modes does not carry expectations along. This is precisely the counterexample of SoSe26 P2a, worth 3 credits there.

(iii) In probability: for any \(\epsilon>0\), by Chebyshev (Theorem 2.40; \(\E[W_n]=0\)) \[\P(|W_n|\ge\epsilon)\le\frac{\Var[W_n]}{\epsilon^{2}}=\frac{1}{n\epsilon^{2}}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0,\] so \(W_n\xrightarrow{\P}0\), and hence \(W_n\xrightarrow{d}0\) by the ladder. Almost-sure convergence does not follow from this argument, and since the \(W_n\) are independent one can show it fails; but the question only asks which modes you can establish, and the honest answer is "in probability (and therefore in distribution); almost-sure convergence does not follow from Chebyshev". (The exact statement \(2\Phi(-\epsilon\sqrt n)\) is available too: at \(\epsilon=0.1\), \(n=100\), it equals \(0.3173\), which is much smaller than the Chebyshev bound \(\frac{1}{100\cdot0.01}=1\) — a bound of 1 is vacuous, which shows how loose Chebyshev can be.)

(iv) Every \(V_n\) has the same cdf \(F(x)=x\) on \([0,1]\), so trivially \(F_{V_n}(x)=F(x)\to F(x)\) at every \(x\): \(V_n\xrightarrow{d}V\) for any \(V\sim\Unif(0,1)\). But convergence in probability to such a \(V\) fails: \(V_n\) and \(V\) would have to be independent \(\Unif(0,1)\) variables, and \(V_n-V\) is then a fixed non-degenerate random variable, so \(\P(|V_n-V|>\frac12)\) is a positive number that does not depend on \(n\) and cannot tend to 0. This is the standard illustration that \(\xrightarrow{d}\) is a statement about distributions only and says nothing about the variables being close to each other.

(v) Yes. This is the one place where the ladder can be climbed backwards, because the limit is a constant. Reason, in the script's terms: the cdf of the constant 5 is \(F(x)=0\) for \(x<5\) and \(1\) for \(x\ge5\), continuous everywhere except at 5. For \(\epsilon>0\), \[\P(|T_n-5|>\epsilon)=\P(T_n>5+\epsilon)+\P(T_n<5-\epsilon) \le\bigl(1-F_{T_n}(5+\epsilon)\bigr)+F_{T_n}(5-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}),\] and both \(5+\epsilon\) and \(5-\frac\epsilon2\) are continuity points of \(F\), so \(F_{T_n}(5+\epsilon)\to1\) and \(F_{T_n}(5-\frac\epsilon2)\to0\). The right-hand side therefore tends to 0. This is exactly the true/false item SoSe26 P1d, whose answer is "true".

In words, the whole ladder: almost-sure convergence is about the paths settling down; convergence in probability is about the chance of being far off shrinking; convergence in distribution is only about the shapes of the histograms lining up. Each is weaker than the one before, and none of them says anything about expectations.

Where this is examined. WiSe25 P1d and P2b, SoSe25 P2b, SoSe26 P1d and P2a — a convergence-mode question has appeared on every paper so far. The guide's full treatment, with counterexamples and a picture of the ladder, is at §2.4.

The long applied problem

Every one of the three papers closes with a long word problem built on a story: tennis schedules, a duck hunt, a randomized survey. Each is worth 10 to 13 credits, and each chains three to five different subchapters in four sub-parts of rising difficulty. This is the one structural habit that survives all three papers unchanged — and it is still only three papers, so it is "what has been asked", not a forecast.

The three closing problems WiSe25 · P6 (10 cr) · SoSe25 · P5 (12 cr) · SoSe26 · P5 (13 cr)

PaperStoryCrSubchapters chainedSub-parts
WiSe 25/26 · P6Strategic tennis matches10 §1.1 (inclusion–exclusion) → §1.4 (independence, total probability, Bayes) a 4 · b 2 · c 4
SoSe 2025 · P5Duck hunt12 §1.2 (Laplace) → §1.4 (independence) → §2.1 (indicators, expectation, variance) → §2.2 (Chebyshev) a 4 · b 4 · c 4
SoSe 2026 · P5Randomized response13 §1.4 (total probability) → §3.1 (identifiability) → §3.2 (mle, bias, variance) → §3.3 (z-test), with §2.4 (clt) underneath a 3 · b 3 · c 2 · d 5

The common skeleton. Part (a) translates the story into a distribution or a probability. Part (b) computes a first quantity from it — an expectation, or an estimator. Part (c) computes a second-order quantity — a variance, or an unbiasedness check. Part (d), where there is one, runs a test or a bound with numbers. Later parts are always made reachable if an earlier one failed: two of the three papers print an explicit "you may use…" for exactly this reason. Never leave a later part blank because an earlier one went wrong.

Method — how to attack a story problem My addition, distilled from the three official solutions

  1. Name everything before computing anything. Write down the events (\(W_i\) = "win match \(i\)", \(A_i\) = "duck \(i\) survives", \(T\) = "answers truthfully") and the random variables with their index ranges. Every official solution starts with a naming paragraph.
  2. Decide what is independent and say it once, explicitly. Almost every later step either uses independence (to multiply probabilities, to add variances) or must avoid using it (linearity of expectation never needs it). Getting this wrong is the single most expensive error in this problem.
  3. Count with indicators. If the question says "the number of …", set \(X_i=\one_{A_i}\) and \(X=\sum_iX_i\). Then \(\E[X_i]=\P(A_i)\) and linearity gives \(\E[X]=\sum_i\P(A_i)\) even when the \(X_i\) are dependent. SoSe25 P5a printed this as a hint, which shows the examiner expects the move to be known.
  4. For a variance of a sum of indicators, expand \(\E[X^{2}]=\sum_{i,k}\E[X_iX_k]\), note \(\E[X_iX_k]=\P(A_i\cap A_k)\), and split the diagonal \(i=k\) (where \(X_i^{2}=X_i\), since \(0^2=0\) and \(1^2=1\)) from the off-diagonal.
  5. Split events into disjoint pieces before adding probabilities; if the pieces overlap, use inclusion–exclusion (Theorem 1.22) instead.
  6. Sanity-check at extreme parameter values. \(n=0\), \(p=0\), \(q=1\), \(m=2\). Every one of the three problems has an extreme case you can check in ten seconds.
  7. If the last part asks for a decision, give it in a sentence of plain English, not only as an inequality between numbers. A credit was awarded for exactly that in SoSe26 P5d.

Walkthrough 1 — Strategic tennis matches WiSe25 · P6 · 10 credits

The setting. You play a strong opponent (S) and a weak opponent (W). You beat the strong one with probability \(p\) and the weak one with probability \(q\), where \(0<p<q<1\). Matches are independent.

(a) Which schedule? WiSe25 · P6a · 4 credits

You play three matches and win the tournament if you win two consecutive matches. Schedule A is strong–weak–strong (SWS), schedule B is weak–strong–weak (WSW). Compute both winning probabilities in terms of \(p\) and \(q\), say which you prefer, and give a brief intuitive explanation without restating the computation.

Solution

Step 1 — name the events. Let \(W_i\) be the event "you win match \(i\)" and \(L_i=W_i^{c}\) the event "you lose match \(i\)", for \(i\in\{1,2,3\}\).

Step 2 — split the target event into disjoint pieces. "Two consecutive wins in three matches" happens in exactly two ways:

  • you win matches 1 and 2 — the event \(W_1\cap W_2\), whatever happens in match 3;
  • you lose match 1 but win matches 2 and 3 — the event \(L_1\cap W_2\cap W_3\).

These two are disjoint: the first requires \(W_1\), the second requires \(L_1\), and an event and its complement cannot both occur. They also exhaust the possibilities: any run of two consecutive wins must start at match 1 or at match 2. So by additivity of a probability measure on disjoint sets (Proposition 1.19, §1.1), \[\P(\text{win})=\P(W_1\cap W_2)+\P(L_1\cap W_2\cap W_3).\] Skipping the word "disjoint" here is the standard way to lose a credit: if the pieces overlapped you would be double-counting.

Step 3 — price each piece by independence. Independent events multiply: \(\P(A\cap B)=\P(A)\P(B)\) (Definition 1.74, §1.4).

Schedule A = SWS, so match 1 is strong (\(\P(W_1)=p\)), match 2 weak (\(q\)), match 3 strong (\(p\)): \[\P(\text{win}\mid\text{SWS})=pq+(1-p)\,q\,p=pq+pq-p^{2}q=2pq-p^{2}q=pq(2-p).\] Schedule B = WSW: match 1 weak (\(q\)), match 2 strong (\(p\)), match 3 weak (\(q\)): \[\P(\text{win}\mid\text{WSW})=qp+(1-q)\,p\,q=pq+pq-pq^{2}=2pq-pq^{2}=pq(2-q).\]

Step 4 — compare. Both expressions are \(pq\) times something. Since \(p<q\), we get \(2-p>2-q\), and \(pq>0\), so multiplying an inequality by a positive number preserves it: \[pq(2-p)>pq(2-q)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textbf{schedule A (SWS) is better.}\]

Step 5 — the intuition, which is separately worth credits. Whatever else happens, you must win match 2: every run of two consecutive matches in a three-match schedule contains the middle one. So the middle slot is the one match you cannot avoid winning, and you should put your weak opponent there. SWS does that; WSW wastes the weak opponent on the two optional slots.

Numbers, as a check. With \(p=0.3\), \(q=0.8\): SWS gives \(0.3\cdot0.8\cdot1.7=0.4080\), WSW gives \(0.3\cdot0.8\cdot1.2=0.2880\). SWS wins by a wide margin.

The guide's full version of this part, with the event diagram, is at §1.4.

(b) Bayes on the schedule WiSe25 · P6b · 2 credits

The organisers pick the schedule by a fair coin flip. Someone is told only that you won. What is the probability that the schedule was SWS?

Solution

Step 1 — the law of total probability (Theorem 1.70(ii), §1.4). The two schedules partition the sample space and each has probability \(\frac12\) (fair coin), so \[\P(\text{win})=\P(\text{SWS})\P(\text{win}\mid\text{SWS})+\P(\text{WSW})\P(\text{win}\mid\text{WSW}) =\tfrac12 pq(2-p)+\tfrac12 pq(2-q)=\tfrac12 pq\,(4-p-q),\] the last step factoring out \(\frac12pq\) and adding \((2-p)+(2-q)=4-p-q\).

Step 2 — Bayes' rule (Theorem 1.70(iii)): \(\P(A\mid B)=\frac{\P(B\mid A)\P(A)}{\P(B)}\), with \(A=\{\text{SWS}\}\) and \(B=\{\text{win}\}\): \[\P(\text{SWS}\mid\text{win})=\frac{\P(\text{win}\mid\text{SWS})\,\P(\text{SWS})}{\P(\text{win})} =\frac{pq(2-p)\cdot\frac12}{\frac12pq(4-p-q)}=\frac{2-p}{4-p-q}.\] The factors \(\frac12\) and \(pq\) cancel top and bottom.

Check. The answer must lie in \((0,1)\) and must be larger than \(\frac12\), because SWS is the more likely winner and so winning is evidence for SWS. Indeed \(2-p>\frac{4-p-q}{2}\iff 4-2p>4-p-q\iff q>p\), which is given. With \(p=0.3,q=0.8\): \(\frac{1.7}{2.9}=0.5862\). More than a half, as expected.

Worked in full at §1.4, and the Bayes machinery itself at §1.4.

(c) Four matches, inclusion–exclusion WiSe25 · P6c · 4 credits

You now play SWWS (four matches). You win if you win at least two non-consecutive matches. Compute the probability of winning.

Solution

Step 1 — enumerate. Let \(A_i\) be "win match \(i\)". Non-consecutive index pairs from \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) are \((1,3)\), \((1,4)\) and \((2,4)\) — the pairs \((1,2)\), \((2,3)\), \((3,4)\) are consecutive. Set \(E_{13}:=A_1\cap A_3\), \(E_{14}:=A_1\cap A_4\), \(E_{24}:=A_2\cap A_4\). The target event is \(E_{13}\cup E_{14}\cup E_{24}\).

Step 2 — why a plain sum is wrong. These three events overlap: winning matches 1, 3 and 4 puts you in both \(E_{13}\) and \(E_{14}\). Adding \(\P(E_{13})+\P(E_{14})+\P(E_{24})\) would count such outcomes more than once. And they are not independent either, even though the \(A_i\) are, because \(E_{13}\) and \(E_{14}\) share the factor \(A_1\). So neither addition nor multiplication works: this is why inclusion–exclusion is needed, and recognising that is the heart of the problem.

Step 3 — price every intersection. The schedule SWWS means \(\P(A_1)=p\), \(\P(A_2)=q\), \(\P(A_3)=q\), \(\P(A_4)=p\). Intersections of the \(E\)'s are intersections of \(A\)'s over the union of the index sets, and independence lets us multiply:

eventas an intersection of \(A_i\)probability
\(E_{13}\)\(A_1\cap A_3\)\(pq\)
\(E_{14}\)\(A_1\cap A_4\)\(p\cdot p=p^{2}\)
\(E_{24}\)\(A_2\cap A_4\)\(qp\)
\(E_{13}\cap E_{14}\)\(A_1\cap A_3\cap A_4\)\(p\,q\,p=p^{2}q\)
\(E_{13}\cap E_{24}\)\(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3\cap A_4\)\(p\,q\,q\,p=p^{2}q^{2}\)
\(E_{14}\cap E_{24}\)\(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_4\)\(p\,q\,p=p^{2}q\)
\(E_{13}\cap E_{14}\cap E_{24}\)\(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3\cap A_4\)\(p^{2}q^{2}\)

Step 4 — inclusion–exclusion for three events (Theorem 1.22, §1.1): singles minus pairs plus the triple. \[\P(\text{win})=\bigl(pq+p^{2}+pq\bigr)-\bigl(p^{2}q+p^{2}q^{2}+p^{2}q\bigr)+p^{2}q^{2} =2pq+p^{2}-2p^{2}q-p^{2}q^{2}+p^{2}q^{2}=2pq+p^{2}-2p^{2}q .\] Factor out \(p\): \(\P(\text{win})=p\,(2q+p-2pq)\).

Checks. With \(q=1\) (you always beat the weak opponent, so \(A_2\) and \(A_3\) are certain) the formula gives \(p(2+p-2p)=p(2-p)=2p-p^{2}\), which is \(\P(A_1\cup A_4)\) — correct, since with \(A_3\) certain, winning match 1 alone already gives the non-consecutive pair \((1,3)\), and likewise match 4 gives \((2,4)\). With \(p=0\) the formula gives 0 — correct, since every non-consecutive pair contains match 1 or match 4, both of which are against the strong opponent. Numerically at \(p=0.3\), \(q=0.8\): \(0.3\,(1.6+0.3-0.48)=0.3\cdot1.42=0.4260\), which a direct enumeration of all 16 outcomes confirms.

Two typesetting slips in the official solution

(1) It writes \(\P(E_{13}\cup E_{14}\cup E_{14})\) — the last term should be \(E_{24}\). (2) The bracket opened after the minus sign closes only after the triple-intersection term, so as printed the triple term is subtracted rather than added. The very next line has the signs right and the final answer \(p(2q+p-2pq)\) is correct, so this is a typographical problem, not a mathematical one — but if you are checking your own work against the model answer, do not be confused by it. The guide documents this at §1.1.

Walkthrough 2 — Duck hunt SoSe25 · P5 · 12 credits

The setting. \(n\) hunters with perfect aim shoot simultaneously at \(m\) ducks. Each hunter picks its target uniformly at random and independently of the others, so two hunters may pick the same duck. \(X\) is the number of surviving ducks.

(a) \(\E[X]\) by the counting trick SoSe25 · P5a · 4 credits

Solution

Step 1 — name. Index ducks by \(i\in\{1,\dots,m\}\) and hunters by \(j\in\{1,\dots,n\}\). Let \(S_j\) be the (random) index of the duck that hunter \(j\) aims at. "Uniformly at random" means \(S_j\sim\Lap[m]\), the Laplace or uniform distribution on \(\{1,\dots,m\}\) (§1.2, §1.2): \(\P(S_j=i)=\frac1m\) for every \(i\). "Independently of the others" means \(S_1,\dots,S_n\) are independent. Let \(A_i\) be the event "duck \(i\) survives".

Step 2 — the probability that one duck survives. Duck \(i\) survives exactly when no hunter aims at it: \[\P(A_i)=\P(S_1\ne i,\ S_2\ne i,\ \dots,\ S_n\ne i) =\prod_{j=1}^{n}\P(S_j\ne i)=\Bigl(\frac{m-1}{m}\Bigr)^{\!n},\] where the middle equality is independence and \(\P(S_j\ne i)=1-\frac1m=\frac{m-1}{m}\) counts the \(m-1\) other ducks out of \(m\) equally likely choices.

Step 3 — indicators. Set \(X_i:=\one_{A_i}\), the indicator of \(A_i\): it is 1 if duck \(i\) survives and 0 otherwise. Then \(X=\sum_{i=1}^{m}X_i\) counts the survivors, since each surviving duck contributes exactly one 1.

Step 4 — linearity. An indicator's expectation is the probability of its event: \(\E[X_i]=1\cdot\P(A_i)+0\cdot\P(A_i^{c})=\P(A_i)\). By linearity (Proposition 2.4(i)), \[\E[X]=\E\Bigl[\sum_{i=1}^{m}X_i\Bigr]=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\E[X_i]=m\Bigl(\frac{m-1}{m}\Bigr)^{\!n}.\]

The crucial remark. The indicators \(X_1,\dots,X_m\) are not independent — if many ducks survive, few hunters were spread out, which makes the remaining ducks more likely to have been hit. Linearity of expectation does not care: it holds for any random variables whose expectations exist. Say this out loud; it is what makes the four-line computation legitimate.

Checks. \(n=0\) (no hunters): \(\E[X]=m\cdot1=m\), all ducks survive. \(n=1\): \(\E[X]=m\cdot\frac{m-1}{m}=m-1\), exactly one duck dies. With \(m=10\), \(n=2\): \(10\cdot0.9^{2}=8.100\).

Worked in full, with the general indicator recipe, at §2.1.

(b) \(\Var[X]\) with dependent indicators SoSe25 · P5b · 4 credits

Solution

Step 1 — the right formula. Because the \(X_i\) are dependent, variances do not add. Use \(\Var[X]=\E[X^{2}]-\E[X]^{2}\) (Proposition 2.8(i)) and expand the square of a sum: \[\E[X^{2}]=\E\Bigl[\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{m}X_i\Bigr)^{2}\Bigr]=\E\Bigl[\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}X_iX_k\Bigr] =\sum_{i,k=1}^{m}\E[X_iX_k].\] There are \(m^{2}\) terms: \(m\) diagonal ones (\(i=k\)) and \(m(m-1)\) off-diagonal ones.

Step 2 — the product of two indicators is the indicator of the intersection. \(X_iX_k=\one_{A_i}\one_{A_k}=\one_{A_i\cap A_k}\) (the product is 1 exactly when both are 1), so \(\E[X_iX_k]=\P(A_i\cap A_k)\).

Step 3 — the diagonal. For \(i=k\): \(X_i^{2}=X_i\), because \(0^{2}=0\) and \(1^{2}=1\). So \(\E[X_i^{2}]=\E[X_i]=\bigl(\frac{m-1}{m}\bigr)^{n}\), and the \(m\) diagonal terms contribute \(m\bigl(\frac{m-1}{m}\bigr)^{n}\).

Step 4 — the off-diagonal. For \(i\ne k\), both ducks survive exactly when no hunter picks either of them. Each hunter must avoid two specific ducks, which happens with probability \(\frac{m-2}{m}\), and the hunters are independent: \[\P(A_i\cap A_k)=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\P(S_j\ne i,\ S_j\ne k)=\Bigl(\frac{m-2}{m}\Bigr)^{\!n}.\] There are \(m(m-1)\) ordered pairs with \(i\ne k\), contributing \(m(m-1)\bigl(\frac{m-2}{m}\bigr)^{n}\).

Step 5 — assemble. \[\Var[X]=\underbrace{m\Bigl(\frac{m-1}{m}\Bigr)^{n}+m(m-1)\Bigl(\frac{m-2}{m}\Bigr)^{n}}_{\E[X^{2}]} -\underbrace{m^{2}\Bigl(\frac{m-1}{m}\Bigr)^{2n}}_{\E[X]^{2}} .\]

Checks. \(n=1\): exactly \(m-1\) ducks survive with certainty, so the variance must be 0. The formula gives \(m\frac{m-1}{m}+m(m-1)\frac{m-2}{m}-m^{2}\frac{(m-1)^{2}}{m^{2}} =(m-1)+(m-1)(m-2)-(m-1)^{2}=(m-1)\bigl[1+(m-2)-(m-1)\bigr]=0\). ✓ With \(m=10\), \(n=2\): the formula gives \(0.09000\); a direct simulation of the experiment gives \(0.0868\pm0.002\). ✓

(c) A Chebyshev window SoSe25 · P5c · 4 credits

With \(n=2\) hunters, find \(k\in\N\) as a function of \(m\) such that the number of survivors lies in \([\E[X]-k,\ \E[X]+k]\) with probability at least 90 %. Hint on the exam: rewrite the condition so that Chebyshev can be used.

Solution

Step 1 — reshape the condition. \[\P\bigl(X\in[\E X-k,\ \E X+k]\bigr)\ge0.9 \iff\P\bigl(X\notin[\E X-k,\ \E X+k]\bigr)\le0.1 \iff\P\bigl(|X-\E X|>k\bigr)\le0.1 ,\] using \(\P(A^{c})=1-\P(A)\) and the fact that being outside the interval means being further than \(k\) from the centre. Chebyshev bounds \(\P(|X-\E X|\ge k)\), and \(\{|X-\E X|>k\}\subseteq\{|X-\E X|\ge k\}\), so a bound on the latter bounds the former.

Step 2 — the variance at \(n=2\). Put \(n=2\) in the formula of part (b): \[\Var[X]=m\Bigl(\frac{m-1}{m}\Bigr)^{2}+m(m-1)\Bigl(\frac{m-2}{m}\Bigr)^{2}-m^{2}\Bigl(\frac{m-1}{m}\Bigr)^{4}.\] Simplify each term by cancelling powers of \(m\): \[m\cdot\frac{(m-1)^{2}}{m^{2}}=\frac{(m-1)^{2}}{m},\qquad m(m-1)\cdot\frac{(m-2)^{2}}{m^{2}}=\frac{(m-1)(m-2)^{2}}{m},\qquad m^{2}\cdot\frac{(m-1)^{4}}{m^{4}}=\frac{(m-1)^{4}}{m^{2}} .\] Put all three over the common denominator \(m^{2}\) and factor the common \((m-1)\) out of the numerator: \[\Var[X]=\frac{m(m-1)^{2}+m(m-1)(m-2)^{2}-(m-1)^{4}}{m^{2}} =\frac{(m-1)\bigl[m(m-1)+m(m-2)^{2}-(m-1)^{3}\bigr]}{m^{2}} .\] Now expand the bracket term by term: \[m(m-1)=m^{2}-m,\qquad m(m-2)^{2}=m(m^{2}-4m+4)=m^{3}-4m^{2}+4m,\] \[(m-1)^{3}=m^{3}-3m^{2}+3m-1 .\] Adding the first two and subtracting the third: \[(m^{2}-m)+(m^{3}-4m^{2}+4m)-(m^{3}-3m^{2}+3m-1) =m^{3}-m^{3}+(1-4+3)m^{2}+(-1+4-3)m+1=1 .\] Every power cancels and only the constant 1 survives. Therefore \[\Var[X]=\frac{m-1}{m^{2}}\qquad(n=2).\] Check: \(m=10\) gives \(\frac{9}{100}=0.09000\), matching part (b). ✓

Step 3 — apply Chebyshev and solve. Theorem 2.40: \(\P(|X-\E X|\ge k)\le\frac{\Var[X]}{k^{2}}\). Demand that this be at most \(0.1\): \[\frac{\Var[X]}{k^{2}}\le0.1\iff k^{2}\ge10\,\Var[X]=\frac{10(m-1)}{m^{2}} \iff k\ge\frac{\sqrt{10(m-1)}}{m}.\] Since \(k\) must be a natural number, take \[k=\Bigl\lceil\frac{\sqrt{10(m-1)}}{m}\Bigr\rceil,\] rounding up, because rounding down would make \(k\) smaller and the bound \(\Var/k^{2}\) larger, which could break the 10 % requirement.

Numbers. \(m=2\): \(\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}=1.581\to k=2\). \(m=5\): \(\frac{\sqrt{40}}{5}=1.265\to k=2\). \(m=10\): \(\frac{\sqrt{90}}{10}=0.9487\to k=1\). \(m=100\): \(\frac{\sqrt{990}}{100}=0.3146\to k=1\).

Two things about the official solution

(1) An inequality sign slips. "At least 90 %" translates to \(\P(\text{outside})\le0.1\), but the printed solution writes \(<0.1\) and then sets \(\Var[X]/k^{2}=0.1\) — which is consistent only with \(\le\). The final \(k\) is unchanged; the consistent version uses \(\le\) throughout, as above.

(2) The answer is correct but far from sharp. With \(n=2\) hunters, at most 2 ducks can die, so \(X\in\{m-2,m-1\}\) whenever \(m\ge2\), and \(\E[X]=\frac{(m-1)^{2}}{m}=m-2+\frac1m\). Both possible values are therefore within distance 1 of \(\E[X]\): \(|m-1-\E X|=1-\frac1m<1\) and \(|m-2-\E X|=\frac1m\le1\). So \(k=1\) works with probability 1 for every \(m\ge2\), while the Chebyshev answer demands \(k=2\) for small \(m\). The question only asked to "find a \(k\)", so the official answer earns full marks — but it is a clean illustration of how loose a Chebyshev bound can be when you know the support of the variable.

Worked at §2.2.

Walkthrough 3 — Randomized response SoSe26 · P5 · 13 credits

The setting. Each survey participant has a sensitive binary attribute \(A\sim\Ber(p)\) with \(p\in[0,1]\) unknown. We never see \(A\). Instead we see a privacy-protected answer \(Y\): with probability \(r\in(0,1]\) the participant answers truthfully, and with probability \(1-r\) answers by flipping a fair coin, independently of \(A\). We observe iid answers \(Y_1,\dots,Y_n\) with \(r\) known, and write \(\bar Y_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}Y_i\).

Why anyone would do this: a participant who answers "yes" can always say the coin made them, so nothing about any individual can be inferred with certainty. The randomness is deliberately injected to buy privacy, and the statistician's job is to subtract it out again. This is the longest and most recent of the three closing problems and it spans four subchapters.

(a) \(\P(Y=1)\) and identifiability SoSe26 · P5a · 3 credits

Solution

Step 1 — total probability over the mechanism. Let \(T\) be the event "the participant answers truthfully", with \(\P(T)=r\) and \(\P(T^{c})=1-r\). These two partition the sample space, so by Theorem 1.70(ii), \[\P(Y=1)=\P(Y=1\mid T)\P(T)+\P(Y=1\mid T^{c})\P(T^{c}).\] Given \(T\), the answer equals the attribute, so \(\P(Y=1\mid T)=\P(A=1)=p\). Given \(T^{c}\), the answer is a fair coin, so \(\P(Y=1\mid T^{c})=\frac12\). Hence \[\P(Y=1)=r\,p+(1-r)\cdot\tfrac12=rp+\frac{1-r}{2}=:q(p).\] (Credit split printed on the paper: 1.5 for this expression.)

Step 2 — identifiability (Definition 3.11, §3.1). A parameter is identifiable if different parameter values give different distributions of the data — equivalently here, if the map \(p\mapsto q(p)\) is injective (one-to-one). Suppose \(q(p_1)=q(p_2)\). Then \(rp_1+\frac{1-r}{2}=rp_2+\frac{1-r}{2}\), so \(rp_1=rp_2\), and since \(r>0\) we may divide by \(r\) to get \(p_1=p_2\). So \(q\) is injective on \([0,1]\) and \(p\) is identifiable from the distribution of \(Y\). (1 credit for injectivity, 0.5 for the conclusion.)

Why \(r>0\) matters. If \(r=0\) every participant just flips a coin, \(q(p)=\frac12\) for every \(p\), and the data carry no information about \(p\): not identifiable. The problem excludes this by writing \(r\in(0,1]\).

An unstated assumption in the official solution

The step \(\P(Y=1\mid T^{c})=\frac12\) uses that the coin is flipped independently of the attribute \(A\), and that the choice of mechanism itself is independent of \(A\). The problem statement does say the coin is flipped "independently of \(A\)", but the model answer never names the assumption where it is used. Naming it costs one clause and makes the derivation airtight.

Worked at §1.4 (the probability half) and §3.1 (the identifiability half).

(b) The mle for \(p\) by reparametrisation SoSe26 · P5b · 3 credits

Assume the observed \(\bar y_n\) lies in \(\bigl[\frac{1-r}{2},\frac{1+r}{2}\bigr]\). Derive the maximum likelihood estimator for \(p\). Hint on the exam: the mle in a Bernoulli model is the sample mean.

Solution

Step 1 — what the data are. By part (a), each \(Y_i\) is Bernoulli with success probability \(q=q(p)=rp+\frac{1-r}{2}\), and the \(Y_i\) are iid. So the likelihood, as a function of \(q\), is \[L(q\mid y)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}q^{y_i}(1-q)^{1-y_i}=q^{\sum_iy_i}(1-q)^{\,n-\sum_iy_i}.\] (The formula \(q^{y}(1-q)^{1-y}\) is the compact way of writing "\(q\) if \(y=1\), \(1-q\) if \(y=0\)": each exponent switches one factor off.) That is 1 credit.

Step 2 — the mle of \(q\). By the hint, \(\hat q_{\text{mle}}=\bar Y_n\). (Deriving it takes three lines: \(\ell(q)=s\ln q+(n-s)\ln(1-q)\) with \(s=\sum y_i\), \(\ell'(q)=\frac sq-\frac{n-s}{1-q}=0\) gives \(s(1-q)=(n-s)q\), i.e. \(s=nq\), so \(q=\frac sn=\bar y_n\).) That is the second credit.

Step 3 — transform back. The map \(p\mapsto q(p)\) is bijective from \([0,1]\) onto \(\bigl[\frac{1-r}{2},\frac{1+r}{2}\bigr]\) (it is affine with slope \(r>0\)). The maximum likelihood estimator is invariant under such a reparametrisation: maximising over \(p\) is the same as maximising over \(q\) and then reading back the \(p\) that produced it. Solving \(\bar y_n=rp+\frac{1-r}{2}\) for \(p\): subtract \(\frac{1-r}{2}\), then divide by \(r\), \[\hat p_{\text{mle}}=\frac{\bar Y_n-\frac{1-r}{2}}{r}.\] That is the third credit.

What the printed assumption on \(\bar y_n\) is really doing

The official line "the Bernoulli likelihood is maximised at \(\hat q=\bar y_n\)" silently needs \(\bar y_n\) to be a reachable value of \(q\), that is \(\bar y_n\in[\frac{1-r}{2},\frac{1+r}{2}\bigr]\) — which is exactly what the problem assumes. If it failed, the unrestricted formula could return a negative number or one above 1, which cannot be a probability; the true mle would then be the nearest boundary, \(\hat p=0\) or \(\hat p=1\). Say this in one sentence; it shows you know why the assumption is printed.

Worked at §3.2.

(c) Unbiasedness and variance SoSe26 · P5c · 2 credits

Show \(\hat p:=\frac{\bar Y_n-\frac{1-r}{2}}{r}\) is unbiased for \(p\) and compute \(\Var[\hat p]\).

Solution

Unbiasedness (1 credit). \(\E[\bar Y_n]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\E[Y_i]=q(p)\), because each \(Y_i\sim\Ber(q(p))\) has mean \(q(p)\) (Lemma 2.26(iii)) — linearity only, no independence needed. Then, since \(\hat p\) is an affine function of \(\bar Y_n\) and expectation is linear (Proposition 2.4(i)), \[\E[\hat p]=\frac{\E[\bar Y_n]-\frac{1-r}{2}}{r}=\frac{q(p)-\frac{1-r}{2}}{r} =\frac{rp+\frac{1-r}{2}-\frac{1-r}{2}}{r}=\frac{rp}{r}=p .\] The bias is \(p-p=0\): unbiased (Definition 3.20(i)).

Variance (1 credit). Adding the constant \(-\frac{1-r}{2}\) does not change a variance, and dividing by \(r\) divides it by \(r^{2}\) (Proposition 2.8(iii), \(\Var[aX+b]=a^{2}\Var[X]\) with \(a=\frac1r\)): \[\Var[\hat p]=\frac{1}{r^{2}}\Var[\bar Y_n]=\frac{1}{r^{2}}\cdot\frac{q(p)\bigl(1-q(p)\bigr)}{n},\] where \(\Var[\bar Y_n]=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_i\Var[Y_i]=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\cdot n\,q(1-q)=\frac{q(1-q)}{n}\), using \(\Var[\Ber(q)]=q(1-q)\) and, here, the independence of the \(Y_i\) (Proposition 2.8(iv)).

Since \(\hat p\) is unbiased, \(\operatorname{mse}[\hat p]=\Var[\hat p]\).

In words: the \(\frac{1}{r^{2}}\) is the price of privacy. With \(r=\frac12\) the variance is four times what it would be if everyone answered truthfully — you need roughly four times as many participants to reach the same accuracy.

Numbers. With \(r=\frac12\), \(n=100\) and \(q=0.55\): \(\Var[\hat p]=\frac{0.55\cdot0.45}{0.25\cdot100}=\frac{0.2475}{25}=0.009900\), standard deviation \(0.09950\). Worked at §3.2.

(d) A one-sided approximate test SoSe26 · P5d · 5 credits

The organisers want to know whether more than 60 % of the population have the attribute. Take \(r=\frac12\); among \(n=100\) answers, 64 equal 1; \(\alpha=0.05\). Formulate the hypotheses and perform an approximate test: state the statistic, its approximate distribution at the null boundary, the rejection rule, the observed value, and the conclusion. Hints on the exam: \(q(p)=rp+\frac{1-r}{2}\) and \(z_{0.05}\approx1.64\).

Solution, with the official credit split

(1 cr) Hypotheses. The claim we want evidence for goes into \(H_1\), and "more than 60 %" is directional, so the test is one-sided (Definition 3.43): \[H_0:\ p\le0.6\qquad\text{against}\qquad H_1:\ p>0.6 .\]

(1 cr) The null boundary and its numbers. With \(r=\frac12\), \(q(p)=\frac12p+\frac{1-\frac12}{2}=\frac p2+\frac14\), which is strictly increasing in \(p\). So among all \(p\) allowed by \(H_0\), the one that makes the data look most like \(H_1\) is the boundary \(p_0=0.6\), and \[q_0=q(0.6)=\tfrac12\cdot0.6+\tfrac14=0.3+0.25=0.55 .\] At this boundary, \(\E[\bar Y_{100}]=q_0=0.55\) and \(\Var[\bar Y_{100}]=\frac{q_0(1-q_0)}{100}=\frac{0.55\cdot0.45}{100}=\frac{0.2475}{100}=0.002475\), so the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{0.002475}=0.04975\).

(1 cr) The statistic and its law. By the clt (Theorem 2.64 — the \(Y_i\) are iid Bernoulli with finite mean and finite non-zero variance), \[Z:=\frac{\bar Y_{100}-0.55}{\sqrt{0.55\cdot0.45/100}}\ \text{is approximately}\ \mathcal N(0,1) \ \text{under the null boundary.}\]

(1 cr) The rule and the observed value. One-sided rejection rule at level \(\alpha=0.05\): reject \(H_0\) if \(z_{\text{obs}}>z_{0.05}\approx1.64\). The observed sample mean is \(\bar y_{100}=\frac{64}{100}=0.64\), so \[z_{\text{obs}}=\frac{0.64-0.55}{0.04975}=\frac{0.09}{0.04975}=1.809\approx1.81 .\]

(1 cr) The decision, in words. Since \(1.81>1.64\), we reject \(H_0\) at the approximate significance level 0.05. The data provide evidence that more than 60 % of the population have the attribute.

How to get \(0.09/0.04975\) without a calculator. \(0.55\cdot0.45=0.2475\), so the variance is \(0.002475\) and the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{0.002475}\). Since \(0.05^{2}=0.0025\), the standard deviation is just under \(0.05\); take it as \(0.0498\). Then \(0.09/0.05=1.8\), and the slightly smaller denominator pushes the answer a little above 1.8. That is enough to see \(1.81>1.64\).

The two traps in this part

Trap 1 — the variance is evaluated at the null boundary, not at the observation. Using \(\hat q=0.64\) would give \(\sqrt{0.64\cdot0.36/100}=0.04800\) and \(z=1.875\); the decision happens to be the same here, but it is not what is marked.

Trap 2 — one-sided means \(z_{0.05}=1.64\), not \(z_{0.025}=1.96\). With 1.96 the observed 1.81 would fail to reject and you would lose the rule credit and the decision credit. Both tests ever set on these three papers were one-sided, and both official solutions flag that explicitly.

A footnote on the estimate itself. Part (b)'s estimator gives \(\hat p=\frac{0.64-0.25}{0.5}=0.7800\) — a point estimate of 78 %. Its standard deviation from part (c) is about \(0.0995\), so a rough 95 % Wald interval would be \(0.78\pm1.96\cdot0.0995\), which is very wide. The test's verdict "more than 60 %" is therefore not a strong statement, only a statistically significant one at the 5 % level. No exam has asked for this interval, but Example 3.58 (§3.4) is the recipe.

Worked in full, with the p-value widget, at §3.3.

Two new long problems in the same style

Each has five parts of rising difficulty, a realistic credit total of 13, and chains several subchapters, in the manner of the three above. Work them under time pressure — about 25 minutes each — with paper only.

Long problem A — The flaky test suite My problem · 13 credits · chains §1.4 → §3.1 → §2.2 (Jensen) → §3.2 → §3.3 with §2.4 underneath

A continuous-integration pipeline runs a suite of \(n=5\) test cases. Each test fails independently of the others with the same unknown probability \(\theta\in[0,1)\). The dashboard does not show individual tests: it only records whether the whole run failed, meaning at least one of the five tests failed. We observe \(m\) independent runs and record \(R_1,\dots,R_m\), where \(R_j=1\) if run \(j\) failed and \(R_j=0\) otherwise. Write \(\bar R_m=\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^{m}R_j\).

  1. (3 cr) Compute \(\P(R=1)\) in terms of \(\theta\) and \(n\). Is \(\theta\) identifiable from the distribution of \(R\)?
  2. (3 cr) Derive the maximum likelihood estimator \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\) for \(\theta\).
  3. (2 cr) Decide, with a proof, whether \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\) is unbiased. State the direction of any bias.
  4. (2 cr) For \(\hat q:=\bar R_m\), give \(\E[\hat q]\), \(\Var[\hat q]\), and a Chebyshev bound on \(\P(|\hat q-q|\ge\epsilon)\) that does not involve the unknown \(q\). Evaluate it at \(m=100\), \(\epsilon=0.1\), and compare with the clt value at \(q=\frac12\).
  5. (3 cr) Among \(m=200\) runs, 150 failed. Test \(H_0:\theta\le0.2\) against \(H_1:\theta>0.2\) at \(\alpha=0.05\), using \(z_{0.05}\approx1.64\).
Solution

(i) The distribution of one run. A run passes exactly when all \(n\) tests pass. The tests are independent, and each passes with probability \(1-\theta\), so \[\P(R=0)=(1-\theta)^{n},\qquad\text{hence}\qquad q(\theta):=\P(R=1)=1-(1-\theta)^{n}.\] With \(n=5\): \(q(\theta)=1-(1-\theta)^{5}\).

Identifiability (Definition 3.11). \(q\) is injective on \([0,1)\): the map \(\theta\mapsto1-\theta\) is strictly decreasing, raising a number in \((0,1]\) to the fifth power is strictly increasing on positive numbers, and subtracting from 1 flips the direction once more — so \(q\) is strictly increasing in \(\theta\). A strictly increasing function is injective, so different \(\theta\) give different distributions of \(R\), and \(\theta\) is identifiable.

What earns the credits: the complement step \(\{R=0\}=\{\text{all tests pass}\}\) (1), independence to get the product \((1-\theta)^n\) (1), the injectivity argument and the conclusion (1).

(ii) The mle. The \(R_j\) are iid \(\Ber(q)\) with \(q=q(\theta)\), so exactly as in the randomized response problem, \[L(q\mid r)=q^{\sum_jr_j}(1-q)^{\,m-\sum_jr_j},\qquad \hat q_{\text{mle}}=\bar R_m .\] (The three-line derivation: \(\ell(q)=s\ln q+(m-s)\ln(1-q)\) with \(s=\sum_jr_j\); \(\ell'(q)=\frac sq-\frac{m-s}{1-q}=0\Rightarrow s(1-q)=(m-s)q\Rightarrow s=mq\Rightarrow q=\bar r_m\); \(\ell''(q)=-\frac{s}{q^{2}}-\frac{m-s}{(1-q)^{2}}<0\) for \(0<s<m\), so it is the global maximum.)

Now invert \(q(\theta)=1-(1-\theta)^{5}\). Solve for \(\theta\): \[q=1-(1-\theta)^{5}\iff(1-\theta)^{5}=1-q\iff1-\theta=(1-q)^{1/5}\iff\theta=1-(1-q)^{1/5}.\] (Taking a fifth root is legitimate because \(1-q\in(0,1]\).) The map is bijective, so the mle transforms with it: \[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=1-\bigl(1-\bar R_m\bigr)^{1/5}.\] Guard clause: if \(\bar R_m=1\) (every run failed) this returns \(\hat\theta=1\), which is outside the stated parameter set \([0,1)\); the mle then sits on the boundary, exactly as in SoSe26 P5b. Say so.

(iii) Unbiasedness — and this is where Jensen enters. Write \(h(u):=1-(1-u)^{1/5}\), so \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=h(\bar R_m)\) and \(\theta=h(q)\).

Is \(h\) convex? Let \(f(u)=(1-u)^{1/5}\). Then, by the chain rule, \[f'(u)=\tfrac15(1-u)^{1/5-1}\cdot(-1)=-\tfrac15(1-u)^{-4/5},\qquad f''(u)=-\tfrac15\cdot\bigl(-\tfrac45\bigr)(1-u)^{-9/5}\cdot(-1)=-\tfrac{4}{25}(1-u)^{-9/5}<0\] for \(u<1\). So \(f\) is strictly concave, hence \(h=1-f\) is strictly convex on \([0,1)\).

Jensen's inequality (Theorem 2.42) applied to the convex \(h\) and the random variable \(\bar R_m\) gives \[\E[\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}]=\E\bigl[h(\bar R_m)\bigr]\ \ge\ h\bigl(\E[\bar R_m]\bigr)=h(q)=\theta .\] So \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\) is biased, and the bias is \(\ge0\): it systematically overestimates \(\theta\). The inequality is strict as soon as \(\bar R_m\) is not degenerate, which it is not for \(0<q<1\) and \(m\ge1\), because \(h\) is strictly convex.

Numbers (by simulation, \(\theta=0.2\), \(n=5\) so \(q=0.6723\)): at \(m=5\) the mean of \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}\) is \(0.3014\) (bias \(+0.101\)); at \(m=20\) it is \(0.2077\) (bias \(+0.0077\)); at \(m=200\) it is \(0.2007\) (bias \(+0.0007\)). The bias is real but vanishes as \(m\) grows — the mle is asymptotically unbiased, which is all Remark 3.30 promises.

The general lesson: applying a non-linear function to an unbiased estimator destroys unbiasedness, and Jensen tells you in which direction. Only affine maps preserve it — which is why the randomized-response estimator, built from an affine inverse, stayed unbiased.

(iv) \(\hat q=\bar R_m\). Unbiased: \(\E[\hat q]=q\) by linearity. Variance: \(\Var[\hat q]=\frac{q(1-q)}{m}\), using independence (Proposition 2.8(iii)(iv)) and \(\Var[\Ber(q)]=q(1-q)\). Chebyshev (Theorem 2.40): \[\P(|\hat q-q|\ge\epsilon)\le\frac{q(1-q)}{m\epsilon^{2}}\le\frac{1}{4m\epsilon^{2}},\] the last step because \(q(1-q)\le\frac14\) for every \(q\in[0,1]\): the parabola \(q-q^{2}\) has its maximum at \(q=\frac12\), where it equals \(\frac14\). This version contains no unknown, which is what makes it usable.

At \(m=100\), \(\epsilon=0.1\): the bound is \(\frac{1}{4\cdot100\cdot0.01}=0.2500\). The clt value at \(q=\frac12\), where the standard deviation of \(\hat q\) is \(\sqrt{\frac{0.25}{100}}=0.05\), is \(2\Phi\bigl(-\frac{0.1}{0.05}\bigr)=2\Phi(-2)=0.04550\). The guarantee is about 5.5 times larger than the realistic value — the same picture as Drill E7 of the previous block.

(v) The test. "More than 0.2" is directional, so the test is one-sided: \[H_0:\ \theta\le0.2\qquad\text{against}\qquad H_1:\ \theta>0.2 .\] Since \(q(\theta)\) is strictly increasing, the hypothesis \(\theta\le0.2\) is the same as \(q\le q(0.2)\), and the null boundary is \[q_0=q(0.2)=1-0.8^{5}=1-0.32768=0.67232 .\] (\(0.8^{2}=0.64\), \(0.8^{4}=0.64^{2}=0.4096\), \(0.8^{5}=0.4096\cdot0.8=0.32768\).)

At the boundary, \(\E[\bar R_{200}]=0.67232\) and \(\Var[\bar R_{200}]=\frac{0.67232\cdot0.32768}{200}=\frac{0.22028}{200}=0.0011014\), so the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{0.0011014}=0.033189\). By the clt, under the null boundary \[Z=\frac{\bar R_{200}-0.67232}{0.033189}\ \text{is approximately}\ \mathcal N(0,1).\] Rejection rule: reject \(H_0\) if \(z_{\text{obs}}>z_{0.05}\approx1.64\). Observed: \(\bar r_{200}=\frac{150}{200}=0.75\), so \[z_{\text{obs}}=\frac{0.75-0.67232}{0.033189}=\frac{0.07768}{0.033189}=2.341 .\] Since \(2.341>1.64\), we reject \(H_0\) at the approximate level 0.05: the data give evidence that the per-test failure probability exceeds 0.2.

Point estimate, for context: \(\hat\theta_{\text{mle}}=1-(1-0.75)^{1/5}=1-0.25^{0.2}=0.2421\).

What this problem drills that the past three do not. The randomized-response problem had an affine link \(q(p)\), so inverting it kept unbiasedness and everything stayed linear. Here the link \(q(\theta)=1-(1-\theta)^{5}\) is non-linear, which (a) makes the null boundary a genuine computation rather than a substitution, and (b) forces the bias question to be answered with Jensen rather than with linearity. Both moves are inside the course: Theorem 2.42 and Definition 3.20.

Long problem B — Handing back the exam sheets My problem · 13 credits · chains §1.2 → §2.1 (indicators, covariance, conditional expectation) → §2.2 → §2.4 → §3.3

At the end of a tutorial, \(n\ge2\) students hand in one exam sheet each. The tutor shuffles the pile uniformly at random — every one of the \(n!\) orderings is equally likely — and hands back one sheet to each student in that order. Let \(X\) be the number of students who receive their own sheet.

  1. (3 cr) Compute \(\E[X]\).
  2. (3 cr) Compute \(\Var[X]\). Are the indicators independent?
  3. (2 cr) Bound \(\P(X\ge4)\) with Markov and with Chebyshev. Which is better, and why?
  4. (2 cr) Given that student 1 received their own sheet, what is the expected number of students who receive their own sheet?
  5. (3 cr) A tutor is suspected of not shuffling properly. Over \(m=400\) independent tutorials the average number of own-sheet matches was \(\bar x=1.12\). Test, at \(\alpha=0.05\) with \(z_{0.05}\approx1.64\), whether the shuffling produces more matches than a uniform shuffle would.
Solution

(i) \(\E[X]\). Let \(A_i\) be the event "student \(i\) receives their own sheet", \(i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), and \(X_i:=\one_{A_i}\), so that \(X=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\).

By symmetry, student \(i\)'s sheet is equally likely to end up in any of the \(n\) positions, so \(\P(A_i)=\frac1n\). (Counting version: the orderings in which position \(i\) holds sheet \(i\) number \((n-1)!\), out of \(n!\) in total, and \(\frac{(n-1)!}{n!}=\frac1n\) — a Laplace probability, §1.2, §1.2.)

Then \(\E[X_i]=\P(A_i)=\frac1n\), and by linearity (Proposition 2.4(i)), \[\E[X]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\E[X_i]=n\cdot\frac1n=1 .\] Whatever the class size, on average exactly one student gets their own sheet.

(ii) \(\Var[X]\). Use \(\Var[X]=\E[X^{2}]-\E[X]^{2}\) and expand as in the duck hunt: \(\E[X^{2}]=\sum_{i,k=1}^{n}\E[X_iX_k]=\sum_{i,k}\P(A_i\cap A_k)\).

Diagonal (\(i=k\)): \(X_i^{2}=X_i\), so each of the \(n\) terms is \(\frac1n\); total \(1\).

Off-diagonal (\(i\ne k\)): both students get their own sheet when two specified positions are fixed. The number of such orderings is \((n-2)!\), so \[\P(A_i\cap A_k)=\frac{(n-2)!}{n!}=\frac{1}{n(n-1)} .\] There are \(n(n-1)\) ordered pairs with \(i\ne k\), so the off-diagonal total is \(n(n-1)\cdot\frac{1}{n(n-1)}=1\).

Hence \(\E[X^{2}]=1+1=2\) and \[\Var[X]=2-1^{2}=1 .\] Again independent of \(n\).

Are the indicators independent? No. Compare: \[\P(A_i\cap A_k)=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\qquad\text{against}\qquad\P(A_i)\P(A_k)=\frac{1}{n^{2}} .\] Since \(n(n-1)<n^{2}\), the joint probability is strictly larger than the product, so the events are not independent. The covariance (Definition 2.9, §2.1) is \[\Cov[X_i,X_k]=\E[X_iX_k]-\E[X_i]\E[X_k]=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}-\frac{1}{n^{2}} =\frac{n-(n-1)}{n^{2}(n-1)}=\frac{1}{n^{2}(n-1)}>0 .\] Positively correlated: knowing that one student got their own sheet makes it slightly more likely for another. At \(n=10\) the covariance is \(\frac{1}{900}=0.001111\), small but not zero.

The reason the variance still comes out as 1: the \(n(n-1)\) small positive covariances add up to \(n(n-1)\cdot\frac{1}{n^{2}(n-1)}=\frac1n\), which exactly cancels the shortfall \(\sum_i\Var[X_i]=n\cdot\frac1n(1-\frac1n)=1-\frac1n\) relative to 1.

(iii) Bounding \(\P(X\ge4)\).

Markov (Theorem 2.38; \(X\ge0\)): \(\P(X\ge4)\le\frac{\E[X]}{4}=\frac14=0.2500\).

Chebyshev (Theorem 2.40): first put the event into the required shape. Since \(\E[X]=1\), \(\{X\ge4\}=\{X-1\ge3\}\subseteq\{|X-1|\ge3\}\), and probabilities respect inclusion, so \[\P(X\ge4)\le\P(|X-1|\ge3)\le\frac{\Var[X]}{3^{2}}=\frac19=0.1111 .\]

Chebyshev is better here (0.1111 against 0.2500), and that is the usual situation when the variable is concentrated around its mean: Markov uses only the mean and therefore cannot know that \(X\) rarely strays, while Chebyshev also uses the variance. The price is that Chebyshev needs a finite variance, which Markov does not.

How good are they? For large \(n\) the true value is about \(0.01899\) (the distribution of \(X\) approaches \(\Poi(1)\), for which \(\P(X\ge4)=1-e^{-1}(1+1+\frac12+\frac16)=1-\frac{8}{3e}=0.01899\)). The exact value at \(n=10\) is \(0.01899\) as well, to four digits. So Chebyshev overshoots the truth by a factor of about 6, and Markov by about 13. Both are valid; neither is sharp.

One caution: for \(n=5\) the exact value is \(0.008333=\frac1{120}\), because with five sheets it is impossible for exactly 4 students to be matched — if four are right the fifth must be too — so \(\P(X\ge4)=\P(X=5)=\frac{1}{5!}\). Small \(n\) has its own combinatorics.

(iv) \(\E[X\mid A_1]\). Given \(A_1\), student 1's sheet is fixed in place and the remaining \(n-1\) sheets form a uniformly random ordering of the remaining \(n-1\) students. So, for \(k\ne1\), \[\P(A_k\mid A_1)=\frac{\P(A_k\cap A_1)}{\P(A_1)}=\frac{1/(n(n-1))}{1/n}=\frac{1}{n-1},\] which is the same formula as before with \(n\) replaced by \(n-1\) — exactly what "a uniform shuffle of \(n-1\) sheets" predicts. Therefore, writing \(X=X_1+\sum_{k=2}^{n}X_k\) and using linearity of conditional expectation, \[\E[X\mid A_1]=\underbrace{\E[X_1\mid A_1]}_{=1,\ \text{since }X_1=1\text{ on }A_1} +\sum_{k=2}^{n}\P(A_k\mid A_1)=1+(n-1)\cdot\frac{1}{n-1}=2 .\] Two, for every \(n\ge2\) — one guaranteed match plus one expected match among the rest.

In words: the "expected one match" is remarkably robust. Take one match as given and the rest of the class still produces one on average, so the total is two.

(v) The test. Model the \(m=400\) tutorials as iid copies \(X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(400)}\) of \(X\). Under a uniform shuffle, \(\E[X]=1\) and \(\Var[X]=1\) from parts (i) and (ii).

"More matches than a uniform shuffle would produce" is directional, so the test is one-sided. Writing \(\mu\) for the true mean number of matches per tutorial: \[H_0:\ \mu\le1\qquad\text{against}\qquad H_1:\ \mu>1 .\] At the null boundary \(\mu_0=1\), and with variance 1 per tutorial, \[\E[\bar X_{400}]=1,\qquad\Var[\bar X_{400}]=\frac{1}{400},\qquad\text{sd}=\frac{1}{20}=0.05 .\] By the clt (Theorem 2.64 — iid, finite mean, finite non-zero variance), the statistic \[Z=\frac{\bar X_{400}-1}{1/20}\ \text{is approximately}\ \mathcal N(0,1)\ \text{under the null boundary.}\] Rejection rule: reject if \(z_{\text{obs}}>z_{0.05}\approx1.64\). Observed: \[z_{\text{obs}}=\frac{1.12-1}{0.05}=\frac{0.12}{0.05}=2.400 .\] Since \(2.400>1.64\) we reject \(H_0\) at the approximate level 0.05: there is evidence that this tutor's shuffling produces more own-sheet matches than a uniform shuffle.

One honest caveat to state: the variance 1 used in the denominator is the variance under the null hypothesis of a uniform shuffle. That is the correct choice for a test (Trap 1 of SoSe26 P5d), and it is also the only variance we can compute without knowing the tutor's actual shuffling mechanism.

What this problem drills that the past three do not. The duck hunt's indicators were also dependent, but there the dependence came from independent hunters colliding; here it comes from a permutation, where a sheet placed in one spot is removed from all the others. Part (iv) brings in conditional expectation, which appeared on the exams only as the true/false item SoSe26 P2c and never as a computation. Part (v) turns a combinatorial quantity into a test, which is the move all three closing problems make in their last part. Everything used is in the course: Laplace probabilities (§1.2), indicators and covariance (§2.1), Markov and Chebyshev (§2.2), the clt (§2.4), the one-sided z-test (§3.3).

The standing warning, once more My addition

Three papers — two endterms and one retake — are a tiny sample, and they disagree with each other on problem count, credit total and topic mix. The closing story problem is the one habit all three share, and even that tells you only what a full-credit answer has looked like, never what the next paper will contain. Drill these chains because the moves inside them (indicators, linearity, covariance, a bound, a test) are the moves the whole course is built from — not because the next problem will be about ducks.

Recipes for the recurring task types

The three official Musterlösungen keep re-using the same fifteen moves. Below, each one is written as a method box: how you recognise the task, the numbered steps, the place where credits are usually lost, and chips saying in which paper (and for how many credits) it has appeared. The chips are evidence of what has been asked, nothing more.

The standing warning

Three papers is a tiny sample: two endterms [Endklausur] and one retake [Wiederholungsklausur], and the retake had a visibly different shape from its own endterm. Nothing on this page predicts the next exam. Use the recipes to know what a full-credit answer looks like, never to decide what to skip.

TT1 · Decide a true/false statement and justify it WiSe25 · P1a–d · 12 cr SoSe25 · P1a–d · 12 cr SoSe26 · P1a–e · 5 cr SoSe26 · P2a–d · 12 cr

Trigger. A short sentence with a tick box, or the words "decide whether the following statement is true or false". 41 credits across the three papers — the largest single task type.

  1. Read the quantifier. "For any", "for all", "then it already holds" means one single witness refutes it. If the sentence is a named theorem in disguise, the answer is the theorem plus its one line.
  2. Compare the hypotheses printed with the hypotheses the result needs. Missing independence [Unabhängigkeit], missing finiteness, missing non-degeneracy — the counterexample lives exactly in that gap.
  3. True: name the script item (Thm 2.35, Prop 2.12(iii)(v), Rem 2.57, …) and write the one or two lines it needs.
  4. False: build the smallest counterexample — a sample space \(\Omega\) with 2 to 4 points and an explicit probability mass function [Wahrscheinlichkeitsfunktion], or \(\Ber(\tfrac12)\), or \(\Unif(0,1)\). Then verify both halves with numbers: the hypothesis holds, and the conclusion fails.
  5. Write the verdict word first. SoSe26's printed marking scheme gives 1 credit for the bare verdict, before any justification.

Pitfall. Reading "iid" into a statement that only says "identically distributed". That single reflex is worth 3 credits on WiSe25 P1d and it is the most examined error on these papers.

Counterexample kit: \(X_i := X_1\) for all \(i\) (destroys independence, keeps the marginal law); \(X_n := n\cdot\one_{\{U\le 1/n\}}\) with \(U\sim\Unif(0,1)\) (converges to 0 in every mode, yet \(\E[X_n]=1\)); \(X\) uniform on \(\{-1,0,1\}\) with \(Y=X^2\) (uncorrelated, \(\E[X\mid Y]=\E[X]\), still dependent); a finite collection whose size is not a power of 2 (cannot be a \(\sigma\)-algebra).

Taught on: \(\sigma\)-algebras · covariance · modes of convergence · what a level means. Drill: the true/false bank.

TT2 · State a named theorem or definition with all assumptions WiSe25 · P2a, P2b · 3+3 cr SoSe25 · P2a, P2b · 3+3 cr SoSe26 · P3a · 3 cr

Trigger. "State the … with all required assumptions", or "Give the full definition of …". 15 credits of pure recall [Reproduktion], present in all three papers.

  1. Set the stage: what objects exist and where they live. "Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be a sequence of iid real random variables on a common probability space \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\)."
  2. List every finiteness and regularity assumption separately, one clause each: finite mean; finite and non-zero variance; \(g\) convex. The marking is per assumption.
  3. State the conclusion in the script's own notation and name the mode of convergence.
  4. For a mode of convergence, include the exceptional-set clause — "for every \(x\in\R\) at which \(F_X\) is continuous" (Def 2.56(iii)), "\(\P(\{\omega:\lim_n X_n(\omega)=X(\omega)\})=1\)" (Def 2.56(ii)). That clause is the part people drop and the part that is marked.
  5. Do not add unasked extras. SoSe26 P3a states that the parenthetical additions were not graded — and a wrong extra can still cost you.

Pitfall. Writing the central limit theorem as \(\bar X_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)\). A limit law cannot depend on \(n\). Write the standardised version, \(Z_n=(\bar X_n-\mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1)\).

Taught on: the laws of large numbers · the central limit theorem · modes of convergence · Jensen. Drill: the state-it bank.

TT3 · A density with an unknown constant: find it, then cdf / mean / median SoSe25 · P3a, P3b, P3c · 2+2+2 cr

Trigger. "Determine \(c\) such that \(p_X(x)=x/c\) on \([0,2]\) is a valid probability density function." A probability density function [Dichte] is a function \(p\ge 0\) whose total integral is 1 (Def 1.45).

  1. Write \(\int p(x)\,\mathrm dx = 1\), integrating only over the stated support — the set where \(p\) is allowed to be non-zero.
  2. Solve for the constant, then check \(p\ge 0\) there. SoSe25's own solution says this out loud.
  3. cdf: \(F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}p(y)\,\mathrm dy\) (Lem 1.49(i)); write all three branches — 0 below the support, the formula on it, 1 above. Full credit needed all three.
  4. Mean: \(\E[X]=\int x\,p(x)\,\mathrm dx\) over the support (Def 2.1(ii)).
  5. Median: solve \(F(m)=\tfrac12\) (Def 2.20) and discard roots outside the support — \(m=\sqrt 2\), not \(-\sqrt2\).

Pitfall. Integrating over all of \(\R\) instead of the support, and forgetting the two constant branches of the cdf.

Taught on: densities · quantiles and the median. Drill: the density drills.

TT4 · Transform a random variable: the density of \(g(X)\) WiSe25 · P3a · 4 cr SoSe25 · P3d · 3 cr SoSe25 · P1d · 3 cr SoSe26 · P4b · 3 cr

Trigger. "\(U\sim\Unif(0,1)\) and \(X=-\tfrac1\lambda\ln U\): derive the density of \(X\)", or "determine the pdf of \(Y=\ln X\)". 13 credits, present in all three papers in some form.

  1. Push the support of \(X\) through \(g\) first. WiSe25 P3a prints "Be sure to correctly specify the support" — the support is separately worth credit.
  2. Decide whether \(g\) is increasing or decreasing there. \(-\tfrac1\lambda\ln u\) is decreasing, so the inequality flips when you invert it.
  3. Then either route — both scored full marks:
    • cdf route: \(F_Y(y)=\P(g(X)\le y)\), invert the inequality (flip if \(g\) is decreasing), differentiate.
    • Prop 2.51: \(p_Y(y)=p_X\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr)\cdot\bigl|\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dy}g^{-1}(y)\bigr|\) — the change-of-variables formula [Transformationsformel], which the exam supplies as a hint when it wants this route.
  4. State \(p_Y(y)=0\) off the support, explicitly.
  5. Check \(\int p_Y = 1\).

Pitfall. A ratio \(X/Y\) is a different task: build the joint density as the product of the marginals (independence, Def 1.77), then integrate over \(\{x < t\,y\}\) as an iterated integral. The change-of-variables formula for one variable does not apply.

Taught on: transformation of densities · the cdf method. Drill: the density drills.

TT5 · Compute a maximum likelihood estimator WiSe25 · P4a · 4 cr SoSe25 · P4a · 4 cr SoSe26 · P5b · 3 cr

Trigger. "Derive the maximum likelihood estimator [Maximum-Likelihood-Schätzer] for \(\theta\)". 11 credits, in all three papers.

  1. \(L(\theta\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p_\theta(x_i)\) (Def 3.13, iid case). Collect the powers of \(\theta\) and merge the exponentials.
  2. \(\ell=\ln L\). Drop additive terms with no \(\theta\) in them (\(\sum\ln x_i\), \(-\ln\prod x_i!\)) — and say that you are dropping them and why (they do not move the maximiser).
  3. \(\mathrm d\ell/\mathrm d\theta = 0\), solve for \(\theta\).
  4. Verify it is a maximum. A second derivative gives only a local statement; the sign of \(\ell'\) on both sides of the candidate gives a global one. Write the extra line.
  5. If the model is a reparametrisation: find the mle of the easy parameter (\(\hat q=\bar y_n\) for a Bernoulli), then invert the known map — from \(q(p)=rp+\tfrac{1-r}{2}\) you get \(\hat p = (\bar y_n-\tfrac{1-r}{2})/r\) — and check that the result lies inside the parameter set.

Pitfall. WiSe25 P4a's official solution stops at \(\ell''(\hat\theta)<0\); since \(\ell''(\theta) = \tfrac{2}{\theta^3}(n\theta-s)\) is positive for \(\theta > s/n\), that argument alone proves only a local maximum. This guide adds the missing line on the mle page.

Taught on: the likelihood function · maximum likelihood estimation. Drill: the estimation drills.

TT6 · Bias, variance and mean squared error of an estimator WiSe25 · P5b, P5c · 2+2 cr SoSe25 · P1b, P4b · 3+2 cr SoSe26 · P5c, P1e · 2+1 cr

Trigger. "Is \(\hat\theta\) unbiased [erwartungstreu]?", "Compute \(\mathrm{mse}[\hat\theta]\)". In all three papers.

  1. Write the estimator as \(c\cdot\sum_i X_i\), or as a sample mean \(\bar Y_n\) after a linear map.
  2. Mean: pull the constant out and use linearity, \(\E[aX+bY]=a\E[X]+b\E[Y]\) (Prop 2.4(i)). No independence is needed here. Compare with \(\theta\) to read off the bias, \(\mathrm{bias}[\hat\theta] =\E[\hat\theta]-\theta\) (Def 3.20(i)).
  3. Variance: constants come out squared, \(\Var[aX+b]=a^2\Var[X]\) (Prop 2.8(iii)); then the variances of independent summands add (Prop 2.8(iv)). Independence is needed here and nowhere else — say so.
  4. If the bias is 0 then \(\mathrm{mse}=\Var\); otherwise \(\mathrm{mse}=\Var+\mathrm{bias}^2\) (Def 3.20(iv)). Two exam sub-parts turn on exactly that sentence.
  5. If the estimator is a count divided by \(n\), recognise the \(\Bin(n,p)\) behind it and reuse \(\E=np\), \(\Var=np(1-p)\) (Lem 2.26(iv)) instead of re-deriving. Those two values were not hinted on WiSe25.

Pitfall. Forgetting that "the mle is good" is an asymptotic statement (Rem 3.30). For a fixed finite \(n\) the mle need not have the smallest mse — that is exactly SoSe26 P1e.

Taught on: properties of estimators · variance. Drill: the estimation drills.

TT7 · Bound a tail with Chebyshev or Markov WiSe25 · P4b · 3 cr SoSe25 · P5c · 4 cr SoSe26 · P4d · 3 cr

Trigger. "Give an upper bound for \(\P(|\hat\theta-\theta|\ge\varepsilon)\)", or "find \(k\) such that \(X\in[\E[X]\pm k]\) with probability at least 90 %". 10 credits, in all three papers.

  1. Rewrite the event into the shape the inequality wants. Chebyshev (Thm 2.40) needs \(\{|Y-\E[Y]|\ge\varepsilon\}\); Markov (Thm 2.38) needs a non-negative variable over a threshold. For \(\P(|Z_n|\ge a)\) the official move is \(|Z_n|\ge a \iff Z_n^2\ge a^2\), then Markov on \(Z_n^2\). For "within \([\E[X]\pm k]\) with probability at least 90 %", it is \(\P(X\notin[\E[X]\pm k])\le 0.1\).
  2. Compute \(\E[Y]\) and \(\Var[Y]\) (or \(\E[Z^2]=\Var[Z]+\E[Z]^2\)) first, as a separate labelled step.
  3. Apply the theorem by name: \(\P(|Y-\E[Y]|\ge\varepsilon)\le \Var[Y]/\varepsilon^2\), or \(\P(Z\ge\varepsilon)\le\E[Z]/\varepsilon\) for \(Z\ge0\).
  4. If a value is wanted, set the bound equal to the allowed failure probability and solve.
  5. Round in the safe direction and say why ("rounding up, so that the inequality still holds the way we want it").

Pitfall. Using Markov on a variable that can be negative. Markov's special case needs \(X\ge0\); that is why the official route squares first.

Taught on: Markov · Chebyshev. Drill: the estimation drills.

TT8 · clt approximation of an estimator, answer in terms of \(\Phi\) WiSe25 · P4c · 3 cr SoSe25 · P4c · 2 cr SoSe26 · P4d · part of 3 cr

Trigger. "Use the central limit theorem to approximate …". Here \(\Phi\) is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal \(\mathcal N(0,1)\): \(\Phi(z)=\P(Z\le z)\) for \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\). In all three papers.

  1. Check Thm 2.64's hypotheses out loud: iid, finite mean, finite non-zero variance.
  2. Standardise: \((\hat\theta-\E[\hat\theta])/\sqrt{\Var[\hat\theta]}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1)\).
  3. Write the approximate law: \(\hat\theta\approx\mathcal N(\theta,\Var[\hat\theta])\) — for example \(\bar X_n\approx\mathcal N(\lambda,\lambda/n)\) or \(\hat\theta\approx\mathcal N(\theta,\theta^2/2n)\).
  4. Two-sided tail: \(\P(|\hat\theta-\theta|\ge\varepsilon)\approx 2\Phi(-\varepsilon/\mathrm{sd}) = 2\bigl(1-\Phi(\varepsilon/\mathrm{sd})\bigr)\), where \(\mathrm{sd}=\sqrt{\Var[\hat\theta]}\). Leave \(\Phi\) symbolic — no table has ever been supplied.
  5. Use the word approximation. WiSe25 P4d is one whole credit for saying that Chebyshev is a valid but loose guarantee decaying like \(1/n\), while the clt is only approximate but far sharper.

Pitfall. "Improving" the answer by substituting \(\hat\theta\) for the unknown \(\theta\) inside the \(\Phi\). WiSe25 P4c's answer \(2\Phi(-\sqrt{2n}\,\varepsilon/\theta)\) is meant to keep \(\theta\) in it.

Taught on: the central limit theorem · the \(\Phi\) table. Drill: the estimation drills.

TT9 · Choose and run an approximate one-sided z-test SoSe25 · P4d · 4 cr SoSe26 · P5d · 5 cr

Trigger. A story sentence with a direction in it ("has increased above", "more than 60 %"), a number \(\alpha\), and a data summary. 9 credits, in two of the three papers; both were one-sided.

  1. Put the claim you want evidence for into \(H_1\). Directional wording means one-sided (Def 3.43). Both official solutions write "note that this is one-sided".
  2. Identify the null boundary \(\theta_0\) and compute the mean and variance of the statistic there, not at the observed value. SoSe26 P5d: with \(r=\tfrac12\), \(q(p)=\tfrac12 p+\tfrac14\) is increasing, so the worst case of \(H_0:p\le0.6\) is \(p_0=0.6\), giving \(q_0=0.55\), \(\E[\bar Y_{100}]=0.55\), \(\Var=0.55\cdot0.45/100\).
  3. Statistic \(Z=\dfrac{\text{estimate}-\text{null mean}}{\sqrt{\text{null variance}}}\); state that it is "approximately \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) under the null boundary, by the clt".
  4. Rejection rule: reject if \(z_{\mathrm{obs}} > z_\alpha\) (one-sided) — \(z_{0.05}\approx1.64\) is supplied — or \(|z_{\mathrm{obs}}| > z_{\alpha/2}\) (two-sided).
  5. Plug in, compare, and state the decision in words. SoSe26's scheme: 1 credit each for the hypotheses, the null-boundary numbers, the standardised statistic and its law, the rule together with \(z_{\mathrm{obs}}\), and the decision.

Pitfall. Two of them, both worth a credit: standardising with the observed variance instead of the null one, and using \(z_{\alpha/2}=1.96\) where the one-sided \(z_\alpha=1.64\) is meant.

Taught on: constructing tests in practice · quantiles \(z_\alpha\). Drill: the story-problem bank.

TT10 · Approximate confidence interval for a proportion (Wald) WiSe25 · P5d · 2 cr

Trigger. "Give an approximate \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval [Konfidenzintervall] for …". One of the three papers.

  1. Recognise the quantity as a mean of iid Bernoulli indicators and name its parameter \(p\). For the empirical cdf, \(\one_{(-\infty,t]}(X_i)\sim\Ber(F(t))\), so \(p=F(t)\).
  2. \(\hat p=\bar Y_n\), the sample mean of those indicators.
  3. clt: \((\hat p-p)/\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\) is approximately \(\mathcal N(0,1)\).
  4. Replace the unknown \(p\) in the standard error by \(\hat p\) (Example 3.58). That substitution is what makes it the Wald interval.
  5. Answer: \(\hat p \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}\), with \(z_{\alpha/2}\) left symbolic.

Pitfall. Saying "the parameter lies in this interval with probability \(1-\alpha\)". The interval is random, the parameter is a fixed unknown number (Rem 3.55). The correct sentence is about the procedure.

Taught on: the Wald interval · what a confidence interval is. Drill: the estimation drills.

TT11 · Decide a convergence claim, or place it on the ladder WiSe25 · P1d, P2b · 3+3 cr SoSe25 · P2b · 3 cr SoSe26 · P1d, P2a · 1+3 cr

Trigger. An arrow \(\xrightarrow{\P}\), \(\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\) or \(\xrightarrow{d}\) in the statement, or the words "converges in probability / almost surely / in distribution". In all three papers.

  1. Name the mode claimed and write its definition (Def 2.56(i)(ii)(iii)).
  2. Recall the only implications that hold in general: \(\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\Rightarrow\xrightarrow{\P}\Rightarrow\xrightarrow{d}\) (Rem 2.57). The converses fail — except that convergence in distribution to a constant does imply convergence in probability.
  3. If the claim is a law of large numbers or the clt, audit the assumption list: iid, or merely identically distributed? finite mean? finite non-zero variance?
  4. For counterexamples use the two machines: \(X_i:=X_1\) (kills independence) and \(X_n:=n\cdot\one_{\{U\le1/n\}}\) (kills convergence of expectations).
  5. Name the mode and the exact reason in the last sentence.

Pitfall. Believing that \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\) carries expectations along. \(X_n=n\cdot\one_{\{U\le1/n\}}\) converges to 0 but \(\E[X_n]=n\cdot\tfrac1n=1\) for every \(n\).

Taught on: modes of convergence · the laws of large numbers. Drill: the true/false bank and the state-it bank.

TT12 · Characteristic-function computation SoSe26 · P1c · 1 cr SoSe26 · P4a, P4b · 1+3 cr

Trigger. The symbol \(\varphi_X\). The characteristic function [charakteristische Funktion] is \(\varphi_X(t)=\E[e^{itX}]\) (Def 2.46), where \(i\) is the imaginary unit, \(i^2=-1\). 5 credits, one of the three papers.

  1. For a finite discrete \(X\), just sum \(\sum_x e^{itx}p_X(x)\) and apply Euler's formula \(e^{iu}=\cos u + i\sin u\) (supplied as a hint when needed).
  2. Affine scaling: \(\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)\) (Rem 2.47(ii)).
  3. Independence turns sums into products: \(\varphi_{X+Y}=\varphi_X\cdot\varphi_Y\) (Rem 2.47(iv)); for an iid sum, \(\varphi_{S_n}(t)=\varphi_X(t)^n\).
  4. Combine both for a scaled sum: \(\varphi_{Z_n}(t)=\varphi_{X_1}(t/\sqrt n)^n=\cos^n(t/\sqrt n)\). The marking split this 1/1/1 for the \(t/\sqrt n\) scaling, for using independence, and for the final expression.
  5. Moments from derivatives at 0: \(\E[X^n]=i^{-n}\varphi_X^{(n)}(0)\) (Rem 2.47(iii)) — an alternative route to \(\E[Z_n]\) and \(\Var[Z_n]\) that scored full marks.

Pitfall. Over-simplifying under time pressure. SoSe26 P4a's note says that turning \(\tfrac12 e^{it}+\tfrac12 e^{-it}\) into \(\cos t\) was not required for the credit.

Taught on: characteristic functions · the complex-number primer. Drill: the estimation drills.

TT13 · Build a random variable out of indicators (the counting trick) SoSe25 · P5a, P5b · 4+4 cr WiSe25 · P5a · 3 cr

Trigger. "How many … survive / exceed / succeed?" An indicator [Indikatorfunktion] \(\one_A\) is the random variable that is 1 when \(A\) happens and 0 otherwise. 11 credits; SoSe25 P5a printed the hint telling you to do this, which shows the examiner expects the move to be learned.

  1. Define the event \(A_i\) per item ("duck \(i\) survives", "\(X_i\le t\)").
  2. Set \(X_i:=\one_{A_i}\) and \(X:=\sum_i X_i\), so \(X\) counts the items.
  3. \(\E[X_i]=\P(A_i)\) — the mean of a Bernoulli variable is its success probability. Then linearity gives \(\E[X]=\sum_i\P(A_i)\), with no independence needed. That matters, because in the duck hunt the indicators are genuinely dependent.
  4. For the variance, expand \(\E[X^2]=\sum_{i,k}\E[X_iX_k]\) and use \(\E[X_iX_k]=\P(A_i\cap A_k)\), splitting the diagonal \(i=k\) (where \(X_i^2=X_i\), because \(0^2=0\) and \(1^2=1\)) from the off-diagonal terms.
  5. Sanity-check at extreme parameter values (0 hunters: all ducks survive; 1 hunter: exactly \(m-1\) survive, variance 0).

Pitfall. Adding variances as if the indicators were independent. They are not, and \(\Var[\sum_i X_i]=\sum_i\Var[X_i]+2\sum_{i<k}\Cov[X_i,X_k]\) (Prop 2.12(vi)) keeps the cross terms.

Taught on: expectation and linearity · covariance. Drill: the story-problem bank.

TT14 · A story problem solved by total probability and Bayes WiSe25 · P6a, P6b · 4+2 cr SoSe26 · P5a · 3 cr

Trigger. A mechanism in two stages: a coin or a schedule decides something first, then the outcome of interest happens. 9 credits, two of the three papers.

  1. Name the events and the conditioning variable explicitly (\(W_i\) / \(L_i\) for match outcomes; \(T\) = "answers truthfully").
  2. Split the event of interest into disjoint pieces and price each by independence. For "two consecutive wins in three matches", \(W_1\cap W_2\) and \(L_1\cap W_2\cap W_3\) are disjoint and exhaust it.
  3. Law of total probability (Thm 1.70(ii)) for the unconditional probability: \(\P(A)=\sum_i\P(A\mid B_i)\P(B_i)\) over a partition \(\{B_i\}\).
  4. Bayes' rule (Thm 1.70(iii)) for the reverse conditional: \(\P(B_i\mid A)=\P(A\mid B_i)\P(B_i)\big/\sum_j\P(A\mid B_j)\P(B_j)\).
  5. Compare the branches algebraically and give the intuition in one sentence. WiSe25 P6a asks for the intuition explicitly, "without just restating the computational results", and it is part of the 4 credits.

Pitfall. Splitting into pieces that overlap. Then the probabilities may not simply be added; check disjointness before you sum.

Taught on: conditional probability and Bayes · independence. Drill: the story-problem bank.

TT15 · Inclusion–exclusion on overlapping events WiSe25 · P6c · 4 cr

Trigger. "At least two non-consecutive wins", "at least one of the following happens" where the "following" share ingredients. One of the three papers — the only appearance of Thm 1.22 anywhere.

  1. Enumerate the events whose union is the target. For four matches and non-consecutive index pairs, these are \((1,3), (1,4), (2,4)\).
  2. Price each single event by independence.
  3. Price each pairwise and the triple intersection by taking the union of the index sets: \(E_{13}\cap E_{14}=A_1\cap A_3\cap A_4\).
  4. Apply Thm 1.22 with alternating signs: \(+\)singles \(-\) pairs \(+\) triple.
  5. Simplify and sanity-check at extreme parameter values.

Pitfall. The derived events \(E_{13}\) and \(E_{14}\) are not independent even though the \(A_i\) are, because they share \(A_1\). Multiplying \(\P(E_{13})\P(E_{14})\P(E_{24})\) is the intended wrong turn, and it is precisely why inclusion–exclusion is needed.

Taught on: probability measures and inclusion–exclusion · independence. Drill: the story-problem bank.

Master sheet — the results to know

This is the pool to compress your handwritten sheet from, not the sheet itself: it is deliberately longer than one A4 page. Every item is here because some sub-part of the three papers was marked on it, or because one of the fifteen recipes above needs it to run. The numbering is the script's own. Each entry carries a one-line note saying where the exams used it.

§1.1–§1.2 · Probability spaces and discrete distributions

Def 1.6 · \(\sigma\)-algebra
\(\Aa\subseteq\pow(\Omega)\) with (i) \(\Omega\in\Aa\); (ii) \(A\in\Aa\Rightarrow A^c\in\Aa\); (iii) \((A_i)_{i\in\N}\subseteq\Aa\Rightarrow\bigcup_{i\in\N}A_i\in\Aa\). WiSe25 P1a (3 cr): the listed collection fails (ii). SoSe26 P2b (3 cr): a forward image fails (ii). Speed fact: on a finite \(\Omega\), a \(\sigma\)-algebra has \(2^k\) members, so a 5-element collection can never be one.
Prop 1.7 · intersection
An arbitrary intersection \(\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}\Aa_\alpha\) of \(\sigma\)-algebras on \(\Omega\) is again a \(\sigma\)-algebra. The object \(\mathcal S\) in WiSe25 P1c is exactly this.
Lem 1.8 · generator
\(\sigma(\mathcal E)=\bigcap\{\Aa : \Aa\ \text{a}\ \sigma\text{-algebra},\ \mathcal E\subseteq\Aa\}\) is the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra containing \(\mathcal E\). WiSe25 P1c (3 cr): two measures agreeing on a generator need not agree on \(\sigma(\mathcal E)\) unless the generator is closed under intersection; \(\{1,2\}\cap\{2,3\}=\{2\}\) is exactly the set the counterexample measures disagree on.
Cor 1.10 · closure
\(A,B\in\Aa\Rightarrow A\cup B,\ A\cap B,\ A\setminus B,\ A\triangle B\in\Aa\); countable intersections too. WiSe25 P1c, to close \(\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\}\}\) up to the full power set.
Def 1.17 · measure
\(\mu:\Aa\to[0,\infty]\) with (i) \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\); (ii) \(\mu\ge0\); (iii) \(\sigma\)-additivity: \(\mu(\bigcup_i A_i)=\sum_i\mu(A_i)\) for countably many pairwise disjoint \(A_i\). Background to WiSe25 P1c: you must check the counterexamples really are measures.
Prop 1.19 · properties
(i) \(\mu(A\cup B)+\mu(A\cap B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\); (iii) monotone: \(A\subseteq B\Rightarrow\mu(A)\le\mu(B)\); plus continuity from below and above and \(\sigma\)-subadditivity. (iii) is used silently whenever \(\{X\ge10\}\subseteq\{X\ge5\}\) (WiSe25 P3b).
Def 1.20 · probability measure
A measure \(\P\) with \(\P(\Omega)=1\); then \((\Omega,\Aa,\P)\) is a probability space.
Thm 1.22 · inclusion–exclusion
\(\P\bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i\bigr)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(-1)^{k-1}\!\!\sum_{1\le i_1<\dots<i_k\le n}\!\! \P(A_{i_1}\cap\dots\cap A_{i_k})\). For \(n=3\): \(\P(A\cup B\cup C)=\P(A)+\P(B)+\P(C)-\P(A\cap B)-\P(A\cap C)-\P(B\cap C)+\P(A\cap B\cap C)\). WiSe25 P6c (4 cr) — the only appearance in three papers. Carry the \(n=3\) line verbatim; it is easy to misremember.
Def 1.23 / 1.56 · cdf
\(F_\P(x)=\P((-\infty,x])\); for a random variable \(F_X:=F_{\P_X}\), and \(p_X:=F_X'\) where \(F_X\) is (weakly) differentiable. SoSe25 P3b (2 cr), SoSe25 P1d (3 cr), WiSe25 P3a (4 cr), WiSe25 P5a.
Lem 1.24 · cdf properties
Increasing; right-continuous; \(F(x)-F(x^-)=\P(\{x\})\); \(F\to0\) at \(-\infty\), \(F\to1\) at \(+\infty\). The three boundary facts catch algebra errors when you write a cdf with all its branches.
Def 1.34 / Lem 1.35 · pmf
For countable \(\Omega\), \(p(\omega):=\P(\{\omega\})\); any \(p:\Omega\to[0,1]\) with \(\sum_\omega p(\omega)=1\) defines a discrete probability measure via \(\P(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}p(\omega)\). WiSe25 P1c (3 cr) hands its counterexample as two pmfs; SoSe25 P1a (3 cr) uses a two-point space.

§1.3–§1.4 · Densities, random variables, independence

Def 1.45 · pdf
\(p:\R^n\to\R_{\ge0}\) with \(\int_{\R^n}p(x)\,\mathrm dx=1\). SoSe25 P3a (2 cr) is exactly "impose \(\int p=1\), solve for the constant, check \(p\ge0\)".
Lem 1.49 · pdf ↔ cdf
(i) \(F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}p(y)\,\mathrm dy\); (ii) \(p=F'\) where \(F\) is differentiable. SoSe25 P3b (2 cr); the cdf route of WiSe25 P3a and SoSe25 P3d.
Def 1.50 · random variable
\(X:\Omega\to\Omega'\) is measurable if \(X^{-1}(A')\in\Aa\) for every \(A'\in\Aa'\). SoSe26 P2b (3 cr): pre-images of a \(\sigma\)-algebra always form one, forward images need not.
Def 1.53 · induced law
\(\P_X(A')=\P(X^{-1}(A'))=\P(\{X\in A'\})\); write \(X\sim\P_X\).
Def 1.54 / 1.79 · identically distributed vs iid
Identically distributed: all \(\P_{X_i}\) are equal. iid: independent and identically distributed. WiSe25 P1d (3 cr) turns entirely on the difference. Write the two definitions next to each other.
Def 1.69 · conditional probability
For \(\P(B)>0\), \(\P(A\mid B):=\P(A\cap B)/\P(B)\). SoSe25 P1a (3 cr): it is not symmetric. WiSe25 P3b (4 cr): with \(\{X\ge10\}\subseteq\{X\ge5\}\) the intersection is \(\{X\ge10\}\), so \(\P(X\ge10\mid X\ge5)=e^{-10\lambda}/e^{-5\lambda}=e^{-5\lambda}\).
Thm 1.70(ii) · total probability
For a measurable partition \(\{B_i\}\) of \(\Omega\) with \(\P(B_i)>0\): \(\P(A)=\sum_i\P(A\mid B_i)\P(B_i)\). WiSe25 P6b (2 cr); SoSe26 P5a (3 cr) gives \(q(p)=rp+\tfrac{1-r}{2}\).
Thm 1.70(iii) · Bayes' rule
\(\P(B_i\mid A)=\dfrac{\P(A\mid B_i)\P(B_i)}{\sum_j\P(A\mid B_j)\P(B_j)}\) for \(\P(A)>0\). WiSe25 P6b (2 cr): \(\P(\text{SWS}\mid\text{win})=(2-p)/(4-p-q)\).
Def 1.74 · independent events
\(A\perp\!\!\!\perp B\) iff \(\P(A\cap B)=\P(A)\P(B)\); a family is independent iff \(\P(\bigcap_{j\in J}A_j)=\prod_{j\in J}\P(A_j)\) for every finite \(J\). WiSe25 P6a, P6c (4+4 cr). The trap: derived events \(E_{ij}=A_i\cap A_j\) are not independent.
Def 1.77 · independent random variables
The joint cdf factorises, \(F_{(X_1,\dots,X_n)}(x)=\prod_i F_{X_i}(x_i)\); consequently joint densities factorise. SoSe25 P1d (3 cr): the joint density is \(\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\cdot\lambda e^{-\lambda y}\).
Def 1.78 · conditional pmf / pdf
Discrete \(p_{Y\mid X=x}(y)=\P(\{X=x\}\cap\{Y=y\})/\P(X=x)\); continuous \(p_{Y\mid X=x}(y)=p_{X,Y}(x,y)/p_X(x)\) where \(p_X(x)>0\). Background to SoSe26 P2c.

§2.1 · Expectation, variance, covariance — the heaviest topic on the papers

Def 2.1 · expectation
Discrete \(\E[X]=\sum_x x\,p_X(x)\) provided \(\sum_x|x|p_X(x)<\infty\); continuous \(\E[X]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x\,p_X(x)\,\mathrm dx\) provided \(\int|x|p_X(x)\,\mathrm dx<\infty\). SoSe25 P3c (2 cr); the integrability proviso is what SoSe26 P2a exploits.
Lem 2.2 · LOTUS
\(\E[g(X)]=\sum_x g(x)p_X(x)\) or \(\int g(x)p_X(x)\,\mathrm dx\) — you never need the distribution of \(g(X)\) itself. WiSe25 P3c (3 cr) runs it backwards: from \(\E[X]=1/\lambda\) and \(X=-\tfrac1\lambda\ln U\) you read off \(\int_0^1\ln u\,\mathrm du=-1\) without integrating.
Prop 2.4 · expectation rules
(i) linearity \(\E[aX+bY]=a\E[X]+b\E[Y]\); (ii) \(\E[c]=c\); (iii) \(X\ge0\Rightarrow\E[X]\ge0\); (iv) monotone; (v) \(X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\Rightarrow\E[XY]=\E[X]\E[Y]\). The most-used item on the papers. Linearity needs no independence — say so wherever the summands are dependent (SoSe25 P5a).
Def 2.5 · variance
\(\Var[X]=\E[(X-\E[X])^2]=\E[X^2]-\E[X]^2\); \(\sigma[X]=\sqrt{\Var[X]}\). SoSe25 P5b (4 cr) is computed exactly through \(\E[X^2]-\E[X]^2\).
Prop 2.8 · variance rules
(i) \(\Var\ge0\), \(=0\) iff \(X\) is almost surely constant; (iii) \(\Var[aX+b]=a^2\Var[X]\); (iv) \(X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\Rightarrow\Var[X+Y]=\Var[X]+\Var[Y]\). (iii)+(iv) give every estimator variance on the papers: \(\Var[\tfrac{1}{2n}\sum X_i]=\theta^2/2n\), \(\Var[Z_n]=1\), \(\Var[\hat p]=q(1-q)/(r^2n)\).
